• Beck’s triad (JVD, hypotension, muffled heart sounds)

• In question stem, neck veins are flat, so cardiac tamponade ❌

Option B: Dilated left ventricle with apical hypokinesis ❌

• Seen in cardiogenic shock or myocardial infarction.
• Associated with:

• Poor cardiac contractility
• Reduced ejection fraction

• Trauma patient with hemorrhage → not cardiogenic shock.

Option C: Inferior vena cava engorgement ❌

• Seen in obstructive shock :

• Tension pneumothorax
• Cardiac tamponade
• Massive pulmonary embolism

• These cause raised venous pressure → distended neck veins, not flat neck veins.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25 year old male after high speed RTA is slightly hypotensive but eFAST is negative. He has a widened mediastinum, chest wall ecchymosis and a pulse deficit in the left radial artery. Which is the next most appropriate step?
options: Give a 2L fluid rush and obtain a CT angiography for the patient.
Proceed to do an emergent thoracotomy.
Initiate permissive hypotension and perform CT angiography.
Stabilize the airway, avoid excessive fluids and perform a TEE immediately.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stabilize the airway, avoid excessive fluids and perform a TEE immediately.

High-speed deceleration trauma with widened mediastinum, chest wall ecchymosis, and upper-limb pulse deficit strongly suggests blunt thoracic aortic injury (BTAI). A negative eFAST does not exclude this diagnosis because eFAST primarily evaluates for hemoperitoneum and pericardial tamponade, not aortic disruption.

In suspected BTAI, the key priorities are:

1.   ATLS stabilization (airway and breathing first)

2.  Prevent worsening hemorrhage by avoiding aggressive fluid boluses and maintaining controlled blood pressure (“anti- impulse therapy”)

3.  Obtain urgent definitive imaging to confirm injury

For imaging:

• CT angiography (CTA) is the standard confirmatory test in stable patients
• If the patient is borderline unstable or CT transfer is unsafe, Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is preferred because it:

o    can be performed immediately at bedside

o    rapidly detects aortic transection/pseudoaneurysm

o    avoids delays and transport-related collapse

Therefore, in a slightly hypotensive trauma patient with strong signs of BTAI, the best next step is Stabilize the airway, avoid excessive fluids, and perform immediate TEE.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25 year old man presents to the emergency department with profuse facial bleeding and loss of consciousness after an RTA. His GCS is noted to be 6. He has a smashed nasal bridge, periorbital swelling and a possible Mandibular fracture. A C-spine collar is placed immediately. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this patient’s management?
options: Head tilt-chin lift followed by bag and mask ventilation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediate cricothyroidotomy.

• In ATLS trauma care, airway with cervical spine protection is the first priority. Any patient with GCS ≤ 8 requires a definitive airway. However, the choice of airway depends on whether intubation is feasible and safe.
• In patients with severe maxillofacial trauma (smashed nasal bridge/midface injury, mandibular fracture) accompanied by profuse facial bleeding, oral intubation with RSI is often unsafe or likely to fail because:

o   blood/secretions obscure the glottic view → failed laryngoscopy

o   facial fractures distort anatomy → difficult mask ventilation and intubation

o   mandibular fracture may prevent mouth opening and causes posterior displacement of tongue → airway obstruction

o   aspiration risk is very high

o   cervical spine precautions limit airway maneuvers
• In this setting, the patient is at risk of a “cannot intubate, cannot ventilate/oxygenate” (CICO) situation. Therefore, the most appropriate immediate definitive airway is a surgical airway, i.e. cricothyroidotomy, which bypasses the obstructed/contaminated upper airway and rapidly restores oxygenation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with epigastric pain with migration to right lower quadrant with tenderness, nausea, anorexia, and low-grade fever. Labs show leukocytosis. Based on these findings, what is his total Alvarado score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 8

The Alvarado score is a clinical scoring system used to assess the likelihood of acute appendicitis and guide further management (observation vs imaging vs surgery).

MANTRELS mnemonic (Total = 10)

• Migration of pain to RLQ — 1

• Anorexia — 1

• Nausea/vomiting — 1

• Tenderness in RLQ — 2

• Rebound tenderness — 1

• Elevated temperature (fever) — 1

• Leukocytosis — 2

• Shift to left (neutrophilia) — 1

Calculation in this patient

• RLQ pain + tenderness → Tenderness RLQ = 2
• Nausea → 1
• Anorexia → 1
• Low-grade fever → 1
• Leukocytosis → 2
• Migration of pain → 1
• Total = 8/10.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after falling approximately 3m from a ladder, landing on his left side. There was no loss of consciousness. The patient has left shoulder and left-sided chest pain, as well as abdominal pain. Blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg and pulse is 116/min. Physical examination shows bruising to the left side of the chest wall and abdomen. There is sharp, left-sided chest pain with deep inspiration but equal breath sounds on both sides. The left costal margin and the left upper quadrant of the abdomen are tender to palpation. Range of motion of the left shoulder is normal. eFAST is shown below. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
options: Obtain CT scan of the abdomen
Obtain dedicated radiographs of the ribs
Obtain plain radiographs of the left shoulder
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Obtain CT scan of the abdomen

In hemodynamically stable blunt abdominal trauma, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen is the investigation of choice to evaluate for solid organ injury (especially splenic injury), even if FAST is positive.

Key concepts

• eFAST positive + stable patient → CT scan

• CT defines:

o Grade of splenic/liver injury

o Active bleeding

o Need for embolization vs surgery

o Associated intra-abdominal injuries

Trauma algorithm pearl

• Unstable + FAST positive → immediate laparotomy

• Stable + FAST positive → CT scan

• Stable + FAST negative but high suspicion → CT scan

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with weight loss and fever. The patient reports a history of blood in the stool and vomiting two weeks ago. Upon examination, tenderness is noted in the right hypochondrium along with an enlarged liver. An abdominal CT scan is shown below. What is the next step?
options: Broad spectrum antibiotics to cover GNB
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Start metronidazole

A young patient with fever, weight loss, right hypochondrial tenderness, hepatomegaly, and a recent history of blood in stool suggests amoebic infection (Entamoeba histolytica) with extraintestinal spread causing an amoebic liver abscess (ALA). On CT, ALA classically appears as a solitary hypodense lesion in the right lobe (often subcapsular).

First-line management of uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess is Metronidazole therapy because:

• Most ALAs respond dramatically to anti-amoebic treatment
• Drainage is not routinely required

When drainage (pigtail) is needed:

• Large abscess (commonly >5 cm)
• Left lobe abscess (risk of rupture into pericardium)
• Failure to improve after 48–72 hours of metronidazole
• Impending rupture or uncertain diagnosis

PAIR is used for hydatid cysts, and broad-spectrum antibiotics are primarily for pyogenic liver abscess. Therefore, the next step is start metronidazole.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a blunt injury to the left flank in a road traffic accident. He is hemodynamically stable but complains of abdominal distension and discomfort 12 hours later. On examination, there is left flank tenderness and abdominal distension with a tympanic note on percussion. Bowel sounds are decreased. Ultrasound shows perirenal hematoma without intraperitoneal free fluid. Which of the following best explains the cause of meteorism in this patient?
options: Paralytic ileus due to retroperitoneal irritation from renal injury
Urinary ascites due to collecting system rupture
Pneumoperitoneum due to associated bowel perforation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paralytic ileus due to retroperitoneal irritation from renal injury

The kidney is a retroperitoneal organ. Following renal trauma, bleeding leads to a perirenal or retroperitoneal hematoma. Irritation of the retroperitoneum can reflexly inhibit intestinal peristalsis, leading to paralytic ileus.

Meteorism in this setting refers to gaseous distension of bowel loops due to accumulation of gas in the setting of ileus, producing a tympanic abdomen.

Other Options:

Option B. Intraperitoneal hemorrhage would present with signs of peritonitis and shifting dullness rather than tympany

Option C. Urinary ascites causes dullness on percussion, not meteorism

Option D. Pneumoperitoneum presents with free air under diaphragm and acute peritonitis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 27-year-old man is being managed conservatively for an appendicular mass using the Ochsner–Sherren regimen. Which of the following findings do not indicate failure of conservative therapy and require surgical intervention?
options: Increasing size of the palpable mass
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreasing pulse rate

The Ochsner–Sherren regimen is conservative management for an appendicular mass, consisting of bowel rest, IV fluids, antibiotics, and close monitoring.

Signs indicating failure of conservative management (need surgery)

• Rising pulse rate (tachycardia)

• Increasing abdominal pain or tenderness

• Increasing size of appendicular mass

• Persistent or high fever

• Leukocytosis or sepsis

• Development of peritonitis or abscess

These findings suggest:

• Ongoing infection

• Abscess formation

• Impending perforation

Finding NOT indicating failure

• Decreasing pulse rate → indicates clinical improvement and response to therapy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 27-year-old man presents with a painless enlargement of the right testis noticed over the past 3 months. There is no history of trauma or infection. On examination, the testis is firm and non-tender. Serum tumor markers show elevated β-hCG and LDH. Ultrasound reveals a heterogeneous intratesticular mass. Which group of lymph nodes is the earliest and most characteristic site of metastasis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes

Testicular tumors metastasize primarily via lymphatic drainage that follows embryologic origin rather than scrotal location.

• Testes develop in the retroperitoneum near kidneys and descend into scrotum.

• Therefore, lymphatic drainage remains to para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes, not inguinal nodes.

Lymphatic spread pattern

• Right testis → interaortocaval & para-aortic nodes

• Left testis → para-aortic (left lumbar) nodes

• Later spread → mediastinal & supraclavicular nodes

Important distinction

• Testicular tumor → para-aortic nodes (first)

• Scrotal skin tumor → superficial inguinal nodes

• Penile cancer → inguinal nodes

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 27-year-old man presents with a painless, fluctuant scrotal swelling separate from the testis. Transillumination is positive. The swelling is located above and behind the testis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epididymal cyst

A painless, fluctuant scrotal swelling that is separate from the testis and shows positive transillumination suggests a cystic lesion containing clear fluid rather than a solid mass. When the swelling is specifically located above and behind the testis, it points to a lesion arising from the epididymis, making epididymal cyst the most likely diagnosis. Epididymal cysts are benign collections of serous fluid within the epididymis and are typically smooth, non-tender, and transilluminant.

This helps distinguish it from:

• Hydrocele: surrounds the testis and is not separate from it
• Varicocele: “bag of worms,” does not transilluminate, usually above testis and increases on standing
• Spermatocele: also arises from epididymis but classically contains sperm and is often described as a cystic swelling at the upper pole; clinically the term is sometimes used interchangeably, but exam descriptions of a clear-fluid transilluminant swelling above/behind testis are most consistent with an epididymal cyst.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a high-velocity road traffic accident. He complains of lower abdominal pain. He is hemodynamically stable. Examination shows no blood at the urethral meatus; high-riding prostate absent. Pelvic compression produces pain. Foley catheter is inserted easily, but gross hematuria appears. Pelvic X-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT cystography

In a hemodynamically stable patient with blunt pelvic trauma, the presence of gross hematuria, especially with a pelvic fracture, is highly suggestive of bladder rupture. The best next investigation is CT cystography, which confirms bladder injury and differentiates intraperitoneal rupture (requires surgical repair) from extraperitoneal rupture (usually managed with Foley catheter drainage).

Other Options:

A) Retrograde urethrogram (RUG):

• Used when urethral injury is suspected
• Indications of urethral injury:

• Blood at urethral meatus
• High-riding/non-palpable prostate
• Inability to pass Foley
• Perineal/scrotal hematoma

C) Immediate exploratory laparotomy:

• Indication: hemodynamic instability
• Used when:

• Patient unstable despite resuscitation
• Suspected intra-abdominal bleeding
• Peritonitis

D) Suprapubic catheter insertion:

Indicated when:

• Urethral injury suspected and Foley cannot be passed
• Need urinary diversion without urethral instrumentation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old man is brought after a high-speed RTA. He is agitated, tachycardic (HR 132/min), hypotensive (BP 80/40 mmHg), and cold peripherally. GCS is 14. FAST shows fr ee fluid in Morrison’s pouch. Pelvis is stable clinically. After 1 liter balanced crystalloid and 1 unit PRBC, BP remains 82/44 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Immediate exploratory laparotomy

In hemodynamically unstable trauma patients with a positive FAST, the next step is immediate exploratory laparotomy without further imaging.

Key principles of trauma management:

• FAST positive + hypotension = intra-abdominal bleeding until proven otherwise

• Persistent shock despite fluid and blood resuscitation indicates ongoing hemorrhage

• Do NOT delay for CT scan in unstable patients

• Definitive management = damage control surgery (exploratory laparotomy)

Trauma algorithm pearl:

| Patient Status | FAST Result | Next Step

| -------------- | ----------- | ---------

| Unstable | Positive | Immediate laparotomy

| Unstable | Negative | Search other bleeding sources (chest, pelvis, long bones)

| Stable | Positive | CT scan abdomen

| Stable | Negative | Observation / secondary survey

other options

• CT abdomen → only for stable patients

• DPL → rarely needed when FAST already positive

• Observation → contraindicated in shock with suspected internal bleeding

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motorcycle collision. He is alert and oriented but complains of neck pain and weakness in all limbs. His BP is 78/42 mm Hg and pulse is 58 bpm. Skin is warm and flushed. There are no obvious external bleeding sites, the FAST scan is negative, and his CVP is normal. Despite receiving 1 L of isotonic fluid, his blood pressure remains low. Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains his persistent hypotension?
options: Massive vasodilation due to loss of sympathetic tone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Massive vasodilation due to loss of sympathetic tone

Neurogenic shock occurs after acute cervical or high thoracic spinal cord injury due to loss of sympathetic outflow, resulting in massive vasodilation and bradycardia.

• Hypotension is therefore due to vasodilation, not volume loss.

Pathophysiology :-

• Spinal cord injury → interruption of sympathetic pathways (T1–L2)

• Unopposed parasympathetic (vagal) tone → bradycardia

• Loss of peripheral vascular tone → systemic vasodilation

• Leads to hypotension with warm, flushed skin

Key clinical features

• Hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation

• Bradycardia (unlike hypovolemic shock → tachycardia)

• Warm extremities

• Normal CVP and negative FAST (no bleeding)

Differentiation from other shocks :-

• Hypovolemic shock: tachycardia, cold clammy skin, low CVP

• Cardiogenic shock: high CVP, pulmonary edema

• Obstructive shock: tamponade, PE, tension pneumothorax signs

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 29-year-old man presents after a high-impact motor vehicle collision. He is hemodynamically stable but complains of left-sided chest and upper abdominal pain. Breath sounds are decreased on the left. Bowel sounds are faintly audible over the left lower chest. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected injury?
options: Perform needle decompression of the chest
Insert a nasogastric (NG) tube and perform chest X-ray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Insert a nasogastric (NG) tube and perform chest X-ray

In blunt thoracoabdominal trauma, bowel sounds in the chest with decreased breath sounds strongly suggest traumatic diaphragmatic rupture with herniation of abdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity.

• Insert nasogastric (NG) tube and repeat chest X-ray

• NG tube would be seen coiled in thoracic cavity confirms stomach herniation through ruptured diaphragm

• Helps differentiate from pneumothorax and prevents misdiagnosis

Other options

• Needle decompression: Only if tension pneumothorax suspected

• FAST: May miss diaphragmatic injury

• Immediate surgery: Done after confirmation with CXR and decompression

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 29-year-old man presents with a midline neck swelling that moves upward on deglutition. The mass is non-tender and there are no signs of infection. Which of the following structures may present in this manner?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

A midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition typically indicates attachment to structures that move during swallowing (thyroid gland, hyoid bone, larynx, or pretracheal fascia).

Causes of midline swelling moving on deglutition

• Thyroid swelling → moves with deglutition due to attachment to pretracheal fascia and larynx

• Thyroglossal duct cyst → moves with deglutition (and classically also with tongue protrusion) because of attachment to hyoid bone

• Pretracheal lymph nodes → can move with swallowing because of fascial attachment to trachea

Key distinguishing feature

• Moves with deglutition only → thyroid, thyroglossal cyst, pretracheal lesions

• Moves with deglutition + tongue protrusion → thyroglossal duct cyst (most specific sign)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman with untreated hyperthyroidism presents with diffuse bone pain. Her DEXA scan shows osteopenia. Which of the following best explains why thyroid hormone causes osteopenia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroid hormone increases RANKL expression

Untreated hyperthyroidism is an important secondary cause of osteopenia/osteoporosis because excess thyroid hormone accelerates bone remodeling. Thyroid hormone stimulates osteoblast-lineage cells to increase expression of RANKL (Receptor Activator of Nuclear factor κB Ligand). RANKL binds to RANK receptors on osteoclast precursors, promoting osteoclast differentiation and activation, leading to increased bone resorption.

Although both bone formation and resorption increase in hyperthyroidism, resorption predominates, resulting in net loss of bone mineral density (osteopenia/osteoporosis) and increased fracture risk. Therefore, the best explanation is: B. Thyroid hormone increases RANKL expression.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with a soft, reducible umbilical swelling. The fascial defect is 1.2 cm. The child is asymptomatic with no episodes of pain or incarceration. Parents are concerned and request surgical correction. What is the best next step in management?
options: Immediate surgical repair using Mayo’s overlap technique
Elective mesh repair of the hernia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Reassurance and observation

Umbilical hernia in children is a common congenital condition due to incomplete closure of the umbilical ring. Most pediatric umbilical hernias—especially those with a small fascial defect (<1.5–2 cm)—close spontaneously as the abdominal wall muscles strengthen. In an asymptomatic child (no pain, incarceration, or skin changes), the best management is reassurance and observation, as spontaneous closure commonly occurs by 4–5 years of age.

Surgical repair is indicated if the hernia:

• Persists beyond 4–5 years
• Has a large defect (>1.5–2 cm)
• Becomes symptomatic (pain, non-reducibility, incarceration/strangulation)
• Has complications such as ulceration or rupture

Therefore, a 3-year-old with a reducible, asymptomatic umbilical hernia and 1.2 cm defect should be managed with reassurance and observation rather than immediate surgery or mesh repair.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed road traffic accident. He is hypotensive (BP 80/50 mmHg), tachycardic, and hypothermic (core temperature 34°C). FAST is positive for intra-abdominal fluid. On laparotomy, multiple liver lacerations with active bleeding and bowel edema are noted. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.1, serum lactate markedly elevated, and INR is prolonged. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Definitive surgical repair of all injuries with primary bowel anastomosis
Perihepatic packing with temporary abdominal closure and transfer to ICU
Immediate liver resection to control bleeding
Closure of abdomen after thorough lavage and observation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Perihepatic packing with temporary abdominal closure and transfer to ICU

This patient is in the “lethal triad” of trauma:

• Hypothermia
• Acidosis
• Coagulopathy

This is a classic indication for damage control surgery.

The principles include:

1.    Rapid control of bleeding (e.g., perihepatic packing)

2.    Control of contamination

3.    Temporary abdominal closure (e.g., vacuum-assisted closure)

4.    Transfer to ICU for correction of physiology

5.    Planned re-exploration after stabilization

Other Options:

Option A. Definitive repair is contraindicated in unstable patients with lethal triad

Option C. Major resections worsen physiology and increase mortality

Option D. Simple closure without controlling bleeding is inappropriate

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32 year old woman on long term OCPs presents with sudden severe upper quadrant pain. She is tachycardic and pale. USG shows a 4 cm hypervascular hepatic lesion with free fluid around the liver. No venous washout is seen with the lesion and AFP is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis and what is the most important associated risk with it?
options: Focal nodular hyperplasia; risk of malignant transformation.
Hepatic adenoma (HNF1 alpha subtype); risk of rupture and hemorrhage.
Hepatic adenoma (Beta catenin subtype); risk of central scar formation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hepatic adenoma (HNF1 alpha subtype); risk of rupture and hemorrhage.

Young women on long-term oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are at increased risk of developing a hepatic adenoma, a benign hepatocellular tumor. Hepatic adenomas are typically hypervascular lesions and may present dramatically with sudden severe right upper quadrant pain, pallor, tachycardia, and free intraperitoneal fluid due to spontaneous rupture and intra-abdominal hemorrhage, which is a surgical emergency. Key diagnostic clues in this case:

• OCP use (major risk factor for hepatic adenoma)
• Sudden RUQ pain + shock features
• Hypervascular hepatic lesion
• Free fluid around liver → suggests bleeding/rupture
• AFP normal → argues against HCC
• No venous washout → not typical of HCC

The most important clinical risk associated with hepatic adenoma is Rupture with hemorrhage, especially when:

• lesion is >5 cm
• pregnancy/OCPs
• subcapsular location

Among hepatic adenoma subtypes:

• HNF1α-inactivated adenoma is strongly associated with OCP use, often in women, and has a major risk of hemorrhage/rupture (malignant transformation is more typical of β-catenin subtype).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32 year old woman underwent total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection for papillary thyroid cancer. On post op day 2, she presents with a breathy voice but no stridor. Laryngoscopy shows unilateral incomplete abduction of vocal cords and is in paramedian position. Her serum calcium levels are normal. Which of the following is the next best step?
options: Medialisation of the affected vocal cords within 24-48 hours.
Urgent wound re exploration to relieve a suspected deep cervical hematoma that is causing RLN compression.
Voice rest for 4 weeks and repeat laryngoscopy.
Immediate CT scan of neck and mediastinum to rule out recurrent tumor encasing the RLN.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Voice rest for 4 weeks and repeat laryngoscopy.

Post-thyroidectomy voice change is most commonly due to recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) neuropraxia or temporary vocal cord dysfunction from surgical traction, edema, or inflammation. Unilateral RLN injury typically presents with:

• Breathy/hoarse voice
• Weak cough
• No respiratory distress
• Laryngoscopy shows the affected vocal cord in a paramedian position with impaired abduction.

In the absence of stridor or airway compromise, this is usually a benign, transient neuropraxia that often resolves spontaneously within weeks to months. Therefore, initial management is conservative with:

• Voice rest
• Observation and/or speech therapy
• Repeat laryngoscopy follow-up to document recovery

Urgent interventions are not indicated unless there are signs of airway obstruction or compressive complications.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Medialisation within 24–48 h is reserved for severe aspiration risk or persistent paralysis, not immediate routine management on POD2.
• Wound re-exploration is indicated in suspected hematoma causing airway compromise (neck swelling, stridor, respiratory distress), which is absent here.
• CT neck/mediastinum is unnecessary immediately after surgery in a clear postoperative setting and with no evidence of recurrence.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old female patient arrives at the emergency department with a history of stabbing injury to her arm. Upon examination, there is a noticeable hematoma, and the patient reports not feeling any radial or ulnar pulses in the affected arm. Imaging reveals a 3cm longitudinal tear in the brachial artery. The medical team is faced with deciding the best treatment option for the patient. Which option should they choose?
options: Repair with great saphenous vein graft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Repair with great saphenous vein graft

Penetrating extremity trauma with absent distal pulses and imaging showing a brachial artery tear represents a major arterial injury requiring urgent revascularization to prevent limb ischemia. For arterial repair, the choice depends on whether the artery can be repaired without tension:

• Small clean transection / short defect → primary repair or end-to-end anastomosis possible.
• Large defect / longitudinal tear requiring segment excision → interposition graft is needed.

In this case:

• 3 cm longitudinal tear in brachial artery

→ After debridement and trimming of damaged edges, there will be a significant segmental loss, making direct end-to-end repair tensioned and unsafe (risk of thrombosis/rupture).

Therefore, the preferred reconstruction is an autologous vein graft, most commonly: Great saphenous vein (reversed) interposition graft because it:

• has excellent long-term patency
• is less thrombogenic than prosthetic grafts
• has lower infection risk (important in traumatic wounds)
• is ideal for small/medium caliber arteries like brachial artery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man has a CE2 liver hydatid cyst (multiseptated, “honeycomb”) on USG. What is the best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laparoscopic pericystectomy

• Management of hepatic hydatid disease is guided by the WHO-IWGE ultrasound classification, which predicts cyst activity and response to therapy.
• A CE2 cyst is an active hydatid cyst characterized by multiple daughter cysts giving a multiseptated “honeycomb/rosette” appearance on ultrasound. These cysts contain a high parasitic load and thick internal septations, making them poor candidates for PAIR because:

o   the contents are not easily aspirated

o   multiple daughter cysts prevent complete evacuation

o   higher risk of persistence/recurrence after percutaneous therapy
• Therefore, CE2 cysts are best treated surgically, typically by pericystectomy (partial/total) or cystectomy, often performed laparoscopically when feasible, with appropriate scolicidal precautions and perioperative antihelminthic therapy.

Other options:

• PAIR: preferred for CE1 and selected CE3a (unilocular fluid cysts), not CE2.
• Albendazole alone: insufficient for CE2 due to complexity/high burden (used as adjunct).
• Observation: reserved for inactive cysts (CE4/CE5).
• Omentopexy only: a cavity management step, not definitive treatment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a fall from height. He is hypotensive and tachycardic. An eFAST examination is performed. Findings: • No free fluid in Morrison’s pouch, splenorenal recess, or pelvis • No pericardial effusion • On lung ultrasound following findings are seen. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of these findings?
options: False negative scan; pneumothorax cannot be diagnosed on ultrasound
Left-sided pneumothorax with high specificity due to lung point sign
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left-sided pneumothorax with high specificity due to lung point sign

eFAST (extended FAST) is a rapid bedside ultrasound tool used in trauma to detect both intra-abdominal fluid and thoracic injuries (pneumothorax/hemothorax).

• Absence of lung sliding suggests pneumothorax but is not specific
• Lung point sign (transition point between sliding and no sliding) is highly specific for pneumothorax
• Normal abdominal windows → no hemoperitoneum
• No pericardial effusion

Thus, isolated left-sided pneumothorax is diagnosed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. He is hypotensive on arrival. Following initial fluid resuscitation, his blood pressure improves transiently but soon falls again. On further evaluation, central venous pressure is low, serum lactate is elevated, and FAST examination does not reveal any free intraperitoneal fluid. There are no obvious external sources of bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism?
options: Cardiogenic shock due to myocardial contusion
Obstructive shock due to tension pneumothorax
Occult hemorrhagic shock with ongoing blood loss
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Occult hemorrhagic shock with ongoing blood loss

In trauma, a patient with transient response to fluid resuscitation (initial BP improvement followed by deterioration) should be assumed to have ongoing hemorrhage until proven otherwise.

• Occult hemorrhagic shock is characterized by:

• Transient responder pattern to fluids
• Low central venous pressure (CVP) → suggests hypovolemia
• Elevated serum lactate → ongoing tissue hypoperfusion
• No obvious external or intraperitoneal bleeding → think hidden sources (retroperitoneum, pelvis, long bones, thorax)

• FAST negative ≠ no bleeding

→ It misses retroperitoneal, pelvic, and some thoracic hemorrhage

• Key differentiation from other shocks:

• Cardiogenic → high CVP
• Obstructive → high CVP (e.g., tension pneumothorax, tamponade)
• Neurogenic → hypotension with bradycardia, not high lactate initially

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He is tachypneic and hypotensive. On examination, there is decreased breath sound on the left side with dullness to percussion. A chest tube is inserted, and 1700 mL of blood is immediately drained. Over the next 2 hours, an additional 250 mL/hour of blood continues to drain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Continue observation with chest tube drainage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emergency thoracotomy

Massive hemothorax is defined by:

• Immediate drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood after chest tube insertion, or
• Persistent bleeding of more than 200 mL/hour for 3 consecutive hours

This patient has:

• Initial output = 1700 mL
• Ongoing bleeding = 250 mL/hour

Both criteria are met, indicating ongoing major intrathoracic bleeding requiring surgical intervention.

Emergency thoracotomy is indicated to:

• Identify and control the source of bleeding
• Prevent hemorrhagic shock and death

Other Options:

Option A. Observation is inappropriate due to massive and ongoing blood loss

Option B. Second chest tube does not address the source of bleeding

Option D. Tranexamic acid may be adjunctive but not definitive management

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents with a painless scrotal swelling located superior to the testis. On examination, the mass is cystic, transilluminates brilliantly, and shows multiple internal loculations giving a characteristic “Chinese lantern pattern” on transillumination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epididymal cyst

An epididymal cyst presents as a painless cystic swelling superior and posterior to the testis that transilluminates brilliantly and may show a “Chinese lantern” pattern due to multiple internal loculations.

• Located above and behind the testis

• Separate from testis

• Painless, cystic swelling

• Brilliant transillumination

• Multiloculated → “Chinese lantern” appearance

• Common in young and middle-aged men

Differentiation from other scrotal swellings

• Hydrocele: surrounds testis, not separate; uniform transillumination

• Varicocele: “bag of worms”, non-transilluminant, increases on standing

• Hematocele: painful, non-transilluminant, history of trauma/infection

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man sustains deep partial-thickness burns to the upper torso after a kitchen fire. Over the next several hours, the area surrounding the central necrotic burn shows progressive tissue hypoperfusion. This region demonstrates vascular constriction and platelet microthrombus formation. Which zone of burn injury does this describe?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Zone of stasis

Burn wounds are divided into three concentric zones described by Jackson: coagulation, stasis, and hyperemia.

Zone of stasis (Correct answer)

• Surrounds central zone of coagulation

• Characterized by reduced perfusion, vasoconstriction, and microvascular thrombosis

• Tissue is initially viable but at risk of progressing to necrosis if perfusion is not restored

• Major target of burn resuscitation and wound care

Zone of coagulation:

• Central area of burn

• Irreversible tissue necrosis

• Protein denaturation and cell death

Zone of hyperemia:

• Outer zone

• Increased perfusion and inflammation

• Usually recovers completely

Proper burn management aims to:

• Maintain perfusion (adequate fluids)

• Prevent infection

• Avoid pressure or hypoxia

→ to salvage the zone of stasis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man underwent radical inguinal orchiectomy for stage II seminoma two months ago. He was initially placed on surveillance. On follow-up, serum LDH is elevated and CT abdomen reveals enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes. There is no evidence of disease elsewhere. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Systemic chemotherapy with bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin (BEP)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Systemic chemotherapy with bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin (BEP)

Stage II seminoma with retroperitoneal lymph node involvement is best treated with systemic platinum-based chemotherapy (BEP regimen).

Key principles in seminoma management

• Seminomas spread first to para-aortic lymph nodes
• Elevated tumor markers (LDH ± β-hCG) and nodal disease indicate progression
• Stage II disease = nodal metastasis below diaphragm

Treatment approach

• Stage I: surveillance or adjuvant radiotherapy/chemotherapy
• Stage II (nodal disease):

• Bulky nodes or marker elevation → systemic chemotherapy (BEP)
• Highly chemosensitive tumor with excellent prognosis

Other Options

• RPLND: mainly for non-seminomatous germ cell tumors
• Radiotherapy: option for small-volume stage II seminoma but chemotherapy preferred in progressive disease with markers
• Repeat orchiectomy: not indicated after complete removal

BEP regimen

• Bleomycin
• Etoposide
• Cisplatin

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man with traumatic spinal cord injury and recurrent episodes of urinary incontinence is evaluated with the investigation shown in the figure. With respect to this investigation, which of the following statements are correct? 1. It records intravesical pressure, abdominal pressure and detrusor pressure simultaneously. 2. Detrusor pressure is calculated as Pdet = Pves − Pabd. 3. It is the investigation of choice to characterise neurogenic bladder dysfunction. 4. It is primarily used to differentiate obstructive from non-obstructive hydronephrosis by comparing renal pelvic and bladder pressures.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 3

The trace shown is a multichannel urodynamic study (cystometry with pressure–flow). It simultaneously records intravesical pressure (Pves), abdominal pressure (Pabd via rectal/vaginal catheter), and computes detrusor pressure(Pdet = Pves − Pabd). In spinal cord injury and other suspected neurogenic bladders, multichannel urodynamics is the investigation of choice to characterize storage and voiding physiology (compliance, detrusor overactivity/areflexia, sphincter dyssynergia, outlet obstruction vs poor contractility) and to guide therapy and renal-risk stratification.

Other Options :

• 4. “Differentiate obstructive vs non-obstructive hydronephrosis by comparing renal pelvic and bladder pressures” describes the Whitaker pressure-perfusion test, not standard urodynamics.

Key Facts:

• Pdet = Pves − Pabd; Pabd subtraction removes cough/strain artifact.
• Channels commonly displayed: flow, volume infused, Pves, Pabd, Pdet, and sometimes pelvic floor EMG.
• Neurogenic bladder assessment needs urodynamics to detect detrusor overactivity, poor compliance (<10 mL/cmH₂O), DSD, and underactive detrusor.
• In outlet evaluation, pressure–flow parameters (e.g., Bladder Outlet Obstruction Index) distinguish obstruction from weak detrusor.

Trick points / Common confusions:

• Do not confuse urodynamics with the Whitaker test; the latter assesses upper tract obstruction using renal pelvic perfusion pressures, not lower tract pressures.
• Uroflowmetry alone is not diagnostic in neurogenic bladder; multichannel studies with Pabd subtraction are required for accurate interpretation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old primigravida woman comes to the emergency department with recent onset right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and low-grade fever. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis of appendicitis?
options: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MRI of the abdomen

Acute appendicitis in pregnancy can present with right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and low-grade fever, but diagnosis is challenging due to physiologic leukocytosis of pregnancy and altered anatomy. Imaging is therefore essential to confirm appendicitis while minimizing fetal risk. In pregnant patients, the recommended diagnostic approach is:

1.     Ultrasound as the initial test (safe, no radiation), but it is often inconclusive because the gravid uterus can obscure the appendix.

2.     If ultrasound is nondiagnostic, the best confirmatory test is MRI of the abdomen, which has high sensitivity and specificity for appendicitis and avoids ionizing radiation, making it safer for the fetus.

3.     CT abdomen/pelvis is reserved only when MRI is unavailable or diagnosis remains unclear because it exposes the fetus to radiation.

CBC alone is not confirmatory and is unreliable due to pregnancy-related leukocytosis. Therefore, the most appropriate test to confirm appendicitis in a pregnant woman is MRI abdomen (Option D).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33 year old male presents with a feeling of heaviness in the left scrotum, worse on prolonged standing. Examination reveals a bag of worms appearance. His semen analysis shows oligospermia with reduced motility. Doppler ultrasound confirms the diagnosis of varicocele. What is the most appropriate management?
options: High ligation of testicular vein (Palomo procedure)
Embolization of internal spermatic vein since fertility is not a concern
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High ligation of testicular vein (Palomo procedure)

• "Bag of worms” → clinical varicocele
• Worse on standing → venous pooling (gravity effect)
• Oligospermia + reduced motility → impaired fertility

This is a functionally significant varicocele affecting spermatogenesis.

| Scenario | Action

| -------- | ------

| No symptoms, normal fertility | Ignore (watchful waiting)

| Pain only | Conservative first (NSAIDs, support)

• Infertility + abnormal semen + clinical varicocele

• Testicular atrophy in adolescents

| Surgery

Why not other options:

Option A. NSAIDs and scrotal support: only when mild symptoms are present; not when infertility is present.

Option C. Kettle–Torek procedure: surgery for undescended testes

Option D. Embolization: can be used but no in this scenario, because fertility is a concern here.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 34-year-old female presents with a lump in her left breast for 2 years. On examination, a 6 x 4 cm mass is palpated. Dimpling of the skin and bloody discharge from the nipple is present. The lesion is invading the pectoralis major muscle. Ipsilateral Level I and Level II matted axillary lymph nodes and C/L Level 1 axillary nodes are present. There was no distant metastasis. What is the TNM staging.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. T3N2M1

Breast cancer staging (TNM) depends on tumor size, local invasion, nodal status, and metastasis.

Tumor (T):

• T3: Tumor >5 cm in greatest dimension

• T4: Tumor of any size with chest wall/skin invasion

o T4a: Chest wall invasion (excluding pectoralis muscle alone)

o T4b: Skin changes (ulceration, peau d’orange, satellite nodules)

Nodes (N):

• N2: Fixed/matted ipsilateral axillary nodes or internal mammary nodes

• N3: Infraclavicular/supraclavicular LN

Metastasis (M):

• M1: Distant metastasis (includes contralateral axillary nodes)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with a gradually enlarging, painless mass in the medial thigh for 6 months. The swelling is firm, deep to fascia, and measures 8 cm in size. MRI shows a well-defined heterogeneous mass with areas of necrosis, located between muscle planes without bone involvement. Core biopsy reveals spindle-shaped cells arranged in fascicles with high mitotic activity. Immunohistochemistry is positive for vimentin and shows a characteristic chromosomal translocation t(X;18). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synovial sarcoma

The clinical picture is suggestive of a high-grade soft tissue sarcoma due to the following red flag features:

• Size greater than 5 cm
• Deep to fascia
• Painless and progressively enlarging

The presence of spindle cells with high mitotic activity suggests a malignant mesenchymal tumor. The key diagnostic clue is the chromosomal translocation t(X;18), which is characteristic of synovial sarcoma.

Differentiation:

• Liposarcoma → fat-containing tumor
• Leiomyosarcoma → smooth muscle markers (desmin, SMA)
• MFH (UPS) → pleomorphic, no specific translocation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old car racer is brought to the emergency department after a car accident on the race track. He is unconscious and is immediately put on mechanical ventilation. He opens his eyes on verbal command and moves all four limbs spontaneously. Calculate his GCS.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eyes-3, Verbal-NT, Motor-6

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) assesses level of consciousness using Eye opening (E), Verbal response (V), and Motor response (M). It is essential in trauma assessment and guides airway protection and prognosis.

Stepwise scoring in this patient

Eye opening (E):

• Opens eyes to verbal command → E3

Verbal response (V):

• Patient is intubated/mechanically ventilated, so verbal response cannot be assessed.
• Record as V-NT (Not testable) rather than giving a score of 1.

Motor response (M):

• “Moves all four limbs spontaneously”
• Best motor response corresponds to obeying commands / purposeful movement.
• In this question framing, spontaneous purposeful movement indicates M6 (best motor response).

Therefore, GCS is: E3, V-NT, M6 → Option D

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents to the trauma center after RTA with shortness of breath. The supine CXR is shown below. The BP is 109/88mm Hg and pulse is 98/min. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ICD insertion

In trauma patients, a massive hemothorax or large pleural collection on chest X-ray requires immediate intercostal chest drain (ICD) insertion.

• Supine CXR showing white-out of hemithorax → suggests hemothorax/large effusion
• Patient symptomatic (dyspnea) but hemodynamically stable
• Definitive management: tube thoracostomy (ICD)

Why not others:

A. Needle thoracocentesis → only for tension pneumothorax

C. ET intubation → if airway compromise/respiratory failure

D. NG tube → unrelated

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male who recently had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy presents on postoperative day 3 with fever. An ultrasonographic evaluation reveals a 5x5 cm fluid collection in the right subdiaphragmatic space. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient's condition?
options: Re-explore the wound with T-tube insertion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pigtail insertion and drainage

Post-laparoscopic cholecystectomy fever with a localized subdiaphragmatic (subhepatic) fluid collection on ultrasound suggests a postoperative intra-abdominal collection/abscess (commonly infected bile/seroma/hematoma). In this patient:

• POD 3 fever

• USG: 5 × 5 cm collection in right subdiaphragmatic space

→ size is significant and likely symptomatic/infected.

Most appropriate next step: Image-guided percutaneous drainage (pigtail catheter) because it:

• provides source control (key step in sepsis/collection management)

• allows pus/fluid culture

• avoids morbidity of reoperation

• is standard for postoperative collections >3–4 cm

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man came with complaints of dark-colored tarry stools to the OPD. Which of the following structures is the likely site of the bleed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proximal to Ligament of Treitz

Melena refers to black, tarry, foul-smelling stools caused by digestion of blood as it passes through the gastrointestinal tract. It typically occurs when bleeding originates from the upper gastrointestinal tract, because hemoglobin is degraded by gastric acid and intestinal enzymes into hematin, producing the black color and sticky consistency.

Clinically, GI bleeding is divided using the ligament of Treitz (duodenojejunal junction) as the anatomical landmark:

• Upper GI bleed: proximal to the ligament of Treitz (esophagus, stomach, duodenum)
• Lower GI bleed: distal to the ligament of Treitz (jejunum onward, colon, rectum)

Therefore, dark-colored tarry stools (melena) most commonly indicate bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz (Option A). Bleeding from the anal canal or sigmoid diverticulosis more often causes hematochezia (fresh red blood per rectum), not melena.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a blunt abdominal trauma. He is initially hypotensive but responds to fluid resuscitation. Contrast-enhanced CT scan shows a large laceration involving more than 50% of the right hepatic lobe with active contrast extravasation. There is no other intra-abdominal injury. On monitoring, his blood pressure stabilizes but he requires ongoing transfusion support. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Immediate exploratory laparotomy with right hepatectomy
Non-operative management with close observation only
Perihepatic packing with temporary abdominal closure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Angiographic embolization of bleeding vessel

This patient has a high-grade liver injury with active contrast extravasation on CT, indicating ongoing arterial bleeding. However, he is hemodynamically stabilized after resuscitation.

Management principles:

• Hemodynamically stable or transient responders → CT-based evaluation
• Active contrast extravasation (“contrast blush”) → indicates arterial bleeding
• Best next step → angiographic embolization

Other Options:

Option A. Hepatectomy is rarely first-line and reserved for uncontrollable bleeding

Option B. Observation alone is inadequate in presence of active bleeding

Option D. Perihepatic packing is indicated in unstable patients undergoing damage control surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents to the ER after falling off a horse. His vitals are stable, but he complains of pain and tenderness in lower abdomen and has not passed urine yet. On examination, there is a visible bruise over his lower abdomen, and blood is seen at the urethral meatus. The bladder is not palpable. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
options: Wait for the bladder to fill and perform suprapubic cystostomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wait for the bladder to fill and perform suprapubic cystostomy

In pelvic/straddle trauma, blood at the urethral meatus is a classic sign of urethral injury, and it is an absolute contraindication to blind urethral catheterization.

Key clinical clues in this case

• Fall with lower abdominal trauma

• Blood at urethral meatus → anterior urethral injury likely

• Inability to void

• Bladder not palpable (may be empty or decompressed)

• Lower abdominal bruise (“butterfly”/perineal bruising pattern may be associated)

Management principle

Do NOT attempt Foley catheter insertion when urethral injury is suspected. First priority is urinary diversion.

Since the patient is stable and needs bladder drainage but urethral catheterization is unsafe, the appropriate step is Suprapubic cystostomy (SPC) — usually done once bladder is adequately distended (or with ultrasound guidance).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman complains of fatigue, weight gain, and increased sensitivity to cold. On physical examination, she has noticeable swelling in her neck the histological image is shown below. Additionally, an ultrasound examination shows that her thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged and has an uneven texture. Which of the following conditions is most likely the cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hashimoto's thyroiditis

A woman with fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance has symptoms of hypothyroidism. When hypothyroid symptoms occur together with a diffusely enlarged thyroid (goiter) and ultrasound showing heterogeneous/uneven texture, the most likely cause is Hashimoto thyroiditis, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune thyroid disorder characterized by:

• Destruction of thyroid follicles by anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies
• Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration with germinal center formation (as seen on histology)
• Progressive thyroid failure → hypothyroidism
• Goiter with firm, diffusely enlarged gland; ultrasound typically shows heterogeneous echotexture

Important clinical associations:

• Other autoimmune diseases (e.g., type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia)
• Increased risk of primary thyroid lymphoma (MALT lymphoma)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old man with BMI 52 kg/m², uncontrolled type 2 diabetes and severe obstructive sleep apnea seeks bariatric surgery with maximum weight loss and improvement in metabolic profile. The surgeon plans the procedure with a short common channel of about 50 cm shown in the figure. Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding this operation?
options: It is primarily restrictive with minimal malabsorption and carries the lowest risk of nutritional deficiency
It is biliopancreatic diversion and is associated with significant fat-soluble vitamin deficiency if supplementation is poor
It is Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and is contraindicated when BMI >50 kg/m²
It is single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass (SADI-S) and routinely preserves the entire gastric volume.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is biliopancreatic diversion and is associated with significant fat-soluble vitamin deficiency if supplementation is poor

Biliopancreatic diversion (BPD) is a predominantly malabsorptive bariatric procedure designed for maximum weight loss and metabolic improvement, especially in patients with morbid obesity (BMI >50).

• Creates a short common channel (\~50 cm) where food mixes with bile and pancreatic enzymes

• Causes marked fat and nutrient malabsorption

• Produces maximum weight loss among bariatric surgeries

• Highly effective for type 2 diabetes remission

High risk of deficiencies due to severe malabsorption:

• Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)

• Iron

• Calcium

• Vitamin B12

• Protein malnutrition

Requires lifelong supplementation and strict follow-up

Comparison with other bariatric procedures

• Sleeve gastrectomy: Restrictive

• Roux-en-Y gastric bypass: Restrictive + mild malabsorption

• BPD/duodenal switch: Maximum malabsorption and weight loss

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department for right flank pain radiating to the groin. She also has hematuria but no dysuria or urinary frequency. The patient has no costovertebral angle tenderness. Abdominal imaging shows a 6-mm calculus in the distal right ureter with no hydronephrosis. The patient's symptoms improve with intravenous hydration and analgesics. Which of the following medications will be most helpful in facilitating stone passage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tamsulosin

Medical expulsive therapy (MET) with α-1 blockers (e.g., tamsulosin) facilitates passage of distal ureteric stones (5–10 mm).

• Stones ≤5 mm usually pass spontaneously.

• Stones 5–10 mm, especially in distal ureter, benefit from MET.

• Tamsulosin (α1A-blocker) relaxes ureteric smooth muscle →

o ↓ ureteric spasm

o ↓ intraluminal pressure

o ↑ stone passage rate

o ↓ colicky pain episodes

Distal ureter has high α-adrenergic receptor density → α-blockade improves relaxation and stone expulsion.

• Bethanechol: increases bladder contraction; no role in ureteric stone passage

• Furosemide: increases urine flow but does not aid passage; may worsen colic

• Imipramine: used for nocturnal enuresis; no role in urolithiasis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the physician by his father because of swelling of his left hemiscrotum. Physical examination shows a nontender left scrotal mass that transilluminates. The mass increases in size when the boy cries but is easily reducible. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Patent processus vaginalis

Persistence of the processus vaginalis is the underlying embryologic defect responsible for communicating hydrocele and congenital indirect inguinal hernia in infants.

• The processus vaginalis is a peritoneal outpouching that accompanies testicular descent through the inguinal canal.

• Failure of its obliteration after birth maintains communication between the peritoneal cavity and tunica vaginalis.

• This allows peritoneal fluid (or bowel) to enter the scrotum → swelling that transilluminates and varies in size with crying/straining.

• Most communicating hydroceles resolve spontaneously by 1 year; persistent cases may require herniotomy.

Other options:

• Sperm collection in epididymis → spermatocele (adults)

• Inguinal floor weakness → direct hernia (elderly)

• Lack of fixation → torsion risk, not hydrocele

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 4-week-old infant presents with persistent jaundice, progressive abdominal distension, pale clay-colored stools, and dark urine since birth. Examination reveals hepatomegaly and poor weight gain. Ultrasound shows a contracted/absent gallbladder, and HIDA scan demonstrates no excretion into the intestine even after delayed imaging. Liver biopsy suggests bile duct proliferation with portal fibrosis. Which of the following congenital anomalies is associated with this condition? 1. Situs inversus 2. Malrotation 3. Annular pancreas 4. Polysplenia 5. Renal agenesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 4

• A 4-week-old infant with persistent jaundice, pale (clay-colored) stools, dark urine, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, absent/contracted gallbladder on ultrasound, and no tracer excretion into the intestine on HIDA scan is most consistent with biliary atresia.
• Liver biopsy classically shows bile duct proliferation with portal tract edema and fibrosis, reflecting progressive obliteration of extrahepatic bile ducts causing cholestasis.
• Biliary atresia is associated with a syndromic form called biliary atresia splenic malformation (BASM) syndrome, which is strongly linked to congenital laterality defects and anomalies such as:

o   Situs inversus / heterotaxy

o   Intestinal malrotation

o   Polysplenia (multiple spleens)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male with history of alcohol use presents with high-grade fever and right upper quadrant pain for 6 days. Ultrasound shows a solitary hypoechoic lesion in the right lobe 5cm. Aspiration produces sterile brown, semi-liquid material. His serology for E. histolytica is negative at admission. What is the best next step?
options: Start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics + repeat imaging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start metronidazole therapy

This patient has features that are highly suggestive of an amoebic liver abscess (ALA) despite a negative serology at admission.

Clues favoring amoebic liver abscess

• Middle-aged male with alcohol use (strong risk factor)
• High-grade fever + right upper quadrant pain
• Solitary abscess in the right lobe (5 cm)
• Aspiration yields sterile brown, semi-liquid material ("anchovy sauce" pus), which is characteristic of amoebic liver abscess
• Culture-negative aspirate supports ALA rather than pyogenic liver abscess

Why is the serology negative?

The patient has had symptoms for only 6 days.

• Antibodies to Entamoeba histolytica usually become detectable after 7–10 days of illness.
• Therefore, early serology may be falsely negative.
• A negative serology does not exclude amoebic liver abscess during the first week.

Why is metronidazole the best next step?

The clinical picture is almost diagnostic of amoebic liver abscess, and treatment should not be delayed waiting for repeat serology.

Treatment

• Metronidazole (or tinidazole)
• Followed by a luminal amoebicide (e.g., diloxanide furoate or paromomycin) to eradicate intestinal cysts.

Why are the other options incorrect?

A. Start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics + repeat imaging ❌

• Appropriate for pyogenic liver abscess, which usually presents with:

• Multiple abscesses
• Purulent aspirate
• Positive bacterial cultures

• Here, the aspirate is sterile brown ("anchovy sauce"), favoring amoebic abscess.

C. Repeat USG-guided aspiration ❌

• Aspiration is not routinely required for amoebic liver abscess.
• Indications include:

• Left lobe abscess
• Large abscess (>5 cm with impending rupture)
• No improvement after 48–72 hours of metronidazole
• Diagnostic uncertainty

The aspiration has already established the characteristic appearance.

D. Plan for surgical drainage ❌

Reserved for:

• Ruptured abscess
• Failure of percutaneous drainage
• Complicated abscesses

Not indicated initially.

High-yield points for exam (ZVrecommended!):

| Feature | Amoebic liver abscess | Pyogenic liver abscess

| ------- | --------------------- | ----------------------

| Number | Usually solitary | Often multiple

| Location | Right lobe | Variable

| Aspirate | Sterile, brown "anchovy sauce" | Thick yellow pus

| Culture | Usually sterile | Positive bacterial culture

| Serology | Positive in >90% after 7–10 days | Negative

| Treatment | Metronidazole + luminal agent | Broad-spectrum antibiotics ± drainage

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being shot in the right thigh during an attempted robbery. The patient is awake, alert, and in moderate distress. Blood pressure is 101/49 mm Hg and pulse is 122/min. Records indicate that his last tetanus vaccine was a year ago. Physical examination shows a gunshot entry wound on the anteromedial upper right thigh with an exit wound on the lateral thigh. There is a hematoma at the entry site but no active bleeding from either wound. The right lower extremity is cool to the touch and distal pulses are feeble. Radiography of the lower extremity shows no fracture. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
options: Doppler ultrasonography of the lower limb vessels
Urgent surgical exploration of the wound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urgent surgical exploration of the wound

Key Findings

• Gunshot wound to thigh
• Cool limb
• Feeble distal pulses
• No fracture
• Hematoma present

That is arterial injury until proven otherwise.

Trauma vascular signs

Hard signs (→ immediate surgery)

• Absent distal pulses
• Expanding hematoma
• Pulsatile bleeding
• Bruit/thrill
• Limb ischemia (cool, pale, painful)

Soft signs (→ imaging first)

• History of bleeding
• Nonexpanding hematoma
• Nerve deficit
• Proximity to vessel

Most appropriate next step: Urgent surgical exploration

• Do NOT delay for Doppler or CT angiography when ischemia signs are present.
• Time = limb.

A. Blood transfusion

Vitals are stable. No shock. no need of blood transfusion.

B. Compression + antibiotics

Inadequate for suspected arterial injury with limb ischemia.

C. Doppler ultrasonography

• Imaging is done only if soft signs of vascular injury are present.
• Here ischemia signs are present → go to OR.

Exam Rule

Penetrating trauma + ischemic limb → straight to surgery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 41-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, pruritus, and jaundice over several months. Lab results show a serum alkaline phosphatase level of 285 U/L. MRCP is shown below. Which of the following morphologic features is most likely present in his liver?
options: Piecemeal hepatocellular necrosis at the interface of portal tracts
Portal bridging fibrosis with nodular hepatocyte regeneration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Concentric "onion-skin" bile duct fibrosis

MRCP showing multifocal strictures and dilatations (“beading”) of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts with cholestatic symptoms (pruritus, jaundice, ↑ALP) is characteristic of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).

• Concentric periductal fibrosis (“onion-skin” fibrosis) around bile ducts → progressive obliteration and cholestasis.

High-yield associations:

• Strongly associated with ulcerative colitis

• ↑ Risk of cholangiocarcinoma

• p-ANCA positive

• Can progress to secondary biliary cirrhosis

Other options:

• PBC: Granulomatous bile duct destruction, AMA positive, middle-aged women

• Autoimmune hepatitis: Interface (piecemeal) hepatitis

• Cirrhosis: Bridging fibrosis with nodules

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42 year old woman presents with intermittent RUQ colicky pain radiating to the back. She has a history of dyslipidemia and has been on OCPs for over 15 years. Her BMI is 38kg/m2. Ultrasound reveals a contracted gallbladder with multiple radiolucent stones. There are no signs of jaundice. Her liver function tests are also normal. Which of the following is the most likely type of gallstone in this woman?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mixed cholesterol stones

Gallstones are classified into cholesterol stones and pigment stones, and the type can be predicted by risk factors and clinical setting. This patient has classic risk factors for cholesterol gallstones:

• Female
• Obesity (BMI 38)
• Dyslipidemia
• Long-term OCP use → ↑ estrogen → ↑ hepatic cholesterol secretion and supersaturation of bile
• Typical symptoms: intermittent RUQ colicky pain radiating to the back (biliary colic)
• Radiolucent stones on ultrasound (cholesterol stones are usually radiolucent)

In practice, the most common gallstones overall are mixed cholesterol stones (cholesterol + calcium salts + bile pigments), rather than 100% pure cholesterol stones. Pigment stones are less likely here:

• Brown pigment stones → infected bile ducts, biliary stasis, parasites
• Black pigment stones → chronic hemolysis (sickle cell), cirrhosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with episodic upper gastrointestinal bleeding, right hypochondrial pain, and progressive jaundice for 3 days. He had undergone percutaneous liver biopsy 10 days ago. On examination, he is mildly icteric and hemodynamically stable. Ultrasound abdomen reveals echogenic contents within the gallbladder lumen and dilated intrahepatic bile ducts, without gallstones. What is the most appropriate next investigation to establish the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CT angiography of hepatic artery

A patient presenting with the triad of upper GI bleeding, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice following a hepatic intervention (e.g., percutaneous liver biopsy) most likely has hemobilia, classically due to an arteriobiliary fistula or hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm. Ultrasound findings of echogenic material within the gallbladder (blood clots) with dilated intrahepatic bile ducts (biliary obstruction from clot) support this diagnosis in the absence of gallstones.

The most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis and identify the bleeding source is CT angiography of the hepatic artery, as it can demonstrate contrast extravasation, pseudoaneurysm, or arterio-biliary fistula, and guides definitive management (angiographic embolization). Endoscopy may show blood at the ampulla but does not localize the vascular lesion; MRCP outlines biliary anatomy but does not reliably identify active vascular bleeding; ERCP is primarily therapeutic (clot extraction/stenting) after diagnosis is established.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old man undergoes split-thickness skin grafting for a post-burn defect on the neck. Three months later, he develops progressive tightening of the grafted area leading to restricted neck extension. This secondary contracture is most likely due to which underlying mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pull of myofibroblasts

Post-burn contractures following split-thickness skin grafting are primarily caused by myofibroblast-mediated wound contraction.

Pathophysiology

• During wound healing, fibroblasts differentiate into myofibroblasts.

• Myofibroblasts contain actin–myosin filaments similar to smooth muscle.

• They generate contractile forces → wound contraction.

• Excessive or prolonged activity → secondary contracture and deformity.

contractures occur after split-thickness graft:

• More dermal loss → greater contraction

• Less structural support than full-thickness graft

• Common in mobile areas (neck, axilla, joints)

Other options

• Collagen cross-linking → contributes to scar strength, not primary contraction

• Epidermal hyperproliferation → hypertrophic scar, not contracture

• Lymphatic congestion → edema, not contracture

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old man with long-standing peripheral arterial disease presents with severe rest pain in the lower limb. Imaging shows diffuse distal arterial disease not amenable to revascularization. He undergoes a lumbar sympathectomy. Postoperatively, which of the following changes is most likely to be observed in the affected limb?
options: Decreased skin temperature due to loss of vasodilatory tone
Increased sweating due to parasympathetic overactivity
Vasodilation of cutaneous vessels with improved collateral flow
Loss of pain sensation due to interruption of somatic nerves
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vasodilation of cutaneous vessels with improved collateral flow

Lumbar sympathectomy works by interrupting sympathetic vasoconstrictor fibers (L2–L4) to the lower limb, leading to:

• Persistent arteriolar vasodilation → ↑ cutaneous blood flow
• Increase in skin temperature
• Reduction in rest pain (due to improved microcirculation)
• Decreased sweating (anhidrosis) in the affected limb

Indications:

• Inoperable peripheral arterial disease
• Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)
• Severe vasospastic disorders

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with a thyroid nodule. FNAC suggests papillary carcinoma. She undergoes total thyroidectomy. Histopathology reveals multifocal tumors with cervical lymph node metastasis. Postoperatively, serum thyroglobulin is undetectable. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Residual tumor suppressed by TSH suppression therapy
Presence of anti-thyroglobulin antibodies interfering with assay
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Presence of anti-thyroglobulin antibodies interfering with assay

Educational objective:

• Thyroglobulin is used as a tumor marker for follow-up in differentiated thyroid carcinoma after total thyroidectomy
• It should be undetectable; detectable levels suggest residual or recurrent disease
• Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies can interfere with assays and cause falsely low or undetectable values
• Always interpret thyroglobulin along with anti-thyroglobulin antibody status
• Undetectable thyroglobulin does not rule out disease if antibodies are present

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman underwent total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection for a solitary thyroid nodule. Histopathology confirmed medullary carcinoma of the thyroid with RET mutation positivity. She is asymptomatic at 1-year follow-up. Levels of tumor marker is raising and imaging suggests locoregional recurrence. Which of the following tumor markers would not be useful in monitoring for recurrence in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thyroglobulin

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from parafollicular C cells, not follicular cells; therefore thyroglobulin is NOT a useful tumor marker for monitoring recurrence.

Useful tumor markers in MTC

• Calcitonin → most sensitive marker for residual or recurrent disease

• CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) → correlates with tumor burden and prognosis

• CGRP (calcitonin gene–related peptide) → may also be elevated

Additional high-yield points

• MTC associated with RET mutation and MEN2 syndromes

• Family screening and prophylactic thyroidectomy may be required

• Rising calcitonin after surgery → suspect recurrence/metastasis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 43-year-old man is being evaluated for suspected lymphoma-related obstruction of the lymphatic system. The radiology team plans to perform pedal lymphangiography. Which of the following best describes how this procedure is performed?
options: The lymphatic channels on the dorsum of the foot are cannulated after injecting a blue dye, and an oily contrast agent is slowly infused to opacify the lymphatic system.
A peripheral intravenous line is placed in the dorsal venous arch and water-soluble contrast is rapidly injected to visualize lymphatics under fluoroscopy.
A CT-guided direct puncture of para-aortic lymph nodes is performed and contrast medium is infused retrogradely.
A radionuclide-labeled tracer is injected subcutaneously and lymphatic drainage is evaluated with a gamma camera.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The lymphatic channels on the dorsum of the foot are cannulated after injecting a blue dye, and an oily contrast agent is slowly infused to opacify the lymphatic system.

Pedal lymphangiography is a specialized imaging technique used to visualize lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes, especially in suspected lymphatic obstruction or lymphoma.

Procedure technique

• A blue dye (e.g., isosulfan blue) is injected into the web spaces of the toes to identify lymphatic channels.

• Small lymphatic vessels on the dorsum of the foot are surgically cannulated.

• An oil-based contrast agent (e.g., Lipiodol) is slowly injected.

• Serial radiographs/fluoroscopy visualize lymphatic channels and nodes.

Uses

• Evaluation of lymphatic obstruction

• Lymphoma staging

• Detection of lymphatic leaks (chylous ascites, chylothorax)

• Preoperative planning for lymphatic surgery

Differentiation from other techniques

• Lymphoscintigraphy: radionuclide tracer + gamma camera (functional study)

• CT/MRI: anatomic imaging only

• Venography: evaluates venous system, not lymphatics

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 43-year-old man presents with progressively worsening dysphagia to both solids and liquids over several months, along with retrosternal discomfort and occasional regurgitation of undigested food. He has a history of chronic smoking and alcohol use. Physical examination is unremarkable. Esophageal manometry performed after a test swallow demonstrates the following. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Achalasia

Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder caused by degeneration of inhibitory neurons (Auerbach/myenteric plexus), leading to:

• Failure of LES relaxation
• Increased LES tone
• Absent peristalsis

Patients present with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, and chest discomfort.

Why not other options?

A. Cricopharyngeal dysfunction → Problem at upper esophageal sphincter → oropharyngeal dysphagia

C. Diffuse esophageal spasm → Simultaneous contractions but normal LES relaxation

D. Esophageal stricture → Mechanical → dysphagia to solids first

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45 year old man with a long standing history of alcohol abuse is admitted to the emergency with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, persistent vomiting and tachycardia for the last 4 days. On admission, his serum lipase was markedly elevated and a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis was made. Despite aggressive IV fluids and supportive management, he continues to have low grade fever and rising leukocyte count but procalcitonin levels are normal. his blood cultures are sterile. He is hemodynamically stable and has no organ failure. A CECT is done which shows a non enhancing necrotic mass involving 40-50% of the pancreas. No gas bubbles are seen with the necrotic tissue. What is the next best step?
options: Attempt a CT guided FNA of the necrotic area to classify the type of pancreatitis.
Continue conservative management and IV fluids.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Continue conservative management and IV fluids.

Acute pancreatitis may progress to necrotizing pancreatitis, which is diagnosed on contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) by non-enhancing pancreatic parenchyma. Management depends primarily on whether necrosis is sterile or infected, and on the presence of organ failure. In this patient:

• CECT shows 40–50% pancreatic necrosis
• No gas bubbles in the necrotic collection (gas strongly suggests infection)
• Procalcitonin is normal, blood cultures sterile
• Hemodynamically stable, no organ failure

→ This most consistent with sterile pancreatic necrosis (or at least no clear evidence of infection).

Sterile necrosis is treated conservatively, even if leukocytosis and low-grade fever are present, because systemic inflammatory response (SIRS) can mimic infection. Routine prophylactic antibiotics do not improve outcomes and are not recommended in sterile necrosis.

• Sterile necrosis → Conservative management
• Infected necrosis → Antibiotics + delayed drainage/necrosectomy (“step-up approach”)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids and regurgitation. High-resolution manometry shows integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) 22 mmHg and 100% failed peristalsis in the distal esophagus. Which of the following best describes this finding according to Chicago classification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type I achalasia

Type I (classic) achalasia is characterized on high-resolution manometry by:

• Elevated integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) → impaired LES relaxation

• 100% failed peristalsis in distal esophagus

• Absence of panesophageal pressurization or spasm

This represents complete loss of esophageal body peristalsis with non-relaxing LES.

Chicago classification of achalasia

• Type I (classic):

o ↑ IRP + absent peristalsis

o No panesophageal pressurization

o Most advanced neuronal degeneration

• Type II:
