o ↑ IRP + absent peristalsis

o Panesophageal pressurization present

o Best treatment response

• Type III (spastic):

o ↑ IRP + premature/spastic distal contractions

o Chest pain common

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden severe headache and vomiting. He also reports having “mass” in both his kidneys. His BP is 160/100 mmHg. A non-contrast CT head is shown below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT angiography

• Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) classically presents with a sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache ± vomiting and meningismus.
• The first-line diagnostic test is a non-contrast CT head (most sensitive early).
• Once SAH is confirmed, the next critical step is to identify the bleeding source, most commonly a ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm, particularly in patients with ADPKD (bilateral kidney masses).
• Therefore, CT angiography (CTA) is the best next investigation to localize the aneurysm and guide definitive therapy (endovascular coiling or surgical clipping) to prevent rebleeding.
• Nimodipine is subsequently given to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischemia due to cerebral vasospasm, but aneurysm localization and securing is the priority immediately after CT-confirmed SAH.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man sustains deep flame burns involving the entire trunk circumferentially, along with extensive burns elsewhere on the body. He is aggressively resuscitated using the Parkland formula, but 6 hours later he develops worsening hypotension, tense abdominal distension, rising peak airway pressures, and urine output < 0.3 mL/kg/hr. What is the next best step in management?
options: Shift to ICU and begin colloid-based resuscitation
Start intravenous vasopressors to maintain MAP
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Perform an emergency decompressive laparotomy

Severely burned patients who undergo aggressive fluid resuscitation (eg, with the Parkland formula) are at risk of developing abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) due to massive capillary leak, bowel edema, and third-spacing.

ACS is suggested by the classic combination of tense abdominal distension, worsening hypotension, oliguria (urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/hr; here < 0.3), and increased peak airway pressures from diaphragmatic elevation. This is a life-threatening condition causing impaired venous return, reduced renal perfusion, and respiratory compromise. The definitive treatment is urgent abdominal decompression, and in a rapidly deteriorating patient with clinical ACS, the next best step is emergency decompressive laparotomy.

Escharotomies are indicated for circumferential chest/limb burns causing restrictive ventilation or limb ischemia, but they do not relieve intra-abdominal hypertension. Vasopressors or switching fluids may temporarily support blood pressure but will not correct the underlying elevated intra-abdominal pressure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man undergoes emergency laparotomy for perforation peritonitis. On postoperative day 5, he develops feculent discharge from the abdominal wound. The output is approximately 800 mL/day. He is febrile, tachycardic, and has electrolyte imbalance. There is no evidence of distal obstruction on imaging. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management strategy?
options: Immediate re-exploration and surgical closure of fistula
Aggressive fluid and electrolyte correction with control of sepsis and nutritional support
Primary skin closure over the fistula site
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aggressive fluid and electrolyte correction with control of sepsis and nutritional support

This patient has a postoperative enterocutaneous (fecal) fistula with high output (>500 mL/day).

Key principles of management can be summarized as “SNAP”:

• Sepsis control
• Nutritional support (often total parenteral nutrition)
• Anatomy definition (imaging later)
• Plan for definitive surgery if needed

Initial management focuses on stabilization:

• Correct fluid and electrolyte imbalance
• Control infection (antibiotics, drainage if required)
• Protect skin from effluent
• Provide nutritional support

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with portal hypertension due to extrahepatic portal vein obstruction presents with recurrent esophageal variceal bleeding despite endoscopic therapy. Surgical shunting is being considered. The surgical team recommends a procedure that selectively decompresses the gastroesophageal varices while preserving portal perfusion to the liver, resulting in a lower risk of postoperative hepatic encephalopathy compared to nonselective shunts. Which procedure is being described?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Distal splenorenal shunt

The distal splenorenal shunt (Warren shunt) is a selective portosystemic shunt that decompresses gastroesophageal varices while preserving portal venous flow to the liver.

Mechanism

• Connects splenic vein → left renal vein

• Selectively decompresses:

o Splenic vein

o Short gastric veins

o Esophageal varices

• Maintains portal flow through superior mesenteric vein to liver

Clinical advantage

• Controls variceal bleeding

• Preserves hepatic perfusion

• Lower risk of hepatic encephalopathy than nonselective shunts

Comparison with other shunts

• Portocaval shunt: total diversion of portal blood → high encephalopathy risk

• Mesocaval shunt: nonselective decompression

• Central splenorenal shunt: nonselective

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old postoperative patient is reviewed on day 3 after an inguinal hernia repair. The wound shows clear, serous discharge at a single point measuring less than 2 cm, without pus or spreading erythema. According to the Southampton wound grading system, what is the correct grade?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Grade IIIa

The Southampton wound grading system is used to classify postoperative wound healing and infection severity based on the presence of erythema, discharge, and deeper involvement. It helps differentiate normal inflammatory changes from true surgical site infection and guides management. In this case, the key finding is:

• Clear serous discharge
• From a single point
• < 2 cm
• No pus
• No spreading erythema

Key distinctions:

• Grade I: normal healing (may have mild bruising/erythema only)
• Grade II: erythema/inflammation only (no discharge)
• Grade III: discharge present

• IIIa: serous discharge
• IIIb: seropurulent discharge

• Grade IV/V: deep or severe infection (abscess/dehiscence/systemic sepsis)

Thus, a clean postoperative wound with localized clear serous discharge is best classified as Southampton Grade IIIa.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with colicky pain in the right upper quadrant. Her pain started about an hour ago after a large, fatty meal and is associated with nausea. The patient had a similar episode a week ago that resolved spontaneously. The patient had a cholecystectomy 2 years ago due to symptomatic cholelithiasis. Her other medical problems include hyperlipidemia and obesity. Laboratory results are as follows: Leukocytes: 8,000/mm³ Total bilirubin: 1.3 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase: 120 U/L Aspartate aminotransferase (SGOT): 37 U/L Alanine aminotransferase (SGPT): 49 U/L Amylase: 91 U/L Abdominal ultrasonography reveals a mildly dilated common bile duct but no stones. While in the emergency department, the patient receives morphine for pain control, but the pain worsens. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction

Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction should be suspected in patients with post-cholecystectomy biliary-type pain and a dilated common bile duct without visible stones, especially when pain worsens after morphine.

Key learning points

• Occurs due to functional obstruction or spasm of the sphincter of Oddi.

• Seen commonly in middle-aged women after cholecystectomy.

• Presents with:

o Recurrent RUQ or epigastric biliary colic

o Normal or mildly abnormal LFTs

o Dilated CBD without stones on imaging

• Morphine increases sphincter of Oddi tone → can worsen biliary pain (classic clue).

• Diagnosis: Sphincter of Oddi manometry (gold standard).

• Treatment: Endoscopic sphincterotomy or medical therapy (e.g., nitrates, CCBs).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with persistent vomiting for 5 days due to gastric outlet obstruction. On admission, she is dehydrated. Laboratory findings: • pH: 7.55 • HCO₃⁻: 36 mEq/L • K⁺: 2.8 mEq/L She is started on intravenous fluids, but her metabolic alkalosis persists despite initial resuscitation. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism responsible for the persistence of alkalosis?
options: Renal bicarbonate retention due to volume depletion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Renal bicarbonate retention due to volume depletion

Educational Objective

Metabolic alkalosis due to vomiting initially results from loss of gastric HCl, but its persistence depends on renal mechanisms, not ongoing acid loss.

• Volume depletion → activates RAAS
• ↑ Aldosterone leads to:

• ↑ H⁺ secretion
• ↑ K⁺ loss (hypokalemia)
• ↑ renal bicarbonate reabsorption

This leads to “contraction alkalosis”, where alkalosis is maintained despite correction of the primary cause.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal cramping, diarrhea, nausea, light-headedness, and diaphoresis occurring 15–20 minutes after meals. She underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery 4 weeks ago for obesity. She is asymptomatic between episodes and at night. Physical examination shows a well-healed surgical scar and mild epigastric tenderness. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this patient’s symptoms?
options: Bacterial overgrowth due to a surgically created blind loop
Increased gastric motility due to vagal nerve injury
Anastomotic stricture causing delayed gastric emptying
Rapid delivery of hyperosmolar contents into the small intestine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rapid delivery of hyperosmolar contents into the small intestine

This patient has early dumping syndrome, a common complication after gastric bypass surgery. It occurs due to rapid emptying of hyperosmolar gastric contents into the small intestine, leading to:

• Fluid shift from plasma into intestinal lumen → diarrhea, hypotension
• Release of vasoactive substances → diaphoresis, light-headedness

Symptoms typically occur within 15–30 minutes after meals.

Why not other options?

A. Blind loop bacterial overgrowth → Causes malabsorption, bloating, steatorrhea—not acute postprandial symptoms

B. Vagal nerve injury → Causes delayed gastric emptying (gastroparesis), not rapid transit

C. Anastomotic stricture → Leads to vomiting and obstruction, not diarrhea

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman receives neo-adjuvant chemotherapy for invasive ductal carcinoma. Clinical assessment shows that the tumor has shrunk to 3 cm on mammography with no nodal involvement or metastasis. Which of the following accurately represents the current staging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. уT2N0M0

Breast cancer staging uses TNM categories, and the stage can be modified with prefixes that indicate when and how the staging assessment was performed. This becomes especially important after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT), because treatment alters tumor size and nodal status.

Prefix “y” is used when the TNM stage is assessed after neoadjuvant therapy (chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, targeted therapy, etc.

So, in this patient:

• Tumor has shrunk to 3 cm → T2 (>2 cm and ≤5 cm)
• No nodal involvement → N0
• No metastasis → M0
• Assessed after NACT → prefix y

Therefore, the correct staging is yT2N0M0 (Option B)

Key prefixes (high yield):

• cTNM = clinical stage (before any definitive treatment; based on exam/imaging/biopsy)
• pTNM = pathologic stage (after surgery)
• yTNM = stage assessed after neoadjuvant therapy
• rTNM = stage at recurrence/restaging after a disease-free interval
• aTNM = stage determined at autopsy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman undergoes a screening mammography that shows spiculated stellate lesion in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. No associated mass is palpated. Ultrasound reveals an architectural distortion with no discrete mass. Core biopsy needle was done which revealed benign proliferative changes with sclerosing ducts, without atypia. The histopathology for the same is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radial scar

A radial scar (complex sclerosing lesion) is a benign proliferative breast lesion that is clinically important because it mimics carcinoma on imaging. It typically appears on screening mammography as a spiculated stellate lesion with architectural distortion and often no palpable mass, closely resembling invasive breast cancer. Histology shows a central fibroelastotic scar with radiating ducts and lobules entrapped within sclerotic stroma, usually without cytologic atypia.

Key learning point: Although a radial scar is benign, it is associated with an increased risk of concurrent malignancy or high-risk lesions, and therefore requires careful correlation between imaging and core biopsy, often prompting surgical excision when imaging-pathology discordance exists or when atypia is present.

Thus, a spiculated stellate lesion with architectural distortion and benign sclerosing ducts on biopsy most likely represents a radial scar.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old female patient undergoes a mammography for a lump in the right breast. Based on the imaging report, she is advised to undergo a biopsy. Which of the following could have been reported?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. BIRADS 4b or BIRADS 5

The BI-RADS (Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System) classification standardizes mammography/US/MRI reporting and directly guides management by estimating the risk of malignancy.

Key categories and action:

• BI-RADS 1 (Negative) → routine screening
• BI-RADS 2 (Benign) → routine screening
• BI-RADS 3 (Probably benign, <2% risk) → short-interval follow-up imaging (not biopsy)
• BI-RADS 4 (Suspicious) → biopsy recommended

o  4A: low suspicion (2–10%)

o  4B: moderate suspicion (10–50%)

o  4C: high suspicion (50–95%)
• BI-RADS 5 (Highly suggestive of malignancy, >95%) → biopsy mandatory
• BI-RADS → known biopsy-proven malignancy

Therefore, a report advising biopsy would typically be: BI-RADS 4 (especially 4B/4C) or BI-RADS 5

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use presents with recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back and significant weight loss. He reports steatorrhea for the past 6 months. Imaging shows pancreatic calcifications and a dilated pancreatic duct measuring 9 mm with multiple intraductal calculi. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive surgical management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Puestow procedure

This patient has chronic pancreatitis with:

• Dilated pancreatic duct (>7 mm)
• Intraductal calculi
• Pain and exocrine insufficiency

The preferred surgical treatment in such cases is a drainage procedure, specifically longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (Puestow procedure).

• “Large duct disease” (duct >7 mm) → drainage procedure
• “Small duct disease” → resection procedures

Why Puestow procedure:

• Longitudinal opening of pancreatic duct
• Anastomosis with jejunum
• Relieves ductal hypertension → pain relief

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Whipple is indicated for malignancy or head-dominant disease without ductal dilatation

B. Distal pancreatectomy is for disease limited to tail

D. Total pancreatectomy leads to brittle diabetes and is rarely first-line

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman has a 2.8 cm breast lump that is firm and irregular. She has a palpable ipsilateral axillary node. Mammogram shows a spiculated mass with microcalcifications. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: Core needle biopsy of breast lesion plus tissue diagnosis of axillary node
Start neoadjuvant chemotherapy without tissue diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Core needle biopsy of breast lesion plus tissue diagnosis of axillary node

This is a high-suspicion breast malignancy. The lump is firm and irregular, mammogram shows a spiculated mass with microcalcifications, and there is a palpable ipsilateral axillary node. The most appropriate next diagnostic step is to obtain tissue diagnosis in a way that provides histology and biomarker assessment. Core needle biopsy of the breast lesion is preferred because it preserves architecture, confirms invasive versus in situ disease, and allows estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 testing. Because there is a clinically abnormal axillary node, a tissue diagnosis of the axillary node should also be done, typically by ultrasound-guided FNAC or core biopsy, to confirm nodal metastasis and guide staging and treatment planning.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman undergoes FNAC for thyroid nodule as shown below. USG Neck: Thyroid nodule + central nodes suspicious. No distant metastasis on CT neck–chest–abdomen. According to current management guidelines, what is the most appropriate surgical treatment?
options: Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection only
Total thyroidectomy with central + lateral neck dissections
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Total thyroidectomy with central + lateral neck dissections

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is a neuroendocrine tumor arising from parafollicular C cells and is suggested on FNAC by cytology showing plasmacytoid/spindle-shaped cells with granular cytoplasm and may show amyloid in the background. Unlike papillary thyroid carcinoma, MTC demonstrates early lymphatic spread, commonly involving the central compartment (Level VI) and frequently spreading to both lateral neck compartments (Levels II–V) even when lateral nodes are not clinically obvious.

Therefore, current surgical guidelines recommend that patients with MTC and suspicious/positive central nodes undergo total thyroidectomy with therapeutic central neck dissection and bilateral lateral neck dissections, as this provides the best chance of complete loco-regional disease clearance and reduces recurrence. In MTC, lateral neck clearance is often performed more aggressively because occult lateral node metastasis is common, and incomplete nodal dissection leads to persistent disease and elevated calcitonin post-operatively.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 48-year-old male with a history of chronic NSAID use presents with sudden epigastric pain and abdominal rigidity. Imaging confirms pneumoperitoneum due to a perforated duodenal ulcer. Intraoperatively, a 2.5 cm anterior duodenal perforation is identified with healthy surrounding tissue and no evidence of malignancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management?
options: Closure of the defect with gastrojejunostomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Graham patch repair

Graham patch repair (omentopexy) is the standard surgical treatment for most perforated duodenal ulcers.

Indications

• Acute perforated duodenal ulcer

• Healthy surrounding tissue

• No suspicion of malignancy

• Hemodynamically stable after resuscitation

Procedure

• Peritoneal lavage

• Closure of perforation using sutures

• Reinforcement with pedicled omental patch (Graham patch)

• Omentum provides vascular supply and promotes healing

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 48-year-old man presents with chronic watery diarrhea, epigastric pain, and significant weight loss over 3 months. His diarrhea persists during fasting. Upper GI endoscopy reveals multiple duodenal ulcers. During hospitalization, nasogastric tube decompression leads to a marked reduction in gastric secretion. Which of the following best explains this observation?
options: Hormone-mediated diarrhea from medullary thyroid carcinoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acid-mediated diarrhea due to gastrinoma

Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) causes acid hypersecretion, leading to multiple refractory peptic ulcers and acid-mediated secretory diarrhea.

Pathophysiology

• Gastrinoma → excessive gastrin secretion

• Marked ↑ gastric acid production

• Acid inactivates pancreatic enzymes and damages intestinal mucosa

→ malabsorption + secretory diarrhea

• Diarrhea persists during fasting

Key clinical clues

• Multiple or recurrent duodenal ulcers

• Ulcers beyond first part of duodenum

• Chronic watery diarrhea

• Weight loss

• May be part of MEN1 syndrome

Differentiation from other causes

• VIPoma: watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria

• Carcinoid syndrome: flushing + serotonin diarrhea

• Medullary thyroid carcinoma: calcitonin-mediated diarrhea

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 48-year-old man with a long history of GERD presents with progressive dysphagia. Endoscopy shows salmon-colored mucosa extending above the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy reveals intestinal-type epithelium with goblet cells. Which of the following classification is used to know the extent of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prague criteria

Barrett esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia). Endoscopically it appears as salmon-colored mucosa extending proximally above the gastroesophageal junction. To describe the extent of Barrett’s esophagus, the standard system used is the Prague C & M classification, which reports:

• C (Circumferential extent): length of continuous circumferential Barrett mucosa
• M (Maximal extent): maximum length of Barrett mucosa including tongues

This classification provides a reproducible way to document disease length, guide surveillance, and assess risk of progression to dysplasia and esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Other Options:

A. Milan criteria:

• Used in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
• Determines eligibility for liver transplantation (single tumor ≤5 cm or ≤3 tumors each ≤3 cm).
• Not related to esophageal disease.

B. Tokyo criteria:

• Used in acute cholangitis and cholecystitis.
• Helps in diagnosis and severity grading (Tokyo Guidelines).
• No role in Barrett esophagus or dysphagia evaluation.

C. Chicago criteria:

• Used in esophageal motility disorders based on high-resolution manometry.
• Classifies disorders like achalasia, distal esophageal spasm, EGJ outflow obstruction.
• Applies to motility disorders, not mucosal metaplasia like Barrett.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman undergoes hemithyroidectomy for a suspicious thyroid nodule. On postoperative day 1, she is comfortable and tolerating oral intake. Her voice is mildly hoarse. Neck drain shows minimal serosanguinous output and her airway is patent. Which of the following postoperative findings would be least expected after hemithyroidectomy?
options: Airway compromise due to neck hematoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypocalcemia with tetany

Hypocalcemia is due to parathyroid injury or devascularization and classically occurs after total thyroidectomy rather than hemithyroidectomy.

In hemithyroidectomy, at least one lobe and most parathyroids remain intact → calcium levels are usually preserved.

Hypocalcemia with tetany is least expected after hemithyroidectomy because at least two parathyroid glands remain intact on the contralateral side, preserving calcium homeostasis.

Expected complications after hemithyroidectomy

• Hoarseness of voice: due to transient recurrent laryngeal nerve neuropraxia

• Postoperative hemorrhage: can cause neck swelling

• Neck hematoma → airway compromise: surgical emergency requiring immediate wound opening

Why hypocalcemia is uncommon

• Significant hypocalcemia usually occurs after total thyroidectomy due to:

o Removal of parathyroids

o Devitalization of parathyroid blood supply

• In hemithyroidectomy, contralateral parathyroids maintain normal calcium levels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 49-year-old male with a history of acute alcoholic pancreatitis 8 weeks ago presents with upper abdominal fullness and mild epigastric pain. An abdominal CT scan image shows a well-defined, round, homogeneous, non-enhancing fluid collection in the lesser sac, measuring 5 cm, with a thin wall but no internal septations. There is mild compression of the stomach but no signs of infection or hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient’s pancreatic condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Conservative management and observation

A pancreatic pseudocyst following acute pancreatitis should be managed conservatively if it is asymptomatic, <6 cm, and without complications (infection, hemorrhage, obstruction).

Key management principles:

• Most pseudocysts resolve spontaneously within weeks.

• Indications for intervention:

o Size >6 cm

o Persistence >6 weeks with symptoms

o Infection/hemorrhage

o Gastric/biliary obstruction

o Rapid enlargement

• Preferred treatment when indicated: endoscopic drainage (first line), then percutaneous or surgical.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50 year old carpenter complains of swelling throbbing pain and heaviness in his left leg for the past 5 months. A duplex scan done showed great saphenous vein incompetence. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endothermal ablation

Chronic symptoms of varicose veins (heaviness, throbbing pain, swelling worsened by prolonged standing) with duplex-confirmed great saphenous vein (GSV) incompetence indicate superficial venous reflux. Duplex ultrasound is the diagnostic gold standard and helps plan definitive management.

For symptomatic GSV reflux, the current treatment of choice is endothermal ablation (radiofrequency ablation or endovenous laser ablation) because it:

• directly closes the incompetent GSV
• is minimally invasive (day-care procedure)
• has less postoperative pain, quicker recovery, and fewer wound complications
• has comparable or better long-term occlusion rates compared with open surgery

Why other options are not preferred:

• Trendelenburg procedure (flush ligation at SFJ) is an older open procedure with higher recurrence.
• Dodd/Cockett surgeries address incompetent perforators/varicosities, not primary GSV reflux as first-line.
• SEPS is mainly for perforator incompetence with venous ulcers (CEAP C5–C6).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50 year old man with chronic hepatitis B presents for evaluation of an incidentally detected liver lesion. MRI shows a 3.2 cm arterially enhancing lesion with venous washout in segment VII consistent with HCC. His investigation reveal: ● Child Pugh A ● No clinically significant portal hypertension (HPVG < 10mmHg) ● Performance status ● AFP mildly elevated ● No vascular or extrahepatic invasion However the MRI shows additional 2 nodules, both <2.5cm in different segments of the liver. What is the best definitive treatment option?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liver transplantation work up

The BCLC (Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer) staging system guides definitive management of hepatocellular carcinoma by integrating: tumor burden, liver function (Child-Pugh), portal hypertension, and performance status (PS).

This patient has:

• Chronic HBV
• Child-Pugh A
• No portal hypertension
• Good PS
• No vascular invasion / extrahepatic spread
• But importantly: multifocal HCC (3 lesions: 3.2 cm + two additional nodules <2.5 cm in different segments)

Even with preserved liver function, the presence of multiple tumors in different segments suggests multicentric disease and higher risk of recurrence if resected.

The best curative/definitive option for eligible multifocal early HCC is liver transplantation according to USCF criteria: Transplantation may be done for 2-3 lesions upto 4.5cm.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old female presents with painless hematuria. Imaging shows a bladder mass. Biopsy reveals transitional cell carcinoma. Which risk factor is most commonly associated with this cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tobacco smoking

Tobacco smoking is the most important and common risk factor for urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the bladder.

• Cigarette smoke contains aromatic amines and carcinogens that are metabolized in the liver and excreted in urine → prolonged exposure of urothelium → malignant transformation.

• Smoking accounts for \~50–60% of bladder cancers.

Other risk factors:

• Occupational exposure to aniline dyes, aromatic amines (benzidine, β-naphthylamine)

• Cyclophosphamide therapy

• Chronic irritation (stones, catheters)

• Pelvic radiation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presents with jaundice, progressive fatigue, and weight loss. Seven months ago, he underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for alcoholic cirrhosis. On examination, scleral icterus is noted. Laboratory studies reveal elevated ALT, AST, and bilirubin levels. Liver biopsy shows perivenular fibrosis, intimal inflammation, and loss of bile ducts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic transplant rejection

• Chronic transplant rejection in liver transplant patients is characterized by progressive bile duct loss (vanishing bile duct syndrome), perivenular fibrosis, and intimal inflammation.
• These histological findings, coupled with the timeline (several months post-transplant), elevated liver enzymes, and bilirubin, strongly point toward chronic rejection.

Other Options:

Option A. Graft-versus-host disease: This typically occurs in bone marrow or hematopoietic stem cell transplants rather than liver transplants. It is associated with skin, gut, and liver involvement but not bile duct loss.

Option C. Acute transplant rejection: Acute rejection usually occurs within the first 3 months post-transplant. It is characterized by mixed inflammatory infiltrate in the portal tracts and endothelial inflammation but not bile duct loss or fibrosis.

Option D. Recurrence of primary disease: Recurrence of alcoholic cirrhosis is unlikely within this short timeframe and does not typically result in the histological findings of bile duct loss or perivenular fibrosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presents with rectal bleeding, a change in bowel habits, and tenesmus for 6 months. Examination reveals a mass in the rectum 2 cm from the anal verge extending to the anal sphincters, and biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma. What surgical intervention is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abdominoperineal resection

The choice of surgery for rectal adenocarcinoma depends primarily on the distance from the anal verge and whether the anal sphincter complex can be preserved while achieving an adequate distal margin and oncologic clearance.

A tumor located very low in the rectum (2 cm from the anal verge) and extending to involve the anal sphincters is not amenable to sphincter-sparing surgery. In such cases, the appropriate curative operation is Abdominoperineal resection (APR)

This involves en bloc removal of: rectum, anal canal, sphincter complex followed by a permanent end colostomy.

Why other options are not appropriate:

A. Total mesorectal excision (TME) is a technique (part of oncologic rectal surgery) but does not specify the required operation when sphincters are involved; APR includes TME.

B. Low anterior resection (LAR) is used for upper/mid rectal tumors where sphincters can be preserved.

D. Hartmann’s procedure is typically for obstructed/perforated cases or high-risk patients; it is not the standard definitive surgery for a very low sphincter-involving tumor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52 year old patient with findings of hypercalcemia of 12.8 mg% and elevated PTH levels is found to have a 1.5 cm mass below the thyroid on USG neck. Which of the following investigations can be performed for the localisation and management of this condition? a. Unilateral focussed neck exploration. b. Sestamibi scan c. Casanova test d. Intra-operative measurement of serum PTH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A, B, D

Hypercalcemia (12.8 mg%) + ↑PTH → suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism

• USG shows a 1.5 cm mass below thyroid → likely parathyroid adenoma

The aim before surgery is to = localise the lesion.

Option a. Unilateral focused neck exploration

• it’s a minimally invasive surgical procedure where one side of the neck is explored to remove the adenoma
• Done AFTER localization of adenoma

Option b. Sestamibi scan

• Gold standard for localizing parathyroid adenoma
• Tc 99 sestamibi is taken up by thyroid and parathyroid gland
• Parathyroid adenomas have:

• High mitochondrial activity; More blood flow
• So on delayed imaging, when the radio tracer is washed out form normal tissue, adenoma still retains it.
• This bright appearing tissue gives apt localization of adenoma.

Option c. Casanova test

Not used for localization of parathyroid adenoma.

The test helps determine whether a recurrent high PTH level is “graft-dependent” (from the transplanted forearm tissue) or “neck-dependent” (remnant neck tissue)

• Ischemic Procedure: A blood pressure cuff is inflated to supra-systolic levels on the graft-bearing arm for 10–30 minutes

• Key Indicator: A decrease in systemic PTH levels by over 50% after 10 minutes of ischemia suggests a graft-dependent recurrence (positive Casanova test), while a drop of less than 20% indicates a neck-dependent recurrence

Option d. Intra-op assessment of serum PTH

• PTH has a short half-life (\~3–5 min)

o   A significant fall after excision (Miami criterion: >50% drop) confirms successful removal and avoids unnecessary bilateral exploration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old diabetic presents with fever, chills, tachycardia, and severe right flank pain. CT KUB shows a 7 mm distal ureteric stone causing hydronephrosis with perinephric fat stranding. Urine has pus cells. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: IV antibiotics and wait for 48 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Percutaneous nephrostomy

An obstructing ureteric stone with infection (fever, chills, tachycardia, pyuria, CT showing hydronephrosis + perinephric fat stranding) represents acute obstructive pyelonephritis / pyonephrosis, which is a urological emergency. In such cases, the most important next step is urgent decompression of the collecting system, because antibiotics alone cannot adequately sterilize an obstructed kidney. Therefore, immediate drainage is required via percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) (or ureteric stenting), followed by IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, with definitive stone removal planned later once sepsis resolves.

Do not perform ureteroscopy/stone extraction during active infection due to risk of precipitating severe sepsis. Conservative measures (tamsulosin/diuretics) or waiting with antibiotics alone are inappropriate when there is infected obstruction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old man is planned for elective low anterior resection for rectal cancer in a high-volume centre. The surgical resident is revising the key elements of ERAS for colorectal surgery. Which of the following statements regarding it is/are correct? 1. Patients are kept nil per oral from midnight, as prolonged fasting reduces aspiration risk. 2. Multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia with thoracic epidural is preferred over systemic opioids alone. 3. Routine nasogastric tubes and intra-peritoneal drains are avoided unless there is a specific indication. 4. Early oral feeding and ambulation within 24 hours after surgery are encouraged.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol in colorectal surgery.

• Avoid prolonged fasting:

Patients are not kept NPO from midnight; clear fluids are allowed up to 2 hours and solids up to 6 hours preoperatively.

Why prolonged fasting is avoided?

• because it causes dehydration , Increases insulin resistance , Delays recovery
• and,

Carbohydrate loading is encouraged-->helps maintain normal metabolism (overcomes stress induced insulin resistance).

and prevents the body from entering a catabolic (muscle-breaking) state during surgery.

• Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia:

Thoracic epidural analgesia, regional blocks, NSAIDs, and acetaminophen Preferred over opioid use.

Problems caused by opioids when used as analgesics

• Post-operative ileus

• Opioids reduce gastrointestinal motility, causing delayed bowel function.

• Respiratory depression

• Suppress respiratory center in the brain, leading to slow or shallow breathing.

• Nausea and vomiting

this reduces infection and post operative ileus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old man presents with dilated, tortuous veins over the medial aspect of his left leg. He complains of heaviness that worsens by evening and improves on limb elevation. On examination, there is hyperpigmentation around the medial malleolus. A bedside test is performed: the leg is elevated, a tourniquet is applied just below the saphenofemoral junction, and the patient is asked to stand. The veins remain collapsed initially but rapidly fill after the tourniquet is released. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Incompetent perforators are the primary pathology
Deep venous thrombosis is the underlying cause
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Saphenofemoral junction incompetence is present

Varicose veins are caused by valvular incompetence leading to venous reflux, most commonly at the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) in the great saphenous system.

Trendelenburg (Brodie–Trendelenburg) test helps localize the site of incompetence:

• Rapid filling before releasing tourniquet → incompetent perforators
• Rapid filling after releasing tourniquet → SFJ incompetence

Chronic venous insufficiency features:

• Medial malleolus involvement
• Hyperpigmentation (hemosiderin deposition)
• Edema, lipodermatosclerosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old man presents with fever, chills, dysuria, and perineal pain for 2 days. DRE reveals a warm, tender, and boggy prostate. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Prostate massage for prostatic secretion culture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start empiric fluoroquinolone therapy

Acute bacterial prostatitis presents with fever, dysuria, and a tender, warm, boggy prostate on DRE and requires immediate empiric antibiotic therapy.

Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (commonly fluoroquinolones or TMP-SMX) targeting gram-negative organisms:

• E. coli (most common)

• Klebsiella

• Proteus

Early treatment prevents complications such as:

• Prostatic abscess

• Sepsis

• Chronic prostatitis

Important precautions

• Avoid prostate massage → may cause bacteremia and septicemia

• Avoid transrectal biopsy in acute phase

• Foley catheterization only if urinary retention; suprapubic preferred if needed

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a palpable breast lump. Targeted breast ultrasound shows a hypoechoic lesion with angular margins and significant asymmetry compared with surrounding parenchyma. Which of the following ultrasound findings is NOT typically associated with malignant breast lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior acoustic enhancement

Malignant breast lesions on ultrasound typically show suspicious features such as:

• Irregular or angular margins

• Poorly circumscribed/spiculated borders

• Hypoechoic solid mass

• Architectural distortion and asymmetry

• Posterior acoustic shadowing (due to dense fibrous stroma)

Posterior acoustic enhancement is more commonly seen in benign lesions (e.g., cysts, fibroadenomas) because sound waves pass easily through fluid or uniform tissue, producing increased echoes behind the lesion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman is scheduled for elective colorectal surgery for carcinoma sigmoid colon. She is being optimized preoperatively as part of an Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol. Which of the following interventions is not recommended as part of the ERAS protocol?
options: Preoperative carbohydrate loading up to 2 hours before surgery
Routine use of nasogastric tube postoperatively
Early mobilization within 24 hours after surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Routine use of nasogastric tube postoperatively

ERAS protocol is an evidence-based perioperative care pathway aimed at:

• Reducing surgical stress

• Enhancing recovery

• Decreasing hospital stay and complications

Key components of ERAS:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman presents with a right breast lump measuring 3.6 cm. Clinical examination reveals multiple hard, fixed axillary lymph nodes on both sides. No skin ulceration or chest wall invasion is noted. What is the TNM staging of this breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T2N2M1

Breast cancer staging uses the TNM system, where T is based on tumor size/local invasion, N describes regional lymph node involvement, and M denotes distant metastasis.

A breast lump measuring 3.6 cm falls into T2 (tumor >2 cm but ≤5 cm) with no skin ulceration or chest wall invasion (so not T4). The presence of multiple hard fixed axillary lymph nodes suggests matted/fixed ipsilateral axillary nodes, corresponding to N2 disease. In addition, axillary lymph nodes on both sides (contralateral axillary nodes) are considered distant metastasis, not regional nodal disease; therefore, this is classified as M1. Hence, the correct staging is T2N2M1.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Ultrasound reveals gallstones with a dilated common bile duct measuring 11 mm. She is hemodynamically stable. MRCP is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with stone extraction followed by cholecystectomy
Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage as definitive treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with stone extraction followed by cholecystectomy

This patient has choledocholithiasis with features suggestive of ascending cholangitis (Charcot’s triad: pain, fever, jaundice).

Management principles:

• Priority is biliary decompression
• ERCP is the treatment of choice:

o    Allows visualization

o    Stone extraction

o    Sphincterotomy

• After stabilization → definitive surgery (cholecystectomy) to prevent recurrence

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Cholecystectomy alone does not address CBD stone

C. Percutaneous drainage is reserved when ERCP is not feasible

D. Antibiotics alone are insufficient without biliary drainage

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 53-year-old man with a midgut carcinoid and single large liver metastasis has uncontrolled symptoms despite maximal octreotide therapy. The metastatic lesion is not resectable. What is the next treatment option?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy

Midgut carcinoid tumors (well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors) often secrete serotonin and other vasoactive substances, producing carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm), which typically becomes clinically significant when there are liver metastases because hepatic first-pass metabolism is bypassed. Somatostatin analogs (octreotide/lanreotide) are first-line to control hormone-mediated symptoms and can also slow tumor progression.

In patients with unresectable metastatic neuroendocrine tumor who have persistent symptoms despite maximal octreotide, the next best treatment is Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) (e.g., ¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE). PRRT delivers targeted radiation to tumors that express somatostatin receptors, improving symptom control, reducing tumor burden, and prolonging progression-free survival.

Local liver-directed therapies like RFA are most useful for small/limited lesions and are not ideal for a single large unresectable metastasis; external beam radiation has limited benefit for diffuse liver disease and is mainly palliative for focal painful metastases. Conventional chemotherapy has limited effectiveness in well-differentiated midgut carcinoids and is not the preferred next step.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 54 year old diabetic man presents with acute onset left leg pain, numbness and weakness for 3 hours. Doppler shows absent dorsalis pedis flow but audible posterior tibial artery flow. Sensation is reduced over the toes, motor sensation is intact. Capillary refill is sluggish. Using Rutherford classification, the limb is what category?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Marginally threatened (category 2a)

Acute limb ischemia (ALI) is a vascular emergency defined by a sudden reduction in limb perfusion (typically <14 days) producing the classic 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia. Management urgency is guided by the Rutherford classification, which predicts limb viability based on sensory loss, motor deficit, and Doppler signals.

These findings correspond to Rutherford Category IIa (Marginally threatened):

• No motor deficit
• Minimal sensory loss (toes only)
• Arterial Doppler often inaudible at distal vessel, but venous Doppler remains audible (some flow preserved)

This category indicates the limb is salvageable with prompt intervention, but not immediately threatened like IIb.

Key distinctions:

• Category I (Viable): no sensory/motor deficit; both arterial and venous Doppler audible
• Category IIa (Marginally threatened): minimal sensory deficit (toes), no motor deficit
• Category IIb (Immediately threatened): more than toe sensory loss + motor weakness → needs urgent revascularization
• Category III (Irreversible): profound anesthesia + paralysis; limb non-salvageable

Therefore, this limb is Marginally threatened — Rutherford IIa (Option B).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 54-year-old male undergoes elective abdominal surgery for colon carcinoma. In the immediate postoperative period, he develops tachycardia and mild hyperglycemia. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated cortisol levels. Which of the following is NOT expected to increase as part of the acute surgical stress response?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Triiodothyronine (T3)

The acute surgical stress response is characterized by activation of the neuroendocrine and inflammatory pathways, leading to a catabolic, hypermetabolic state.

Hormonal and cytokine changes in surgical stress

Increase:

• ACTH → stimulates cortisol release

• Cortisol → gluconeogenesis, insulin resistance

• Growth hormone → protein catabolism, lipolysis

• Catecholamines → tachycardia, hyperglycemia

• Glucagon

• Pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6)

Decrease:

• Triiodothyronine (T3)

• Thyroxine (T4) may be normal/low

• Conversion of T4 → T3 reduced

Known as euthyroid sick syndrome (low T3 syndrome)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 54-year-old woman with symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism (serum calcium 11.8 mg/dL, elevated PTH) is planned for parathyroidectomy. Pre-operative localization studies are performed. Neck ultrasound suggests a left inferior parathyroid adenoma, whereas sestamibi scintigraphy localizes uptake to the right superior gland. The results are discordant. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Four-dimensional CT scan

When preoperative localization studies for primary hyperparathyroidism are discordant (USG vs sestamibi), the next best step is four-dimensional CT (4D-CT) for accurate localization.

• Successful minimally invasive parathyroidectomy depends on precise localization.

• If first-line imaging is discordant or negative:

o Perform 4D-CT → highest sensitivity for detecting ectopic or small adenomas.

• Provides:

o Anatomical detail

o Vascular perfusion pattern

o Delayed washout characteristics of adenoma

Management algorithm

1. Confirm biochemical hyperparathyroidism (↑Ca, ↑PTH)

2. Initial localization:

o Ultrasound

o Sestamibi scan

3. If concordant → minimally invasive surgery

4. If discordant/negative → 4D-CT

5. If still unclear → bilateral neck exploration

other options

• MRI: less sensitive than 4D-CT

• Immediate four-gland exploration: reserved when localization fails

• Minimally invasive surgery: requires concordant localization

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with intermittent upper GI bleeding associated with sudden epigastric pain. Endoscopy reveals blood emerging from the ampulla of Vater, but no mucosal lesion is seen in the stomach or duodenum. Which diagnosis best fits this picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hemosuccus pancreaticus

Hemosuccus pancreaticus is a rare cause of upper GI bleeding characterized by bleeding from the pancreatic duct into the duodenum via the ampulla of Vater.

• Intermittent upper GI bleeding

• Blood seen emerging from ampulla on endoscopy

• Associated with chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic pseudocyst

• Often accompanied by epigastric pain

Pathophysiology

• Chronic pancreatitis → pseudoaneurysm (usually splenic artery)

• Pseudoaneurysm ruptures into pancreatic duct

• Blood flows through pancreatic duct → ampulla → duodenum

Differentiation from other causes

• Hemobilia: bleeding from biliary tree → blood from ampulla but usually after trauma/procedure

• Dieulafoy lesion: gastric mucosal artery bleed

• Mallory-Weiss tear: mucosal tear at GE junction after vomiting

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of swelling and unusual heaviness of his scrotum that he first noticed a few weeks ago. The symptoms improve when he is lying in bed. He also reports a 5-kg weight loss and increasing fatigue over the past 6 months. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the past 15 years. Physical examination shows tenderness to palpation of his right flank. There are soft strands palpable in the right hemiscrotum superior of the right testis. The strands increase with Valsalva maneuver. Applying a bright light to the right hemiscrotum shows no transillumination. Obstruction of venous drainage into which of the following vessels is most likely responsible for this patient's scrotal enlargement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inferior vena cava

A scrotal swelling described as “soft strands/bag of worms” that increases with Valsalva, does not transilluminate, and improves on lying down is characteristic of a varicocele (dilated pampiniform plexus). Varicoceles are usually left-sided, but a new-onset right-sided varicocele, especially in an older man, is a red flag for secondary obstruction of venous drainage due to an intra-abdominal malignancy. This patient also has:

• Weight loss and fatigue
• Right flank tenderness
• Smoking history

→ strongly suggests renal cell carcinoma or retroperitoneal tumor causing venous obstruction.

• The right testicular (gonadal) vein drains directly into the IVC.
• So obstruction/compression of the inferior vena cava can back up blood into the right gonadal vein → dilated pampiniform plexus → right-sided varicocele. (whereas the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, explaining the higher incidence of left varicocele.)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old man undergoes a Whipple procedure for suspected pancreatic adenocarcinoma of the head of the pancreas. Prior to the procedure, the patient receives a dose of prophylactic antibiotics. Toward the end of the operation, he is given 2 units of packed red blood cells. The patient is then extubated and transferred to the postanesthesia care unit for recovery. One hour later, he develops fever and chills. Temperature is 38.5 C (101.3 F), blood pressure is 130/76 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 16/min. Examination shows a mildly tender abdominal wound without erythema. There is serosanguinous discharge from the pancreatic suction drain. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A Foley catheter and right subclavian central venous access are present, both placed at the time of surgery. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's fever?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Transfusion reaction

Fever and chills occurring within hours of blood transfusion in the immediate postoperative period are most commonly due to an acute transfusion reaction, especially a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction.

• Timing is crucial:

o Fever within 1–6 hours after transfusion → think transfusion reaction

o Surgical site or catheter infections usually occur after 24–48 hours

• Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction:

o Most common transfusion reaction

o Caused by recipient antibodies against donor leukocytes or cytokines in stored blood

o Presents with fever, chills, rigors shortly after transfusion

• Other causes less likely here:

o Surgical site infection → typically ≥48 hours

o Catheter infection → days later

o Drug fever → not immediately after single dose

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman is diagnosed with mid-rectal carcinoma on colonoscopy and biopsy. The surgeon wants to assess depth of invasion and relationship of tumor to the mesorectal fascia to plan total mesorectal excision (TME). Which is the investigation of choice?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. MRI pelvis

MRI pelvis is the investigation of choice for local staging of rectal carcinoma, especially to evaluate:

• Depth of tumor invasion (T stage)

• Circumferential resection margin (CRM)

• Relationship to mesorectal fascia

• Nodal involvement in mesorectum

• Planning for total mesorectal excision (TME) and neoadjuvant therapy

• Provides excellent soft-tissue resolution

• Accurately predicts CRM involvement, the most important predictor of local recurrence

• Helps decide neoadjuvant chemoradiation vs upfront surgery

Comparison with other modalities

• CT abdomen/pelvis: For distant metastasis staging, not local rectal staging

• Endorectal ultrasound: Good for early T staging (T1–T2) but limited for mesorectal fascia/CRM

• PET-CT: Used for metastatic or recurrent disease, not primary staging

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56 year old male labourer presents with long standing groin discomfort. On examination, a reducible swelling is noted medial to the inferior epigastric vessels and another reducible swelling is noted lateral to the same vessels on the same side. Ultrasound confirms two separate sacs straddling the inferior epigastric artery and a diagnosis of pantaloon hernia is made. What is the grading of this hernia according to the NYHUS classification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type IIIb

The Nyhus classification is an anatomic system used to categorize inguinal hernias based on the status of the internal ring and the presence/extent of posterior wall weakness, and it helps guide operative repair.

A pantaloon hernia refers to the coexistence of:

• a direct inguinal hernia (medial to inferior epigastric vessels), and
• an indirect inguinal hernia (lateral to inferior epigastric vessels)

with two separate sacs straddling the inferior epigastric vessels, resembling a “pantaloon.”

In the Nyhus classification:

• Type III = posterior wall defect (large hernias)

• IIIa = direct hernia
• IIIb = indirect hernia with posterior wall weakness (often large/scrotal) and includes combined/direct-indirect patterns such as pantaloon

• Type IV = recurrent hernia

Therefore, a pantaloon hernia is classified as Nyhus Type IIIb (Option C).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old woman comes to the OPD with skin lesions on her right arm that she noticed 3 weeks ago. She underwent a right mastectomy for advanced breast cancer 7 years ago and was treated with radiation and chemotherapy. Since her treatment, the patient has had swelling of the right arm. Her mother was recently diagnosed with shingles. Physical examination shows nonpitting edema of the right upper extremity. There are 3 firm purple papules on the inner surface of the right arm. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lesion biopsy

In patients with chronic lymphedema after breast cancer surgery, the appearance of new violaceous or firm nodular skin lesions should be considered malignant until proven otherwise, most commonly cutaneous angiosarcoma, and mandates prompt tissue diagnosis.

High-yield points

• Stewart–Treves syndrome = angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema

• Typically develops 5–10 years after mastectomy + axillary dissection/radiation

• Early lesions may resemble:

o Bruises

o Purple papules

o Small vascular nodules

easily misdiagnosed as infection or dermatitis

Management principle

• Any suspicious lesion in a lymphedematous limb → immediate biopsy

• Imaging alone is insufficient

• Early surgical/oncologic management improves survival

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old woman presents with weight loss, newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus and a painful erythematous rash over the perineum and lower abdomen. Over the last 3 months she has also developed low mood with anhedonia and has been treated for a left lower limb deep vein thrombosis. Investigations show fasting plasma glucose of 212 mg/dL and markedly elevated fasting plasma glucagon levels. Which of the following clinical features is classically included in the “4 Ds” of glucagonoma syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dermatitis

To recognize glucagonoma syndrome, a rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor characterized by the classic “4 Ds”:

1. Dermatitis – Necrolytic migratory erythema (NME)

o Painful erythematous rash in perineum, groin, lower abdomen, and extremities

o Most characteristic and diagnostic feature

2. Diabetes mellitus

o Due to excess glucagon causing hyperglycemia

3. Depression

o Neuropsychiatric symptoms including depression, lethargy

4. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)

o Hypercoagulable state commonly seen

Key clinical triad to remember

• Weight loss

• New-onset diabetes

• Necrolytic migratory erythema

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 57-year-old white man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance because of sudden-onset, bright red emesis. His blood pressure is 80/40 mmHg and heart rate is 124/min. Physical examination is notable for jaundice and an enlarged abdomen that is dull to percussion and positive for a fluid wave. Which of the following vessel anastomoses is responsible for the patient’s bleeding?
options: Left gastric vein and azygos vein
Paraumbilical vein and inferior epigastric vein
Portal vein and inferior vena cava
Splenic vein and left renal vein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left gastric vein and azygos vein

Massive bright red hematemesis with hypotension in a patient with signs of chronic liver disease and portal hypertension (jaundice, ascites with fluid wave) is most consistent with bleeding esophageal varices. Varices form when elevated portal venous pressure diverts blood through portosystemic (portal–systemic) anastomoses, leading to dilation of submucosal veins that can rupture and cause life-threatening hemorrhage. The most clinically important portosystemic anastomosis causing esophageal varices is:

• Portal side: Left gastric vein (coronary vein)
• Systemic side: Esophageal veins draining into the azygos system

Thus, bleeding occurs due to anastomosis between the left gastric vein and the azygos vein. Other portal-systemic sites:

• Paraumbilical vein ↔ superficial epigastric veins → caput medusae
• Superior rectal vein ↔ middle/inferior rectal veins → hemorrhoids
• Retroperitoneal venous collaterals

Therefore, the vessel anastomosis responsible is Left gastric vein and azygos vein (Option A).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old diabetic patient presents with a chronic heel ulcer containing necrotic slough. The surgeon plans biological debridement using sterile maggots. Which organism is commonly used for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lucilia sericata

• Chronic diabetic foot ulcers often contain necrotic slough and devitalized tissue, which delays healing and promotes infection.
• When surgical/sharp debridement is difficult or risky, biological debridement (maggot therapy) is an effective alternative.
• It uses sterile larvae that selectively digest necrotic tissue while sparing viable tissue.
• The organism most commonly used is the green bottle blowfly, Lucilia sericata.

Its larvae aid wound healing by:

• Proteolytic enzymes that liquefy necrotic tissue (selective debridement)
• Antibacterial action (secretions inhibit bacterial growth and disrupt biofilms)
• Reducing wound odor and bacterial burden
• Stimulating granulation tissue formation

Thus, sterile larvae of Lucilia sericata are the standard organism for medical maggot debridement therapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old female has Bismuth Type IIIa Klatskin tumor. What is the preferred surgical procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right hepatectomy + caudate lobe resection

Klatskin tumor refers to perihilar cholangiocarcinoma arising at the hepatic duct confluence. Surgical planning is guided by the Bismuth–Corlette classification, which describes the longitudinal extent of biliary duct involvement and determines which hepatic resection is needed for an R0 (margin-negative) resection.

In Bismuth Type IIIa, the tumor involves:

• the common hepatic duct and confluence, and
• extends into the right hepatic duct (right secondary biliary radicals), while the left duct is relatively spared.

Therefore, the preferred curative operation is Right hepatectomy + caudate lobe resection with en bloc bile duct excision and biliary reconstruction.

The caudate lobe (segment I) drains directly into the hilar bile ducts and is frequently involved early in perihilar cholangiocarcinoma; removing it improves chances of complete clearance.

Other options are incorrect because:

• Left hepatectomy is preferred for Type IIIb (left duct involvement).
• Whipple’s procedure is for distal bile duct/pancreatic head tumors, not perihilar tumors.
• Simple bile duct excision has high positive-margin rates and is inadequate for Type III lesions.

Thus, Type IIIa Klatskin tumor → Right hepatectomy + caudate lobe resection (Option B).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old male presents with hematemesis and melena. Emergency upper GI endoscopy reveals a bleeding gastric ulcer with a visible vessel but no active bleeding. According to the Forrest classification, what is the ulcer’s grade and the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Forrest IIa ; endoscopic treatment recommended

Forrest classification guides risk of rebleeding and need for endoscopic therapy in peptic ulcer bleeding.

• Forrest IIa = visible non-bleeding vessel → high risk of rebleeding (≈40–50%)

• Requires urgent endoscopic hemostatic therapy (injection + thermal/coagulation/clips) even if active bleeding is absent.

Forrest classification summary:

• Ia: Spurting bleeding → emergency endoscopic therapy

• Ib: Oozing bleeding → endoscopic therapy

• IIa: Visible vessel → endoscopic therapy recommended

• IIb: Adherent clot → remove clot + treat

• IIc: Flat pigmented spot → PPI, no endoscopic therapy

• III: Clean base → low risk, conservative management

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department with suspected sepsis. The junior resident calculates a NEWS score to assess the severity of illness and guide escalation of care. When asked during rounds, the resident incorrectly expands the acronym “NEWS.” Which of the following is the correct full form of NEWS in this context?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. National Early Warning Score

• NEWS = National Early Warning Score
• Updated version: NEWS2 (National Early Warning Score 2)

It is a standardized scoring system developed by the Royal College of physicians to:

• Detect early clinical deterioration
• Trigger timely escalation of care
• Improve patient outcomes in acute settings

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with hematemesis and melena. He is tachycardic but normotensive. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin of 8.7 g/dL. After resuscitation with IV crystalloids, high-dose proton pump inhibitor infusion is started. Upper GI endoscopy reveals a bleeding duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Endoscopic combination therapy with epinephrine injection and thermal coagulation
Continue PPI infusion alone and observe
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endoscopic combination therapy with epinephrine injection and thermal coagulation

A bleeding peptic ulcer with a visible vessel (Forrest IIa) carries a high risk of rebleeding and requires urgent endoscopic hemostatic therapy, even if active bleeding is not seen.

Standard management sequence in upper GI bleed

1. Hemodynamic stabilization (IV fluids, blood if needed)
2. High-dose IV PPI infusion
3. Urgent endoscopic therapy for high-risk lesions

High-risk endoscopic stigmata requiring therapy

• Active spurting/oozing bleeding (Forrest Ia/Ib)
• Visible vessel (Forrest IIa)
• Adherent clot (IIb, after clot removal)

Combination therapy is superior to monotherapy:

• Epinephrine injection (vasoconstriction + tamponade)
• Thermal coagulation or hemoclips → definitive hemostasis

This reduces rebleeding, need for surgery, and mortality.

Other Options

• PPI alone → insufficient for visible vessel
• Surgery → reserved for failed endoscopic therapy
• TAE → for persistent/recurrent bleeding after endoscopy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive post-prandial abdominal pain for 3 months. The pain begins 20–30 minutes after meals, lasts 1–2 hours, and forces him to avoid eating. He reports significant weight loss, early satiety, and fear of eating (“food fear”). He is a long-standing diabetic, hypertensive, and smokes 20 cigarettes/day. Abdominal exam is normal except for a faint epigastric bruit. Routine labs and endoscopy done previously were normal. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT angiography of abdominal vessels

Progressive post-prandial abdominal pain (intestinal angina) beginning 20–30 minutes after meals, lasting 1–2 hours, associated with food fear and significant weight loss in an older patient with major atherosclerotic risk factors (smoking, diabetes, hypertension) is classic for chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) due to atherosclerotic stenosis/occlusion of mesenteric arteries (most commonly SMA ± celiac). A faint epigastric bruit further supports vascular disease. Because endoscopy and routine labs are often normal in CMI, diagnosis requires vascular imaging.

The most appropriate confirmatory investigation is CT angiography (CTA) of abdominal vessels, as it provides rapid, high-resolution visualization of the celiac, SMA, and IMA, identifies the site and severity of stenosis, evaluates collateral flow, and simultaneously aids planning for revascularization (endovascular stenting or bypass). Duplex mesenteric Doppler can be used as a screening test but is operator dependent and limited in obese/bowel gas; CTA is the preferred confirmatory test in most patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with weight loss and intermittent hematuria. CT abdomen shows a 6.2 cm enhancing upper-pole renal mass, confined to the kidney, with tumor thrombus extending into the renal vein but not into the IVC. No lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis is seen. Renal function is normal. Biopsy shows clear cell RCC with VHL gene inactivation. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Radical nephrectomy with renal vein thrombectomy
Targeted therapy with sunitinib followed by surgery
Immunotherapy with nivolumab + ipilimumab as first line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Radical nephrectomy with renal vein thrombectomy

Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) commonly arises due to VHL gene inactivation, leading to increased HIF activity and overexpression of pro-angiogenic factors (e.g., VEGF), which explains the typical enhancing renal mass on CT. Management of RCC is primarily surgical when disease is localized.

A renal mass measuring 6.2 cm confined to the kidney corresponds to T1b, but the presence of tumor thrombus in the renal vein upstages the tumor to T3a, even without IVC extension. In patients with localized RCC with renal vein tumor thrombus and no metastasis, the recommended definitive treatment is radical nephrectomy with renal vein thrombectomy, because complete surgical resection offers the best chance of cure and prevents progression/embolization of thrombus.

Partial nephrectomy is preferred for small localized tumors (especially ≤4 cm or selected T1b) when feasible, but is generally not appropriate for T3 disease with venous thrombus. Targeted therapy (e.g., sunitinib) and immunotherapy (nivolumab + ipilimumab) are primarily used in metastatic or unresectable advanced RCC, not as first-line treatment for resectable localized RCC with venous involvement. Therefore, the most appropriate management is radical nephrectomy with renal vein thrombectomy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with Child–Pugh A cirrhosis is being evaluated for right hepatectomy for hepatocellular carcinoma. As part of preoperative assessment, an Indocyanine Green (ICG) retention test at 15 minutes (ICG-R15) is performed and found to be significantly elevated. Which of the following best explains what this test is assessing?
options: Hepatic arterial perfusion to the tumor-bearing segment
Overall functional capacity of hepatocytes and hepatic reserve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Overall functional capacity of hepatocytes and hepatic reserve

Indocyanine Green (ICG) clearance test is a dynamic assessment of functional hepatic reserve, widely used in preoperative evaluation before liver resection.

• ICG is:

• Taken up exclusively by hepatocytes
• Not metabolized
• Excreted unchanged into bile

• Therefore, its clearance depends on:

• Hepatocellular function
• Effective hepatic blood flow

Clinical Significance:

• Impaired ICG clearance → reduced functional liver reserve
• Predicts risk of post-hepatectomy liver failure (PHLF)
• Helps determine extent of safe liver resection

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with long-standing diabetes mellitus presents with a non-healing ulcer over the plantar aspect of the foot. Peripheral pulses are palpable. Ankle–brachial index (ABI) is reported as 1.3. However, ischemia is still suspected. Toe pressure is measured as 30 mmHg, and brachial systolic pressure is 120 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: ABI is reliable and rules out peripheral arterial disease
TBI is normal, indicating adequate perfusion
Medial arterial calcification is likely causing falsely elevated ABI
Toe pressure is unreliable due to small vessel size
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial arterial calcification is likely causing falsely elevated ABI

In diabetic patients, peripheral arteries (especially tibial vessels) often develop medial arterial calcification (Monckeberg sclerosis), making them non-compressible.

• This leads to a falsely elevated ABI (>1.3) → ABI becomes unreliable
• Despite “normal/high” ABI, true ischemia may still be present

Role of Toe–Brachial Index (TBI):

• Toe vessels are less affected by calcification → more reliable
• TBI = Toe pressure / Brachial pressure = 30 / 120 = 0.25

• <0.7 = abnormal
• <0.4 = severe ischemia

• Toe pressure <30 mmHg → poor wound healing

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old metal factory worker presents with lower urinary tract symptoms and is found to have an elevated PSA. Core biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma of the prostate. Occupational history reveals long-term exposure to heavy metals used in battery manufacturing. Which environmental exposure has been linked to an increased risk of prostate cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cadmium

Cadmium exposure is an established environmental and occupational risk factor associated with an increased risk of prostate carcinoma.

• Chronic exposure occurs in:

o Battery manufacturing

o Metal smelting

o Electroplating

o Cigarette smoke (major source)

Mechanism

• Cadmium acts as a metalloestrogen and carcinogen

• Induces oxidative stress and DNA damage

• Accumulates in prostate tissue → promotes malignant transformation

Other risk factors for prostate cancer

• Increasing age (most important)

• Family history (BRCA2)

• African ancestry

• High-fat diet

• Androgen exposure

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old woman with BMI 42, uncontrolled hypertension, and a history of two previous midline laparotomies (for bowel obstruction and hysterectomy) is posted for laparoscopic ventral hernia repair. The surgeon decides to insert the Veress needle at Palmer’s point. During insertion, the surgeon feels only one click, and on connecting the insufflator, the pressure initially rises to 17 mmHg, then slowly falls to 12 mmHg but does not drop further. There is minimal abdominal expansion, and the saline drop test shows intermittent bubbling, not free fall. A small amount of bloody fluid is aspirated from the needle. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue insufflation as the needle is likely intraperitoneal
Advance the Veress needle further until pressure drops
Stop the attempt and switch to open (Hasson) technique
Withdraw the needle and attempt insertion at the umbilicus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stop the attempt and switch to open (Hasson) technique

Safe creation of pneumoperitoneum is the critical first step in laparoscopy. Correct Veress needle placement in the peritoneal cavity is suggested by two distinct “clicks” (fascia then peritoneum), low initial insufflation pressure (<10 mmHg) with free flow of gas, good abdominal distension, and a positive saline drop test (free fall without bubbling).

In this obese patient with multiple previous midline laparotomies, the risk of intra-abdominal adhesions and visceral/vascular injury is high, even when using an alternative entry site like Palmer’s point. In this case, multiple findings indicate incorrect/unsafe placement and possible injury: only one click, high opening pressure (17 mmHg) that fails to fall below 12, minimal abdominal expansion, intermittent bubbling on saline drop test, and bloody aspirate (suggesting preperitoneal placement or vascular/visceral trauma).

Therefore, the safest and most appropriate next step is to abort the Veress attempt and switch to an open (Hasson) technique to obtain direct visual entry and reduce the risk of further injury. Continuing insufflation or advancing the needle risks worsening extraperitoneal insufflation or penetrating bowel/major vessels and attempting umbilical entry is unsafe due to likely adhesions from prior surgeries.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60 year old male with history of long standing goitre visits the OPD. Surgeon performs this manoeuver- which makes the patient breathless. This finding implies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Post operative airway risk

The maneuver shown (lateral compression of thyroid swelling producing breathlessness) indicates tracheal compression by long-standing goitre, suggesting risk of postoperative airway collapse (tracheomalacia).

Chronic large goitres compress and soften the tracheal cartilages over time → after thyroidectomy, removal of external support can lead to tracheal collapse and airway obstruction.

Clinical significance:

• Breathlessness on compression → significant tracheal narrowing

• Indicates postoperative airway risk

• May require delayed extubation or elective tracheostomy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man comes to the office due to pain, redness, and swelling in his right arm. The patient was recently diagnosed with unresectable lung cancer. He received the first cycle of chemotherapy 2 weeks ago through a right-sided peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, pulse is 78/min, and respirations are 14/min. Oxygen saturation is normal. Examination shows right arm swelling and mild erythema. Capillary refill is normal. No discharge is seen around the PICC line. The remainder of the examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Duplex ultrasonography

Patients with cancer who have an indwelling central venous catheter (eg, PICC line) are at high risk for upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis (UEDVT) due to malignancy-associated hypercoagulability and catheter-related venous endothelial injury. UEDVT typically presents with unilateral arm swelling, pain, and mild erythema, often without fever or discharge at the catheter site.

→ Most concerning diagnosis is catheter-associated UEDVT.

The most appropriate next step is Duplex ultrasonography, which is the first-line diagnostic test for suspected UEDVT because it is noninvasive and can identify venous thrombosis (noncompressibility, absent flow).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with painless jaundice and a dilated common bile duct on ultrasound. MRCP shows a stricture in the distal common bile duct suspicious for dysplastic changes. To obtain a tissue diagnosis and relieve obstruction, which procedure is most appropriate?
options: Diagnostic laparoscopy with biliary brush cytology
ERCP with biliary stenting and brush cytology
