Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC) with aspiration cytology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ERCP with biliary stenting and brush cytology

In patients with obstructive painless jaundice and distal common bile duct (CBD) stricture, the best initial procedure is ERCP with brush cytology and biliary stenting.

• Provides tissue diagnosis via brush cytology/biopsy.

• Allows simultaneous therapeutic decompression with biliary stent placement.

• Best for distal CBD obstruction (e.g., pancreatic head cancer, cholangiocarcinoma).

Other options:

• PTC → used when ERCP fails or for proximal/hilar obstruction.

• UGIE → cannot evaluate biliary tree.

• Diagnostic laparoscopy → staging tool, not first-line for diagnosis/relief.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man undergoes resection for sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma. Histology shows tumor extending through the serosa but with no regional lymph node metastases. According to Dukes classification for colorectal carcinoma, which stage and approximate 5-year survival best correspond to this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dukes B2, 5-year survival 75 %

The Dukes classification of colorectal carcinoma correlates tumor depth and nodal involvement with prognosis.

Dukes staging overview

• Dukes A: Tumor confined to mucosa/submucosa → 5-year survival \~90–95%

• Dukes B: Tumor extends through bowel wall but no lymph node metastasis

o B1: Extends into muscularis propria

o B2: Penetrates through serosa or beyond → 5-year survival \~70–75%

• Dukes C: Any depth with regional lymph node involvement → survival \~40–65%

• Dukes D: Distant metastasis → poor prognosis

Key concept in this question

Tumor extends through serosa but no nodal metastasis

→ corresponds to Dukes B2

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with weakness, regurgitation and weight loss was diagnosed with gastric carcinoma. Which of the following findings is incorrect?
options: Sister Mary Jaseph nodules: Paraumbilical nodules
Virchow lymph nodes: Left supraclavicular lymph nodes
Troisier's sign: Left axillary lymph nodes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Troisier's sign: Left axillary lymph nodes

A.    Sister Mary Joseph nodule → Paraumbilical metastasis

B.    Virchow node → Left supraclavicular node

C.    Troisier’s sign → actually refers to palpable Virchow node (left supraclavicular) (not axillary)

D.    Pyloric tumor → causes gastric outlet obstruction → non-bilious vomiting

Key concept:

Troisier’s sign = enlarged, hard left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) due to abdominal malignancy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 61-year-old man with distal esophageal adenocarcinoma located 5 cm above the gastroesophageal junction is scheduled for curative resection. The surgical team plans an esophagectomy with a right thoracotomy and laparotomy, followed by intrathoracic anastomosis. Which of the following operative approaches is being described?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ivor-Lewis esophagectomy

Ivor–Lewis esophagectomy is the preferred surgical approach for distal and mid-esophageal cancers, especially adenocarcinoma near the gastroesophageal junction.

Key components of Ivor–Lewis procedure

• Two-incision approach:

o Laparotomy (abdominal phase)

o Right thoracotomy (thoracic phase)

• Gastric mobilization and creation of gastric conduit

• Intrathoracic esophagogastric anastomosis

Indications

• Distal esophageal carcinoma

• Gastroesophageal junction tumors

• Good oncologic exposure with mediastinal lymphadenectomy

Comparison with other approaches

• Transhiatal esophagectomy (THE): abdominal + cervical incision, no thoracotomy, cervical anastomosis

• McKeown (three-stage): laparotomy + right thoracotomy + cervical incision, cervical anastomosis

• Left thoracoabdominal: older approach for distal tumors

Advantages of Ivor–Lewis

• Better visualization of thoracic esophagus

• Adequate lymph node clearance

• Lower cervical anastomotic leak risk than McKeown

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62 year old man with moderate COPD and hypertension is undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. After creation of pneumoperitoneum with CO2 at an intra-abdominal pressure of 15 mmHg, the following findings are noted: - Sudden rise in EtCO2 from 34 to 54mmHg - Increase in peak airway pressure - HR- 50 bpm Which of the following scenarios can explain these findings?
options: CO2 embolism leading to acute right heart obstruction.
Vagal mediated JT reflex due to peritoneal stretch.
Absorption of CO2 from peritoneum causing hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis.
Decreased venous return due to high IAP causing obstructive shock.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Absorption of CO2 from peritoneum causing hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis.

Creation of CO₂ pneumoperitoneum during laparoscopy increases intra-abdominal pressure and exposes the peritoneum to a highly diffusible gas. CO₂ is rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream, especially at higher pressures (e.g., IAP 15 mmHg), leading to hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis unless ventilation is increased. The most characteristic physiologic response to increased CO₂ absorption is:

• Rise in EtCO₂ (as seen from 34 → 54 mmHg)
• Increased airway pressures due to diaphragmatic splinting and reduced lung compliance from pneumoperitoneum

The accompanying bradycardia can occur with acute hypercarbia/acidosis or may coexist with peritoneal stretch reflexes, but the key unifying finding here is the marked rise in EtCO₂, which is best explained by CO₂ absorption from the peritoneum.

This differs from:

• CO₂ embolism → typically causes a sudden fall in EtCO₂ (due to increased dead space) with cardiovascular collapse.
• Vagal stretch reflex → causes bradycardia but does not explain a significant EtCO₂ rise.
• Reduced venous return from high IAP → hypotension/tachycardia; not primarily a large EtCO₂ rise.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62-year-old diabetic patient has an ABI of 1.4. Which of the following is the best next investigation to assess peripheral arterial disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Toe-brachial index (TBI)

ABI is calculated as: ABI = Ankle systolic pressure / Brachial systolic pressure

Normally:

• 0.9–1.3 = normal
• <0.9 = PAD
• >1.3 = non-compressible artery

In diabetes (and elderly/CKD), arteries of the leg often become stiff and calcified, so when the cuff inflates it cannot compress the artery properly. This causes:

• Falsely high ankle systolic pressure
• Falsely high ABI (e.g., 1.4)

So the ABI becomes invalid for assessing PAD severity.

Best next investigation: Toe-brachial index (TBI) because:

• Toe arteries are smaller and are much less affected by medial calcification
• Hence, toe pressure measurements remain compressible and reliable
• Therefore, TBI is the preferred test when ABI is >1.3

Interpretation (useful exam values):

• TBI > 0.7: normal
• TBI 0.4–0.7: PAD
• TBI < 0.4: severe ischemia

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with a history of jaundice that fluctuates over time. His jaundice intermittently worsens and then improves, without significant changes in his symptoms otherwise. He has no history of recent infections but reports occasional mild abdominal discomfort. MRCP is shown below. What is the most likely cause of this waxing and waning jaundice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Periampullary carcinoma

Fluctuating (waxing and waning) obstructive jaundice is classically associated with periampullary tumors. Periampullary carcinoma Causes intermittent obstruction (unlike pancreatic head cancer → progressive painless jaundice)

• Mechanism:

• Tumor near the ampulla of Vater intermittently obstructs bile flow
• Partial/variable obstruction → jaundice improves and worsens over time

• MRCP finding (concept):

• Dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts
• Obstruction at distal CBD/ampullary region

• Differentiation:

• CBD stones → colicky pain, more acute episodes
• Stricture → persistent, not fluctuating
• Parasites → rare, episodic but different imaging features

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with hematuria and flank pain. Contrast-enhanced CT shows a 9 cm renal mass confined within Gerota’s fascia. The tumor extends into the renal vein and further into the inferior vena cava below the diaphragm. There is no lymph node enlargement or distant metastasis. According to the TNM staging system, what is the stage of this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. T3b N0 M0

RCC staging is based on tumor size and extent of spread:

• T1: ≤7 cm, confined to kidney
• T2: >7 cm, confined to kidney
• T3: Tumor extends into major veins or perinephric tissues but not beyond Gerota’s fascia

o    T3a: Involves renal vein or perinephric fat

o    T3b: Extends into inferior vena cava below diaphragm

o    T3c: Extends into inferior vena cava above diaphragm or invades its wall

• T4: Tumor invades beyond Gerota’s fascia

In this case:

• Tumor extends into IVC below diaphragm → T3b
• No nodes (N0), no metastasis (M0)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 63-year-old thin elderly woman presents with intermittent episodes of small bowel obstruction. She has no visible abdominal or groin swelling. On examination, there is mild abdominal distension. Deep palpation over the medial thigh elicits pain radiating to the knee. Peripheral pulses are normal. During one episode, exploratory imaging reveals a hernia sac protruding through a defect in the pelvic wall, lying inferior to the superior pubic ramus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Obturator hernia

Obturator hernia is an occult pelvic hernia that commonly presents as recurrent small bowel obstruction without a visible swelling, especially in elderly, thin women.

• Hernia passes through the obturator canal
• Howship–Romberg sign: pain along medial thigh due to obturator nerve compression
• Often missed clinically → diagnosis usually by imaging or during surgery
• Has a high risk of strangulation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old female patient comes to the clinic with a history of rapidly enlarging swelling in her right breast for the last 15 days. During the physical examination, there was a local rise in temperature, and the lump was partially mobile over the chest wall. What could be the probable diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inflammatory carcinoma

A rapidly enlarging breast swelling in an elderly woman with local warmth (raised temperature) strongly suggests inflammatory breast carcinoma, an aggressive form of invasive breast cancer caused by tumor emboli obstructing dermal lymphatics. This lymphatic blockage produces acute inflammatory signs that mimic mastitis, but unlike infection it occurs in non-lactating older women and progresses rapidly.

Key features of inflammatory carcinoma:

• Rapid enlargement of breast over days–weeks
• Warmth, erythema, edema
• Peau d’orange appearance may develop
• Often no discrete well-circumscribed lump
• High likelihood of early nodal/distant spread → poor prognosis

Why other options are less likely:

B. Giant fibroadenoma: occurs in adolescents/young women, not 65-year-old.

C. Phyllodes tumor: rapid growth but typically a well-circumscribed, large, firm mass without marked warmth/skin inflammatory changes.

D. Galactocele: occurs during/after lactation, cystic and not associated with inflammatory signs in elderly.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to nausea, vomiting, and increasing abdominal pain over the last 3 hours. Four weeks ago he was discharged from the hospital following an inpatient admission for acute myocardial infarction. His other medical problems include type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and peptic ulcer disease. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg, pulse is 110/min and irregular, and respirations are 22/min. The patient appears to be in severe distress due to pain. There is diffuse abdominal tenderness, but it is more pronounced over the lower right quadrant. Liver function studies: Amylase: 275 U/L Lipase: 80 U/L (normal, 0-160 U/L) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bowel ischemia

Acute mesenteric (bowel) ischemia is a life-threatening abdominal emergency caused by sudden reduction in intestinal blood flow, most commonly due to arterial embolism. The classic high-risk patient is an elderly individual with cardiovascular disease and atrial fibrillation. In this case, the patient has several strong clues for bowel ischemia:

• Recent myocardial infarction (4 weeks ago) → predisposes to mural thrombus and embolization
• Irregular tachycardia → suggests atrial fibrillation, a major cause of arterial emboli
• Severe abdominal pain with distress
• Exam shows tenderness but the key concept is “pain out of proportion to physical findings” (early ischemia may have minimal peritoneal signs)
• Mild fever and tachycardia support systemic inflammatory response

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man undergoes elective anterior resection for rectal carcinoma. On postoperative day 4, he develops tachycardia, low-grade fever, and mild abdominal discomfort. There is no obvious peritonitis. Drain output is minimal. CRP is elevated. What is the most sensitive early investigation to detect the likely complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Contrast-enhanced CT with rectal contrast

Postoperative anastomotic leak is a life-threatening complication that often presents with subtle early signs, the most sensitive being tachycardia, followed by low-grade fever and raised inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP), even before overt peritonitis develops.

• Contrast-enhanced CT with rectal (or oral) contrast is the most sensitive early investigation

o    Detects contrast extravasation, perianastomotic collections, and air-fluid levels

• Plain X-ray and ultrasound have low sensitivity in early stages
• Diagnostic laparoscopy is invasive and reserved when imaging is inconclusive but suspicion remains high

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to a 5-day history of left lower abdominal pain, nausea, and poor appetite. Although she has a history of chronic constipation, she has been having 2–3 loose, nonbloody bowel movements daily. History is notable for hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy 15 years ago. Rectal and pelvic examinations elicit exquisite left-sided tenderness. Stool testing for occult blood is negative. Laboratory results include a white blood cell count of 16,500/mm³. Which of the following is the best next step in diagnosis?
options: Stool PCR testing for Clostridioides difficile
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT scan of the abdomen

Older patients presenting with acute left lower quadrant (LLQ) abdominal pain, leukocytosis, nausea/anorexia, and localized tenderness are most suspicious for acute diverticulitis, even if they report loose stools (diarrhea can occur due to colonic irritation around an inflamed diverticulum). A history of chronic constipation is a common predisposing factor. The presence of exquisite LLQ tenderness and elevated WBC count supports an intra-abdominal inflammatory process rather than infectious diarrhea.

The best next diagnostic step in suspected acute diverticulitis is a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast, because it:

• Confirms the diagnosis (colonic wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding)
• Detects complications: abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction
• Helps guide management (antibiotics vs drainage vs surgery)

Endoscopy (flexible sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy) is avoided in the acute setting due to risk of perforation and is performed later (after resolution) if needed to rule out malignancy. Stool cultures and C. difficile testing are appropriate when infectious diarrhea predominates, but here the clinical picture is primarily localized LLQ abdominal pain with systemic inflammation, favoring diverticulitis. Therefore, the next best diagnostic step is CT abdomen (Option A).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 66-year-old man presents with lower limb pain on walking. He describes three different patterns over time: • Initially, he noticed pain in his calves after walking a fixed distance, which was relieved within minutes of stopping. • Later, he developed pain that worsens on standing and walking downhill, but improves when he leans forward or sits. • More recently, he complains of knee pain with stiffness lasting <30 minutes in the morning, along with crepitus on movement. On examination: • Peripheral pulses are reduced in one condition but normal in the others. • Neurological examination is normal except for mild sensory symptoms in one condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: All three patterns represent progression of a single vascular disease
First = neurogenic claudication, second = intermittent claudication, third = osteoarthritis
First = intermittent claudication, second = neurogenic claudication, third = osteoarthritis
First = osteoarthritis, second = intermittent claudication, third = neurogenic claudication
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. First = intermittent claudication, second = neurogenic claudication, third = osteoarthritis

Lower limb pain on walking is best differentiated by pattern of pain, relieving factors, and associated findings:

Intermittent claudication (vascular):

• Pain after a fixed walking distance
• Relieved by rest (standing still)
• Diminished peripheral pulses
• Due to muscle ischemia

Neurogenic claudication (lumbar canal stenosis):

• Posture-dependent pain
• Worse on extension (walking downhill/standing)
• Relieved by flexion (sitting, leaning forward, cycling)
• Pulses normal, may have sensory symptoms

Osteoarthritis:

• Localized joint pain (commonly knee)
• Worse with activity, relieved by rest
• Crepitus + short morning stiffness (<30 min)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 67-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to abdominal discomfort and distension. Five days ago, he began having large-volume watery stools 6-8 times daily after eating at a new restaurant. He self-treated with increased oral fluids and the stool frequency and consistency began to improve. However, his bowel movements abruptly stopped yesterday, and the diffuse abdominal discomfort and distension worsened. The abdomen is distended, tympanic, and mildly tender to palpation with no guarding or rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are decreased. Abdominal CT scan shows diffuse colonic dilation with nondilated small bowels. Which of the following most likely contributed to this patient's current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Electrolyte abnormality

This patient’s presentation is classic for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome), characterized by massive colonic dilation without a mechanical obstruction.

Ogilvie syndrome occurs due to autonomic dysfunction of colonic motility (↓ parasympathetic / ↑ sympathetic tone), leading to impaired colonic peristalsis and progressive dilation.

A major precipitating factor is electrolyte abnormalities, especially after diarrheal illness:

• Hypokalemia
• Hypomagnesemia
• Hypocalcemia

These electrolytes are essential for normal smooth muscle contraction and intestinal motility, so their depletion can trigger colonic pseudo-obstruction.

Why other options are incorrect

A. Adhesions → usually cause small bowel obstruction, not isolated colon dilation.

B. Colonic hypoperfusion → causes ischemic colitis (bloody diarrhea, pain).

C. Colonic mass → causes true mechanical large bowel obstruction with a transition point, not diffuse dilation without small bowel dilation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 67-year-old man with a history of chronic skin infections presents with fever, severe back pain, and malaise. CT angiography of the abdomen reveals an irregularly shaped, saccular aneurysm involving the infrarenal abdominal aorta with surrounding inflammatory changes. Which of the following best describes this condition?
options: Inflammatory aneurysm secondary to autoimmune vasculitis
Mycotic aneurysm caused by bacterial infection of the aortic wall
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mycotic aneurysm caused by bacterial infection of the aortic wall

A mycotic aneurysm is an infected arterial aneurysm caused by bacterial invasion of the arterial wall, most commonly due to bacteremia or septic emboli.

• Fever and systemic toxicity

• Severe localized pain (e.g., back or abdominal pain)

• History of infection (skin infections, endocarditis, bacteremia)

• Rapidly enlarging or tender aneurysm

Imaging findings

• Saccular, irregular aneurysm

• Peri-aneurysmal inflammation or soft tissue stranding

• Rapid progression on imaging

• Often involves abdominal aorta (especially infrarenal)

Common causative organisms

• Staphylococcus aureus (most common)

• Salmonella species

• Streptococci

Management

• Urgent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics

• Surgical excision or endovascular repair

• High risk of rupture → emergency condition

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 68-year-old woman is found to have a cystic lesion in the head of pancreas. CT shows a microcystic lesion with central stellate scar and central calcification. Cyst fluid has low CEA and low amylase. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serous cystadenoma

The combination of a microcystic “honeycomb” mass in the pancreatic head, a central stellate scar with central calcification, and cyst fluid with low CEA and low amylase is classic for serous cystadenoma (SCN). SCNs are benign, often in older women, frequently head-predominant, and characteristically have very low cyst fluid CEA (non-mucinous) and low amylase (no ductal communication).

Other Options::

• MCN: Typically macrocystic, body/tail of pancreas in middle-aged women, ovarian-type stroma, and high CEA; amylase usually low.
• Main-duct IPMN: Ductal dilation, mucin extrusion, cyst fluid amylase high (duct communication) and CEA often elevated.
• Pseudocyst: History of pancreatitis, no epithelial lining, amylase very high; imaging lacks central scar.

Trick points / common confusions

• Central scar with calcification strongly favors SCN, not MCN.
• Low CEA rules against all mucinous entities (MCN/IPMN).
• High amylase suggests IPMN or pseudocyst; low amylase supports SCN or MCN, but the microcystic pattern clinches SCN.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 69-year-old woman presents with an irreducible, tender swelling below the inguinal ligament. Imaging confirms a femoral hernia. For emergency strangulated femoral hernia, which surgical approach (as shown in the diagram) is preferred?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High (McEvedy’s) approach

A femoral hernia presents as a groin swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, classically in elderly women, and has a high risk of incarceration and strangulation due to the narrow femoral ring. Therefore, once diagnosed—especially when irreducible and tender (strangulated)—it requires urgent surgical repair.

In emergency strangulated femoral hernia, the preferred approach is the High (McEvedy’s) approach, because it provides:

• Rapid access to the femoral canal
• Direct entry into the peritoneal cavity if needed
• Ability to inspect bowel viability and perform resection-anastomosis if ischemic bowel is present
• Better exposure in emergency settings compared to low/inguinal approaches

Other approaches:

• Lockwood’s (low) approach: used mainly for elective femoral hernia repair, limited access to bowel.
• Lotheissen’s (transinguinal) approach: elective option, less ideal for strangulation.
• Stoppa repair: mainly for bilateral/recurrent hernias, not for acute strangulated cases.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 7-month-old baby boy is brought to the clinic by his mother due to “empty scrotum”. On examination, hemiscrotum on right side is not developed and testis is not palpable in the inguinal region. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diagnostic laparoscopy

• Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) is diagnosed when the testis has not descended into the scrotum by 6 months of age (corrected for prematurity).
• After 6 months, spontaneous descent is unlikely, and timely evaluation is essential because untreated cryptorchidism increases the risk of subfertility, malignancy (testicular cancer), torsion, and inguinal hernia.

In a 7-month-old infant with an empty hemiscrotum and a nonpalpable testis (not felt in the inguinal canal), the testis may be:

• intra-abdominal
• atrophic/vanished
• ectopic

The next best step is diagnostic laparoscopy, which is the gold standard investigation for a nonpalpable undescended testis because it:

• accurately determines presence and location of the testis
• identifies blind-ending vessels (vanishing testis)
• allows simultaneous therapeutic management (laparoscopic orchiopexy/orchiectomy as appropriate)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 7-year-old child with MEN2B and a confirmed RET mutation is planned for prophylactic total thyroidectomy for medullary thyroid carcinoma risk. Regarding postoperative adjuvant management in MTC, which statement is true?
options: Radioiodine ablation is recommended after surgery
There is no role for radioiodine or thyroid scan in MTC
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. There is no role for radioiodine or thyroid scan in MTC

Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and is not iodine-avid. Therefore radioiodine ablation and diagnostic radioiodine scans are not useful post-thyroidectomy. Definitive management is total thyroidectomy with prophylactic central compartment dissection in MEN2B, with postoperative follow-up using serum calcitonin and CEA and cross-sectional imaging when indicated. Targeted TKIs (e.g., vandetanib, cabozantinib, or selective RET inhibitors like selpercatinib/pralsetinib) are reserved for unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic progressive disease, not as a replacement for curative surgery. Levothyroxine is given for replacement to maintain euthyroidism, and TSH suppression is not required because C cells are not TSH-driven.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 9 years old child was brought to the hospital after burns. There was involvement of half of anterior chest wall and abdomen towards left side, left arm and left thigh. Calculate the burnt surface area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 20-25%

In children, burn surface area is estimated using the Rule of Nines (modified for pediatrics) or the Lund–Browder chart (most accurate). TBSA estimation is essential for:

• guiding fluid resuscitation (Parkland formula)

• predicting severity/prognosis

• deciding referral to burns unit

Pediatric Rule of 9s

For a 9-year-old :

• Each arm = 9%

• Anterior trunk (chest + abdomen) = 18%

• Each leg ≈ 14% (anterior leg = 7%)

• Head and neck = 9%

Calculation in this case

Burns involving:

1. Half of anterior chest + abdomen on left side

• Anterior trunk = 18%

• Half of anterior trunk = 9%
2. Left arm = 9%
3. Left thigh

• Thigh corresponds to about half of one leg

• One leg = \~14%

• Thigh ≈ half of leg = 7%

Total approximate TBSA:

• 9% (half anterior trunk) + 9% (left arm) + \~7% (left thigh)

= 25%

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A breast cancer tissue shows ER and PR positivity but negative HER2 expression. Which of the following is true regarding treatment response?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Poor response to paclitaxel

Breast cancers are commonly classified into molecular subtypes using immunohistochemistry markers:

• ER/PR status

• HER2 status

A tumor that is ER+ and PR+ with HER2 negativity is most consistent with a Luminal A subtype, which has:

• Hormone-driven biology

• Lower proliferation index (often low Ki-67)

• Better overall prognosis

Good response to endocrine therapy

• Tamoxifen (premenopausal)

• Aromatase inhibitors (postmenopausal)

• ± ovarian suppression

Poorer response to chemotherapy, especially compared to triple-negative or HER2-positive cancers

• Hence, poorer response to paclitaxel is true.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A hemicolectomy specimen biopsy shows adenocarcinoma invading the subserosa with deposits in the mesentery but no lymph node involvement or distant spread. What is the tumor stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T3 N1c M0

In colon cancer staging, two findings are crucial: depth of invasion (T stage) and presence of nodal disease or tumor deposits (N stage).

• A tumor that invades through muscularis propria into subserosa/pericolic tissue is staged as T3 (it has not penetrated the serosal surface, which would make it T4a).

• Tumor deposits are discrete cancer nodules in the mesocolic/mesenteric fat that lack identifiable lymph node tissue. Importantly, when tumor deposits are present but no regional lymph nodes are involved, the nodal stage is classified as N1c (even if all lymph nodes are negative).

• Absence of distant spread corresponds to M0.

Therefore, adenocarcinoma invading subserosa with mesenteric tumor deposits, no lymph node involvement, and no metastasis = T3 N1c M0.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male newborn is born at 37 weeks' gestation after spontaneous vaginal delivery. The mother had no prenatal care. Physical examination shows a urethral opening on the dorsal aspect of the penis, 4 mm proximal to the glans. The physical appearance is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's findings?
options: Incomplete union of the labioscrotal swellings
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malpositioning of the genital tubercle

A urethral opening on the dorsal surface of the penis indicates epispadias, which occurs due to malpositioning of the genital tubercle during embryologic development.

Key embryologic concept

• Normal development: genital tubercle migrates and elongates → urethral folds fuse ventrally → urethra forms in correct position.

• Epispadias: genital tubercle develops too dorsally → urethral opening forms on dorsal penis.

Clinical correlations

• Epispadias often associated with:

o Bladder exstrophy

o Pubic diastasis

o Urinary incontinence

• Distinguished from hypospadias (ventral opening).

Why other options are incorrect

• Persistence of urogenital membrane → cloacal abnormalities

• Incomplete fusion of labioscrotal swellings → bifid scrotum

• Abnormal gubernaculum → undescended testis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A newborn is diagnosed with a complete right cleft lip, complete right alveolar cleft, intact hard palate, incomplete soft palate cleft, and incomplete left alveolar cleft, with no cleft of the left lip. Which of the following LAHSAL codes correctly represents this anomaly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LAsa

The LAHSAL classification is a standardized system used to describe cleft lip, alveolus, and palate defects precisely and completely.

Structure of LAHSAL (Right → Left):

L A H S S A L

• L = Lip

• A = Alveolus

• H = Hard palate

• S = Soft palate

• S = Soft palate (left side)

• A = Alveolus

• L = Lip

Rules:

• Uppercase letter → complete cleft

• Lowercase letter → incomplete cleft

• Dot or omission → no cleft

• Written from patient’s right → left

Applied to this case:

• Right lip: complere cleft → L

• Right alveolus: complete → A

• Hard palate: intact; Soft palate incomplete → s

• Left alveolus incomplete → a

• Left lip intact

Correct LAHSAL code: LAsa

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A newborn presents with bilateral lower limb swelling since birth. Family history is positive. Genetic testing shows FLT-4 gene mutation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Milroy disease

• Primary (hereditary) lymphedema is a group of genetic disorders caused by abnormal development of lymphatic vessels, leading to impaired lymph drainage and chronic, non-pitting swelling of limbs.

• The age of onset and associated genetic mutation are key to diagnosis.

• Milroy disease is the classic form of congenital hereditary lymphedema.

• It presents with bilateral lower limb swelling present at birth or in early infancy, often with a positive family history (typically autosomal dominant inheritance).
• The most characteristic molecular association is mutation in the FLT4 gene, which encodes VEGFR-3 (vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-3), a receptor crucial for lymphangiogenesis (formation of lymphatic vessels).
• Defective VEGFR-3 signaling leads to hypoplastic/aplastic lymphatic channels, causing lifelong lower limb lymphedema.

Other Options:

A) Meige disease

• Actually a subtype of lymphedema praecox
• Onset: puberty/adolescence
• Most common primary lymphedema overall
• No classic FLT-4 mutation

C) Lymphedema tarda:

• Onset: after 35 years
• Rare
• Usually unilateral lower limb

D) Lymphedema praecox:

• Onset: before 35 years, typically around puberty
• Includes Meige disease
• Most common primary lymphedema

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient after severe traumatic brain injury opens eyes, is awake, recognizes family, but requires assistance for dressing, feeding, and daily activities. What is the GOS category?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Severe disability

• The Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) is used to assess functional outcome after traumatic brain injury (TBI) by categorizing recovery based on the patient’s level of consciousness, independence, and ability to resume normal life.
• It has 5 outcome categories: Death, Vegetative state, Severe disability, Moderate disability, and Good recovery.
• A patient who is awake, can open eyes, and recognizes family is clearly not vegetative (vegetative patients have wakefulness without awareness).
• However, if the patient requires assistance for dressing, feeding, and daily activities, they are dependent for activities of daily living (ADLs).
• This level of dependence corresponds to Severe Disability on GOS.

Analysing all options:

• A. Vegetative state: Awake but no awareness/interaction
• B. Severe disability: Conscious but dependent, needs help with ADLs
• C. Moderate disability: Independent but with deficits (cannot fully return to work/social activities)
• D. Good recovery: Returns to normal life with minimal deficits

Thus, an awake patient with awareness but dependence for daily care = GOS Severe disability (Option B).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient following head injury with 2 episodes of vomiting, and GCS of 15/15 undergoes CT scan as shown. The diameter of the EDH is 1cm. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wait and watch

Epidural hematoma (EDH) is a neurosurgical emergency typically caused by arterial bleeding (classically middle meningeal artery) and appears on CT as a biconvex/lentiform hyperdense extra-axial collection that does not cross suture lines. Management depends on hematoma size, mass effect, and neurological status. Indications for urgent surgical evacuation (craniotomy/burr hole) include:

• EDH thickness > 15 mm (1.5 cm)
• Volume > 30 mL
• Midline shift > 5 mm
• GCS ≤ 8 with pupillary abnormalities or neurological deterioration

In this case:

• EDH diameter/thickness = 1 cm → below surgical threshold
• Patient has vomiting but no mention of focal deficits/pupillary changes
• Therefore, if neurologically stable and imaging criteria are not met, EDH can be managed with Conservative management (wait and watch) with close neurological monitoring and repeat CT.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient had history of burns on the site shown in the image below, one year ago. He recently noticed a growth at the scar site. What is the like diagnosis of pathology shown?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Squamous cell carcinoma

A chronic non-healing ulcer or new growth arising in a previous burn scar is classically a Marjolin ulcer, which is a Squamous cell carcinoma

• Pathogenesis:

• Chronic inflammation and repeated tissue damage → malignant transformation
• Most commonly occurs in burn scars

• Key clinical features:

• Long-standing scar → recent ulceration or proliferative growth
• Often irregular, indurated margins, may bleed
• Typically develops years after injury (can occasionally be earlier)
• More aggressive than typical SCC
• Higher risk of local invasion and metastasis

• Important associations:

• Burn scars
• Chronic ulcers
• Sinus tracts (e.g., osteomyelitis)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is referred with variceal bleeds which are not responding to medical management. A TIPSS procedure is advised for the patient. Which of the following is a contraindication for this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Portal vein occlusion

TIPS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt) is an interventional radiology procedure that creates a low-resistance channel between the portal vein and a hepatic vein, thereby reducing portal hypertension. It is used in patients with portal hypertensive complications such as:

• Refractory variceal bleeding not controlled with endoscopic + medical therapy
• Refractory/intractable ascites (important indication)

For TIPS to be performed, there must be patent portal venous inflow so that blood can be shunted into systemic circulation. Therefore, Portal vein occlusion is a major contraindication (often absolute/technical), because the shunt cannot function if the portal vein cannot be accessed or has no flow.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with a rectal mass protruding through the anal opening after straining. Which of the following statements regarding this condition’s management is incorrect?
options: Abdominal procedure is preferred in younger patients.
Perineal approach is not preferred if there is a high operative risk.
Altemier’s procedure is used in cases of a strangulated prolapse.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perineal approach is not preferred if there is a high operative risk.

A rectal mass protruding through the anal opening after straining suggests rectal prolapse (full-thickness protrusion of rectal wall). Management is surgical and depends on patient age, comorbidities, operative risk, and whether the prolapse is strangulated. Rectal prolapse surgeries are broadly divided into:

1. Abdominal procedures:

• Examples: rectopexy (with/without sigmoid resection)
• Preferred in younger/fit patients because they have:

• Lower recurrence rates
• Better functional outcomes

Therefore, statement (B) is correct.

2. Perineal procedures:

• Examples: Delorme’s procedure, Altemeier’s procedure
• Preferred in elderly or high operative risk patients, because:

• Less physiologic stress
• Can be done under regional anesthesia

Hence (C) is the incorrect statement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents 6 months postpartum with complaints of occasional weakness and myalgia. Serum TSH is elevated, T3 and T4 are normal. Physical examination shows slight enlargement of the thyroid gland. What is the next step in management?
options: Reassure her and follow up thyroid profile
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reassure her and follow up thyroid profile

Women in the first year after delivery may develop postpartum thyroiditis, a painless autoimmune thyroid inflammation caused by immune rebound after pregnancy. It often follows a triphasic course:

1.     transient hyperthyroid phase

2.     hypothyroid phase

3.     recovery to euthyroid state in most patients

This patient is 6 months postpartum with:

• mild symptoms (weakness, myalgia)
• elevated TSH with normal T3/T4 → subclinical hypothyroidism
• mild, painless thyroid enlargement

Most cases of postpartum thyroiditis are self-limited, and subclinical hypothyroidism typically resolves without treatment. Therefore, the next best step is: Reassurance with follow-up thyroid function tests (repeat TSH/free T4 in 4–6 weeks).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with abdominal pain and vomiting. The CT abdomen reveals features suggestive of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cholelithiasis

Cholelithiasis refers to the presence of gallstones within the gallbladder. On CT abdomen, gallstones may be seen as hyperdense foci within the gallbladder lumen (especially calcified stones), sometimes with a layering appearance.

Clinical correlation

Cholelithiasis classically presents with:

• episodic RUQ/epigastric pain (biliary colic)

• nausea/vomiting after fatty meals

• no fever or leukocytosis unless inflammation develops

Differentiation from other gallbladder conditions

• Acute cholecystitis → gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign

• Gallbladder abscess/empyema → thick irregular wall, intraluminal pus, systemic toxicity

• Gallbladder carcinoma → mass replacing gallbladder, irregular wall thickening, invasion into liver

Thus, the CT findings are most consistent with cholelithiasis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was found to have an elevated 24-hour urinary cortisol level and elevated ACTH. On administration of high dose dexa, ACTH levels were suppressed. MRI of pituitary shows no gland enlargement. What is the next recommended step?
options: Venous sampling from inferior petrosal sinus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Venous sampling from inferior petrosal sinus

In ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, the key clinical task is to localize the source of ACTH. Elevated 24-hour urinary cortisol with elevated ACTH confirms ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism. Suppression of ACTH with high-dose dexamethasone suggests Cushing disease (pituitary ACTH adenoma) rather than ectopic ACTH secretion, but this test is not perfectly definitive.

When pituitary MRI is negative or non-diagnostic (no adenoma/enlargement seen), the next recommended step is Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling (IPSS). IPSS is the gold standard to confirm a pituitary source by demonstrating a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient, and it helps lateralize the lesion before surgery. Therefore, next step = Venous sampling from inferior petrosal sinus (Option C)

Why not others:

• Adrenal MRI is for ACTH-independent Cushing (low ACTH), not here.
• Plasma cortisol adds little after elevated urinary cortisol and ACTH.
• Transsphenoidal surgery should not be performed without confirming pituitary source when MRI is negative (risk of unnecessary surgery).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient who sustained blunt abdominal trauma after a road accident is admitted to the ICU overnight. He is hemodynamically stable. On abdominal examination, he now has tenderness, rigidity, and rebound tenderness. Which is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Laparotomy

• In blunt abdominal trauma, management is guided primarily by hemodynamic status and the presence or absence of peritonitis.
• Although stable patients are often observed or evaluated with imaging, the development of tenderness with rigidity and rebound tenderness indicates peritonitis, strongly suggesting a hollow viscus injury (eg, bowel perforation) or ongoing intra-abdominal contamination/bleeding.
• Investigations like eFAST or diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) are used when the diagnosis is unclear, especially in unstable patients.
• However, in a patient who has clear peritoneal signs, imaging tests should not delay definitive treatment.
• Therefore, the next best step is immediate exploratory laparotomy (Option A).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with acute pancreatitis has BP 84/50, HR 140, cold extremities. • PCWP: normal • SVR: high • CVP: low • CO: low What is the type of shock?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypovolemic

Shock is classified based on hemodynamic parameters such as cardiac output (CO), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and filling pressures (CVP and PCWP). In acute pancreatitis, massive third spacing of fluid into the retroperitoneum and peritoneal cavity can cause significant intravascular volume depletion, leading to hypovolemic shock.

Hypovolemic shock is characterized by:

• Low preload → low CVP
• Low left-sided filling pressure → normal/low PCWP
• Low CO due to reduced venous return
• High SVR as a compensatory vasoconstrictive response
• Clinical findings of cold extremities and poor perfusion

This differs from:

• Cardiogenic shock: high PCWP, high CVP, low CO, high SVR
• Distributive shock (sepsis/anaphylaxis): low SVR with warm extremities early
• Obstructive shock (PE/tamponade): high CVP with low CO

Thus, the given hemodynamic profile (↓ CVP, normal PCWP, ↓ CO, ↑ SVR with cold extremities) confirms hypovolemic shock.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with cirrhosis has: mild encephalopathy (grade 1), moderate ascites controlled with diuretics, bilirubin 3 mg/dL, albumin 2.8 g/dL and INR 2.1. What is his Child–Pugh class?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Class C

Child–Pugh uses 5 parameters, each scored 1–3. Sum classifies severity:

• Total score 5–6 = A, 7–9 = B, 10–15 = C.

Scoring this patient

1.   Encephalopathy: grade 1 → 2 points

2.   Ascites: described as “moderate and controlled with diuretics”. In standard tables: none = 1, slight/diuretic-controlled = 2, moderate/tense or poorly controlled = 3.

3.   Bilirubin 3 mg/dL:

o    ≤2 = 1, 2–3 = 2, >3 = 3 → 2 points

4.   Albumin 2.8 g/dL:

o    ≥3.5 = 1, 2.8–3.5 = 2, <2.8 = 3 → 2 points

5.   INR 2.1:

o    <1.7 = 1, 1.7–2.3 = 2, >2.3 = 3 → 2 points

Total = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10 → Class C.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with severe right-sided abdominal pain shows no findings on X-ray, but USG reveals a 6 mm renal stone. Which stone is most likely present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Uric acid

Renal calculi differ in their chemical composition and therefore in their visibility on plain X-ray (KUB). When a patient has classic renal colic but X-ray shows no stone, the most likely stone is radiolucent.

Radiolucent stone

Uric acid stone

• Not visible on X-ray (KUB negative)

• Detected on USG (echogenic focus with posterior shadow) and best seen on non-contrast CT KUB

• Forms in acidic urine (pH < 5.5)

• Associated with gout, high purine intake, myeloproliferative states, tumor lysis

Radiopaque stones (visible on KUB)

• Calcium oxalate/phosphate (most common overall)

• Struvite (infection/staghorn stones)

• Cystine (faintly radiopaque, “ground-glass”)

Therefore: Stone seen on USG but not seen on X-ray → Uric acid calculus.

Disclaimer: Even though we have studied that struvite may be radiolucent calculus, it is usually radio-opaque. Hence uric acid is a better answer here.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A person receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is at risk of developing a deficiency in which of the following nutrients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Zinc

Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) provides calories and macronutrients intravenously, but patients remain at risk of micronutrient deficiencies, especially trace elements, if they are not supplemented adequately or if requirements are increased (eg, burns, sepsis, diarrhea, fistulas). Among the nutrients listed, the most commonly deficient in patients on prolonged TPN is Zinc

Why zinc deficiency occurs with TPN

• Zinc is a trace element often depleted with:

o high GI losses (diarrhea, fistula output)

o poor intake/omission from TPN formulation

• Zinc must be added separately to TPN in appropriate doses

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A surgeon performs an appendicectomy with a grid iron incision. He later converts the incision to Rutherford Morrison incision. Which of the following are cut?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

When a gridiron (McBurney’s) incision for appendicectomy is extended to a Rutherford Morrison incision, the incision becomes a muscle-cutting approach for wider exposure of the right lower abdomen and pelvis.

• Gridiron incision: Muscle-splitting incision

o External oblique aponeurosis is cut

o Internal oblique and transversus abdominis are split along fibers (not cut)

• Rutherford Morrison incision (hockey-stick extension of gridiron): Becomes a muscle-cutting incision

o Used when greater exposure is needed (e.g., complicated appendicitis, cecal pathology)

o Requires division of: External oblique, Internal oblique, Transversus abdominis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A trauma patient suffered a renal laceration with urine extravasation. He was managed conservatively. However, after a few days, he presented with a urinoma. The next best management for this patient would be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ureteral stenting

After renal trauma with urine extravasation, most stable patients are managed conservatively. However, if a patient later develops a urinoma, it indicates persistent urinary leak from the collecting system.

Therefore, the next best step is ureteral stenting (Double J stent) because it:

• reduces pressure in the collecting system
• promotes sealing of the leak
• allows urine to drain normally into the bladder
• avoids ongoing extravasation and expansion of urinoma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A wide mouth non-indurated Meckel's diverticulum is found during surgery for acute appendicitis. What should be done?
options: Take consent from patient and re-explore
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nothing to be done

Meckel’s diverticulum is a congenital true diverticulum of the ileum due to persistence of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct. It is often found incidentally during abdominal surgery (eg, appendicectomy). The key decision is whether to resect an incidental Meckel’s diverticulum.

A wide-mouthed, non-indurated Meckel’s diverticulum without inflammation, ulceration, or palpable ectopic tissue is considered low risk for future complications (obstruction, bleeding, diverticulitis). Resection in such cases adds:

• risk of bowel leak

• bleeding

• postoperative adhesions/obstruction

Therefore, incidental wide-based Meckel’s diverticulum should be left alone. Resection is considered only when high-risk features are present, such as:

• narrow neck (higher obstruction/diverticulitis risk)

• induration/thickening or palpable ectopic tissue

• fibrous bands

• inflammation/ulceration

• bleeding or symptoms

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young 28 year old patient came to the OPD with complains of palpitation and excessive sweating. His general examination was normal. Blood sugar levels were within the normal range. His BP however came out to be 184/106 mmHg. BP was recorded again after 15 mins and it remained in the same range. The patient went through a full intensive work up and was diagnosed to be a case of pheochromocytoma. Which of the following genes related to this condition is not associated with hereditary pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NF2 gene

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor arising from adrenal medulla chromaffin cells and classically presents with episodic symptoms such as palpitations, sweating, and hypertension. A significant proportion of pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas are hereditary, so identifying genetic associations is important for screening, family counseling, and detecting associated tumors. The major hereditary syndromes/genes associated with pheochromocytoma include:

• RET proto-oncogene → MEN 2A / MEN 2B
• VHL gene → Von Hippel–Lindau syndrome
• Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) complex mutations (SDHB, SDHD, SDHC, SDHA, SDHAF2) → familial paraganglioma–pheochromocytoma syndromes

In contrast, the NF2 gene is associated with Neurofibromatosis type 2 (bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas) and is NOT linked to pheochromocytoma. (Pheochromocytoma is associated with NF1, not NF2.) Therefore, the gene not associated with hereditary pheochromocytoma is NF2.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young man presented to the emergency with an open fracture of Gustilo Anderson Stage IIIC. Which of the following suture materials would you use for the repair of the artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Polypropylene

In Gustilo-Anderson type IIIC open fractures, there is an associated arterial injury requiring urgent vascular repair to salvage the limb. Repair of arteries requires a suture that is:

• Non-absorbable
• Monofilament (less thrombogenic, less infection risk)
• Has high tensile strength
• Causes minimal tissue reaction
• Maintains long-term integrity in a pulsatile vessel

Polypropylene (Prolene) is the suture of choice for arterial anastomosis/repair because it is a non-absorbable monofilament with excellent handling and low thrombogenicity.

Why others are incorrect:

• A. Silk: Braided, higher tissue reaction and thrombogenicity → not preferred for vascular anastomosis.
• C. Polyglycapron (Monocryl): Absorbable → loses strength quickly, unsuitable for artery repair.
• D. Polydioxanone (PDS): Slowly absorbable → used in fascia/soft tissue, not ideal for permanent arterial repair.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: After a fall from a height, a 10-year-old child presented to the emergency department with complaints of abdominal pain. Upon examination, the child's vital signs were stable, but tenderness was noted in the left lumbar region. Hematuria was found on bladder catheterisation. What would be the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT urography

Blunt abdominal trauma with left flank/lumbar tenderness and hematuria strongly suggests a renal injury. The most important next step is to grade the renal trauma and identify associated injuries (laceration, urinary extravasation, vascular injury). Since the child is:

• hemodynamically stable
• has hematuria
• has flank tenderness

The investigation of choice is contrast-enhanced CT of abdomen with delayed excretory phase (CT urography) because it:

• best evaluates renal parenchymal injury
• detects collecting system injury and urine extravasation
• assesses renal vessels and retroperitoneal hematoma
• guides management (conservative vs intervention)

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Retrograde urethrogram → indicated with blood at meatus, pelvic fracture, high-riding prostate, or inability to void (urethral injury signs).

C. CT cystography → indicated when bladder rupture is suspected (gross hematuria + pelvic fracture).

D. Single shot IVP → outdated; may be used intraoperatively when CT is unavailable.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All are known risk factors for gastric cancer, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blood group O

Gastric carcinoma is strongly associated with environmental and infectious factors that promote chronic gastritis → atrophy → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → cancer.

Established risk factors include:

• Diet rich in salted/smoked meats (nitrosamines) → increased gastric cancer risk

• Menetrier disease (hypertrophic gastropathy with protein loss) → increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma

• EBV infection → associated with a subset of gastric adenocarcinomas (EBV-positive gastric cancer)

Blood group association:

• Blood group A, not O, is associated with increased risk of gastric carcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All are true about hernia, except:
options: Grynfelt triangle is superior lumbar triangle
Left side more common than right
Petit triangle bounded by iliac crest, lat dorsi, external oblique
Spigelian hernia occurs near inguinal region
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spigelian hernia occurs near inguinal region

Abdominal wall hernias may occur through anatomical weak areas such as the lumbar triangles and the Spigelian fascia. Knowledge of these landmarks helps identify uncommon hernias clinically.

Lumbar hernias

• Grynfelt triangle = superior lumbar triangle

Boundaries:

o Superior: 12th rib

o Medial: quadratus lumborum

o Lateral: internal oblique

• Lumbar hernias are more commonly left-sided due to relatively weaker left posterior abdominal wall.

• Petit triangle = inferior lumbar triangle

Boundaries:

o Inferior: iliac crest

o Posterior: latissimus dorsi

o Anterior: external oblique

• Spigelian hernia

Occurs through the Spigelian fascia (along the semilunar line), most commonly at the Spigelian belt near the level of the arcuate line.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All are true regarding factors preventing spontaneous closure of a fistula, except:
options: Presence of foreign body in the tract
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Presence of fibrosis

Spontaneous closure of an enterocutaneous fistula (ECF) depends on fistula output, anatomy, and presence of factors that prevent healing. Clinicians remember the major causes of failure of spontaneous closure using the “FRIEND” mnemonic:

F – Foreign body

R – Radiation

I – Infection/Inflammation

E – Epithelialization of the tract

N – Neoplasm

D – Distal obstruction

Additional important poor prognostic factors include:

• High-output fistula (>500 mL/day)

• Short tract, multiple fistulas, proximal small bowel origin

• Ongoing sepsis/malnutrition

Presence of fibrosis is not a standard factor preventing spontaneous closure and is not part of FRIEND.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are at an increased risk in the condition below except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. RCC

A horseshoe kidney is a congenital fusion anomaly in which the lower poles of the kidneys fuse across the midline and remain trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent.

Because of abnormal position and rotation:

• Ureters pass anteriorly over the isthmus

• Drainage becomes impaired

• Leads to urinary stasis

Conditions commonly associated

Urinary stasis predisposes to:

• Renal calculi (most common complication)

• Hydronephrosis/PUJ obstruction

• Recurrent infections

• Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) due to chronic irritation and stasis

• Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is not significantly increased compared to general population in horseshoe kidney

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are Class I indications for CABG, except:
options: Sudden cardiac arrest survivors with ischemia-mediated VT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Two-vessel disease without LAD involvement

Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is recommended when revascularization provides a clear survival benefit or reduces major adverse cardiac events. Class I indications (strong evidence/benefit >> risk) include:

✅ Left main coronary artery disease

• CABG improves survival significantly.

✅ Three-vessel coronary artery disease

• Especially with reduced LV function or diabetes; CABG improves long-term outcomes.

✅ Survivors of sudden cardiac arrest / sustained ischemia-mediated VT

• If ventricular arrhythmia is due to reversible ischemia, revascularization (often CABG) is indicated to prevent recurrence.

❌ Two-vessel disease without LAD involvement

• Does not generally carry a survival advantage with CABG.

• CABG is most beneficial in 2-vessel disease with proximal LAD involvement or significant ischemic burden.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are included in TRISS except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Limb ischemia

TRISS (Trauma and Injury Severity Score) is used to predict probability of survival in trauma patients by combining physiological and anatomical data.

• Components of TRISS:

• RTS (Revised Trauma Score) → physiological parameters (GCS, BP, RR)
• ISS (Injury Severity Score) → anatomical injury severity
• Age of the patient
• Mechanism of injury (blunt vs penetrating)

• Not included:

• Limb ischemia (a local clinical finding, not part of scoring)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are lab findings in acute pancreatitis, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypercalcemia

Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when at least 2 of 3 are present:

1. Characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back

2. Serum lipase or amylase ≥ 3× normal

3. Imaging evidence of pancreatitis

Typical laboratory findings in acute pancreatitis include:

• Elevated serum lipase (most sensitive/specific)

• Leukocytosis due to inflammation/SIRS

• Elevated ALT (especially >150 IU/L suggests gallstone pancreatitis)

However, calcium levels in acute pancreatitis are characteristically:

• Low (hypocalcemia) due to fat saponification (binding of calcium in necrotic fat)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are risk factors for breast cancer except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oophorectomy

Breast cancer risk is strongly influenced by genetic predisposition and cumulative lifetime estrogen exposure. Factors that increase estrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy) increase risk, while factors that reduce estrogen exposure decrease risk. Risk factors in the options:

• Cowden syndrome (PTEN mutation) → increases breast cancer risk

• Late menopause → prolonged estrogen exposure → higher risk

• Nulliparity → fewer periods of breast differentiation and more lifetime estrogen cycles → higher risk

• Oophorectomy → removes ovaries → reduces estrogen production → protective, especially in high-risk women (eg, BRCA carriers)

Therefore, the exception (not a risk factor) is: C) Oophorectomy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 18 year old football player presents with progressively worsening deep groin pain for 3 months. The pain increases during sprinting and sit ups. He denies any swelling in the groin. On examination, there is tenderness over the pubic tubercle. No visible bulge is seen on performing the cough impulse test. Hip range of motion is normal and FADIR test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Athletic pubalgia

Chronic deep groin pain in athletes that worsens with sprinting, twisting, kicking, and sit-ups in the absence of a visible/palpable groin bulge is most consistent with athletic pubalgia (sports hernia). Despite the term “hernia,” this condition is not a true hernia; instead it is caused by strain or tearing of the musculotendinous structures of the lower abdominal wall and groin, most commonly involving the rectus abdominis insertion, conjoint tendon, and/or posterior inguinal wall near the pubic tubercle. Key features supporting athletic pubalgia in this case:

• Gradual progressive deep groin pain over months
• Pain provoked by sit-ups (abdominal contraction) and sprinting
• Tenderness over pubic tubercle
• No cough impulse / no bulge → argues against inguinal hernia
• Normal hip ROM and negative FADIR → rules out femoroacetabular impingement

Differentiation:

• Occult inguinal hernia: may have cough impulse/bulge or pain with raised intra-abdominal pressure; imaging may show hernia.
• Osteitis pubis: inflammatory pain at pubic symphysis, often midline with pain on adductor squeeze; imaging shows symphyseal changes.
• Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI): hip pathology with reduced hip ROM and positive FADIR.

Thus, the most likely diagnosis is athletic pubalgia (sports hernia).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after falling and striking his chest. He had been playing an interactive video game when he lost his balance and hit his left chest against the coffee table. The patient now has moderate left-sided chest pain, worse with deep inspiration. Blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg, pulse is 122/min, and respirations are 28/min. Jugular veins are flat. The trachea is midline. The left chest wall has intact, bruised skin and is exquisitely tender to palpation. Breath sounds are present on the right but diminished in the left lung base, which is dull to percussion. Heart sounds are normal without murmurs. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intercostal vessel injury

Blunt chest trauma with hypotension, flat neck veins, unilateral decreased breath sounds, and dullness to percussion suggests hemothorax — most commonly due to intercostal vessel injury.

• Hypotension + tachycardia → hemorrhagic shock

• Flat JVP → excludes cardiac tamponade/tension pneumothorax

• Dullness to percussion + decreased breath sounds → pleural fluid (blood)

• Blunt chest trauma → rib fracture → intercostal artery tear → hemothorax

Most common cause of traumatic hemothorax: Intercostal vessel injury (often from rib fractures)

• Ascending aortic tear: severe deceleration injury; mediastinal widening, unequal pulses

• Bronchial rupture: massive air leak, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax

• Diaphragmatic rupture: bowel sounds in chest, herniation, respiratory distress (not acute shock from blood loss)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 45-year old female comes to your clinic reporting feelings of constant fatigue. Upon performing USG, you discover that she has a scleroatrophic gallbladder containing impacted stones. In addition, a 6mm stone is detected within the common bile duct, causing dilation of the biliary tree. What should be the subsequent course of action in her treatment?
options: Immediately take up patient for cholecystectomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ERCP

A patient with gallbladder stones plus a CBD stone (choledocholithiasis) and dilated biliary tree has an obstructing stone in the common bile duct that must be cleared before definitive gallbladder surgery. In this case:

• Scleroatrophic gallbladder with impacted stones → chronic cholecystitis (“burnt-out” gallbladder)
• CBD stone 6 mm + biliary dilatation → confirmed choledocholithiasis

The next step in management is ERCP, because it is both:

• Diagnostic, and more importantly
• Therapeutic (endoscopic sphincterotomy + stone extraction/stenting)

After duct clearance, the patient should undergo elective cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence, but CBD obstruction must be treated first.

Why not MRCP?

• MRCP is used when CBD stone is suspected but not confirmed. Here the stone is already detected.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man comes to the OPD with a non healing ulcer over the glans penis accompanied by intermittent bleeding and foul smelling discharge. He has a long history of poor genital hygiene. On examination, the ulcer has indurated edges. While counselling the patient about risk factors for carcinoma penis, which of the following would you not include on your list?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Peyronie’s disease

Carcinoma penis is most commonly a squamous cell carcinoma and typically presents in elderly men as a non-healing ulcer or growth on the glans/prepuce with foul-smelling discharge, bleeding, and indurated edges. A major contributor is chronic irritation and inflammation, often related to poor genital hygiene and smegma accumulation.

Important established risk factors for penile carcinoma include:

• High-risk HPV infection (HPV 16 and 18) → especially associated with basaloid/warty SCC
• Phimosis and poor genital hygiene
• Chronic balanitis/posthitis (long-standing inflammatory changes)
• Premalignant lesions such as leukoplakia (keratosis), erythroplasia of Queyrat, Bowen disease
• Smoking, lichen sclerosus (BXO), immunosuppression

Peyronie’s disease (fibrous plaque of tunica albuginea causing penile curvature) is not a recognized risk factor for carcinoma penis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An otherwise healthy 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother 2 hours after the sudden onset of scrotal pain. Physical examination shows nontender testes and a tender, 5-mm, bluish nodule at the superior pole of the left testis. The patient undergoes urgent surgical exploration of the scrotum. During the operation, the nodule on the superior pole of the testis is found to be necrotic. In the process of embryologic development, this nodule forms as a result of the activity of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MIF

Torsion of appendix testis presents with acute scrotal pain and a “blue dot sign” at the superior pole of the testis. The appendix testis is a remnant of the Müllerian (paramesonephric) duct.

During male embryologic development:

• Müllerian Inhibiting Factor (MIF) from Sertoli cells causes regression of Müllerian ducts.

• Incomplete regression can leave remnants → appendix testis.

Embryology pearls:

• MIF → regression of Müllerian ducts → appendix testis remnant

• Testosterone → Wolffian duct development

• DHT (via 5-α reductase) → external genitalia

• LH → stimulates Leydig cells (testosterone production)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: As per the ANDI classification of benign breast disorders, all of the following would be considered under disorders of early reproductive years, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nipple eversion

The ANDI classification (Aberrations of Normal Development and Involution) groups benign breast disorders according to the phase of breast development/involution in which they occur. It helps distinguish normal physiologic variations from true disease.

In the early reproductive years (adolescence to early adulthood), common ANDI conditions include:

• Adolescent hypertrophy (juvenile macromastia)
• Fibroadenoma (most common benign breast lump in young women)
• Nipple inversion (may be developmental/physiologic in younger females)

Nipple eversion, however, is normal anatomy and is not considered a benign breast disorder under ANDI categories (it is not a pathologic aberration). Therefore, the condition NOT included under disorders of early reproductive years is Nipple eversion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Circumcision is contraindicated in
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypospadias

Circumcision is contraindicated in hypospadias because the prepuce is required for future urethral reconstruction (urethroplasty).

• Hypospadias = ventral urethral opening with dorsal hooded prepuce.

• Foreskin tissue is used in surgical repair of urethra.

• Performing circumcision removes essential tissue → complicates definitive repair.

Other options:

• Balanitis: Circumcision often indicated if recurrent.

• Paraphimosis: Emergency reduction; circumcision done later to prevent recurrence.

• Bladder exstrophy: Genital reconstruction required, but absolute classical contraindication tested in exams = hypospadias.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Duodenum preserving pancreatic head resection surgery for chronic pancreatitis is also known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Berger operation

Surgery for chronic pancreatitis is chosen based on whether the disease is dominated by a dilated pancreatic duct, an inflammatory mass in the pancreatic head, or both. When chronic pancreatitis causes an enlarged/fibrotic pancreatic head producing pain and obstruction, procedures that remove diseased head tissue while preserving the duodenum are preferred to reduce morbidity and maintain gastric/duodenal continuity.

Duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (DPPHR) is classically known as the Beger (Berger) procedure, in which the pancreatic head is resected while keeping the duodenum intact, followed by pancreatic drainage reconstruction.

Key distinctions:

• Puestow operation = longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy for dilated duct.
• Frey’s operation = local “coring out” of pancreatic head + longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (for head-dominant disease with duct dilation).
• Beger (Berger) operation = true DPPHR.
• Duval operation = distal pancreatectomy with pancreaticojejunostomy (older operation).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During a surgical scrub, a resident misses a specific area consistently. Surveillance data shows this area is the most commonly missed during routine hand washing. Which area is it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The thumb

The thumb is the single most commonly missed area during routine hand hygiene and surgical hand scrubbing. Studies evaluating hand-washing technique using fluorescent markers have consistently shown that the thumb, fingertips, and interdigital web spaces are inadequately cleaned despite routine washing. Since the thumb frequently contacts patients and equipment, inadequate cleaning increases the risk of healthcare-associated infections (HAIs).

The WHO six-step hand hygiene technique specifically includes rotational rubbing of each thumb to ensure complete coverage and effective reduction of transient microorganisms.

• Other commonly missed sites: Interdigital web spaces and fingertips/nail folds
• WHO 6-step hand hygiene specifically includes:

• Palm to palm
• Palm over dorsum
• Interdigital spaces
• Backs of fingers
• Rotational rubbing of thumbs
• Rotational rubbing of fingertips on palm

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon carefully dissects to obtain the “critical view of safety”. Which of the following is not a boundary of this triangle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystic artery

In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the “critical view of safety” (CVS) described by Strasberg requires full clearance of the hepatocystic (Calot’s) triangle, which is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct, and the inferior surface of the liver. Within this cleared triangle, only two structures leading into the gallbladder should be visible, which are then identified as the cystic duct and cystic artery. The cystic artery itself is not a boundary of the triangle. It lies inside the triangle after dissection.

Learning Points:

• Hepatocystic triangle – Bounded by cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver, and is the key area dissected for CVS.
• Original Calot’s triangle – Calot’s original description used the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and cystic artery, but in modern hepatobiliary surgery the superior boundary is taken as the liver edge, not the artery.
• Critical view of safety – Requires that the hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue and only two structures entering the gallbladder are seen, minimizing risk of bile duct injury.
• Cystic artery location – The cystic artery typically runs within the triangle and is one of the two structures to be clipped and divided, but it is not a boundary in the modern definition used for CVS.
• Bile duct injury prevention – Proper identification of the cystic duct versus common hepatic duct within the hepatocystic triangle is essential to avoid catastrophic common bile duct injury.

Other Options:

A. Cystic duct – Correct boundary. Forms the inferior edge of the hepatocystic triangle.

B. Inferior surface of the liver – Correct boundary. The superior border of the hepatocystic triangle in modern usage.

D. Common hepatic duct – Correct boundary. Forms the medial edge of the hepatocystic triangle.

C. Cystic artery – Not a boundary in the modern hepatocystic triangle used for critical view of safety, so this is the correct answer.

Trick points / Common confusions:

• Exam questions often mix original Calot’s triangle and modern hepatocystic triangle. For a critical view of safety, think cystic duct, common hepatic duct, liver edge, not the artery.
• A useful memory aid is that the two structures you finally clip (cystic duct and artery) are inside the triangle, whereas the triangle boundaries include only one duct twice and the liver edge.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During surgery for a hydatid cyst of the liver, the surgeon removes the endocyst and drains the cyst cavity. To prevent residual cavity complications, he performs spiral suturing of the hydatid cavity walls. This surgical step is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Capitonnage

In hepatic hydatid disease (Echinococcus granulosus), after endocystectomy (removal of the germinal membrane/endocyst) and evacuation of cyst contents, a large residual pericyst cavity may remain. This cavity can lead to postoperative complications such as infection, bile leakage, prolonged drainage, hemorrhage, and residual cavity abscess. To prevent these residual cavity problems, surgeons may obliterate the cavity by in-folding and suturing the cavity walls in a spiral/continuous manner, thereby collapsing the space and eliminating dead space. This technique is called capitonnage.

Key differentiations:

• Marsupialization: exteriorization of cyst cavity by suturing it to the skin/open wound for continuous drainage.
• PAIR: percutaneous aspiration–injection–reaspiration (image-guided minimally invasive technique).
• Cystojejunostomy: internal drainage procedure connecting cavity to jejunum (rarely used; for selected complicated cysts).

Thus, spiral suturing of the hydatid cavity walls to obliterate the residual cavity = Capitonnage.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During the examination of which of the following swellings would you expect to see transillumination? 1. Meningomyelocele 2. Spermatocoele 3. Ranula 4. Cystic hygroma 5. Lipoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3, 4

Transillumination is a clinical test used to identify swellings that contain clear fluid (cystic lesions).

• When a light is placed behind such a swelling in a dark room, the swelling glows-->indicating fluid content.

Swellings that transilluminate (fluid-filled)

✅ Spermatocoele – cystic swelling arising from epididymis, filled with fluid/sperm

✅ Ranula – mucus retention cyst in the floor of mouth (salivary origin)

✅ Cystic hygroma – congenital lymphatic malformation, multiloculated fluid-filled swelling

So: 2, 3, 4 are correct.

Swellings that do NOT transilluminate

❌ Meningomyelocele – contains neural tissue/CSF but has thick coverings and solid elements; not classically transilluminant in exam setting

❌ Lipoma – solid fat tumor, does not transilluminate

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During total mesorectal excision for mid-rectal cancer, the surgeon carefully dissects in the correct avascular planes around the rectum. Which statement regarding the fascial planes is most accurate?
options: Fascia of Denonvilliers lies posterior to the rectum and separates it from the sacrum.
Fascia of Waldeyer lies anterior to the rectum and separates it from the prostate or vagina.
Fascia of Denonvilliers is an important anterior plane between rectum and genitourinary organs.
Both fasciae are routinely excised along with mesorectum in TME.
questions.explanation:
