Correct answer: C. Fascia of Denonvilliers is an important anterior plane between rectum and genitourinary organs.

During total mesorectal excision (TME) for rectal cancer, precise dissection along embryologic fascial planes ensures oncologic clearance while preserving autonomic nerves.

• Fascia of Denonvilliers lies anterior to the rectum, separating it from the prostate/seminal vesicles in males and vagina in females.

• It forms a key anterior surgical plane in TME and must be carefully identified to avoid injury to genitourinary structures and autonomic nerves.

Key fascial relationships in TME

• Mesorectal fascia (holy plane): Avascular plane surrounding mesorectum used for TME dissection

• Denonvilliers fascia: Anterior plane between rectum and genitourinary organs

• Waldeyer’s fascia: Posterior rectosacral fascia connecting rectum to sacrum

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer, which of the following steps will not lead to hoarseness of voice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ligation of Superior thyroid artery

Hoarseness after thyroidectomy is most commonly due to injury to the nerves supplying the larynx:

• Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) → vocal cord paralysis → hoarseness (most important)
• External branch of superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN) → loss of pitch/voice fatigue (not classic hoarseness, but voice change)

Several surgical steps during thyroidectomy place the RLN at high risk, especially where it is closely related to thyroid structures:

Berry’s ligament

• RLN is tightly adherent near the ligament of Berry as it enters the larynx

o   highest risk zone for RLN injury → hoarseness

Zuckerkandl tubercle

• Posterolateral projection of thyroid tissue
• RLN often runs just medial/posterior to it

o   dissection can injure RLN

Beahr’s triangle

• Anatomical area used to locate RLN (between trachea, esophagus and thyroid region)

o   dissection here risks RLN trauma

Ligation of Superior thyroid artery

• Done at superior pole, mainly risks EBSLN
• Does not typically injure RLN, hence does not lead to hoarseness in the classical sense

Therefore, the step least likely to cause hoarseness is Ligation of superior thyroid artery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: For performing a transurethral resection in cases of bladder tumors, which of the following lasers is most commonly used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nd-YAG laser

Lasers are used in urology for cutting, coagulation, and tissue vaporization. In transurethral management of bladder tumors (laser TURBT/fulguration), the preferred laser is one that provides deep coagulation and good hemostasis, especially for superficial tumor ablation.

Nd:YAG (Neodymium-doped Yttrium Aluminium Garnet) laser is most commonly used because it:

• has deep tissue penetration

• provides excellent coagulation

• is effective for tumor coagulation/fulguration via endoscopic approach

Why others are less suitable:

• Ho:YAG: mainly used for stone fragmentation and prostate enucleation (HoLEP); more precise cutting with shallow penetration.

• Argon: limited depth, less commonly used for TUR of bladder tumors.

• CO₂ laser: not practical endoscopically in bladder due to poor transmission through fluids.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Histopathological examination of a polyp shows dysplasia up to the submucosa. What is the correct Haggitt classification level?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Level 4

The Haggitt classification is used for malignant pedunculated colorectal polyps to describe the depth of invasion of carcinoma arising within the polyp. It helps determine whether endoscopic polypectomy is sufficient or whether formal bowel resection is needed.

In this question:

• Dysplasia/carcinoma extends up to the submucosa (implying invasion beyond mucosa into bowel wall submucosa)

→ corresponds to Haggitt Level 4, which is the highest-risk category

| Level | Description

| ----- | -----------

| Level 0 | Carcinoma in situ / intramucosal carcinoma (no invasion beyond muscularis mucosae)

| Level 1 | Invasion into the head of the polyp

| Level 2 | Invasion into the neck of the polyp

| Level 3 | Invasion into the stalk of the polyp

| Level 4 | Invasion into the submucosa of the bowel wall (below stalk)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: I-VITROS in relation to minimally invasive surgery refers to:
options: Incise, View, Identify, Tie, Repair, Observe, Seal
Incise, Visualise, Insuffulate, Triangulate, Retract, Operate, Seal
Insuffulate, Visualise, Incise, Triangulate, Repair, Operate, Seal
Insuffulate, Visualise, Identify, Triangulate, Retract, Operate, Seal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Insuffulate, Visualise, Identify, Triangulate, Retract, Operate, Seal

Minimally invasive surgery (MIS)/laparoscopy follows a structured sequence of steps to ensure safe access, adequate visualization, proper tissue handling, and secure closure. The mnemonic I-VITROS describes the standard workflow of laparoscopic surgery.

I-VITROS =

• I – Insufflate: create pneumoperitoneum (usually CO₂) to form working space
• V – Visualise: introduce telescope and confirm safe intraperitoneal access
• I – Identify: identify anatomy, pathology, and key landmarks
• T – Triangulate: correct port placement for ergonomic instrument alignment and precision
• R – Retract: expose operative field safely without tissue trauma
• O – Operate: perform the intended surgical steps (dissection, clipping, cutting, suturing)
• S – Seal: ensure hemostasis/secure closure (energy sealing, clips, sutures) and final check

Thus, I-VITROS in MIS refers to “Insufflate, Visualise, Identify, Triangulate, Retract, Operate, Seal” (Option D).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the incision shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gibson incision

Gibson incision is an oblique extraperitoneal lower abdominal incision commonly used for renal transplantation and access to the distal ureter, iliac vessels, and pelvic kidney.

Key features

• Curved oblique incision in right or left iliac fossa

• Parallel to inguinal ligament

• Provides extraperitoneal approach to pelvis

• Avoids entering peritoneal cavity → ↓ bowel complications

Common uses

• Renal transplantation (most common)

• Distal ureteric surgery

• Pelvic vascular procedures

Differentiation from other incisions

• Kocher incision → Right subcostal (open cholecystectomy)

• Maylard incision → Transverse suprapubic with rectus muscle division

• Mercedes Benz incision → Bilateral subcostal with midline extension (liver transplant)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the incorrect pair: A. Esophageal web B. Feline esophagitis C. Candidiasis D. Barrett's esophagus
options: [Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. [image not included in this edition]

Esophageal web is a thin mucosal membrane seen in the upper esophagus (post-cricoid region) and is classically associated with Plummer–Vinson syndrome (iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, glossitis).

On endoscopy it appears as a thin shelf-like projection, not a circumferential narrowing or inflammatory mucosal change (Image shown is that of a Shatzki ring)

Other options:

• Eosinophilic esophagitis: concentric rings (“trachealization”), linear furrows

• Candidiasis: white adherent plaques

• Barrett esophagus: salmon-colored columnar mucosa in distal esophagus

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the incorrect statement regarding rectal carcinoma.
options: Hartmann's operation is done in elderly debilitated patients
Adenocarcinoma is a rare variant of rectal carcinoma
Early morning spurious diarrhea and tenesmus can occur
Growth into muscularis propria is stage B1 of modified Duke's staging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenocarcinoma is a rare variant of rectal carcinoma

Rectal carcinoma is most commonly adenocarcinoma, arising from glandular epithelium of the colorectal mucosa. In fact, >90–95% of rectal cancers are adenocarcinomas, making it the predominant histologic type, not a rare variant. Rare histologic subtypes include squamous cell carcinoma, neuroendocrine tumors, lymphoma, and GIST.

Clinical features of rectal cancer may include:

• Tenesmus
• Spurious/false diarrhea, especially early morning, due to rectal irritation and partial obstruction
• Altered bowel habits and bleeding

Surgical considerations:

• Hartmann’s procedure (resection with end colostomy and rectal stump closure) is often chosen in elderly/debilitated patients or in emergencies when primary anastomosis is unsafe.

Staging:

• In Modified Dukes staging, B1 refers to tumor invasion into the muscularis propria without nodal involvement (B2 extends through it).

Therefore, the incorrect statement is: B) Adenocarcinoma is a rare variant of rectal carcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the slide given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spleen

The spleen is identified histologically by the presence of white pulp (lymphoid follicles) scattered within red pulp (vascular sinusoids and cords).

• White pulp: Basophilic lymphoid nodules surrounding central arterioles (PALS)
• Red pulp: Eosinophilic areas with splenic cords (of Billroth) and venous sinusoids
• No cortex–medulla distinction (unlike lymph node or thymus)

Key differentiating points:

• Lymph node: Distinct cortex & medulla, no red pulp
• Tonsil: Surface epithelium with crypts
• Thymus: Lobulated with cortex & medulla + Hassall corpuscles

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the suture:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Horizontal mattress

The suture shown is a Horizontal Mattress Suture.

Key identifying features:

• Two bites taken parallel to the wound edge
• Needle passes back and forth on the same side of the wound
• Creates a rectangular pattern on the skin surface
• Provides good tension distribution and eversion of wound edges

Commonly used in:

• High-tension wounds
• Fragile skin (with caution)
• To achieve hemostasis along wound edges

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of suture material given in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monofilament

Suture materials are classified based on filament structure into monofilament and polyfilament (Braided)

Monofilament sutures (e.g., polypropylene, polydioxanone/PDS):

• Single smooth strand

• Low tissue drag

• Less infection risk (no capillarity)

• Poor knot security → needs more knots

• Used in contaminated wounds, vascular and subcuticular closure

Multifilament/braided sutures (e.g., silk, vicryl):

• Multiple strands braided together

• Better handling and knot security

• Higher infection risk due to capillarity and bacterial harboring

• More tissue drag

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify what is depicted in the abdominal X-Ray.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retrograde pyelogram

A retrograde pyelogram (RGP) is a fluoroscopic urologic imaging procedure in which contrast is injected retrograde into the ureter via a cystoscope and ureteric catheter, allowing visualization of the ureter, renal pelvis, and calyces.

Clinical significance / uses (high-yield):

• Evaluation of ureteric obstruction/stricture
• Localization of ureteric injury
• Assessment when IVU/CT urography is contraindicated (eg, renal failure, contrast allergy)
• Intraoperative guidance during urological procedures (stenting, ureteroscopy)

Differentiation from similar studies:

• IVU (intravenous urogram): contrast given IV → kidneys excrete dye over time.
• MCU: bladder is filled with contrast to assess reflux; ureters opacify only if reflux occurs.
• Ureteric stent: would show characteristic “double J” curls in kidney and bladder.
• Therefore, the image depicts a Retrograde pyelogram.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a case of head injury, which patient would not require an immediate CT scan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. One episode of vomiting

In head injury, the decision to obtain an immediate CT head is based on the presence of high-risk features that predict intracranial injury or need for neurosurgical intervention. CT is mandatory when any of the following are present:

• Post-traumatic seizure (especially in children) → suggests cortical irritation/bleed
• Suspected skull fracture (basal or depressed) → high risk of intracranial hemorrhage
• GCS < 13 or fall in GCS (eg, GCS 12 in RTA victim) → moderate/severe head injury requiring urgent imaging

In contrast, a single isolated episode of vomiting, with otherwise normal neurological examination and no additional high-risk features, does not by itself mandate immediate CT, since minor vomiting can occur after concussion. (Repeated vomiting or vomiting with other risk factors would require CT.) Therefore, the patient who would not require immediate CT is One episode of vomiting (Option D).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a child with unilateral undescended testis, diagnostic laparoscopy shows blind-ending testicular vessels on the right side. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. No further exploration

In the evaluation of a non-palpable undescended testis, diagnostic laparoscopy is the gold standard because it identifies the location and viability of the testis and guides further management. During laparoscopy, the key structures to follow are the vas deferens and testicular vessels.

If laparoscopy shows blind-ending testicular vessels (vessels end abruptly and do not enter the inguinal canal), this indicates testicular agenesis or a vanished testis (usually due to intrauterine/perinatal torsion with atrophy and resorption). In this situation, there is no viable testis to retrieve or fix, and further inguinal/scrotal exploration will not provide benefit.

Therefore, when blind-ending vessels are seen, the appropriate management is No further exploration (Option D).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with a head injury who presents with fixed dilated pupils and rapidly deteriorating neurological signs, where is the burr hole made?
options: Temporal region contralateral to the side of pupillary dilatation
Midline as it is not known which side of pupil dilated first
Left temporal region if no localising sign found
Right temporal region if no localising sign found
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left temporal region if no localising sign found

A head injury patient with fixed dilated pupil(s) and rapid neurological deterioration is presumed to have a life-threatening intracranial mass lesion, most commonly an acute extradural hematoma or subdural hematoma causing uncal herniation. The classic mechanism is compression of the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III) → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, followed by brainstem compromise.

In such a scenario, if CT imaging is not immediately available and the patient is crashing, an emergency decompressive burr hole (life-saving “rescue burr hole”) is performed to relieve pressure.

Principle:

• If there is a unilateral dilated pupil → burr hole is made in the ipsilateral temporal region (at the pterion) to evacuate likely EDH.

• If the side is uncertain/no localizing signs are available → the recommended first burr hole is made in the left temporal region.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In the preparation for a standard VATS (Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery), which of the following is considered the first essential step before port insertion?
options: Collapse of the lung using double-lumen endotracheal intubation
Positioning of the patient in lateral decubitus position
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Collapse of the lung using double-lumen endotracheal intubation

Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) requires a clear operative field within the pleural cavity, which is only possible if the ipsilateral lung is collapsed. Therefore, the first essential step in standard VATS preparation is establishing one-lung ventilation (OLV), most commonly achieved with a double-lumen endotracheal tube (DLT) (or bronchial blocker when DLT is not feasible).

Collapsing the operative lung:

• Creates adequate intrathoracic working space
• Improves visualization of pleura, lung, mediastinum
• Reduces risk of lung injury during port placement
• Facilitates safe manipulation and dissection

Only after confirming effective lung isolation and collapse should the team proceed with lateral decubitus positioning and subsequent port/camera insertion. Thus, lung collapse using double-lumen intubation is the first essential step before port insertion in VATS.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Match the following question on signs of testicular torsion:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-A, 2-B, 3-E, 4-D, 5-C

Testicular torsion is a urological emergency caused by twisting of the spermatic cord → acute ischemia, and is primarily a clinical diagnosis.

| Sign | Finding | Mechanism

| ---- | ------- | ---------

| Prehn sign | Pain not relieved by elevation of the testis (negative Prehn sign) | Distinguishes torsion from epididymitis

| Gouverneur sign | Horizontal (transverse) lie of the affected testis | Twisting of the spermatic cord rotates the testis

| Angell sign | Horizontal lie of the contralateral testis due to bilateral bell-clapper deformity | Indicates bilateral predisposition; supports bilateral orchidopexy

| Brunzel sign | High-riding (elevated) testis | Shortening of the twisted spermatic cord pulls the testis upward

| Ger sign | Absent cremasteric reflex | Ischemia and twisting abolish the reflex

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Match the following question on types of liver transplantation:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A, 5-E

Liver transplantation is classified based on source of graft and surgical technique, and understanding the core concept of each type is key:

• Orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT) → Entire diseased liver removed and replaced in the same anatomical position
• Living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) → Partial liver graft from a healthy donor (liver regeneration capacity is crucial)
• Split liver transplantation → One donor liver divided → transplanted into two recipients (e.g., adult + child)
• Auxiliary liver transplantation → Native liver retained, partial graft added. Used in acute liver failure (temporary support)
• Domino liver transplantation → Liver from a patient with metabolic disease (e.g., familial amyloidosis) transplanted into another recipient

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Match the following suture materials (List I) with their most characteristic property/clinical use (List II):
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-3, B-4, C-5, D-2, E-1

• Polydioxanone (PDS) → Monofilament absorbable, very slow hydrolysis → retains strength >6 weeks → (3)
• Vicryl (Polyglactin 910) → Braided synthetic absorbable → loses strength relatively fast → (4)
• Silk → Natural, braided → high capillarity → infection risk → (5)
• Prolene (Polypropylene) → Non-absorbable, inert, high memory → ideal for vascular anastomosis → (2)
• Chromic catgut → Natural absorbable → degraded by proteolytic enzymes → more tissue reaction → (1)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Match the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A–4, B–1, C–5, D–3, E–2

To understand and differentiate the classical bedside clinical tests used in the evaluation of varicose veins, specifically to assess saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) competence, perforator incompetence, superficial reflux, and deep venous patency.

• Brodie–Trendelenburg test

→ Assesses SFJ incompetence by observing rapid venous filling after releasing proximal occlusion following leg elevation.

• Modified Perthes test

→ Evaluates deep venous patency while the patient walks with a thigh tourniquet; pain or venous distension suggests deep venous obstruction.

• Fegan’s method

→ Used to localize incompetent perforator veins by digital pressure over perforator sites.

• Morrissey cough test

→ Detects SFJ incompetence by feeling a transmitted impulse at the SFJ during coughing.

• Schwartz tap test

→ Demonstrates superficial venous reflux when a tapping impulse is transmitted proximally along the vein.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: McLaughlin score in trauma is used to determine which of the following?
options: To know the amount of fluid that has to be used for resuscitation.
To access the extent of neurological deficit post trauma.
To predict the need of a massive blood transfusion.
To evaluate the grade of shock.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. To predict the need of a massive blood transfusion.

Trauma patients can rapidly deteriorate due to occult hemorrhage, and early identification of those who will require massive transfusion is crucial to reduce mortality. The McLaughlin score is a trauma scoring system used to predict the need for massive blood transfusion (commonly defined as ≥10 units of PRBCs within 24 hours or significant blood requirement in early hours).

It uses early clinical and physiologic parameters (such as hypotension, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis/low base excess, and laboratory markers of hypoperfusion) to estimate the likelihood of major ongoing bleeding and the need for activation of a massive transfusion protocol (MTP).

Thus, the McLaughlin score is specifically applied to Predict the need for a massive blood transfusion in trauma, enabling prompt initiation of balanced blood product resuscitation and damage control strategies.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: On day 6 of hospitalization for aneurysmal SAH, a patient develops acute neurologic deficits. Transcranial Doppler shows elevated flow velocities. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypervolemia and induced hypertension

Delayed neurological deterioration 3–14 days after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is most commonly due to cerebral vasospasm, which leads to delayed cerebral ischemia.

• New focal neurological deficits around day 4–10

• Transcranial Doppler: elevated cerebral artery flow velocities → indicates vasospasm

Most appropriate management

Induced hypertension with hypervolemia (hemodynamic augmentation)

• Improves cerebral perfusion across vasospastic vessels

• Often combined with nimodipine (standard prophylaxis in SAH)

other options

• Immediate craniotomy: for rebleed or mass lesion, not vasospasm

• Anticoagulation: increases bleeding risk

• Rapid sodium correction: for severe hyponatremia, not focal deficits from vasospasm

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Presence of which of the following is a contraindication for surgical resection of the tumor ina patient with carcinoma of the head of the pancreas?
options: Para-aortic lymph nodes in operative field
Tumor surrounding celiac axis for 90 degree
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hepatic metastasis

• Distant metastasis (e.g., liver) = absolute contraindication to curative resection in carcinoma head of pancreas.
• Tumor size >5 cm → not a contraindication if resectable.
• Para-aortic nodes → considered M1 disease in many protocols, but often detected intraoperatively; still strongest classic answer remains liver metastasis.
• Celiac axis involvement <180° (e.g., 90°) → borderline resectable, not absolute contraindication.

Key takeaway:

• Any distant metastasis (especially liver) = unresectable disease

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Regarding cold ischemia time (CIT) during organ preservation, which statement is most accurate?
options: Heart can safely tolerate >24 hours of cold ischemia
Kidney typically tolerates the longest CIT among solid organs
Liver tolerates longer CIT than kidney
CIT has no effect on graft survival if UW solution is used
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kidney typically tolerates the longest CIT among solid organs

Cold ischemia time (CIT) is the duration an organ remains preserved at low temperature between procurement and transplantation.

Clinical importance

• Longer CIT → increased risk of delayed graft function

• Higher acute rejection rates

• Reduced long-term graft survival

• Even with preservation solutions (e.g., UW solution), prolonged CIT worsens outcomes.

Organ tolerance to cold ischemia (approximate safe limits)

• Kidney: 24–36 hours (longest tolerance)

• Liver: 8–12 hours

• Pancreas: 12–18 hours

• Heart: 4–6 hours (least tolerant)

• Lung: 6–8 hours

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The following flap was being used for facial reconstruction surgery. Identify the flap:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thoracoacromial artery

The pectoralis major myocutaneous flap (PMMC) is a commonly used pedicled flap for head and neck/facial reconstruction, especially when microvascular free flaps are not feasible. It provides a large, reliable bulk of well-vascularized tissue that can be rotated to cover facial and oral cavity defects.

The vascular pedicle of the PMMC flap is the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery (branch of the axillary artery). Recognition of this pedicle is essential because the flap is designed and raised based on this blood supply, allowing it to be transferred while maintaining intact vascularity.

Thus, when a flap is harvested from the anterior chest wall for facial reconstruction and is based on the pectoralis major muscle, the supplying vessel is Thoracoacromial artery (pectoral branch).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Ultrasound image is shown below for a particular condition. Which of the following ultrasound criteria is most diagnostic of this condition?
options: Target sign with alternating hypoechoic and hyperechoic rings in ileum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) is a classic cause of gastric outlet obstruction in early infancy, best diagnosed by ultrasound with objective measurements.

• Most reliable parameter:

o    Pyloric muscle thickness > 3 mm

• Supportive parameter:

o    Pyloric channel length > 15–18 mm

Clinical correlation:

• Age: 3–6 weeks
• Vomiting: non-bilious, projectile
• Exam: palpable “olive” in epigastrium
• Labs: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis"

Imaging signs:

• Target/doughnut sign (transverse)
• Cervix/shoulder sign (longitudinal)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What are the different levels of triage in emergency care?
options: Head neck, thoracic and abdominal triage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediate, delayed, and minimal triage

Triage is the process of sorting patients in the emergency setting (especially during disasters/mass casualty incidents) based on severity of injury and urgency of treatment, with the goal of achieving the maximum number of survivors using limited resources.

The classic disaster triage categories are:

• Immediate (Red): life-threatening but treatable injuries requiring urgent intervention (airway compromise, major hemorrhage, shock)
• Delayed (Yellow): serious injuries but stable enough to wait (fractures without shock, moderate burns)
• Minimal (Green): minor injuries (“walking wounded”)

(Often a fourth category is included: Expectant/Dead (Black) for nonsurvivable injuries or deceased.)

Thus, the levels of triage described in the question correspond to Immediate, delayed, and minimal triage (Option B).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is root value of nerve which is most commonly injured in laparoscopic hernia surgery, resulting in sensory loss over the lateral thigh?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. L2-L3

The most commonly injured nerve in laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair is the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, which leads to meralgia paresthetica (burning pain and sensory loss over lateral thigh).

Root value: L2–L3 → Correct answer: A

• Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve arises from lumbar plexus (L2–L3)

• Purely sensory nerve

• Supplies anterolateral thigh

• Vulnerable during:

o Laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair

o Mesh fixation/tacker placement near ASIS

o Retroperitoneal dissection

Clinical manifestation of injury:

• Burning pain/paresthesia over lateral thigh

• Numbness without motor deficit

• Known as meralgia paresthetica

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis based on the ERCP image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Biliary ascariasis

Biliary ascariasis occurs when Ascaris lumbricoides migrates from the duodenum through the ampulla of Vater into the common bile duct (CBD) or intrahepatic ducts. It is an important cause of biliary colic and obstructive symptoms in endemic regions.

ERCP appearance (classic)

On ERCP, biliary ascariasis produces a characteristic linear, elongated filling defect within the contrast-filled bile duct, often described as:

• “Strip sign” / “linear filling defect”
• Sometimes a “rail/parallel line” appearance if the worm’s outline is seen

This differs from stones, which appear as round/oval filling defects, and from choledochal cyst or Caroli disease, which show ductal dilatations rather than intraductal linear defects.

Management principle

• Endoscopic extraction via ERCP (preferred when symptomatic obstruction/cholangitis)
• Followed by antihelminthic therapy (e.g., albendazole) after removal to prevent recurrence

Therefore, the ERCP image is diagnostic of biliary ascariasis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common mediastinal mass in children?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Neurogenic tumor

Mediastinal masses in children most commonly arise from the posterior mediastinum, and the most common mediastinal tumors in pediatric patients are neurogenic tumors. These include neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma, ganglioneuroma, and other tumors of sympathetic chain origin. Neurogenic tumors are particularly frequent in young children and often present with respiratory symptoms (cough, wheeze) due to airway compression or may be detected incidentally on chest imaging.

In contrast, thymoma is rare in children and typically occurs in adults. Bronchogenic cysts are congenital mediastinal lesions, commonly in the middle mediastinum, but they are less common overall than neurogenic tumors as a cause of pediatric mediastinal masses. Hence, the most common mediastinal mass in children is a neurogenic tumor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most frequent cause of adrenal incidentaloma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Non-functioning adenoma

The most common cause of adrenal incidentaloma is a non-functioning adrenal adenoma.

• Adrenal incidentaloma = adrenal mass detected incidentally on imaging done for unrelated reasons.

• Majority (\~70–80%) are benign, non-secretory cortical adenomas.

• Functional tumors are less common and include:

o Subclinical Cushing syndrome (most common functional lesion)

o Pheochromocytoma

o Aldosterone-producing adenoma

All adrenal incidentalomas must be evaluated for:

1. Hormonal activity (cortisol, catecholamines, aldosterone if hypertensive)

2. Malignancy risk (size >4–6 cm, irregular margins, heterogeneity)

Even if asymptomatic, biochemical screening is mandatory to rule out functional tumors.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is the most appropriate management strategy for the following hepatic hydatid cysts in a fit adult?
options: Single 3 cm CE1 cyst – immediate surgery
Large 8 cm CE1 cyst – albendazole plus PAIR
CE2 honeycomb cyst 7 cm – watch and wait only
CE5 heavily calcified cyst with no symptoms – emergency surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Large 8 cm CE1 cyst – albendazole plus PAIR

Management of hepatic hydatid cysts is based on the WHO (CE) ultrasound classification, cyst size, and symptoms.

Active cysts (CE1, CE2): require treatment

Inactive cysts (CE4, CE5): often managed conservatively if asymptomatic

CE classification and management

• CE1 (simple, unilocular cyst):

o <5 cm → Albendazole alone

o >5 cm → Albendazole + PAIR (puncture–aspiration–injection–reaspiration)

• CE2 (multiseptated “honeycomb” cyst):

o Usually requires surgery (PAIR less effective due to multiple daughter cysts)

• CE3: individualized (PAIR or surgery)

• CE4/CE5 (degenerating/calcified):

o Observation (“watch and wait”) if asymptomatic

Why option B is correct

Large active CE1 cyst (>5 cm) in fit adult →

Albendazole + PAIR is first-line minimally invasive treatment.

Why others are wrong

• Small CE1 → medical therapy first, not immediate surgery

• CE2 honeycomb → surgery preferred, not observation

• CE5 calcified → inactive cyst → no emergency surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which MRI kinetic curve is most concerning for invasive carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type III: Washout pattern

Refers to dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) kinetic curves used in breast MRI.

Type I – Progressive enhancement

• Slow and continuous increase in signal intensity
• Contrast keeps accumulating over time
• Usually benign lesions
• Examples: fibroadenoma, benign proliferative lesions

Type II – Plateau pattern

• Initial rapid enhancement
• Then signal intensity stabilizes (plateau)
• Intermediate suspicion
• Seen in both benign and malignant lesions.

Type III – Washout pattern (Most suspicious)

• Rapid initial enhancement
• Followed by decrease in signal intensity (washout)
• Indicates high vascularity and leaky tumor vessels
• Most concerning for invasive carcinoma

Type 0 – No enhancement

• No contrast uptake
• Usually normal tissue or non-enhancing benign lesion

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary indication for Stoppa’s repair?
options: Umbilical hernia in a cirrhotic patient
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Recurrent inguinal hernias

Stoppa’s repair (Giant prosthetic reinforcement of the visceral sac) is an open preperitoneal mesh repair used primarily for recurrent and bilateral inguinal hernias.

Principle of Stoppa repair

• Large mesh placed in preperitoneal space

• Covers entire myopectineal orifice bilaterally

• Reinforces all potential hernia sites:

o Direct

o Indirect

o Femoral

Main indications

• Recurrent inguinal hernia (most important)

• Bilateral inguinal hernias

• Large or multiple groin hernias

• Failed anterior mesh repair

Advantages

• Avoids scarred anterior plane in recurrent hernia

• Wide preperitoneal reinforcement

• Low recurrence rate

• Treats bilateral defects through single incision

Not indicated for

• Small primary uncomplicated hernias

• Strangulated hernia requiring emergency surgery

• Umbilical hernia

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the BRCA genes?
options: BRCA1 is located on the long arm of chromosome 17
BRCA2 carcinomas are Luminal A type
BRCA2 mutation is associated with male breast carcinoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. BRCA1 mutation causes well-differentiated cancer

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes involved in DNA double-strand break repair via homologous recombination. Germline mutations lead to hereditary breast–ovarian cancer syndromes with early-onset breast cancer and increased risk of ovarian and other cancers. Key facts:

• BRCA1 is located on chromosome 17q (long arm of chromosome 17).
• BRCA2 is located on chromosome 13q and is strongly associated with male breast cancer.

Tumor phenotype differences:

• BRCA1-associated breast cancers are typically high grade, poorly differentiated, and often triple-negative (basal-like).
• BRCA2-associated breast cancers are more often ER/PR positive and resemble Luminal-type tumors (commonly Luminal A pattern).

Therefore, the incorrect statement is “BRCA1 mutation causes well-differentiated cancer” because BRCA1 cancers are characteristically poorly differentiated/high-grade.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication for placement of the device?
options: Long-term feeding in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Head and neck malignancy undergoing radiotherapy
Persistent dysphagia expected to last more than 6 weeks
Requirement of enteral nutrition for 2 weeks after acute stroke
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Requirement of enteral nutrition for 2 weeks after acute stroke

The device shown is a PEG tube. A PEG tube (Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy) is a feeding tube inserted through the abdominal wall directly into the stomach, placed using an endoscope.It is used for short-term enteral nutrition and gastric decompression. The general rule for enteral feeding access is based on duration:

• < 4–6 weeks → Nasogastric / nasoenteric tube (Ryle’s tube)
• > 4–6 weeks → Gastrostomy/jejunostomy (PEG/PEJ)

Therefore, NG feeding is indicated in conditions needing temporary feeding support, such as:

• Acute stroke with dysphagia expected to improve
• Short-term inability to swallow

However, NG tubes are NOT ideal when long-term feeding is required, because of:

• aspiration risk
• tube dislodgement
• nasal/esophageal ulceration
• poor long-term tolerance

Long-term indications instead require PEG:

• ALS
• Head and neck malignancy during radiotherapy
• Dysphagia expected > 6 weeks

Hence, requirement of enteral nutrition for 2 weeks after acute stroke is not an indication for PEG-type long-term access (and is managed by NG tube), making it the correct “NOT an indication” option.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate matching of ulcer type with its characteristic feature?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4, E-5

• Arterial ulcer → Due to ischemia (PAD) → Punched out + very painful + worse at night (rest pain) → (2)
• Venous ulcer → Due to venous hypertension → Medial malleolus + hyperpigmentation (hemosiderin) + induration → (3)
• Neuropathic (diabetic) ulcer → Loss of sensation → repeated trauma → Pressure points + callus + painless → (1)
• Marjolin ulcer → SCC arising in chronic scar/burn ulcer → (4)
• Rodent ulcer (Basal cell carcinoma) → Rolled edges, pearly margins, central ulceration on face→ (5)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following patients comes under the category III non-heart-beating donor?
options: A patient who died during transportation to the hospital
A patient who died after failed resuscitation after reaching the hospital
A patient who was brought dead to the hospital
A patient who is awaiting death in the hospital
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A patient who is awaiting death in the hospital

Non-heart-beating donors refer to :

• donation after circulatory death (DCD).
• These donors are classified by the Maastricht classification,--> categorizes DCD based on the circumstances of cardiac arrest.

Maastricht categories (high yield)

• Category I: Dead on arrival / brought dead

• Category II: Unsuccessful resuscitation (unexpected arrest, CPR fails)

• Category III: Awaiting cardiac arrest after planned withdrawal of life support (controlled DCD)

• Category IV: Cardiac arrest in a brain-dead donor

Category III non-heart-beating donor = controlled DCD patient:

A patient who is awaiting death in the hospital (after withdrawal of ventilatory/circulatory support)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following represent features of a suspicious thyroid nodule:
options: [Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. [image not included in this edition]

Ultrasound features suggestive of a malignant (suspicious) thyroid nodule include:

• Hypoechoic solid nodule

• Irregular or ill-defined margins

• Microcalcifications (psammoma bodies → classic for papillary carcinoma)

• Taller-than-wide shape

• Increased internal vascularity

• Extrathyroidal extension or abnormal cervical nodes

Among these, microcalcifications within a hypoechoic solid nodule are one of the most specific signs of thyroid malignancy (especially papillary carcinoma).

In contrast, benign features include:

• Pure cystic or spongiform appearance

• Smooth margins

• Peripheral (eggshell) calcification

• Isoechoic/hyperechoic nodules

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are true?
options: Lymphoedema in the arm after treatment usually indicates a recurrence.
Radiotherapy after implant reconstruction of the breast gives a good cosmetic result.
Male breast cancer carries a poor prognosis when compared with female breast cancer stage by stage.
Chemotherapy is safe in second and third trimester in women with pregnancy associated breast cancer.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chemotherapy is safe in second and third trimester in women with pregnancy associated breast cancer.

Breast cancer management requires awareness of treatment-related complications, reconstructive outcomes, prognostic factors, and special clinical situations such as pregnancy.

• Arm lymphedema after breast cancer treatment is most commonly due to axillary lymph node dissection and/or radiotherapy causing lymphatic obstruction. It does not usually indicate recurrence unless accompanied by other concerning findings (eg, new hard nodes, progressive mass, skin changes). Therefore, it is not a reliable sign of recurrence.
• Radiotherapy after implant-based breast reconstruction is associated with a higher risk of complications such as capsular contracture, implant deformity, fibrosis, pain, and poor cosmetic outcome. Hence, cosmesis is often worse when radiotherapy is delivered after implant reconstruction.
• Male breast cancer prognosis, when compared stage-for-stage, is generally similar to female breast cancer. The overall survival may appear worse in men largely because they present later and are older, not because of intrinsically poorer biology stage-for-stage.
• Chemotherapy during pregnancy-associated breast cancer can be given safely in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, as organogenesis is complete after the first trimester. Standard regimens such as anthracycline-based therapy are commonly used. Chemotherapy is avoided in the 1st trimester due to teratogenicity risks and avoided near delivery due to neonatal myelosuppression.

Therefore, the correct true statement is:

d) Chemotherapy is safe in second and third trimester in women with pregnancy associated breast cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements best reflects the “rule of 12” for thyroid swellings?
options: Malignancy risk is higher in women than men
Cystic nodules carry higher risk than solid
Isolated nodules have higher risk than dominant
Generalized swelling carries the highest risk
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isolated nodules have higher risk than dominant

The Rule of 12 is a classical heuristic used for determining risk of malignancy is thyroid nodules.

1. Isolated Thyroid Swelling

• Solid nodule → 24% risk

• Male → 48%
• Female → 12%

• Cystic nodule → 12% risk

• Male → 24%
• Female → 6%

Key idea:

• Solid > Cystic in malignancy risk
• Male > Female

2. Dominant Thyroid Swelling (within multinodular goiter)

• Solid → 12% risk

• Male → 24%
• Female → 6%

• Cystic → 6% risk

• Male → 12%
• Female → 3%

Compared to isolated nodules, dominant nodules have half the risk.

3. Generalized Thyroid Swelling

• Overall malignancy risk → \~3%

Lowest risk category.

Core Concept (Rule of 12)

• Baseline risk halves as you go:

• Isolated → Dominant → Generalized

• Within each:

• Solid = double cystic
• Male = double female

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding retrosternal goitres?
options: Operated only if patient is symptomatic
Almost always operated by a midline sternotomy
Majority of the goitres derive their blood supply from mediastinal vessels
CT/MRI has to be done routinely in all patients
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT/MRI has to be done routinely in all patients

All patients with retrosternal (substernal) goitre should undergo cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) to assess the extent and anatomical relations of the goitre.

Why CT/MRI is routinely required:

• Determines inferior extent of the goitre into mediastinum

• Assesses tracheal compression, deviation, or narrowing

• Evaluates relation to great vessels and esophagus

• Helps plan surgical approach (cervical vs sternotomy)

• Detects posterior mediastinal extension

Key surgical pearls:

• Most retrosternal goitres can be removed via cervical approach (sternotomy rarely needed)

• Blood supply usually arises from inferior thyroid vessels (not mediastinal vessels)

• Surgery is recommended even if asymptomatic due to risk of:

o Sudden airway compression

o Malignancy

o Progressive enlargement

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) is not true?
options: Vaccination must be given at least 2 weeks prior to elective splenectomy.
It is more common when splenectomy is done for malignancy and hematological disorder than for trauma
Initial presentation involves fever and chills
Most cases occur after 2 years of splenectomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Most cases occur after 2 years of splenectomy

OPSI is caused by encapsulated organisms:

• Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common)
• Haemophilus influenzae
• Neisseria meningitidis

Timing:

• Risk is highest within the first 2 years after splenectomy
• Can occur lifelong, but early period is most critical
• Hence, statement “most cases occur after 2 years” is false

Clinical presentation: Sudden onset fever, chills → rapidly progresses to septic shock

Risk factors: Higher risk in hematological disorders and malignancy compared to trauma

Prevention:

• Vaccination at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy
• Post-splenectomy vaccines if emergency
• Prophylactic antibiotics in high-risk patients

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following symptoms are part of storage LUTS (lower urinary tract symptoms)? 1 - Frequency 2 - Nocturia 3 - Hesitancy 4 - Straining 5 - Urgency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 5

• Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) are classified according to the phase of micturition in which they occur: storage (filling), voiding (emptying), and post-micturition symptoms.
• Storage LUTS occur during the bladder filling phase and are classically remembered by the mnemonic FUN—Frequency, Urgency, Nocturia.
• Therefore, frequency (1), nocturia (2), and urgency (5) are storage LUTS, whereas hesitancy (3) and straining (4) are voiding/obstructive LUTS, typically seen in bladder outlet obstruction such as BPH.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of these is incorrect about management of hepatoma?
options: Milan criteria is applicable for single tumor up to 5 cm or three tumors each less than 3 cm
A FLR (future liver remnant) of at least 40% normal liver is a pre-requisite for resection
Colorectal metastasis to liver can be excised
Percutaneous ablation is used for hepatomas
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A FLR (future liver remnant) of at least 40% normal liver is a pre-requisite for resection

Management of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC/hepatoma) depends on tumor burden, liver function, and the feasibility of curative therapy (resection, transplantation, ablation). Key concepts:

• Milan criteria define eligibility for liver transplantation in HCC: single tumor ≤5 cm OR up to 3 tumors each ≤3 cm, with no vascular invasion or metastasis.
• Percutaneous ablation (RFA/MWA) is a curative option for small HCC (typically ≤3 cm, selected up to 5 cm).
• Liver metastasis from colorectal cancer is often resectable, and metastasectomy can be curative in selected patients.

Future Liver Remnant (FLR) requirement

The amount of liver that must remain after resection depends on baseline liver quality:

• Normal liver: FLR ≥ 20–25%
• Steatosis/chemotherapy-injured liver: FLR ≥ 30%
• Cirrhotic liver: FLR ≥ 40%

Thus, saying FLR must be at least 40% in normal liver is incorrect (40% is required for cirrhosis, not normal liver).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of these is the incorrect statement concerning the the appendix?
options: The base of the appendix is found at the confluence of the three taeniae coli of the caecum.
The appendicular artery is an end artery
Neuroendocrine tumors of the appendix arise from the argentaffin cells (Kulchitsky) at the base of the crypts
Pseudomyxoma peritonii is a frequent complication of appendiceal carcinoids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pseudomyxoma peritonii is a frequent complication of appendiceal carcinoids

• Anatomy of Appendix:

o The base of the appendix is located at the convergence of the three taeniae coli → reliable surgical landmark

o Appendicular artery (branch of ileocolic artery) is an end artery → predisposes to ischemia and gangrene

• Tumors:

o Appendiceal carcinoids (neuroendocrine tumors) arise from argentaffin (Kulchitsky) cells at the base of crypts

o Usually slow-growing and often found incidentally

• Important distinction:

o Pseudomyxoma peritonei is classically associated with mucinous tumors of the appendix/ovary, NOT carcinoids

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which statement best describes the Palomo procedure for varicocele?
options: Subinguinal ligation of pampiniform plexus preserving artery and lymphatics
High retroperitoneal ligation of testicular vein and testicular artery
Endovascular embolization of the internal spermatic vein
Inguinal approach isolating and preserving testicular artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High retroperitoneal ligation of testicular vein and testicular artery

The Palomo procedure is a surgical treatment for varicocele involving high retroperitoneal ligation of the testicular vein along with the testicular artery.

• Approach: Retroperitoneal (high ligation)

• Ligation of:

o Testicular vein

o Often the testicular artery (classical Palomo)

• Lymphatics usually preserved or may be sacrificed depending on technique

• Reduces venous reflux responsible for varicocele

Indications

• Symptomatic varicocele

• Infertility with abnormal semen analysis

• Testicular atrophy in adolescents

Comparison with other techniques

• Microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy: preserves artery & lymphatics (lowest recurrence)

• Ivanissevich procedure: inguinal vein ligation with artery preservation

• Embolization: radiologic occlusion of testicular vein

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: You are evaluating a patient in the burns unit in your ward. The patient is suffering from 3rd degree circumferential burns along the thorax and abdominal area. The patient received 8L of Ringer lactate at the primary facility before being referred to your hospital. His BP is 82/54 mmHg, HR is 130 BPM. His urine output for the last 3 hours is less than 20 mL. What is the next step in this case?
options: Measure urine output after 1 hour and continue fluids.
Give a diuretic to help with the possible urinary retention
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Measure bladder pressure.

Severe burn patients with circumferential full-thickness (3rd degree) thoracoabdominal burns who receive large-volume fluid resuscitation are at high risk of developing abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) due to massive capillary leak, visceral edema, and third spacing. ACS leads to intra-abdominal hypertension, causing impaired venous return and organ hypoperfusion.

Key clinical clues suggesting ACS in this patient:

• Circumferential trunk burns (restrictive “burn eschar” + raised compartment pressures)
• Received massive fluids (8 L RL)
• Persistent hypotension (82/54) and tachycardia
• Oliguria (<20 mL over 3 hours) despite aggressive resuscitation

→ suggests renal hypoperfusion, not urinary retention

The next best step is to measure intra-abdominal pressure, most commonly via bladder pressure measurement, which is the standard bedside method for diagnosing intra-abdominal hypertension/ACS.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is brought by her mother with concerns about asymmetrical breast development. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Reassure and reassess

Breast asymmetry is a common physiological finding during puberty. In adolescent girls with isolated asymmetrical breast development and no red-flag features (e.g., mass, pain, skin changes, nipple discharge, or lymphadenopathy), the appropriate management is reassurance and follow-up, as breast development usually becomes symmetrical over time.

Why not the other options?

• A. Biopsy of the larger breast: Not indicated in physiological pubertal breast asymmetry.
• B. Mammography: Not recommended in adolescents due to dense breast tissue and low likelihood of malignancy.
• D. Breast ultrasound: Reserved for a palpable breast mass or other suspicious clinical findings, not for isolated asymmetry.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 29-year-old lady presents with a history of discharge from the nipple of the left breast since 1 month duration. Which one of the following is not warranted in the initial assessment of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Histo/Cytopathology

A 29-year-old woman with nipple discharge requires an initial clinical and imaging assessment to identify an underlying breast lesion.

1. Clinical examination — Correct

• Assess the breast and nipple for a palpable mass, skin/nipple changes, and characteristics of the discharge.

2. Histo/Cytopathology — Incorrect / Not routinely warranted initially

• Routine cytological examination of nipple discharge has limited diagnostic value and is not part of the standard initial evaluation.
• Tissue diagnosis is performed when imaging or examination identifies a suspicious lesion.

3. Mammography — Correct

• May be performed when clinically indicated, particularly when the discharge is pathological or there are suspicious findings.

4. Ultrasonography — Correct

• Ultrasound is particularly useful in women <30 years and is generally the preferred initial imaging modality for a breast abnormality in this age group.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of spontaneous, unilateral, blood-stained discharge from a single duct of the right nipple. There is no palpable breast lump. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intraductal papilloma

Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of spontaneous, unilateral, blood-stained nipple discharge from a single duct in women aged 35–55 years. It is a benign papillary tumor arising within a major lactiferous duct, usually located beneath the areola.

Why not the other options?

• B. Fibroadenoma: Presents as a painless, mobile breast lump; nipple discharge is uncommon.
• C. Duct ectasia: Usually occurs in perimenopausal women and causes multiduct, thick green/brown, sticky discharge with nipple retraction.
• D. Breast carcinoma: May cause bloody nipple discharge, but is usually associated with a palpable hard irregular lump, skin changes, or axillary lymphadenopathy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with a palpable lump in the left breast. Mammography suggests malignancy, and tissue diagnosis is required. Which is the preferred biopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Core needle biopsy

• Core needle biopsy (CNB) is the preferred initial biopsy for suspected breast cancer.
• It provides tissue architecture, unlike FNAC which provides only cytology.
• Histology allows assessment of tumor type, grade, ER/PR status, and HER2 expression.
• It guides neoadjuvant therapy and surgical planning.
• FNAC cannot reliably distinguish in situ from invasive carcinoma.
• Excision biopsy is no longer the first-line diagnostic procedure.
• Incisional biopsy is rarely required.
• CNB is usually performed under ultrasound or stereotactic guidance.
• It has high sensitivity and specificity with minimal morbidity.
• Triple assessment = Clinical examination + Imaging + Core needle biopsy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with a rapidly growing, painless mass in her right breast that she first noticed about 3 months ago. On physical examination, the mass is well-circumscribed, lobulated, and larger than 5 cm in diameter. A history of a similar lesion occurred 2 years back also. A core needle biopsy is performed, and the histological examination reveals the image as shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phyllodes tumour

• Age: 42 years (phyllodes usually occurs in middle-aged women).
• Rapidly growing mass; Large size (>5 cm).
• Well-circumscribed and lobulated; History of recurrence.

Histopathology shows:

• Leaf-like (phyllodes) architecture with Cleft-like spaces
• Hypercellular stroma

Suggests phyllodes tumor > fibroadenoma.

| Condition | Key features

| --------- | ------------

| Phyllodes tumour | Rapid growth, large (>5 cm), leaf-like histology

| Fibroadenoma | Small, slow growing, common in young women

| Invasive ductal carcinoma | Irregular infiltrative mass

| Ductal papilloma | Usually causes nipple discharge

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 43-year-old woman presented with serous discharge from a single duct of the nipple of her right breast which was sent for evaluation. She is unlikely to be suffering from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fibrocystic disease

Pathological nipple discharge is typically spontaneous, unilateral, and from a single duct. A serous discharge from a single duct is most commonly caused by intraductal papilloma, but it can also occur in duct ectasia and carcinoma. It is uncommon in fibrocystic disease.

Why is A correct?

• A. Fibrocystic disease ✅: Correct (unlikely).

• Usually presents with cyclical breast pain, nodularity, and multiple cysts.
• Nipple discharge, if present, is usually non-spontaneous and from multiple ducts, making single-duct serous discharge uncommon.

About other options:

• B. Intraductal papilloma ❌

• Most common cause of spontaneous unilateral single-duct nipple discharge.
• Discharge is typically serous or blood-stained.

• C. Duct ectasia ❌

• Can present with unilateral nipple discharge, which is often green, brown, or serous, along with nipple retraction and periareolar tenderness.

• D. Carcinoma ❌

• May present with spontaneous unilateral single-duct serous or blood-stained discharge, especially if associated with a breast lump.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents with a right-sided breast lump of size 20x15 cm with a recent increase in size. The lump is erythematous, ill-defined, and fixed to the chest wall. She has a positive family history of breast cancer in her mother. A diagnosis of inflammatory breast cancer is made. What is the next step in management?
options: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by modified radical mastectomy
Modified radical mastectomy followed by chemotherapy
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by breast conservation surgery and sentinel lymph node biopsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by modified radical mastectomy

Inflammatory breast cancer presents with rapid breast enlargement, erythema, peau d’orange, and skin involvement due to dermal lymphatic invasion, indicating locally advanced (T4d) disease. Primary surgery is avoided initially because the disease is diffuse.

Management follows a sequence: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy → Modified radical mastectomy → Postoperative radiotherapy, followed by targeted or hormonal therapy depending on receptor status.

Breast-conserving surgery is contraindicated in inflammatory breast cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady presents with a hard lump in the left breast. On examination, the lump is found to be 4 cm × 6 cm in size, not fixed to the skin, but fixed to the underlying pectoralis major muscle. The T stage of this is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. cT3

The breast lump measures 4 × 6 cm, so its largest dimension is 6 cm.

Breast cancer T staging by tumor size:

• T1: ≤2 cm
• T2: >2 cm to ≤5 cm
• T3: >5 cm
• T4: Tumor of any size with extension to the chest wall and/or skin

Although the tumor is fixed to the pectoralis major muscle, involvement of the pectoralis muscle alone does not qualify as chest-wall invasion for T4 staging.

Therefore:

• 6 cm tumor + no skin involvement/chest-wall invasion → cT3

Why not the other options?

• (a) cT4a: Requires invasion of the chest wall; pectoralis muscle involvement alone is not sufficient.
• (b) cT3 — Correct: Tumor >5 cm without T4 features.
• (c) cT4b: Requires features such as ulceration, satellite skin nodules, or edema/peau d’orange.
• (d) cT2: Tumor is >5 cm, so it exceeds the T2 range.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady presents with history of a painless lump in the right breast since 1 month. On examination, the lump is hard, 3 × 4 cm in size in the upper outer quadrant and is not fixed to the skin or the underlying structures. The axilla reveals firm mobile lymph nodes (level I). Rest of systemic examination is normal. The clinical stage of this disease is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. cT₂N₁Mₓ

This patient has carcinoma of the breast. Clinical staging is based on the TNM classification (AJCC).

• Tumor size: 3 × 4 cm → Largest dimension is 4 cm, which is >2 cm but ≤5 cm → T₂
• Lymph nodes: Mobile ipsilateral level I axillary lymph nodes → N₁
• Metastasis: No evidence of distant metastasis has been evaluated → Mₓ

Therefore, the clinical stage is cT₂N₁Mₓ.

• T₂: Tumor >2 cm but ≤5 cm.
• N₁: Metastasis to mobile ipsilateral level I or II axillary lymph nodes.
• Mₓ: Distant metastasis cannot be assessed clinically.

Why not the other options?

• A. cT₁N₁Mₓ: Incorrect because T₁ tumors are ≤2 cm.
• C. cT₃N₁Mₓ: Incorrect because T₃ tumors are >5 cm.
• D. cT₃N₂Mₓ: Incorrect because the tumor is not >5 cm, and N₂ requires fixed/matted axillary nodes or internal mammary node involvement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old female underwent MRM (Modified Radical Mastectomy). After few years, she developed lymphedema of the ipsilateral arm. Which of the following malignancy can develop in her arm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymphangiosarcoma

Stewart–Treves syndrome refers to the development of lymphangiosarcoma in a limb affected by chronic lymphedema, classically occurring years after Modified Radical Mastectomy (MRM) with axillary lymph node dissection.

Why not other options?

• B. Malignant melanoma: Associated with UV exposure, dysplastic nevi, and genetic predisposition; not related to post-mastectomy lymphedema.
• C. Lymphoma: Not a recognized complication of chronic lymphedema after MRM.
• D. Malignant fibrous histiocytoma: A soft tissue sarcoma with no specific association with chronic lymphedema.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old patient underwent a lumpectomy and was found to have low-grade DCIS with 2 mm clear margins. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radiotherapy

Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast malignancy in which malignant epithelial cells are confined to the ductal system without breaching the basement membrane. It is Stage 0 (TisN0M0) breast cancer. In a patient with:

• Low-grade DCIS
• Breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy)
• Clear surgical margins (≥2 mm)

The standard next step is adjuvant whole-breast radiotherapy, which significantly reduces the risk of ipsilateral local recurrence.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mastectomy: Reserved for multicentric/extensive DCIS, persistently positive margins, or when breast conservation is not feasible.
• B. BCT (Breast-Conserving Therapy): Lumpectomy has already been performed; breast-conserving therapy consists of lumpectomy + radiotherapy.
• D. Tamoxifen: May be offered in ER-positive DCIS after surgery ± radiotherapy to reduce recurrence but is not a substitute for radiotherapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old female presents with pain in her back of recent onset, which has become severe of late. During the course of investigations, she was found to have lytic lesions in the vertebrae and ribs. Which of the following organs should be carefully screened now for detecting the primary cause of these lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Breast

In an older woman presenting with multiple osteolytic lesions involving the vertebrae and ribs, metastatic carcinoma should be strongly suspected. Among women, the breast is the most common primary site causing skeletal metastases, particularly to the axial skeleton (vertebrae, ribs, pelvis, skull, and proximal femur). Can present initially with back pain, pathological fractures, or hypercalcemia before the primary tumor is diagnosed.

Therefore, the breast should be carefully screened to identify the primary malignancy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Small intestine: Primary malignancies are uncommon and rarely present with isolated lytic bone metastases.
• B. Large intestine: Colorectal cancer more commonly metastasizes to the liver and lungs before bone.
• C. Adrenal: Primary adrenal malignancies are rare and are not a common source of multiple lytic bone lesions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman undergoes screening mammography. The figure suggests a likely diagnosis of: (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Involuting Fibroadenoma

The mammogram shows coarse, popcorn-like calcifications within a well-circumscribed mass. This characteristic "popcorn" pattern of calcification is the classic radiographic appearance of an involuting fibroadenoma. These benign breast tumors typically develop in younger women and often undergo calcification during the involution process as women age, particularly after menopause.

Visual Support: The image demonstrates the typical popcorn calcification pattern within a well-defined mass - the hallmark radiographic appearance of an involuting fibroadenoma.

Other Options:

Option A. Intraductal Carcinoma Breast - Incorrect because DCIS typically presents with fine\, linear\, branching or pleomorphic microcalcifications in a segmental or ductal distribution\, not the coarse popcorn-like calcifications seen here.

Option C. Fibroadenosis - Incorrect as fibroadenosis (fibrocystic changes) typically shows multiple small cysts and areas of increased density without the characteristic popcorn calcifications visible in this image.

Option D. Fat Necrosis - Incorrect because fat necrosis typically appears as an oil cyst with a thin calcified rim\, or as spiculated masses with architectural distortion. It lacks the typical popcorn calcification pattern seen in this mammogram.

Educational Objective:

Coarse "popcorn" calcifications within a well-circumscribed mass on mammography are pathognomonic for an involuting fibroadenoma, representing the degenerative calcification of a previously non-calcified fibroadenoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female presented with an ulcerated breast lump. Nipple retraction was seen, with some warmth and redness. On biopsy, it was diagnosed as invasive ductal carcinoma. Which of these correctly represents the AJCC stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T4b

• Ulcerated breast lump, Warmth + redness, Nipple retraction —> These indicate skin involvement

T4b definition (AJCC): includes:-

• Ulceration of skin
• Satellite skin nodules
• Oedema (peau d’orange)

Hence, fits T4b staging.

❌Stage IV with N1–N2

Stage IV requires M1 (distant metastasis)--> No metastasis mentioned in question stem

❌Stage IIIB

• Includes T4 lesions, but this stage depends on N status also
• Nodal status not given → cannot be stage IIIB

❌ It cannot be M1

• Not a valid staging option ( because AJCC staging needs N/M stage, which isn't mentioned in the Question stem)

AJCC staging for CA BREAST ➖

| T Stage | Meaning

| ------- | -------

| Tis | Carcinoma in situ

| T1 | Tumour ≤ 2 cm

| T2 | Tumour > 2 cm but ≤ 5 cm

| T3 | Tumour > 5 cm

| T4 | Tumour of any size with skin/chest wall involvement

| N Stage | Meaning

| ------- | -------

| N0 | No lymph node involvement

| N1 | 1–3 lymph nodes involved

| N2 | 4–9 lymph nodes involved

| N3 | ≥10 lymph nodes or major node involvement

| M Stage | Meaning

| ------- | -------

| M0 | No distant metastasis

| M1 | Distant metastasis present

According  to AJCC classification

Stage 0

• Tis N0 M0

In situ disease (DCIS/LCIS), no invasion

Stage I (early)

• T1 N0 M0

• Tumor ≤ 2 cm, no nodal or distant spread

• T1 N1mi M0 (Stage IB)

• Micrometastasis in nodes

Stage II (localized spread)

• T0–T2 N1 M0

• Small tumor with mobile ipsilateral nodes

• T2 N0 M0

• Tumor 2–5 cm, no nodes

• T3 N0–N1 M0

• Tumor >5 cm, limited nodes

Stage III (locally advanced)

• T0–T3 N2–N3 M0

• Extensive nodal involvement (fixed/matted, supraclavicular, internal mammary)

• Any T with N3
• May include T4

• Chest wall or skin involvement (e.g., inflammatory breast cancer)

Stage IV (metastatic)

• Any T, Any N, M1
• Distant metastasis present (bone, liver, lung, brain)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female with breast cancer undergoes investigation which reveals the presence of ER positivity. Presence of ER is important as it is a:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prognostic marker

• ER positivity tells you how well the tumour will respond to endocrine therapy (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors), making it a prognostic > predictive marker (remains controversial)
• Although ER status correlates with a better prognosis, its clinical value also lies in predicting the benefit of hormonal treatment; it is not diagnostic, nor a surrogate molecular subtype marker on its own.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A middle-aged, obese P3L3 woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding and is diagnosed with an endometrial polyp with a single feeding vessel, as shown on hysteroscopy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hysteroscopic polypectomy

Hysteroscopic polypectomy is the treatment of choice for symptomatic endometrial polyps. It allows direct visualization and complete removal of the polyp along with its stalk (feeding vessel), reducing recurrence and providing tissue for histopathological examination to exclude malignancy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Dilatation and curettage (D&C): Blind procedure with a high chance of missing focal lesions or incomplete removal.
• B. LNG-IUS: May reduce abnormal uterine bleeding but does not remove the polyp.
• C. Hysterectomy: Not first-line for a benign endometrial polyp; reserved for selected cases with coexisting pathology or confirmed malignancy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A mother presents on day 8 of normal vaginal delivery with painful left breast, fever with chills. On examination, her left breast is tender and red with raised local temperature. What should be the line of management?
options: Analgesics and antibiotics, plenty of fluids, breastfeeding continued from right breast
Hot fomentation, analgesics, restricted fluids, avoid breastfeeding from either breast
Antibiotics, incision and drainage, avoid breastfeeding from either breast
Antibiotics, analgesics, restricted fluids, breastfeeding continued from right breast
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Analgesics and antibiotics, plenty of fluids, breastfeeding continued from right breast

The presentation is most consistent with acute puerperal mastitis:

• Day 8 postpartum
• Fever with chills
• Painful, tender breast
• Redness and increased local temperature

Management includes:

• Antibiotics → Treat bacterial mastitis, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
• Analgesics → Relieve pain and inflammation.
• Adequate fluids → Maintain hydration.
• Continue breastfeeding → Breastfeeding should generally be continued because milk stasis worsens mastitis. Feeding/pumping from the affected breast is also usually encouraged if tolerated.

Why not the other options?

• (b) Restricted fluids and stopping breastfeeding are incorrect; both can worsen milk stasis.
• (c) Incision and drainage is indicated for a breast abscess, not uncomplicated mastitis. Breastfeeding usually does not need to be stopped.
• (d) Restricted fluids are inappropriate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient has been diagnosed with Luminal A type of breast carcinoma. Which of the following best describes the marker profile in her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ER+, PR+, HER2- Low Ki67

Option B: Luminal A breast carcinoma →  characterized by strong hormone receptor positivity.

| Subtype | ER/PR | HER2 | Ki-67 | Behavior

| ------- | ----- | ---- | ----- | --------

| Luminal A | +/+ | − | Low | Best prognosis

| Luminal B | +/+ | ± | High | Intermediate

| HER2-enriched | −/− | + | High | Aggressive

| Triple-negative | −/− | − | High | Most aggressive

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a 4.5 cm breast lump and ipsilateral mobile axillary lymph nodes, without distant metastasis. What is the most appropriate stage of this breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stage 2B

Breast cancer staging is based on the TNM (Tumor–Node–Metastasis) classification. In this patient:

• Tumor size = 4.5 cm → T2 (>2 cm but ≤5 cm)
• Ipsilateral mobile axillary lymph nodes → N1
• No distant metastasis → M0

TNM: T2N1M0 = Stage IIB

Why not the other options?

• A. Stage 2A: Includes T2N0M0 or T1N1M0.
• C. Stage 3A: Usually N2 disease (fixed/matted axillary nodes or internal mammary nodes) or larger tumors with advanced nodal involvement.
• D. Stage 3B: Tumor with chest wall or skin involvement (T4) regardless of N status.

| Stage | TNM

| ----- | ---

| IIA | T0–1N1M0 or T2N0M0

| IIB | T2N1M0 or T3N0M0

| IIIA | T0–2N2M0 or T3N1–2M0

| IIIB | T4, any N, M0

| IIIC | Any T, N3, M0

| IV | Any T, any N, M1

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a breast lesion as shown in the image. According to the TNM staging system, which stage does this lesion most likely represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. T4D

The image demonstrates inflammatory breast carcinoma (T4D),

• Identified by extensive peau d'orange involving more than one-third of the breast skin→ due to dermal infiltration into lymphatics→ causing lymphedema and prominent hair follicles.

T4 subcategories in TNM staging:

• T4a: Chest wall invasion (excludes pectoralis muscle alone)
• T4b: Skin involvement (ulceration/peau d'orange/satellite nodules)
• T4c: Both T4a + T4b features
• T4d: Inflammatory breast cancer (peau d'orange >1/3 of skin)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An Intraoperative image of MRM (Modified Radical Mastectomy) is shown. What nerve is marked with black arrow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Median pectoral nerve

Intraoperative view during Modified Radical Mastectomy (MRM).

The nerve marked is piercing the pectoralis minor muscle  feature of the medial pectoral nerve.

Important nerves encountered in MRM

| Nerve | Course | Clinical importance

| ----- | ------ | -------------------

| Long thoracic nerve | Runs on chest wall along serratus anterior | Injury → winging of scapula

| Thoracodorsal nerve | Runs with thoracodorsal vessels to latissimus dorsi | Injury → weak arm adduction

| Medial pectoral nerve | Pierces pectoralis minor | Supplies pectoralis minor & major

| Subscapular nerves | Supply subscapularis and teres major | Seen deeper near axilla

Ruling out other options:

Long thoracic nerve

• Lies on serratus anterior along chest wall, not piercing pectoralis minor.

Thoracodorsal nerve

• Runs with thoracodorsal vessels to latissimus dorsi.

Subscapular nerve

• Lies deeper near subscapularis muscle.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Breast cancer of size 6 x 8 cm with dimpling with invasion of Pectoralis Major and ipsilateral matted axillary nodes belongs to what TNM stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. T3N2M0

Tumor size = 6 × 8 cm

Largest dimension = 8 cm

So tumor is:

• 5 cm → T3

Dimpling of skin

Skin dimpling/tethering alone does not make it T4.

T4 requires:

• Ulceration
• Satellite skin nodules
• Peau d’orange
• Chest wall invasion

Invasion of Pectoralis Major

Invasion of pectoralis major muscle alone is NOT chest wall invasion.

Chest wall invasion (T4a) means invasion of:

• Ribs
• Intercostal muscles
• Serratus anterior

NOT pectoralis muscle.

Hence still T3, not T4.

Ipsilateral matted axillary lymph nodes

Matted/fixed ipsilateral axillary nodes = N2

No distant metastasis mentioned

→ M0

Final TNM Stage

| Component | Stage

| --------- | -----

| Tumor >5 cm | T3

| Matted axillary nodes | N2

| No metastasis | M0

Final Answer: T3N2M0

| T Stage | Definition

| ------- | ----------

| T1 | Tumour ≤ 20 mm in greatest dimension

| T1mi | Tumour ≤ 1 mm

| T1a | Tumour > 1 mm but ≤ 5 mm (round 1.0–1.9 mm to 2 mm)

| T1b | Tumour > 5 mm but ≤ 10 mm

| T1c | Tumour > 10 mm but ≤ 20 mm

| T2 | Tumour > 20 mm but ≤ 50 mm

| T3 | Tumour > 50 mm

| T4 | Tumour of any size with extension to chest wall and/or skin (dermis alone not included)

| T4a | Extension to chest wall (pectoral muscle involvement alone does not qualify)

| T4b | Skin ulceration, satellite nodules, or oedema (peau d’orange), not inflammatory carcinoma

| T4c | Both T4a and T4b present

| T4d | Inflammatory carcinoma (peau d’orange, redness > 1/3rd breast ± lump)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the imaging modality shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mammography

Mammography is a specialized low-dose X-ray imaging technique used to evaluate the breast for:

• Breast cancer screening
• Detection of palpable lumps
• Microcalcifications
• Architectural distortion and asymmetry

It is the screening test for breast carcinoma.

• Each breast is compressed between two plates to improve image quality and reduce radiation dose.
• Standard views:

• Craniocaudal (CC) view
• Mediolateral oblique (MLO) view

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Image of a patient with large ulcerated breast cancer with liver metastasis. What is the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Simple mastectomy

This patient has:

• Large ulcerated/fungating Breast cancer
• Already has liver metastasis → indicates Stage IV disease

In metastatic breast cancer:

• Surgery is usually palliative, not curative.

Why Simple Mastectomy?
