A fungating/ulcerated breast mass can cause:

• Bleeding
• Infection
• Foul discharge
• Pain
• Difficulty in wound care

Hence, toilet/simple mastectomy is done for palliation and local symptom control.

Simple mastectomy:

• Removes breast tissue only
• No formal axillary clearance

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Infiltration of which anatomical structure leads to the characteristic defect in the breast shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cooper's ligament

Skin dimpling in breast malignancy occurs due to fibrosis and traction on Cooper’s ligaments,  tether the skin to the pectoral fascia.

This infiltration shortens these ligaments, pulling the skin inward.

Duct involvement causes nipple retraction, while dermal lymphatic blockage produces peau d’orange.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Most important prognostic factor for Carcinoma Breast is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Axillary lymph node status

Option A: Axillary lymph node status

It reflects the extent of disease spread beyond the primary tumor.

• The number of involved lymph nodes strongly correlates with:

• Risk of recurrence
• Overall survival

• It is a key component of staging (TNM system).

Option B: Tumor size → Important for staging, but less predictive than nodal involvement.

Option C: Distant metastasis → Indicates advanced disease (Stage IV), but among early-stage cases, lymph nodes guide prognosis more precisely.

Option D: Hormonal status (ER/PR, HER2) → Important for treatment decisions, but not the single strongest prognostic factor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The malignancy associated with Stewart-Treves syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymphangiosarcoma

Stewart–Treves syndrome is the development of lymphangiosarcoma, a rare but highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor, in the setting of chronic lymphedema. It classically occurs after radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection, although it can develop in any cause of longstanding lymphedema.

Why not other options?

• B. Malignant melanoma: Associated with UV exposure, dysplastic nevi, and genetic syndromes, not chronic lymphedema.
• C. Basal cell carcinoma: Related to chronic sun exposure and fair skin.
• D. Liposarcoma: A malignant tumor of adipose tissue with no association with Stewart–Treves syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the cause for the following skin change?
options: Spread of tumor to anterior chest wall
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Infiltration of subdermal lymphatics

Peau-d’orange results from lymphatic obstruction by tumor cells, causing dermal edema and accentuated skin pores. Cooper’s ligament involvement causes dimpling, not peau-d’orange. Lactiferous duct or chest wall involvement do not produce this characteristic appearance.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the mainstay of treatment for Zuska’s Disease? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hadfield operation

Zuska's Disease, also known as duct ectasia or chronic periductal mastitis, is characterized by segmental ductal dilation with accumulation of secretions that become infected, leading to ductal abscesses and potential mammary fistula formation. The definitive treatment for this challenging condition is the Hadfield procedure, which involves conical excision of the ductal system. This surgical approach requires shaving the back of the nipple to ensure removal of all terminal ducts, which is critical for preventing recurrence. Without complete excision of the affected ducts, this notoriously difficult condition frequently persists.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct in the treatment of cracked nipple? I. Correct attachment (Latch on) will provide immediate relief from pain and rapid healing. II. If pain, mother should use breast pump and the infant is fed with the expressed milk. III. Miconazole lotion is applied over the nipple as well as in the baby’s mouth if there is oral thrush. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and III

Cracked nipples are a common cause of painful breastfeeding, especially during the first few weeks postpartum. The most common cause is poor attachment (improper latch) of the baby to the breast. Management aims to correct the underlying cause, relieve pain, and continue breastfeeding whenever possible.

All the given statements are correct:

• I. Correct attachment (Latch on) will provide immediate relief from pain and rapid healing: The most important treatment is correcting the baby’s latch and positioning. Proper attachment reduces trauma to the nipple and promotes healing.
• II. If pain, mother should use breast pump and the infant is fed with the expressed milk: If direct breastfeeding is too painful, expressing breast milk with a breast pump and feeding the infant with expressed milk helps maintain lactation while allowing the nipple to heal.
• III. Miconazole lotion is applied over the nipple as well as in the baby’s mouth if there is oral thrush: Candida infection can cause persistent nipple pain and cracking. Both the mother and the infant must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection. Miconazole is commonly used for the mother, while the infant receives appropriate antifungal therapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is a good prognostic factor for breast cancer patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ER+

Estrogen receptor (ER) positivity →  favorable prognostic factor in breast cancer.

ER+ tumors are biologically less aggressive,  show better differentiation; respond well to hormonal therapy.

High Ki-67, BRCA1 mutation, and p53 positivity are associated with aggressive behavior and poorer prognosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not considered a contraindication to BCT?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tumour limited to one quadrant

Breast-conserving therapy (BCT) = lumpectomy + radiotherapy.

Pre requisites for BCT: Tumor must be localised, preferably-  within a single quadrant.

Because:

• Clear tumor margins are obtained  →  lower risk of local recurrence
• Normal breast tissue preserved → better cosmetic appearance.
• Remaining microscopic disease —> treated with radiotherapy.**

Hence,results of BCT become comparable to mastectomy with better cosmetic result —>

✅ Option D. Tumour limited to one quadrant

Prior chest radiation — ❌

• BCT requires postoperative radiotherapy.
• If the patient already received radiation to the chest, additional RT can cause severe tissue damage→ hence, BCT is contraindicated.

Involved margins after resection — ❌

• Positive margins mean residual tumour.
• BCT requires clear margins; otherwise re-excision or mastectomy is needed→ hence, BCT is contraindicated.

Scleroderma — ❌

• It is a collagen vascular disease.
• Such patients have severe radiation toxicity, fibrosis, and poor healing after RT—> hence, BCT is contraindicated.

Key contraindications to BCT

Absolute

• Prior chest RT
• Pregnancy (when RT required)
• Multicentric disease
• Persistent positive margins
• Collagen vascular diseases

Relative

• Large tumour relative to breast size
• Locally advanced breast cancer (LABC)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following stains cause brown color to Her 2 neu cells of breast carcinoma as shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diamino benzidene

HER2/neu expression in breast carcinoma → detected by IHC (immunohistochemistry)

Diaminobenzidine (DAB) is the chromogen that produces a brown precipitate at the site of antigen–antibody binding. → This brown membranous staining indicates HER2 protein overexpression.

Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)is used in immunofluorescence, not routine IHC. and produces green colour, not brown stain.

Alkaline phosphatase is an enzyme, not a chromogen ; not responsible for brown staining.

Benzene has no role in staining.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of these is not included in the TNM stage T4b of breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Skin erythema involving > 1/3rd surface

T4b breast cancer includes:

• Peau d’orange (skin edema)
• Ulceration of skin
• Ipsilateral satellite skin nodules

These are features of direct skin involvement by breast carcinoma.

“Skin erythema involving >1/3 of breast surface” is a criterion for: Inflammatory breast cancer which is classified as T4d, not T4b.

| Stage | Feature

| ----- | -------

| T1 | Tumor < 2 cm

| T2 | Tumor 2 – 5 cm

| T3 | Tumor > 5 cm

| T4a | Chest wall invasion (ribs, intercostal muscles, serratus anterior; pectoralis major not included)

| T4b | Skin involvement – ulceration, satellite nodules, peau d’orange (< 1/3 of breast skin)

| T4c | Combination of T4a + T4b

| T4d | Inflammatory breast cancer – erythema/peau d’orange > 1/3 of breast skin

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is not associated with BRCA1/BRCA2 genes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Liver cancer

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes involved in the homologous recombination repair of double-stranded DNA breaks. Germline mutations in these genes significantly increase the risk of several hereditary cancers, most notably breast and ovarian cancer.

• A. Breast cancer ✅

• Strongly associated with both BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations.
• BRCA1 is commonly associated with triple-negative breast cancer.

• B. Ovarian cancer ✅

• Both BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations markedly increase the lifetime risk of high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

• C. Prostate cancer ✅

• Particularly associated with BRCA2 mutations.
• BRCA2 carriers have a higher risk of aggressive prostate cancer.

• D. Liver cancer ❌

• Not a recognized BRCA1/BRCA2-associated malignancy.
• Hepatocellular carcinoma is more commonly associated with HBV/HCV infection, cirrhosis, aflatoxin exposure, and alcohol.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old morbidly obese male patient presented with complaints of severe abdominal pain and urinary disturbances. His urine microscopy shows the following type of crystals and an ultrasound of the kidney revealed a renal stone of size 2.5 cm. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL)

Urine microscopy shows hexagonal crystals, typical of cystine stones that are radio-opaque (due to high sulfur content). The treatment of choice for renal calculi of size 2.5 cm is percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL).

Indications of PCNL:

* Staghorn calculi

* Stones >2 cm in size

* Stone composition - struvite, calcium oxalate monohydrate and cystine stones

* Multiple stones

* Obese patients in whom ESWL is contraindicated

* Stones not responding for ESWL

Endoscopic instruments are passed into the kidney using a percutaneous technique and stones are removed.

Complications of percutaneous nephrolithotomy include:

* Haemorrhage from the punctured renal parenchyma

* Perforation of the collecting system with extravasation of saline irrigant

* Perforation of the colon or pleural cavity during placement of the percutaneous track

Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy:

ESWL is a non-invasive method that generates shockwaves outside the body, which are focused on the stones. It is the commonest method of treating urinary tract stones nowadays. Stones up to approximately 2 cm in size are suitable for this form of treatment.Cystine stones are very hard stones as a result of disulphide bonds and do not fragment with ESWL. Other stones that are difficult to disintegrate by ESWL include cystine, brushite, and calcium oxalate monohydrate stones.

ESWL is only 45-60% effective in the treatment of large stones. It causes frequent complications including pain, hydronephrosis, fever, and occasional urosepsis, due to difficulties in the passage of stone particles, especially in cases of insufficient disintegration.

Complications: Infection, haematuria, parenchymal haemorrhage, and perirenal hematoma.

Contraindications: Obese patients, pregnant patients, and patients taking oral anticoagulants.

Stone fragments collecting in the distal ureter following ESWL are called steinstrasse  (a german word, which means 'street of stones'). The most common site of the column of stone fragments obstruction is the distal ureter, followed by the proximal ureter and mid ureter. The postoperative image is attached below.

Ureteroscopic removal: Ureteric calculi are directly visualized through semi-rigid ureteroscopes. Stones are then fragmented and extracted using a dormia basket.

These are generally preferred for stones <6mm and specifically those present in the distal ureter. The most significant complications relate to injury to the ureteric mucosa or wall and include ureteric perforation and extravasation, avulsion of the ureter and ureteric stricture.

Open surgery: A longstanding obstructing calculus can result in chronic inflammatory change in the kidney. Open surgeries are generally indicated for xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP). Generally, in such cases, a subcapsular nephrectomy is performed.

In extremely rare cases where both PCNL and ESWL are contraindicated open/laparoscopic surgery is used.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 27-year-old man came to the clinic with headache, palpitations, sweating. As there is history of renal problems in his brother and father he requests for an abdominal ultrasound which revealed the presence of multiple renal and pancreatic cysts.A 24-hour urinary metanephrine was sent which was elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Von Hippel-Lindau disease

The clinical scenario with elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine  (suggestive of pheochromocytoma) along with multiple renal and pancreatic cysts is most likely to be von Hippel- Lindau disease.

It is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by the development of highly vascularized tumors in multiple organs. These include:

* Haemangioblastomas of the retina and central nervous system

* Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors

* Pheochromocytoma

* Renal cysts- develop into clear renal cell cancer.

* Pancreatic cysts

* Ovary cystadenoma

* Epididymal cystadenoma

Other options:

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2:  (RET gene on chromosome 10q11.2) Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) describes conditions with tumours involving two or more endocrine glands.  They have an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance and can also be sporadic. MEN type 2 is classified into MEN 2A and MEN 2B.

MEN 2A is also called Sipple syndrome and characterized by:

* Pheochromocytoma

* Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid

* Parathyroid hyperplasia.

MEN 2B is characterized by:

* Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid

* Pheochromocytoma.

* Mucosal neuromas of lips and tongue, intestinal ganglioneuromas, marfanoid habitus, and lax joints.

* Parathyroid hyperplasia is absent.

Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome: is characterized by:

* Folliculin gene is involved

* Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma

* Pulmonary cysts

* Facial fibrofolliculomas

Tuberous sclerosis (Bourneville disease): is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in either the TSC1 or the TSC2 gene. It is characterized by:

* Seizures

* Mental retardation

* Adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas)

* Shagreen patch

* Hypomelanotic macules

* Periungual fibromas

* Renal angiomyolipomas

* Cardiac rhabdomyoma

* Cortical tubers

* Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma

* Subependymal nodules

Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome present with skin lesions on face similar to tuberous sclerosis but the age of presentation is much later than TSC.

VHL: von Hippel–Lindau

RCC: renal cell carcinoma

PTEN: phosphatase and tensin homolog gene

TSC: Tuberous sclerosis complex

SEGA: Subependymal Giant-cell astrocytoma

Pearl PF1539: Pheochromocytoma

Features:

* When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant.

* Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised.

* Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen.

Factors indicating more chances of malignancy:

* An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score)

* High number of Ki-67-positive cells

* Vascular invasion or a breached capsule

Diagnosis:

* Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test.

* MRI is the IOC.

* Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis.

Treatment:

* Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC.

* Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy

* Preop Alpha blockers should be given

* Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and fever. On examination of the affected side, there is localized erythema, warmth, point tenderness, fluctuation test is positive. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and contralateral breast is normal. What is the management plan for this patient?
options: Aspiration under USG guidance and antibiotics and repeated aspiration as necessary
Punch biopsy under ultrasound guidance followed by a course of IV antibiotics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspiration under USG guidance and antibiotics and repeated aspiration as necessary

The given case scenario points towards a diagnosis of breast abscess. The latest guidelines for the management of breast abscess specify that multiple aspirations under antibiotic cover should be attempted before an incision and drainage is done. This often allows resolution without the need for an incision scar and also allows the patient to continue breastfeeding.

Breast abscess is a sequelae of untreated bacterial mastitis which occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis.

Signs and symptoms:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

The initial treatment should involve providing pain relief with analgesics. The abscess should then be localized preferably under USG guidance and percutaneous aspiration carried out. The pus should be sent for microbiological examination to find the organism and antibiotic sensitivity. Repeated aspirations may be carried out under antibiotics cover if needed.

In some conditions mentioned below, the breast abscess may be unresponsive to repeated aspirations and antibiotic cover. In such cases, incision and drainage is performed. The conditions include:

* Presence of thick pus

* Bacteria resistant to antibiotics

* If just superficial part has been aspirated in the presence of a multiloculated abscess

* A non-healing breast abscess due to tuberculosis of breast or Inflammatory carcinoma of the breast, or an immunocompromised host.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35 year old man suffered a blow on distended bladder following which he developed sudden severe pain in hypogastrium associated with syncope. Later on as the pain subsided the abdomen began to distend. However he had no desire to micturate. Which among the following is true regarding his condition?
options: This a typical case of Extra peritoneal bladder rupture.
MRI is the ideal investigation to diagnose bladder rupture.
Repaired in two layers of absorbable suture
Laparoscopic method is avoided as it can be done only on laparotomy.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Repaired in two layers of absorbable suture

The above scenario depicts a typical case of intraperitoneal bladder rupture. Repair is usually done by a laparotomy in which the edges of the bladder are sutured using two layers of absorbable suture.

Bladder rupture :

It can be intraperitoneal (20 per cent) or extraperitoneal (80 per cent).

* Intraperitoneal rupture is usually secondary to a blow or falls on a distended bladder, more rarely to surgical damage.

* Intraperitoneal rupture is associated with sudden severe pain in the hypogastrium, often accompanied by syncope. The shock subsides and the abdomen distends and there is no desire to micturate. Peritonitis does not follow immediately if the urine is sterile; varying degrees of rigidity is present on examination

CT cystogram is the investigation of choice for diagnosing bladder rupture in a stable patient. Intravenous urography (IVU) may confirm a leak. Retrograde cystography will confirm the diagnosis.

Intraperitoneal bladder injuries can be repaired in two layers of absorbable suture and the bladder drained with a Foley catheter or suprapubic cystostomy tube. Laparotomy is the usual treatment for intraperitoneal injuries. Laparoscopic repair is an option for certain patients with isolated intraperitoneal bladder injuries.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is brought into casualty with a history of swelling in the right groin for the past 6 months. On examination, a reducible hernia is present in the right groin with no features of strangulation. What is the next step in the management of the patient?
options: Reduce the swelling and do elective surgery later
Reduce the swelling and later observe
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reduce the swelling and do elective surgery later

As this patient is asymptomatic now and has no features of obstruction or strangulation and is a reducible hernia, the best option is to reduce the swelling and do elective surgery later.

Emergency Surgery should be offerred ,if there are features of

* strangulation

* bowel obstruction

* bowel infarction

Elective surgery should be given for

* all femoral hernias which has high risk of strangulation,

* increasing size of the swelling,

* increasing difficulty in reduction of the swelling

* young patients who might have high risk of complications later in life.

Note:

Any patient who presents with acute pain in a hernia, particularly if irreducible, should be offered surgery .

In most irreducible hernia cases , after giving adequate analgesia the hernia will reduce due to muscle relaxation.

In the elderly, if the hernia is asymptomatic, small in size,can be reduced easily and is not causing anxiety then observation alone is enough.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with a lesion on his left ear that has gradually increased in size over the past three months. He has a history of chronic smoking with a 20-pack-year history. His vital signs are within normal limits, and the rest of his physical examination reveals no abnormalities. Histopathological evaluation of the lesion shows keratin pearls. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Squamous cell carcinoma

The image shows a picture of cutaneous horn and it is associated with squamous cell carcinoma.

Cutaneous horn: Cutaneous horns are hard conical projections from the skin, made of compact keratin. They arise from benign, premalignant, or malignant skin lesions. Approximately 9% showed SCC pathological features at the base.

SCC is the second most common skin cancer. The primary risk factor and driving force for the development of this common cancer is UV exposure(ex: gardener), previous chronic wounds, or chemical carcinogens

Variants :

* Bowen's disease

* Erythroplasia of Queyrat

SCC initially presents as smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous lesions. All these lesions later ulcerate and have a characteristic everted edge and are surrounded by inflamed, indurated skin.

Keratin pearls are seen on histopathologic evaluation.

Treatment : Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Other modalities include cautery ablation, cryotherapy, drug therapy including imiquimod, Moh’s microsurgery and Radiation therapy.

Differential:

Basal cell carcinoma

It presents as a small, slowly growing pearly nodule, often with tortuous telangiectatic vessels on its surface, rolled borders, and a central crust (nodular BCC). The occasional presence of melanin in this variant of nodular BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

Most common site is the inner canthus of the eye.

Different edges of ulcers are seen as:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old lady presented with a 1.5cm pigmented lesion on the face which is growing rapidly in size and associated with itching. The lesion is shown below. Which of the following is likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Malignant melanoma

The given clinical scenario of a >6mm pigmented lesion on the face which is asymmetrical, with an irregular border, made of black and brown pigments, and increasing rapidly in size, points towards a diagnosis of malignant melanoma.

Types of melanoma:

* Lentigo maligna

* Superficial spreading

* Acral lentiginous

* Nodular

Histopathology of melanoma:

* Individual melanoma cells are larger than normal melanocytes

* They have large nuclei with irregular contours, chromatin is characteristically clumped at the periphery of the nuclear membrane with prominent red eosinophilic nucleoli

* All tumors have a vertical and radial phase of growth. The appearance of melanocytes is similar in both phases. The vertical growth has is often heralded by the appearance of a nodule.

* The possibility of metastasis correlates with the depth of invasion which is called the Breslow thickness.

Other options:

Acquired melanocytic nevus (common mole) is rarely more than 1cm in size. It also does not show atypical network

Congenital melanocytic nevus may be small, medium or large size(>20cm). A large-sized mole may show an atypical network and have a risk of melanoma growth. But a history of being present since birth or infancy needs to be present.

A dysplastic nevus is formed at the dermo-epidermal junction. They are usually smaller in size than melanoma, have a fuzzy border, and more likely to show brown-tan pigmentation. Any blue-black pigmentation should raise suspicion of melanoma. The majority of them regress on their own

Pearl PF0159: Clinical findings suggestive of melanoma

The ABCDE of Melanoma consists of the rules for the examination of a nevus to assess its malignant potential:

A : Asymmetry

* Melanoma lesions are irregular, or not symmetrical, in shape.

B : Border irregular

* Melanoma lesions usually have irregular borders that are ill defined.

C : Color variegation

* The presence of multiple colors (blue, black, brown, tan, etc.) or the uneven distribution of color.

D : Diameter >6 mm

* Melanoma lesions are often greater than 6 millimeters in diameter (approximately the size of a pencil eraser).

E : Evolution

* There is a change in the size, shape, symptoms (such as itching or tenderness), surface (especially bleeding), or color of a mole.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents to OPD with low backache. His PSA level are 100ng/ml. Which of the following drug is indicated for treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Goserelin

The clinical features and investigations showing elevated PSA levels are suggestive of prostate cancer. Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used in the treatment of prostate cancer.

Androgen deprivation therapy is the primary medical therapy for prostate cancer. The drugs approved for this indication include leuprolide, goserelin, histrelin, buserelin, and triptorelin.

The agonist action of the GnRH analogues causes increased testosterone production, causing a tumour flare. It can be prevented by concomitant administration of an androgen receptor antagonist such as flutamide, bicalutamide, or nilutamide until downregulation of testosterone is complete.

The combined androgen deprivation therapy with continuous GnRH agonist and an androgen receptor antagonist is as effective as surgical castration in reducing the levels of serum testosterone and its effects.

Other options:

Option A: Somatostatin analogs acts as growth hormone antagonist and are used in the treatment of acromegaly, gigantism, acute control of bleeding from esophageal varices.

Option B: Terlipressin is a vasopressin analog used in the treatment of hepatorenal syndrome.

Option D: Anabolic steroids like testosterone are used to treat osteoporotic bone pain and counteract the effects of long-term corticosteroid use.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A car driver was brought into the A&E following a RTA with complaints of breathlessness. On examination his vitals are PR-112/min, BP-100/70, SpO2-90% and there is extensive bruising on his chest.Chest Xray is as below. What is the management of this patient?
options: Internal operative fixation of the fractures segments
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. IPPV

The diagnosis here is flail chest with respiratory failure and the management with respiratory failure is IPPV.

Flail Chest :

* A flail chest occurs when a segment of the chest wall does not have bony continuity with the rest of the thoracic cage.

* This condition results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, i.e. 2 adjacent ribs or 3 or more ribs fractured in two or more places.

* The blunt force required to disrupt the integrity of the thoracic cage typically produces an underlying pulmonary contusion as well.

Clinical Features:

On inspiration the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards and less air therefore moves into the lungs.On expiration, the segment moves outwards(paradoxical respiration).

Diagnosis - Made clinically, not by radiography. To confirm the diagnosis the chest wall can be observed for paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment for several respiratory cycles and during coughing. Voluntary splinting as a result of pain, mechanically impaired chest wall movement and the associated lung contusion are all causes of the hypoxia and respiratory failure.

The patient is also at high risk of developing a pneumothorax or hemothorax.

Treatment

* Chest strapping or splinting should be avoided

* Currently, treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates) or epidural analgesia and physiotherapy.

* IPPV (Intermitent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is reserved for cases developing respiratory failure despite adequate analgesia and oxygen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A factory worker working in a plastic pipe factory presented to the OPD with weight loss and right upper quadrant abdominal pain of 6 months duration. He had hepatomegaly. Further investigation revealed that most of the liver was replaced by a hemorrhagic tumor with extensive necrosis. What can be the likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Angiosarcoma of the liver

The diagnosis is angiosarcoma of the liver.

Angiosarcoma of the liver is usually seen in individuals having occupational exposure to agents such as vinyl chloride, arsenic, or thorotrast. The gross specimen of the liver  shows greyish white lesions, with multiple reddish-brown hemorrhagic foci and several blood-filled spaces .

Option A: Cavernous hemangiomas appear as red-blue, soft nodules, usually less than 2 cm in diameter. Their clinical significance is that they might be mistaken radiographically or intraoperatively for metastatic tumors.

Option B: Metastatic carcinoma of the liver has a gross appearance that shows multiple nodular lesions of variable size, replacing much of the normal parenchyma.

Option D: Primary hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has a peak incidence around 20 to 40 years of age and is predominantly seen in men. The gross appearance shows unifocal or multifocal or diffusely infiltrative lesions that are paler than the surrounding tissue. The lesions may be greenish due to the presence of bile. Cirrhosis may be seen in about 50% of the cases. Intrahepatic metastases may be seen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with progressive difficulty in swallowing for both solids and liquids for 8 months. Barium swallow done is shown below. Upper GI endoscopy and manometry are performed in this patient. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?
options: Loss of lower esophageal sphincter pressure causing reflux
incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter
It is is a primary motility disorder
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of lower esophageal sphincter pressure causing reflux

The given clinical scenario and the barium swallow showing bird beak appearance is suggestive of Achalasia cardia.  The diagnostic criteria for achalasia with manometry are impaired lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent peristalsis with elevated LES pressure.

Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the absence of esophageal peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) in response to swallowing. There is incomplete(<75%) relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter

Manometry is considered the most sensitive investigation to diagnose achalasia as it identifies early disease before esophageal dilatation and food retention.

Endoscopy is useful for ruling out pseudoachalasia.

Note: 24 hours pH monitoring is ideal and most accurate in patients with the features of gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Pearl PF0313: Achalasia Cardia

Achalasia is a rare disease caused by the loss of ganglion cells within the esophageal myenteric plexus.

Their absence leads to increased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), and absent peristalsis.

Achalasia is the only true motility disorder of the esophagus.

Primary achalasia is due to ganglion cell degeneration and is thought to be due to an autoimmune process attributable to latent infection with human herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) combined with genetic susceptibility.

Secondary achalasia may arise in Chaga's disease

Clinical features:

* dysphagia (solid and liquid food)

* regurgitation

* chest pain

* weight loss

* bronchitis, pneumonia, or lung abscess from aspiration

Differential diagnosis: Diffuse esophageal spasm, Chagas’ disease, and pseudoachalasia

On barium swallow: Bird beak-appearance

Investigation of choice: Manometry (most sensitive)

Treatment: Pneumatic dilatation and Heller myotomy

Pearl PF1482: Barium swallow

Diffuse esophageal spasm: Corkscrew appearance

Feline esophagus: Transient transverse bands seen in the mid and lower esophagus on a double-contrast barium swallow. It is seen in active gastroesophageal reflux, hiatus hernia, and eosinophilic esophagitis.

Achalasia: Dilated esophagus with a retained column of barium and bird beak sign.

Zenker's diverticulum: Posterior outpouching of the hypopharynx through a weakness in the muscle layer called Killian dehiscence.

Esophageal carcinoma: Irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction, and shouldered margins.

Schatzki's ring: Thin submucosal circumferential ring in the lower esophagus at the squamocolumnar junction.

Esophageal web in a patient with Plummer Vinson syndrome. Esophageal webs are thin membranes of normal esophageal tissue consisting of mucosa and submucosa. Translucent part denotes esophageal web.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient on steroids as part of her psoriasis medication presents with mild fever which is present only during the night and weight loss. She had an ulcer on her neck which had undermined edges as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tubercular lymphadenitis

The clinical scenario of immunosuppression, symptoms of fever at night, weight loss, and the neck finding of an ulcer with undermined edges is suggestive of tubercular lymphadenitis.

The image shows long-standing tubercular adenitis with a sinus.

In tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis any group of lymph nodes can be involved. Symptoms include evening pyrexia, malaise, and cough (from pulmonary tuberculosis) while in children-failure to thrive can be seen. A matted lymph nodal mass is the typical clinical feature. In later stages the mass may be cystic, denoting an abscess.

The abscess denotes underlying caseation and does not show any features of inflammation hence it is called a 'cold abscess'. The pus is initially confined by the deep cervical fascia, but after weeks or months, this may become eroded at one point and the pus flows through the small opening into the space beneath the superficial fascia. The process has now reached the stage of a ‘collar stud abscess'. An abscess may burst through the skin to form an ulcer with undermined edges which is typical of a tubercular ulcer with undermined edges and can develop into a discharging sinus.

Diagnosis is by the culture of pus and biopsy of the lymph node. The involvement of other systems must be excluded. Treatment is with antitubercular drugs.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was brought to casualty following a road accident. The patient is unconscious; the following image shows the CT scan. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subdural hematoma (SDH)

The plain computed tomography (CT) scan shows a concave-convex shaped hematoma on the left side suggestive of subdural hematoma.

An acute SDH is the result of the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid membrane and the dura. It is usually due to the rupture of bridging veins running from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses. The level of consciousness is usually impaired at presentation and may deteriorate further as the hematoma expands. Elderly and alcoholic patients are at a higher risk of acute SDH formation after head trauma due to brain atrophy. On CT scan, acute SDH appears as a hyperdense, crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) lesion.

Open craniotomy for the evacuation of acute SDH is indicated for the following:

* Thickness >1 cm

* Midline shift >5 mm

* Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score drops by two or more points from the time of injury to hospitalization.

Chronic subdural hematoma results from a hematoma that expands over days or weeks by osmosis, ultimately producing symptoms of raised ICP or focal deficits. On a CT scan, diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface would be seen as shown in the image below.

Pearl PF0339: Intracranial Hemorrhage (ICH)

Extradural hemorrhage (EDH):

* Source: Arterial bleed

* MC- Middle meningeal artery

* Cause- Trauma

* Clinical features: Lucid interval is characteristic

* CT – Lentiform opacity

* Treatment: A large or rapidly evolving EDH requires surgical evacuation

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH)

* Source: Venous bleed

* Bridging dural veins

* Causes: Trauma, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, alcohol abuse, shaken baby syndrome

* Clinical features

* Acute SDH: may be associated with lucid interval

* Chronic SDH: drowsiness, headache

* CT- crescentic opacity

* Treatment: May resolve spontaneously or require surgical drainage

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)

* Source: Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – Trauma

* 2nd MC – Rupture of berry aneurysm

* MC sites: Terminal ICA, MCA bifurcation, top of basilar artery

* Clinical features: Thunderclap headache with neck stiffness +/- FND

* Investigations:

* Non-contrast CT brain,

* CSF xanthochromia (peaks in 2 days and subsides in 2 weeks)

* Treatment:

* Clipping/coiling of berry aneurysm,

* Triple H therapy – hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution to prevent vasospasm

Intraparenchymal hemorrhage- (MC type of ICH)

* Source- Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – hypertension

* Trauma, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, bleeding disorders, neoplasms, vascular malformations

* MC sites:

* Putamen (basal ganglia)

* Thalamus

* Cerebellum

* Pons

* Treatment:

* Correction of any identified coagulopathy by infusing prothrombin complex concentrates, FFP or fresh platelets as required

* Surgical evacuation for cerebellar hematoms >3 cm in size

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient who underwent Nissen's fundoplication was seen in the ward during evening rounds. He is asymptomatic at present with stable vitals. What is the next line of management for this patient?
options: Nasogastric tube to prevent gas bloat syndrome
Insert chest tube to prevent pneumothorax
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Monitor vitals

The patient is asymptomatic, therefore no further action needs to be taken other than monitoring his vitals.

The most common complication of Nissen’s fundoplication is gas-bloat syndrome.

Fundoplication is a procedure in which the fundus of the stomach is wrapped around the lower end of the esophagus. After this procedure, most patients are unable to belch gas from the stomach into the esophagus. This causes increased gas in the stomach resulting in bloating sensation, abdominal discomfort, and flatulence. This is known as gas bloat syndrome and occurs more commonly with Nissen total fundoplication.

Other options:

During the early postoperative period, patients who report persistent nausea and demonstrate inadequate intake of a liquid diet should undergo abdominal radiography. If significant gastric distention is identified, a nasogastric tube can safely be placed to decompress the stomach for 24 hours.

Pneumothorax is the most common complication that occurs intraoperatively. Chest tube needs to be inserted if pneumothorax takes place, which is not seen in this case.

Pearl PF1544: Types of Fundoplication

Types of fundoplication

Degree of wrap

Dor

anterior 180–200° fundoplication

Thal

270° anterior fundoplication

Lind

300° posterior fundoplication

Toupet

posterior 180 - 270° fundoplication

Belsey Mark IV

270° anterior transthoracic fundoplication

Nissen

360° fundoplication

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: According to Weigert Meyer's rule of duplication of the ureter, the lower pole ureter in the urinary bladder is:
options: Lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter
Lateral and caudal to the upper pole ureter
Medial and cephalad to the upper pole ureter
Medial and caudal to the upper pole ureter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter

The lower pole ureter is lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter.

According to Weigert Meyer's rule of congenital complete duplication of the ureter,

* The ureter draining the upper segment of the kidney inserts in the bladder inferior and medial to the ureter draining the lower segment of the kidney (Weigert–Meyer rule). The lower moiety of the completely duplicated system is generally normal.

* The upper ureter is considered ectopic and the lower ureter is considered orthotopic.

* Ectopic ureters are more prone to obstruction.

* Orthotopic ureters are more prone to reflux due to perpendicular entry into bladder musculature rather than oblique entry.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following statement regarding ranula are true except
options: Bluish, translucent, cystic swelling in the floor of mouth
Marsupialisation or excision is the treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arises from submandibular salivary gland

The incorrect statement regarding ranula is it arises from the submandibular salivary gland. It is a mucous extravasation cyst occurring as a result of obstruction of one of the sublingual salivary glands in the floor of the mouth.

Features :

* Translucent, bluish, soft, cystic fluctuant swelling present below the tongue pushing it upwards and medially thus interfering with speech, mastication, respiration, and swallowing.

* Plunging ranula presents as asymptomatic, enlarging neck mass.

Management:

* Marsupialisation – unroofing the cyst and tacking the edges of the cyst to adjacent tissues.

* Sclerosing agents like bleomycin.

* Sublingual gland excision – recurrence rate is very low.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 11-month-old boy with had a recent urinary tract infection that resolved with antibiotics. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows reveal an empty scrotum on the right side with normal left testis. But a mass was palpable on the right inguinal canal. The USG revealed the right testicle under the subcutaneous fat near the right inguinal canal as shown in the image below. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Orchidopexy

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of cryptorchidism and the next best step is to perform an orchidopexy.

Orchidopexy is the treatment of choice for incompletely palpable unilateral undescended testis. Orchidopexy is usually performed before the boy reaches 12 months of age.

About 4% of boys are born with one or both testes incompletely descended. About two-thirds of these reach the scrotum during the first 3 months of life, but full descent after that is uncommon.

Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac.  It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. The testes can arrest anywhere during descent, and the most common site is the inguinal region.

Phases of testicular descent:

* Transabdominal phase: Testes come to lie in the lower abdomen or pelvis, and this descent is regulated by Mullerian-inhibiting substances.

* Inguinoscrotal phase: Testes descend along the inguinal canal and reach the scrotal sac, and this phase of the descent is regulated by androgen-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve.

The exact pathogenesis remains unknown; however, deficiency in gonadotropins and Mullerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) and increased expression of estradiol in the placenta are thought to play a role.

Cryptorchidism is histopathologically characterized by the following:

* Testicular atrophy: thickening of the basement membrane, arrested germ cell development, marked hyalinization

* Tubules showing Sertoli cells but no spermatogenesis

* Increase in the interstitial Leydig cells

It is associated with testicular atrophy and dysfunction, which result in sterility. Cryptorchid testes carry a 3–5-fold higher risk for testicular cancer (usually seminoma). Thus, observation is never the policy. (Option -A)

When the testis is impalpable, ultrasound may be helpful in identifying the intracanalicular testis, while laparoscopy may be needed to differentiate between the abdominal testis and a truly absent testis. Since here testis is made out in the inguinal region, laparoscopy is not the next best line of management(Option-C)

Hence, orchidopexy is usually performed before the boy reaches 12 months of age to avoid the following complications remembered by the mnemonic TESTIS:

*

T- Torsion

*

E- Epididymorchitis

*

S- Sterility

*

T- Trauma (Increased risk)

*

I- Increased risk of inguinal hernia (Most commonly occurring complication)

*

S- Seminoma (Increased risk)

The given flowchart summarizes the treatment protocol for undescended testis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the incision for appendicectomy.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lanz incision

* Lanz incision is a Transverse or skin crease incision for appendicitis,2 cm below the  umbilicus, centred on the midclavicular–midinguinal line

* Rockey–Davis incision : Transverse right lower quadrant incision.

* Gridiron incision : Oblique muscle splitting incision in the right lower quadrant. Also called as Mc Burney incision.

* Rutherford–Morrison incision : oblique muscle cutting incision with its lower end over McBurney’s point and extending obliquely upwards and laterally as necessary(Shown on the left side in the image for the sake of clarity)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Revised A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis. Picture of the resected gall bladder is shown as below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gall bladder carcinoma

The diagnosis is gallbladder carcinoma.

The gross specimen shows a resected gallbladder with multiple gallstones impacted in the lumen. The irregularly thickened wall, mucosal changes, and firm, indurated areas indicate tumor growth and inflammation.

Gallbladder carcinoma

* Gallbladder carcinoma is a rare malignancy that affects the elderly population; it is associated with a poor prognosis, except when diagnosed at the early stages.

* The histologic subtypes are papillary, nodular, and tubular carcinomas.

Clinical features:

* It is usually indistinguishable from cholecystitis or cholelithiasis.

* Features include right upper quadrant pain, abdominal discomfort, nausea, and vomiting.

Diagnosis:

* It is usually diagnosed when patients undergo cholecystectomy for gallstones.

* Laboratory diagnosis in 80% of the cases is made by detection of elevated levels of carbohydrate antigen (CA) 19-9 in assays.

* Ultrasonography (USG) is often indicative of a thickened irregular gallbladder wall or a lesion replacing the gallbladder.

* Computed tomography (CT) can detect the presence of a tumour and its invasion and can be used for identifying its stage of development

* Percutaneous transhepatic or endoscopic retrograde cholangiography and subsequent bile cytology can help establish the diagnosis of gallbladder cancer.

* Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography is a non-invasive imaging method that allows for a complete clinical assessment of the vascular, nodal, and hepatic architecture and other adjacent organs.

Treatment options for carcinoma gall bladder found incidentally after cholecystectomy:

* Up to stage Ia and stage Ib with negative margins: Standard cholecystectomy

* Stage Ib with perineural, lymphatic, vascular invasion and stage II: Extended cholecystectomy

* Chemotherapy is not required in an early gall bladder cancer. Radiation has no role.

Treatment of gallbladder carcinoma (in general):

T1a: Simple cholecystectomy

T1b, T2, T3: Radical cholecystectomy

T4: Unresectable, chemotherapy and palliative nonsurgical therapy are provided.

N1: Regional lymphadenectomy

N2: Radical cholecystectomy plus hepatopancreatic duodenectomy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Revised A young sheep farmer presents to the OPD with pain in the right upper part of the abdomen. On examination, there is tenderness and enlargement of the liver. Blood investigations show eosinophilia, elevated liver enzymes, and abdominal ultrasound is as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydatid cyst

The clinical vignette along with the ultrasound image showing multiple septations and rosette or honeycomb appearance is diagnostic of active hydatid cyst.

Hydatid cyst:

Echinococcus granulosus is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases.

The hydatid cyst usually develops three weeks after the infection. The cyst is surrounded by a fibrous capsule called the pericyst that is derived from the host tissue.

The cyst wall is composed of two layers, ectocyst (outer gelatinous membrane), and endocyst (inner germinal membrane). Ectocyst is a laminated membrane, which is acellular. It helps in the passage of nutrients. The endocyst helps in producing the laminated membrane and scoleces.

The brood capsules are cellular masses in the hydatid fluid which consists of scoleces. In a definitive host, these scoleces develop into adult tapeworm while in the intermediate hosts these develop into new hydatid cysts. The brood capsules are attached to the endocyst by a pedicle or stalk. The brood capsules may mature and detach from the mother cyst and become the daughter cysts, which are an exact replica of the mother cysts.

The freed brood capsules and scoleces present in the hydatid fluid are called hydatid sand.

The image attached below shows the C.S of hydatid cyst.

Investigations:

Computed tomography (CT) scan is the best imaging modality for hydatid cyst. It shows the presence of a space-occupying lesion with a smooth outline with septa.

CT scan has an accuracy of 98% in the detection of hydatid cysts and higher sensitivity to demonstrate the daughter cysts and extra-hepatic cysts.
The indirect hemagglutination test and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) have a sensitivity of 80% overall and are the initial screening tests of choice.

Note:

* First/Initial imaging test: USG

* Best imaging test: CT scan

Classification of CE based on ultrasound imaging

Type
Ultrasound features
Stage

CE1
Univesicular fluid collection
Active Cyst

CE2
Honeycomb appearance: Multivesicular fluid collection with daughter cysts separated by septae

CE3A
Water lily sign: Fluid collection with detached membrane
Transitional cyst

CE3B
Daughter cysts present in a solid matrix

CE4
Cysts in a heterogeneous matrix with no daughter cysts

Management:

Class

<5 cm albendazole 400 mg PO BID

>5 cm albendazole 400 mg PO BID+ PAIR

PAIR: puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration

Pearl PF1538: Indications and contraindications of puncture, aspiration, injection, and re-aspiration (PAIR) in hydatid cyst

Indications:

* Relapse cyst, infected cyst, cyst >5 cm in different liver segments

* Patients who refuse surgery or where surgery is contraindicated

* Pregnant women, children < 3 years of age

* WHO - type CE1 and type CE3a.

Contraindications:

* Cysts in lung

* Cysts communicating with bile duct

* Cysts with multiple septae—honeycomb cysts

* Inaccessible cysts

* Hyperechogenic cysts

* Calcified cysts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: This instrument is not used in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute anal fissure

The instrument given in the above image is a proctoscope and proctoscopy is contraindicated in acute anal fissures.

Due to pain, digital rectal examination and anoscopy are not performed immediately in acute anal fissures. Acute anal fissures are examined under anaesthesia in operating room when needed.

Anal fissure:

Clinical features

* Severe pain associated with defecation resolves spontaneously and reappears during the next evacuation

* It may even be associated with the passage of fresh blood noticed on tissue after wiping

* Most of the fissures are located in the posterior midline, with the rest being located in the anterior midline. Fissures located laterally can be possible due to other diseases like HIV, TB, syphilis, Crohn's disease, or carcinoma.

Treatment of Anal fissure

* The focus is to normalise bowel habits. Bowel softeners, dietary fibres, and adequate water should be recommended

* Medical therapy involves the topical application of glyceryl trinitrate. It releases nitric oxide and relaxes the internal anal sphincter. This reduces spasms and pain and improves vasculature to promote healing

* Surgical therapy is recommended for chronic fissures that have failed medical therapy. Lateral internal sphincterotomy is the procedure of choice. The aim of this procedure is to decrease the spasms of the internal sphincter by dividing a portion of the muscle.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is tumour marker of pancreatic cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carcinoembryonic antigen

Carcino Embryogenic Antigen is the tumour marker for pancreatic cancer.

Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)

* Normally detected in glycocalyx of fetal epithelial cells

* May play a role in the metastasis of cancer cells

* CEA levels over 5 ng/dL: ascites fluid A/W malignancy

* Detection, recurrence, and prognosis of adenocarcinoma (lung) and colorectal carcinoma

* Elevated levels also present in cirrhosis, biliary obstruction, hepatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, smokers and post-surgical bowel sequestration with mucocele

* Benign cysts may be CEA+ even when benign

* Hepatocellular carcinoma: canalicular pattern for polyclonal CEA is 50-90% sensitive for hepatocellular carcinoma, > 95% specific

* Pancreatic adenocarcinoma: 92% sensitive for metastases vs. 0% for bile duct adenoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about carcinoid tumours of appendix?
options: Size appears to be the best predictor of malignant behavior and metastatic potential
Arise from Kulchitsky cells of the crypts of Lieberkühn
Most common location is the base of the appendix
Most common tumour of the appendix
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Most common location is the base of the appendix

The most common location of the carcinoid tumor of the appendix is the tip of the appendix (i.e., the distal third of the appendix).

Carcinoid tumor:

* Synonym – Argentaffinoma

* It arises in argentaffin tissue (Kulchitsky cells of the crypts of Lieberkühn).

* It is the most common tumor of the appendix

* It is 10 times more common than any other neoplasm of the appendix.

* Most often, it presents with symptoms of subacute or recurrent appendicitis.

* It is frequently found in the distal third (mostly tip) of the appendix.

* Moderately hard, yellow tumor between the intact mucosa and the peritoneum.

* Microscopically:

* Tumor cells are small, arranged in small nests within the muscle, and have a characteristic pattern using immunohistochemical stain chromogranin A

* Carcinoid tumor of the appendix rarely give rise to metastasis.

Treatment :

* Appendicectomy has been shown to be a sufficient treatment.

* Indications for right hemicolectomy:

* Cecal wall involvement

* Tumour ≥ 2 cm in size

* Lymph nodal involvement

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following tests would a surgeon advise first in a patient with a large thyroid swelling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroid function tests

Assessing the biochemical function of the thyroid i.e. thyroid function test (TFT) is the first investigation done in any thyroid condition.

Evaluation of any thyroid disease should begin with the assessment of TSH, T3, and T4. TSH is the only test necessary in most patients with thyroid nodules that clinically appear to be euthyroid.

If a discrete swelling is associated with hyperthyroidism, it indicates a toxic adenoma. This is followed by an ultrasound of the neck or radioiodine uptake. Findings in thyroid swelling associated with thyroid neoplasia include microcalcification and increased vascularity. FNAC should be used under ultrasound guidance, on all nodules that fall outside a fully benign category.

Modalities for evaluation of thyroid swelling include:

* Laboratory evaluation

* TSH

* T3

* T4

* Thyroid imaging

* Ultrasound

* Radioisotope scanning

* CT/MRI

* Biopsy techniques

* Fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNA)

* Tru-cut/core-needle biopsy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following zones of retroperitoneum need mandatory surgical exploration as management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zone 1

Zone 1 needs mandatory surgical exploration.

Retroperitoneum is divided into 3 zones, based on the types of viscera and their differential management in blunt trauma:

Zone1
Central
Always explored, after proximo-distal vascular control

Zone2
Lateral
Only explored if the hematoma is pulsatile or expanding, else conservative/ angioembolization

Zone3
Pelvic
Only explored if the hematoma is pulsatile or expanding, else conservative/ angioembolization

If there is a penetrative injury in any of the zones, surgical management is done.

Mattox maneuver is left medial visceral rotation to expose the aorta.

Cattell-Braasch maneuver is done by right medial visceral rotation to expose IVC.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient was brought to the ER after RTA, his RR is 25/min, BP is 80/45mmHg. On examination, hyper-resonance is heard over the left side of the chest. The chest X-ray performed is given below. What would be the appropriate management in this case?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the right 5th ICS
Wide bore needle insertion in the left 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wide bore needle insertion in the left 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain

The given clinical scenario and the given chest radiograph are suggestive of tension pneumothorax. It is managed by inserting wide-bore needle in 5th ICS followed by placing an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS.

Tension pneumothorax and simple pneumothorax have similar signs, symptoms, and examination findings, but hypotension qualifies the pneumothorax as a tension pneumothorax.

Immediate management includes inserting a wide-bore needle in the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

Definitive management includes insertion of the intercostal tube in the triangle of safety. If a sucking wound is present, then it is covered with gauze pieces and taped on 3 sides.

Remember: (Acc to ATLS 10th edition)

* In adults, needle thoracotomy location changed to 5th ICS mid axillary line from 2nd ICS midclavicular line.

* In the pediatric age group, the thoracotomy location remains at the 2nd ICS midclavicular line.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old man developed abdominal pain for which he was being evaluated. You notice the following in his CECT. What is the likely condition indicated by the arrow in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horse shoe kidney

The given image shows a horseshoe kidney. It is prone to obstruction, reflux, and stone formation (the likely cause of pain in this case)

Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidneys with male preponderance

Horseshoe kidney is caused due to the fusion of the lower poles of the kidney. The lower border of the kidneys usually lies in front of the L3 vertebra due to the arrest of ascent.

The common associations of horseshoe kidney are:

* Vesicoureteral Reflux

* Wilms Tumor

* Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney

* Turner’s Syndrome

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old male patient presented to surgery OPD with a history of intermittent purulent discharge with a slight blood tinge from an external opening located in the perianal region even after multiple drainage attempts.Examination of the perianal region is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fistula-in-ano

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of fistula-in-ano. Laying open fistulotomy is the surest management method to eradicate the disease.

Fistula-in -ano:

A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal hollow tract or cavity that is lined with granulation tissue and that connects a primary opening inside the anal canal to a secondary opening in the perianal skin.

The most common cause is perianal abscess. Other causes include tuberculosis or Crohn's disease.

Symptoms:

* Perianal pain

* Discharge - intermittent purulent discharge (which may be bloody)

Goodsall's rule:

Goodsall’s rule can be used as a guide in determining the location of the internal opening of the fistula.

* Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract.

* Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly track in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline.

Exceptions to Goodsall’s Rule

However, exceptions to this rule often occur: Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline.

Investigations:

The investigations available for fistula-in-ano are as follows:

* Fistulogram

* Endoanal ultrasound

* MRI

* Computed tomography (CT) scan

* Endocoil MRI

* Hydrogen peroxide–enhanced 3-D endoanal ultrasonography

Fistula-in-ano is surgically managed by fistulotomy, fistulectomy, ligation of the inter-sphincteric fistula tract (LIFT), or setons

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. He has a past history of peptic ulcer disease. Physical examination reveals rigidity. X-ray abdomen is as shown below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent surgical exploration

The clinical vignette with physical examination findings of rigidity, x-ray findings showing free air under the diaphragm with an underlying history of peptic ulcer disease is indicative of peptic ulcer perforation. The next best step in the management of this patient is urgent surgical exploration.

GI tract perforation:

Common causes include surgery, blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, corrosive agents, or particular medications.

Patients may present with acute pain, abdominal/pelvic mass due to an abscess or phlegmon formation, fistula formation(such as in Crohn's disease), sepsis

Physical examination shows subcutaneous gas (mediastinal gas might be heard as a systolic "crunch" - Hamman's sign). When free intraperitoneal perforation has occurred, signs of peritonitis are present.

Diagnosis may be made based on clinical exam findings of peritonitis and history. However, confirmation is obtained by demonstrating pneumoperitoneum. X-ray, USG, or CT scan may be used to quickly identify free air. Erect X-ray is commonly used and it shows the presence of free air under the diaphragm(shown in the image below)

Management - Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Indications for immediate bowel exploration are

* Sepsis/diffuse peritonitis(as in this patient)

* Bowel ischemia

* Complete or closed-loop bowel obstruction

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman comes to the OPD with a history of a lump in the left breast. On clinical examination, the size of the lump in the left breast is 9×10 cm with the following appearance and no axillary lymphadenopathy. The histopathology of the biopsy from the lump shows increased stromal cellularity and typical leaflike architecture. What is your likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phyllodes tumour

The given clinical scenario and the image are suggestive of phyllodes tumour or cystosarcoma phyllodes of the breast.

Phyllodes tumour is also known as cystosarcoma phyllodes presents as a large tumour with an unevenly bosselated surface. The histopathology of the biopsy of the lump shows increased stromal cellularity, overgrowth, and typical leaflike architecture.

Phyllodes tumours usually occur in women over the age of 40 years but can appear in younger women. It is mostly benign even though it is also called cystosarcoma phyllodes or serocystic disease of Brodie. They are usually mobile over the chest wall despite their large size. Histologically, there is a wide variation with some having low malignant potential and others having a higher mitotic index.

This tumour does not infiltrate the skin though the overlying skin becomes thin and tense due to swelling. Nipple retraction is not seen in this condition. Axillary dissection is not done if malignant transformation occurs because the lymphatic spread is rare. Treatment of phyllodes tumor:

* Benign type- Enucleation or wide local excision

* Massive tumours, recurrent tumours and malignant type- Mastectomy

Other options:

Giant fibroadenomas are usually seen in the early reproductive years. These are benign, solid, encapsulated, and biphasic tumour consisting of fibroblastic stroma and epithelium-lined glands. It is a slow-growing tumour and presents as a painless lump in the breast.

Inflammatory breast cancer is the most aggressive subtype of breast cancer. Axillary nodal metastases are common, and there is a significant risk for distant metastases. Patients with inflammatory carcinoma usually have a rapid onset of disease with progression over weeks to 3 months.

The hallmark of inflammatory breast cancer is diffuse tumor involvement of the dermal lymphatic channels within the breast and overlying skin, often without an underlying tumor mass. Inflammatory breast cancer manifests clinically as erythema, edema, and warmth of the breast as a result of lymphatic obstruction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought by her mother to the outpatient department with an abdominal swelling. She has mild discomfort but no other symptoms of pain or vomiting. On examination, the swelling is fluctuant, soft in consistency, and moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the attachment of mesentery. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chylolymphatic cyst

The given clinical scenario is typical of the mesenteric cyst with a positive Tillaux sign. The most common type of cyst is chylolymphatic cyst.

In chylolymphatic cyst there is congenitally misplaced lymphatic tissue which has no efferent communication with the lymphatic system.The thin wall of the cyst, is composed of connective tissue, lined by flat endothelium, and is filled with clear lymph or chyle.

Mesenteric cyst:

* Cysts may occur in the mesentery of the small intestine or the colon and can be of different types:

* Chylolymphatic

* Enterogenous

* Urogenital remnant

* Dermoid.

* Most commonly presents as painless abdominal swelling with the following characteristic physical signs,

* Fluctuant swelling near the umbilicus

* Swelling moves freely in a plane at right angles to the attachment of the mesentery (Tillaux’s sign)

* Presence of zone of resonance around the cyst

* Investigations- USG and CT scan demonstrate the type of cyst.

* Treatment of choice is enucleation with or without resection of the bowel.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presents with low backache and weight loss. He has progressive difficulty in urination and had an episode of urinary retention 2 days back which was relieved by catheterization.PSA was done which was 5.2 ng/ml and an X-Ray LS spine shows osteoblastic changes. What is the clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prostate cancer

The given clinical details with elevated PSA and blastic changes in the LS spine suggest a diagnosis of carcinoma prostate.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumour in men over the age of 65 years. The growth and survival of prostate cancer cells depend on androgens.  Approximately 70% of carcinomas of the prostate arise in the peripheral zone of the gland, classically in a posterior location.

Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.

Grading of prostate cancer by the modified Gleason system correlates with pathologic stage and prognosis.

Measurement of serum PSA levels is widely used to assist in the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of prostate cancer.

Prostatic biopsy specimen showing foci of small crowded glands, some showing cribriform pattern of arrangement.

Pearl PF0895: Types of metastasis(osteoblastic or osteolytic) and their primary:

Predominantly osteoblastic:

* Prostate cancer

* Osteosarcoma

* Medullary carcinoma thyroid

Mixed osteoblastic and osteolytic:

* Breast cancer(preponderance toward osteolytic)

* Lymphoma

* Urothelial carcinoma

* Lung cancer

Predominantly osteolytic:

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Multiple myeloma

* Thyroid carcinoma(except medullary carcinoma thyroid)

* Gastrointestinal tract carcinoma

* Malignant melanoma

questions.text: A 70-year-old woman had her routine follow up and her USG of the liver is shown below. She is asymptomatic at present but has a history of mild right hypochondriac pain which is relieved by taking analgesics. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gallstones

The USG shows a gallbladder wall that is thickened with no edema in the pericholecystic fat. The gallbladder contains biliary sludge and gallstones, shown as the acoustic shadowing. There are no signs of current cholecystitis and thus the diagnosis is gallstones.

Ultrasonography is the most accurate initial imaging modality of choice for the diagnosis of gallbladder stones. They appear as echogenic foci producing acoustic shadows. Size of the gallbladder, presence of stones or polyps, and the thickness of the wall are measured. Inflammation around the gallbladder, the size of the common bile duct, and stones in the extrahepatic biliary tree can also be determined. The sensitivity of UG is > 95%. Small stones can be differentiated from small polyps by the presence of mobility or of an acoustic shadow.

The image below shows ultrasonography of the gall bladder:

Amoebic liver abscess ( Option b)  shows necrotic material and debris on usg without any acoustic shadows. Diagnosis is often found using aspiration.

Hydatid cysts (option c) can present similarly. There is tenderness and enlargement of the liver with blood investigations show eosinophilia, elevated liver enzymes. USG can show various stages, classical being multiple septations and rosette or honeycomb appearance, Water Lilly sign when the cyst wall detaches

The image below shows the multiple septations in ultrasonography of hydatid cyst.

An ultrasound scan in acute cholecystitis (Option d ) demonstrates a distended gallbladder with a thickened wall of >3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, the presence of gallstone( when it is due to associated cholelithiasis), and the sonographic Murphy's sign. Gallbladder distension (diameter >5 cm), pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder wall striations, and, occasionally, wall hyperemia on Doppler examination may also be seen in USG.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A barber aged 42 years presented with a healed ulcer as below, over the lower medial aspect of the right leg. On examination, he has varicose veins on both his legs. What is the most likely type of ulcer he had?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Venous ulcer

The history of varicose veins and the presence of an ulcer at the lower 1/3rd of the leg with eczema and pigmentation is characteristic of a venous ulcer.

Venous ulcers are due to chronic venous insufficiency and are particularly seen in the area between the muscles of the calf and ankle. They are accompanied by lipodermatosclerosis and hemosiderosis(If these features are not present then the ulcer is probably not of venous origin). Ambulatory venous hypertension is the most acceptable theory in the pathophysiology of venous ulcers. It has a sloping edge and the floor contains granulation tissue covered by slough and exudate. Marjolin’s ulcer is a type of squamous cell carcinoma seen in chronic long-standing venous ulcers.

Management of venous ulcers:

* Bisgaard's regimen

* Education

* Elevation of the affected limb to reduce the edema

* Elastic compression stockings - The ideal interface pressure in venous ulceration is 35-40 mmHg.

* Evaluation

* 4 layer bandaging system comprising of:

* Orthopedic wool

* Cotton crepe

* Elastic bandage - first compressive layer

* Cohesive bandage - second compressive layer

* Antibiotics are given only if the wound is infected.

* Regular dressing.

* Medical management by oral pentoxifylline is considered which helps in reducing the viscosity and improving circulation.

* Surgery- ulcer excision with pinch mesh grafting has a good outcome and helps in preventing recurrence.

Ischaemic/ Arterial
Venous

Toes, feet, legs, or even upper limb digits.
The lower limb, commonly on the medial side of the ankle, is never above the middle third of the leg

Characteristics

Deep, penetrating the fascia exposes the tendons, muscles, and underlying bone.

The ulcer is painful, with irregular margin tenderness, and hyperesthetic.

Vertically oval, and painless, the floor may have pale to no granulation tissue, induration, and tenderness at the base.
painless, punched-out with regular calloused margins.

Edges are thin, reddish blue, and undermined with pale granulation tissue, scanty discharge on the floor, and slight induration at the base.
