questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old mother presents with pain in her left breast. Which of the following is the most likely cause of acute mastitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Crack in the nipple

Acute mastitis is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

Mastitis occurs due to a combination of factors such as inadequate milk drainage and the introduction of bacteria present on the skin. The cracks in the nipple serve as an entry point, thus resulting in infection. The most common organism causing acute mastitis is Staphylococcus aureus.

Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the 1st month of breastfeeding (lactational breast abscess).

Staphylococcal acute mastitis typically results in localized abscesses. Signs and symptoms of this condition involve:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

Management includes analgesia, continued expression from the breast, antibiotics such as amoxiclav, and repeated aspiration of pus. In case of aspiration and antibiotics failure, incision and drainage can be done.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old female patient involved in a road traffic accident had nausea and vomiting. She was brought unconscious to the emergency room. NCCT brain reveals the following findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extradural hemorrhage

The given history and CT image showing a typical biconvex hyperdense lesion are characteristic of an extradural hemorrhage (EDH), and it is most commonly due to bleeding from the middle meningeal artery.

EDH refers to the accumulation of blood in the potential space between the inner table of the skull and the dura mater. The hematoma arises from arterial disruption, especially of the middle meningeal artery. The middle meningeal vein and diploic veins may also be implicated.

Patients present with head injury with lucid interval, ipsilateral mydriasis, and ipsilateral hemiparesis. There is a transient loss of consciousness after injury; 6-12 hours later the condition of the patient deteriorates. The time period between which the patient appears normal is known as the lucid interval. The patient presents with features of raised intracranial pressure such as high blood pressure, vomiting, bradycardia, and convulsions. Cushing's triad involves bradycardia, respiratory irregularities, and hypertension.

On head CT, the blood clot is biconvex or lentiform in shape and has a well-defined border. An EDH is typically associated with a fracture of the temporoparietal region.

Immediate surgical intervention is necesary to save life. A craniotomy is indicated for EDH.

Pearl PF0339: Intracranial Hemorrhage (ICH)

Extradural hemorrhage (EDH):

* Source: Arterial bleed

* MC- Middle meningeal artery

* Cause- Trauma

* Clinical features: Lucid interval is characteristic

* CT – Lentiform opacity

* Treatment: A large or rapidly evolving EDH requires surgical evacuation

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH)

* Source: Venous bleed

* Bridging dural veins

* Causes: Trauma, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, alcohol abuse, shaken baby syndrome

* Clinical features

* Acute SDH: may be associated with lucid interval

* Chronic SDH: drowsiness, headache

* CT- crescentic opacity

* Treatment: May resolve spontaneously or require surgical drainage

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)

* Source: Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – Trauma

* 2nd MC – Rupture of berry aneurysm

* MC sites: Terminal ICA, MCA bifurcation, top of basilar artery

* Clinical features: Thunderclap headache with neck stiffness +/- FND

* Investigations:

* Non-contrast CT brain,

* CSF xanthochromia (peaks in 2 days and subsides in 2 weeks)

* Treatment:

* Clipping/coiling of berry aneurysm,

* Triple H therapy – hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution to prevent vasospasm

Intraparenchymal hemorrhage- (MC type of ICH)

* Source- Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – hypertension

* Trauma, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, bleeding disorders, neoplasms, vascular malformations

* MC sites:

* Putamen (basal ganglia)

* Thalamus

* Cerebellum

* Pons

* Treatment:

* Correction of any identified coagulopathy by infusing prothrombin complex concentrates, FFP or fresh platelets as required

* Surgical evacuation for cerebellar hematoms >3 cm in size

Pearl PF1866: Intracranial haemorrhage

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old patient who is a chronic tobacco chewer presents with a whitish lesion on the gingivobuccal sulcus for 7 months. What is the next best step in the management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Local excision and biopsy

The most likely diagnosis in the given scenario is leukoplakia. The next best step in management is local excision and biopsy.

Leukoplakia is a premalignant condition of the oral cavity characterized by well-circumscribed whitish patches or plaques that involve large areas of the oral mucosa. Smoking, chronic candidiasis, tobacco chewing, alcohol, spices, and sepsis are some of the risk factors.

They appear as small, well-circumscribed lesions and can extensively involve a large area of the oral mucosa.

Variants of leukoplakia are:

* Homogenous: Most common type; presents has uniform white patches

* Nodular: Fine nodules on the surface, has more malignant potential

* Speckled leukoplakia is whitish lesions on an erythematous base. They have the highest risk of malignant transformation.

* Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is rare and has a high risk for malignant transformation.

Hairy leukoplakia is more commonly seen in AIDS patients, characterized by severe hyperkeratosis and acanthosis. The most common cause of this condition is Epstein-Barr virus.

Leukoplakia in the elderly and of long duration has more risk of turning into malignancy. So an excisional biopsy confirms the diagnosis and also helps to rule out carcinoma. Management includes smoking cessation and reduction in alcohol consumption.

questions.text: A 44-year-old lady presents to the hospital with a flank mass that is ballotable. On CT imaging, the mass measures 4cm. Urine examination shows malignant cells. What is the most appropriate management for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Partial nephrectomy

Partial nephrectomy (also known as nephron-sparing surgery) is performed for renal cell carcinoma(RCC) tumors less than 4 cm in size. It is also performed for:

Indications for partial nephrectomy:

* Tumors < 4cm

* Well-selected tumors between 4-7 cm

* Bilateral tumors

* Tumor in solitary kidneys

* Patients with pre-existing renal dysfunction.

Recently, partial nephrectomy is also increasingly being performed for stage T1b tumors.

Treatment of renal cell carcinoma:

RCC is a radio and chemoresistant tumor.

Staging
Description
Management

Stage 1
Tumor <7 cm, confined to the kidney
Partial nephrectomy

Stage 2
Tumor >7 cm, confined to the kidney
Radical nephrectomy

Stage 3
Tumor extends into the major veins or adrenal gland with intact Gerota’s fascia or regional lymph nodes involved.
Radical nephrectomy

Stage 4
Tumor invades beyond Gerota fascia (including contiguous extension into the ipsilateral adrenal gland)

• Debulking surgery
• mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus, sirolimus
• Tyrosine kinase inhibitors: sunitinib, sorafenib

Radical nephrectomy consists of the removal of the kidney, perirenal fat, adrenal gland, and regional lymph nodes. The adrenal gland is no longer removed except in cases of obvious tumor involvement. Lymphadenectomy is indicated only in high-risk patients with large primary tumors and enlarged lymph nodes.

Cryoablation is indicated in the T1a stage of RCC if surgery cannot be performed. It is also indicated in advanced/metastatic tumors.

Note: Sunitinib and sorafenib are also used in GIST and hepatocellular carcinoma.

* Associated with sickle cell trait

Sarcomatoid change can occur infrequently in all types of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and is an ominous feature.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient underwent an emergency laparotomy for grossly contaminated peritonitis due to a perforated hollow viscus. On postoperative day 7, the patient developed signs of wound infection, including erythema, tenderness, and serosanguinous discharge. Subsequently, the wound showed evidence of dehiscence with exposure of underlying tissues. The patient's vital signs are stable, with no evidence of ongoing intra-abdominal sepsis. Considering the current wound status, what should be the most appropriate management strategy for the laparotomy wound?
options: Vaccum assisted negative pressure wound therapy
Antibiotic irrigation of the wound followed by delayed primary closure
Initiating primary wound closure to reduce risk of further contamination
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vaccum assisted negative pressure wound therapy

The clinical scenario is suggestive of burst abdomen and the most appropriate management would be Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy.

Burst abdomen/Acute wound dehiscence is the mechanical wound failure causing separation of the closed abdominal wound associated with abdominal content evisceration. It usually occurs between the 5th and 8th postoperative days.

A sudden giving way feeling from the wound precipitated by bouts of cough, and pinkish serosanguinous discharge can be seen. Omentum or coils of the intestine are forced out of the wound.

Management includes delayed closure with initial mesh wrap or Bogota bag, placing a subcutaneous drain, suitable antibiotic therapy, and prevention of abdominal compartment syndrome as described above and VAC.

Vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) is a method of wound management, which uses negative pressure for spontaneous healing or by lesser reconstructive options. Negative pressure therapy stabilizes the wound environment by reducing wound edema and bacterial load,as well as improves tissue perfusion by angiogenesis and thereby stimulating granulation tissue formation. All this improves the possibility of primary closure of wounds and reduces the need for plastic procedures.The ideal pressure applied is 125 mm Hg.

Indications of VAC therapy includes diabetic foot ulcers, bed sores,burn injuries,crush injuries, sternal/abdominal wound dehiscence, fasciotomy wounds and animal bites/frostbite wounds.

VAC therapy is contraindicated in patients with malignant wounds such as Marjolin’s ulcer,untreated osteomyelitis, presence of fistulae or necrotic tissue underneath the dressing.

Below is an image showing VAC.

Other Options:

Option B: Antibiotic irrigation followed by delayed primary closure is insufficient because it doesn't address the immediate need for ongoing drainage and decompression, and local antibiotics aren't effective for managing severe contamination.

Option C: Primary closure of the abdomen immediately after laparotomy would be dangerous in this scenario as it risks abdominal compartment syndrome due to ongoing edema and doesn't allow for adequate drainage of contamination; forced closure could lead to tissue necrosis and organ dysfunction.

Options D: Normal saline-soaked gauze dressing is inadequate because it doesn't provide active negative pressure, fails to effectively remove edema and inflammatory exudates, and requires frequent dressing changes that increase infection risk and nursing workload; additionally, it can lead to tissue maceration and doesn't promote wound edge approximation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman after thyroidectomy comes to you for 2nd opinion for further treatment of papillary thyroid cancer. What would you recommend for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radioiodine scan

A radioiodine scan will be recommended to this patient following the thyroidectomy, to look for residual or metastatic disease.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy. It is more commonly seen in women between the ages of 30 and 50. Radiation exposure and a family history of thyroid malignancies are the common etiologies. Genetic abnormalities in either the RET gene or the BRAF gene can be seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Clinical features include an asymptomatic thyroid swelling with cervical lymph node enlargement. In advanced disease, there may be features like hoarseness, dysphagia, cough, or dyspnea.

An ultrasound scan accurately assesses the size and number of nodules, as well as categorizes the lesions as benign, indeterminate, or malignant. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is a diagnostic test, helpful in investigating an indeterminate or malignant lesion.

Histopathology shows the following features:

* Branching papillae

* Orphan Annie eye nuclei: optically clear nuclei with fine nuclear chromatin

* Pseudo inclusions: invaginations of the nuclear membrane

* Psammoma bodies: concentric calcifications in the core of the papillae.

Below is the histopathological image of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid with characteristic Orphan Annie eye nuclei.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is known to spread via lymphatics, hence lymph node metastasis is commonly seen.

Treatment of Papillary thyroid carcinoma is as follows:

Total thyroidectomy is the treatment of choice. Routine central neck dissection is not recommended. Neck dissection is indicated in higher-risk situations, such as

* Tumor size > 4 cm (T3 stage) or gross extrathyroidal extension (T4 stage) or enlarged central lymph nodes - Total thyroidectomy + Central Neck Dissection

* Lateral Aberrant Thyroid - Total thyroidectomy + Modified Radical Neck Dissection + Central Neck Dissection

For occult papillary cancer (<1 cm tumor size, with no lymphatic, vascular or capsular invasion) - Lobectomy can be sufficient.

Radio-iodine ablation is undertaken when a whole-body iodine scan is positive after a total thyroidectomy for any differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary or follicular carcinoma).

The presence of any metastatic or residual thyroid tissue after total thyroidectomy can be detected by observing the uptake of radio-iodine in the entire body. To achieve effective uptake of radio-iodine, TSH levels need to be greatly increased, for example, by withdrawing thyroxine after the surgery for 4-6 weeks.

A positive whole-body iodine scan after total thyroidectomy indicates that there is either a metastatic or residual disease present. These patients are treated with I131 for radio-iodine ablation.

A negative scan means there is no metastasis or residual thyroid tissue. They are followed up regularly with serum thyroglobulin, TSH and USG-neck.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 51-year-old lady presents with complaints of a mass in the right breast. On examination, the mass was larger than 2cm and ipsilateral mobile axillary lymph nodes were present. What is the staging, considering the mass is malignant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. cT4N1M0

The clinical scenario of a 51-year-old lady with a breast mass >2cm, lymph node involvement (N1), and the image showing an ulcerative mass near the nipple of the right breast (T4), is clinically suggestive of inflammatory breast carcinoma. Its likely staging is cT4N1M0

Inflammatory breast carcinoma (stage T4) is an aggressive form of locally advanced breast cancer (LABC) and is associated with the worst prognosis among all subtypes of breast cancer. It accounts for <3% of breast cancers. It is characterized by skin changes of brawny induration, erythema, and edema (peau d’orange). The term peau d’orange describes the orange-peel appearance of the skin resulting from edema and dimpling at sites of hair follicles.

In order to determine the best course of treatment for a patient with IBC, it is important to stage cancer. Staging is the process of determining the extent to which cancer has spread within the breast and to other parts of the body. Some prefixes and suffixes are used with the cTNM (clinical) and pTNM (pathologic) staging systems to designate special cases. These do not affect the stage group but indicate that they must be analyzed separately. The “y” prefix, denotes patients who have received systemic therapy before surgery. In this patient, since the staging is being done clinically, "c" is added as a prefix.

The diagnostic criteria for inflammatory breast cancer are -

*

Rapid onset of breast erythema, edema and/or peau d’orange, and/or warm breast (with or without an underlying palpable mass)

*

Duration of history no more than six months

*

Erythema occupies at least one-third of the breast

*

Pathologic confirmation of invasive carcinoma

The pathologic hallmark is the presence of tumor cells within dermal lymphatics in skin biopsy specimens, but it is not a prerequisite for diagnosis. Mammography may be normal or show skin thickening. A PET-CT scan should be considered at the time of diagnosis to rule out concurrent metastatic disease.

Axillary nodal metastases are common, and there is a significant risk for distant metastases.

Combined-modality treatment is used, which includes

* Neoadjuvant chemotherapy

* Modified radical mastectomy

* Radiation therapy

* Hormonal therapy (for ER-positive tumors)

* Trastuzumab (for HER-2-positive tumors)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old male patient presents with hematuria and a neovascular mass in bilateral kidney on a CT scan, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal angiomyolipoma

The CT image showing renal lesions that has hypo-attenuating components consistent with macroscopic fat is highly suggestive of renal angiomyolipoma.

Angiomyolipomas are benign tumors that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. The mean age of presentation is 43 years and there is a female predilection. It can present as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, especially with larger tumors. The patient can present with flank pain, palpable mass, hematuria, urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure.

Imaging in renal angiomyolipoma: Demonstration of macroscopic fat is the main part of making a diagnosis. USG may show hyperechoic lesions in the cortex with posterior acoustic shadowing. In patients with tuberous sclerosis, the entire kidney is affected and produces an echogenic appearance with loss of normal corticomedullary junction.

CT findings:

* Cortical lesions that demonstrate macroscopic fat (less than -20 HU)

* Absence of ossification or calcification

* The presence of macroscopic fat is strongly suggestive of this condition, but not pathognomonic as RCC may rarely demonstrate macroscopic fat.

* Approximately 5% may be fat-poor.

MRI: It is an excellent tool to demonstrate intramural fat components. Two sequences are used:

* Fat-saturated techniques

* Phase-in and phase-out imaging that shows India ink artifacts at the junction between fat and non-fat components.

Digital subtraction angiography: They are hypervascular lesions showing a 'sunburst appearance' in the arterial phase and an 'onion peel appearance' in the venous phase.

They usually do not require any intervention. mTOR inhibitors like everolimus can be used to decrease the size of the lesion.

Other options:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC): It is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC and hence it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases.

Renal cyst: It is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions needs evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification of renal cysts is given above.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient presents with painless hematuria. He is diagnosed with bladder cancer involving the muscle layer. What is the next best step in the treatment of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Radical cystectomy

Radical cystectomy is the preferred mode of management for a patient with bladder cancer involving the muscle layer.

Smoking and exposure to chemicals are strongly associated with the development of bladder cancer.

Activation of oncogenes such as ras, c-erbB, E2F3, and inactivation of tumor-suppressor genes such as p53, p21, p16, and Rb gene is implicated in the cancer formation of the bladder.

Clinical features of bladder carcinoma include:

* Painless gross haematuria - Most common symptom and is indicative of a bladder carcinoma until proven otherwise

* Urinary retention

* Constant pelvic pain

* Increased urinary frequency

* Discomfort while urinating

* If there is nerve involvement, pain is referred to the suprapubic region, groins, perineum, and thighs.

Investigations done for bladder cancer are:

* Urine cytology - Low sensitivity

* Intravenous urography, non-contrast CT, and MRI show a filling defect.

* Cystourethroscopy and biopsy - Mainstay for diagnosis.

The most important prognostic factor in bladder carcinoma is the depth of invasion.

Management:

* Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer:

* Intravesical instillations of a chemotherapeutic agent such as mitomycin C or epirubicin

* Regular cystoscopic check-ups and repeat biopsy if required

* Immunotherapy with regular intravesical instillations of Bacille Calmette Guerin (BCG)

* Muscle invasive bladder cancer:

*

* Systemic chemotherapy with a combination of drugs – cisplatin, methotrexate, doxorubicin, and vinblastine (M-VAC) or cisplatin along with gemcitabine is given before radical cystectomy(neoadjuvant).

* Radical cystectomy along with urinary diversion procedure and lymph node dissection +/- neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

* Radical beam external radiotherapy is also used for invasive bladder cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 73 old male smoker with a past history of coronary artery disease presents with blackening of the toes. An image of the foot is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atherosclerosis

The given clinical scenario of an elderly smoker with past history of coronary artery disease and gangrene of the first three toes is likely to have atherosclerosis.

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease in which there is a build-up of plaques inside arteries.  It is common after 50 years.These plaques are principally composed of lipids that induce an inflammatory reaction causing turbulent flow leading to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease(ASCVD). This results in atheroma formation in arteries throughout the body hampering the blood flow and leading to ischemia.

Risk factors include smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and elevated cholesterol. The infrarenal part of the abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, iliofemoral vessels, carotid bifurcation, and popliteal arteries are the common arteries involved. The presence of atherosclerotic disease in one part of the body suggests there could be blockade in other parts as well.

Patients with chronic limb ischemia present with rest pain and tissue loss such as gangrene and ulceration. An ischemic ulcer is painful, pale, and cyanotic in appearance with absent pulsations. It may be associated with transient ischemic attacks, chest pain, eye problems, mesenteric ischemia, and altered renal function.

Doppler or angiogram can be done to identify the block. It is important to evaluate these patients for intercurrent cardiac disorders.

Management involves cessation of smoking and modification of other risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia. High-intensity statins should be given irrespective of cholesterol levels in ASCVD. Other drugs that can be used include pentoxifylline, aspirin, clopidogrel, and cilostazol. Surgical options include thrombectomy, endarterectomy, bypass grafting, and amputations if the limb is gangrenous.

Complications of atherosclerosis include

* Narrowing of the arteries: Coronary, cerebral, renal, mesenteric, iliofemoral. > 70% narrowing (severe) causes reduced blood flow.

* lschaemia, ulcerations, gangrene

* Embolism: From atheromatous plaques

* Aneurysm formation: Mainly abdominal aorta and also in peripheral arteries

Option A: Buerger’s disease is a progressive nonatherosclerotic segmental inflammatory disease that most often affects small- and medium-sized arteries, veins, and nerves of the upper and lower extremities.

* Typically presents in young male smokers, with symptoms beginning prior to age 40.

* Patients initially present with the foot, leg, arm, or hand.

* Claudication may progress to rest pain to calf claudication and eventually ischemic rest pain and ulcerations on the toes, feet, or fingers and even gangrene.

If the patient continues to smoke, the disease progresses into the collaterals, blocking them eventually, leading to severe ischemia which is called decompensatory peripheral vascular disease/ critical limb ischemia which presents as rest pain, ulceration, and gangrene.

Option C: Raynaud's disease usually occurs in females and affects bilateral upper limbs. Patients present with pallor/blanching (syncope), dusky cyanosis (asphyxia), and rubor/painful red de-engorgement (recovery). Peripheral pulses are normal.

Option D: Giant cell arteritis is characterized by giant cell infiltration of the arterial wall (giant cell arteritis) involving superficial temporal, facial, retinal, upper limb, coronary and vertebral arteries. Patients present with severe headaches, visual abnormalities, jaw claudication, and a tender superficial temporal artery.

Pearl PF1741: Ankle–brachial Pressure Index (ABPI)

The ankle-brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is the ratio of systolic pressure at the ankle to that in the arm.

The numerator is the highest pressure in the dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, or peroneal artery and the denominator is the highest brachial systolic pressure.

ABPI Reading
Interpretation

>0.91 < 1.3
Normal

<0.9
Diagnostic of occlusive arterial disease in patients with symptoms of claudication or other signs of ischemia

0.5 to 0.9

<0.3

>1.4
Signifies poor compressibility of the arteries. Mostly due to calcification because of increased age, diabetes etc.

Note: A fall in the resting ABPI of more than 20% after exercise is indicative of arterial disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic presents to the emergency room with acute pain abdomen in the epigastric region radiating to the back with nausea, anorexia, and occasional vomiting. Investigations showed elevated amylase levels and total count. Likely diagnosis is__________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute pancreatitis

History of epigastric pain radiating to the back in a chronic alcoholic patient with elevated serum amylase levels are most consistent with the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis.

Pearl PF0602: Clinical features of acute pancreatitis

Symptoms:

* Acute onset of epigastric pain, which is severe, constant, and refractory to usual doses of analgesics.

* Typically radiates to back

* Relieved in the sitting forward position

* Nausea, repeated vomiting, retching, and hiccups

Signs:

* Hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea

* Grey Turner sign (A): bluish discoloration of the flanks

* Cullen’s sign (B): bluish discoloration around the umbilicus

* Fox sign: discoloration below the inguinal ligament

* Pleural effusion (left > right): dullness on percussion, decreased breath sounds

Pearl PF1357: Laboratory findings in acute pancreatitis

* Elevated serum amylase and serum lipase

* Serum amylase level rises immediately and peaks in few hours and returns to normal in 3–5 days

* Serum amylase level lacks specificity.

* Serum amylase levels do not correlate with the severity of pancreatitis.

* Serum lipase is more specific, and it is more useful when the patient presents 24–48 hours later.

* Hyperglycemia

* Hypocalcemia, hypoalbuminemia

* Leukocytosis

* Elevated serum levels of hepatic enzymes like alanine aminotransferase (ALT).

* Azotemia, due to prerenal acute renal failure in case of severe fluid loss

Pearl PF1586: X-Ray Findings in Acute Pancreatitis

Radiographic findings of acute pancreatitis are non-specific.

Sentinel loop sign: Generalized or local ileus, with isolated dilation of a segment of the gut (sentinel loop) consisting of jejunum, transverse colon, or duodenum adjacent to the pancreas

Colon cut-off sign: Functional spasm at the splenic flexure due to the extension of inflammation to phrenicocolic ligament via transverse mesocolon.

Renal halo sign: Edema around the kidney due to the involvement of paranephric fat resulting in:

* Obliteration of psoas shadow

* Localised ground-glass appearance

questions.text: A diabetic patient developed DVT with a necrolytic migratory rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glucagonoma

Necrolytic migratory erythema skin lesion along with a history of long standing diabetes and recurrent deep vein thrombosis is suggestive of glucagonoma.

* In maternal diabetes, the fetal islets respond to hyperglycemia by increasing their size and number. In the postnatal period, these hyperactive islets may be responsible for serious episodes of hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A homosexual man complains of painful defecation and mass protruding from the anal canal. Biopsy reveals squamous cell carcinoma of anus. Correct management for this patient is ___________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Combined chemoradiation

The management of choice for squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal is combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy also called Nigro regimen.

Treatment of squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal:

* The primary treatment for squamous cell carcinoma is by chemoradiotherapy (Nigro regimen)

* A combination of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) with mitomycin C/ cisplatin is followed by external beam radiation to the pelvis with a minimum dose of 45 Gy.

* Metastases are rare at presentation (5%), and treatment is aimed at local control.

* Patients with T2 lesions and residual disease after 45 Gy, T3 or T4 tumors, or node-positive disease are usually treated with an additional 9 to 14 Gy for a total dose of 54 to 59 Gy.

* Patients with persistent disease up to 6 months after treatment generally require APR. Those who have local recurrence are also recommended for APR.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presented with a sudden onset tearing type of chest pain radiating to the back, shortness of breath, and nausea. CT chest image is given.What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Labetolol and urgent surgery

The above clinical scenario of a male patient with tearing chest pain is suggestive of aortic dissection. Beta-blockers such as Labetalol should be given to all patients with aortic dissection and surgical repair is done after stabilizing the patient. So, option A is the correct answer.

Aortic dissection occurs when a tear or flap occurs in the intima or inner media of the aorta resulting in progressive separation of the layers of the aorta.

Risk factors for aortic dissection are:

* Smoking

* Hypertension

* Atherosclerosis

* Hypercholesterolemia

* Aortopathy, aortitis, bicuspid aortic valve, or preexisting medial degenerative disease.

* Aortic injury during cardiac catheterization, surgery, endovascular aortic repair (Iatrogenic)

* Cocaine or amphetamine abuse

The most typical presentation of aortic dissection is tearing chest pain. Other clinical features include dyspnea, nausea, vomiting, murmurs due to aortic valvular insufficiency, and shock. A discrepancy between the extremities in pulse, blood pressure, or both is the classic physical finding in patients with aortic dissection.

The dissection can extend distally down the aorta to involve the:

* Renal arteries (renal pain and renal failure)

* Mesenteric arteries (abdominal pain and bowel ischemia)

* Spinal arteries (paraplegia, incontinence)

* Iliofemoral arteries (leg pain, pallor, loss or reduced pulses, and limb ischemia).

The dissection may track proximally to involve the:

* Head and neck vessels (syncope and focal neurological deficits)

* Coronary vessels (cardiac ischemia, cardiac tamponade)

* Aortic root (aortic regurgitation)

Investigations in aortic dissection:

* Transesophageal echocardiography can be done at the bedside in patients who are hemodynamically unstable; it can give information about flow in the true and false lumen and shows very high sensitivity for confirmation of the aortic dissection.

* Currently, a CT scan is the initial best investigation for the diagnosis of aortic dissection in the hemodynamically stable patent. Additionally, it tells about the segments involved and the acuity, and complications of the dissection. The classic feature seen in the CT scan is a double-lumen aorta.

Treatment:

The initial management of patients diagnosed with aortic dissection is beta-blocker medication to control hypertension, along with pain management. The preferred beta-blocker drug is esmolol, a cardio-selective beta blocker. These reduce cardiac contractility and blood pressure. It can be used in patients with bronchospastic disorders. Labetalol, a non-selective beta blocker decreases systemic vascular resistance without impairing the cardiac output. Enalapril and other angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors can be used if there is decreased renal perfusion.

Calcium channel blockers like diltiazem may be used IV if beta-blockers cannot be employed.

Once hypertension is controlled, definitive surgical repair of aortic dissection is done. Nitroprusside, a direct vasodilator is given after adequate beta-blockade is achieved. Definitive management is by surgical repair.

Types:

* Stanford type A (DeBakey types I and II) requires surgical intervention once the patient's blood pressure is stabilized.

* Stanford type B (DeBakey type III) is best managed by antihypertensive drugs. Surgical intervention is indicated in complicated cases if the pain increases (signaling impending rupture) or when there is evidence of malperfusion of organs or neurological symptoms.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presented with complaints of hematuria and recurrent urinary tract infection. You notice the following finding in his CECT. What is the likely condition indicated by the arrow in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horse shoe kidney

The given image shows a horseshoe kidney. It is prone to obstruction, reflux, and stone formation.

Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidneys. Horseshoe kidneys are a type of renal fusion anomaly. They are formed when the lower poles of the two kidneys fuse during organogenesis to form an isthmus. They are typically low-lying as the inferior mesenteric artery interferes with its ascent due to its size and the presence of an isthmus.

It presents as a fixed, nonmobile, firm mass in the midline at the level of the 4th lumbar vertebra and is resonant on percussion. It is associated with an increased risk of infection, stone formation, hydronephrosis, and tuberculosis.

It has a 2:1 male preponderance. Individuals with horseshoe kidneys are prone to reflux, obstruction, and stone formation.

Other options:

Option A: The image of polycystic kidney disease on CT abdomen is shown below: Multiple bilateral cysts are seen.

Option C: Hydronephrosis is aseptic dilatation of the pelvicalyceal system due to partial or intermittent obstruction to urinary outflow.

Option D: Pancake kidney (also known as discoid kidney, disc kidney, lump kidney, fused pelvic kidney, or cake kidney) is a rare renal fusion anomaly where both the upper and lower poles of the kidney are fused giving it an appearance of a pancake. The MRI image of the pancake kidney is shown below:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man came with complaints of recurrent discharge and pain due to lesions around the anus for 3 years. A diagnosis of fistula-in-ano is made. What is the gold standard investigation for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MRI

In cases of fistula-in-ano, MRI is the gold standard investigation.

A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal connection between the anal canal and the perianal skin, lined with granulation tissue. It may follow the drainage of a perianal abscess or may be seen in association with diseases like tuberculosis or Crohn's disease.

Clinical features are perianal pain, swelling, and intermittent purulent discharge, which might be blood-stained. On examination, one or more external openings may be visible.

Goodsall’s rule can be used as a guide in determining the location of the internal opening of the fistula. Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract. Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly track in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline.

However, exceptions to this rule often occur. Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline.

The investigations done for fistula-in-ano can include a fistulogram, endoanal ultrasound with hydrogen peroxide, MRI, and computed tomography (CT) scan. An MRI is the gold standard investigation for fistula imaging. It helps us to identify the secondary extensions of the track, which when missed may cause persistence of the fistula.

Surgical management includes fistulotomy, fistulectomy, ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract (LIFT), setons, or advancement flaps.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with urinary symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia. Which of the following is used to manage the urinary symptoms in the initial stage of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tamsulosin

Tamsulosin is used for the management of urinary symptoms in the initial stages of Benign prostatic hyperplasia(BPH). It improves the urinary flow by inhibiting the smooth muscle contraction of the prostate thereby reducing the resistance at the bladder neck.

BPH is characterized by symptoms of urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, incontinence, slow urinary stream, straining to void, urinary intermittency (stream starting and stopping during micturition), or hesitancy, splitting of the voiding stream, and terminal dribbling. Physical examination reveals a smooth enlarged and non-tender prostate. Lab investigations reveal a normal PSA (prostate-specific antigen). Diagnosis is made based on clinical presentation and a lack of lab findings suggestive of malignancy (elevated PSA). A biopsy is rarely indicated.

Conservative treatment is recommended for men with mild symptoms, flow rate >10ml/s, and good bladder emptying with residual urine <100ml.

Medical management includes alpha-adrenergic blocking agents that inhibit the contraction of smooth muscle that is found in the prostate. Tamsulosin is an adrenoreceptor antagonist with receptor selectivity at α1A. It is used in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia.

The other class of drugs is the 5α-reductase inhibitors, which inhibit the conversion of testosterone to DHT, the most active form of androgen. Finasteride is a 5α-reductase enzyme inhibitor. It is effective in the treatment of palpable enlarged prostate. These drugs result in a 25% shrinkage of the prostate gland.

Indications for surgical management:

* Lower urinary tract symptoms that are refractory to medical therapy

* Refractory urinary retention

* Recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI)

* Hematuria

* Stone formation

* Hydronephrosis, hydroureter with renal functional impairment

Surgical management involves the use of the transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). Laser ablative techniques using holmium YAG can also be done.

* Static component: 5 alpha-reductase inhibitor [eg: Finasteride]

* Dynamic component: Alpha 1 blockers [eg: Tamsulosin, terazosin etc]

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. Skin grafting was done wherein the graft was taken from the same person. Which type of graft is it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autograft

The given image shows a split skin graft obtained from the same person. This type of graft is autograft.

Skin grafting is the transfer of skin from the donor area to the recipient area. The most preferable donor site is the buttocks in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children. The most commonly used donor site is the thigh.

Autograft is the transfer of tissue from one location to another location on the same patient.

Skin grafts can be broadly divided into two categories:

Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis are called split-thickness skin grafts. Less dermis in the split-thickness skin graft translates into less primary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks in surface area after harvesting and before grafting) and more secondary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks during healing).

Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. More dermis in the full-thickness skin graft translates into more primary contraction and less secondary contraction.

Other options:

Option B:Xenograft is tissue transfer from a donor of one species to a recipient of another species. It is also known as heterograft.

Option C: Allograft is the tissue transfer between two genetically different members, e.g. kidney transplantation (human to human). It is also known as homograft.

Option D: Isograft is the tissue transfer between two genetically identical individuals, i.e. between two identical twins.

Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft

The take of skin graft occurs in three phases:

* Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries.

* Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses

* Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft

Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later.

Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)

questions.text: A patient who was diagnosed with prostate cancer is being investigated. The bone scan is reported as a super scan with increased uptake in the bones and reduced activity in the spleen. What is the reason for this super scan appearance?
options: Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis
Decreased uptake by adrenal glands and kidney
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis

The super scan appearance is due to increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis.

Diffuse osteoblastic metastatic diseases such as carcinoma breast and prostate carcinoma lead to a generalized increase in the skeletal uptake relative to soft tissue and absent or faint renal activity on a bone scan. This is known as a super scan. It may also be seen in generalized bone diseases such as hyperparathyroidism.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.

Prognosis and staging: The Gleason grading system correlates with the pathological stage, spread, and prognosis. Measurement of serum PSA levels may be useful to assist with the diagnosis and management.

Pearl PF0895: Types of metastasis(osteoblastic or osteolytic) and their primary:

Predominantly osteoblastic:

* Prostate cancer

* Osteosarcoma

* Medullary carcinoma thyroid

Mixed osteoblastic and osteolytic:

* Breast cancer(preponderance toward osteolytic)

* Lymphoma

* Urothelial carcinoma

* Lung cancer

Predominantly osteolytic:

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Multiple myeloma

* Thyroid carcinoma(except medullary carcinoma thyroid)

* Gastrointestinal tract carcinoma

* Malignant melanoma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A soldier presents to a referral hospital one day after sustaining a high-velocity shrapnel injury to his right thigh. He complains of severe pain at the wound site. On examination, crepitus is present. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clostridium perfringens

The most likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario is gas gangrene/ clostridial myonecrosis, which is caused by clostridium perfringens.

Military wounds provide an ideal environment for gas gangrene as the kinetic energy of high-velocity missiles or shrapnel causes extensive tissue damage. Patients who are immunocompromised, diabetic, or have malignant disease are also at greater risk. The usual incubation period is <24 hours of injury.

Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues). The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate, in which Gram staining will reveal bacteria. Edema and spreading gangrene occur due to the release of collagenase, hyaluronidase, other proteases, and alpha-toxin. Early systemic complications like circulatory collapse and organ failure can occur without adequate treatment.

Management includes high doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues. Amputations should be performed under antibiotic prophylaxis.

Other options:

C. difficile, a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus, causes Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile infection (CDI) after ingestion of spores of the organism. The more severe form of the condition is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC). It is most commonly associated with prolonged antimicrobial use which interferes with the commensal colonic microflora. The most commonly implicated antibiotics are cephalosporins, ampicillin, and clindamycin.

questions.text: All of the following are true about nephroblastoma except:
options: Treatment is chemotherapy followed by surgery
Most common intraabdominal malignancy in children
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Most common intraabdominal malignancy in children

Neuroblastoma, not nephroblastoma, is the most common intra-abdominal malignancy in children.

Wilms tumor/nephroblastoma is an embryonal renal neoplasm caused by faulty renal development that results in the metanephric blastema multiplying excessively. It is usually diagnosed before the age of five.

Children may present with a mass abdomen, fever, and hematuria, which is indicative of the extension of the tumor into the renal pelvis. Hypertension is also observed in a considerable percentage of patients.

Prognostic factors for Wilms tumor:

* Histology

* Stage

* Age

* Tumor weight

* Response to therapy

* Loss of heterozygosity at 1p and 16q

The two most important factors are the histology and the stage of the tumor.

Most of the tumors have favorable histology and are characterized as the “classic” type that consists of three components—blastemal, stromal, and epithelial (tubules) tissues.

Unfavorable tumors are those with focal or diffuse anaplasia. Two principal staging systems are used:

* The COG system is based on findings prior to the initiation of treatment. There exists a local stage and a disease stage. The local stage defines the extent of abdominal disease while the disease stage considers both local disease and metastasis. Metastasis commonly occurs in the lungs.

* The SIOP classification is based on the histologic appearance of the tumors at resection and the outcomes. They are classified as completely necrotic (low risk), blastemal (high risk) and other histological types.

Imaging with USG abdomen and pelvis, CT scan, MRI, etc., shows a solid space-occupying lesion in the kidney.

Management is mainly by chemotherapy and nephrectomy.

questions.text: Four patients were brought to the casualty after sustaining trauma. Which of the following is the correct match of injuries and signs among the following?
options: Extra dural hemorrhage (EDH)- Pin point pupil
Penetrating injury to eustachian tube- CSF otorrhea
Penetrating injury to eye- Battle sign
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gaze paresis- Mid brain lesion

Gaze paresis- Mid-brain lesion, is the correctly matched pair among the given options.

Traumatic injury to the brain affecting the mid-brain or brainstem dysfunction produces:

* Gaze paresis - Inability of the eye to look across beyond the midline.

* Dysconjugate gaze - Inability of the eyes to work together.

* Roving eye movements.

Battle sign and CSF rhinorrhea are features of a middle cranial fossa fracture.

Middle cranial fossa fracture is associated with:

* CSF otorrhea or rhinorrhea

* Hemotympanum

* Ossicular disruption

* Battle sign: Bruising behind the ear

* 7th and 8th cranial nerve palsies

A double target sign is seen in patients with CSF rhinorrhea. The nasal discharge in a patient with CSF rhinorrhea after head trauma is mixed with blood. When this discharge is collected on a filter paper, it shows a double target sign with a central red spot and a peripheral lighter halo as seen in the image below.

The image below shows the 'battle' sign.

Anterior cranial fossa fracture is associated with:

* Subconjunctival hematoma

* CSF rhinorrhea

* Periorbital hematoma or “Raccoon eyes”

Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes): Pooling of blood surrounding the eyes, associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa (given below).

The pinpoint pupil is seen in patients with pontine hemorrhage and opioid overdose.

questions.text: Genetic testing for BRCA 1/BRCA 2 is indicated for all of the following except:
options: Breast cancer diagnosed in a post menopausal female >50 years of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Breast cancer diagnosed in a post menopausal female >50 years of age

Genetic testing is not recommended in post-menopausal females >50 years of age.

Genetic counselling is the process of discussing various genetic testing such as BRCA testing and multiple gene panel testing.

Genetic counselling and testing for genetic mutations (BRCA 1, BRCA 2 and others such as TP53, PTEN) are recommended for high-risk women with:

* Breast cancer diagnosed before age 50

* Triple-negative breast cancer

* Bilateral breast cancer

* Breast and ovarian cancer in the same individual

* Breast cancer in men

* Family history (maternal or paternal) of two or more individuals with breast and ovarian cancer

* A close male relative with breast cancer

* A close relative with early-onset (<50 years) breast or ovarian cancer

* Known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation in the family

questions.text: Involvement of which of the following structures leads to the clinical presentation as shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superficial lymphatics

The peau d'orange appearance of the breast occurs due to the blockade of superficial lymphatics.

The dermal lymphatic blockade gives rise to edema in the breast. The sweat glands and hair follicles get buried due to the edema resulting in a typical orange peel appearance. Infiltration of the ligaments of Cooper results in dimpling of the skin. Infiltration of the lactiferous glands gives rise to retraction of the nipple. Spread into the chest wall results in fixation of the breast into the chest wall. This leads to restricted mobility of the breast.

Spread to the axillary lymph nodes can give rise to lymphedema. Venous edema of the upper limb develops due to the compression of the axillary vein on lymph nodes.

questions.text: Revised Which of the following is not a component of qSOFA score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LDH- Lactate dehydrogenase

Lactate dehydrogenase is not a component of the qSOFA score.

qSOFA scoring is a simplified derivative of SOFA for bedside assessment that is particularly useful outside the ICU setting as it does not require laboratory values.

The qSOFA assigns one point for each component and suggests potentially life-threatening sepsis when at least two of the following parameters are met.

* Altered mental status (GCS <15)

* Systolic blood pressure ≤ 100 mmHg

* Respiratory rate ≥ 22 breaths/min.

A qSOFA score of ≥2 is associated with a significant risk of death or prolonged ICU stay.

SOFA is a more comprehensive and accurate scoring system which is particularly superior to qSOFA in the ICU setting. This includes:

* Circulation - Systolic BP & need for vasopressors and platelet count

* Respiration - PaO2/FiO2 & need for mechanical ventilation

* Mentation - Glasgow coma score

* Hepatic function - Bilirubin

* Renal function - Creatinine

Organ dysfunction is identified by a SOFA score of ≥ 2

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is the least commonly used graft for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intercostal artery

The intercostal artery is the least likely to be used as a graft in CABG.

The left internal mammary artery (LIMA) provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). The conduit with the highest patency rate is the left internal mammary artery or internal thoracic artery. Long patency rates of >98 percent have been reported.

Venous grafts:

* The long saphenous vein is the most common vein used as a conduit as it is straightforward to harvest, provides good length, and is easy to handle.

* The ten-year patency rate for long saphenous vein grafts is reported to be 50–60 percent.

Arterial grafts:

* The Left internal mammary artery (LIMA) or internal thoracic artery has become the conduit of choice for the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. The radial artery can be used as a second or alternative arterial bypass graft. Other arterial bypass grafts include the gastroepiploic artery and the inferior epigastric artery.

Pearl PF1920: Indications for Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)

Class I indications for CABG from the American College of Cardiology(ACC) and American Heart Association(AHA).

* Left main disease

* Three-vessel disease with or without proximal LAD disease

* Two vessel disease with proximal LAD disease

* Survivors of sudden cardiac death with presumed ischemia-mediated VT

Other indications for CABG include the following:

* Disabling angina

* Ongoing ischemia in the setting of a non–ST-segment elevation (MI) that is unresponsive to medical therapy

* Poor LV function but with viable, nonfunctioning myocardium above the anatomic defect that can be revascularized

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which lymph node is most commonly involved in prostate cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pelvic

The most common lymph node of metastatic disease in prostate cancer is the pelvic or retroperitoneal lymph nodes.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the pelvic, obturator, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.

Prognosis and staging: The Gleason grading system correlates with the pathological stage, spread, and prognosis. Measurement of serum PSA levels may be useful to assist with the diagnosis and management.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about CHPS? CHPS- Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
options: Caused by hypertrophy of longitudinal muscles
USG is very sensitive in diagnosing this condition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Caused by hypertrophy of longitudinal muscles

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is caused by the hypertrophy of circular muscles, not longitudinal muscles.

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS):

It most commonly presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 3 and 6 weeks of age. It is associated with hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus. This results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. First-born male infants are at the highest risk.

Infants usually present with projectile, non-bilious vomiting. Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right (not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting.

Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality i.e hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.

Ultrasound examination is the investigation of choice for this condition. Ultrasound examination confirms the diagnosis of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) in the majority of cases. The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis is a muscle thickness of ≥4 mm and a pyloric length of ≥16 mm.

Cervix sign and Nipple sign are signs of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis in USG. Double-layered hypertrophic mucosa protrudes into the stomach, creating the so-called Nipple sign. The sonographic appearance of the hypertrophied pylorus resembles that of the uterine cervix and is sometimes referred to as the cervix sign.

Management includes the correction of metabolic abnormality before the correction of the pylorus. The hypertrophic pylorus is surgically corrected by Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy.

The image below shows the cervix and nipple sign seen in IHPS.

Hypovolemic shock: It is due to reduced circulating volume. Causes include hemorrhage, dehydration, vomiting, and third spacing.

Obstructive Shock: This leads to a reduction in preload due to mechanical obstruction of cardiac filling. Causes include cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolus, or air embolus.

Cardiogenic shock: Due to the failure of the heart to pump blood to tissues. Causes include myocardial infarction, cardiac dysrhythmias, valvular heart disease, blunt myocardial injury, and cardiomyopathy.

Distributive shock: Distributive shock is the condition of reduced oxygen delivery where the primary physiologic disturbance is a reduction in systemic vascular resistance leading to vasodilation. It is unique among the types of shock in that there is a compensatory increase in cardiac output. Causes include spinal shock, anaphylaxis, and septic shock.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the best imaging modality to diagnose neuroendocrine tumours (NETs)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. PET

Positron emission tomography (PET) is the best modality to diagnose Neuroendocrine tumors(NETs).

The initial imaging investigation is standard cross-sectional imaging with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). In patients of suspected NETs, CTs of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis are done for staging, and consideration of an MRI of the liver or pancreas in cases where further definition is required.

PET scans with 111In (indium) labeled pentetreotide somatostatin and 68Ga (gallium) linked somatostatin analogues take advantage of the overexpression of somatostatin receptors commonly seen in NETs. These radiolabeled somatostatin analogues localized with PET scan are the best imaging modality for NETs.

questions.text: Which of the following is the gold standard treatment for the condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endothermal ablation

The gold standard for the treatment of varicose veins is endothermal ablation. The given image shows tortuous dilated veins suggestive of varicose veins.

The management of varicose veins is as follows:

Incompetence
Management

Great saphenous vein (GSV) and saphenofemoral (SFJ)

• Endothermal ablation (gold standard treatment for varicose veins). It includes:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

• Trendelenburg procedure (Flush Ligation of Saphenofemoral Junction (SFJ) after ligation of 6 tributaries) ± stripping (retrogradely up to the knee, to prevent saphenous nerve injury.)

• Subfascial endoscopic perforator surgery (SEPS) - smaller incision, so cosmetically better

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

New treatment modalities:

* Foam sclerotherapy - The Tessari method is a widely used method to prepare foam for sclerotherapy. Sclerosant: air ratio taken is 1:3 or 1:4

* Endovenous glue therapy - endoluminal application of cyanoacrylate adhesive

* Transilluminated powered phlebectomy

Option B: Injection sclerotherapy: In this technique, a detergent is injected directly into the veins.

* Most commonly used sclerosant is Sodium tetradecyl sulfate.

* The detergent causes endothelial damage leading to thrombosis, fibrosis, and obliteration (sclerosis) of veins.

* Injection sclerotherapy alone can be successful in varicose veins <3 mm in diameter and in telangiectatic vessels.

* Complications from sclerotherapy include allergic reaction, local hyperpigmentation, air embolism, stroke and pain at the site of injection.

Option C: Phlebectomy -Small stab incisions are made to revert the reflux by occluding the refluxing tributaries of the veins.

Option D: Saphenous vein ligation and stripping is the preferred therapy for patients with GSVs of very large diameter (>2 cm).

C4b-Lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche
