*The descriptor A (asymptomatic) or S (symptomatic) is placed after the C clinical class.

Telangiectases are less than 1 mm, reticular veins are between 1 and 3 mm, and varicose veins are greater than 3 mm measured in the upright position.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the recommended treatment for the condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ureteroscopy

The given X-ray image shows a lower/distal ureteric stone. Ureteroscopic removal is generally preferred for stones <6mm and specifically those present in the distal ureter. Ureteric calculi are directly visualized through semi-rigid ureteroscopes. Stones are then fragmented and extracted using a dormia basket. Complications are related to injury to the ureteric mucosa such as ureteric perforation and extravasation, avulsion of the ureter, and ureteric stricture.

Ureteroscopic stone removal using a dormia basket is depicted in the image below.

Option A: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) - Endoscopic instruments are passed into the kidney by percutaneous technique and stones are fragmented and removed. It is mainly used in treating large stones in the renal pelvis and calyces and stones in the proximal ureter.

Indications of PCNL:

* Obstructions caused by anatomical abnormalities like pelviureteric junction obstruction, calyceal diverticula or ureteric obstruction

* Staghorn calculi

* Stones >2.5 cm in size

* Stone composition - struvite, calcium oxalate monohydrate , and cystine stones

* Multiple stones

* Obese patients in whom ESWL is contraindicated

* Lower calyceal stones

* Stones not responding to EWSL

Other options:

Option C: Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL) is a non-invasive method that generates shockwaves outside the body, which are focused on stones. It is the commonest method of treating renal calculi nowadays.

Stones up to approximately 1.5 cm in size are suitable for this form of treatment. Cystine stones which are often multiple, and very hard are relatively resistant to ESWL due to their hardness. Contraindications for ESWL include obese patients, pregnant patients, and patients taking oral anticoagulants.

Option D: Wait and watch is done for small stones <5mm as they are more likely to pass spontaneously.

Pearl PF1959: Management of renal and ureteric calculi

ESWL: Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy

PCNL: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy

URS: Ureteroscopic retrieval of stones

Pearl PF0036: Microscopic Appearance of Various Stones

* Cystine stones: Hexagonal

* Uric acid stones: Varying shapes (rhomboids or parallelograms)

* Calcium oxalate

* Monohydrate: Dumbbell shaped

* Dihydrate: Octahedral or envelope shaped

* Struvite stones: Rectangular or coffin lid

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following procedures has the highest risk to cause the recurrence of duodenal ulcers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Highly selective vagotomy

Highly selective vagotomy (HSV) has the highest risk to cause the recurrence of duodenal ulcers among the given options.

HSV retains the vagal innervation to the antrum, pylorus, and the remaining abdominal viscera while cutting off the vagal nerve supply to the proximal two-thirds of the stomach, which houses nearly all of the parietal cells. As a result, the procedure reduces overall gastric acid secretion by around 75%, and GI side effects are uncommon. However, HSV has not had great success treating type II (gastric and duodenal) and type III (prepyloric) gastric ulcers, possibly as a result of hypergastrinemia brought on by prolonged antral stasis and gastric outlet obstruction.

Option A: Resective procedures like gastrectomy have the least rates of recurrence but are less preferred nowadays due to higher rates of morbidity and mortality.

Option C: Unlike HSV, vagotomy and drainage is widely accepted as a successful definitive operation for complicated PUD, with lower rates of recurrence.

Option D: Gastrojejunostomy is a good choice in patients with gastric outlet obstruction or a severely diseased proximal duodenum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about the following image?
options: Staph. aureus is the causative organism
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Staph. aureus is the causative organism

The image above indicates that the patient has Fournier's gangrene. It is caused due to mixed infection of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.

Concurrent illnesses like diabetes mellitus and alcoholism, predispose patients to Fournier's gangrene.

The sequence of events is as follows: A mixed infection of the aerobic and anaerobic bacteria → fulminating inflammation of subcutaneous tissue → obliterative arteritis of the arterioles that supply the scrotal skin → gangrene

The testes are usually not affected due to their intraabdominal-origin blood supply.

It is a surgical emergency. In Fournier's gangrene, despite the best therapy, mortality rates are high at 50%.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following will not have bilateral hydronephrosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Retrocaval ureter

Retrocaval ureter does not lead to bilateral hydronephrosis.

Circumcaval or retrocaval ureter is a developmental anomaly of the inferior vena cava (IVC). It is due to abnormal development of the right supracardinal system. There is a persistent right posterior cardinal vein that ends up passing in front of the ureter. The anomaly always occurs on the right side, as this is the side of the normal IVC.

The given image shows a right-sided fish hook or S-shaped ureter. It describes the appearance of a retrocaval ureter as the right ureter hooks behind the IVC.

Pearl PF1540: Causes of Hydronephrosis

Unilateral hydronephrosis

Extramural obstruction

* Tumor from adjacent structures, e.g., cervix, prostate, rectum, colon, or cecum

* Retrocaval ureter

Intramural obstruction

* Congenital stenosis

* Ureterocele

* PUJ obstruction

* Congenital small ureteric orifice

* Inflammatory stricture following removal of ureteric calculus, repair of a damaged ureter, or tuberculous infection

* Neoplasm of the ureter or bladder cancer involving the ureteric orifice

Intraluminal obstruction

* Calculus in the pelvis or ureter

* Sloughed papilla in papillary necrosis (especially, in patients with diabetes, analgesic abuse, or sickle cell disease)

Bilateral hydronephrosis

Congenital:

* Posterior urethral valves (associated with pulmonary hypoplasia)

* Urethral atresia

* PUJ obstruction

Acquired:

* Benign prostatic hypertrophy or carcinoma of the prostate

* Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Ormond's disease)

* Postoperative bladder neck scarring

* Urethral stricture

* Phimosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: While doing an endoscopy, constriction is felt at the oesophageal junction at 25 cm from the incisor. This is due to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arch of aorta

The arch of aorta and left bronchus crosses the esophagus at 25 cm from the upper incisor teeth.

Normally esophagus shows 3 constrictions at the following levels measured from upper incisors:

* Junction of the esophagus with cricopharynx (15 cm from the incisor teeth)

* Crossed by arch of aorta and left bronchus (25 cm from the incisor teeth)

* It pierces the diaphragm (40 cm from the incisor teeth)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: 74 year old gentleman presents to the OPD with history of significant unintentional weight loss, loss of appetite and iron deficiency anemia. A chest x-ray was done and is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metastasis

The above scenario indicates the patient may be suffering from colon carcinoma. The X-ray depicts cannon ball appearance classical of lung metastasis.
Pulmonary metastasis typically appears as peripheral, rounded nodules of variable size, scattered throughout both lungs. The most common primaries to result in pulmonary metastases in adults include:

* Breast carcinoma

* Colorectal carcinoma

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Uterine leiomyosarcoma

* Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old female patient presented with painless, fleshy, exophytic lesions on the surface of the genitalia. She is 14-weeks pregnant. It is found to be caused by low-risk strains of HPV. Which of the following is the safest and can be used to manage this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cryotherapy

The given clinical scenario of painless exophytic lesions on the genitalia and caused by low-risk HPV strains is suggestive of Anogenital warts. Cryotherapy is the safest management that can be used in pregnant women for treating warts.

Anogenital warts is a genital infection caused by the human papillomavirus(HPV) commonly HPV‐6 and HPV‐11. Transmission of HPV commonly occurs sexually or through the genital lesions of the mother during delivery. Giant warts are called Condyloma acuminata.

The lesions present as soft, pink and flesy warts. These growths may be pedunculated discrete or verrucous and coalesce to form large cauliflower-like growths. It commonly occurs on the glans, corona, and frenulum in men and the posterior fourchette in women. Diagnosis is done by HPV DNA PCR (polymerase chain reaction).

Management (non-pregnant):

The first-line drugs used in the treatment are podophyllin and imiquimod. Podophyllin is the most commonly used drug for anogenital warts and is used as a local application of podophyllin 25% in alcohol or podophyllin 20% in tincture benzoin or podophyllin cream. Imiquimod is also used as a first-line drug next to podophyllin and is used as a 5% cream applied 3 times per week.

Second-line management includes Cryotherapy, Surgical removal of warts, laser and 80-90% trichloroacetic acid. Fluorouracil 5% and 25% trichloroacetic acid combination causes small warts to fall off by 3-4 days and is also used as a second-line management. Cryotherapy is the safest management that can be used in pregnant women for treating warts.

As imiquimod, podophyllin, and podofilox should not be used during pregnancy, cryotherapy is considered relatively safer.

Interferon therapy can be used for severe extensive warts.

Cryotherapy:

This treatment is physician administered. Dimethyl ether spray, carbon dioxide snow and liquid nitrogen all produce cold thermal damage to the skin.

Liquid nitrogen produces the coldest freeze and is commonly used in practice. It is applied using a cotton wool bud or a cryospray until a rim of iced tissue (seen as a white discoloration) develops around the wart. The freeze is maintained for 5–30 sec depending on the size and site of the wart. Scarring is unlikely with freezing times under 30 secs.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman receiving cyclosporin A after renal transplantation develops multiple and bilateral breast lumps that regress after cessation of treatment. Biopsy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fibroadenoma

Almost half the women receiving cyclosporin A after renal transplantation develop multiple and bilateral fibroadenomas that regress after cessation of treatment.

Fibroadenomas are the most common benign tumor of the female breast. They are frequently multiple and bilateral and usually occur in women<30 years of age. They are called "breast mouse" due to their high mobility within the breast.

Complex fibroadenomas are grouped with “proliferative changes without atypia” and are associated with 1.5-2 times increased risk of subsequent cancer. Complex fibroadenomas contain cysts larger than 0.3 cm, sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications, or papillary apocrine change.

Histological image of Fibroadenoma showing proliferation of ducts arranged in intracanalicular (compressed) and pericanalicular pattern surrounded by fibromyxoid stroma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old female undergoes emergency laparotomy. Which of the following is the surest sign of wound dehiscence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Copious sero-sanguinous discharge

The surest sign of wound dehiscence is copious serosanguinous discharge.

Burst abdomen/Acute wound dehiscence is the mechanical wound failure causing separation of the closed abdominal wound associated with abdominal content evisceration. It usually occurs between the 5th and 8th postoperative days.

A sudden giving way feeling from the wound precipitated by bouts of cough, and pinkish serosanguinous discharge can be seen. Omentum or coils of the intestine are forced out of the wound.

Management includes delayed closure with initial mesh wrap or Bogota bag, placing a subcutaneous drain, suitable antibiotic therapy, and prevention of abdominal compartment syndrome as described above.

Below is an image showing a burst abdomen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man sustained a spinal cord injury as a result of a road traffic accident. On examination, his blood pressure is found to be 90/60 mmHg. The patient most likely suffered from which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neurogenic shock

The clinical scenario of the presence of hypotension associated with the spinal cord injury is suggestive of neurogenic shock.

Neurogenic shock refers to reduced tissue perfusion due to loss of vasomotor tone to peripheral arterial beds. Neurogenic shock is usually secondary to spinal cord injuries due to vertebral body fractures of the cervical or high thoracic region that disrupts the sympathetic regulation of peripheral vascular tone. Loss of vasoconstrictor impulses results in increased vascular capacitance, decreased venous return and decreased cardiac output.

Primary injury in neurogenic shock occurs due to damage to axons and the membrane of neurons. Secondary injury occurs doe to vascular damage hours to days after the primary insult.

The clinical features are bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, hypotension and autonomic dysreflexia. The skin often appears warm and flushed and there is also presence of radiological evidence of vertebral fracture.

Treatment involves securing of airways, adequate ventilation and perfusion with fluids and blood products followed by administration of vasoconstrictors to improve vascular tone.

Other options:

Option A: Cardiogenic shock is caused due to the failure of the myocardial pump.

Option B: Septic shock is not likely in this clinical scenario, as there is no evidence of any infection.

Option D: Hypovolemic shock is caused due to a significant decrease in blood or plasma volume, caused by the loss of fluid from the vascular compartment. Haemorrhage, fluid loss from severe burns, diarrhea, excessive urine formation, perspiration, and trauma are some of the major mechanisms of fluid loss that can lead to hypovolemic shock.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with gynecomastia. Ultrasonography (USG) reveals a 1-cm solid mass within the body of the testis. His serum testosterone is 600 ng/dL and estradiol is 35 pg/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leydig cell tumour

A 40-year-old man presenting with gynecomastia, testicular mass, and increased sex hormones is most likely to have  Leydig cell tumor of the testis.

Leydig cell tumor:

* It is the most common sex-cord stromal type of testicular neoplasm.

* It is mostly benign and invariably unilateral.

* Most cases occur between 20 and 60 years of age; however, it can present at any age.

* The most common presenting feature is testicular swelling or gynecomastia (~15% of cases).

* In children, hormonal effects manifested primarily as sexual precocity, are the dominant features.

* Tumors of Leydig cells may secrete androgens and estrogens, and even corticosteroids.

Grossly: Golden brown, homogeneous circumscribed nodules <5 cm in diameter.

Histologically:

* large, round, or polygonal cells

* round central nucleus and prominent nucleoli

* abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm containing lipid droplets, vacuoles, or lipofuscin pigment

* crystalloids of Reinke, rod-shaped eosinophilic cytoplasmic bodies are seen in about 25% of the tumors

Other options:

* Sertoli cell tumor mostly presents as a painless testicular mass. They are usually hormonally silent but sometimes produces estrogen. In this patient, increased testosterone along with gynaecomastia make Leydig cell more likley.

* Spermatocytic tumor mainly occurs in older adults as a slow-growing testicular mass. They do not secrete any hormones.

* Granulosa cell tumor usually presents as a slow-growing and non-functioning testicular mass. Gynecomastia is rare.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old alcoholic obese male patient presented to the emergency department with severe pain abdomen radiating to the back. Blood investigations revealed increased serum amylase and lipase levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute pancreatitis

The clinical presentation of the patient is suggestive of acute pancreatitis.

Acute pancreatitis is a condition characterized by inflammatory damage to the pancreas. Various causes of acute pancreatitis are:

* Gallstone-induced (most common cause)

* Alcohol (2nd most common cause)

* Trauma (most common cause in children)

* Iatrogenic- Post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)

* Drug-induced pancreatitis (Thiazides, Azathioprine, Anti-cancer drugs, etc)

* Hypertriglyceridemia

* Hypercalcemia

* Scorpion bite

* Idiopathic

Clinical presentation of acute pancreatitis is characterized by epigastric pain radiating to the back which is relieved by bending forward, nausea, and vomiting. Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis can present with certain named signs like:

* Cullen’s sign: Discoloration around the umbilicus

* Grey Turner’s sign: Discoloration in the flanks

* Fox sign: Discoloration in the inguinal region

* Bryant’s sign: Discoloration on the scrotum

Blood investigations show increased serum amylase and lipase levels. Serum lipase is more sensitive and specific than serum amylase but it rises late. USG cannot help establish the diagnosis of pancreatitis. Plain erect chest x-ray and abdominal radiographs are not diagnostic of acute pancreatitis and can only be used to rule out certain differentials. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) is the imaging investigation of choice, but may not always be needed. Various scoring systems are used to grade the severity of acute pancreatitis based on blood investigations and radiographic findings.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old alcoholic obese male patient presented to the emergency department with severe pain abdomen radiating to the back. Blood investigations revealed increased serum amylase and lipase levels. Which of the following should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5% dextrose

The clinical presentation of the patient is suggestive of acute pancreatitis. 5% dextrose should be avoided in this condition.

Acute pancreatitis is a condition characterized by inflammatory damage to the pancreas. Various causes of acute pancreatitis are:

* Gallstone-induced (most common cause)

* Alcohol (2nd most common cause)

* Trauma (most common cause in children)

* Iatrogenic- Post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)

* Drug-induced pancreatitis (Thiazides, Azathioprine, Anti-cancer drugs, etc)

* Hypertriglyceridemia

* Hypercalcemia

* Scorpion bite

* Idiopathic

Clinical presentation of acute pancreatitis is characterized by epigastric pain radiating to the back which is relieved by bending forward, nausea, and vomiting. Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis can present with certain named signs like:

* Cullen’s sign: Discoloration around the umbilicus

* Grey Turner’s sign: Discoloration in the flanks

* Fox sign: Discoloration in the inguinal region

* Bryant’s sign: Discoloration on the scrotum

Blood investigations show increased serum amylase and lipase levels. Serum lipase is more sensitive and specific than serum amylase but it rises late. USG cannot help establish the diagnosis of pancreatitis. Plain erect chest x-ray and abdominal radiographs are not diagnostic of acute pancreatitis and can only be used to rule out certain differentials. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) is the imaging investigation of choice, but may not always be needed. Various scoring systems are used to grade the severity of acute pancreatitis based on blood investigations and radiographic findings.

Management:

In the management of acute pancreatitis, it's crucial to avoid stimulating the pancreas further, as it can exacerbate inflammation and worsen symptoms. Therefore, solutions containing glucose, such as 5% dextrose, should be avoided because they can trigger pancreatic enzyme secretion.

5% Dextrose is also a hypotonic solution and cannot maintain plasma oncotic pressure and will exaggerate the underlying third space loss.

Instead, fluids should be administered intravenously as necessary, but they should be non-stimulating to the pancreas, such as normal saline or lactated Ringer's solution.

Early initiation of oral feeds is encouraged as soon as vomiting and abdominal pain is controlled. In severe acute pancreatitis, if the patient cannot stop vomiting or cannot tolerate enteral feeds, total parenteral nutrition is then given. TPN is based on clinical status, nutritional needs, and response to other management strategies. However, enteral feeds are the mainstay of nutritional therapy in acute pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 49-year-old man presented to the OPD with complaints of a gradually progressive swelling over his abdomen for 1.5 years. He has a history of penetrating stab injury at the same site. On examination, the swelling was 12 cm and was partially reducible with a palpable cough impulse. Which of the following is the best way to manage this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fascial closure with a mesh

Incisional hernias are repaired by fascial closure augmented with a mesh.

Incisional hernia refers to an abdominal wall hernia at the site of a previous surgical incision. It is a type of ventral hernia. Incisional hernias are usually asymptomatic, but can occasionally present with pain. Strangulation and bowel obstruction is rare due to the large neck of the defect. In general, incisional hernias are repaired by fascial closure augmented with a mesh. There are different options for mesh placement:

* Onlay (above the anterior fascia, over the defect)

* Inlay (between the fascial edges without overlap)

* Sublay (below the fascial components) - this includes retrorectus, preperitoneal, and intraperitoneal (IPOM) mesh placements

Primary suture repair using Mayo’s technique is reserved only for very small hernias with < 2cm defect. This involves closing the fascial edges with a 2 cm overlap using an interrupted suture and then reinforcing it with a continuous running suture (double-breasting).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presented with complaints of dull pain over the right lower abdomen for the past 2 months. CT scan revealed a pseudomyxoma peritonei. Which of the following is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucinous cystadenoma

The above clinical scenario and findings confirms the diagnosis of pseudomyxoma peritonei. It is associated with mucinous cystadenoma.

Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is a rare clinical entity characterized by diffuse intra-abdominal gelatinous and mucoid material on peritoneal surfaces. Spontaneous perforation of a mucinous cystadenoma leads to implantation of low-grade malignant tumor cells in the peritoneum.

However, the most common cause of pseudomyxoma peritonei is carcinoma of the appendix.

Diagnosis is by CT, MRI, and laparoscopy. Even after the removal of the ovarian tumor, these cells continue to secrete mucin. Recurrence rates are high.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man has the following lesion over the face. He complains of bleeding while itching. Which of the following is seen in the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rolled out edge

The given history with the image showing an ulcer over the face with pearly, rolled-out borders points to a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is an epithelial tumor arising from basal cells. It is the most common type of skin cancer most commonly seen over the face, above the line joining corner of the mouth, and lobule of the ear. Risk factors for BCC include ultraviolet radiation (strongest risk factor), age 40-80 years with excessive sun exposure, light-skinned people, and exposure to arsenic compounds, coal tar, aromatic hydrocarbons, and infrared light. It is more common in males than females. It is also associated with syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum and Gorlin's syndrome.

Features of BCC include:

* Pearly nodule with rolled border

* Tortuous telangiectatic vessels

* Surface which can get ulcerated with raised and beaded edge, often with a central depression or umbilication

* Bleeding on minor trauma

BCC has various subtypes such as nodular (most common type), pigmented, nodulocystic, morphoeic, infiltrative, and fibroepithelioma of Pinkus.

It is locally aggressive and can erode the bone or facial sinuses. It rarely metastasizes via lymph nodes.

The occasional presence of melanin in the nodular variant of BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

Diagnosis is confirmed by a wedge biopsy. X-ray or CT may be needed if there is a local invasion. Histology shows peripheral palisading of cells.

Treatment:

* Surgical: Wide excision (4-6 mm clearance) with a skin graft or flap or primary suturing

* Mohs' surgery for BCC close to the eyes, nose, or ear to preserve more tissue.

* Non-surgical: Radiotherapy, vismodegib and sonedegib.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman with breast carcinoma develops right upper limb lymphedema after mastectomy as a result of axillary lymph node dissection. 10 years later, she presents with multiple confluent, hemorrhagic, necrotic, and elevated purple-black papules over the right upper limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lymphangiosarcoma

The most likely diagnosis in this setting is lymphangiosarcoma.

Angiosarcoma may develop in areas affected by lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral upper extremity, several years after radical mastectomy with lymph node resection for breast cancer known as Stewart–Treves syndrome (STS). Lymphatic vessels are most likely the source of the tumour.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A newborn is brought with severe respiratory distress soon after birth. A chest X-ray was done and is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing herniation of the bowel loops into the chest is suggestive of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).

CDH is a structural diaphragmatic defect with or without abdominal contents in the thorax. It allows the abdominal organs to push into the chest cavity resulting in pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension. The most common type of CDH is a bochdalek hernia involving the left side. They may also have a scaphoid abdomen.

Babies with CDH present with respiratory distress immediately after birth characterized by tachypnea, grunting, use of accessory muscles, and cyanosis. Auscultation of the chest may reveal bowel sounds with reduced breath sounds.

Diagnosis is done by a chest radiograph showing herniated bowel loops hemithorax, displacement of the mediastinum to the contralateral side, and reduced lung space. Prenatal diagnosis can be made using ultrasonography between 16 to 24 weeks of gestation.

The immediate step in the management is to place a naso- or orogastric tube for decompression. The airway is to be secured with endotracheal intubation. Bag and mask ventilation should be avoided. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation have been used as a part of the ventilation strategy.

Bag and mask ventilation should be avoided. Surgical repair of the defect is to be considered at least 48 hours after stabilization and resolution of pulmonary hypertension.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A newborn presents with jaundice. Biliary atresia is suspected when jaundice is persistent and exceeds:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 weeks

Newborns with persistent jaundice for more than 2 weeks suggests a diagnosis of biliary atresia.

Biliary atresia may also be termed as noncystic obliterative cholangiopathy. It is a disease of the intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts of unknown etiology.

Clinical features include persistent jaundice, clay-colored stools, and hepatomegaly. Untreated newborns will show signs of liver cirrhosis and failure (ascites, portal hypertension, and failure to thrive).

Laboratory evaluation will show elevated levels of direct and indirect bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase. Ultrasound will show a hypoplastic or absent gall bladder and triangular cord sign.

Hepatobiliary scintigraphy can also be performed.

Classification of biliary atresia and its treatment are:

Management of extrahepatic biliary atresia

Type I

Atresia restricted to the common bile duct

Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy

Type II

Atresia of the common hepatic duct

Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y hepatoportoenterostomy)

Type III

Atresia of the right and left hepatic duct

In the Kasai procedure, the extrahepatic biliary tree is dissected proximally till the liver capsule, the porta hepatis is transected and a jejunal loop is anastomosed in order to provide a drainage pathway for bile.

Infants with biliary atresia, who do not achieve successful drainage after Kasai's procedure, require liver transplantation within the first year of life. This is the most common reason for liver transplantation in children.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient complains of experiencing pain in the calf region after walking a certain distance. He reports that he needs to rest to relieve the pain. Which grade of Boyd's grading system does this symptom correspond to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Grade 3

This patient's pain typically resolves with rest. This indicates that he can be classified as Grade III according to Boyd's classification of claudication.

Boyd's grading system is commonly used to classify the severity of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) based on the presence and severity of symptoms.

Grade III corresponds to symptoms of intermittent claudication, where the patient experiences reproducible muscle pain, cramping, or weakness in the lower limbs (usually the calf muscles) after a specific distance of walking or physical activity. The pain typically resolves with rest. Grade III indicates moderate PAD severity.

Boyd's classification of claudication:

* Grade I: Patient complains of pain after walking. If the patient continues to walk, due to increased blood flow in muscle and opening of collaterals metabolites causing pain are washed away and the pain subsides.

* Grade II: Pain still persists on continuing to walk; but can walk with effort.

* Grade III: The patient has to rest to relieve the pain.

* Grade IV: Pain at rest.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident (RTA) presents with signs of seat belt abdominal trauma on the anterior abdominal wall. What should be the primary concern in terms of potential injuries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hollow viscus injury

The clinical scenario of a seat belt injury most likely indicates a hollow viscus injury. In cases of blunt abdominal trauma, particularly those involving seat belt injuries, there is a risk of sustaining injuries to the hollow viscera, which includes organs such as the stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and bladder.

Seat belt injuries can lead to compression forces against the abdomen, potentially causing shearing or tearing injuries to these structures.

Hollow viscus injuries can be challenging to diagnose clinically and may require imaging studies such as CT scans or exploratory surgery for confirmation.

Other Options:

Options A & B: While liver and spleen injuries are also common in blunt abdominal trauma, especially in cases of seat belt injuries, the question specifies signs of seat belt abdominal trauma on the anterior abdominal wall, which suggests a concern beyond these solid organs.

Option C: While the pancreas can be injured in cases of blunt abdominal trauma, the primary concern in this scenario, given the history of RTA and signs of seat belt abdominal trauma, should be focused on potential injuries to hollow viscera rather than the pancreas specifically.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is suspected to have MEN-1 syndrome. Which of the following is the most common gastro-entero-pancreatic tumor seen in this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastrinoma

MEN 1 syndrome is characterized by the triad of tumors involving the parathyroids, pancreatic islets, and anterior pituitary. Gastrinoma is the most common gastro-entero-pancreatic tumor in MEN 1 syndrome.

Most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome is the first and second part of duodenum.

Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer is called Zollinger Ellison syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was undergoing the ERCP for the removal of gallstones. However, it required multiple attempts to retrieve the stone. What is the commonest complication expected in such cases after the procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute pancreatitis

Pancreatitis is the most common complication of ERCP. (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangio Pancreatography). The Pancreatitis is usually mild and resolves in a few days.

Multiple attempts at cannulation, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction or history of recurrent pancreatitis and therapeutic procedures instead of diagnostic ones impart a higher risk of pancreatitis

In this procedure, a side-viewing endoscope is passed through the pylorus of the stomach into the second part of the duodenum to visualize the papilla.

It is then cannulated, and dye is injected into the pancreatic or bile duct to visualize the pancreatic or biliary tree. Minor procedures like biopsy and endoscopic stone removal can be done via this itself.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male patient presented with a sudden onset of scrotal pain and discharge. Based on the image below, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fournier's gangrene

The given scenario of an elderly male patient with sudden-onset scrotal pain and discharge, with the image showing a blackish discoloration of the scrotum, is likely to be Fournier's gangrene.

Fournier's gangrene is an uncommon polymicrobial infection involving the perineal soft tissue, external genitalia, and perianal region. There is subcutaneous tissue inflammation leading to obliterative arteritis and gangrene. It typically follows minor injuries or procedures in the perineal area, urethral dilatation, and injection for hemorrhoids are some of the etiological factors.

Clinically, sudden scrotal pain with associated prostration, pallor, and pyrexia can be seen. Other features such as crepitus and foul-smelling exudate can be present.

Emergency surgical debridement is needed after initial measures like fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics are undertaken. Urinary diversion and other supportive measures are useful in the management of the condition.

Other options:

Option A: Torsion of testis is a surgical emergency typically seen in the age group of 10-25 years. It is characterized by sudden groin and lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Examination findings reveal a swollen, tender scrotum and testis with a twisted tender cord above it and loss of cremasteric reflex.

Option B: Acute epididymo-orchitis is an infection of the epididymis and testis. It is seen in sexually-active young men. In older men, it is seen following a urinary tract infection, secondary to an indwelling catheter. The features include groin ache, fever, swollen and painful epididymis and testis.

Option C: Scrotal carcinoma is a rare carcinoma that is seen in workers exposed to oil, coal products, and aromatic hydrocarbons. It starts as a wart or ulcer in the scrotum and can extend to the testis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male with a history of chronic smoking is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip stage. Further investigations revealed that the lymph nodes are not involved. What is the treatment of choice in this patient?
options: Wide local excision with negative margins
Wide local excision with frozen borders
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wide local excision with negative margins

This pateint has an early stage squamous cell carcinoma. Wide local excision with negative margins is the preferred treatment for this type of cancer.

Lip cancer most commonly occurs in men from 50 to 70 years but can be seen in younger patients. Risk factors include sunlight exposure, smoking, and tobacco use. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of lip cancer. But commonly occurring cancer in the upper lip is basal cell carcinoma.

Surgical resection (wide local excision with negative margins) is the preferred treatment modality. The typical lip length is 6 to 7 cm. For defects of <1/3rd of the lip, resection with primary closure is the preferred treatment.

For defects of more than 1/3rd of the lip, require local flaps for reconstruction after resection:

* Johansen step technique- local flap for large central defects

* Lip-switch (Abbe-Estlander) flap- based on the sublabial or superior labial artery. When the defect involves only the commissure, the Estlander flap is used, and the Abbé flap is used for midline defects. Abbe-Estlander Flap is used for mixed defects. The markings of the Abbe-Estlander flap are shown below.

* Karapandzic flap - circumoral advancement flap. It is a neuromuscular flap that includes the remaining orbicularis oris muscle with its innervation.

In the presence of neck metastasis, neck dissection is indicated. Postoperative radiation is administered to patients with positive margins, lymph node metastases, tumor thickness >4mm, or perineural invasion. If the mandible is involved, mandibulectomy and free flap reconstruction is required.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Following a road traffic accident, a 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with maxillofacial trauma and inability to open the mouth. To establish an airway, an emergency laryngotomy is performed. Where is the opening made?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cricothyroid membrane

In laryngotomy, an opening is made on the cricothyroid membrane.

Laryngotomy is also called cricothyrotomy or mini-tracheostomy. It is done as an emergency life-saving procedure to buy some time to allow a patient to be carried to the operation theatre. Once stable, it is replaced by intubation or tracheostomy.

Most of the laryngeal foreign bodies are arrested above the vocal cords, i.e. above the middle of the thyroid cartilage. Thus, an effective airway can be provided by piercing the cricothyroid membrane.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the lesion depicted in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Penile urethral stricture

The given image shows retrograde cystourethrogram with findings consistent with penile urethral stricture.

The male urethra can be visualized by retrograde urethrography (RGU) or voiding cystourethrogram (VCU), also known as micturating cystourethrogram (MCU).

In RGU, the urethra is visualized with the instillation of contrast into the anterior urethra (penile urethra and bulbar urethra). It is helpful for diagnosing anterior urethral abnormalities.

The following image shows an RGU with bulbar urethral stricture:

In VCU, after injecting contrast into the bladder using a Foleys catheter, the posterior urethra (membranous urethra and prostatic urethra) is visualized during micturition. It is helpful for diagnosing posterior urethral abnormalities and bladder abnormalities. It is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and posterior urethral valve.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a triage system, highest priority patients are respectively colour coded by
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Red

Highest priority patients are coded red in the triage system.

* Triage consists of rapidly classifying the injured on the basis of the severity of their injuries and the likelihood of their survival with prompt medical intervention.

* Triage is the only approach that can provide maximum benefit to the greatest number of injured in a major disaster situation.

Pearl PF1015: Triage Colour Coding

Triage system consists of four colour codes:

Color code
Priority
Type of patients

Red
High
Need for immediate resuscitation or surgery in the next 6 hours or transfer (Eg. massive hemorrhage, tension pneumothorax)

Yellow
Medium
Possible resuscitation or surgery in next 24 hours (Eg. Isolated simple fracture)

Green
Low
Ambulatory patients or minor illness (Eg. Isolated abrasions, contusions, sprains)

Black
Least
Dead or moribund patients (Eg. massive head injuries, 95% third degree burns)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Structure(s) preserved in case of MRND 1 are:
options: Accessory nerve and internal jugular vein
Accessory nerve, sternocleidomastoid, and internal jugular veins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only spinal accessory nerve

Structure preserved in MRND 1 is only the spinal accessory nerve.

There are three types of modified radical neck dissection (MRND). Structures preserved are:

* MRND 1 - Only spinal accessory nerve

* MRND 2 - Accessory nerve and internal jugular vein

* MRND 3 i.e., functional neck dissection - Accessory nerve, sternocleidomastoid, and internal jugular veins.

Radical neck dissection involves the removal of:

* All ipsilateral cervical lymph node groups extending from the inferior border of the mandible to the clavicle and from the lateral border of the sternohyoid muscle, hyoid bone, and contralateral anterior belly of the digastric muscle medially to the anterior border of the trapezius muscle laterally.

* All lymph nodes from Levels I through to V

* The spinal accessory nerve

* Internal jugular vein

* Sternocleidomastoid muscle

* Tail of parotid

* Submandibular gland

A radical neck dissection does not include the removal of the following.

* sub-occipital nodes

* peri-parotid nodes (except infraparotid nodes located in the posterior aspect of the submandibular triangle)

* buccinator nodes

* retropharyngeal nodes

* midline visceral (anterior compartment) nodes

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the best management approach for gastroschisis in a neonate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primary closure

A neonate with gastroschisis would need an immediate primary closure. Primary closure under general anesthesia or gradual reduction using a preformed silo may be performed. Parenteral nutrition is often needed for several weeks to support intestinal recovery.

Gastroschisis is an abdominal wall defect located on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly) allowing protrusion of the intestines, stomach, bladder, and sometimes ovaries or undescended testes. The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion as they herniate through the abdominal wall directly into the amniotic cavity. The affected bowel loops can be damaged by exposure to amniotic fluid.

Risk factors include teenage pregnancy, recreational drug use, smoking, and genitourinary infection during pregnancy. After birth, careful management is required to prevent twisting or kinking of the blood supply to the intestines. The abdomen is wrapped with transparent plastic wrap, a nasogastric tube is inserted, and fluid resuscitation is initiated.

Management: Immediate surgical intervention is required after birth to prevent complications such as infection, dehydration, and damage to the exposed abdominal organs. Surgical repair typically involves gently placing the protruding abdominal contents back into the abdominal cavity and closing the abdominal wall defect surgically. This approach helps protect the exposed organs, prevent complications, and facilitate normal abdominal wall development.

Pearl PF0342: Difference between gastroschisis and omphalocele

Characteristic
Gastroschisis
Omphalocele

Defect size (diameter)
2-3 cm
2-15 cm

Sac
Never
Always, may be ruptured

Gestational age
Prematurity
Term

Umbilical cord
Adjacent to the defect (defect is seen usually on its right side)
Attached to sac

Herniated viscera
Small bowel, stomach, colon
Small bowel, stomach, colon, liver

Malrotation
Yes
Yes

Bowel character
Inflammatory, edematous
Normal

Enternal nutrition
Delayed
Normal

Associated abnormalities
Uncommon (10% atresia)
Common (50%)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the correct order of the normal phases of wound healing?
options: Proliferative phase > Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Remodeling phase
Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase
Inflammatory phase > Hemostatic phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase
Remodeling phase > Proliferative phase > Destructive phase > Inflammatory phase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase

The correct order of the normal phases of wound healing is as follows: Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase.

Inflammatory phase: begins immediately after wounding and lasts 2-3 days. Bleeding is followed by vasoconstriction and thrombus formation to limit blood loss. Occasionally, the early part of inflammatory phase is called hemostatic phase.

Proliferative phase lasts from 3rd day to 3rd week consisting mainly of fibroblast activity with production of collagen and ground substance, growth of new blood vessels and re-epithelialization of the wound surface.

Remodeling phase is characterized by maturation of collagen- type 1 replacing type 3 until a ratio of 4:1 is achieved. The mature collagen leads to increased tensile strength and represents approximately 80% of the uninjured skin strength.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the type of hernia in which the internal organ composes a portion of the wall of the hernia sac?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sliding hernia

* Sliding hernia occurs when an internal organ composes a portion of the wall of the hernia sac.

* The most common viscus involved are as follows:

* Left side: sigmoid colon and its mesentry

* Right side: cecum

* It is more common on the left side.

* Most sliding hernias are variants of indirect inguinal hernias.

* The primary danger associated with a sliding hernia is the failure to recognize the visceral component of the hernia sac before injury to the bowel or bladder.

Other options:

Option A: Lumbar hernia is a rare type of hernia occurring in the lumbar region

Option C: Spigelian hernia occurs along the Spigelian fascia

Option D: In Richter’s hernia only a part of the bowel wall (typically the antimesenteric border) is trapped, leading to strangulation without complete bowel obstruction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication for parathyroidectomy in a patient?
options: Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limits of normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Creatinine clearance < 90 ml

Creatinine clearance <90 mL/min is not an indication of parathyroidectomy in primary hyperparathyroidism.

Indications for parathyroidectomy in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism:

* Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limits of the normal level.

* GFR < 60mL/ min, 24-hour urine calcium >400 mg/dL and increased risk of or the presence of nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis

* Decreased bone mineral density at the lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, or distal radius (>2.5 SD below peak bone mass, T score below −2.5; vertebral fracture)

* Age <50 years

* Long-term medical surveillance not desired or possible

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following structures does not form the boundary of Hesselbach’s triangle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vas deferens

Vas deferens does not form the boundary of Hesselbach’s triangle.

Hesselbach's triangle (also called the inguinal triangle) is a region of the deep part of the anterior abdominal wall.

Pearl PF0034: Boundaries of Hesselbach’s triangle

* Lateral - inferior epigastric artery

* Medial - lateral border of rectus abdominis

* Inferior - inguinal ligament

Direct inguinal hernia emerges through Hesselbach’s triangle (Hence situated medial to inferior epigastric artery)

Indirect inguinal hernia enters deep inguinal ring (Hence it is lateral to inferior epigastric artery)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of refeeding syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperphosphatemia

Refeeding syndrome is associated with Hypophosphataemia, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia.

Refeeding syndrome is a potentially lethal condition that can occur with rapid and excessive feeding of patients with severe underlying malnutrition due to starvation, alcoholism, delayed nutritional support, anorexia nervosa, or massive weight loss in obese patients.

* It can occur with either enteral or parenteral nutrition, but is more common with the latter.

* Symptoms: Electrolyte abnormalities can result in cardiac failure and dysrrhythmias, respiratory failure, neurologic disturbances, and renal and hepatic dysfunction.

Prevention and treatment:

* Correct underlying electrolyte and volume deficits.

* Additionally, thiamine should be administered before the initiation of feeding. Caloric replenition should be instituted slowly and should gradually increase over the first week.

* Vital signs, fluid balance, and electrolytes should be closely monitored and any deficits corrected as they evolve.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old female patient presented to OPD with the given presentation. On examination, it seems gelatinous in consistency. She reports fluctuation in size, mild numbness in hand and occasional pain. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ganglion cyst

The history and image are suggestive of a patient with a ganglion cyst.

Ganglion cyst arises from the leakage of synovial fluid from a joint or tendon sheath and thus contains a glary, viscous fluid.

It can appear anywhere in the wrist but the most common area is the dorsal surface of the scapholunate ligament.

Patients usually present with painless, well-defined, cystic, transillumination-positive, and non-tender swelling. If there is an impingement on a nearby nerve or structure it can cause pain.

It disappears spontaneously, but the aspiration of the swelling or operative removal can be done for reassurance or when there is pressure on the nerve. Even if treatment is done, the rates of recurrence are high.

Other Options:

Option B: Lipomas are benign tumors of adipose tissue. It can occur anywhere and at any depth. It can be encapsulated or diffuse, superficial or deep. On examination, they are nontender and non-pulsatile. Because of the soft consistency, they may appear to be fluctuant but they are not. The slip sign is positive.

Option C: Dermoid Cyst presents as asymptomatic, slowly enlarging, painless, superficial localized swellings over the volar aspect of the hand, especially the distal portion of the digits.

Option D: An extremity hematoma is a localized collection of blood in the soft tissues of an extremity, typically occurring after trauma, surgery, or in patients with bleeding disorders. The hematoma can develop in various tissue planes: subcutaneous, intramuscular, or subfascial compartments.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old male was brought to the ER after sustaining an astride injury. Following the trauma, he experienced an urge to urinate but was unable to pass urine. On examination, blood was present at the urethral meatus. What is likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bulbar urethra

The given clinical scenario with a history of an astride injury, blood at the tip of the meatus, and inability to pass urine are all suggestive of an injury to the bulbar urethra.

Astride injury refers to trauma that occurs when a person falls with their perineum straddling a hard object, leading to blunt perineal trauma.

Urethral injuries can be classified into:

Type
Proximal urethral injury
Distal urethral injury

Site of injury

• Prostatic urethra
• Membranous urethra

• Bulbar urethra
• Penile urethra

Mechanism
Secondary to pelvic fracture

Occurs due to a blow to the perineum by:

• Straddle injury
• Gymnasium accidents

Clinical features

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• High-riding prostate on digital rectal examination (Vermooten sign)
• Deep perineal hematoma

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• Perineal hematoma (Butterfly hematoma)

Note: Urinary bladder rupture occurs due to an injury to the suprapubic region. Extraperitoneal bladder rupture is more common and associated with pelvic fracture. Intraperitoneal bladder rupture is caused by a blow or a fall on the distended bladder. It manifests as sudden severe pain in the hypogastrium and syncope.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man is brought to ER after a car accident. He had multiple injuries and a femoral shaft fracture. He was treated and stabilized. But 48 hours later, he suddenly develops breathing difficulty, increased heart rate and petechial rashes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fat embolism

History of sudden onset breathlessness and rashes on 3rd day of admission after femoral shaft fracture should raise suspicion of fat embolism.

Fat embolism is the presence of fat globules in vital organs and peripheral circulation after fracture of the long bone or other major trauma.

Pathogenesis- release of free fatty acids by the action of lipases on the neutral fats and actual obstruction of small pulmonary vessels by fat globules.

Clinical features:

* Early signs are fever and tachycardia

* Presenting features are of 2 types- Cerebral type: drowsiness, restlessness, disorientation or Pulmonary type: tachypnoea, tachycardia

* Other features: petechial rash in front of neck/anterior axillary fold/ chest/ conjunctiva

The classical clinical triad consists of respiratory distress, neurological abnormalities, and petechial haemorrhages

Treatment of fat embolism is mainly supportive:

* Respiratory support (oxygen)

* Heparinization (increases lipoprotein lipase activity)

* Intravenous low molecular weight dextran

* Corticosteroids: To avoid pneumonitis

* Prompt stabilization of long-bone fractures

Other Options:

Option A: Beck's triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds) is seen in cardiac tamponade.

Option B: Pneumothorax can cause sudden, sharp chest pain and difficulty breathing, but it often presents with hyper-resonant percussion (tapping on the chest) and decreased breath sounds on the affected side.

Option C: Sudden onset dyspnoea and bilateral fine basal crackles are signs of Pulmonary edema.

Pearl PF1166: Gurd's criteria for diagnosing fat embolism syndrome

Major criteria

* Axillary or subconjunctival petechiae

* Hypoxemia with PaO2 <60 mmHg, FIO2 < 0.4

* CNS depression disproportionate to the hypoxemia

* Pulmonary edema

Minor criteria

* Tachycardia (HR >110 beats per minute)

* Pyrexia (temp >38.50C)

* Emboli visible in retina

* Fat globules in urine

* Fat globules in sputum

* Unexplanied drop in hematocrit or platelet count

* Increased ESR

At least one major criterion and four minor criteria are required to make a diagnosis of fat embolism syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old lactating female presents 2 weeks after delivery, with a 3 cm subareolar mass in her right breast. The mass is associated with redness, tenderness, and mild warmth. She reports no fever but mentions difficulty in breastfeeding from the affected breast. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lactation Mastitis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lactational mastitis.

Lactational mastitis is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

Mastitis occurs due to a combination of factors such as inadequate milk drainage and the introduction of bacteria present on the skin. The cracks in the nipple serve as an entry point, thus resulting in infection. The most common organism causing acute mastitis is Staphylococcus aureus.

Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the 1st month of breastfeeding (lactational breast abscess).

Staphylococcal acute mastitis typically results in localized abscesses. Signs and symptoms of this condition involve:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

Management includes analgesia, continued expression from the breast, antibiotics such as amoxiclav, and repeated aspiration of pus. In case of aspiration and antibiotics failure, incision and drainage can be done.

Other Options:

Option A: Mondor’s disease is characterized by thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the breast and anterior chest wall.

Option B: Breast abscess is a sequela of untreated bacterial mastitis, which occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. Patients usually present with fever and malaise, localised pain and tenderness, redness and swelling of the affected breast and fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess, which is a late sign of breast abscess.

Option C: A galactocele is a milk-filled cavity in the breast of a woman who is usually lactating. It can be caused due to lactation problems, prolactin stimulation by drugs, or duct obstruction. It presents as a palpable, round, well-circumscribed, and freely mobile mass with no fever, pain, or inflammation. It is usually subareolar and unilateral.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with persistent swelling and discomfort over the dorsal aspect of the index finger. He gave a history of penetrative trauma to the area a few days ago. On examination, there is a firm, tender mass with limited mobility of the distal interphalangeal joint. The image is shown below. If left untreated, what is the most likely complication?
options: Gangrene of the fingertip due to compromised vascular supply
Secondary infection requiring removal of the nail bed
Frog-like deformity of the finger caused by chronic inflammation and tendon dysfunction
Injury to blood vessels during wound cleaning leading to ischemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Frog-like deformity of the finger caused by chronic inflammation and tendon dysfunction

In the given clinical scenario of penetrating trauma followed by swelling over the dorsal aspect of the index finger that could progress to a "frog-like" deformity, making this the correct answer.

A "frog-like" finger refers to a Boutonnière deformity - a condition where the middle joint of a finger is bent inward while the tip joint is bent excessively outward, creating a distinctive appearance similar to a frog's leg bent at the knee; essentially, the finger looks like it's making a "buttonhole" shape.

The progressive tendon dysfunction leading to the frog-like deformity represents the natural history of untreated cases due to the anatomical relationship between the central slip of the extensor tendon and the dorsal aspect of the middle phalanx where the infection is located.

This deformity occurs when chronic inflammation and infection of the extensor tendon mechanism leads to destruction of the central slip at the dorsal aspect of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint. This results in the characteristic deformity where the PIP joint becomes flexed while the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint becomes hyperextended.

Other Options:

Option A: Gangrene of the fingertip is unlikely as the vascular supply to the digit remains intact in these cases unless there's significant compartment syndrome, which would present with more severe symptoms.

Option B: Removal of the nail bed would not be necessary as the pathology is centred over the phalanx rather than the nail complex.

Option D: Injury to blood vessels during wound cleaning is not a natural complication of the condition itself but rather an iatrogenic possibility.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with a 3 cm soft, non-tender, and fluctuant swelling on the upper back. The lesion has been present for several months and occasionally drains a foul-smelling, cheesy material. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
options: Complete surgical excision including the capsule
Surgical excision of the cyst content leaving behind a portion of the wall
Incision and drainage of the cyst
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Complete surgical excision including the capsule

The clinical vignette is suggestive of a sebaceous cyst and the best management is complete surgical excision including the capsule.

A sebaceous cyst is derived from hair follicle infundibulum or traumatic inclusion. The most common site of a sebaceous cyst is the postauricular sulcus or below and behind the ear lobule. Malignancy is rare.

Clinical features of a sebaceous cyst include:

* Benign swelling that is mobile, fluctuant, and fixed to the skin. It presents with a central punctum in about 70% of cases.

* It is generally an asymptomatic, non-tender swelling. It can be painful and red if inflamed.

* It may ooze out a foul-smelling, cheese-like discharge.

Treatment depends on the clinical state of the cyst. When inflamed or infected, they should be incised and drained initially. After the inflammation subsides, a total surgical excision of the cyst is performed. If the cyst wall is not removed, there is a risk of recurrence. Perilesional triamcinolone injection helps with inflammation resolution but not cyst eradication.

The complications include sebaceous horn, cock’s peculiar tumor, and abscess formation. The treatment involves the excision of the cyst along with normal skin using an elliptical incision.

Below is an image showing an inflamed sebaceous cyst with a central punctum:

Other Options:

Option A: Topical application of antibiotics wont be correct choice for the given case scenario beacuse Antibiotics alone are not indicated for management of sebaceous cyst.

Option C: Surgical excision of the cyst content leaving behind a portion of the wall is also not indicated as it may lead to high rate of recurrence.

Option D: Only Incision and drainage is also not enough .When cyst is inflamed or infected, they should be incised and drained initially. After the inflammation subsides, total surgical excision of the cyst is performed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with a 3cm sub-areolar mass in her left breast. She reports bloody nipple discharge but denies pain, redness or systemic symptoms. On examination, the mass is firm and non-tender. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intraductal papilloma

The given clinical scenario of unilateral bloody nipple discharge with a palpable mass beneath the areola and histopathology showing a central fibrovascular core with papillae arborizing within the lumen are suggestive of a solitary intraductal papilloma.

Intraductal papilloma is a benign, proliferative breast disorder without atypia. It is defined as Localized hyperplasia of the ductal epithelium within the duct. According to the ANDI (Aberrations of normal development and involution of breast tissue) classification, it is an aberration of normal epithelial turnover. It comprises a central fibrovascular core and papillary projections of the epithelium and myoepithelial cells. The papillary lesions in a duct are of three types:

* Solitary papilloma

* Papillomatosis: five or more papillomas

* Juvenile papillomatosis, also called Swiss cheese disease

Intraductal papilloma is commonly seen in premenopausal women. It is the most common cause of spontaneous nipple discharge from a single duct. These papillomas are located close to the nipple and are associated with bloody nipple discharge. Sometimes, a palpable mass under the areola may be present.

A triple assessment, consisting of clinical examination, imaging, and pathology, should be performed to exclude carcinoma. Ultrasonography may reveal a dilated subareolar duct and a papillary growth within. A ductoscopy shows a firm, palpable nodule inside the duct. Most duct papillomas are located up to a distance of 5 cm from the nipple.

The treatment for single-duct discharge is microdochectomy, which involves making a tennis racquet-shaped incision and removing the papilloma and a single duct involved. Hadfield’s procedure(cone excision of ducts) is used when multiple ducts are involved.

Other options:

Option A. Ductal carcinoma in situ: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a neoplastic proliferation of epithelial cells limited by the basement membrane. It involves the ducts and lobules. It is not associated with a loss of E-cadherin expression. It typically presents as a suspicious area on a mammogram rather than a palpable mass with bloody discharge.

Option C. Lobular carcinoma in situ: Histologically, LCIS consists of a monomorphic population of cells with oval or round nuclei and small nucleoli involving ducts and lobules. Mucin-positive signet ring cells are commonly present. The histological image is given below:

Option D. Fibroadenoma: This is a benign breast tumor that is usually firm, rubbery, and mobile. They occur in women in their 20s and 30s, and they are frequently multiple and bilateral. Histology shows delicate and often myxoid stroma that resembles normal intralobular stroma. The epithelium may be surrounded by stroma (pericanalicular pattern) or compressed and distorted by it (intracanalicular pattern) as shown below:

questions.text: A 4-year-old-boy was brought to emergency department with complaints of acute radiating pain in right iliac region and during surgery the following structure was found. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meckel’s Diverticulum

The clinical history and the image are both suggestive of Meckel's Diverticulum.

Meckel’s diverticulum is a true diverticulum, which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel. The diverticula which contain all the layers of the intestine are called true diverticula. It is caused by a failure of normal regression of the vitelline duct that develops during weeks 5-7 of gestation.

The rule of 2's (Mnemonic for Meckel’s diverticulum) :

* 2 types of heterotopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic)(Option d).

* 2% incidence

* located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve

* approximately 2 inches in length

* Usually symptomatic by 2 years of age

The most common presentation is painless, massive, lower GI bleed in children younger than 5 years. Meckel's diverticulum can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.

A bleeding Meckel's diverticulum may be confirmed by a 99 mTc-pertechnetate isotope scan to detect ectopic gastric mucosa.

Surgical treatment is the definitive therapy for Meckel’s diverticulum. A simple V-shaped diverticulectomy with transverse closure of the ileum is the ideal surgical approach.

The following diagram shows the various anomalies that arise as a result of the failure of normal regression of vitellointestinal duct:

Other Options:

Option A: The most common tumor of the appendix is the well-differentiated neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor. This neoplasm, which is almost always benign, most frequently forms a solid bulbous swelling at the distal tip of the appendix.

Option B: Adenocarinoma of  the appendix is very rare, accounting for 0.5% of all gastrointestinal cancers. They are detected in 0.08 to 0.1% of appendectomy specimens. Mucinous is a subtype of the adenocarinoma of  the appendix.

Option D: In bowel loop obstruction, the obstructed bowel loops are centrally located and lie transversely. In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect. Additionally, a distended cecum may exhibit a gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.

questions.text: A 53-year-old male patient was admitted following a road traffic accident. Paradoxical respiration was seen. His chest X-ray is shown below. He was given analgesics and oxygen was administered via face mask but he developed respiratory failure. What is the best line of management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mechanical ventilation

The given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing contiguous rib fractures on the right side suggest flail's chest.

It is characterized by contiguous rib fractures and paradoxical respiration following blunt trauma to the chest wall. Mechanical ventilation (like Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is the management of flail chest with respiratory failure.

Flail Chest :

* A flail chest occurs when a segment of the chest wall does not have bony continuity with the rest of the thoracic cage.

* This condition results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, i.e. 2 adjacent ribs or 3 or more ribs fractured in two or more places.

* The blunt force required to disrupt the integrity of the thoracic cage typically produces an underlying pulmonary contusion as well.

Clinical Features:

On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards and less air, therefore, moves into the lungs. On expiration, the segment moves outwards(paradoxical respiration).

Diagnosis - Made clinically, not by radiography. To confirm the diagnosis the chest wall can be observed for the paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment for several respiratory cycles and during coughing. Voluntary splinting as a result of pain, mechanically impaired chest wall movement, and the associated lung contusion are all causes of hypoxia and respiratory failure.

The patient is also at high risk of developing a pneumothorax or hemothorax.

Treatment

* Chest strapping or splinting should be avoided

* Currently, treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates) or epidural analgesia and physiotherapy.

* IPPV (Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is reserved for cases developing respiratory failure despite adequate analgesia and oxygen.

Other options:

Option A: Chest tube drainage can be done in traumatic pulmonary contusion associated with pneumothorax or hemothorax

Option B: Intrapleural local analgesia can be given if the patient has a chest tube inserted. Since the chest tube drainage is only done after stabilising the patient, intrapleural analgesia is not the best line of treatment at this stage.

Option D: Surgical fixation of the fracture is done only in patients with severe chest injury and pulmonary contusion. Also, surgery should be proceeded only after the patient's condition is stabilised.

questions.text: A 64-year-old man is rushed to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and obstipation. His erect X-ray abdomen is as shown. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sigmoid volvulus

The given clinical scenario of a 64-year-old man with severe abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and obstipation along with the radiograph showing the coffee bean sign is likely to be sigmoid volvulus.

Sigmoid volvulus is a condition that occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on the sigmoid mesocolon.

A sigmoid volvulus can be differentiated from a cecal volvulus by swirl sign, location of the obstructed loop, and anatomical appendages. The swirl with sigmoid volvulus is located on the right quadrant while the swirl with cecal volvulus is located at the pelvic brim.

Other options:

Option B: Colonic diverticulosis refers to the condition where multiple outpouchings occur along the gastrointestinal tract without any inflammation. The barium enema given below shows multiple outpouchings in the ascending, transverse, and descending colon resembling a saw-tooth.

Option C: Cecal volvulus is more common in females in the 4th to 5th decade. It is characterized by ischemia.

Option D: Paralytic ileus occurs secondary to neuromuscular failure. This leads to the failure of transmission of peristaltic waves. It mainly occurs following laparotomy. The image given below is an X-ray of a patient with a paralytic ileus.

questions.text: A 65-year-old male presents with lower urinary tract symptoms, including weak urinary stream, hesitancy, and nocturia. On digital rectal examination (DRE), a hard, irregular prostate is palpated. He has no significant past medical history but reports mild back pain over the past few weeks. The physician suspects prostate cancer. Which enzyme is elevated in prostate cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acid phosphatase

Prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) is commonly increased in prostatic cancer.

The form of acid phosphatase that is found in the prostate gland is called prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP). PAP is a glycoprotein that is synthesized by the epithelial cells of the prostate gland. It is secreted into the prostatic fluid, where it plays a role in the liquefaction of semen.

PAP is also a potential target for monoclonal antibody therapy. Sipuleucel-T is a cell-based approach to induce an immune response against prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) that is commonly expressed in prostatic cancer.

Option A: Alkaline phosphatase is increased in primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma.  Similarly, cancers that metastasize to the bones or primary bone cancers like osteosarcoma.

Option C: Lactate dehydrogenase elevations can occur in a range of malignancies. It is often observed in hematological cancers like lymphomas and leukemias, reflecting the rapid cell turnover characteristic of these diseases. Lung cancers, both small cell and non-small cell types, can also lead to increased LDH levels.

Option D: Alpha-fetoprotein is a protein that is produced by the liver and yolk sac during fetal development. Alpha-fetoprotein levels are typically elevated in certain types of cancer, such as liver cancer and testicular cancer, but not in prostate cancer.
