Pearl PF1160: NICE Guidelines for CT in Head Injury

National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) Guidelines for Computed Tomography (CT) in Head Injury

Indications for CT imaging within 1 hour of following risk factors being identified:

* Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) <13 at any point

* GCS <15 at 2 hours after injury on assessment in emergency department

* Focal neurological deficit

* Suspected open, depressed, or basal skull fracture

* More than one episode of vomiting

* Post-traumatic seizure

Indications for CT imaging within 8 hours

* Age >65 years

* Coagulopathy (e.g., aspirin, warfarin, or rivaroxaban use)

* Dangerous mechanism of injury (e.g., fall from a height, road traffic accident)

* Retrograde amnesia >30 minutes

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient was brought to the ER after a road traffic accident. On examination, left-sided hydropneumothorax was noted. Thoracostomy was done and around 1800 ml of blood was drained in 1 hour. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Continue resuscitation for the next 6 Hours
Administer a hemostatic agent through the chest tube
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Emergency thoracotomy

Given the significant blood loss (1800 ml) and the patient's critical condition, the most appropriate management in this scenario would be an emergency thoracotomy.

A thoracotomy is a surgical procedure in which an incision is made into the chest to access the thoracic cavity. It is performed in critical situations to control bleeding and repair injuries to the chest structures, including the lung and blood vessels.

In this case, the patient's condition is serious due to the combination of pneumothorax, hydrothorax, and a rapid blood loss of 1800 ml in just 1 hour. This level of bleeding suggests a severe injury to blood vessels or vital structures within the chest. Emergency thoracotomy would provide direct access to the bleeding source, allowing for immediate control of bleeding, repair of injuries, and restoration of stable conditions.

Indications for thoracotomy:

* Initial tube thoracostomy drainage of >1000 ml (penetrating injury) or >1500 ml (blunt injury) of frank blood

* Ongoing tube thoracostomy drainage of >200 ml/ hr for 3 consecutive hours in non-coagulopathic patients with hemothorax

* Caked hemothorax despite the placement of two chest tubes

* Massive air leak from chest tube with inadequate ventilation

* Open pneumothorax

* Great vessel injury

* Pericardial tamponade

* Cardiac herniation

* Tracheobronchial injury

* Esophageal perforation

Other Options:

Option A: Thoracentesis involves the removal of fluid or air from the pleural space using a needle or catheter. However, given the severity of the situation with rapid blood loss, this procedure alone would not adequately address the underlying issues or stop the significant bleeding.

Option B: Continued resuscitation for the next 6 hours is not appropriate in this scenario due to the patient's critical condition and substantial blood loss. Immediate intervention is required to stabilize the patient's condition and address the underlying causes of the blood loss.

Option C: While hemostatic agents can be useful in certain bleeding situations, the rapid blood loss and critical nature of the presented case call for a more immediate and direct approach, such as an emergency thoracotomy, to achieve rapid control of bleeding and prevent further complications.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient with a history of burns in his left lower limb presented to the OPD with the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Marjolin’s ulcer

This patient's history of burns and the image is suggestive of a Marjolin's ulcer. It is a rare and aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma that grows from burns, scars, or poorly healing wounds. It presents as an indurated, non-tender ulcer with raised and everted edges with scarring in the surrounding area with marked fibrosis

The ulcer can spread to the lymph nodes when it reaches the normal skin. A wedge biopsy and MRI of the region involved confirm the diagnosis.

Management is by wide excision, for larger ulcers, amputation is done.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man was brought after he fell into a manhole and injured his perineum. He was unable to pass urine and blood was seen at the tip of the urethra. A diagnosis of bulbar urethral injury was made. Where do you expect the urine to get collected in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior abdominal wall

In bulbar urethral injury, the anterior abdominal wall is one of the sites for the collection of urine.

The rupture of the urethra below the urogenital diaphragm will result in extravasation of urine into the superficial perineal pouch, penis and scrotum in males and labia majora in females, and the anterior abdominal wall.

The superficial fascia of the abdomen is divided below the umbilicus into a superficial fatty layer (fascia of Camper) and a deep membranous layer (fascia of Scarpa). Scarpa's fascia is continuous with the membranous layer of the superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia).

Colles' fascia is attached to fascia lata (the deep fascia of the thigh) along the Holden's line that extends from the pubic tubercle laterally for 8 cm. Extravasated fluid cannot pass into the medial thigh below Holden's line due to the firm attachment of Colles' fascia to the fascia lata.

Urethral injuries can be classified as follows:

Type
Proximal urethral injury
Distal urethral injury

Site of injury

• Prostatic urethra
• Membranous urethra

• Bulbar urethra
• Penile urethra

Mechanism
Secondary to pelvic fracture

Occurs due to a blow to the perineum by:

• Straddle injury
• Loose manhole covering
• Gymnasium accidents

Clinical features

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• High-riding prostate on digital rectal examination (Vermooten sign)
• Deep perineal hematoma

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• Perineal hematoma (Butterfly hematoma)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought in to the casualty with maxillofacial trauma after an RTA. He is unconscious with a dropping SpO2. The ER doctor decides to intubate him. What is the preferred method of securing airway for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tracheostomy

Patients with severe maxillofacial trauma are very likely to experience severe airway compromise or obstruction. Hence to maintain airway competency, intubation is necessary and in the above case, the presence of facial trauma, tracheostomy is ideal.

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea.

Functions:

* Provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction.

* Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance

* Uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood

* Allows suction of secretions in the setting of the impaired cough reflex.

* Allows positive pressure respiration

* Allows administration of anesthesia

Indications:

* Respiratory obstruction due to

* Infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis, diphtheria)

* Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures

* Neoplasms

* Foreign bodies or edema

* Bilateral abductor paralysis

* Congenital anomalies

* Retained secretions

* Inability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles

* Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions

* Painful cough

* Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis

Other options:

Option A and B: Mask ventilation and LMA are not enough as the patient has severe airway compromise.

Option D:  Nasotracheal intubation is contraindicated in the presence of facial trauma because there may be an undiscovered fracture at the base of the skull. The tube could be forced through it and into the brain.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with fever and flank pain. History revealed that he underwent kidney stone removal 4 years back. Imaging was done and a foreign body was detected. What is the appropriate course of action?
options: Cystoscopy and removal of the foreign body
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cystoscopy and removal of the foreign body

In a patient who has previously undergone kidney stone removal and now presents with fever, flank pain, and a foreign body detected on imaging, the most appropriate course of action is to perform a cystoscopy and remove the foreign body.

Cystoscopy is a minimally invasive procedure that involves inserting a thin, flexible tube with a cystoscope into the bladder through the urethra. It allows to visualize the interior of the bladder and urethra and can be used to directly identify and remove foreign bodies.

Leaving a foreign body inside the urinary tract can lead to complications such as infection, obstruction, or further tissue damage. Therefore, prompt removal of the foreign body through cystoscopy is the recommended approach to address the patient's symptoms and prevent potential complications.

Other options:

Option B (laparotomy and cystoscopic removal) and option C (retro-urethral approach) involve more invasive procedures and are not typically the first-line approach for foreign body removal in the urinary tract.

Option D (leave the foreign body inside) is not an appropriate choice as it could lead to ongoing symptoms and complications, as mentioned earlier. The foreign body should be removed to ensure the patient's well-being.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with aortic dissection. He continuously complains of hiccups. Which of the following nerves is most likely compressed in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. D

Hiccups can be caused by irritation or stimulation of the phrenic nerve, which controls the diaphragm's movements. The structure marked as D is the phrenic nerve.

The structures marked in the image are:

A. Right vagus nerve

B. Left vagus nerve

C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve

D. Right phrenic nerve

The phrenic nerve originates from the cervical spine (C3-C5) and travels down through the chest to the diaphragm.

Aortic dissection occurs due to rupture in the inner layer of the aorta, and depending on the location of the tear, it can lead to a variety of symptoms, including pain, altered blood flow, and involvement of adjacent structures.

If the tear involves the ascending aorta or the arch of the aorta, it can potentially affect the adjacent structures, including the phrenic nerve. Irritation or compression of the phrenic nerve due to the dissection could lead to hiccups as a symptom.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was rushed to the emergency department after being hit in the head in a road traffic accident The patient was unconscious. CT-scan revealed an extradural hematoma. Which of the following is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pterion

The pterion is most likely to be injured. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.

Pterion is an H shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

* Frontal bone

* Squamous part of the temporal bone

* Greater wing of sphenoid bone

* Parietal bone.

It is an important structure as it overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a direct hernia is posted for Lichtenstein repair. Which of the following is used in the mesh?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Polypropylene

A Lichtenstein mesh repair is currently one of the most frequently used methods for treating an inguinal hernia. In this technique, a cone-shaped plug of polypropylene mesh is used.

Polypropylene is a monofilament, non-absorbable suture material. It is a propylene polymer. It is used in plastic surgery, cardiovascular surgery, hernia repair, ophthalmic surgery, and general surgical subcuticular skin closure. Polypropylene mesh is used for hernia repair.

A Lichtenstein mesh repair is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. It is an anterior tension-free mesh repair that reduces the chances of recurrence of a hernia. A piece of prosthetic nonabsorbable mesh is used to fit the canal to bridge the defect in this repair.

Other surgical methods used for the repair of a hernia are:

* Bassini repair - It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. In this method, a mesh is not used. It is associated with a high recurrence and is not used frequently now. It is used only in cases of hernial strangulation and peritonitis where the use of a mesh is not preferred. It is performed by suturing the transversus abdominis and internal oblique musculoaponeurotic arches/conjoined tendon to the inguinal ligament.

* Shouldice repair - It is a multilayered repair, where the posterior wall of the inguinal canal is strengthened by continuous sutures. It involves double-breasting of the transversalis fascia. It is associated with a very low recurrence rate.

* Gilbert repair (plug and patch repair) - It is an extension of Lichtenstein’s original mesh repair and has now become the most commonly performed primary anterior inguinal hernia repair. In this technique, a cone-shaped plug of polypropylene mesh is used. It is deployed like an upside-down umbrella when inserted into the internal inguinal ring to occlude the hernia

* McVay repair (Cooper's ligament repair) is used for the correction of direct inguinal hernia, large indirect hernia, recurrent hernia, femoral hernias (particularly suited for strangulated femoral hernias). In this method, the transversus abdominis aponeurosis is approximated to Cooper's ligament.

* Stoppa-Rives repair - It is used for the repair of large, recurrent, or bilateral hernias. In this method, a sub-umbilical midline incision is given to place a large mesh into the preperitoneal space.

* Herniotomy - It is used to treat inguinal hernia in a child which occurs due to the presence of a patent processus vaginalis. Therefore in herniotomy, the repair of the inguinal ring is not done

Other options:

* Polyglactin (Vicryl)- This is an absorbable suture material and is commonly used in gut anastomoses, biliary anastomoses, and kidney and ureter surgeries.

* Polyglycolic acid- Used for other absorbable sutures, in particular where slightly longer wound support is required.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young boy presented with a bluish-red cystic swelling on the left side of the floor of the mouth as shown below. On examination, it showed fluctuation and transillumination. It was initially 1.5 cm, and progressed to 5 cm in the last few months. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ranula

The given scenario and the image of a cystic swelling on the floor of the mouth are suggestive of a ranula.

Ranula is a transilluminant mucocele. It is also known as "frog's belly", as it resembles the vocal sacs of a frog.

It is of two types:

* Oral ranula - It is a benign cystic lesion formed by extravasation of mucus, involving the sublingual gland. Clinically present as cystic swelling in the floor of the mouth. On examination fluctuation test and transillumination test is positive. It is conservatively managed by marsupialization. Definitive management is the excision of the cyst. Some may resolve spontaneously.

* Cervical or plunging ranula- is a rare type of retention cyst arising from the sublingual gland. The mucous passes through the mylohyoid muscle diaphragm to enter the neck. Clinically present as intraoral and cervical swelling. Diagnosis is made by USG or MRI. Management includes excision of the sublingual gland + aspiration of saliva out of the sac.

Other options:

Options A: Ectopic thyroid tissue is a developmental defect of the thyroid gland and is frequently found along the course of the thyroglossal duct. Lingual thyroid is the most common presentation of ectopic thyroid (shown below).

Option B: Cystic hygroma is usually seen in neonates and early childhood. They are cystic swellings filled with lymph fluid and are characteristically brilliantly translucent. They occur in the neck and can involve the parotid, submandibular, tongue, etc. The swelling is soft and partially compressible. Definitive treatment is the excision of the swelling.

Option C: Ludwig's angina is a brawny swelling of the submandibular region that is caused by streptococcal infection. The infection tracks down to the mylohyoid muscle causing inflammation that displaces the tongue leading to dysphagia and painful airway obstruction. Management is by antibiotic therapy and decompression of the floor of the mouth by incising mylohyoid muscle.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young male patient developed abdominal pain for which he was being evaluated. CT and IVU findings are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horse shoe kidney

The given images show a horseshoe kidney. It is prone to obstruction, reflux, and stone formation (the likely cause of pain in this case)

Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidneys with male preponderance

Horseshoe kidney is caused due to the fusion of the lower poles of the kidney. The lower border of the kidneys usually lies in front of the L3 vertebra due to the arrest of ascent.

The common associations of horseshoe kidney are:

* Vesicoureteral Reflux

* Wilms Tumor

* Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney

* Turner’s Syndrome

IVU findings of a Horseshoe kidney:

* Handshake sign - due to the position of the lower poles closer to the spine, and the lower calyces closer to each other

* Flower vase sign - due to medially rotated calyces

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly diabetic patient presents with extreme pain in the right side of his trunk. On examination, blisters and a woody surface are noted. The image of his trunk is shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Necrotizing fasciitis

The given clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of necrotizing fasciitis, which is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus).

Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressive necrosis of the subcutaneous tissues and fascia. The source of the infection is either the skin following trauma or a surgical incision. Diabetes mellitus is the most common comorbidity associated with the condition.

Local symptoms and signs are pain, erythema, edema, warmth, crepitus, blisters, bullae, greyish drainage (‘dishwater pus’), necrosis, and gangrene. Systemic features are fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, shock, coagulopathy, and multiorgan failure.

Treatment involves appropriate intravenous antibiotics with urgent radical surgical debridement.

Other options:

Option A: Gas gangrene is a form of myonecrosis caused by Clostridium perfringens. Patients who are immunocompromised are at a greater risk. Features are severe local wound pain and crepitus. Large doses of intravenous antibiotics and aggressive debridement of affected tissues are required.

The below image shows bluish-black discoloration and hemorrhagic bullae due to gas gangrene.

Option C: Cellulitis is an infection involving the skin and subcutaneous tissues. The point of entry may be a traumatic or surgical wound. Group B streptococci are the major causative organism. There is poor localisation and tissue destruction, gangrene and ulceration may follow, which are caused by the release of proteases.

Option D: Erysipelas is an infection of the superficial epidermis. It presents as an erythematous raised lesion with sharply demarcated edges that differentiate it from the surrounding skin. The given image shows erysipelas.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly female patient presented with diarrhea occurring approximately 20 minutes after meals. She underwent a Billroth I gastrectomy operation. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
options: Prescribe proton pump inhibitors in combination with amoxicillin.
Consider reversing the surgical procedure from Billroth II to Billroth I
Advise the patient to consume small, frequent meals and increase protein content in their diet.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Advise the patient to consume small, frequent meals and increase protein content in their diet.

This patient most likely has dumping syndrome, and the initial management for this patient is to recommend small frequent meals and increased protein content in the diet to manage symptoms and slow down gastric emptying.

Dumping syndrome is a common complication after gastrectomy, particularly after procedures like Billroth I, where the stomach's capacity is reduced. It occurs due to the rapid emptying of the stomach contents into the small intestine, leading to symptoms like diarrhea, nausea, sweating, and palpitations, typically occurring shortly after meals.

The initial management of dumping syndrome involves dietary modifications. Recommending small, frequent meals can help slow down the rate at which food is emptied from the stomach and prevent the sudden surge in glucose absorption that triggers the symptoms. Increasing the protein content of meals can also help stabilize blood sugar levels and reduce the severity of symptoms.

Other Options:

Option A: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and amoxicillin are not the primary treatments for dumping syndrome. PPIs are used to reduce stomach acid production, while amoxicillin is an antibiotic. Neither directly addresses the underlying issue of rapid gastric emptying and glucose absorption seen in dumping syndrome.

Option B: Insulin and glucose are not typically used as initial management for dumping syndrome. Dumping syndrome involves rapid glucose absorption, and managing it through dietary adjustments is usually the first step.

Option C: Reversing the surgical procedure to Billroth 1 or Roux-en-Y is a more drastic option that might be considered if dietary modifications do not effectively manage the symptoms of dumping syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male patient presents with persistent fatigue and anemia. Given his clinical profile, what is the recommended screening protocol for colon cancer in this patient?
options: Fecal occult blood testing every 2 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Colonoscopy every 10 years

Anemia and fatigue in an elderly patient can be indicative of gastrointestinal bleeding, possibly from colorectal cancer, the most appropriate protocol for screening for colon cancer is a colonoscopy every 10 years.

Current ACS guidelines advocate screening the average-risk population for colorectal carcinoma beginning at age 50 years. Screening recommendations include the following:

* Annual faecal occult blood test (FOBT), or

* Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, or

* FOBT and flexible sigmoidoscopy in combination every 5 years, or

* Air-contrast barium enema every 5 years, or

* Colonoscopy every 10 years.

A positive FOBT should be followed by a colonoscopy.

Patients with other risk factors (considered a high-risk population) should be screened earlier and more frequently, as shown below:

Population
Initial age
Recommendation

Familial colorectal cancer first-degree relative
40 years of age or 10 years before the age of the youngest affected relative (whichever is earlier)
Colonoscopy every 5 years

Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis)
At diagnosis; then 8 years after diagnosis
Colonoscopy with multiple biopsies every 1–2 years

Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
10–12 years of age
Annual flexible sigmoidoscopy

Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)
20–25 years of age
Colonoscopy every 1–2 years

For individuals at average risk of colon cancer, current guidelines recommend colonoscopy as the gold standard for screening. Colonoscopy allows direct visualization of the entire colon and is effective at detecting both polyps and cancers. Given the patient's age, symptoms of anemia, and potential risk factors, a colonoscopy every 10 years is an appropriate protocol for colorectal cancer screening.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An intern is observing the procedure of thoracocentesis. What is the site of needle insertion in this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper border of lower rib

The correct site for needle insertion during thoracentesis is usually at the upper border of the lower rib. This location helps to prevent any injury to the intercostal nerve and vessels.

For thoracocentesis, a posterior approach is preferred. The patient should sit on the edge of the bed, leaning forward with the arms abducted onto a pillow on a bedside stand. The patient might have severe dyspnea, so it is important to assess whether they can maintain this position for 10 minutes before performing the procedure. The entry site for the thoracocentesis is at the superior aspect of the rib.

This prevents any injury to the intercostal nerve and vessels.

While maintaining gentle negative pressure, the needle should be slowly advanced into the pleural space. If a diagnostic tap is being performed, 30-50 mL of fluid will be adequate. If a therapeutic thoracocentesis is being performed, a maximum of 1 liter of pleural fluid should be withdrawn at a given time. Withdrawal of quantities more than this can cause re-expansion pulmonary edema. A chest radiograph should be obtained post-procedure to evaluate for a pneumothorax. The patient should be instructed to inform the doctors if new shortness of breath develops.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is the following clinical finding seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior cranial fossa fracture

The image shows bilateral periorbital ecchymoses, which is called the panda sign, and it is seen in anterior cranial fossa fractures. It is also known as panda eyes/raccoon eyes.

Anterior cranial fossa fracture occurs due to direct impact. It is a contrecoup injury that occurs when there is a direct blow to the chin (in boxing). The impact is transmitted to the maxilla and base of the skull and results in a contrecoup fracture of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid. It presents with CSF rhinorrhea and periorbital hematoma or raccoon eyes and the image is shown below.

The pooling of blood surrounding the eyes is most commonly associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa. This finding is typically not present during the initial evaluation.  It is delayed by 1 to 3 days. If bilateral, this finding is highly predictive of a basilar skull fracture.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Management of an appendicular mass in appendicitis is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ochsner–Sherren regimen

Ochsner–Sherren regimen is indicated for patients with appendicular mass in whom conditions are stable.

The patient's temperature and pulse rate are recorded 4-hourly and adequate fluid balance is maintained. CECT abdomen is done and antibiotic therapy is started. Abscess if present is drained. Improvement is usually seen within 24–48 hours.

Ochsner–Sherren regimen:

Principle :

* The inflammatory process is already localised and that inadvertent surgery is difficult and may be dangerous.

* It may be impossible to find the appendix and, occasionally, a faecal fistula may form.

* Antibiotic therapy should be given after performing CECT abdomen

* Abscess if present can be drained radiologically.

Outcome :

* Improvement in 24–48 h

* 90% cases resolve

* Failure should raise suspicion of Crohn’s disease and carcinoma.

Criteria for stopping conservative treatment of Appendicular mass:

* Rising pulse rate

* Increasing or spreading abdominal pain

* Increasing size of the mass

Other options:

* Alvarado score is a clinical scoring system used in the diagnosis of appendicitis.

* If the patient's condition deteriorates or if there is evidence of peritonitis, laparotomy is performed.

* Incision and drainage are not done in appendicitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What nutrient deficiency is commonly associated with delayed wound healing following minor surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin C

Delayed wound healing after minor surgery can be attributed to a deficiency in vitamin C.

Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, plays a crucial role in collagen synthesis, a protein that is essential for wound healing and tissue repair. Collagen provides structural support to the skin, blood vessels, and other connective tissues. A deficiency in vitamin C can lead to impaired collagen formation, weakening of blood vessels, and delayed wound healing.

Factors influencing healing:

* Infection: one of the most important causes of delay in healing; prolongs inflammation; increases the local tissue injury

* Diabetes: most important systemic cause of abnormal wound healing

* Nutritional status: protein deficiency and vitamin C deficiency inhibit collagen synthesis and retard healing.

* Glucocorticoids (steroids): anti-inflammatory effects; results in weakness of the scar due to inhibition of TGF-β production and diminished fibrosis

* Mechanical factors: such as increased local pressure or torsion; may cause wounds to pull apart or dehisce

* Poor perfusion: due to arteriosclerosis, diabetes, or obstructed venous drainage; also impairs healing

* Foreign bodies: such as fragments of steel, glass, or even bone; impede healing

* Type and extent of tissue injury: affect subsequent repair;

* Location of the injury and the character of the injured tissue: also important

Even though zinc also causes poor wound healing, Vitamin C is more commonly implicated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which gas is commonly used in pneumoperitoneum, which involves inflating the abdominal cavity during laparoscopic surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carbondioxide

The correct gas used in pneumoperitoneum is carbon dioxide. Pneumoperitoneum is a technique used in laparoscopic or minimally invasive surgery to create a working space within the abdominal cavity.

CO2 is the preferred gas for this purpose due to several reasons:

*

Non-Flammable: CO2 is non-flammable, making it safer to use in surgical procedures where electrical equipment is in close proximity.

*

Minimal Absorption: CO2 is minimally absorbed by the body, which means it can be introduced into the abdominal cavity without causing significant physiological changes.

*

Rapid Absorption: CO2 is quickly absorbed into the bloodstream and can be eliminated through respiration after the procedure, reducing the risk of post-operative complications.

*

Low Cost: CO2 is readily available and cost-effective.

Other Options:

* Oxygen is not used for pneumoperitoneum due to its flammable nature. In the presence of electrical equipment and surgical tools, using oxygen would pose a significant fire hazard.

* Nitrous oxide is not commonly used for pneumoperitoneum because it is a greenhouse gas and has poor absorption characteristics. It can lead to increased intra-abdominal pressure and potential complications.

* Nitrogen is not typically used for pneumoperitoneum because it is also a non-absorbable gas. This means it would remain in the body after the surgery, potentially causing discomfort and complications.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about triage, according to the internationally accepted four-color-coded system?
options: Yellow - Significant injuries, hemodynamically stable patients, required monitoring
Green - Patients in life threatening conditions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Yellow - Significant injuries, hemodynamically stable patients, required monitoring

The yellow color tag is given for the patients who have significant injuries but are hemodynamically stable, and need monitoring. They are the medium priority patients.

Triage is used to classify the priority of treatment.

It is carried out at the site of the disaster to determine the priority for immediate medical attention, transportation, and admission to the hospital.

The internationally accepted four-color coded system is commonly used. It includes:

Color code
Type of patients
Examples

Red (High priority) (option A).

Need for immediate resuscitation or surgery in the next 6 hours or transfer.

May survive if timely medical intervention can be given

• Tension pneumothorax
• Airway obstruction
• Hemothorax
• Cardiac tamponade
• Acute circulatory arrest
• Major intra-abdominal bleed etc.

Yellow (Medium priority)(option C).

Possible resuscitation or surgery in the next 24 hours.

Likely to survive if prompt treatment is given.

• Compound fractures
• Degloving injuries
• Pelvic fracture
• Spinal injuries
• Moderate head injury

Green (Low priority)(option D).

Ambulatory patients or minor illnesses.

Likely to survive if treatment is slightly delayed.

• Simple fractures
• Minor lacerations etc.

Black (Least priority)(option B).

Dead or moribund patients.

• Severe brain injury
• Major damage / disruption to chest wall and abdominal structures

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following should be used for pre-operative management in a patient with pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alpha adrenergic blockers

Alpha-blockers like phenoxybenzamine are given pre-operatively to manage hypertension in pheochromocytoma. Beta-blockers such as propranolol are given only after adequate alpha blockade is achieved.

The drug of choice to control blood pressure prior to surgery is oral phenoxybenzamine at 0.5–4 mg/kg of body weight. It is a non-specific α-blocker and is preferred due to its long action (3-4 days).

Pheochromocytoma:

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

It can be sporadical or hereditary. Hereditary pheochromocytoma occurs in association with syndromes such as MEN 2 (Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), familial paraganglioma syndrome, Von Hippel Lindau (VHL) syndrome, and neurofibromatosis (NF) type 1.

Clinical features:

It most commonly presents as a classic triad of intermittent headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating along with hypertension. The patient can also present with anxiety, panic attacks, nausea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and weakness.

Symptoms may be precipitated by surgery, pregnancy, position changes, exercise, and medications such as metoclopramide and tricyclic antidepressants.

Investigations:

* Biochemical screening test - measurement of urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines.

* MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor. It is preferred over a CT scan as the contrast used in CT scans can precipitate paroxysms.

* Other imaging modalities like MIBG scintigraphy, DOPA- or FDG- PET scan are used in identifying the primary tumor as well as the extra-adrenal tumors and metastases.

Treatment:

Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma.

Preoperatively, hypertension is managed initially with alpha-blockers followed by beta-blockers.

Postoperatively, lifelong yearly follow-up should be done.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 15-year-old male patient presented to emergency with pain in the right lower quadrant. He was diagnosed with acute appendicitis. Which of the following is the most commonly used incision for appendectomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gridiron incision

The most commonly used incision for an appendectomy is McBurney's Gridiron incision.

The incision is made at McBurney’s point (two-thirds from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine). They involve passing through all of the abdominal muscles, transversalis fascia, and then the peritoneum, before entering the abdominal cavity.

Other options:

Option A: Mildline laparotomy incision is commonly used when the diagnosis is uncertain and in cases where an appendicular perforation is suspected. It is for better abdominal exposure.

Option B: Pfannential incision is used for the lower segment caesarean section.

Option D: Kocher's subcostal incision is used for open cholecystectomy.

The major anterior abdominal incisions have been illustrated below:

* 1 is Kocher incision - A subcostal incision used to gain access for gall bladder and/or biliary tree pathology.

* 2 is midline incision - The most common incision for laparotomy, a vertical incision which follows the linea alba which is particularly favored in diagnostic laparotomy, as they allow wide access to most of the abdominal cavity.

* 3 is McBurney's incision (also called gridiron incision) is an oblique incision (superolateral to inferomedial) passing along McBurney's point. It is popularly used for open appendicectomy.

* 4 is battle incision a lower right paramedian incision but placed more laterally than the standard paramedian incision. It is suitable for dealing with acute appendicitis and pathologies in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen.

* 5 is Lanz incision, a transverse or skin crease incision for appendicitis, 2 cm below the umbilicus, centered on the midclavicular–mid-inguinal line. Due to its continuation with Langer’s lines, the Lanz incision produces much more aesthetically pleasing results with reduced scarring.

* 6 is paramedian incision - this incision runs 2-5 cm away from the midline used to access much of the lateral viscera, such as the kidneys, spleen, and the adrenal glands.

* 7 is transverse incision - A supraumbilical transverse incision offers excellent exposure of the upper abdomen. A transverse incision may be superior to a midline incision in terms of recovery and complications postoperatively.

* 8 is Rutherford Morrison incision, an oblique muscle cutting incision used for access to sigmoid colon and pelvis in patients where the midline is scarred due to previous surgery.

* 9 is Pfannenstiel incision - An infraumbilical transverse incision in the lower abdomen, often used for gynecological and obstetric procedures.

questions.text: A 24-year-old presents with a scrotal swelling as shown in the image. The swelling is brilliantly transilluminant and the testes cannot be palpated separately. A CT scan was done which showed fluid collection in tunica vaginalis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydrocele

In the above clinical scenario, there is a unilateral scrotal swelling where the testes cannot be palpated separately, and is transilluminant points towards a diagnosis of hydrocele.

Hydrocoele is an accumulation of fluid within the tunica vaginalis. Hydrocele can be congenital or acquired. Congenital hydrocele is seen in children due to patent processes vaginalis. Acquired hydrocele can be secondary to inflammation or infection of the epididymis or testes. It is translucent on transillumination test and testes will not be separately palpable due to tense fluid collection. As it arises in the scrotum, it is possible to get above the swelling. Cough impulse is absent.

USG will show anechoic (due to fluid) reflection.

CT scan shows fluid collection within the scrotal sac.

Treatment involves Jaboulay's operation, in which the eversion of the sac upon itself is done to prevent refilling of the hydrocoele sac. The other method of treating the hydrocele is plicating the redundant tunica which can be done when the sac wall is thin. This is known as the Lord's operation.

Other options:
Option A:  Hernia is a reducible swelling in which the examiner cannot get above the swelling and testes are palpable.

Option B: Varicocele is a dilatation of the pampiniform plexus which feels like a dragging sensation to the patient. A scrotal swelling is not a usual presentation.

Option C: Seminoma is the most common germ cell tumour of the testes. They are hard on palpation. The CT scan will show homogenous hyperdensity and not fluid collection.

questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presented with severe pain and swelling in her right hand which is increasing in size and severity. She had a prick injury while in the garden 5 days back. On examination, she cries out in pain when you try to extend the hand and palpate the palmar aspect passively. Which of the following statements is true about this condition?
options: It is more common on the dorsal aspect of the hand
X ray imaging will aid in location of the foreign body in all patients.
Oral analgesics are the mainstay of treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It requires incision and drainage.

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of a deep palmar abscess secondary to a foreign body and it requires incision and drainage.

Foreign body intrusions into the hand are among the most common injuries to the upper extremity seen in the Emergency Department. They can present with pain and swelling initially. The patient also presents with partial foreign bodies after the partial removal of the object. The delayed presentation can lead to the development of deep palmar abscesses with severe pain and systemic signs (fever, tachycardia)

Diagnosis: History is useful. If a metal object is suspected, an X-ray can be used to locate the object. In patients with non-metallic objects, high-frequency ultrasound can be used.

Treatment requires exploration under anesthesia to remove the foreign body along with incision and drainage of the abscess.

Other options:

Option A: It is more common in the palmar space.

Option B: X-ray imaging can detect metallic objects. In the above case of splinters/thorns- high frequency musculoskeletal ultrasound probe can be used.

Option D: Analgesics are necessary but not the mainstay of treatment.

questions.text: A 25-year-old male came to OPD with a complaint of midline neck swelling which has been persistent for many years. Recently, it has become painful and inflamed. There has been a clear watery discharge from the wound since last week. On examination, the swelling moves with protrusion of the tongue and also on deglutition. Which of the following statements is true about this condition?
options: Untreated condition may lead to squamous cell carcinoma
They are remnants of thyroid tissue
Acid fast bacilli (AFB) staining should be done to come to a diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. They are remnants of thyroid tissue

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a thyroglossal cyst which has been complicated by a sinus fistula. These are the remnants of thyroid tissue.

A thyroglossal duct cyst is a congenital midline neck swelling that typically presents during childhood. It represents the persistence of the thyroglossal tract. It can occur anywhere along the migratory course of the duct:

Beneath foramen cecum → Floor of mouth → Suprahyoid → Region of thyroid cartilage → Subhyoid (most common site)

Clinically, the cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion. This indicates attachment to the hyoid bone. Swelling is smooth, soft, fluctuant (cystic), non-tender, mobile, and often transilluminate.

The most common complication is infection. Thyroglossal fistula is an acquired condition that either follows infection of the cyst which bursts open or due to inadequate removal of the cyst.

Option A: An untreated thyroglossal duct cyst can rarely lead to malignant transformation, with papillary thyroid carcinoma (85%) being the most common type. It is not associated with squamous cell carcinoma.

Option B: Sistrunk’s operation is performed to excise the cyst. It involves the excision of the whole thyroglossal tract, involving removal of the body of the hyoid bone, and the suprahyoid tract.

Option D: AFB staining is required when a suspicion of cervical lymph node tuberculosis. They present with the associated systemic signs and symptoms of TB. Swellings are laterally located and don't move with protrusion of the tongue or deglutition.

questions.text: A 30-year-old presents on postpartum day 10 with high-grade fever, malaise and pain in her left breast. She has been exclusively breastfeeding her child. She had presented to the OPD a few days back with mild pain and congestion of the breast and was prescribed oral analgesics and antibiotics. On examination, the left breast appears engorged and a fluctuant swelling is present. Ultrasound showed fluid collection. What is the next most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Breast abscess

A lactational mother with high-grade fever and fluctuant swelling which did not resolve with analgesics and antibiotics points towards a diagnosis of breast abscess.

The most common aetiology of breast abscess is Staph. aureus and occurs commonly in lactational mothers. It occurs due to the colonisation of obstructed lactiferous ducts. It is commoner in new mothers at the beginning of lactation who are inexperienced with breastfeeding or during weaning when nipple trauma occurs due to the infant's growing teeth.

Signs and symptoms: Fever and malaise, localized pain and tenderness, redness and swelling of the affected breast, fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

The initial treatment should involve providing pain relief with analgesics. The abscess should then be localized preferably under USG guidance and percutaneous aspiration carried out. The pus should be sent for microbiological examination to find the organism and antibiotic sensitivity. Repeated aspirations may be carried out under antibiotics cover if needed. In some conditions mentioned below, the breast abscess may be unresponsive to repeated aspiration and antibiotic cover. In such cases, incision and drainage are performed. The conditions include:

* Presence of thick pus

* Bacteria resistant to antibiotics

* If just a superficial part has been aspirated in the presence of a multiloculated abscess

Other options:

Option B: Mastitis occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. This occurs secondary to blockage of the lactiferous duct due to incomplete emptying of breast milk or due to a retracted nipple. Overgrowth of these bacteria results in the development of breast abscesses.

questions.text: A 35-year-old male patient presents with a bulky scrotal swelling. On evaluation, malignancy is suspected. Orchidectomy is done and the gross section is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seminoma

The given cut section of testicular mass is homogenous, grey-white, and does not show haemorrhage or necrosis suggesting a diagnosis of seminoma.

Seminoma is the most common testicular tumour. In about 15% of cases, serum HCG levels are raised as these seminomas contain syncytiotrophoblasts. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels are also measured to assess tumour burden. They are bulky, homogenous, pale, and well-circumscribed masses that do not show any haemorrhage or necrosis, as shown in the image below.

Microscopically, sheets of uniform tumour cells divided into poorly demarcated lobules by fibrous septa are seen. Each cell is large, and round, and has a distinct cell membrane, abundant clear cytoplasm, and a large central nucleus with a few nucleoli.

Therapy depends on the stage of the tumour. Seminoma has the best prognosis. Most cases of seminoma stages I and II can be cured by orchidectomy with or without chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

Other options:

Option B, C: Yolk sac tumour and endodermal sinus tumour  will not present with a homogenous appearance on gross examination.

Option D: Teratoma has origins from ectodermal, mesodermal and endodermal germ cell layers. The gross cut section will have tissues from this origin.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presented to a surgical emergency with complaints of severe epigastric pain for 1 day. On examination, HR was 120/min and BP was 100/60 mm Hg. On palpation, there is tenderness, guarding and rigidity. What is the probable cause of the condition shown in the X-ray below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hollow viscus perforation

The clinical scenario of hypotension and tachycardia with abdominal tenderness, guarding and rigidity with free air under the diaphragm in X-ray is indicative of hollow viscus perforation.

Acute abdomen is a common surgical emergency. Common causes include appendicitis, hollow viscus perforation, cholecystitis, and pancreatitis. An erect abdominal X-ray is commonly done as the first investigation. Free air under the diaphragm can result from hollow viscus perforation including Gastric, duodenal, small bowel and large bowel perforations.

Causes of hollow viscus perforation are blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, infections(TB, typhoid, Crohn's), corrosive agents etc.

Clinical features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

Investigations include estimation of the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel suggestive of paralytic ileus. However, CECT is the most sensitive investigation to detect minimal/ suspected pneumoperitoneum.

Management of a hollow viscous perforation mainly includes resuscitation, analgesics, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency exploratory laparotomy.

Other options: None of the other options have free air under the diaphragm.

Option A: Acute cholecystitis presents with pain in the right upper quadrant with fever and nausea. They may have tenderness and guarding. Rigidity is uncommon. Additionally, free air under the diaphragm may be seen in cases of gall bladder perforation only.

Option B: Sigmoid volvulus shows a large, dilated loop of the colon, often with a few air-fluid levels. Specific signs include the coffee bean sign and the absence of rectal gas. On the x-ray abdomen, the apex of the sigmoid volvulus extends towards the right upper quadrant and the haustrations are usually lost.

Option D: In small bowel obstruction, the obstructed bowel loops are centrally located and lie transversely. In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect. Additionally, a distended cecum may exhibit a gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presented with diffuse abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed rigidity and guarding. Abdominal X-ray demonstrated free air under the diaphragm. The patient was taken up for surgery and intraoperatively, ileal perforation was noted with gross contamination of the abdomen with enteric and purulent content. What is the appropriate management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent surgical exploration with ileostomy

The clinical vignette with Ileal perforation and physical examination findings of rigidity and guarding suggest peritonitis due to perforation. The next best step in the management of this patient is urgent surgical exploration with an ileostomy.

Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition that occurs following the rupture of the alimentary tract. Common causes include iatrogenic (surgery, scopes) blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, infections( TB, typhoid) peptic ulcer disease, corrosive agents, or particular medications

This leads to the leakage of the enteric contents, thereby leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. Peritonitis is the generalized or localized inflammation of the peritoneum due to the free spillage of fluids into the peritoneal cavity or secondary bacterial infection.

Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation occur due to the developed peritonitis and the features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

Investigations include estimating the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus. The below image shows a hollow viscus perforation.

Management - Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Indications for immediate bowel exploration are

* Sepsis/diffuse peritonitis(as in this patient)

* Bowel ischemia

* Complete or closed-loop bowel obstruction

Other options:

Option A: Resection is considered in a patient with multiple perforation, suspected gangrene or malignancy. Anastomosis is avoided in patients in shock, peritonitis with gross contamination

Option B: Primary repair is usually taken for small perforation with minimal contamination and no sign of peritonitis. It is commonly done for traumatic enteric perforation

Option D: Duodenal perforations, on the other hand, are generally treated with omental patch repair without resection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45 year male presented to OPD with complaints of swelling on the upper back. It has been present for nearly a year and has not increased in size. On examination, the swelling is non pulsatile, and slip sign is positive approximately measuring 5*5 cm. Which of the following statements is likely true?
options: Excision can be done if the patient makes a request
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Excision can be done if the patient makes a request

The clinical scenario of a 45-year-old male presenting with a non-pulsatile swelling on the upper back, which has not increased in size for nearly a year and measures approximately 5*5 cm with a positive slip sign, suggests a benign lesion like a lipoma. If the patient requests it, excision can be performed.

Lipomas are benign tumors of adipose tissue. It can occur anywhere and at any depth. It can be encapsulated or diffuse, superficial or deep.
On examination, they are nontender and non-pulsatile. Because of the soft consistency, they may appear to be fluctuant but they are not. The slip sign is positive.
Diagnosis is mostly clinical. Biopsy is rarely indicated in case of clinical doubt of malignant transformation. All lipomas need not be excised. Lipomas can be excised on suspicion of malignant transformation and sometimes at the patient's request.
Imaging is required in cases of deep-seated tumors only.

Other options:

Option A: Lipomas have a very low risk of malignant transformation into liposarcoma.
Option B: While FNAC (Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology) can be used to confirm the diagnosis, it is not always necessary for a typical lipoma.
Option C: PET scans are generally not needed for benign conditions like lipomas. They are used in cases where malignancy is suspected.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient came with pain in the left loin. An intravenous urogram was done and the image is shown below. There is non-visualisation of the right kidney. Which of the following is a true statement? DMSA- Dimercaptosuccinic acid
options: Visualized kidney has a remnant function of 10%.
This abnormality can be due to compression of ureter by artery/vein on the same side.
The best test to evaluate the functioning of a kidney is through a Tc99 DMSA scan.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. This abnormality can be due to compression of ureter by artery/vein on the same side.

The given intravenous urogram (IVU) shows a dilated pelvicalyceal system and ureter on the left side suggesting a left-sided hydroureteronephrosis which occurs secondary to compression of distal ureter by a vessel- artery/vein.

Hydroureteronephrosis is a pathological condition which occurs due to dilatation of the renal pelvis and ureter secondary to a distal obstruction. The extramural causes of hydroureteronephrosis include tumours from adjacent structures (e.g., cervix, prostate, rectum, colon, or cecum), retrocaval ureter, aberrant renal vessels, idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Ormond’s disease). (See pearl attached). If the obstruction is not relieved, it can lead to kidney scarring and permanent kidney damage with the compromise of glomerular and tubular function.

Other options:

Option A: Renal function cannot be predicted using IVU alone.

Option C:  Renal function is best assessed by the Tc-99m MAG3 (mercaptoacetyltriglycine) scan. It is eliminated through the kidney through both glomeruli filtration and tubular excretion and is a measure of both. Tc-99m DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) is used to evaluate renal structure and morphology, particularly in pediatric imaging for detecting scarring and pyelonephritis. It is an ideal agent for the assessment of the renal cortex. Tc-99m DTPA (diethylene-triamine-pentaacetate) is cleared only via glomeruli with no tubular excretion. Hence, it is used for direct measurement of GFR.

Option D: The characteristic sign in the given IVP depicts cobra head/ adder head deformity seen in the ureterocele.

* It refers to the cystic dilatation of the distal collecting tubules

* Drooping lily sign

* It refers to the inferolateral displacement of the lower pole due to an obstructed upper pole in a duplicated collecting system

* Handshake sign - due to the position of the lower poles closer to the spine, and the lower calyces closer to each other

* Flower vase sign - due to medially rotated calyces

* It refers to the medially drawn ureters caused by fibrosis at the lumbosacral junction

* Right ureter hooks behind the IVC as it passes posterior to it

Ureterocele

* It refers to the dilation of the distal ureter

* Goblet sign

* It is due to the focal dilation of the ureter by an intraluminal mass

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 47-year-old female comes with complaints of severe chest pain since last night. She had gone to a party where she remembers binge drinking following which she had multiple episodes of vomiting which was also mixed with blood. On examination, she appeared sick and had fast breathing. Her BP-90/50 mg Hg, HR-112/min and crepitus can be palpated. An X-ray was done and is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Esophageal perforation

The given clinical scenario with a history of recurrent episodes of vomiting mixed with blood, and now presenting with chest pain, hypotension, and palpable crepitus with a given X-ray showing pneumomediastinum is suggestive of esophageal perforation.

Oesophageal perforation is a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs through the transmural perforation of the esophageal wall. It can occur secondary to trauma, endoscopic instrumentation, corrosive ingestion, or severe repetitive vomiting against a closed GE junction. It presents with retrosternal chest pain and other symptoms depending on the size of the perforation and contamination of the mediastinum. Late signs may include mediastinitis as well as surgical emphysema. The initial investigation that is performed in this condition is a contrast esophagogram (gastrograffin) which will show the extravasation of the contrast. Water-soluble contrast (iohexol) should be used instead of barium contrast to prevent barium-related inflammation of the mediastinum if there is perforation. If the esophagogram is normal, contrast-enhanced CT is useful in identifying the injury. If the suspicion of esophageal perforation is high and the radiological investigations are normal, then the endoscopy can be performed to confirm the diagnosis.

Other options
Options A: Mallory-Weiss tear is characterized by mucosal lacerations at the gastroesophageal junction, typically following forceful vomiting. It usually presents with hematemesis and epigastric pain but does not typically cause severe chest pain or crepitus.

Option C: Pulsion Diverticulum (e.g., Zenker's Diverticulum) is an outpouching of the esophageal mucosa due to increased intraluminal pressure.
Patients may have dysphagia, regurgitation, and possibly halitosis. However, it does not typically present with acute severe chest pain or crepitus.

Option D: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, often presenting with sharp chest pain that may worsen with deep breaths or when lying down. Acute pericarditis is unlikely given the history of vomiting, hematemesis, and crepitus.

questions.text: A 47-year-old man presented with a chronic non-healing painless ulcer over his scalp for 8 years. He gave a history of sustaining electric burns injury to the scalp 8 years back. The examination findings are shown below. Which of the following statements is true?
options: It can progress to squamous cell cancer
Long duration antibiotics will improve the condition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It can progress to squamous cell cancer

The given scenario and image show a long-standing ulcer with crusting and irregular borders can progress to Marjolin's ulcer which is an aggressive type of squamous cell carcinoma.

Marjolin ulcers most commonly arise from burn scars. The most common cell type identified is squamous cell carcinoma. All suspicious lesions should be biopsied. Confirmed cases of Marjolin ulcers should be excised with clear margins. Marjolin ulcers can be prevented with early excision and grafting of burn wounds. The prognosis is poor with a high rate of recurrence.

SCC is the second most common skin cancer. The primary risk factor and driving force for the development of this common cancer is UV exposure.

Variants :

* Bowen's Disease

* Erythroplasia of Queyrat

SCC initially presents as smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous lesions. All these lesions later ulcerate and have a characteristic everted edge and are surrounded by inflamed, indurated skin.

Treatment:  Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Other modalities include cautery ablation, cryotherapy, drug therapy including imiquimod, Moh’s microsurgery and Radiation therapy.

Other options:

Option A: A malignancy cannot be incised. Some malignancies can have local control through wide local excision.

Option C: Squamous cell carcinomas spread lymphatogenously.

Option D: Chronic antibiotic therapy is not recommended for SCC. It is used in the treatment of chronic osteomyelitis, actinomycosis and tuberculosis.

Pearl PF0158: Marjolin’s Ulcer

* Low-grade cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arising from

* Long-standing ulcer like venous ulcer

* Post-burn scar

* Chronic osteomyelitis

* Post-radiation ulcer.

* Slow progression to malignancy (SCC) since it is relatively avascular.

* Painless due to the absence of nerves in scar tissue.

* No secondary deposits since there are no lymphatics in scar tissue.

* Radioresistant due to avascularity.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trophic ulcer

The given picture showing an ulcer with punched-out edges over a pressure point is most likely that of a trophic ulcer/neuropathic ulcer.

A neuropathic ulcer is one that occurs as a result of peripheral neuropathy. In peripheral neuropathy, lack of sensation over the pressure points leads to cumulative microtrauma, minor wounds, or cuts that remain unnoticed but eventually develop into ulcers.

Features of a neuropathic ulcer include

* Painless ulcer

* Punched out ulcer with regular margins

* Often located on the plantar surface of the foot

* Ulcer margins show the presence of calluses

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with pain abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen was done. What is the likely source of pain in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kidney

The history of an elderly male presenting with pain abdomen and an axial CECT image showing renal lesions with irregular enhancement is suggestive of renal origin of pain likely renal cell carcinoma (RCC).

It is the most common malignant tumour of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50–70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It usually presents with painless gross hematuria, flank pain, or painless flank mass.

Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice for RCC. On CT, small lesions enhance homogeneously, whereas larger lesions have irregular enhancement due to areas of necrosis. The clear cell subtype may show much stronger enhancement is a differential for angiomyolipoma. Still, it is essential to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Surgeries done for RCC:

Partial nephrectomy, the goal is the complete removal of the primary tumor while preserving healthy renal parenchyma. It is used for renal tumors <7cm in size.
Classic radical nephrectomy involves the removal of the kidney, perirenal fat, adrenal gland, and regional lymph nodes.
Targeted therapies for RCC include tyrosine kinase inhibitors (sorafenib, sunitinib), anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) monoclonal antibodies (bevacizumab), and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors (everolimus and temsirolimus).

Given below is the image showing the anatomy in the axial section of the CT scan

1- Liver, 2-Spleen, 3-Pancreas, 4-Gallbladder, 5-Right Adrenal Gland, 6-Left Adrenal Gland, 7-Inferior Vena Cava, 8-Aorta, 9-Portal Vein, 11- Ascending Colon, 12-Descending Colon, 14- Stomach.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62-year-old female presented to the OPD with complaints of a gradually progressive swelling over his abdomen for 1.5 years. She had a history of midline surgery done as a child. On examination, the swelling was 4 cm and was reducible with a palpable cough impulse. She is planned to undergo fascial closure with a mesh repair. What is the likely location of the mesh as shown in image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Onlay

The above clinical scenario of a reducible swelling with cough impulse and palpable defect in a patient with a previous surgery points toward a diagnosis of incisional hernia.  Incisional hernias are repaired by fascial closure augmented with a mesh. It is an onlay type of mesh repair.

An incisional hernia refers to a ventral abdominal wall hernia at the site of a previous surgical incision.  Incisional hernias are usually asymptomatic, but can occasionally present with pain. Strangulation and bowel obstruction are rare due to the large neck of the defect. In general, incisional hernias are repaired by fascial closure augmented with a mesh. There are different options for mesh placement:

* Onlay (above the anterior fascia, over the defect)

* Inlay (between the fascial edges without overlap)

* Sublay (below the fascial components) - this includes retrorectus, preperitoneal, and intraperitoneal (IPOM) mesh placements

Primary suture repair using Mayo’s technique is reserved only for very small hernias with < 2cm defect. This involves closing the fascial edges with a 2 cm overlap using an interrupted suture and then reinforcing it with a continuous running suture (double-breasting).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old chronic smoker presented with a bright red velvety plaque on the floor of the mouth. Which of the following statements is correct about the diagnosis and management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Erythroplakia and biopsy

The given clinical scenario of a chronic smoker presenting with a bright red velvety plaque on the floor of the mouth is suggestive of erythroplakia and the next best step is to do an excision biopsy of the lesion.

Erythroplakia is a pre-malignant oral lesion that presents as a bright red velvety patch or plaque commonly at the lower alveolar mucosa, gingivobuccal sulcus and the floor of the mouth. The red colour is due to decreased keratinization and as a result, the red vascular connective tissue of the submucosa shines through.  Grossly, the lesion may be of three varieties—homogenous, speckled or granular, and erythroplakia, interspersed with areas of leukoplakia. Malignant potential is 17 times higher than in leukoplakia, hence excision biopsy and follow-up are indicated in such cases.

Other options:
Option A, B, D:  Leukoplakia is a premalignant condition of the oral cavity characterized by whitish patches or plaques that cannot be rubbed off. Management includes smoking cessation and reduction in alcohol consumption. A biopsy should be done and a photographic record of the lesion is used for follow-up. Both erythroplakia and leukoplakia have malignant potential. Hence, only observation will not be appropriate.

questions.text: A 65-year-old male patient presents with a direct inguinal hernia on the left side. He underwent open hernioplasty with mesh repair. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ilioinguinal nerve

The ilioinguinal nerve is most commonly injured within open hernia repair due to traction or thermal injury. The ilioinguinal nerve provides innervation to the groin and medial aspect of the thigh, the upper part of the scrotum, and the penile root.

Other options:

Option B: The iliohypogastric nerve carries the sensory supply from the suprapubic area. Injury to this nerve in the right iliac fossa rarely causes sensory disturbances, as the suprapubic area has a rich nerve supply from other sources too. If the nerve is severed above the anterior superior iliac spine, it can lead to the weakened posterior wall of the inguinal canal resulting in a direct inguinal hernia. The iliohypogastric nerve can also get injured following appendicectomy.

Option C: Injury to the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve results in loss of sensation in the skin of the scrotum of males, and loss of sensation of the mons pubis and labia majora in females.

Option D: Injury to the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve causes hypoesthesia over the anterior thigh below the inguinal ligament.

Note: The femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve are injured less commonly.

Pearl PF0305: The triangle of pain/Electrical hazard zone:

The triangle of pain/Electrical hazard zone:

It is bounded

* Superio-medially by gonadal vessels

* Laterally by peritoneum

* Inferio-laterally by the iliopubic tract

Contents:

* Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve

* Anterior femoral cutaneous nerve

* Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve

* Femoral nerves

Pearl PF0304: The triangle of doom

The triangle of doom is bounded

* Medially by the vas deferens

* Laterally by the vessels of the spermatic cord (gonadal vessels)

* Inferiorly by peritoneal reflection

Apex oriented superiorly at internal ring.

The contents of the space include

* External iliac vessels

* Deep circumflex iliac vein

* Femoral nerve

* Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve

questions.text: A 65-year-old male patient presents with a left groin swelling for a few years. The swelling increases in size on standing and decreases while lying on the bed. On examination, the swelling has a positive cough impulse. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Reduction of content, repair of the defect and reinforcement with a mesh
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Reduction of content, repair of the defect and reinforcement with a mesh

The given clinical scenario is an uncomplicated inguinal hernia.  An uncomplicated inguinal hernia is repaired by the reduction of the content, repair of the defect and reinforcement with mesh placement(Lichtenstein mesh repair).

A hernia is a protrusion of the contents outside the cavity containing it. Groin hernias arising lateral to the inferior epigastric artery are indirect and hernia arising medial to it are direct inguinal hernias. Hernias have two cardinal features- reducibility and cough impulse. A Lichtenstein mesh repair is currently one of the most frequently used methods for treating an inguinal hernia. It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. It is an anterior tension-free mesh repair that reduces the chances of recurrence of a hernia. A piece of prosthetic nonabsorbable mesh is used to fit the canal to bridge the defect in this repair.

Other surgical methods used to repair a hernia are:

Bassini repair is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. In this method, a mesh is not used. It is associated with a high recurrence and is not used frequently now. It is used only in cases of hernial strangulation and peritonitis where the use of a mesh is not preferred. It is performed by suturing the transversus abdominis and internal oblique musculoaponeurotic arches/conjoined tendons to the inguinal ligament.  Shouldice repair is a multilayered repair, where the posterior wall of the inguinal canal is strengthened by continuous sutures. It involves double-breasting of the transversalis fascia. It is associated with a very low recurrence rate. These are herniorraphies (Option C)

Herniotomy is used to treat inguinal hernia in a child which occurs due to the presence of a patent processus vaginalis. Therefore in herniotomy, the repair of the inguinal ring is not done. (Option B)

McVay repair (Cooper's ligament repair) is used for the correction of direct inguinal hernia, large indirect hernia, recurrent hernia, femoral hernias (particularly suited for strangulated femoral hernias). In this method, the transversus abdominis aponeurosis is approximated to Cooper's ligament.

Stoppa-Rives repair is used for the repair of large, recurrent, or bilateral hernias. In this method, a sub-umbilical midline incision is given to place a large mesh into the preperitoneal space.

Pearl PF0034: Boundaries of Hesselbach’s triangle

* Lateral - inferior epigastric artery

* Medial - lateral border of rectus abdominis

* Inferior - inguinal ligament

Direct inguinal hernia emerges through Hesselbach’s triangle (Hence situated medial to inferior epigastric artery)

Indirect inguinal hernia enters deep inguinal ring (Hence it is lateral to inferior epigastric artery)

Pearl PF1778: Types of indirect inguinal hernia

* Bubonocele – Hernia limited to the inguinal canal.

* Funicular – Hernia stops just above the testis.

* Complete/scrotal – Hernia reaches bottom of scrotum.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic smoking came with complaints of ulcerative lesions on his lower lip for a year. On examination, there is a presence of a palpable ipsilateral submental node approximately 5*5 cm. Biopsy from the lesion was suggestive of squamous cell cancer. What is the next step in the management of this patient? MRND-Modified radical neck dissection
options: Resection of primary lesion with lip reconstruction and MRND
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Resection of primary lesion with lip reconstruction and MRND

The given patient has a squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with a primary lesion on the lower lip with ipsilateral lymph node metastasis to the submental node. This patient will need resection of the primary lesion with reconstruction and modified radical neck dissection (MRND).

Lip cancer most commonly occurs in men from 50 to 70 years old but can be seen in younger patients. Risk factors include sunlight exposure, smoking, and tobacco use. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of lip cancer. But commonly occurring cancer in the upper lip is basal cell carcinoma.

Most lip cancers occur in the lower lip followed by the upper lip and commissure. The most common site is the vermilion border of the lower lip. Ulcerative lesion on the vermilion border of the lower lip is the most common clinical manifestation. Mass can extend and fix on the underlying bone. Loss of sensation over the chin indicates mental nerve involvement. The most frequently involved nodes are the submental and submandibular nodes.

Surgical resection (wide local excision with negative margins) is the preferred treatment modality. The typical lip length is 6 to 7 cm. For defects of <1/3rd of the lip, resection with primary closure is the preferred treatment.

For defects of more than 1/3rd of the lip, require local flaps for reconstruction after resection:

* Johansen step technique- local flap for large central defects

* Lip-switch (Abbe-Estlander) flap- based on the sublabial or superior labial artery. When the defect involves only the commissure, the Estlander flap is used, and the Abbé flap is used for midline defects. Abbe-Estlander Flap is used for mixed defects. The markings of the Abbe-Estlander flap are shown below.

* Karapandzic flap - circumoral advancement flap. It is a neuromuscular flap that includes the remaining orbicularis oris muscle with its innervation.

In the presence of neck metastasis, neck dissection is indicated. Postoperative radiation is administered to patients with positive margins, lymph node metastases, tumor thickness >4mm, or perineural invasion. If the mandible is involved, mandibulectomy and free flap reconstruction is required.
