questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 67-year-old patient with a history of thromboembolic stroke is currently taking aspirin and warfarin. He is complaining of a headache and appears confused after a fall in the toilet last night. NCCT of the head was done. What is the next best step in management? NCCT- Non contrast CT head
options: Vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma and neurosurgery consultation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma and neurosurgery consultation

The above clinical scenario and the plain computed tomography (CT) scan show a concave-convex-shaped hematoma on the left side suggestive of an acute subdural hematoma (SDH). Since, the patient is on anticoagulants, reversal with Vitamin K, FFP and immediate neurosurgical consultation would be the next best step.

Acute SDH results from the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid membrane and the dura. The tearing of a bridging vein running from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses is the most common cause of acute SDH.

Radiographic features of subdural haemorrhages-Crescent-like distribution around the periphery of the brain.
Crescent-shaped hypodense lesion on axial CT: Chronic subdural haemorrhage
Crescent-shaped hyperdense collections on CT: Acute subdural haemorrhage.

On head CT scan, acute SDH appears as a hyperdense, crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) lesion (as seen in this question)

Open craniotomy for the evacuation of acute SDH is indicated for the following:

* Thickness >1 cm

* Midline shift >5 mm

Emergent decompression is also recommended for a comatose patient with an acute subdural hematoma less than 1 cm in thickness causing a midline shift of less than 5 mm if any of the following criteria are met:

*  GCS drops by two or more points from the time of injury to the hospitalization

*  The patient presents with fixed and dilated pupils

* ICP is >20mm Hg

Other options:

Option A: Aspirin and Clopidogrel are given in patients with ischemic stroke. It is not required for this patient.

Option C: Mannitol is used to lower intracranial pressure. Raised features of intracranial pressure like vomiting, papilledema are not mentioned.

Option D: Only observation would be inappropriate in the case of Acute SDH.

Pearl PF1866: Intracranial haemorrhage

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought with complaints of headache, vomiting and neck stiffness for a few days. He had undergone a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement for hydrocephalus a year back. Which of the following is the most common cause of shunt malfunction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Shunt obstruction

Obstruction of the shunt is the most common cause of shunt malfunction.

A ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is used to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) due to an obstruction in the normal outflow or there is a decreased absorption of the fluid.

Complications of the shunting procedure include the following -

* Shunt obstruction - most common cause for shunt malfunction

* Shunt infection due to skin flora entering the shunt, most commonly from Staphylococcus epidermidis.

* Intracerebral or intraventricular haemorrhage

* Tip migration or malposition

* Shunt overdrainage (slit ventricle syndrome) - usually occurs after many years

* Shunt nephritis

* Shunt disconnection or breakage or kinking

* Inguinal hernia

* Seizures

Shunt obstruction -

* It is the most common cause of shunt malfunction.

* The most common site is the ventricular catheter.

* Obstruction occurs due to clogging of the shunt by blood, proteinaceous material, choroid plexus, glial adhesions or secondary to infection.

* The patient comes with features of raised intracranial pressure like headache, vomiting and eye examination showing papilloedema.

* Diagnosis is done by CT Brain imaging which shows ventriculomegaly. On performing a lumbar puncture, the CSF flow is found to be slow despite the raised CSF pressure.

* Treatment is by revision of the shunt.

The image below shows the location of the shunt in the brain

The image below shows a CT scan of the brain with some proteinaceous material deposited in the ventricles and shunt insitu.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient following an accident presented with complex injuries including degloving injuries of the foot and leg. What type of flap/graft was used during surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thiersch graft

The image given shows a Thiersch graft which is also known as a split-thickness skin graft.

Skin grafts can be broadly divided into two categories:

Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis are called split-thickness skin grafts. Less dermis in the split-thickness skin graft translates into less primary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks in surface area after harvesting and before grafting) and more secondary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks during healing).

Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft- Option A) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. More dermis in the full-thickness skin graft translates into more primary contraction and less secondary contraction.

Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft:

* Large grafts can be harvested.

* In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such as burns.

* Uptake is good. Meshing can be done i.e. small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this and this improves graft takeup.

* Meshing also allows the graft to expand.

Advantages of full-thickness skin graft over split skin graft:

* It has a lesser degree of post-graft contraction.

* Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements.Other options:

Grafts derive their blood supply from the target bed while flaps carry their own blood supply.

Option B: Free flaps - A flap where its blood vessel is disconnected and the vessel is reconnected using microsurgery at the new site.

Option C: Pedicled/islanded flaps - They are the repositioned flaps which maintain their original blood supply even after the transfer.

Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft

The take of skin graft occurs in three phases:

* Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries.

* Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses

* Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft

Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later.

Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A middle-aged woman with a history of renal calculi complaints of bone pain and abdominal cramps. X-ray shows subperiosteal resorption of 2nd and 3rd metacarpals and phalanges. On investigation, serum calcium and PTH were raised and phosphate levels were decreased. Which of the following investigations will help localise the primary pathology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 99Tc-Radiolabelled Sestamibi scan

The given clinical picture is highly suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a solitary parathyroid adenoma arising sporadically. It is best localised using a 99Tc- Radiolabelled sestamibi scan.

Hyperparathyroidism is caused by elevated parathyroid hormone and is classified into primary, secondary, and tertiary types.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism

an autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH)

compensatory hypersecretion of PTH in response to prolonged hypocalcemia
persistent hypersecretion of PTH even after the cause of prolonged hypocalcemia is corrected

Parathyroid  adenoma or hyperplasia
chronic renal failure
after renal transplant.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is one of the most common endocrine disorders, and it is an important cause of hypercalcemia. Tumours of the parathyroid glands usually come to attention because of excessive secretion of PTH rather than mass effects. It can also be associated with MEN1 and MEN 2A syndromes.

The clinical manifestations of hyperparathyroidism can be summarized as “painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans.” Skeletal manifestations of hyperparathyroidism include bone resorption, osteitis fibrosa cystica, and brown tumours. Renal changes include nephrolithiasis (stones) and nephrocalcinosis.

Localisation of parathyroid is difficult. Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabeled Sestamibi is a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue. It is now regarded as the most accurate and reliable method for imaging the parathyroid glands.

Other options:

Option B: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is not commonly used to image the parathyroid glands

Option C: Ultrasonography of the neck is a safe and widely used technique for the localization of abnormal parathyroid glands. However, ultrasonography is operator, lesion size and location dependent. Ectopic locations are difficult to locate.

Option D: Multiphase CT imaging has become widely utilized to localize the disease. It gives both anatomical as well as functional information about the parathyroid glands. The disadvantage is the higher radiation dose when compared to others.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient came to OPD with a complaint of dilated and tortuous veins in the left leg and mild pain while walking. On palpation, the vein is pulsatile. He had a history of road traffic accident, including a left leg fracture 10 years ago. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arteriovenous (AV) fistula

This patient with a history of trauma and a recently developed pulsatile swelling of the same side has a traumatic arteriovenous fistula.
An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal communication between an artery and a vein and tends to occur when two structures are in proximity. Traumatic AVF can occur secondary to penetrating and blunt trauma. The most common traumatic AV fistula is a carotid-cavernous fistula secondary to the base of the skull fracture.
Clinical features: pulsatile swelling and in chronic cases- limb lengthening, arterialisation of veins and heart failure. Large extremity fistula may present with skin warmth in contrast to cool extremity and signs of venous hypertension which is usually seen in varicosities.

Diagnosis: Ultrasonography can detect flow anomalies. CT angiography can provide anatomic delineation.

Other options

Option A: Varicose veins can present with dilated tortuous veins. However, they are not pulsatile and with a history of trauma AV fistula is more likely.

Option B: Pseudoaneurysms do not present with dilated and tortuous veins.

Option D: Atherosclerosis doesn't present with dilated veins and pulsatile swellings.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient fell from a train onto the railway tracks and injured both his legs severely. He was urgently taken to the hospital and the following procedure was done as shown in the image below. What is the rationale for performing this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Life saving procedure

The above patient shown in the image had undergone a below-knee amputation. In the background of trauma with a severely injured, crushed or septic limb amputation is a life-saving procedure.

Major amputations can be done for,

* Dead limb -Gangrene

* Deadly limb- Wet gangrene, spreading infection (gas gangrene), malignancy

* Dead loss limb- Severe critical rest pain which cannot be revascularized, paralysis, trauma etc

Even though, the below-knee amputations provide a better fit for a prosthesis(Option A), it is not the main rationale behind this procedure.

Mangled extremity score system (MESS) is commonly used to decide whether the limb should undergo amputation. Components of the score: Shock, Ischemia, Soft tissue injury and age.

Other options:

Option C: Amputation can be used for the treatment of cancer but it does not reduce the risk of cancer.

Option D: Good cosmetic outcomes are not the indications for amputation in a trauma patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought to the casualty following a road traffic accident. He is tachypneic and uses accessory neck muscles for respiration. His BP is 90/60 mm Hg. On percussion, the right chest is hyper-resonant. On auscultation, breath sounds could not be heard on the right chest. An urgent chest X-ray is done. What is the next best step of management?
options: Tube thoracostomy at 5th intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line
Needle decompression at 5th intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line
Needle decompression at 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
Needle decompression at 2nd intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Needle decompression at 5th intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line

The above patient with hemodynamic instability, tachypnea and hyper-resonant sounds on percussion with absent breath sounds on auscultation along with the radiolucency and mediastinal shift on X-ray is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. Immediate management is done with needle decompression or needle thoracostomy i.e. insertion of a wide-bore needle in the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line.

Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency when air leaks from the lungs into the pleural cavity and cannot escape. This leads to compression of the lung field with mediastinal shift and collapse of lung parenchyma. This can be diagnosed clinically with high index of suspicion and immediate decompression with wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space should be done.

Definitive management - tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th ICS in the triangle of safety.

Triangle of safety:

The boundaries are

* Anteriorly - lateral border of the pectoralis major

* Posteriorly- latissimus dorsi

* Inferiorly- a line perpendicular to the nipple going to the back

For pediatric patients, needle decompression is done at the midclavicular line in the 2nd intercostal space.

The images below show the triangle of safety and technique of chest drain insertion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with polyuria, polydipsia, lethargy and abdominal pain. She also gives a history of mood disorders and recurrent kidney stones. Which of the following investigations would not be useful in arriving at a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Angiography of renal arteries

The given clinical scenario of recurrent kidney stones, mood disorder and features of hypercalcemia (polyuria, polydipsia) is suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. Angiography of renal arteries is not a useful investigation for hyperparathyroidism.

Investigations in primary hyperparathyroidism: Ultrasonography of the neck is a safe and widely used technique for localising abnormal parathyroid glands.

Dual-energy radiographic absorptiometry (DEXA) is useful for demonstrating skeletal involvement in primary hyperparathyroidism. Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabelled Sestamibi is also a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue. The image given below shows a radiolabeled Sestamibi scan.

Clinical features of hyperparathyroidism:

* Bones:

* Pathological fractures Subperiosteal bone resorption - 2nd and 3rd digits, most common in radial aspect.

* Salt and pepper skull

* Osteitis fibrosa cystica or VonReckling Hausen’s disease

* Stones:

* Multiple and recurrent renal stones - most common

* Nephrocalcinosis

* Abdominal groans - colicky due to pancreatitis
Psychiatric overtones - raised PTH causing CNS depression and psychiatric symptoms
Band keratopathy
Features of hypercalcemia - vomiting, confusion, ECG changes: increased PR interval, shortened QT interval

The image given below shows a salt and pepper skull seen in hyperparathyroidism.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a history of recurrent pilonidal sinus underwent surgery as shown in the image. What kind of flap procedure is used here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rhomboid flap

The following image shows a rhomboid flap done in pilonidal sinus surgery.

A pilonidal sinus is defined as a blind track lined by granulation tissue leading from an epithelial surface to surrounding tissue. Pilonidal sinus disease, also called jeep/driver’s bottom, is commonly seen in the natal cleft, more in men, usually after puberty.

Buttock friction and shearing forces (drivers are commonly affected) in this area allow broken hairs to enter the skin and create a subcutaneous, chronically infected midline track. An infected hair follicle can also form such a track. Secondary tracks can also form and are lined with granulation tissue and discharge.

Patients complain of intermittent pain, swelling, and discharge at the base of the spine. A foreign-body-type reaction may then lead to the formation of an abscess.

Treatment includes non-surgical and surgical approaches:

Non-surgical approaches include conservative treatment with proper hygiene and regular shaving of hair in the area. In case of an abscess- adequate rest, baths, local antiseptic dressings, and broad-spectrum antibiotics are advised.

Surgical approaches for the management of pilonidal sinus disease include:

Incision and drainage- for pilonidal abscess refractory to medical treatment.
Bascom's procedure- is a cleft lift procedure in which hair follicles parallel to the natal cleft are removed under local anesthesia
Others- VY advancement flaps, and Z-plasty.

A rhomboid flap is an example of a transposition flap that are rectangular or square and turn laterally to reach the defect . They rely on the looseness of adjacent skin to transfer a rhomboid-shaped flap into a defect that has been converted into a similar rhomboid shape.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An alcoholic male patient diagnosed with hollow viscus perforation is taken up for laparotomy. Intraoperatively, a 2 cm-sized perforation is seen in the gastric region as shown below. How can this patient be managed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Omental pedicle repair

The given scenario of an alcoholic male patient of gastric perforation showing intra-op large 2 cm size perforation can be managed by an Omental pedicle repair.

Gastroduodenal perforations are a common surgical emergency in developing countries. Causes: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD), Smoking, alcohol, chronic analgesic use. Patients present with hypotension and signs and symptoms of peritonitis- tenderness, guarding and rigidity. Management: Multiple surgical options exist depending on the perforation's location and size. Larger perforations and ulcers with fibrotic edges can be managed by an omental pedicle flap repair. A tongue of omentum is brought up to cover the ulcer defect and secured with a series of interrupted sutures. (Modified Graham's patch)

Option A: Small subcentric perforations with healthy margins can undergo primary repair and buttressed with an omental patch. (Graham's repair)

Option C: Removal of gastric antrum (antrectomy) with gastroduodenostomy is Billroth I reconstruction. It was done historically and avoided now due to higher morbidity with high rates of post-gastrectomy syndromes. In PUD, the duodenum may be scarred as well.

Option D: In Billroth II, two-thirds of the stomach is removed, the duodenal stump is closed and the stomach is anastomosed to the jejunum. It is now reserved for gastric malignancy and perforations associated with malignancy. It has higher rates of post-gastrectomy syndromes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man with a chronic history of IV drug use presented with a progressively increasing swelling in the groin on the right side. It is is non fluctuant but pulsatile on examination. He has diminished pulses on the same side distal to the swelling. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
options: CT angiography followed by surgical intervention
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT angiography followed by surgical intervention

The patient most likely has a pseudoaneurysm of the femoral artery, caused by repeated penetrating injuries during intravenous drug administration. The recommended approach includes conducting a CT angiography for diagnosis, followed by surgical intervention.

In pseudoaneurysm, the intimal and medial layers are disrupted and the dilated segment is lined by adventitia only compared to a true aneurysm where all three layers are involved. It usually occurs secondary to trauma- arterial samples, arterial catheterization and IV drug users. It is usually pulsatile and systolic bruit can be heard on auscultation.

Doppler ultrasound reveals a bidirectional, 'to-and-fro' flow of blood which is known as the yin-yang sign. Management includes the delineation of anatomy using CT-Angiography. Treatment options include open or endovascular surgery.

Other options

Option B: Antibiotics are used when the local wound appears infected with pus discharge or systemic symptoms of malaise and fever. However, imaging and surgical intervention will be needed.

Option C: Compression stockings are used in the management of chronic venous insufficiency.

Option D: Incision and drainage are required for the management of abscesses.  It should be avoided in the case of a pseudoaneurysm.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon is attempting to identify the Calot’s triangle. Identify the marked structure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cystic artery

In the given intra-op image during laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the structure marked is the cystic artery.

During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the importance of achieving a critical view of safety (CVS) is paramount for safe ligation and division of the cystic duct and artery.

CVS can be achieved by following these 3 principles:

* Dissecting the hepatocystic triangle. It is the triangle formed by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct, and the inferior border of the liver.

* Cystic plate, or the liver bed of the gallbladder, is exposed to create a window behind the gallbladder.

* To prevent harm to other nearby structures, only two structures—the cystic duct and artery—should enter the gallbladder.

The inferior surface of the liver does not form the boundary of Calot’s triangle. It forms the superior boundary of the hepatobiliary triangle.

The boundaries of Calot’s triangle are: 3C's

* Medially – Common hepatic duct

* Inferiorly – Cystic duct

* Superior – Cystic artery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure shown in the image: ERCP- Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography CBD- Common bile duct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ERCP+CBD stenting

The image shown is of ERCP and CBD stenting.

This is an invasive procedure similar to Upper GI endoscopy. Ampulla of Vater is cannulated and then a contrast-filled dye is injected for evaluation of the biliary and pancreatic tree. After a pathology has been diagnosed in CBD, a CBD stent can be placed.
CBD stenting is useful in indicated in cases of

* CBD stones

* CBD strictures

* management of mild bile duct injury leaks

* palliative drainage of malignant bile duct obstructions.

* ERCP shows filling of the main pancreatic duct (MPD), and CBD. The MPD and CBD drain into the major papillary.

* The most common significant complication is acute pancreatitis.

Other options:

(Option A) The pancreatic duct is seen below.

Option B: PTBD is a form of external biliary drainage where either biliary ductal systems are drained outside percutaneously. It is not done endoscopically.

Option D: PEG is a minimally invasive procedure used for enteral feeding. Endoscopically, a light source is placed in the stomach and a percutaneous puncture is made. A tube is entered through the ostomy and secured to the skin. Enteral feeding can be through nasogastric and nasojejunal tubes. Surgically, tube gastrostomy and feeding jejunostomy can be done.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 13-year-old male presents to the OPD with severe pain in the right testis after being hit by a cricket ball 2 hours ago. On examination, there is severe testicular pain and an absent cremasteric reflex. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Surgical exploration

The given clinical vignette of severe pain in the right testis along with a negative cremasteric reflex is highly suggestive of testicular torsion.  It is a surgical emergency, and if left untreated, the testes may become gangrenous. Early surgery undertaken to untwist the testis gives a better outcome.

Testicular torsion is the twisting of the spermatic cord and its contents such that the testicular blood supply becomes compromised.

Etiology and risk factors-

* High investment of the tunica vaginalis(like a clapper in a bell). Most common cause.

* Inversion of the testis.

* Separation of the epididymis from the body of the testis.

Clinical features of testicular torsion are - scrotal pain and swelling, erythema, negative cremasteric reflex, nausea, and vomiting, the testis seems high in the scrotum and the twisted cord can sometimes be palpated.

* Prehn’s Sign is used to differentiate the torsion of testis from acute epididymo orchitis. In the case of acute epididymo orchitis, the pain gets relieved on the elevation of the testis but not in torsion of testes.

* Deming’s sign: Spasm of the cremaster muscle and the cord twisting cause the affected testis to be positioned higher in torsion testes.

Even though Doppler ultrasound scanning can confrm the absence of the blood supply to the affected testis, false-positive results are commonly seen, hence it is not routinely recommended.

Urgent scrotal exploration in case of doubtful diagnosis.  A transverse scrotal incision is taken. If the testis is viable, twisting is prevented by fixation with three non-absorbable sutures between the tunica albuginea of the testis and the scrotal raphe.

If the testis is infarcted after the cord is untwisted, an orchidectomy must be undertaken and the opposite testis must be fixed to the scrotum to preserve fertility and prevent torsion. If the affected testis is viable after the cord is untwisted, both the affected and the contralateral testes are fixed to the scrotum (bilateral orchiopexy) using non-absorbable sutures.

Other options:

Option A and D: The optimal timeframe for surgical intervention and testicular salvage is within 6 hours from the onset of pain. Hence, seeking early urological consultation at presentation is essential, even if confirmatory tests are not yet available.

Option B: Ultrasound guided arterial doppler has to be taken, not venous. Also even for USG arterial doppler false positives are commonly seen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 16-year-old female presents with multiple episodes of abdominal pain and a history of passing blood in stools. On examination, she has dark pigmented spots on her lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome

The clinical scenario of passage of blood in stools with mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark pigmented spots on lips and oral mucosa) and the presence of hamartomatous polyps in the small intestines in endoscopy is highly suggestive of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. Due to germline heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the gene STK11. The hyperpigmentation typically appears as dark blue to brown macules on the lips, nostrils, buccal mucosa, palmar surfaces of the hands, genitalia, and perianal region.

Complications:

* Intussusception

* Risk for gastric and small intestinal cancers, and subsequently for colon, pancreatic, breast, lung, ovarian, and uterine cancers.

Treatment of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome mainly involves resection of polyps when there is heavy, persistent, or recurrent bleeding, or if intussusception develops. Polyps may be removed surgically by enterotomy or laparotomy, or endoscopically using a colonoscope introduced via an enterotomy. In severe cases where large segments of the small intestine are involved, resection of the affected portion may be required.

Other options:

Option A: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) is an inherited disorder presenting with numerous colorectal adenomatous polyps. It is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the APC gene, which is a regulator in the Wnt signaling pathway. At least 100 polyps are required to make a diagnosis of FAP.

Option C: Juvenile polyposis (JPS) is an autosomal dominant inherited condition that presents with hamartomatous polyps due to mutations in the BMPR1A, SMAD4 or ENG genes. Pigmentation is not present.

Option D: Cowden disease is characterised by polyps of stomach or colon with mucocutaneous lesions, thyroid adenomas and goitre, fibroadenomas and fibrocystic disease of the breast, Uterine leiomyomas, macrocephaly.

Pearl PF0932: Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome

* Autosomal-dominant disease

* Germline defects in the tumor suppressor serine-threonine kinase 11 (STK11) gene on chromosome 19.

Features:

* Hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, lips, and digits

* Hamartomatous polyps of the intestinal tract

* Increased (2% to 10%) risk for cancer of the intestinal tract, with cancers reported throughout the intestinal tract, from the stomach to the rectum.

* Increased risk for extraintestinal malignant neoplasms, including cancer of the breast, ovary, cervix, fallopian tubes, thyroid, lung, gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas, and testicles.

Screening: Baseline colonoscopy and upper endoscopy at age 20 years, followed by annual flexible sigmoidoscopy thereafter.

Pearl PF0293: Features of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis

Gastrointestinal manifestations:

* Colon and rectum: Multiple adenomatous polyp usually >100

* Gastric and duodenal polyps are present in 50% cases.

* Gastric polyp: fundal gland polyp, gastric adenoma.

* Duodenal polyp usually in the ampullary region: Adenomatous and premalignant

Extraintestinal manifestations

* Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) seen in 75% of cases; it is detected by indirect ophthalmoscopy.

* Epidermoid cysts

* Desmoid tumors in the abdomen

* Osteoma: In the skull, mandible, and tibia

* Brain tumors

* Tumors of the thyroid, adrenal, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, and bile duct

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-month-old male infant presents with a scrotal swelling that has been present since birth and is exacerbated by crying. The swelling has suddenly become painful, red, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Strangulated inguinal hernia

The clinical scenario of a 2-month-old male infant with a reducible scrotal swelling that is exacerbated by crying present since birth (congenital) and has become suddenly painful, red, and irreducible is most suggestive of a strangulated inguinal hernia. Infants are at high risk for incarceration of an inguinal hernia because of the narrow inguinal ring.

An inguinal hernia represents a protrusion of abdominal contents through a patent processus vaginalis into the inguinal canal and sometimes into the scrotum. It is a common indication for surgical repair in children. When a hernia becomes incarcerated and is not reducible, it can lead to strangulation of its contents.

Management of a strangulated inguinal hernia requires emergency surgical repair. It is usually performed by open inguinal repair, and a contralateral side evaluation may be considered. Laparoscopic approaches can also be used in certain cases. The repair of a patent processus vaginalis is emphasized to prevent recurrence.

Other options:

Option A: Epididymitis occurring before 6 months of age is usually due to infected urine ascending through the vas deferens. In contrast, epididymo-orchitis typically develops after puberty in sexually active boys and presents with acute testicular pain, fever, dysuria, increased frequency of urination, and urethral discharge. Pain may subside on elevation of the testis (Prehn’s sign).

Option B: Testicular torsion presents with acute scrotal pain associated with vomiting and absent cremasteric reflex.

Option D: A hydrocele refers to the accumulation of fluid between the parietal and visceral layers of the tunica vaginalis, usually limited to the scrotum. They are generally asymptomatic, non-tender, and may fluctuate in size, often decreasing overnight; they can also occur bilaterally. In infants, hydroceles may sometimes be tense and cause discomfort.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presented with pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen 4 days after undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. On ultrasonography, a significant collection was detected in the right upper quadrant. What is the next appropriate step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the collection

The clinical scenario of a patient presenting with pain in the right upper quadrant and a significant collection after laparoscopic cholecystectomy (4 days) points towards a bile duct injury with a possible leak. So, The next step of management is ultrasound-guided aspiration, followed by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) and stenting.

Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the most common cause of bile duct injury. Major biliary leakage is usually seen 2 to 10 days after cholecystectomy. Affected patients typically present with:

* Pyrexia

* Abdominal pain

* Bilious ascites

* Mild jaundice

* Leukocytosis

* Elevations in the serum levels of ALP and GGT.

Iatrogenic bile duct injury should be considered in any patient who develops new or worsening symptoms following laparoscopic cholecystectomy. In the absence of an external drainage site, bile leakage may present as a localized biloma, either sterile or infected, or as biliary ascites. Additional warning signs include persistent or increasing postprandial or shoulder pain, generalized malaise, and fever, all of which should prompt strong suspicion of a bile duct injury.

Management of bile duct injury:

* If detected on table with

* Duct injury less than 3 mm or those draining less than single segment of the liver: Ligation

* Lateral injury—Ducts larger than 4 mm or those that drain multiple hepatic segments: Repair using T-tube.

* Transection with minimal loss of duct length: Repair using T-tube is used; in case of extensive loss of duct length, billiary enteric anastomosis is performed.

* Cystic duct leaks can be treated by the percutaneous drainage of intra-abdominal collection and endoscopic biliary drainage.

* Radiological workup: Abdominal ultrasonography to determine the extent of the leak.

* For definitive leaks, ultrasound-guided aspiration is performed; alternatively, the collection is drained and a transhepatic biliary drain is placed. After 6–8 weeks, the definitive repair is ascertained.

* Ultrasonography confirmation and aspiration of the leak is followed by ERCP and stenting.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a history of penetrating chest trauma. On examination, breath sounds are absent on the right side of the chest, and there is severe tracheal deviation. What is the immediate step in management?
options: Wide-bore needle insertion in the 2nd intercostal space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Needle decompression at 5th intercostal space

The given clinical presentsation of tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds on right side on auscultation following a penetrating chest trauma is highly suggestive of tension pneumothorax. Immediate management is done with needle decompression or needle thoracostomy i.e. insertion of a wide-bore needle in the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line.

Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency when air leaks from the lungs into the pleural cavity and cannot escape. This leads to compression of the lung field with mediastinal shift and collapse of lung parenchyma. This can be diagnosed clinically with high index of suspicion and immediate decompression with wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space should be done.

The most common causes of a tension pneumothorax are:

* Penetrating chest trauma.

* Blunt chest trauma leading to a parenchymal lung injury and a persistent air leak.

* Iatrogenic lung injury, such as that caused by central venipuncture.

* Mechanical positive-pressure ventilation.

The clinical presentation is dramatic, with the patient appearing increasingly restless, dyspneic, and tachypneic. Physical examination reveals distended neck veins, hyper-resonance, and decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side.

Current medical practice for the treatment of tension pneumothorax involves immediate decompression. Historically, this was taught as the rapid insertion of a large-bore cannula into the second intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line on the affected side. This was then followed by the insertion of a chest tube through the fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line. However, the current recommendation is to perform the initial decompression within the "safe triangle."

Definitive management - tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th ICS in the triangle of safety.

Triangle of safety:

The boundaries are

* Anteriorly - lateral border of the pectoralis major

* Posteriorly- latissimus dorsi

* Inferiorly- a line perpendicular to the nipple going to the back

For pediatric patients, needle decompression is done at the midclavicular line in the 2nd intercostal space.

The images below show the triangle of safety and technique of chest drain insertion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old male had a tumor in his left lobe of liver, so left-sided hemi hepatectomy was planned. Which of the following lobes of liver will be resected in this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2,3,4a,4b

In the left hemi-hepatectomy (also called left hepatectomy) the segments marked as 2, 3 and 4(a, b) should be removed.

Couinaud classification is the commonly used classification of the liver. It divides the liver is divided into eight segments. Each segment has its own vascular supply, biliary drainage, and lymphatic drainage. Segment I corresponds to the caudate lobe of the liver and segment IV corresponds to the quadrate lobe of the liver.

A horizontal plane known as the portal plane divides the liver where the portal vein bifurcates and becomes horizontal. This divides each section of the liver into superior and inferior segments:

* Left lateral section: segment II above and segment III below the portal plane

* Left medial section: segment IVa above and segment IVb below the portal plane

* Right anterior (or medial) section: segment VIII above and segment V below the portal plane

* Right posterior (or lateral) section: segment VII above and segment VI below the portal.

The Couinaud's Liver Segments are as follows:

Pearl PF2018: Couinaud's liver segments

The Couinaud classification is currently the most widely used system to describe functional liver anatomy.

* Based on the distribution of hepatic portal venous branches in the parenchyma

* Each segment has its own dual vascular inflow, biliary drainage and lymphatic drainage

Segment I corresponds to the gross anatomical caudate lobe and is considered as posterior segment.

Other segments:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 7-year-old male child weighing 40 kg presents with thermal burns involving 22% of the total body surface area. What is the approximate amount of fluid that should be administered in the first 8 hours of resuscitation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1,320 mL

The amount of fluid that needs to be administered in the first 8 hours in this case is 1,320 mL

Hartmann’s solution or Ringer’s lactate is the crystalloid most commonly used for burn resuscitation, as it closely matches the osmolality of plasma. It is cheaper compared to colloid solutions and is effective in maintaining intravascular volume.

The modified Parkland formula is the standard method for fluid calculation, expressed as:

* TBSA% burn × weight (kg) × 3 = Volume in mL.

* substituiting the given values, 22 ✖️ 3 ✖️ 40 = 2,640 mL.

To complete 24-hour resuscitation, half (1,320 mL) of this is given in the first 8 hours and the other half over the remaining 16 hours. Urine output serves as a reliable endpoint to guide resuscitation and should be maintained at 0.5–1.0 mL/kg/hour in children. Urine output greater than 2 mL/kg/hour indicates the need to reduce the infusion rate.

Resuscitation fluids in burn patients must always be commenced from the time of burn injury, and if there is any delay, the deficit should be compensated. Intravenous fluid therapy is indicated for adults with burns exceeding 15% of total body surface area (TBSA) and for children with burns exceeding 10% TBSA.

In children, maintenance fluids are required in addition to resuscitation fluids, usually in the form of dextrose–saline. The regimen is weight-based:

* 100 mL/kg for 24 hours for the first 10 kg

* 50 mL/kg for the next 10 kg

* 20 mL/kg for each kilogram above 20 kg body weight

Pearl PF2125: Burns – Formulae for Fluid Calculation(Updated according to ATLS 10th edition 2018 guidelines)

Parkland’s formula gives the total fluid requirement for 24hours. Half of this volume is infused in the first 8 hours, and the remaining half is infused in the next 16 hours.

This formula is recommended for those who have sustained large deep partial-thickness or full-thickness burns that cover more than 20% of the TBSA in adults and more than 10% in children.

Formulas provide a starting target rate; Subsequently, the amount of fluid provided should be adjusted based on urine output.

Evan’s formula is used for normal saline.

* 6 portions of colloid are administered over 36 hours

questions.text: A child is rescued from a major train accident. During triage, the child is found to be stable and can walk, but he has a large laceration on the leg with severe inflammation around the wound. What is the most appropriate triage category for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Yellow

A child with a large laceration on the thigh which is inflamed but is stable, will be classified under the yellow category.

The yellow (medium priority) category includes patients who need resuscitation or surgery within 24 hours and have a good chance of survival with prompt treatment. Spinal injuries, along with moderate head injuries, compound fractures, and pelvic fractures, typically fall under this category due to the potential for delayed complications.

Triage includes rapid classification of the injured based on their injuries and the chances of survival with prompt medical intervention into four categories- red (high priority), yellow (medium priority), green (low priority) and black (least priority). It provides maximum benefit to the greatest number of injured in a disaster situation. It lessens the burden on medical facilities.

Pearl PF2180: Triage Colour Coding

Triage system consists of four colour codes:

Color code
Type of patients
Examples

May survive if timely medical intervention can be given

• Tension pneumothorax
• Airway obstruction
• Hemothorax
• Cardiac tamponade
• Acute circulatory arrest
• Major intra-abdominal bleed etc.

Yellow (Medium priority)

Possible resuscitation or surgery in the next 24 hours.

Likely to survive if prompt treatment is given.

• Compound fractures
• Degloving injuries
• Pelvic fracture
• Spinal injuries
• Moderate head injury

Green (Low priority)

Ambulatory patients or minor illnesses.

Likely to survive if treatment is slightly delayed.

• Simple fractures
• Minor lacerations etc.

Black (Least priority)

Dead or moribund patients.

• Severe brain injury
• Major damage / disruption to chest wall and abdominal structures

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A neonate presents with thickened, edematous intestines protruding from the abdomen without any external covering. What will be the next best line of management?
options: Cover the contents with a silo bag and wait
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cover the contents with a silo bag and wait

The clinical scenario of a neonate presenting with thickened and edematous protruding intestines without any covering points towards a diagnosis of gastroschisis. The next best line of management would be to cover the contents with a silo bag and wait.

A neonate with gastroschisis would need an immediate primary closure. However, in the given scenario, in neonates with thickened and edematous intestines, it may not be possible to return the bowel to the peritoneal cavity immediately after birth. In such cases, a plastic spring-loaded silo bag can be placed over the bowel, facilitating the gradual reduction of the bowel wall edema. This is followed by definitive surgical closure in about 1–2 weeks.

Gastroschisis is an abdominal wall defect located on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly), allowing protrusion of the intestines, stomach, bladder, and sometimes ovaries or undescended testes. The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion as they herniate through the abdominal wall directly into the amniotic cavity. The affected bowel loops can be damaged by exposure to amniotic fluid.

The intestines are matted and covered by a thick peel. Longer exposure in utero to amniotic fluid can cause trauma to the intestines. The intestines are also not fully rotated, and these factors increase the risk of intestinal volvulus, postnatal intestinal dysfunction with delayed mobility, and prolonged need for hospitalization and enteral feeding.

Risk factors include teenage pregnancy, recreational drug use, smoking, and genitourinary infection during pregnancy. After birth, careful management is required to prevent twisting or kinking of the blood supply to the intestines.

Management: Immediate surgical intervention is required after birth to prevent complications such as infection, dehydration, and damage to the exposed abdominal organs. In the immediate postoperative period, if abdominal wall closure is tight, aggressive fluid resuscitation may be required to ensure adequate tissue perfusion and prevent metabolic acidosis. Patients are supported with TPN until bowel function returns.

Surgical repair typically involves gently placing the protruding abdominal contents back(primary reduction) into the abdominal cavity and closing the abdominal wall defect surgically. Primary reduction is successful in 50% to 80%, with eviscerated contents placed into the abdominal cavity without excessive tension. Parenteral nutrition is often needed for several weeks to support intestinal recovery.

Note: Covering the bowel with saline-soaked gauze is a temporary measure to prevent fluid loss and infection, but it’s not the next best line of management. The definitive step is silo placement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of severe head injury following a road traffic accident (RTA) and a poor Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score. CT scan of the brain appears normal, but the patient dies within a few hours. Brain biopsy shows multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diffuse axonal injury

The clinical vignette of an initially poor GCS score and later death following a high-energy accident(RTA) with a normal CT scan and brain biopsy showing multiple haemorrhages is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury.

Diffuse axonal injury is a type of primary brain injury commonly associated with high-energy accidents. It is caused by damage to axons throughout the brain due to rotational acceleration followed by deceleration. There is disruption and shearing of axons leading to microhemorrhages. Most commonly, it occurs in automobile accidents. Patients are usually unconscious from the moment of impact and remain the same until death.

The immunohistochemistry marker with beta-amyloid precursor protein is considered to be the most reliable indicator of axon damage. Seen earliest at 2-3 hours.

The histological features :

Initially, there will be dilation of the axons, followed by the formation of club-shaped structures known as retraction balls. These retraction balls later decrease in number over 2-3 weeks, followed by microglial cell proliferation.

Later in the course, astrocytosis and demyelination will be observed.

Diffuse axonal injury is characterized by multiple focal lesions with a characteristic distribution:

* CT may be normal.

* MRI is the modality of choice for assessing suspected diffuse axonal injury even in patients with entirely normal CT of the brain. It detects the micro-bleeds within the brain.

Other options:

Option B: Cerebral contusion occurs due to traumatic brain injury, at the sites that come in direct contact with the skull. Imaging may show microhemorrhages and edema. Usually, no treatment is required.

Option C: Subdural hemorrhage is caused by rupture of cerebral bridging veins. In subdural hemorrhage, the CT shows crescentic opacity.

The image below shows a CT of a subdural hemorrhage.

Option D: Extradural hemorrhage is mostly due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Since the dura mater tends to adhere to the skull, the hemorrhage is seen in CT as a biconvex dense area. They are confined by cranial sutures.

The image below shows a CT of an extradural hemorrhage.

Pearl PF1100: Diffuse Axonal Injury

Features of diffuse axonal injury

Mechanism
Primarily a non-impact rotational acceleration-decceleration injury (this leads to deformation of the axons by stretching them)

Pathology

Changes in permeability of the axolemma

Axonal swelling

Intracellular calcium accumulation

Proteolysis

Collapse of the cytoskeleton

Histology

'Retraction balls or globes' - bulbous and clubbed axons. Seen earliest at 12-18 hours.

Immuno-histochemistry

Beta-amyloid precursor protein - considered to be the most reliable indicator of axon damage. Seen earliest at 2-3 hours.

Retraction balls:

* The force generated by violent shaking or rotational injury (as in a passenger ejected from the moving vehicle) can produce stretching of axons in cerebral white matter.

* Microscopic examination does not show any axonal injuries up to 12 hrs after injury

* After 12 hrs the axons first appear dilated then club shaped and finally appear as round balls known as retraction balls which indicates transected axons.

* The number of retraction balls begins to decrease after 2-3 weeks after injury and cluster of microglial cells appear followed by astrocytosis and demyelination.

Image shows scattered axonal retraction balls stained with Congo Red (arrows):

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on the lateral aspect of the nasal fold, below the eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Squamous Cell Carcinoma

The clinical description of a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on a sun-exposed site like the lateral nasal fold is characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma(SCC).

SCC is a malignant tumour of keratinising cells of the epidermis or its appendages. It arises from the stratum basalis of the epidermis and is the second most common skin cancer. The primary risk factor and driving force for the development of this common cancer is UV exposure. Variants of SCC include, Bowen's disease and Erythroplasia of Queyrat.

It initially presents as smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous lesions. All these lesions later ulcerate and have a characteristic everted edge and are surrounded by inflamed, indurated skin. When a SCC appears in a scar it is known as a Marjolin’s ulcer.

Surgical excision is the treatment of choice SCC. It provides both histological confirmation and complete clearance. The excision margins depend on tumor size:

* lesions <2 cm require a 4-mm margin,

* while those >2 cm need a 1-cm margin.

Other options:

Option B: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumor that originates from pluripotential epithelial cells of the basal epidermis and hair follicles, typically involving pilosebaceous skin.

Option C: Malignant Melanoma is a malignancy of melanocytes and may develop in the skin, mucous membranes, retina, or leptomeninges. There are four common macroscopic variants of malignant melanoma. It doesn’t present as an edged-out ulcer.

Option D: Keratoacanthoma presents with a reddish papule with a horny crust in the centre. It is a rapidly evolving tumour of the skin considered as a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a severe headache and neck stiffness. There is no history of fever. The CT brain taken is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subarachnoid haemorrhage

The given clinical scenario of an afebrile patient with a severe headache, neck stiffness with CT head showing hyperdense areas in the basal cisterns and sulci, is highly suggestive of Subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. It usually occurs due to bleeding from a ruptured aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. Most of the ruptured aneurysms are located at the circle of Willis.

Patients present with a sudden and severe headache referred to as thunderclap headache, which may be associated with vomiting, decreased consciousness, and seizures. Neck stiffness and photophobia may develop after a few hours.

Non-contrast CT scan is the imaging modality of choice if done within 12 hours. It shows an increased density of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces. A lumbar puncture should be done if there is a strong suspicion of SAH but negative CT findings. It is ideally done 12 hours later. This allows for red blood cell lysis to occur and bilirubin to be detected in the CSF.

Other options:

Option A: Bacterial meningitis is characterised by high fever, neck stiffness, and positive Brudzinski's sign.

Option B: Subdural haemorrhage is often due to the rupture of bridging veins that crosses the subdural space. In subdural hemorrhage, the CT shows crescentic opacity.

Option D: Extradural haemorrhage is mostly due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Since the dura matter tends to adhere to the skull, the hemorrhage is seen in CT as a biconvex dense area. They usually do not cross cranial sutures.

Pearl PF2181: Types of Intracranial Hemorrhage

1. Extradural hemorrhage/epidural hematoma (EDH)

* Source: Arterial - middle meningeal artery (m/c)

* Cause: Trauma - fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone

* Lens or lentiform shaped opacity

* Presence of a characteristic lucid interval

* Treatment: Surgical evacuation of large/rapidly evolving EDH

2. Acute subdural hemorrhage (SDH)

* Source: Venous - bridging veins

* Cause: Trauma

* Common in old age, alcoholics, patients on anticoagulants, shaken baby syndrome (a form of child abuse seen in infants and toddlers)

* Clinical features: Acute SDH may be associated with a lucid interval; chronic SDH is associated with drowsiness, headache

* CT findings: Crescent opacity

* Treatment: May resolve spontaneously or require surgical drainage

3. Acute on chronic SDH

* Source: Venous - bridging veins

* Cause: Usually, trivial trauma in old age or patients on anticoagulants

* Crescent clots

* Presence of a history of headache, confusion, and being prone to falls

4. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

* Source: Arterial

* Causes: Trauma (most common), berry aneurysm (2nd most common)

* M/c sites: Terminal ICA, MCA bifurcation, top of basilar artery

* Clinical features: Characteristic thunderclap headache

* CSF: Xanthochromia

* Hyperdensity in the subarachnoid space

* Treatment: Early repair by clipping/coiling of berry aneurysm. Nimodipine and IV fluids with monitoring to prevent vasospasm.

5. Intra-parenchymal hemorrhage

* Most common type of intracranial hemorrhage

* Cause: Hypertension (most common cause)

* Hyperdensity within the brain parenchyma

* Site: Putamen of the basal ganglia (most common)

* Treatment: Correction of any identified coagulopathy by infusing prothrombin complex concentrates, FFP, or fresh platelets as required; surgical evacuation for cerebellar hematoma >3 cm in size

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with breast skin dimpling as shown in the image. This occurs due to the infiltration of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cooper's ligament

Skin dimpling of the breast occurs due to traction on Cooper’s ligaments by a carcinoma. The fibrous bands shorten as they are infiltrated and pulled by tumor or associated fibrosis, producing the characteristic puckering or dimpling on the breast surface.

The condition is most often seen in carcinoma of the breast, where the tumor induces fibrosis and collagen deposition (desmoplastic reaction). As the tumor increases in size and invades adjacent breast parenchyma, it contracts the fibrous tissue (Cooper’s ligaments), leading to tethering of the overlying skin. This leads to the signs of dimpling or puckering during clinical examination.

Other options:

Option B: Lactiferous duct: Infiltration of these ducts results in nipple retraction.

Option C: Dermal lymphatics: Their involvement causes peau d’orange (orange peel appearance) due to edema.

Option D: Suspensory fascia: It is part of the superficial fascia.
