questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with dilation of veins as shown in the image. Which vein is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Great Saphenous Vein

The image shows prominent, tortuous, dilated veins(varicosities) on the medial aspect of the leg and thigh, which is the characteristic course of the Great Saphenous Vein (GSV). The dorsum of the foot, at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, medial aspect of the leg and thigh forms the surface marking of the great saphenous vein.

The surface marking for it is marked by joining the following points from foot to thigh:

* On the dorsum of the foot, at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch.

* On the anterior surface of the medial malleolus.

* On the medial border of the tibia at the junction of the upper 2/3rd and lower 1/3rd of the leg.

* At the adductor tubercle

* Just below the centre of the saphenous opening.

Varicose veins are subcutaneous dilated, tortuous veins 3mm or more in diameter. They commonly present with a sensation of dragging pain, heaviness, itching or burning over the affected area or the whole limb, and swelling of the feet. These symptoms increase throughout the day or with prolonged standing and are relieved by elevation or compression hosiery.

Risk factors:

* Female gender

* Increasing age

* Increasing body mass and height

* Pregnancy

* Family history

* Smoking

* Occupations involving prolonged standing

Management of varicose veins

Incompetence
Management

Great saphenous vein (GSV) and saphenofemoral (SFJ)

• Endothermal ablation (gold standard treatment for varicose veins). It includes:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

• Trendelenburg procedure (Flush Ligation of Saphenofemoral Junction (SFJ) after ligation of 6 tributaries) ± stripping (retrogradely up to the knee, to prevent saphenous nerve injury.)

Short saphenous vein (SSJ) and saphenopopliteal (SPJ)

• Flush ligation of SPJ (Stripping is not done to prevent sural nerve injury)
• Endothermal ablation:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

Perforator

• Dodd and Crockett surgery - Multiple subfascial ligations
• Subfascial endoscopic perforator surgery (SEPS) - smaller incision, so cosmetically better
• Endothermal ablation:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

New treatment modalities:

* Foam sclerotherapy - The Tessari method is a widely used method to prepare foam for sclerotherapy. Sclerosant: air ratio taken is 1:3 or 1:4.

* Endovenous glue therapy - endoluminal application of cyanoacrylate adhesive

* TriVex - Transilluminated powered phlebectomy

Other options:

Option B: The small saphenous vein courses from the lateral of the dorsal venous arch to the center of popliteal fossa.

Option C: The femoral vein runs upward in the thigh, accompanying the femoral artery within the femoral sheath and it is a deep vein.

Option D: Perforators: Connect superficial veins to deep veins. They may become incompetent, causing varicose veins, but the main visible dilated vein here is the GSV.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with weight gain, thinning of hair, and dry skin. The clinical features are suggestive of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which of the following antibodies is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. An elevated TSH and the presence of thyroid peroxidase antibodies usually confirm the diagnosis.

It is an autoimmune disease (associated with HLA DR-3 and HLA-B8) that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure. The most commonly associated antibody is anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody (Anti-TPO), which targets the enzyme thyroid peroxidase, essential for thyroid hormone synthesis.

Clinical features of Hashimoto's thyroiditis are as follows:

* More common in women (10 to 20 times)

* Diffusely enlarged, painless, lobulated gland

* Patients usually present with hypothyroidism (due to alteration in thyroid function by infiltration of lymphocytes and resultant fibrosis)

* Hashitoxicosis: initial transient phase of thyrotoxicosis

Laboratory investigations show,

* Elevated TSH

* Low T3 and T4

* Presence of thyroid autoantibodies-

* Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO)

* Antithyroglobulin (Anti-Tg)

* Thyrotropin Receptor Antibody (Anti-TSH-R)

* Anti sodium/iodide symporter (Anti-NIS)

The management of Hashimoto's thyroiditis is as follows:

* Thyroid hormone replacement therapy

The algorithm used for Thyroid hormone replacement therapy in Hashimoto's thyroiditis is as shown below,

Surgery may be required if there is a suspicion of malignancy or goiters causing compressive symptoms.

Note: All the other options (Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), TSH receptor antibodies (TSHR-Ab), Long-acting thyroid stimulator) are antibodies that are primarily associated with Graves’ disease, leading to hyperthyroidism

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a 40% burn injury on the arm underwent split-thickness skin grafting on post-burn day 3. On post-operative day 5, during physiotherapy, the patient develops stiffness and a limited range of motion in the arm. The graft appears healthy and well-adhered. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Forceful passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Continue physiotherapy without intervention

Supervised movements by physiotherapists, usually under direct vision of any affected joints, should begin after about 5 days in case of burn wounds. In this case, the patient is on post-operative day 5 with a healthy graft and stiffness during physiotherapy, which aligns with the recommendation to continue supervised physiotherapy at this stage.

Physiotherapy and splints are essential in maintaining the range of movement and reducing joint contracture after skin grafting. Elevation of the affected limb is important. After grafting, the hand should be splinted in the functional position, but the graft itself must be placed in the position of maximal stretch.

Grafts are tissues that are transferred without their blood supply and therefore need to be revascularised through the recipient wound bed. For the graft to take successfully, the wound bed must be healthy and well-vascularized to support angiogenesis into the graft tissue. There are two types of skin grafts:

* Split thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis.

* Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft): include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles.

Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft:

* Large grafts can be harvested.

* In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such as burns.

* Uptake is good. Meshing can be done i.e. small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this and this improves graft take up.

* Meshing also allows the graft to expand.

Advantages of full-thickness skin graft over split skin graft:

* It has a lesser degree of post graft contraction

* Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements.

The most preferable donor site is buttock in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children. The most commonly used donor site is the thigh.

* The graft is taken from the donor site with a handheld Humby knife or electric dermatome.

* Grafts are perforated to allow exudates to escape and improve ‘take’. It can further be meshed to allow expansion.

* Grafts will take up only on the beds which are vascularized, hence preparation of wound bed is an essential step.

* Skin grafts are completely dependent on nutrition on the tissue over which they are placed and can heal well over muscle, perichondrium, and periosteum. They do not take well over bone or cartilage or on tissue that has been irradiated or infected or is hypovascular.

* A clean healthy wound bed with a meshed graft tied in place to stop movement will encourage take.

* The presence of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci is a contraindication in grafting as it can destroy split grafts completely and also convert donors to full-thickness defects.

* The donor area is dressed appropriately and the dressing is opened after 10 days and not earlier.

The given image shows Humby's knife. The average thickness of the graft obtained from a Humbys knife is 0.3 mm.

Other options:

Option A: Stricture release(surgical intervention) is indicated when a well-formed contracture or significant scar tissue is restricting joint motion. In this patient’s scenario, the graft appears healthy and well-adhered, and stiffness is expected during early physiotherapy.

Option C: Forceful passive stretching or forceful manipulation is not recommended soon after grafting, as it can damage the delicate graft, impair graft take, and disrupt the healing process. Supervised physiotherapy is recommended.

Option D: Tendon repair not indicated, as there are no signs of tendon rupture in this case.

Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft

The take of skin graft occurs in three phases:

* Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries.

* Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses

* Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft

Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later.

Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with abdominal injury following a road traffic accident (RTA) has lost approximately 200 mL of blood. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, but the heart rate is elevated. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. eFAST

In a trauma patient with abdominal injury, tachycardia along with loss of 200mL blood, early shock should be suspected. Therefore, the immediate step is to evaluate for ongoing intra-abdominal bleeding by eFAST (extended-focused assessment with sonography for trauma)

A quick diagnostic modality called eFAST is used to evaluate patients who may have thoracoabdominal injuries. It is used to determine whether free fluid is present in the abdominal cavity, thoracic cavity, and pericardium. It takes two to four minutes.  More than 100 mL of free fluid can be detected by eFAST.

The standard order of evaluation is:

* Pericardial cavity - subxiphoid

* Flank of right side - perihepatic view or Morison's pouch

* Flank of left side - perisplenic view

* Pelvic cavity - retrovesical views

* Right anterior thoracic

* Left anterior thoracic

Disadvantages:

* It is not reliable in detecting less than 100 mL of free blood.

* Hollow viscus injuries cannot be accurately identified.

* Unreliable in penetrating trauma.

* Subjective findings.

* Unreliable for retroperitoneal injuries

If there is a doubt, eFAST may be repeated or supplemented with other investigations.

Other options:

Option A: Wait and watch cannot be done, as ongoing internal bleeding may be missed and may lead to shock.

Option B: Chest X-ray, not the first-line when abdominal trauma with shock is suspected. Useful for chest injuries, pneumothorax.

Option D: USG abdomen is time-consuming, as it is not done as a bedside assessment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism is scheduled for a total thyroidectomy. Pre-anesthetic check-up (PAC) was not done adequately. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur during surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arrhythmia

A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism undergoing surgery(thyroidectomy) is at significant risk for a thyroid storm (also known as a thyrotoxic crisis), which usually presents with hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, hyperpyrexia and other symptoms.

Thyroid storm is a rare but severe life-threatening complication of hyperthyroidism induced by the release of excessive thyroid hormones.

Causes:

* Abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications

* Infection

* When a thyrotoxic patient has been inadequately prepared for thyroidectomy.

* Thyroid or non-thyroid surgery

* Trauma in patients with untreated thyrotoxicosis

* Amiodarone administration

* Exposure to iodinated contrast agents

* Following RAI (radioactive iodine) therapy

Features:

* They present 12–24 hours after surgery with hyperpyrexia and severe dehydration

* Cardiovascular: Circulatory collapse, hypotension, palpitations, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac failure

* GI symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice.

* Neurological symptoms: restlessness, irritability, delirium, tremor, convulsions, and coma

Treatment:

* Supportive measures – rehydration by proper fluid therapy, tepid sponging, cooling blankets

* Thionamides like Propylthiouracil (PTU), methimazole or carbimazole are used as they inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis. Propylthiouracil blocks the peripheral conversion of thyroxine (T4) into the more active triiodothyronine (T3) and serves as the preferred drug in thyroid storm. However, the risk for severe liver injury and acute liver failure associated with PTU therapy makes either carbimazole or methimazole the first choice thionamides in patients with deranged liver function tests.

* Lugol’s iodide is given one hour after intake of thionamides. They inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by Wolff- Chaikoff effect. Large doses of iodide inhibit the organic binding of the iodide and hence decrease thyroid hormone synthesis.

* Propranolol is used to reduce tachycardia and other adrenergic manifestations. It also reduces the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.

* Glucocorticoids – reduce the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and controls the shock.

* Digoxin, cardiac monitoring is crucial.

Pearl PF1414: Thyroid storm / Thyrotoxic crisis:

It is an emergency caused by an acute exacerbation of hyperthyroidism.

Precipitating factors:

* Abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications

* Infection

* When a thyrotoxic patient has been inadequately prepared for thyroidectomy.

* Thyroid or non-thyroid surgery

* Trauma in patients with untreated thyrotoxicosis

* Amiodarone administration or exposure to iodinated contrast agents

* Following RAI therapy.

Clinical features:

* Fever

* Central nervous system agitation or depression

* Cardiovascular and GI dysfunction, including hepatic failure

Treatment of thyroid storm:

Treatment modality
Effect

IV Fluids, ice packs
Rehydration and external cooling

Propranolol

Block adrenergic effects

Reduces peripheral T4 to T3 conversion

Propylthiouracil
(DOC)

Reduces peripheral T4 to T3 conversion

Corticosteroids

Inhibits the release of thyroid hormone from the gland

Reduces peripheral T4 to T3 conversion

Lugol’s iodine/ sodium ipodate
Inhibits the release of thyroid hormone from the gland

Digoxin
Controls the associated atrial fibrillation

Diuretics and administration of oxygen

To manage the cardiac failure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A person presented with a history of road traffic accident (RTA) and a crush wound in the thigh. He came to the doctor the next day. On examination, the wound appeared black with crepitus. What is the most likely organism involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clostridium perfringens

The given clinical scenario of a present with blackish colored wound with crepitus following a extensive wound injury (crush injury) is highly suggestive of gas gangrene/ clostridial myonecrosis, which is caused by Clostridium perfringens.

Military wounds and trauma which cause extensive tissue damage provide an ideal environment for gas gangrene. C.perfringens is gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-bearing bacilli present in nature, especially in soil and faeces. Patients who are immunocompromised, diabetic, or have malignant disease are also at greater risk. The usual incubation period is <24 hours of injury.

Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues). The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate, in which Gram staining will reveal bacteria. Edema and spreading gangrene occur due to the release of collagenase, hyaluronidase, other proteases, and alpha-toxin. Early systemic complications like circulatory collapse and organ failure can occur without adequate treatment.

Management includes high doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues. Amputations should be performed under antibiotic prophylaxis.

Other options:

Option A: C. tetani is an anaerobic, terminal spore-bearing, Gram-positive bacterium. It causes tetanus following implantation into tissues or a wound, and it usually presents with spasms.

Option B: C. difficile, a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus, causes Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile infection (CDI) after ingestion of spores of the organism. The more severe form of the condition is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC). It is most commonly associated with prolonged antimicrobial use which interferes with the commensal colonic microflora. The most commonly implicated antibiotics are cephalosporins, ampicillin, and clindamycin.

Option C: C. botulinum causes botulism, a paralytic disease that usually presents as a form of food poisoning.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man, a follow-up patient of GERD with recurrent reflux symptoms, is found to have a nodule in the second part of the duodenum on endoscopy. Which hormone is most likely to be raised?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gastrin

The given clinical scenario of a nodule in the second part of the duodenum in a patient with recurrent reflux (GERD) and symptoms suggestive of persistent acid-related disease is suggestive of a gastrinoma, a neuroendocrine tumor that secretes gastrin. Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer, is called Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES)/Gastrinoma is a neuroendocrinal tumour characterized by hypersecretion of gastrin resulting in gastrointestinal tract ulcers. It occurs more commonly in a sporadic pattern but can be associated with MEN-1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia-1) syndromes in the familial pattern. Gastrinoma is most commonly located in the gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's triangle) bounded by the lines connecting the:

* Cystic duct

* Junction between the second and third parts of the duodenum

* Junction between the neck and body of the pancreas

The most common presentations of gastrinoma are epigastric pain, diarrhoea, and peptic ulcers. The ulcers occur at typical locations (proximal duodenum) and atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). Duodenal ulcers are the most common.

Treatment of ZES :

High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitor followed by surgery.

Surgeries that can be done are:

* Distal Pancreatectomy– if lesion in body or tail of the pancreas

* Enucleation– if the lesion is in the head of the pancreas

* Full-thickness excision– if the lesion is in duodenum

* MEN associated– surgery done only if size>2.5cm

Other options:

Option A: VIPoma is characterized by watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). It is caused by the release of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) from the tumor.

Option C: Glucagonomas, α-cell tumors are associated with increased serum levels of glucagon. The patient presents with mild diabetes mellitus, a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema), and anemia. They occur most frequently in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women and are characterized by extremely high plasma glucagon levels.

Option D: Insulinomas, β-cell tumors are the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasms. These are usually benign and often cause symptomatic hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemic symptoms appear when blood glucose levels fall below 50 mg/dL. The symptoms usually develop after fasting or exertion and improve after glucose intake.

Pearl PF2047: Clinical features of gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome)

Most common symptom: Abdominal pain.

Gastrin hypersecretion stimulates gastric acid secretion, leading to peptic ulcers that occur at atypical sites like the duodenum and jejunum and are refractory and multiple.

Diarrhea is due to

* Acid-induced injury to the small intestine mucosa

* Inability of the intestinal tract to absorb large volumes of fluids secreted by the stomach

* Inactivation of pancreatic lipase by low pH

* Precipitation of bile salts.

The unique characteristic of acid-induced diarrhea is that it is controlled by nasogastric aspiration of gastric secretions.

Pearl PF1838: Diagnostic tests in Zollinger Ellison Syndrome

To confirm the diagnosis of ZES,

* Gastric pH <2.5 and

* Serum gastrin >1000pg/ml (normal <100pg/ml)

Provocative tests can be done like the secretin stimulation test when the diagnosis is in doubt. An increase in serum gastrin >200pg/ml following an IV bolus of secretin (2U/kg) is diagnostic.

Other tests:

* BAO >15mEq/h (or >5mEq/h if they have had a procedure for peptic ulcer)

* BAO: MAO ratio is increased (>0.6)

(BAO=Basal acid output; MAO=Maximal acid output)

For localization

* Initial investigation - CT or MRI

* Best investigation - Endoscopic ultrasound

* If the tumor is not localized - Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the pathology in the child shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Umbilical hernia

The hernia appears which as a soft bulge at the umbilicus and covered by normal skin points towards umbilical hernia.

An umbilical defect is present at birth and normally closes as the umbilical cord stump heals within a week. If this process is delayed, herniation may develop during the neonatal period. Umbilical hernia occurs in up to 10% of infants and is more common in premature babies.

It usually appears within a few weeks after birth, often symptomless, but increases in size during crying and assumes a classic conical shape. Both sexes are equally affected, though the incidence is significantly higher in black infants compared to white. Obstruction and strangulation are extremely rare below the age of 3 years.

Treatment of Umbilical Hernia in Children

* Conservative management is preferred for children under 2 years of age when the hernia is symptomless, as about 95% resolve spontaneously. Parental reassurance is essential during this period.

* If the hernia persists beyond 2 years or is large and symptomatic, surgical repair is indicated.

* Surgery involves making a small curved incision below the umbilicus, defining and opening the neck of the sac, reducing the contents, excising the redundant sac, and closing the defect in the linea alba.

Other options:

Option A: In paraumbilical hernia, the hernia is beside the umbilicus & push it to one side taking a crescent shape and the defect in the median raphe is immediately adjacent to the true umbilicus.

Option B: Spigelian hernia is a type of interparietal hernia that occurs at the level of the arcuate line through the Spigelian point.

Option C: A femoral hernia passes through the femoral triangle. Femoral hernia is below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the suturing technique shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Simple interrupted sutures

Simple interrupted sutures involve inserting the needle at right angles to the incision so that it passes through both sides of the wound and exits again at right angles. The needle should be rotated through the tissue to prevent enlargement of the needle hole.

The distance from the needle point to the wound edge should approximately equal the tissue depth, and subsequent sutures should be spaced at twice this distance. Each suture must extend into the wound depth and be placed at right angles to its axis. The suture is then tied using a surgeon's knot in case of nonabsorbable suture or a square knot for absorbable sutures.

Option A and C: Mattress sutures can either be vertical or horizontal. The initial suture is inserted as in an interrupted suture. The needle can then be moved either horizontally or vertically, traversing both edges of the wound once again. Such sutures are very useful in producing an accurate approximation of irregular wound edges. They can produce either eversion or inversion of a wound edge.

The images below show horizontal and vertical mattress sutures respectively:

Option D:  In subcuticular suturing, the suture is anchored at one end of the wound. Small bites of subcuticular tissue are taken on alternate sides of the wound and then pulled together gently at the apex. This approximates the wound edges together. The final bite leaves a trailing loop of the suture, and a knot can be tied. The knots can be tied loosely or secured by means of a collar and bead when non-absorbable sutures are used. If the suture is absorbable, a buried knot is used.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the ulcer shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Venous ulcer

The image of a healing ulcer with a sloping edge in the Gaiter's area indicates a venous ulcer.

Venous ulcers due to chronic venous insufficiency are most commonly seen in the lower ⅓ of the leg and foot. They usually lie just proximal to the medial or lateral malleolus.

Ambulatory venous hypertension is the most acceptable theory in the pathophysiology. They have a sloping edge and the floor contains granulation tissue covered by slough and exudate. Marjolin’s ulcer is a type of squamous cell carcinoma seen in chronic long-standing venous ulcers. These are accompanied by lipodermatosclerosis and hemosiderosis.

Management of venous ulcers:

1) Bisgaard's regimen (4Es)

* Education of the patient

* Elevation of the affected limb to reduce the edema

* Elastic compression stockings - The ideal interface pressure in venous ulceration is 35-40 mmHg.

* Evaluation

2) 4-layer bandaging system comprising of:

* Orthopaedic wool

* Cotton crepe

* Elastic bandage - first compressive layer

* Cohesive bandage - second compressive layer

3) Antibiotics are given only if the wound is infected.
4) Regular dressing.
5) Medical management by oral pentoxifylline is considered which helps in reducing the viscosity and improving circulation.
6) Surgical management by ulcer excision with pinch mesh grafting has a good outcome and helps in preventing recurrence.

Note: Vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) is a negative pressure dressing. An occlusive dressing is placed over the sore and it is connected to VAC that generates -125mmHg of pressure. It is used in chronic non-healing ulcers, venous ulcers, diabetic ulcers, burn wounds, and bed sores.

Type of Ulcer
Ischaemic/Arterial
Venous
Neuropathic

Tuberculous

Underlying condition
Peripheral vascular disease mainly atherosclerosis, thromboangitis obliterans, and Raynaud's phenomenon
Varicose veins, previous deep vein thrombosis
Diabetes, peripheral neuropathy
Tuberculosis lymph nodes, cold abscess from bone and joint tuberculosis

Location
Toes, feet, legs, or even upper limb digits
Lower limb, commonly on the medial side of the ankle, never above the middle third of the leg
The plantar surface of the foot and toes
Neck, axilla, and groin

Characteristics
Deep, penetrates the deep fascia exposing the tendons, muscles, and underlying bone. The ulcer is painful, tender, and hyperaesthetic.
Vertically oval, and painless. The floor may have pale to no granulation tissue, induration, and tenderness at the base.
Punched-out with regular calloused margins.
Edges are thin, reddish blue, and undermined. Pale granulation tissue, scanty discharge on the floor, and slight induration at the base

Other features
Features of ischemia in adjacent areas, like pallor, dry skin, brittle nails, loss of hair
Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged usually the vertical group. The ulcer is recurrent.
Dry, cracked, insensate
Regional lymph nodes are enlarged, non-tender, and matted

Other options:

Option A: The following image depicts an arterial ulcer:

Option C: A callous ulcer is a type of foot ulcer that develops from a pre-ulcerative callus. It's a chronic, non-healing wound that can last for months or years. Callous ulcers are characterized by a hard base, rigid walls, pale tissue inside the ulcer, and a variety of shapes and sizes.

Option D: The following image is that of a neuropathic ulcer:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the correct sequence of Damage control surgery? * Patient selection * Primary exploration * ICU care * Secondary exploration * Abdominal closure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,2,3,4,5

The correct answer is option C: 1,2,3,4,5

The correct sequence  of five stages of damage control surgery are:

* Patient selection

* Control of haemorrhage and control of contamination(primary exploration)

* Resuscitation continued in the intensive care unit

* Deﬁnitive surgery(secondary exploration)

* Abdominal closure

Damage control surgery is minimal intervention done to stabilize the patient and do the definite surgery later. It centers on coordinating staged operative interventions with periods of aggressive resuscitation to salvage trauma patients sustaining major injuries. The aim of the DCS is to restore physiology over anatomy. It is applied to trauma patients with combined vascular and visceral injuries.

The phases are:

*

Phase 1 involves recognition of the severity of the injury. Here,rapid-sequence induction of anesthesia and intubation is done. This is followed by early rewarming and prompt movement of the patient to the operating theatre.

*

Phase 2 involves performing immediate laparotomy. Here, the focus is to control bleeding and contamination. Abdominal packing and temporary wound closure are done.

*

Phase 3 involves movement to the intensive care unit (ICU). The aim is to normalize the biochemical and physiological parameters.

*

Phase 4 involves re-exploration in the operating theatre. Here, definitive repair of all injuries is done. Multiple procedures on multiple occasions may be required.

Pearl PF2177: Damage Control Surgery

Five stages of damage control surgery:

1. Patient selection
2. Control of hemorrhage and control of contamination
3. Resuscitation continued in the intensive care unit
4. Deﬁnitive surgery
5. Abdominal closure

Phases of Damage Control Surgery:

Phase 0: Identification of patient for damage control surgery in emergency room
Phase 1: Emergency laparotomy to stop bleeding and prevent contamination
Phase 2: ICU care for resuscitation
Phase 3: Re-laparotomy for definitive repair
Indications for damage control surgery:
Anatomical

* Inability to achieve haemostasis

* Complex abdominal injury, e.g. liver and pancreas

* Combined vascular, solid and hollow organ injury, e.g. aortic or caval injury

* Inaccessible major venous injury, e.g. retrohepatic vena cava

* Demand for non-operative control of other injuries, e.g. fractured pelvis

* Anticipated need for a time-consuming procedure

Physiological (decline of physiological reserve)

* Temperature <34ºC

* pH <7.2

* Serum lactate >5 mmol/L (normal is <2.5 mmol/L)

* Prothrombin time (PT) >16 s

* Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) >60 s

* Blood transfusion approaching 15 units

* Blood pressure <70 mmHg

Environmental

* Operating time >60 min

* Inability to approximate the abdominal incision

* Desire to reassess the intra-abdominal contents (directed relook)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for an 8 cm chylolymphatic mesenteric cyst?
options: Resection of cyst along with adjacent bowel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enucleation

The most appropriate step in the management of this patient would be complete enucleation. Chylolymphatic cysts have their own independent blood supply, allowing for complete excision by enucleation.

Mesenteric cyst:

* Cysts that occur in the mesentery of the small intestine or the colon and can be of different types:

* Chylolymphatic

* Enterogenous

* Urogenital remnant

* Dermoid

Mesenteric cysts occur most commonly in middle-aged adults and are twice as common in women. Although they are rare, the chylolymphatic type is the most common variant. In chylolymphatic cyst there is congenitally misplaced lymphatic tissue which has no efferent communication with the lymphatic system. The thin wall of the cyst, is composed of connective tissue, lined by flat endothelium, and is filled with clear lymph or chyle.

* Most commonly presents as painless abdominal swelling with the following characteristic physical signs(Tillaux’s triad):

* Fluctuant swelling near the umbilicus

* Swelling moves freely in a plane at right angles to the attachment of the mesentery (Tillaux’s sign)

* Presence of zone of resonance around the cyst

Other presentations include

* Recurrent attacks of abdominal pain due to temporary impaction of a food bolus in a segment of the bowel narrowed by the cyst.

* Vomiting

* Acute abdominal complications, such as:

* Torsion of the cyst

* Rupture of the cyst

* Haemorrhage into the cyst

* Infection

* Investigations - USG and CT scan demonstrate the type of cyst.

* Treatment of choice chylolymphatic mesenteric cyst is enucleation with or without resection of the bowel.

Other options:

Options A and D: Not recommended as there is risk for recurrence(aspiration) and acute abdominal complications(conservative management)

Option C: Resection of cyst along with adjacent bowel is usually done for enterogenous cysts. They arise either from a diverticulum of the mesenteric border of the intestine or from duplication of the intestine. Since they have a common blood supply with the intestine, the removal of enterogenous cysts requires resection of the related portion of the intestine.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for esophageal varices ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endoscopic variceal ligation

The first-line treatment for active variceal bleeding is endoscopic therapy, with endoscopic variceal ligation (banding) preferred.

Esophageal variceal bleeding is a complication of portal hypertension, most commonly due to cirrhosis. . After initial resuscitation and stabilization, endoscopic intervention is the mainstay of treatment for bleeding esophageal varices. The two most commonly used techniques are endoscopic band ligation (EVL), where rubber bands are applied to the base of the varix, and endoscopic sclerotherapy, which involves injecting a sclerosant into or around the varix.

Endoscopy is usually performed in a head-down position with good suction and visualization using a double-channel endoscope and power washers. Once the bleeding site is identified, treatment is focused only on the active varices. Both EVL and sclerotherapy effectively control bleeding, but EVL is preferred as it significantly reduces the risk of rebleeding, and a single session is often sufficient.

Initial management of variceal bleeding involves the following:

* Admission to the intensive care unit

* Placement of two large-bore peripheral cannulae

* Blood transfusion

* Correction of coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma, vitamin K, and tranexamic acid

* Terlipressin, a splanchnic vasoconstrictor

* Prophylactic antibiotic

* Endotracheal intubation for airway protection if bleeding is uncontrolled

* Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy

TIPSS or Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Stent Shunt placement involves the placement of a shunt to redirect blood flow and reduce portal pressure. It is very effective but requires analgesia, sedation, and fluoroscopic guidance. It is done if medical and endoscopic measures fail to control bleeding.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following veins is involved in esophageal varices?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left gastric vein

Varices of the lower end of the esophagus receive their portal venous supply mainly from the left gastric vein, which communicates with the veins of the lower esophagus. Therefore, the vein involved in esophageal varices is the left gastric vein.

It is a tributary of the portal vein. In portal hypertension,when the pressure in the portal vein increases, the submucosal veins of the proximal stomach and distal esophagus which receive portal flow from the short gastric veins and the left gastric vein can become dilated, forming varices with a high risk of hemorrhage.

Esophageal variceal bleeding is a complication of portal hypertension, most commonly due to cirrhosis. Endoscopic intervention is the mainstay of treatment for bleeding esophageal varices. The two most commonly used techniques are endoscopic band ligation (EVL), where rubber bands are applied to the base of the varix, and endoscopic sclerotherapy, which involves injecting a sclerosant into or around the varix.

Endoscopy is usually performed in a head-down position with good suction and visualization using a double-channel endoscope and power washers. Once the bleeding site is identified, treatment is focused only on the active varices. Both EVL and sclerotherapy effectively control bleeding, but EVL is preferred as it significantly reduces the risk of rebleeding, and a single session is often sufficient.

The protocol for the management of variceal bleeding involves the following:

TIPSS or Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Stent Shunt placement involves the placement of a shunt to redirect blood flow and reduce portal pressure. It is very effective but requires analgesia, sedation, and fluoroscopic guidance. It is done if medical and endoscopic measures fail to control bleeding.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: 30 year old female presented with low-grade fever of 1-week duration associated with loss of appetite and weight loss. Barium meal follow through image of the patient is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ileocaecal TB

This case demonstrates the chronic stage of ileocaecal tuberculosis. Ileocaecal junction is the commonest site of tuberculosis in the gastrointestinal tract. Other sites involved in the abdomen are liver, spleen, and peritoneum.

Barium meal follow through study findings:

* Narrowed terminal ileum (string sign) and ileocaecal junction

* Dilatation of proximal ileum

* Caecum appears shrunken and 'pulled-up' away from RIF

* Conical caecum

* Ileocaecal angle becomes obtuse

* Goose neck ileus – ileum hanging from pulled up caecum

* Fleischner sign

* Yellow arrow indicates the shrunken caecum

* Red arrow indicates stricturous narrowing of terminal ileum and ileocaecal junction

* Blue arrow indicates proximal ileal dilatation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with acute onset of pain in his scrotum. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a swollen erythematous scrotum and the right testis has gone up. Cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right testicular torsion

The given clinical vignette along with negative cremasteric reflex and positive Deming's sign (right testes gone up) is suggestive of testicular torsion.

Etiology and risk factors-

* High investment of the tunica vaginalis(like a clapper in a bell). Most common cause.

* Inversion of the testis.

* Separation of the epididymis from the body of the testis.

Clinical features of testicular torsion are - scrotal pain and swelling, erythema, negative cremasteric reflex, nausea, and vomiting, testis seems high in the scrotum and twisted cord can sometimes be palpated.

* Prehn’s Sign is used to differentiate the torsion of testis from acute epididymo orchitis. In the case of acute epididymo orchitis, the pain gets relieved on the elevation of the testis but not in torsion of testes.

* Deming’s sign: Spasm of the cremaster muscle and the cord twisting cause the affected testis to be positioned higher in torsion testes.

Doppler ultrasound scanning can confirm the absence of the blood supply to the affected testis, but the false-positives are high.

Urgent scrotal exploration in case of doubtful diagnosis.  A transverse scrotal incision is taken. If the testis is viable, twisting is prevented by fixation with three non-absorbable sutures between the tunica albuginea of the testis and the scrotal raphe.

Differential diagnosis -

* Epididymo-orchitis - Here dysuria associated with the accompanying urinary infection is commonly present. In epididymo-orchitis elevation of the testis reduces the pain while it makes it worse in torsion.

* Torsion of a testicular appendage - Here the most common structure to twist is the appendix of the testis, which can be visible as a small dark spot. In most cases, it is indistinguishable from torsion testis. Hence in cases of doubt surgical exploration is done.

questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient was brought to the ER after RTA, his RR is 25/min, BP is 80/45mmHg. On examination, hyper-resonance is heard over the left side of the chest. The chest X-ray performed is given below. What would be the appropriate management in this case?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS
Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS

The given clinical scenario and the given chest radiograph are suggestive of pneumothorax. It is managed by inserting wide-bore needle in 5th ICS followed by placing an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS.

Tension pneumothorax and simple pneumothorax have similar signs, symptoms, and examination findings, but hypotension qualifies the pneumothorax as a tension pneumothorax.

Immediate management includes inserting a wide-bore needle in the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

Definitive management includes insertion of the intercostal tube in the triangle of safety. If a sucking wound is present, then it is covered with gauze pieces and taped on 3 sides.

Remember: (Acc to ATLS 10th edition)

* In adults, needle thoracotomy location changed to 5th ICS mid axillary line from 2nd ICS midclavicular line.

* In the pediatric age group, the thoracotomy location remains at the 2nd ICS midclavicular line.

questions.text: A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and fever. On examination of the affected side, there is localized erythema, warmth, point tenderness,fluctuation test is positive. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and contralateral breast is normal.What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Breast abscess

The given case scenario points towards a diagnosis of breast abscess. The latest guidelines for the management of breast abscess specify that multiple aspirations under antibiotic cover should be attempted before an incision and drainage is done. This often allows resolution without the need for an incision scar and also allows the patient to continue breastfeeding.

Mastitis occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. This occurs secondary to blockage of lactiferous duct or due to incomplete emptying of breast milk or due to retracted nipple. Overgrowth of these bacteria results in the development of breast abscess.

It is commoner in new mothers at the beginning of lactation who are inexperienced with breastfeeding or during weaning when nipple trauma occurs due to the infant's growing teeth.

Signs and symptoms of this condition involve:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

The initial treatment should involve providing pain relief with analgesics. The abscess should then be localized preferably under USG guidance and percutaneous aspiration carried out. The pus should be sent for microbiological examination to find the organism and antibiotic sensitivity. Repeated aspirations may be carried out under antibiotics cover if needed.

In some conditions mentioned below, the breast abscess may be unresponsive to repeated aspirations and antibiotic cover. In such cases, incision and drainage is performed. The conditions include:

* Presence of thick pus

* Bacteria resistant to antibiotics

* If just superficial part has been aspirated in the presence of a multiloculated abscess

* A non-healing breast abscess due to tuberculosis of breast or Inflammatory carcinoma of the breast, or an immunocompromised host.

questions.text: A 34-year-old female presented with a painless mass in the right inguinal region. On examination, there is a cough impulse on the index finger and the swelling reduced completely on pressing it through the deep inguinal ring with a gurgling sound. What is the likely diagnosis in this lady?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Indirect inguinal hernia

The presentation of a painless swelling with a cough impulse is suggestive of a hernia. A hernia that reduces when pressing on the deep inguinal ring suggests a case of indirect inguinal hernia while a direct inguinal hernia emerges through the Hesselbach's triangle.

A femoral hernia passes through the femoral triangle whereas an umbilical hernia protrudes through the umbilicus.

The boundaries of Hesselbach’s triangle are:

* Lateral - inferior epigastric artery

* Medial - lateral border of rectus abdominis

* Inferior - inguinal ligament

Indirect inguinal hernias are by far the most common type of hernia in women. It is the most common hernia regardless of gender.

questions.text: A 36-year-old man presents with dull aching epigastric pain. He gives a history of acute abdominal pain following a binge of alcohol 5 weeks back which was managed conservatively. On examination, he appears icteric and a firm mass was palpable in the epigastrium. His CT scan is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pancreatic pseudocyst

The given clinical scenario with a history of acute pancreatitis, epigastric mass, and the CT image showing a cyst is suggestive of pancreatic pseudocyst. The capsule of the cyst is composed of collagen and granulation tissue, and it is not lined by epithelium. Hence, it is called a pseudocyst.

Pseudocysts are post-inflammatory cysts that arise following an attack of mild acute pancreatitis. Formation of a pseudocyst requires 4 weeks or more from the onset of acute pancreatitis. They are also the most common complication of chronic pancreatitis.

Pseudocysts are usually solitary and most commonly seen in the lesser omental sac. The most common artery involved is the splenic artery.

Complications of pancreatic pseudocyst include:

* Abscess

* Systemic sepsis

* GI bleeding

* Fistula formation

* Peritonitis

* Obstructive jaundice

* Bowel obstruction

* Hemorrhage into the cyst

* Hemoperitoneum

Pancreatic pseudocysts can be distinguished from cystic neoplasms by having high amylase levels and absence of mucin and low serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old man is brought to the casualty with severe abdominal pain radiating to the back for the past 1 day and has had 3 episodes of vomiting. The pain typically radiates to the back and is slightly relieved in the sitting forward position. The following signs are seen on examination and lab investigations reveal elevated lipase and amylase. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute pancreatitis

The given clinical scenario with a patient having characteristic abdominal pain radiating to the back and with elevated lipase and Grey Turner sign (A) and Cullen's sign (B) shown in the picture, is suggestive of acute pancreatitis.

Causes of pancreatitis -

* Gallstones

* Alcoholism

* Post ERCP

* Abdominal trauma

* Following biliary, upper gastrointestinal or cardiothoracic surgery

* Ampullary tumor

* Drugs (corticosteroids, azathioprine, asparaginase, valproic acid, thiazides, estrogens)

* Hyperparathyroidism

* Hypercalcemia

* Pancreas divisum

* Autoimmune pancreatitis

* Hereditary pancreatitis

* Viral infections (mumps, coxsackie B)

* Malnutrition

* Scorpion bite

* Idiopathic

Signs and symptoms of pancreatitis-

Abdominal pain classically radiating to the back, vomiting, Cullen's sign(hemorrhagic discoloration of umbilical area, Gray turner's sign(hemorrhagic discoloration of left flank)

Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis -

Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when at least two of the following are present:

* Sudden, intense, persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back

* Marked elevation of pancreatic enzymes- S.amylase or lipase (≥3 times normal)

* Classic features seen on radiological imaging

Management of acute pancreatitis -

* The most important initial step in the management of patients with acute pancreatitis is hydration to ensure pancreatic perfusion and thereby decrease the risk of pancreatic necrosis.

* Early fluid resuscitation (one-third of the total 72-hour fluid volume administered within 24 hours of presentation, 250–500 mL/h initially) reduces the risk of SIRS.

* Food and liquids are restricted by mouth, bed rest is advised.

* Meperidine may be given to reduce pain.

* Oral fluid and food intake are resumed when the patient is free of pain and has bowel sounds.

Complications of acute pancreatitis

Local

*  Pancreatic phlegmon

* Pancreatic abscess

* Pancreatic pseudocyst

* Pancreatic ascites

*

Systemic

* Pulmonary:Acute respiratory distress syndromePleural effusion

* Cardiovascular:Hypotension, Hypovolemia

* Hematologic:Hemoconcentration, DIC

* GI haemorrhage: Portal vein or splenic vein thrombosis with varices.

* Renal: Oliguria, AKI, Renal artery/vein thrombosis

* Metabolic: Hyperglycemia, Hypocalcemia, and Hypertriglyceridemia.

* Sudden blindness (Purtschers retinopathy)

* Fat necrosis: Intra-abdominal saponification, Subcutaneous tissue necrosis

Pearl PF0602: Clinical features of acute pancreatitis

Symptoms:

* Acute onset of epigastric pain, which is severe, constant, and refractory to usual doses of analgesics.

* Typically radiates to back

* Relieved in the sitting forward position

* Nausea, repeated vomiting, retching, and hiccups

Signs:

* Hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea

* Grey Turner sign (A): bluish discoloration of the flanks

* Cullen’s sign (B): bluish discoloration around the umbilicus

* Fox sign: discoloration below the inguinal ligament

* Pleural effusion (left > right): dullness on percussion, decreased breath sounds

Pearl PF1586: X-Ray Findings in Acute Pancreatitis

Radiographic findings of acute pancreatitis are non-specific.

Sentinel loop sign: Generalized or local ileus, with isolated dilation of a segment of the gut (sentinel loop) consisting of jejunum, transverse colon, or duodenum adjacent to the pancreas

Colon cut-off sign: Functional spasm at the splenic flexure due to the extension of inflammation to phrenicocolic ligament via transverse mesocolon.

Renal halo sign: Edema around the kidney due to the involvement of paranephric fat resulting in:

* Obliteration of psoas shadow

* Localised ground-glass appearance

questions.text: A 40-year-old obese female presented with colicky pain in the right hypochondrium. On examination, her temperature is 100°F, her pulse rate is 94 bpm and her blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. There is scleral icterus and tenderness in right hypochondrium. Blood investigations show AST-22 IU/L, ALT-27 IU/L, S.bilirubin-5mg% and ALP- 200 mg%. What should be the initial investigation in this patient? ALP- Alkaline phosphatase, AST- Aspartate aminotransferase, ALT- Alanine aminotransferase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. USG

The symptoms of right hypochondrial pain, fever, scleral icterus, increased serum bilirubin, and ALP is suggestive of choledocholithiasis. The first investigation to be done in this case is a USG to look for biliary duct dilation and whether it is intra or extrahepatic. Once this is confirmed, ERCP can be done as it can remove the stone without operative intervention.

Clinical features of choledocholithiasis:

* Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, which may radiate to the back

* Biliary colic

* Vomiting

* Dyspepsia

* Flatulence

* Food intolerance particularly to fatty foods

* Altered bowel habits

* Jaundice.

Investigations:

Transabdominal ultrasound is the initial investigation to be done.

Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography is the best modality to view the proximal biliary tract while ERCP is used for distal biliary tract.

The most common indication for therapeutic ERCP is the relief of biliary obstruction due to gallstone disease and benign or malignant biliary strictures.  Pancreatic divisum can present with recurrent pancreatitis and ERCP can help diagnose this as well.

Pearl PF0601: Diagnostic Evaluation of the Bile Ducts

Diagnostic Evaluation of the Bile Ducts

* Hepatobiliary ultrasound: Initial procedure of choice in investigating possible biliary tract obstruction

* CT scan: Procedure of choice in investigating possible biliary obstruction if diagnostic limitations prevent HBUS

* MRCP: Useful modality for visualizing pancreatic and biliary ducts

* ERCP: Best visualisation of distal biliary tract

* Endoscopic sphincterotomy and stone removal can also be done

* PTC: Best visualisation of proximal biliary tract

* Indicated when ERCP is contraindicated or failed

* EUS: Most sensitive method to detect ampullary stones

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old female presented with fever, vomiting and right hypochondriac pain that was radiating to the neck. She has had similar on and off episodes in the past.On examination, Murphy's sign is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute cholecystitis

The clinical scenario with positive Murphy's sign is suggestive of acute cholecystitis.

Acute cholecystitis is the inflammation of the gallbladder that develops over hours, usually because a gallstone obstructs the cystic duct. In the majority of cases, the process is limited by the stone slipping back into the body of the gallbladder. Clinical features include:

* Pain in the right hypochondrium with referred pain to the back

* Fever

* Nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia

* Jaundice

* Positive Murphy's sign

* Positive Boas' sign

Murphy's sign: After asking the patient to exhale, the examiner places his hand below the costal margin on the right side at the mid-clavicular line. The patient is then instructed to take deep inspiration. If the patient stops breathing and winces with a ‘catch’ of breath, Murphy’s sign is said to be positive.

Boas' sign: It is the presence of an area of hyperaesthesia at the site where pain is radiated to the back, typically, below the scapula.

An ultrasound scan is sensitive in acute cholecystitis and demonstrates a distended gallbladder with thickened wall, pericholecystic fluid, the presence of gallstone, and the sonographic Murphy's sign. The gold standard investigation of acute cholecystitis is hydroxyiminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan. The radioisotope used is Technetium-99m ( 99mTc)-a labelled derivative of iminodiacetic acid.

The first-line treatment would be medical conservative management to subside the symptoms. The conservative management includes nil per mouth with intravenous fluid administration, administration of analgesics and antibiotics.

Other Murphy's in surgery:

Murphy's punch sign: This test is performed by the examiner using the fist to make jabbing thrusts over the costovertebral angle. The test is positive for infection, inflammation, or obstruction of the kidney.

Murphy's triad is associated with acute appendicitis.

* Pain in the right illiac fossa

* Vomiting

* Fever

Pearl PF1607: Diagnostic Evaluation of the Gall Bladder

* Gallbladder Ultrasound: Investigation of choice for detection of gall stones

* Abdominal X-ray: Useful in

* Calcified gall stones

* Emphysematous cholecystitis

* Porcelain gallbladder

* Limey bile

* Gallstone ileus

* Radioisotope scans (HIDA/DIDA/DISIDA)

* Indicated for confirmation of suspected acute cholecystitis

* Useful in diagnosis of acalculous cholecystopathy

Abbreviations:

* HIDA: Hepatobiliary IminoDiacetic Acid scan

* DIDA/DISDA: Di-isopropyl IminoDiacetic Acid - Dynamic Tc99m DIDA Cholescintigraphy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old alcoholic with a history of binge drinking presents with an episode of vomiting bright red blood. His vitals are stable. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mallory Weiss Tear

The most probable diagnosis for the above-mentioned clinical presentation is Mallory Weiss tear .

Mallory Weiss Syndrome is due to a longitudinal tear in mucosa or submucosa of the gastroesophageal junction. It is a common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to the presence of longitudinal superficial mucosal lacerations (Mallory-Weiss tears). The left gastric artery is the most common vessel to bleed.

It mainly occurs in patients with repetitive forceful retching and vomiting and is associated with heavy alcohol intake. The presence of portal hypertension with oesophagal varices and hiatal hernia may aggravate the condition. The investigation of choice is endoscopy.

Management of Mallory Weiss tear is conservative, as it usually is self-limiting. Endoscopic electrocoagulation or sclerosant therapy is done in some cases. Angiographic embolization or high gastrotomy is necessary only in rare cases that don't respond to conservative management.

Boerhaave syndrome is characterized by a tear in the lower third of the oesophagus which occurs when a person vomits against a closed glottis, causing a leak into the mediastinum, pleural cavity and peritoneum. Here all layers are involved.

The patients initially present with severe chest pain, tachypnea, and shock. Clinical features include Mackler's triad

* Retching

* Chest pain

* Subcutaneous emphysema

This catastrophic event produces severe mediastinitis(deranged vitals tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, and hypotension) and generally requires surgical intervention.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents with a lump in her left breast. Examination reveals a 6 X 4 cm mass in her left breast and a single mobile lymph node palpable under the mass. Which of the following is the best-recommended surgical treatment modality in this case?
options: Modified radical mastectomy and neoadjuvant chemotherapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Modified radical mastectomy and neoadjuvant chemotherapy

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of carcinoma of the breast. This patient has breast cancer at T3N1M0 disease which belongs to stage III A. The preferred treatment of choice in such patients is modified radical mastectomy and neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

Pre-operative chemotherapy and postoperative radiotherapy will add to the benefit of the patients. Considerations for treatment of Stage III A and III B disease are summarized in the flowchart as shown below.

The treatment of breast cancer should be individualized and based on various clinical factors. However, a general idea of it is as follows.

When systemic adjuvant therapy is given before the surgery it is called neoadjuvant therapy.

Early-stage localised cancer(stages 0, I , II) can be treated by mastectomy or breast-conserving therapy(BCT). BCT requires radiation to further improve patient benefit.

Locally advanced breast cancer(stages IIIA, IIIB) breast adenocarcinoma without distant metastases. It includes breast cancer that fulfils any of the following criteria in the absence of distant metastasis (M0):

*

Tumours more than 5 cm in size with regional lymphadenopathy: T3, N1-3

*

Tumours of any size with direct extension to the chest wall or skin, or both (including ulcer, oedema or satellite nodules): Any T4

*

Presence of clinically fixed or matted axillary lymph nodes, or any infraclavicular, supraclavicular, or internal mammary lymphadenopathy: Any N2 or Any N3

LABC is treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy + modified radical mastectomy + adjuvant radiation therapy. If ER/PR receptor positivity is present then hormonal therapy is added, and if Her-2/neu receptor positivity is present, then Trastuzumab / Herceptin is added.

Metastatic cancer(stage IV) Treatment of metastatic cancer is aimed at palliating symptoms, improving quality of life, preventing potential disabling complications and attempting to prolong life.

Pearl PF1896: Important surgeries for breast cancer

Breast conservative surgery is also known as segmental mastectomy, lumpectomy, partial mastectomy, wide local excision, and tylectomy.

* Tylectomy: Excision of lump

* Simple mastectomy: Palpable extent of breast + Nipple–areola complex + overlying skin.

* Subcutaneous mastectomy: Palpable extent of breast without overlying skin.

* Total mastectomy: All breast tissue + Nipple–areola complex + skin.

* Extended simple mastectomy: Simple mastectomy + removal of level I axillary lymph nodes.

* Modified radical mastectomy:  Entire breast tissue + Nipple–areola complex + skin + Axillary lymph nodes (Levels I + II ± III)

* Patey’s: Pectoralis minor is removed

* Scanlon’s: Pectoralis minor incised

* Auchincloss: Pectoralis minor only retracted

* Halsted’s radical mastectomy: Entire breast tissue + Nipple–areola complex + skin + Levels I + II+ III Axillary lymph nodes + Pectoralis major and minor

* Extended radical (Urban) - Halsted’s + Internal mammary lymph nodes

* Extended radical (Dahl-Iversion) mastectomy – Halsted’s + Internal mammary + Supraclavicular lymph nodes

* Super radical mastectomy – Halsted’s + Internal mammary + Supraclavicular + Mediastinal lymph nodes

Pearl PF2291: Contraindications for Breast Conservative Surgery

Absolute contraindications:

* 1st-trimester pregnancy

* Diffuse microcalcifications

* Persistently positive pathologic margin

* Multicentric tumor

Relative contraindications:

* Connective tissue disorders like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE),  scleroderma and rheumatoid arthritis

* Large lump-to-breast ratio, i.e., a big lump in small breast

* Lump beneath the nipple-areola complex

* Multifocal tumor

* History of therapeutic radiation exposure to the chest wall

NOTE : Some authorities do not consider Rheumatoid Arthritis as a relative contraindication as the data on radiation toxicity in RA is sparse.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 48-year-old patient presented with scrotal swelling. Investigations for testicular tumors revealed that LDH was elevated but AFP was within normal limits. Following orchidectomy, the following histological picture was observed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Seminoma

The clinical scenario, high LDH with normal AFP levels, and the given histology picture (fried egg appearance) are highly suggestive of testicular seminoma.

In yolk sac tumors and embryonal carcinoma, AFP is elevated whereas in teratoma LDH is normal.

Seminoma is the most common testicular tumor. It is common in men between 20-40 years of age.

The patients usually present with a painless testicular lump. If a testicular tumor is suspected, blood samples are taken from the patient for the evaluation of the tumor markers (hCG, LDH, and AFP), and the diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasound scanning of the testis. A high inguinal orchidectomy is performed.

Further treatment of seminoma depends on the stage of the tumor. Stage I tumors, whose levels of tumor markers decline after orchidectomy may not require further treatment. Stage II-IV tumors require radiotherapy and chemotherapy. The chemotherapeutic agents used are bleomycin, etoposide, and platin-based agents (BEP).

HCG: Human Chorionic Gonadotropin

questions.text: A 5-year-old child presented with fever and pain in the right iliac fossa. He had a history of nausea and vomiting 3 days back and was not taken to the hospital by his parents, but then symptoms started worsening. The surgeon suggested percutaneous drainage as the CT of the right iliac fossa showed a well-circumscribed fluid collection. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Appendicular abscess

The history of right iliac fossa pain with fever,nausea and vomiting is suggestive of acute appendicitis,which in this case has progressed to an appendicular abscess as suggested by the radiological findings.

An appendicular abscess is a very common complication of an untreated or perforated appendix. It can occur retroperitoneally or intraperitoneally.

Investigations include USG or Computed Tomography which shows a well-circumscribed, rounded, or ill-defined, irregular fluid collection in the appendicular region.

With the recent advances, early laparoscopic drainage or radiologically assisted percutaneous drainage followed by delayed appendicectomy is also done. If these are unsuccessful or there is leakage into the peritoneal cavity a midline laparotomy can be done.

Note:

The popular management of an appendicular mass is the Oschner-Sherren regime which is conservative management as the inflammatory process has already been localized and surgery is difficult now.

If it progresses to an abscess then it has to be drained radiologically or laparoscopically along with intravenous antibiotics given.

The indications for stopping the conservative management include:

* Rising pulse rate

* Increasing or spreading abdominal pain

* Increasing size of the mass.

A follow-up CT is taken in case of conservative management to ensure that there is complete resolution of the inflammatory process.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presented with painful swelling of the right calf muscle, 7 days after her knee replacement surgery. On examination, her heart rate is 70 beats per min, her blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, and her SpO2 is 96% on room air. Homan's test is positive. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Deep vein thrombosis

The clinical vignette describes a case of deep venous thrombosis(DVT).

Deep vein thrombosis:

Causes

* Postoperative thrombosis: (Most common cause)

* Following childbirth

* Trauma- to leg, ankle, thigh, pelvis

* Immobility – Bed-ridden patients, individuals on long-duration air or bus travel (Traveller’s thrombosis).

* Debilitating illness, obesity, immobility, bed rest, pregnancy, puerperium, oral contraceptives, estrogens.

Sites

* Pelvic veins—common

* Leg veins—common in femoral and popliteal veins (Common on the left side).

Features of DVT

* Fever-commonest

* Tense, tender, warm, pale/bluish, shiny swelling calf

* Positive Homan’s, Mose’s sign

* Inverted beer bottle sign/ champagne bottle sign

* Commonly it is asymptomatic

* Features of pulmonary embolism

Note:

Mose's sign- Squeezing of the relaxed calf muscles from side-to-side is also painful as the thrombosed deep veins in the calf are always tender and this test is known as Moses’ sign.

Homans sign - Passive forceful dorsiflexion of the foot with the knee extended will elicit tenderness in the calf. Gentle pressure directly on the calf muscles in the relaxed position will also elicit pain. Care must be taken to be gentle in manipulation lest it may dislodge a clot and cause a pulmonary embolism. The image is attached below.

Treatment

* Rest, the elevation of the limb, bandaging the entire limb with crepe bandage.

* Anticoagulants: Heparin/low molecular weight heparin, warfarin, phenindione.

* Palma operation

* May-Husni operation

Pulmonary embolism is the commonest complication of deep vein thrombosis leading to death.

Pearl PF1496: Risk factors for venous thromboembolism

Patient factors:

* Age

* Obesity

* Varicose veins

* Immobility

* Pregnancy

* Puerperium

* High-dose estrogen therapy

* Previous deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.

Thrombophilia

* Congenital

* Deficiency of antithrombin III, protein C or protein S

* Antiphospholipid antibody or lupus anticoagulant

* Factor V leiden gene defect or activated protein C resistance

* Dysfibrinogenaemias

* Acquired

* Antiphospholipid antibody or lupus anticoagulant

Disease or surgical procedure

* Trauma or surgery, especially of pelvis, hip, and lower limb

* Malignancy, especially pelvic, and abdominal metastatic

* Heart failure

* Recent myocardial infarction

* Paralysis of lower limb(s) infection

* Inflammatory bowel disease

* Nephrotic syndrome

* Polycythaemia

* Paraproteinaemia

* Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

* Behçet’s disease

* Homocysteinemia

Pearl PF1167: Prophylaxis for DVT

Mechanical prophylaxis

Early ambulation

Acts by activating the calf pump mechanism

Pneumatic compression stocking

Prevents stasis by periodically compressing the calves

Pharmacological prophylaxis

Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) - Enoxaparin

Fondaparinux

Prevent thrombus formation by inhibiting factor Xa

Apixaban

Rivaroxaban

Oral factor Xa inhibitors

Unfractionated heparin (UFH)

Prevents action of factors VIII - XII and production of thrombin/fibrin.

Used in renal insufficiency

Warfarin

Inhibits hepatic production of factors II, VII, IX and X

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62 year old chronic smoker presents with painless hematuria. On examination ther was a ballotable mass in the left flank region.Urine examination revealed presence of RBC's with no WBC's. A CECT taken is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal cell carcinoma

The clinical scenario along with the CECT image showing a hypoenhancing mass in contrast-induced CT in the right kidney corresponds to Renal cell carcinoma.

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC):

* Also known as hypernephroma or Grawitz tumor.

* Seen in men in their sixth to the seventh decade.

* The proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron is usually the site of origin of RCC.

Risk factors for renal cell carcinoma include the following:

* Smoking

* Obesity

* Hypertension

* Family history of renal cell carcinoma

* Drugs like phenacetin and diuretics

Pearl PF0896: Histologic subtypes of renal cell carcinoma

Clear-cell Type

* Most common type

* Originate from proximal tubule

* Associated with von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease

Papillary Type

* Psammoma bodies are seen in histology

* Originates from distal convoluted tubules, can be multifocal and bilateral.

Chromophobe type

* Are unique in having multiple losses of entire chromosomes

* Originates from intercalated cells of collecting duct

* Good prognosis

Collecting (Bellini) duct type

* Poor prognosis

Renal medullary carcinoma

* Rare

* Associated with sickle cell trait

* Originates from collecting duct

Note:

Sarcomatoid change can occur infrequently in all types of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and is an ominous feature.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 77-year-old man presented with worsening hip and back pain. He also reports weight loss and loss of appetite. The X-ray revealed the given lesions. His PSA levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prostate cancer

Blastic lesions on X-Ray along with elevated PSA levels, loss of weight, and loss of appetite are suggestive of prostatic carcinoma with metastasis to bones.

Carcinoma of the prostate:

It is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years  They may range from indolent lesions that cause no harm to aggressive metastatic tumors. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements.

Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Prostate carcinoma is a type of adenocarcinoma. Therefore, histopathology shows the malignant cells arranged in the form of glands. In contrast to benign glands, malignant glands have tightly packed cells and characteristically lack branching and papillary infoldings. The outer basal cell layer typical of benign glands is absent. The cells may show increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear atypia, etc. α-methyl acyl-coenzyme A-racemase (AMACR) is positive and is upregulated in prostate cancer.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Advanced disease may produce ureteral obstruction. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in the decreasing order of frequency.

Management of Prostatic Carcinoma

Stage of cancer
Age>70 or Gleason score=6
Age<70 or Gleason score>6

Early prostate cancer: T1, T2A
Active surveillance
Radical prostatectomy

Locally advanced prostate cancer: T2B, T2C, T3, T4, N1
Brachytherapy + Androgen deprivation therapy
Brachytherapy + Radical prostatectomy

Metastatic prostate cancer

Androgen deprivation therapy

Chemotherapy and radiotherapy (hormone-resistant  tumor)

Radiopharmaceutical therapy (hormone-resistant bony metastasis)

Below image shows histopathology of Prostate carcinoma:

Pearl PF0895: Types of metastasis(osteoblastic or osteolytic) and their primary:

Predominantly osteoblastic:

* Prostate cancer

* Osteosarcoma

* Medullary carcinoma thyroid

Mixed osteoblastic and osteolytic:

* Breast cancer(preponderance toward osteolytic)

* Lymphoma

* Urothelial carcinoma

* Lung cancer

Predominantly osteolytic:

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Multiple myeloma

* Thyroid carcinoma(except medullary carcinoma thyroid)

* Gastrointestinal tract carcinoma

* Malignant melanoma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A gross specimen of the colon obtained from a 14-year-old boy is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial adenomatous polyposis

The gross specimen in the image shows the presence of multiple polyps in the colon suggestive of familial adenomatous polyposis.

Familial adenomatous polyposis is an autosomal dominant disease that usually occurs in teenagers

* It is caused by mutations in the APC gene, which is a key negative regulator in the WNT signaling pathway

* 75% of the cases are inherited and a few are sporadic

* The polyps are morphologically indistinguishable from sporadic adenomas. The gross appearance will be a sessile or pedunculated mass between 0.3 to 10 cm in diameter. The texture will be velvet or raspberry. Histologically, the hallmark of epithelial dysplasia is nuclear hyperchromasia, elongation, and stratification. They can be classified as tubular, villous, or tubulovillous based on architecture

* Colorectal carcinoma occurs in 100% of cases before the age of 50.

* Prophylactic colectomy is recommended in patients with APC gene mutations.

* At least 100 polyps are required to make a diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis.

Pearl PF0293: Features of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis

Gastrointestinal manifestations:

* Colon and rectum: Multiple adenomatous polyp usually >100

* Gastric and duodenal polyps are present in 50% cases.

* Gastric polyp: fundal gland polyp, gastric adenoma.

* Duodenal polyp usually in the ampullary region: Adenomatous and premalignant

Extraintestinal manifestations

* Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) seen in 75% of cases; it is detected by indirect ophthalmoscopy.

* Epidermoid cysts

* Desmoid tumors in the abdomen

* Osteoma: In the skull, mandible, and tibia

* Brain tumors

* Tumors of the thyroid, adrenal, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, and bile duct

questions.text: A patient presented with retrosternal chest pain radiating to the jaw and dysphagia. A barium swallow was performed which showed the following image. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse esophageal spasm

The above clinical picture showing retrosternal chest pain and dysphagia with a barium swallow showing cork-screw appearance are characteristic of a diffuse esophageal spasm (DES).

Diffuse Esophageal Spasm - It is a poorly understood hypermotility disorder of the esophagus seen more commonly in women.  Patients usually present with dysphagia and chest pain which is caused by spontaneous, abnormal contractions seen more in the distal two-thirds of the oesophageal body. However, in between the contractions, peristalsis remains normal. Pathologically, there is marked hypertrophy of the circular muscles.

Investigations :

A barium swallow shows corkscrew esophagus.

However, manometry is the gold standard test for diagnosis.

* On classic manometry - simultaneous, multi-peaked contractions of high amplitude (>120 mmHg) or long duration (>2.5 seconds) are suggestive of DES (as given in the question).

* On high-resolution manometry, a DCI (Distal contractile Integral) >450 mmHg is suggestive of DES. This is in accordance with the latest Chicago classification.

Treatment: Calcium-channel antagonists, vasodilators, and endoscopic dilatation have only transient effects. Surgical treatment includes extended/long oesophageal myotomy, up to the aortic arch, if required. The surgical treatment of DES is more successful in improving dysphagia than chest pain.

The older terms "diffuse esophageal spasm" and "jackhammer (nutcracker ) esophagus" have been replaced in the Chicago classification by Distal esophageal spasm and Hypercontractile esophagus respectively.

Pearl PF1589: Barium Studies

Barium swallow: Used to assess the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach.

The image below is a barium swallow showing eosinophilic esophagitis and associated stricture:

Barium meal: Used to assess stomach and duodenum.

Barium meal followthrough: Used to assess the small intestine

Barium enema: Used to assess the large intestine
