questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with increased frequency of micturition, incomplete bladder emptying, and frequent urinary tract infections. What is the diagnosis based on the image shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bladder stones

The clinical scenario along with the X-ray gives the diagnosis of bladder stones. The tip of a catheter can also be seen in the Xray.

Primary bladder stone:

* Develops in sterile urine in the absence of any known functional, anatomic, or infectious factors and does not necessarily imply that stones have formed de novo in the bladder.

* Most common in children younger than 10 years of age

* Most vesical calculi are mixed

* Ammonium acid urate, calcium oxalate, uric acid, and calcium phosphate are the most common components of primary bladder calculi

Secondary bladder stone: Forms during infection, due to bladder outflow obstruction, impaired bladder emptying, or the presence of a foreign body.

Types:

* Calcium oxalate stones

* Uric acid stones - occur in patients with gout but are also observed in patients with ileostomies or with bladder outlet obstruction

* Cystine stones - in cystinuria

* Triple phosphate stones - occur in urine infected with urea-splitting organisms

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was brought to the hospital following a road traffic accident. He was disoriented and a CT head was taken which showed no evidence of bleed but there was raised intracranial tension. Which of the following can be used for the initial management of raised intracranial pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mannitol

Mannitol can be used for the initial management of raised intracranial pressure. It helps decrease the edema associated with the injury.

If there is an associated bleed then craniotomy and evacuation might be needed as well which depends on the clinical picture.

Initial management of raised intracranial pressure (ICP):

* Airway protection

* Positioning the head up 20–30° (reverse Trendelenburg positioning)

* A bolus of mannitol up to 1 g/kg for free water diuresis (the effect is delayed by 20 min)

* Hypertonic saline (3% or 5%)

* Maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance

* Seizure control

* Sedation using a combination of opiates and barbiturates

* Ventriculostomy and/or craniectomy may be needed for definitive decompression.

ICP normally varies between 4 and 14 mmHg. Sustained ICP levels above 20 mmHg can injure the brain. The goal of therapy in raised ICP is to maintain the ICP <20 mmHg.

Note: Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centers, classically producing Cushing’s triad. It is comprised of:

* Bradycardia

* Raised blood pressure

* Irregular respirations.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a history of a road traffic accident 2 hours ago was brought to the emergency department with an altered sensorium. His GCS was 10 and the CT scan is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epidural hematoma

Axial CT shows a hyperdense lentiform (biconvex) opacity consistent with an epidural hematoma.

Extradural hematoma (EDH) is also known as an epidural hematoma. It is a collection of blood that forms between the inner surface of the skull and the outer layer of the dura, which is called the periosteal layer. It is commonly associated with a history of trauma and associated skull fracture.

The source of bleeding is usually a torn meningeal artery (most commonly the middle meningeal artery). It is associated with an underlying fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone.

Investigations to be done include CT and MRI. It is seen as a biconvex lesion. It can cause a mass effect with herniation. They are usually limited by cranial sutures, but not by venous sinuses.

Swirl sign refers to the non-contrast CT appearance of acute extravasation of blood into a hematoma, for example, an extradural hematoma or subdural hematoma. It represents unclotted fresh blood which is of lower attenuation than clotted blood that surrounds it.

The following image shows a CT scan depicting swirl sign:

Pearl PF0338: Intracranial haemorrhage

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a history of blunt abdominal trauma presents to the emergency with abdominal pain. On examination his vitals were HR-122, BP-80/50 mmHg, SpO2-94%, and there were abdominal guarding and rebound tenderness. What is the initial step in the management of this patient?
options: Get a CECT abdomen to rule out intraperitoneal bleed
Get a USG FAST to rule out intraperitoneal bleed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Start resuscitation with intravenous crystalloids

The history of blunt abdominal trauma, hypotension, abdominal guarding, and rebound tenderness is diagnostic of an intra-abdominal bleed. Since he is haemodynamically unstable, the initial management of this patient is to resuscitate him with intravenous crystalloids.

A patient with blunt abdominal trauma who is haemodynamically unstable needs urgent exploratory laparotomy to control the bleeding. But the initial management and evaluation are directed at ATLS protocols based on Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability and Exposure, thus the first step is to stabilize him with IV fluids. In a hemodynamically unstable patient with abdominal trauma, the initial step is to start resuscitation with intravenous crystalloids. This helps restore intravascular volume, improve blood pressure, and stabilize the patient's condition before proceeding with further diagnostic evaluations or interventions.

The management of abdomen trauma depends on the hemodynamic status and the examination findings. Some major indications for laparotomy:

* Peritonitis

* Hemodynamic instability with positive FAST

* Hollow organ injury

* Stab wound with evisceration

* Shock from uncontrolled bleeding

In a patient with hemodynamic instability and no signs of peritonitis, focused assessment with sonography in trauma (FAST) is performed. If FAST is not available, then a diagnostic peritoneal lavage is done. The presence of intraabdominal bleeding on either necessitates further exploration.

If the patient is hemodynamically stable with no signs of peritonitis, then a contrast-enhanced CT scan is done to look for intra-abdominal injuries and decide on the need for operative, nonoperative, or angiographic therapy. In a patient with trauma and signs of peritonitis, an exploratory laparotomy is done.

The most common organs that are affected in blunt abdominal trauma are the spleen followed by the liver. Blood should be urgently typed and transfused in case of unstable patients with large bleeds when needed.

Primary assessment (i.e the primary survey) follows the ABCDE pattern: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (neurologic status), and Exposure. It is crucial to realize that the absence of abdominal pain or tenderness does not rule out the presence of significant intra-abdominal injury.

The following signs strongly correlate with intra-abdominal injury

* Seatbelt sign

* Rebound tenderness

* Hypotension

* Abdominal distension

* Abdominal guarding

* Concomitant femur fracture

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young man presents to the emergency department with a painful scrotum. On examination, the patient is febrile, scrotal erythema is noticed, and on lifting the testis, the pain is relieved. What is the most likely cause of the patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epididymo-orchitis

The clinical scenario with positive Prehn's sign is suggestive of acute epididymo-orchitis.

A positive Prehn’s sign is used to differentiate epididymis from testicular torsion. A Prehn’s sign is said to be positive when the pain gets relieved on lifting the testis. If it persists, it is likely to be testicular torsion.

Epididymo-orchitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the epididymitis and testis. The infection reaches the epididymitis from a primary infection of the urethra, seminal vesicles, or prostate. In young men, it is sexually acquired while in older men it is secondary to a urinary tract infection. It can occur post catheterization or instrumentation as well.

Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of acute epididymitis in young, sexually active males. In older men(>40yrs) with bladder outflow obstruction, epididymitis results from a urinary infection, most commonly due to Escherichia coli.

Clinical features include pain and redness in the scrotum, fever, and tenderness of the scrotum.

Initial investigations include urine specimen for culture, Nucleic acid amplification testing(NAAT), and a urethral swab to check for signs of infection. An ultrasound of the epididymis can show inflammation and abscess formation if any.

Treatment is by antibiotics and scrotal support.

Note:

A common differential is a testicular torsion which needs urgent surgical exploration. A Prehn's sign is used to differentiate torsion from epididymo-orchitis.

Chronic tuberculous epididymo-orchitis presents as a painless swelling of the scrotum with a firm enlarged epididymis, beading of the vas deferens, and a normal testis on palpation.Beading of the vas deferens is due to subepithelial tubercle formation and is specific to genital tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male on digital rectal examination was found to have a rectal mass raising the suspicion of rectal carcinoma. His bowel habits are normal and he visited the outpatient department for a routine check-up. Which of the following should be recommended as the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Full Colonoscopy and biopsy

As the patient is elderly with a rectal mass, presenting to an outpatient department, colorectal carcinoma has to be ruled out and the investigation of choice is a colonoscopy along with a biopsy.

A colonoscopy can be used to view 100–160 cm from the anal verge while a sigmoidoscopy can only see up to 60 cm from the anal verge. Colonoscopy rules out any associated proximal lesions as well.

Moreover, a rigid sigmoidoscopy procedure requires the rectum to be empty and thus a barium enema has to be given prior to the procedure.

Colonoscopy can also be therapeutic in the case of proximal adenomas which are snared via the colonoscope. In case of sensing cancer, a CT colonography or barium enema can be used.

The other investigations used in rectal cancer include:

* Digital rectal examination - for assessing the depth of penetration

* Endorectal ultrasound or MRI - provides an accurate assessment of the extent of invasion of the bowel wall

* MRI with an endorectal coil - is the investigation of choice to assess the 'T' and 'N' stages

* CECT - for evaluation of metastasis.

Screening for colorectal malignancy:

* Start screening at 50 years of age in an average risk patient

* Yearly stool occult blood testing

* Colonoscopy every 10 year

* Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 year

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion of ___
options: Lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Lateral nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Medial nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence

Cleft lip is due to failure of fusion between the medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence.

Various defects of fusion of prominences in the face region are as follows:

* Cleft lip is due to the failure of the fusion of maxillary prominence with medial nasal prominence. It can be unilateral or bilateral. It can vary in severity from a small notch in the upper lip to a double cleft extending into both the nostrils. There is also associated underdevelopment of the part of the maxilla that bears the incisors.

* Median (midline) cleft lip is a rare defect occurring due to failure of fusion of the two medial nasal prominences in the midline.

* Oblique facial cleft is caused by the failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the lateral nasal prominence along the line of the nasolacrimal groove. The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface in these cases.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pancreaticojejunostomy

The image shows the resection of the tail of pancreas followed by longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy i.e. Puestow procedure which is a treatment modality for chronic pancreatitis.

When chronic pancreatitis is accompanied by intractable pain, it is best treated with side-to-side Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy, also known as the modified Puestow procedure or lateral pancreaticojejunostomy.

Note:

Duval procedure is outdated and not in use due to low improvement rates. Restenosis and segmental obstruction of the pancreas is common due to progressive scarring. It is now only used in resectable tumors of the body or the tail of the pancreas.

Pearl PF0325: Drainage procedures for chronic Pancreatitis

Duval procedure: Distal pancreatectomy with Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy

Puestow procedure: Resection of tail followed by longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy

* Partington and Rochelle modification of Puestow procedure: Elimination of resection of pancreatic tail

* A longitudinal pancreatotomy typically discloses segmental stenosis of the pancreatic duct and the presence of intraductal calculi in a patient with chronic calcific pancreatitis.

* Following mobilization of a Roux limb of jejunum, a longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy is performed to permit extensive drainage of the pancreatic duct system.

Pearl PF0333: Resection and Hybrid Surgical Procedures for Chronic Pancreatitis

Beger’s procedure: Duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (DPPHR)

* The completed resection after transection of the pancreatic neck and subtotal removal of the pancreatic head, with preservation of the distal common bile duct and duodenum (Marked A).

* Completion of the reconstruction of the anastomosis to the distal pancreas and to the proximal pancreatic rim by the same Roux limb of the jejunum.

Frey’s procedure:

* The local resection of the pancreatic head with longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (LR-LPJ) provides complete decompression of the entire pancreatic ductal system. Reconstruction is performed with a side-to-side Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy.

Warren’s modification of Beger’s procedure:

Berne modification (Beger + Frey) involves excavation of the central portion of the head without formal division of the neck.

(image below)

Hamburg modification of Frey’s procedure

Note:

Surgical treatments for chronic pancreatitis

Resection

* Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Kausch–Whipple procedure)

* Pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy (Traverso–Longmire)

* Beger procedure

* Near-total or total pancreatectomy

Decompression/Drainage

* Duval procedure

* Puestow–Gillesby procedure

* Partington–Rochelle procedure (Puestow)

* Izbicki procedure

Hybrid (resection+decompression)

* Frey procedure

* Hamburg modification

* Berne modification

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Whipple's procedure

The image shows the Whipple procedure which is a complex surgery done for carcinomas involving the head of the pancreas.

It is done only in cases when:

* The entire duodenum has to be removed e.g. in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)

* Tumor encroaches in the first part of the duodenum, or stomach

* A clear resection margin is not achieved by PPPD

The following structures are removed during Whipple’s procedure:

* Distal stomach

* Duodenum

* Proximal jejunum

* Head of the pancreas

* Gallbladder

* Common bile duct (CBD)

* Regional lymphatics

The reconstruction following Whipple’s procedure or pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy involves anastomosis in the following order:

Pancreaticojejunostomy

↓

Choledochojejunostomy

↓

Gastrojejunostomy

This is controversial since there is a difference in the reconstruction procedures mentioned in standard textbooks:

Bailey and Love, 27th edition (Pg no: 1236) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + choledochojejunostomy + duodenojejunostomy

Schwatrz, 11th edition (Pg no: 1493) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + choledochojejunostomy + gastrojejunostomy/duodenojejunostomy

Sabiston, 20th edition (Pg no: 1546) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + hepaticojejunostomy + duodenojejunostomy

Pearl PF0333: Resection and Hybrid Surgical Procedures for Chronic Pancreatitis

Beger’s procedure: Duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (DPPHR)

* The completed resection after transection of the pancreatic neck and subtotal removal of the pancreatic head, with preservation of the distal common bile duct and duodenum (Marked A).

* Completion of the reconstruction of the anastomosis to the distal pancreas and to the proximal pancreatic rim by the same Roux limb of the jejunum.

Frey’s procedure:

* The local resection of the pancreatic head with longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (LR-LPJ) provides complete decompression of the entire pancreatic ductal system. Reconstruction is performed with a side-to-side Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy.

Warren’s modification of Beger’s procedure:

Berne modification (Beger + Frey) involves excavation of the central portion of the head without formal division of the neck.

(image below)

Hamburg modification of Frey’s procedure

Note:

Surgical treatments for chronic pancreatitis

Resection

* Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Kausch–Whipple procedure)

* Pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy (Traverso–Longmire)

* Beger procedure

* Near-total or total pancreatectomy

* Duval procedure

* Puestow–Gillesby procedure

* Partington–Rochelle procedure (Puestow)

* Izbicki procedure

* Frey procedure

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The following barium swallow is suggestive of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Achalasia cardia

Image shows markedly dilated esophagus and characteristic bird's beak appearance suggestive of achalasia cardia (dilated esophagus with distal narrowing).

In achalasia cardia, the lower esophagral spinchter (LES) is hypertensive and fails to relax appropriately in response to swallowing. Sphincter spasm and delayed emptying through LES are also seen. Esophageal manometry is the gold standard for establishing the diagnosis of esophageal achalasia.

Pearl PF0313: Achalasia Cardia

Achalasia is a rare disease caused by the loss of ganglion cells within the esophageal myenteric plexus.

Their absence leads to increased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), and absent peristalsis.

Achalasia is the only true motility disorder of the esophagus.

Primary achalasia is due to ganglion cell degeneration and is thought to be due to an autoimmune process attributable to latent infection with human herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) combined with genetic susceptibility.

Secondary achalasia may arise in Chaga's disease

Clinical features:

* dysphagia (solid and liquid food)

* regurgitation

* chest pain

* weight loss

* bronchitis, pneumonia, or lung abscess from aspiration

Differential diagnosis: Diffuse esophageal spasm, Chagas’ disease, and pseudoachalasia

On barium swallow: Bird beak-appearance

Investigation of choice: Manometry (most sensitive)

Treatment: Pneumatic dilatation and Heller myotomy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the probable cause of the condition shown in the X-ray below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perforation peritonitis

The Xray shows free air under the diaphragm which is indicative of hollow viscus perforation and among the options, perforation peritonitis is a probable cause.

GI tract perforation:

Common causes include surgery, blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, corrosive agents, or particular medications.

Patients may present with acute pain, abdominal/pelvic mass due to an abscess or phlegmon formation, fistula formation(such as in Crohn's disease), sepsis

Physical examination shows subcutaneous gas (mediastinal gas might be heard as a systolic "crunch" - Hamman's sign). When free intraperitoneal perforation has occurred, signs of peritonitis are present.

Diagnosis may be made based on clinical exam findings of peritonitis and history. However, confirmation is obtained by demonstrating pneumoperitoneum. X-ray, USG, or CT scan may be used to quickly identify free air. Erect X-ray is commonly used and it shows the presence of free air under the diaphragm(shown in the image below)

Management - Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Indications for immediate bowel exploration are

* Sepsis/diffuse peritonitis(as in this patient)

* Bowel ischemia

* Complete or closed-loop bowel obstruction

Deep tenderness at McBurney's point, known as McBurney's sign, is a sign of acute appendicitis. McBurney's point is a point at one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine and umbilicus. It is where the appendix is commonly located.

questions.text: What is the stage of the breast cancer shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. T4b

The image shows Peau d'orange appearance of breast which is T4b according to the TNM staging.

Tumour of any size with overlying skin involvement(Peau d'orange appearance) is T4b.

The peau d'orange appearance of the breast occurs due to blockade of sub-dermal lymphatics.The lymphatic blockade gives rise to edema in the breast and tries to swell up. Since the infiltrated skin is tethered to the ligaments of Cooper, the swelling is restricted. The resultant edema deepens the mouth of the sweat glands and hair follicles giving rise to the typical orange peel appearance.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which classification system is shown in the image below that is used to stage gastric cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bormann's classification

The image shows Bormann classification used for advanced gastric cancer.

Gastric carcinoma can be classified as early gastric cancer and advanced gastric cancer.

* Early gastric cancer involves mucosa, submucosa with or without lymph node involvement. Early gastric cancer can be further classified using the Japanese classification.

* Advanced gastric cancer involves the muscularis layer, with or without adjacent structures. Its macroscopic appearances have been classified using Bormann classification.

The given image shows the pathological types of early gastric cancer as per Japanese system.

Other options:

Option A: AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer) is for squamous cell carcinoma. It is classified based on the extent of differentiation.

Option D: Hinchey classification is used for diverticulitis.

Pearl PF1130: Borrmann’s classification of stomach cancer

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following clinical factors has the worst prognosis in a case of acute limb ischemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Paralysis

Paralysis is seen in a nonviable limb and has the worst prognosis in a case of acute limb ischemia.

The classification of acute limb ischemia is:

a)Viable (I):

* Mild pain

* No sensory or motor deficits

* Capillary refill normal

* Doppler evaluation normal

* Urgent evaluation to be done

b)Marginally threatened(IIa):

* Moderate pain

* Minimal sensory deficit( in toes) with no motor deficit

* Delayed capillary refill is seen here

* Abnormal arterial doppler

* Urgent revascularization is needed

c)Immediately threatened(IIb):

* Severe pain

* Paraesthesia and mild to moderate muscle weakness

* Delayed capillary refill

* Abnormal arterial doppler

* Emergency revascularization is needed.

d)Nonviable(III):

* Irreversible muscle and tissue damage.

* Pain is variable here due to the death of the nerves

* Profound sensory loss, paralysis, and rigor of the limbs

* Abnormal arterial and venous dopplers

* Amputation is needed here

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following conditions has a barium enema as shown in the picture below ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diverticulosis

Saw-tooth appearance on a barium enema is characteristic of colonic diverticulosis.

The segment of colon involved in extensive diverticulosis is often concentrically narrowed along with accompanying hypertrophy of the colonic muscle layers, thus producing an irregular appearance resembling a sawtooth.

Note: Saw-tooth appearance can also occur in Hirschsprung's disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding Marjolin's ulcer?
options: It is seen in sites of chronic wounds or scars.
It can progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
It is radioresistant due to avascularity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It rapidly progresses to malignancy

The incorrect statement regarding Marjolin's ulcer is that it rapidly progresses to malignancy.

Marjolin’s ulcer refers to a rare form of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma . It originates from areas of scarring or chronic wounds.

It progresses to full-fledged SCC gradually. The progression is gradual and slow. It has a long latency period of around 30 years. Since the ulcer occurs in scarred tissue without nerves and vessels, it is painless and radioresistant

Clinical signs of the tumour include:

* Ulceration

* Nodule formation

* An abrupt increase in size

* Everted or rolled wound margins

* Overgrowth of granulation tissue

* Tendency to bleed on manipulation

For the diagnosis, an edge-wedge biopsy can be done. MRI of the part and the regional node area is done to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment involves wide local excision, and in case of a large ulcer, amputation is required.

An image of Marjolin's ulcer is below:

Pearl PF0158: Marjolin’s Ulcer

* Low-grade cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arising from

* Long-standing ulcer like venous ulcer

* Post-burn scar

* Chronic osteomyelitis

* Post-radiation ulcer.

* Slow progression to malignancy (SCC) since it is relatively avascular.

* Painless due to the absence of nerves in scar tissue.

* No secondary deposits since there are no lymphatics in scar tissue.

* Radioresistant due to avascularity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: 10 months old male baby presented with an empty scrotum. Ultrasonography revealed that the right testis was found in the right inguinal canal, while the left testis was found in the perineum. Comment on the diagnosis of this baby.
options: Right side undescended testis and left sided ectopic testis
Right side ectopic testis and left side undescended testis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right side undescended testis and left sided ectopic testis

Since the right testis is found in the inguinal canal which is along the normal path of descent it is called an undescended testis, while the left testis lies in the perineum which is an ectopic site of descent and is called an ectopic testis.

* The ectopic testis is one that has ended up away from the normal path of descent. The commonest site is the superficial inguinal pouch.

* Cryptorchidism or undescended testis is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac.  It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. The testes can arrest anywhere during descent, and the most common site is the inguinal region.

Phases of testicular descent:

* Transabdominal phase: Testes come to lie in the lower abdomen or pelvis, and this descent is regulated by Mullerian-inhibiting substances.

* Inguinoscrotal phase: Testes descend along the inguinal canal and reach the scrotal sac, and this phase of the descent is regulated by androgen-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve.

The exact pathogenesis remains unknown; however, reduced levels of Müllerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) and gonadotropins, together with elevated placental estradiol, are thought to be involved

The image below shows the possible ectopic sites of the testes:

A retractile testis is a normally developed and descended testis that retracts back into the inguinal canal due to hyper reflexive cremasteric muscle contraction.

Therefore any stimulation of the skin of the scrotum or thigh causes the testis to ascend and temporarily disappear into the inguinal canal. When the cremaster relaxes, the testis reappears in the scrotum.

The scrotum of a boy with such a retractile testis is normal (normal rugosity is seen).

Retractile testes require no treatment

Note: Chair test helps to differentiate retractile testis from ectopic testis because both of them describe a condition, wherein the testis lies in an abnormal position.

Chair Test:  Here, The young patient is asked to sit on a chair hugging his knees to his chest. This maneuver helps the retractile testis to get pushed down back to the bottom of the scrotum. By this test retractile testis can be differentiated from the ectopic testis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 3-day-old neonate presents with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. Among the following, which is the most appropriate investigation to diagnose the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CECT abdomen

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of jejunoileal atresia, and among the options CECT abdomen is the most appropriate investigation to diagnose the condition.

Small bowel atresias present with intestinal obstruction soon after birth. Bilious vomiting is the dominant feature in proximal bowel atresia such as duodenal atresia whereas abdominal distension with bilious vomiting is more with distal small bowel atresia such as jejuno-ileal atresia. Jejuno-ileal atresia is the most GI atresia.

Plain abdominal radiographs show a variable number of dilated loops of bowel and fluid levels according to the level of obstruction.

* Jejunal/ileal atresia - Triple bubble appearance

* Duodenal atresia - Double bubble appearance

A contrast study is the next best investigation to exclude other bowel anomalies.

In jejunal/ileal atresia, the distal end of the dilated proximal small bowel is resected and a primary end-to-end anastomosis is possible. If the proximal bowel is extremely dilated, it may need to be tapered to the distal bowel before anastomosis.

Classification of Jejunoileal atresia:

Type

Feature

Type 1

Mucosal web or diaphragm

Type 2

With an atretic cord between two blind ends of bowel with intact mesentery

Type 3 a

Complete separation of the blind ends of the bowel by a V-shaped mesenteric gap

Type 3 b

An apple peel or Christmas tree deformity with a large mesenteric gap

Type 4

Multiple atresias, with a string of sausage appearance

An erect X-ray of the abdomen showing ileal atresia. The image shows a triple bubble appearance and associated finding of apple-peel bowel with loss of dorsal mesentery is a feature of ileal atresia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old female patient presents with the complaint of a palpable painless mass in the left breast. On examination, the mass was highly mobile, measured 3x3 cm, and was rubbery in consistency. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fibroadenoma

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of fibroadenoma of breast. It presents as painless, palpable lump and is rubbery in consistency.

Fibroadenoma is one of the aberrations of normal development and involution of the breast (ANDI). The most common age group affected is 15-25 years (early reproductive period) with a peak incidence in the second decade.

Fibroadenomas can be classified into 2 types:

* Without complex features - classified as a non-proliferative condition

* With complex features -

* Associated with cysts > 0.3 cm, sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications, or papillary apocrine change

* Classified as proliferative changes without atypia

Fibroadenomas are benign tumours, although neoplasia may develop in the epithelial elements within them. Cancer in a newly discovered fibroadenoma is exceedingly rare; 50% of neoplasias that involve fibroadenomas are LCIS, 35% are invasive carcinomas, and 15% are intraductal carcinoma.

It arises from hyperplasia of a single lobule and presents as a well-circumscribed, smooth, firm, non-tender, freely mobile mass (mouse in the breast). It is a biphasic tumor consisting of fibroblastic stroma and epithelium-lined gland. Popcorn calcification is seen in mammography.

Excision is not advised unless there is suspicious histology on fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC). Giant fibroadenomas are >5 cm in size, common in adolescent girls, and require excision by submammary incision.

The ultrasound image depicts a well-circumscribed oval mass with uniform hypoechogenicity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and a fever. On examination, the left breast appears as shown in the image below. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and the contralateral breast is normal. Repeated aspirations under antibiotic cover were unsuccessful. A USG done showed fluid collection. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Incision and drainage

This patient with breast abscess has not responded to multiple attempts of aspirations. The next best step in this scenario is to perform incision and drainage.

The given scenario points towards a diagnosis of breast abscess. The initial management of breast abscess includes aspiration of abscess along with supportive measures like a breast support garment, cold compression on the breast and analgesia to aid in symptomatic relief. This often allows resolution without the need for an incision scar and also allows the patient to continue breastfeeding. But her aspirations have been unsuccessful and thus incision and drainage have to be the next step in the management of this patient.

Mastitis occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. This occurs secondary to blockage of the lactiferous duct or due to incomplete emptying of breast milk or due to a retracted nipple. Overgrowth of these bacteria results in the development of breast abscesses.

It is common in new mothers at the beginning of lactation who are inexperienced with breastfeeding or during weaning when nipple trauma occurs due to the infant's growing teeth.

Signs and symptoms of this condition involve:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

The initial treatment should involve providing pain relief with analgesics. The abscess should then be localized preferably under USG guidance and percutaneous aspiration carried out. The pus should be sent for microbiological examination to find the organism and antibiotic sensitivity. Repeated aspirations may be carried out under antibiotics cover if needed.

In some conditions mentioned below, the breast abscess may be unresponsive to repeated aspirations and antibiotic cover. In such cases, incision and drainage are performed. The conditions include:

* Presence of thick pus

* Bacteria resistant to antibiotics

* If just a superficial part has been aspirated in the presence of a multiloculated abscess

* A non-healing breast abscess due to tuberculosis of the breast or inflammatory carcinoma of the breast, or an immunocompromised host.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old man was referred to the surgery OPD from the infertility clinic. On inspection, the scrotum appeared as in the image. On palpation, a bag of worms sensation was felt. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Varicocele

The clinical scenario with the given image showing abnormal dilation and enlargement of the scrotal venous pampiniform plexus,  like bag of worms is suggestive of a varicocele.

Varicocele is an abnormal dilatation and enlargement of the scrotal venous plexus draining the testis. Left-sided varicocele is more common. Most varicoceles are idiopathic, obstruction of the testicular vein by a renal tumour or nephrectomy is seen in some cases.

The pathogenesis behind varicocele is due to increased blood flow to the testis leading to higher intratesticular temperatures, which inhibits spermatogenesis and results in low sperm count, motility and morphology. Most varicoceles are asymptomatic. Those symptomatic tend to present in adolescence or early adulthood, with a dragging discomfort that is worse on standing at the end of the day. There may be a cough impulse. Additionally, patients may have infertility.

Grades of varicocele

Grade 1
Varicocele only palpable on Valsalva’s maneuver

Grade 2
Varicocele palpable without Valsalva’s maneuver

Grade 3
Varicocele is seen on inspection of the testis

Often, patients may be asymptomatic and do not require treatment. Treatment of symptomatic and young patients includes surgical ligation of the gonadal vein. It may be achieved through embolectomy or varicocelectomy. Approaches to varicocelectomy are:

* Inguinal ( Ivanisevic method )

* Retroperitoneal (Palomo procedure)

* Natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery through the transvesical route

In older patients, NSAIDs and scrotal support are adequate.

Other options :

Option a: Hydrocele is an accumulation of fluid within the tunica vaginalis. In the case of a primary hydrocoele, as the fluid is collected within a closed sac, a cough impulse is unlikely to be seen. Important positive clinical findings in a hydrocoele are that they are irreducible,  the testes cannot be palpated separately, ability to get above the swelling, and transillumination of the swelling.

Option c : Testicular torsion is the twisting of the spermatic cord and its contents such that the testicular blood supply becomes compromised. It is a surgical emergency and if left untreated, the testes may become gangrenous.

Option d : Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac. It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year old alcoholic and a chronic smoker presented with bouts of vomiting and stabbing pain in the epigastrium. He was binge drinking shortly before the symptoms started. He is febrile and tachycardic. The given findings were seen on bedside radiological imaging. Which among the following is a likely cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peptic ulcer perforation

In the given case scenario, the supine abdominal x-ray shows air beneath the diaphragm along with Rigler's double-wall sign indicating pneumoperitoneum. The likely cause for this would be peptic ulcer perforation. Consumption of alcohol and chronic tobacco smoking are high-risk factors for developing peptic ulcers. Fever and tachycardia suggest peritonitis from the perforated ulcer.

Gastric ulcers are more prone to perforate than bleed. Thus, these perforations lead to pneumoperitoneum which is an emergency and warrants immediate surgical intervention.

Other options:

A. Tension pneumothorax - presents with a rapid hemodynamic compromise with absent breath sounds. Pneumoperitoneum rarely is caused by pneumothorax, and downward displacement of air is more likely seen in retroperitoneal spaces.

C. Boerhaave syndrome or spontaneous esophageal rupture - occurs in alcoholics after binge drinking, due to forced vomiting from the closed glottis.  Pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema are seen here.

D. Mallory Weis tear - longitudinal mucosal tear resulting in upper GI bleeding. It is commonly seen in alcoholics.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old alcoholic with a history of binge drinking presents with an episode of vomiting bright red blood. His vitals are stable. What is the probable diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mallory Weiss Tear

The most probable diagnosis for the above-mentioned clinical presentation is Mallory Weiss tear as the patient's vitals are stable.

Mallory Weiss Syndrome:

* It is a common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to the presence of longitudinal superficial mucosal lacerations (Mallory-Weiss tears).

* They occur primarily in the lower esophagus close to the gastroesophageal junction.

* It mainly occurs in patients with repetitive forceful retching and vomiting and is associated with heavy alcohol intake.

* The concurrent presence of portal hypertension with esophageal varices and hiatal hernia in patients with Mallory Weiss syndrome is not uncommon.

Boerhaave syndrome:

* It is a transmural perforation of the esophagus (while the Mallory Weiss tear is a mucosal tear).

* Clinical presentation:

* Mackler's Triad:

* Vomiting

* lower thoracic pain

* subcutaneous emphysema

* Other classical findings include deranged vitals tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, and hypotension.

* Diaphoresis and abdominal rigidity can also be present

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old chronic alcoholic with a history of chronic liver disease presents to the emergency department with massive, sudden onset hematemesis. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bleeding esophageal varices

The given clinical scenario of a chronic alcoholic with sudden onset haematemesis is suggestive of esophageal variceal bleeding.

The management of esophageal variceal bleeding involves:

* Resuscitation with IV fluids, airway protection, and oxygen

* Blood transfusion to maintain Hb between 7-9g/dL

* Antibiotic prophylaxis with ceftriaxone before endoscopy

* An attempt at hemostasis with octreotide or terlipressin or vasopressin

* Fluid resuscitation followed by an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy within 12 hours to determine the cause of the bleeding

* Endoscopic variceal band ligation or sclerotherapy

* In case, of failure or rebleeding - TIPS

Nonselective beta-blockers like propranolol and nadolol are used in the prophylaxis of variceal bleeding.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old diabetic man presents with a progressive increase in pain in his calf, initially after walking a distance of 400m later 200m over the last 6 months. He now prefers to sleep in a seated position by hanging his leg to alleviate pain. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rest pain

The given clinical scenario describes a case of peripheral arterial disease which has worsened over time. This patient who prefers to sleep in a seated position by hanging his leg to alleviate pain now has rest pain.

Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) presents as intermittent claudication (crampy pain in the muscles). As the disease progresses, claudication distance decreases, and pain occurs even at rest called ischemic rest pain. Rest pain is due to ischemia of the somatic nerves. The pain is exacerbated by lying down or elevation of the foot due to the loss of the gravitational effects on perfusion pressure. It may be lessened by hanging the foot down.

Physical exam findings include atrophied skin, pallor on the raising leg (Buerger's test), nail changes, and decreased peripheral pulses.

The initial investigation done is an ABI. Further investigation is done with Doppler imaging, duplex scan, and digital subtraction angiography. Rest pain is seen when ABI becomes <0.5.

Other options:

Option A: Sciatica - The patient complains of pain radiating down the back of the thigh and calf. Sciatica can either be because of inflammation of the sciatic nerve or because of compression of one of the roots constituting the sciatic nerve

Option B:  Neurogenic claudication occurs with changes in the position of the back such as bending forward and straightening. It takes more time to be relieved by rest (more than 5 minutes). In spinal stenosis, there is an abnormal narrowing of the central canal, the lateral recesses, or the intervertebral foramina to the point where the neural elements are compromised.

Option C: Patients with venous claudication have some form of venous diseases like varicose veins, edema and skin changes due to chronic venous diseases like pigmentation, eczema or ulcers.

Pearl PF1741: Ankle–brachial Pressure Index (ABPI)

The ankle-brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is the ratio of systolic pressure at the ankle to that in the arm.

The numerator is the highest pressure in the dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, or peroneal artery and the denominator is the highest brachial systolic pressure.

ABPI Reading
Interpretation

>0.91 < 1.3
Normal

<0.9
Diagnostic of occlusive arterial disease in patients with symptoms of claudication or other signs of ischemia

0.5 to 0.9
Arterial obstruction often associated with claudication

<0.3
Critical limb ischemia (multilevel obstruction i.e any combination of iliac, femoral or tibial vessel disease and may be associated with non-healing ulcerations, ischemic rest pain, or pedal gangrene.

>1.4
Signifies poor compressibility of the arteries. Mostly due to calcification because of increased age, diabetes etc.

Note: A fall in the resting ABPI of more than 20% after exercise is indicative of arterial disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 77-year-old man presented with worsening hip and back pain. He also reports weight loss and loss of appetite. His PSA levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prostate cancer

Blastic lesions on X-Ray along with elevated PSA levels, loss of weight, and loss of appetite are suggestive of prostatic carcinoma with metastasis to bones.

Carcinoma of the prostate:

It is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years  They may range from indolent lesions that cause no harm to aggressive metastatic tumors. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements.

Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Prostate carcinoma is a type of adenocarcinoma. Therefore, histopathology shows the malignant cells arranged in the form of glands. In contrast to benign glands, malignant glands have tightly packed cells and characteristically lack branching and papillary infoldings. The outer basal cell layer typical of benign glands is absent. The cells may show increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear atypia, etc. α-methyl acyl-coenzyme A-racemase (AMACR) is positive and is upregulated in prostate cancer.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Advanced disease may produce ureteral obstruction. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in the decreasing order of frequency.

Management of Prostatic Carcinoma

Stage of cancer
Age>70 or Gleason score=6
Age<70 or Gleason score>6

Early prostate cancer: T1, T2A
Active surveillance
Radical prostatectomy

Locally advanced prostate cancer: T2B, T2C, T3, T4, N1
Brachytherapy + Androgen deprivation therapy
Brachytherapy + Radical prostatectomy

Metastatic prostate cancer

Androgen deprivation therapy

Chemotherapy and radiotherapy (hormone-resistant  tumor)

Radiopharmaceutical therapy (hormone-resistant bony metastasis)

Below image shows histopathology of Prostate carcinoma:

Pearl PF0895: Types of metastasis(osteoblastic or osteolytic) and their primary:

Predominantly osteoblastic:

* Prostate cancer

* Osteosarcoma

* Medullary carcinoma thyroid

Mixed osteoblastic and osteolytic:

* Breast cancer(preponderance toward osteolytic)

* Lymphoma

* Urothelial carcinoma

* Lung cancer

Predominantly osteolytic:

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Multiple myeloma

* Thyroid carcinoma(except medullary carcinoma thyroid)

* Gastrointestinal tract carcinoma

* Malignant melanoma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought to the casualty following a road traffic accident. The patient is in respiratory distress and has visibly dilated neck veins. A large amount of air was noted on the left side in the X-ray as shown below. What is the next best step of management?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space

The given X-ray features and clinical scenario point towards the diagnosis of tension pneumothorax. The next best step in the management is wide bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space.

The chest X-ray shows a well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side with tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed while waiting for radiological confirmation. Imaging modalities used are ultrasound – extended focused assessment with sonar for trauma (eFAST), chest x-ray, and spiral CT.

A tension pneumothorax develops when there is a tear either in the parietal or visceral pleura. This tear acts as a one-way valve i.e. air enters from the lung or chest wall through it during inspiration but has no way to escape during expiration. This ultimately leads to the collapse of the affected lung.

It usually occurs following penetrating or blunt chest trauma, iatrogenic lung injury, or mechanical positive pressure ventilation.

It is characterized by:

* Chest pain

* Tachypnoea, and acute dyspnea

* Sudden onset hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension, low O2 saturation, loss of consciousness)

* Neck vein distention

* Tracheal deviation away from the side of injury

* Decreased chest movements on the affected side

* Hyper-resonance on percussion on the affected side

* Absence or decreased breath sounds on the affected side

The X-ray below shows a left-sided tension pneumothorax. There is a large, well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side. The yellow arrows are pointing to the tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side.

Management of tension pneumothorax:

* Immediate management- needle decompression or needle thoracostomy i.e. insertion of a wide-bore needle in the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line

* Definitive management- tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th ICS in the triangle of safety identified as a triangle that lies anterior to the midaxillary line above the nipple, below, and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle.

The images below show the triangle of safety and technique of chest drain insertion.

Other options:

* Pericardiocentesis is done in cases of cardiac tamponade which is characterized by the presence of hypotension, distended jugular veins, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad). The breath sounds are absent in tension pneumothorax while they are present in cardiac tamponade.

* Surgery for pneumothorax can be performed by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) or as an open procedure (thoracotomy) in cases of spontaneous pneumothorax failing to settle despite chest drainage. Pleural adhesion is achieved by chemical pleurodesis where talc is used and is insufflated into the chest cavity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented to the hospital with a history of increased frequency of micturition. On cystoscopy, a pale ureteric orifice was seen. The patient's KUB X-ray is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bladder tuberculosis

The given clinical scenario and KUB X-ray point to the diagnosis of bladder tuberculosis.

The earliest sign of tuberculosis of the bladder observed by cystoscopy is the pallor of the mucosa around the ureteric orifice due to submucous edema. Subsequently, tubercles may be seen.

A thimble bladder is a small contracted bladder due to fibrosis of the bladder walls. It is seen in bladder tuberculosis and is appreciated in a micturating cystourethrogram (MCU). The X-ray KUB given above shows a thimble bladder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient sustained a crush injury on their right arm as depicted in the given image. He was brought to the hospital and on examination, his arm is pulseless, swollen and dark red. What would be the best way to manage this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fasciotomy

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a crush syndrome with compartment syndrome. If compartment syndrome is confirmed (by measuring intra-compartmental pressure), then fasciotomy is performed.

Crush syndrome can result when a limb is compressed for a prolonged period (e.g. getting crushed or entrapped in a vehicle or rubble) and after extended use of a pneumatic antishock garment. This results in hypoperfusion and myonecrosis in the crushed limb. When the limb is released from the compression, toxic metabolites get released to cause reperfusion injury.

Management of crush syndrome involves aggressive management of the open wound and radical excision of necrosed muscle to avoid sepsis. Encouraging high urine flow, along with alkalization of urine with sodium bicarbonate to prevent precipitation of myoglobin in the renal tubules. Renal hemofiltration is recommended if there is oliguria or renal failure. If compartment syndrome is confirmed (by measuring intra-compartmental pressure), then fasciotomy is performed.

The diagnosis can be confirmed by measuring the intra-compartmental pressure using a split catheter introduced into the compartment. The difference between diastolic pressure and compartment pressure is known as differential pressure (ΔP). If the differential pressure (ΔP) is less than 30 mm Hg (4.00 kilopascals), immediate compartment decompression is indicated.

Treatment:

* Prompt decompression of the affected compartment is done.

* All the dressings, bandages, and cast on the affected limb are removed and the limb is nursed flat.

* Fasciotomy is done if the differential pressure is less than 30 mm Hg

* Fasciotomy wounds are left open and after 2 days if there is necrosis debridement is done. If the wounds are healthy it can be sutured without tension or skin grafting can be done.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A woman who sustained third and fourth-degree burns on her back has been brought to you. What would be the order of sequence in her management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Resuscitation - debridement - allograft or autograft

The correct sequence in management is Resuscitation - debridement - allograft or autograft.

Fluid resuscitation in burns:

Intravenous fluid resuscitation is done in adults with second degree and third degree burns > 15% TBSA (Total body surface area) and in children with burns > 10% TBSA.

According to ATLS 10th edition, 2018, the resuscitation formula used in thermal burns in adults is 2 mL/kg × % TBSA. 50% of the total fluid is given in the first 8 hours after the burns injury and the remaining 50% is given in the subsequent 16 hours. This can be calculated as:

First 8 hours: 1 mL/kg × % TBSA (lactated Ringer solution)
Next 16 hours: 1 mL/kg × % TBSA (lactated Ringer solution)

For a patient presenting 8 hours after sustaining thermal burns, the total volume using resuscitation formula should be given in the next 16 hours i.e; 2 mL/kg × % TBSA in the next 16 hours while maintaining a target urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/hr for adults.

In adults, urine output should be maintained between 30 and 50 cc/hr to minimize potential over-resuscitation.

In case of paediatric burns, the resuscitation formula used in thermal burns is 3 mL/kg × % TBSA.

Pearl PF0276: Burns – Formulae for Fluid Calculation(Updated according to ATLS 10th edition 2018 guidelines)

This formula gives the total fluid requirement for 24hours. Half of this volume is infused in the first 8 hours, and the remaining half is infused in the next 16 hours.

Note:

The goal of resuscitation is to maintain the fine balance of adequate perfusion as indicated by urine output. It is important to understand that formulas provide a starting target rate; subsequently, the amount of fluids provided should be adjusted based on a urine output target of 0.5 mL/kg/hr for adults and 1 mL/kg/hr for children weighing less than 30 kg.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young adult with gastric outlet obstruction presents with vomiting. Which of the following fluids is preferred in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Normal saline

Normal saline is preferred in a patient with gastric outlet obstruction to rectify the electrolyte imbalance.

The recurrent vomiting secondary to the gastric outlet obstruction leads to dehydration and hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis. This abnormality has to be corrected and adequate rehydration ensured before the surgery is undertaken. The patient should be rehydrated with intravenous isotonic saline with potassium supplementation. Replacing the sodium chloride and water allows the kidney to correct the acid–base abnormality. (Normal saline has more chloride than Ringer lactate)

Surgery can be done once the electrolyte imbalance is corrected - Routine preoperative evaluation is conducted, oral feeding is discontinued and the stomach is emptied with a nasogastric tube. Intravenous fluids are given to replace the ongoing gastric losses.

Fluid Resuscitation

* Fluid resuscitation - 0.9% saline with KCl in 5% glucose provides maintenance and corrects deficits in most babies. As the chloride deficit is replaced, the kidneys correct the pH.

* The urine output should be monitored and the electrolyte levels must be checked every 6 hours.

* To ensure that rehydration has occurred, the urine output should be >2 cc/Kg/hr.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery for obesity. He now presents to his physician with complaints of dizziness, fatigue, and tremors 2 hours after the ingestion of a carbohydrate-rich meal. His symptoms occur mainly due to * Hypoglycemia * Small volume of food intake * High osmotic load of food * Increased release of insulin * Increased release of glucagon
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 4

The patient is presenting with features of late dumping syndrome following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. This occurs due to an increased release of insulin and hypoglycemia.

Dumping syndrome occurs due to rapid gastric emptying. It is commonly seen following gastric surgeries. It can be divided into

* Early dumping syndrome is a condition that develops after consuming foods high in osmotic load. Fluid is sequestered from the circulation into the gastrointestinal tract as a result of the increased osmotic load in the intestine. Patients will develop hypovolemia and hypotension.

* Late dumping syndrome develops after ingestion of a large volume of meals and meals which are rich in carbohydrates. Blood sugar levels rise quickly as a result of the intestines absorbing a lot of glucose. This ultimately leads to an increase in insulin release, which results in hypoglycemia.

The mainstay in the management of dumping syndrome is dietary manipulation. The patient is advised to have small volume, regular meals that are rich in protein, fat, and low in carbohydrates. Somatostatin analogue like octreotide is used in the management of intractable syndromes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Five days after a common bile duct injury, there is a leak, and the patient presents with fever and abdominal pain . What will be the next line of management ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ultrasound-guided aspiration

In the case of a common bile duct injury with a leak and patient presenting with signs of localized peritonitis, the next step of management is ultrasound-guided aspiration, followed by ERCP and stenting.

Common bile duct injury: The most common cause of bile duct injury is laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Management

* If detected on table with

* Duct injury less than 3 mm or those draining less than single segment of the liver: Ligation

* Lateral injury—Duct injury more than 4 mm or those draining multiple hepatic segments: Repair using T-tube.

* Transection with minimal loss of duct length: Repair using T-tube is used; in case of extensive loss of duct length, billiary enteric anastomosis is performed.

* Cystic duct leaks can be treated by the percutaneous drainage of intra-abdominal collection and endoscopic biliary drainage.

* Post-operative detection of leak: Major biliary leakage is usually seen 2 to 10 days after cholecystectomy. Patients usually present with pain in the abdominal region, fever, and, in some cases, bilious ascitic fluid.

* Jaundice is usually mild. Leukocytosis and abnormal liver function tests, particularly elevations in the serum levels of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, are common.

* Radiological workup: Upon presentation, transabdominal ultrasonography is initially performed to define the extent of possible bile leak.

* For definitive leaks, ultrasound-guided aspiration is performed; alternatively, the collection is drained and a transhepatic biliary drain is placed. After 6–8 weeks, the definitive repair is ascertained.

* Ultrasonography confirmation and aspiration of the leak is followed by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and stenting.

questions.text: GCS of a patient who had a road-traffic accident is 10. Using the GCS scoring system, the head injury of this patient is classified as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Moderate traumatic brain injury

Using the Glasgow Coma Scale score(GCS) , the head injury of this patient with a GCS 10 is classified as moderate.

GCS is used in the assessment of patients with a head injury. The maximum GCS score is 15 (E4 V5 M6).

Based on the GCS score, the head injury sustained can be classified as follows:

GCS Score

* 13-15 represent mild injury

* 9-12 represent moderate injury

* ≤8 represent severe injury

* If an area cannot be assessed, no numerical score is given for that region, and it is considered “non-testable." (NT)

* In case of endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy, the verbal component of the score is denoted as NT.

Half-hourly for 2 hours,
Then 1-hourly for 4 hours,
Then 2-hourly thereafter.
Should the patient with GCS equal to 15 deteriorate at any time after the initial 2-hour period, observations should revert to half-hourly and follow the original frequency schedule.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the investigation and the lesion depicted in the image given below.
options: Retrograde cystourethrogram with membranous urethra stricture
Retrograde cystourethrogram with penile urethral stricture
Micturating cystourethrography with prostratic urethra stricture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retrograde cystourethrogram with penile urethral stricture

The given image shows retrograde cystourethrogram with findings consistent with penile urethral stricture.

The male urethra can be visualized by retrograde urethrography (RGU) or voiding cystourethrogram (VCU), also known as micturating cystourethrogram (MCU).

In RGU, the urethra is visualized with the instillation of contrast into the anterior urethra (penile urethra and bulbar urethra). It is helpful for diagnosing anterior urethral abnormalities.

The following image shows an RGU with bulbar urethral stricture:

In VCU, after injecting contrast into the bladder using a Foleys catheter, the posterior urethra (membranous urethra and prostatic urethra) is visualized during micturition. It is helpful for diagnosing posterior urethral abnormalities and bladder abnormalities. It is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and posterior urethral valve.

The following image shows a voiding cystourethrogram in a patient with grade V VUR:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the pathology in the given radiograph of a newborn.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Imperforate anus

The given radiograph of a newborn shows imperforate anus/anal atresia.

Anorectal atresia, also known as imperforate anus, refers to a spectrum of abnormalities of the rectum and anus. There are many possible abnormalities as follows:

* The absence of an anal opening.

* The anal opening is in the wrong place.

* A connection, or fistula, joining the intestine and urinary system.

* A connection joining the intestine and vagina.

* In females, the intestine can join with the urinary system and vagina in a single opening, known as a cloaca.

Incidence is one in every 5,000 live births.

The newborn presents with an inability to pass meconium, abdominal distension, anal dimple, and sometimes passing meconium per urethra. It is divided into low intermediate and high lyings according to the Wingspread classification. Diagnosis is done using Wangenstein invertogram . Treatment is surgical.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Split thickness skin graft for wound closure on thigh includes:
options: Epidermis and variable parts of dermis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epidermis and variable parts of dermis

Split-thickness skin graft for wound closure on the thigh includes epidermis and variable parts of the dermis.

Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ) consists of the whole of the epidermis and only a portion of the dermis.

Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft): include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles.

Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft:

* Large grafts can be harvested.

* In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such as burns.

* Uptake is good. Meshing can be done, i.e. small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this and this improves graft take-up.

* Meshing also allows the graft to expand.

Advantages of a full-thickness skin graft over split skin graft:

* It has a lesser degree of post-graft contraction

* Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements.

The most preferable donor site is buttocks in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children. The most commonly used donor site is the thigh.

* The graft is taken from the donor site with a handheld Humby knife or electric dermatome.

* Grafts are perforated to allow exudates to escape and improve ‘take’. It can further be meshed to allow expansion.

* Grafts will take up only on the beds which are vascularized, hence preparation of wound bed is an essential step.

* Skin grafts are completely dependent on nutrition on the tissue over which they are placed and can heal well over muscle, perichondrium, and periosteum. They do not take well over bone or cartilage or on tissue that has been irradiated or infected or is hypovascular.

* A clean healthy wound bed with a meshed graft tied in place to stop movement will encourage take.

* The presence of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci is a contraindication in grafting as it can destroy split grafts completely and also convert donors to full-thickness defects.

* The donor area is dressed appropriately and the dressing is opened after 10 days and not earlier.

The given image shows Humby's knife. The average thickness of the graft obtained from a Humbys knife is 0.3 mm.

Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft

The take of skin graft occurs in three phases:

* Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries.

* Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses

* Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft

Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later.

Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the ideal time and method of removing hair before surgery to avoid surgical site infection?
options: On the OT table with electric hair clippers
With a razor 24 hours before surgery
With a hair removal cream on the previous day
On the OT table with a razor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. On the OT table with electric hair clippers

To avoid surgical site infection, hair should be removed on the OT table with electric hair clippers.

Measures to decrease the incidence of surgical site infections (SSIs)

Patient preparation:

1) Smoking cessation four to six weeks prior to elective surgery is recommended to decrease the incidence of pulmonary complications.

2) Bowel preparation prior to abdominal surgeries is expected to decrease the incidence of SSIs.

Infection control:

1) Timely administration of preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis.

2) All surgical team members must practice appropriate surgical hand hygiene measures.

3) Surgeons and other team members within the premises of the operation theater should routinely wear barrier clothing such as scrubs, caps, and gowns.

4) Preoperatively, the patient must be advised to use topical mupirocin and bathe with chlorhexidine to aid in Staphylococcus aureus decolonization.

5) Shaving hair with razors at the operative site is not advised. If hair removal is absolutely necessary, it may be performed with hair clippers.

Miscellaneous perioperative measures:

1) Maintain normothermic OT

2) Ensure laminar airflow

3) Minimise red cell transfusions

4) Ensure adequate glycemic control.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are storage symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia? * Urgency * Enuresis * Hesitancy * Frequency * Dribbling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 4

Urgency, enuresis and frequency are storage symptoms.

Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) can be classified as:

Storage
Voiding

• Frequency (earliest symptom in BPH)
• Nocturia
• Urgency
• Urge incontinence
• Nocturnal incontinence (enuresis)

• Hesitancy
• Poor flow
• Intermittent stream
• Dribbling
• Sensation of poor bladder emptying
• Episodes of near retention

Clinical features of BPH:

* Urinary urgency

* Urinary nocturia

* Urinary frequency

* Urinary incontinence, terminal dribbling

* Abrupt starting and stopping of the urinary stream

* Splitting of the voiding stream

Physical examination reveals a smooth enlarged and non-tender prostate. Lab investigations reveal a normal PSA (prostate-specific antigen). Diagnosis is made based on clinical presentation and a lack of lab findings suggestive of malignancy (elevated PSA). A biopsy is rarely indicated.

Conservative treatment is recommended for men with mild symptoms, flow rate >10ml/s, and good bladder emptying with residual urine <100ml.

Medical management includes alpha-adrenergic blocking agents that inhibit the contraction of smooth muscle that is found in the prostate. Tamsulosin is an adrenoreceptor antagonist with receptor selectivity at α1A. It is used in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia.

The other class of drugs is the 5α-reductase inhibitors, which inhibit the conversion of testosterone to DHT, the most active form of androgen. Finasteride is a 5α-reductase enzyme inhibitor. It is effective in the treatment of palpable enlarged prostate. These drugs result in a 25% shrinkage of the prostate gland.

Indications for surgical management:

* Lower urinary tract symptoms that are refractory to medical therapy

* Refractory urinary retention

* Recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI)

* Hematuria

* Stone formation

* Hydronephrosis, hydroureter with renal functional impairment

Surgical management involves the use of the transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). Laser ablative techniques using holmium YAG can also be done.

Storage symptoms are seen in conditions where the bladder is irritated. Voiding symptoms are common in conditions causing bladder outlet obstruction. In benign prostatic hyperplasia, both storage and voiding symptoms are present.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following CT findings is not an indication to perform angiography in a splenic trauma patient under conservative management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subcapsular hematoma covering 40% surface area

In a splenic trauma patient under conservative management, angiography is indicated if the CT shows a high-grade injury rather than a low-grade injury (subcapsular hematoma covering 40% surface area is a grade II injury).

In splenic trauma patients that are managed conservatively, angiography is indicated if there is the presence of the following CT findings:

* Contrast extravasation

* Presence of pseudoaneurysm

* Significant hemoperitoneum

* High-grade injury

* Evidence of vascular injury

Management of Splenic trauma:

Grade I and II injuries:

* They are usually hemodynamically stable and are managed non-operatively.

* Initially, these patients are managed conservatively with regular monitoring of vitals and serial CECT.

* If the grade of injury is found to increase, then angiography and embolization of the bleeding vessel are done to achieve hemostasis.

* If angiography and embolization fail to achieve hemostasis, or if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable or if there is a contrast blush, then a splenorrhaphy is done.

Grade III injuries that are hemodynamically stable are managed like that of Grades I and II, while those that are hemodynamically unstable are managed like that of Grades IV and V.

Grade IV and V injuries: These patients are usually hemodynamically unstable and splenectomy is done.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following has the least risk of developing into invasive ductal carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Squamous metaplasia

Squamous metaplasia has the least risk of developing into invasive ductal carcinoma.

Pearl PF0189: Relative risk of invasive breast carcinoma based on pathological examination of benign breast tissue

No increased risk

* Adenosis, sclerosing or florid

* Apocrine metaplasia

* Cysts, macro and/or micro

* Duct ectasia

* Fibroadenoma

* Fibrosis

* Hyperplasia

* Mastitis (inflammation)

* Periductal mastitis

* Squamous metaplasia

Slightly increased risk (1.5–2 times)

* Hyperplasia, moderate or florid, solid, or papillary

* Papilloma with a fibrovascular core

Moderately increased risk (5 times)

* Atypical hyperplasia (ductal or lobular)

Insufficient data to assign a risk

* Solitary papilloma of lactiferous sinus

* Radial scar lesion

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following incisions would be used during an open appendicectomy procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

McBurney's incision (also called gridiron incision), marked 3 in the image, is popularly used for open appendicectomy. It is an oblique incision (superolateral to inferomedial) passing along McBurney's point.

The major anterior abdominal incisions have been illustrated below:

* 1 is Kocher incision - A subcostal incision used to gain access for gall bladder and/or biliary tree pathology.

* 2 is midline incision - The most common incision for laparotomy, a vertical incision that follows the linea alba which is particularly favoured in diagnostic laparotomy, as they allow wide access to most of the abdominal cavity.

* 3 is McBurney's incision (also called gridiron incision) is an oblique incision (superolateral to inferomedial) passing along McBurney's point. It is popularly used for open appendicectomy.

* 4 is a battle incision a lower right paramedian incision but placed more laterally than the standard paramedian incision. It is suitable for dealing with acute appendicitis and pathologies in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen.

* 5 is Lanz incision, a transverse or skin crease incision for appendicitis, 2 cm below the umbilicus, centred on the midclavicular–mid-inguinal line. Due to its continuation with Langer’s lines, the Lanz incision produces much more aesthetically pleasing results with reduced scarring.

* 6 is a paramedian incision - this incision is used to access much of the lateral viscera, such as the kidneys, spleen, and adrenal glands.

* 7 is transverse incision - A supraumbilical transverse incision offers excellent exposure of the upper abdomen. A transverse incision may be superior to a midline incision in terms of recovery and complications postoperatively.

* 8 is Rutherford Morrison incision, an oblique muscle cutting incision used for access to the sigmoid colon and pelvis in patients where the midline is scarred due to previous surgery. Rutherford Morison’s incision is useful if the appendix is para- or retrocaecal and fixed. It is essentially an oblique muscle-cutting incision with its lower end over McBurney’s point and extending obliquely upwards and laterally as necessary

* 9 is Pfannenstiel incision - An infraumbilical transverse incision in the lower abdomen, often used for gynecological and obstetric procedures.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the best investigation to establish a diagnosis of GERD?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring

24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring is the ‘gold standard’ to establish a diagnosis of GERD.

* Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations are the most important manometric findings in GERD.

24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring in GERD:

* In the proximal esophagus (15 cm above the LES), acid exposure normally occurs less than 1% of the time.

* In the distal esophagus (5 cm above the LES), it normally occurs less than 4% of the time.

De Meester score

* An overall score is obtained with the use of a formula that assigns a weight to each item according to its capacity to cause esophageal injury.

* A value greater than 14.7 indicates reflux.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common deficiency observed after gastric bypass/bariatric surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iron
