Iron deficiency is the most common deficiency observed following gastric bypass or bariatric surgery. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, bypass procedures lead to or exacerbate an existing deficiency by impairing absorption. It is more common in the Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) and biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD/DS) procedures than in sleeve gastrectomy (SG).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the next step in the management of an old patient who has undergone complete excision of glioblastoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Radiotherapy

Standard treatment post-surgical resection of glioblastoma includes radiotherapy in older patients. Radiation alone is effective as a single-modality therapy in the elderly owing to the survival benefit of radiation. Moreover, the combined-modality therapy of Chemoradiation has increased the risk of Neurotoxicity.

It is used in combination with temozolomide chemotherapy in younger individuals. Temozolomide is used as a first-line agent for the management of glioblastoma multiforme. It is used for newly diagnosed cases along with radiotherapy and also used for maintenance therapy. Bevacizumab, which is a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) antibody may be used in the treatment of recurrent glioblastoma.

Glioblastoma is the most common adult primary intracranial neoplasm. It affects people usually in the sixth or seventh decade. These tumors may arise de novo or may result from a malignant transformation of lower-grade astrocytomas. Mutations of Isocitrate Dehydrogenase (IDH) and Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor gene (EGFR) are implicated in the pathogenesis of the same.

Clinically, patients usually present with headaches, seizures due to raised intracranial pressure or focal neurologic deficits depending upon the site involved.

Grossly, glioblastomas are found infiltrating the brain tissue and are poorly delineated. They have greyish tumor cells with central yellowish necrosis and multiple areas of hemorrhages. Microscopically, they are composed of poorly differentiated pleomorphic astrocytic cells with nuclear atypia and high mitotic activity. Necrosis and florid microvascular proliferation are characteristic. They exhibit pseudopalisading—dense arrangement of tumor cells lining up around the foci of tumor necrosis.

According to the WHO Classification of CNS diseases 2016, glioblastomas are classified as follows:

* Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype:

* About 90% of cases

* Primary or de novo glioblastoma

* Over 55 years of age

* Worst prognosis

* Glioblastoma, IDH-mutant:

* About 10% of cases

* Secondary glioblastoma, with a history of prior lower-grade diffuse glioma

* Arises in younger patients

* Poor prognosis

* Glioblastoma, NOS (not otherwise specified), where full IDH evaluation cannot be performed.

The given histological image shows foci of necrosis with pseudo-palisading of malignant nuclei and endothelial cell proliferation, which are characteristic of glioblastoma (previously called glioblastoma multiforme).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Internal mammary artery

The left internal mammary artery (LIMA) provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). The most important criterion in conduit selection is graft patency. The conduit with the highest patency rate is the left internal mammary artery or internal thoracic artery.

Left internal mammary artery > Radial artery > long saphenous vein represents the correct order of graft patency in a patient undergoing a CABG procedure.

Venous grafts:

* The long saphenous vein is the most common vein used as a conduit as it is straightforward to harvest, provides good length, and is easy to handle.

* The ten-year patency rate for long saphenous vein grafts is reported to be 50–60 percent.

Arterial grafts:

* The Left internal mammary artery (LIMA) or internal thoracic artery has become the conduit of choice for the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. The radial artery can be used as a second or alternative arterial bypass graft. Other arterial bypass grafts include the gastroepiploic artery and the inferior epigastric artery.

* Long patency rates of >98 percent have been reported.

Pearl PF1920: Indications for Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)

Class I indications for CABG from the American College of Cardiology(ACC) and American Heart Association(AHA).

* Left main disease

* Three-vessel disease with or without proximal LAD disease

* Two vessel disease with proximal LAD disease

* Survivors of sudden cardiac death with presumed ischemia-mediated VT

Other indications for CABG include the following:

* Disabling angina

* Ongoing ischemia in the setting of a non–ST-segment elevation (MI) that is unresponsive to medical therapy

* Poor LV function but with viable, nonfunctioning myocardium above the anatomic defect that can be revascularized

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following represents type III choledochal cyst from the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. C

The figure marked C in the given image represents choledochal cyst type III, a cystic dilation of the intramural common bile duct, within the wall of the duodenum, known as choledochoceles.

Choledochal cysts:

Choledochal cysts are congenital cystic dilations of the intrahepatic and/or extrahepatic biliary tree. They present with a triad of jaundice, a palpable upper quadrant mass, and abdominal pain. They are commonly seen in females.

Choledochal cyst is classified into five types:

The original classification for choledochal cysts by Alonso–Lej, and colleagues has been modified by Todani and associates to include intrahepatic cystic disease.

* Type I: is a simple cyst that can involve any portion of the CBD.

* Type II: It is described as an isolated diverticulum arising from the wall of the CBD

* Type III: They arise from the intraduodenal portion of the common bile duct and are also known as choledochocele.

* Type IVA: The cysts consist of multiple dilatations of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.

* Type IVB: These choledochal cysts are multiple dilatations involving only the extrahepatic bile ducts.

* Type V (Caroli’s disease): It consists of multiple dilatations limited to the intrahepatic bile ducts.

Caroli's disease:

Caroli’s Disease is an autosomal recessive condition of multifocal cystic dilatation of segmental intrahepatic bile ducts. According to Todani's classification, it is classified as a type V choledochal cyst.

USG may show dilated intrahepatic bile ducts in these individuals. The beaded appearance of intrahepatic bile ducts on the HIDA scan and the central dot sign on CT are characteristic findings associated with Caroli's disease. MRCP is the investigation of choice.

Treatment options:

* Type I—excision of the cyst with its mucosa and reconstruction by Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy.

* In type II—excision of the diverticulum and suturing of the CBD wall can be done

* Type III cysts represent Choledochoceles, consisting of cystic dilation of the intramural common bile duct, within the wall of the duodenum. As type III cysts are associated with the lowest malignancy risk of any choledochal cyst, endoscopic sphincterotomy followed by surveillance is generally recommended over cyst excision with pancreaticoduodenectomy.

* Type IV, if the cyst is adherent to the portal vein posteriorly, that part of the cyst wall over the portal vein is left behind. But mucosa of the part should be removed. This is named Lily’s operation.

* Excision of all cystic tissues and reconstruction of the biliary tree is recommended for extrahepatic biliary involvement as in Type 4B and in case of intrahepatic involvement, an additional segmental resection of the liver may be required which can be removed by hepatectomy.

* Liver transplantation is the preferred treatment of choice in type IV and type V.

Pearl PF1150: Classification of Choledochal Cysts

Type

Feature

Type I

The most common choledochal cyst type; it involves only the extrahepatic biliary tree and is generally a fusiform dilation.

Type II

Saccular diverticulum off the common bile duct and may be mistaken for an accessory gallbladder.

Type III

A cystic dilation of the intramural common bile duct, within the wall of the duodenum, known as choledochoceles.

Type IV

Type IVa: Cysts involving the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree

Type IVb: Multiple cysts limited to the extrahepatic biliary tree.

Type V

Also known as Caroli disease, involve the intrahepatic ducts only.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the hospital with symptoms of an inguinal hernia. During the operation, the surgeon observes a segment of necrotic bowel in the hernial sac. What is the appropriate course of action for resection and anastomosis of a necrotic bowel seen during surgery?
options: The surgeon must use chromic catgut.
The surgeon must not include the submucosa in the sutures.
The surgeon must use the single layer, extramucosal suture technique.
The surgeon must use the single-layer seromuscular suture technique.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The surgeon must use the single layer, extramucosal suture technique.

Single-layer extramucosal intestinal anastomosis is the preferred technique for bowel resection and anastomosis because it incorporates the submucosa—the strongest layer of the bowel wall—while minimizing tissue ischemia, luminal narrowing, and foreign-body reaction.

• Submucosa is the holding layer of the intestine and must be included in the sutures for a secure anastomosis.
• Extramucosal (serosubmucosal) sutures approximate the bowel edges without penetrating the mucosa.
• A single-layer anastomosis is associated with:

• Comparable or superior strength to two-layer techniques
• Reduced tissue trauma and ischemia
• Shorter operative time
• Lower risk of luminal narrowing

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

• A. Use chromic catgut → Not mandatory; modern intestinal anastomoses commonly use absorbable synthetic sutures (e.g., polyglactin, PDS).
• B. Must not include the submucosa → Incorrect. The submucosa must be included because it provides the greatest tensile strength.
• D. Single-layer seromuscular technique → Does not reliably include the submucosa and is therefore less ideal.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-year-old child underwent surgery, and the wound took one month to heal. Deficiency of which of the following micronutrients is the most likely cause of delayed wound healing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zinc

Zinc is an essential trace element required for DNA and RNA synthesis, cell proliferation, collagen formation, protein synthesis, and epithelialization, making it critical for normal wound healing. Zinc deficiency results in delayed wound healing, impaired immune function, dermatitis, alopecia, growth retardation, and impaired taste (hypogeusia).

Why not the other options?

• A. Copper: Required for lysyl oxidase, which cross-links collagen and elastin. Deficiency causes connective tissue defects, anemia, and depigmented hair but is a less common cause of delayed wound healing.
• C. Magnesium: Important for enzyme function and neuromuscular activity but is not a classic cause of delayed wound healing.
• D. Iron: Essential for hemoglobin synthesis and hydroxylation of collagen, but deficiency primarily causes microcytic hypochromic anemia rather than isolated delayed wound healing.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old girl presents to the OPD with complaints of a progressively increasing swelling on the dorsum of the left wrist. The swelling is cystic and nontender on examination and becomes more prominent on plantar flexion of the wrist. The swelling is 2 cm × 1 cm in size. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ganglion cyst

A ganglion cyst is the most common soft tissue swelling of the hand and wrist. It is a benign, mucin-filled cyst arising from the joint capsule or tendon sheath. The patient has the classic features:

• Young adult
• Dorsal wrist swelling
• Cystic and non-tender
• More prominent on palmar (volar) flexion of the wrist

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Sebaceous cyst: Occurs in hair-bearing skin, has a central punctum, and is uncommon on the dorsum of the wrist.
• C. Dermoid cyst: Congenital lesion usually occurring along embryonic fusion lines (e.g., lateral eyebrow, midline), not typically over the wrist.
• D. Epidermoid cyst: Usually arises from epidermal inclusion, is attached to the skin, and is less common on the dorsal wrist.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presented to the otolaryngology clinic with complaints of pain and swelling in the right side of his face. Upon examination, the physician noted swelling in the parotid gland, which is located in the cheek area. The patient also reported that his symptoms worsened when he ate food, and he had lost his appetite due to the discomfort. The physician ordered an ultrasound imaging of as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sialolithiasis

The diagnosis is A) Sialolithiasis (salivary gland stone).

• Painful swelling in parotid gland
• Pain worsens while eating
• Loss of appetite due to discomfort

When you eat, saliva production increases → if a duct is blocked by a stone, saliva cannot flow → pressure builds up → pain and swelling.

USG shows: Hyperechoic calculus with posterior acoustic shadowing with associated duct dilation and swollen hyperechoic gland (Typical for salivary calculi)

B) Foreign body

• Rare in salivary glands
• No typical pain during meals

C) Osteoma of floor of mouth

• Bony growth
• Does not cause parotid swelling with eating

D) Cervical lymphadenopathy

• Swollen lymph nodes
• Not related to salivation or meals

Most stones occur in the submandibular gland (\~80–90%) because:

• Saliva is thicker
• Wharton duct is long and uphill

But parotid stones can also occur, which is the case here.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presented to the dermatologist with a small lesion on her right nasolabial fold. Upon examination, the dermatologist noted a 0.4-cm nodule with a smooth surface and well-defined borders. The nodule was located on the upper forehead, just above the eyebrows. It was excised and a pathological examination was done. The image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Basal cell carcinoma

Location: Forehead / face (sun-exposed area)

Pearly nodule with well-defined borders = think Basal Cell Carcinoma. Nevus

The slide shows:

• Nests of basaloid cells
• Peripheral palisading (cells at the edge line up like a fence)
• Tumor islands in dermis
• Clefting artifact between tumor and stroma

These are hallmark histological features of BCC.

B) Melanoma

• Shows atypical melanocytes
• Pagetoid spread; Often pigmented
• Not basaloid nests with palisading

C) Squamous cell carcinoma

• Shows keratin pearls
• Intercellular bridges
• Cells are squamoid, not basaloid

D) Nevus

• Benign melanocytic nests
• No peripheral palisading

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presented with a slowly growing, mobile, variably firm swelling for 2 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parotid tumor

Typical features of pleomorphic adenoma:

• Preauricular swelling (in front of the ear)
• Slow growing (months–years)
• Painless
• Mobile but limited vertically (because of parotid fascia)
• Firm or rubbery consistency

Swelling below and in front of the ear, exactly where the parotid gland lies.

Why the Other Options Are Wrong

❌A) Dermoid cyst

Usually midline (like submental region).; Present since childhood .

Not typically located in the parotid region.

❌C) Sebaceous cyst

Located in skin, not deep gland.

Shows punctum (black dot) ; More superficial and fluctuant.

❌D) Cervical lymph node

Usually associated with infection or malignancy.

Location typically along SCM, not preauricular.

| Feature | Diagnosis

| ------- | ---------

| Most common salivary tumor | Pleomorphic adenoma

| Most common malignant salivary tumor | Mucoepidermoid carcinoma

| Facial nerve palsy + parotid mass | Suggests malignancy

FNAC aids diagnosis of pleomorphic adenoma; treatment is superficial parotidectomy to prevent recurrence.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe pain, swelling and redness in scrotal area. He undergoes a surgical procedure for the same. Based on the image below, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fournier's gangrene

The postoperative picture shows exposed testes after radical debridement, characteristic of Fournier gangrene.

Other listed conditions do not require such extensive debridement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman is diagnosed with locally advanced breast carcinoma. The multidisciplinary tumor board recommends systemic chemotherapy before definitive surgery to reduce tumor size and improve the likelihood of breast-conserving surgery. This treatment strategy is best described as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is systemic chemotherapy administered before definitive surgery (or other local therapy). Its goals are to downstage the tumor, improve resectability, facilitate organ conservation, eradicate micrometastatic disease early, and assess in vivo tumor chemosensitivity. In breast cancer, achieving a pathological complete response (pCR) is associated with a favorable prognosis, especially in HER2-positive and triple-negative tumors.

Why not the other options?

• B. Adjuvant chemotherapy: Given after surgery to eliminate residual microscopic disease and reduce recurrence.
• C. Definitive chemotherapy: Used as the primary treatment without planned surgery, such as in certain leukemias, lymphomas, or metastatic disease.
• D. Concurrent chemoradiotherapy: Chemotherapy administered simultaneously with radiotherapy, not before surgery.

High-Yield Pearl:

"Neo = Before, Adjuvant = After."

Common indications for neoadjuvant chemotherapy:

• Locally advanced or inflammatory breast cancer
• Osteosarcoma
• Rectal carcinoma (often with radiotherapy)
• Esophageal carcinoma
• Muscle-invasive bladder cancer
• Advanced ovarian cancer
• Wilms tumor

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old destitute is brought to the emergency with a foul-smelling wound on his left foot. On examination, the wound is seen to have maggots with a lot of necrotic tissue. What is the class of this wound according to the CDC wound classification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Class 4

According to the CDC wound classification, wounds are classified into four classes:

1. Class 1 – Clean: Uninfected wound; no inflammation; respiratory, gastrointestinal, genital, or urinary tract not entered.
2. Class 2 – Clean-contaminated: Controlled entry into respiratory, gastrointestinal, genital, or urinary tract without unusual contamination.
3. Class 3 – Contaminated: Open, fresh accidental wounds, major breaks in sterile technique, or gross spillage from the GI tract.
4. Class 4 – Dirty/Infected: Old traumatic wounds with devitalized tissue or wounds with existing infection/pus/perforation.

This patient’s foul-smelling wound with maggots and extensive necrotic tissue represents a dirty/infected wound → Class 4.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old female presents to the emergency with pain, swelling and redness over the left foot following a trivial trauma 3 days back. On examination, the swelling over the left foot is poorly localised; local tenderness and erythema are present and crepitus is absent; distal pulsations are palpable. The most likely clinical diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cellulitis

This patient has the classical features of cellulitis, an acute bacterial infection involving the skin and subcutaneous tissue.

• Trivial trauma preceding infection
• Pain, swelling, and redness for 3 days
• Poorly localized swelling (diffuse inflammation)
• Local tenderness and erythema
• No crepitus (argues against necrotizing fasciitis)
• Distal pulses palpable (rules out vascular compromise and makes compartment syndrome less likely)

Why not the other options?

• A. Compartment syndrome ❌

• Presents with severe pain out of proportion to examination, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, paresthesia, and later absent pulses.
• Redness and diffuse erythema are not typical early features.

• C. Abscess ❌

• Usually presents as a localized, fluctuant, tender swelling with a well-defined collection of pus.
• The swelling here is poorly localized.

• D. Fasciitis (Necrotizing fasciitis) ❌

• Rapidly progressive infection with severe pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, skin discoloration, bullae, and often crepitus (if gas-forming organisms are present).
• This patient has no crepitus or signs of severe systemic illness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old lady underwent total abdominal hysterectomy. On the 3rd postoperative day, she suddenly became breathless while returning from washroom. Her blood pressure was 80/50 mmHg. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thromboembolism

• A patient who develops sudden breathlessness and hypotension on the 3rd postoperative day after major surgery is most likely to have pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) due to deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
• Major surgery, immobility, increasing age, and malignancy are important risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE).

Why not other options?

• A. Postural hypotension: Causes dizziness or transient syncope on standing, not sudden severe dyspnea with shock.
• B. Secondary haemorrhage: Usually presents with bleeding, falling hemoglobin, tachycardia, and abdominal distension rather than sudden respiratory distress.
• D. Transient ischaemic attack (TIA): Presents with focal neurological deficits, not isolated breathlessness and hypotension.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A diabetic patient presents with sudden-onset perineal pain. On examination, foul-smelling discharge, and necrotic tissue as seen in the image is noted. Which of the following is true about the given condition?
options: Anti-gas gangrene serum indicated for all cases
Urinary diversion is the next step
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection

The condition shown is Fournier gangrene.

• Sudden perineal pain
• Foul-smelling discharge
• Necrotic black tissue
• Occurs in diabetics

This is a rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the perineum and scrotum,

Most common in diabetic or immunocompromised patients.

D) Mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection

Fournier gangrene is polymicrobial.

Common organisms include:

• Aerobes → Escherichia coli, Streptococcus
• Anaerobes → Bacteroides, Clostridium
• Others → Klebsiella, Proteus

These bacteria cause → rapid fascial necrosis gas formation foul smell  A) Anti-gas

A)   Gangrene serum indicated for all cases ❌

Anti-gas gangrene serum is used for clostridial gas gangrene, which is:

But Fournier gangrene is polymicrobial, not purely clostridial.

B) Urinary diversion is the next step ❌

Urinary diversion (suprapubic catheter) may be done later if urethra is involved, but the first and most important step is:

Emergency surgical debridement  Delay in debridement can cause rapid spread

So urinary diversion is not the immediate next step.

C) Bilateral orchiectomy must be done ❌

In Fournier gangrene Testes are usually spared

Reason: Testes receive blood supply from the testicular artery directly from the abdominal

❌ Orchiectomy is unnecessary.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A middle aged female with bilateral ptosis and muscle weakness getting worse by evening undergoes CT scan of the chest which reveals the presence of a thymoma. Which of the following receptor is likely to be affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Postsynaptic ACh receptor

The clinical features are classic for myasthenia gravis associated with thymoma.

It is caused by autoantibodies directed against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

This reduces neuromuscular transmission, leading to fatigable muscle weakness and ptosis.

Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies are seen in Lambert–Eaton syndrome, not myasthenia gravis.

| Feature | Myasthenia Gravis | Lambert-Eaton

| ------- | ----------------- | -------------

| Target | Postsynaptic ACh receptor | Presynaptic Ca channels

| Weakness | Worse with activity | Improves with activity

| Reflexes | Normal | Reduced

| Tumor association | Thymoma | Small cell lung carcinoma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent abdominal surgery during which a surgical gauze was inadvertently left inside the abdomen. The patient subsequently developed septic shock and died. This incident is best classified as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Never event

A never event is a serious, preventable patient safety incident that should never occur if appropriate safety systems are in place. Leaving a surgical gauze (retained surgical item/gossypiboma) inside a patient after surgery is a classic example of a never event.

• Retained surgical items (e.g., gauze, sponge, instrument) are completely preventable through proper surgical counts and safety checklists.
• In this case, the retained gauze led to sepsis, septic shock, and death, making it a classic never event.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sentinel event: Incorrect in this question. Although the patient’s death qualifies as a sentinel event, the emphasis is on the retained surgical gauze, which is specifically classified as a never event.
• C. Adverse event: Too broad; it includes any injury caused by medical management and may not be preventable.
• D. Active event: Not a recognized patient safety classification.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A surgeon is about to start a laparoscopic procedure on a patient. The floor nurse asks the surgeon about the identity of the patient, site of the procedure to be performed and any anticipated critical events during the surgery. These questions are a part of the:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. WHO surgical safety checklist

The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist is a standardized checklist developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to improve patient safety and reduce surgical morbidity and mortality. It promotes effective communication among the surgical team and ensures that critical safety steps are not missed before, during, and after surgery.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Universal precautions checklist: Refers to infection control measures (e.g., hand hygiene, PPE, safe handling of sharps), not surgical team communication.
• B. Nurses safety checklist: No standard checklist by this name is used internationally.
• C. MCI patient safety checklist: There is no recognized Medical Council of India (MCI) surgical safety checklist.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are features of a major surgical site infection (SSI), except:
options: Excessive pain at the surgical site
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Excessive pain at the surgical site

A major surgical site infection (SSI) is suggested by features indicating significant local infection and/or systemic involvement.

• (a) Significant amount of pus — Correct: A large amount of purulent discharge strongly suggests a significant SSI.
• (b) Delayed return home — Correct: Major SSI can prolong hospitalization and delay discharge.
• (c) Excessive pain at the surgical site — Incorrect / Not a defining criterion: Pain can occur with SSI, but excessive pain alone is not a characteristic criterion used to define a major SSI.
• (d) Patient being systemically ill — Correct: Fever, tachycardia, malaise, or other systemic features suggest a significant/major SSI.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Distributive shock is described by which of the following patterns of cardiovascular responses? 1. Vasodilatation 2. Reduced peripheral vascular resistance 3. Inadequate ‘afterload’ 4. Low cardiac output Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Why is D correct?

• 1. Vasodilatation ✓

• The hallmark of distributive shock is generalized peripheral vasodilatation due to inflammatory mediators or loss of sympathetic tone.

• 2. Reduced peripheral vascular resistance ✓

• Vasodilatation causes a marked decrease in systemic vascular resistance (SVR), leading to hypotension.

• 3. Inadequate ‘afterload’ ✓

• Because SVR is reduced, the afterload decreases, making it difficult to maintain adequate arterial pressure despite preserved cardiac function.

• 4. Low cardiac output ✗

• Early distributive shock usually has a normal or increased cardiac output due to compensatory tachycardia and reduced afterload. Cardiac output may decrease only in the late stages.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a Veress needle is inserted through the umbilicus. After insufflating a small amount of CO₂, the insufflation pressure rises abruptly, and crepitus is felt around the umbilical port. What is the most likely cause?
options: Veress needle failed to enter the peritoneal cavity
Over-insufflation of CO₂ into the peritoneal cavity
Injury to the inferior epigastric artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Veress needle failed to enter the peritoneal cavity

During creation of pneumoperitoneum for laparoscopic surgery, a sudden rise in insufflation pressure immediately after CO₂ insufflation, along with crepitus around the umbilical port, indicates that the Veress needle is in the preperitoneal/subcutaneous tissue rather than the peritoneal cavity. CO₂ accumulates in the subcutaneous tissues, causing subcutaneous emphysema.

• Failure of the Veress needle to penetrate the peritoneum leads to extraperitoneal insufflation.
• CO₂ enters the subcutaneous tissue, producing:

• High initial insufflation pressure (>10–15 mmHg)
• Poor gas flow
• Abdominal distension does not occur appropriately
• Palpable crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema) around the port site

Why not the other options?

• A. Veress needle punctured the bowel: May cause bowel injury, feculent aspirate, or later peritonitis, but does not typically present with immediate subcutaneous crepitus and high insufflation pressure.
• C. Over-insufflation of CO₂ into the peritoneal cavity: Causes elevated intra-abdominal pressure but does not produce localized subcutaneous emphysema around the port.
• D. Injury to the inferior epigastric artery: Causes abdominal wall bleeding or hematoma, not crepitus or high insufflation pressure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Giving TPN (total para-enteral nutrition) in a patient in ICU with metabolic syndrome predisposes to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperglycaemia

Concept: TPN (Total Parenteral Nutrition)  contains a high amount of glucose as its main energy source.

In patients with metabolic syndrome:

• There is insulin resistance
• Cells cannot utilize glucose efficiently

So when large amounts of glucose are infused via TPN, the result is: hyperglycaemia.

Complications of TPN

| Complication | Reason

| ------------ | ------

| Hyperglycaemia | High glucose infusion

| Infection | Central venous catheter

| Electrolyte imbalance | Rapid metabolic shifts

| Refeeding syndrome | Sudden feeding in malnourished patients

| Liver dysfunction | Long-term TPN

Why other options are wrong

B. Reactive hypoglycaemia

Occurs with excess insulin, not with TPN.

C. Hyperlipidaemia

TPN does contain lipids→ But:  not the primary component (glucose is)

Lipid rise is less immediate and less prominent (  As compared to glucose imbalance)

Compared to glucose imbalance, this is not the most expected/important complication.

D. Hyperuricemia

Not directly related to TPN.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Good measure of systemic perfusion by ABG is by measurement of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Base deficit

Serum lactate and base deficit are the most reliable ABG-derived markers of systemic tissue perfusion. They reflect the adequacy of oxygen delivery to tissues and are widely used to assess the severity of shock, trauma, sepsis, and other states of tissue hypoperfusion.

When tissue oxygen delivery is inadequate, cells switch to anaerobic metabolism, resulting in lactate production and metabolic acidosis, which is reflected as an increased base deficit.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻): Reflects metabolic acid-base status but is a less sensitive indicator of tissue perfusion than lactate or base deficit.
• B. pH: May remain normal initially because of respiratory compensation and does not specifically indicate tissue perfusion.
• D. PCO₂: Reflects ventilation, not systemic tissue perfusion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the device in the image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. PEG tube

The PEG tube is a specialized device used for long-term feeding directly into the stomach, identified by its retention bolster and the presence of specific tools in the insertion kit.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the most common site of an intra-abdominal abscess:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Subhepatic space

The right subhepatic space (Morison’s pouch) is the most common site for intra-abdominal abscess formation due to dependent drainage and proximity to hepatobiliary pathology.

Common Causes of Subhepatic Abscess-

| Cause | Mechanism

| ----- | ---------

| Appendicitis | Spread of infection

| Perforated duodenal ulcer | Contamination

| Biliary infections | Ascending infection

| Post-operative complications | Leakage

| Space | Clinical significance

| ----- | ---------------------

| Subhepatic (Morison pouch) | Most common abscess

| Right subphrenic | Post hepatic surgery abscess

| Left subphrenic | Gastric / splenic pathology

| Pelvic pouch (Douglas) | Most dependent space in pelvis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of drain:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Closed suction drain

A Romovac drain is a closed suction drain that uses a vacuum system to actively remove fluids from a surgical site, reducing the risk of infection and aiding in the healing process.

A) Open drain

• Open to air (no collection system)
• High infection risk
• Example: corrugated rubber drain

Not used commonly now

B) Semi-open drain

• Partially closed but not fully sealed
• Some contamination risk

Not as safe/effective as closed suction

D) Penrose drain

• Soft rubber tube, passive drainage
• Works by gravity/capillary action, no suction
• Open type → higher infection risk

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the types of suturing technique, demonstrated in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Simple interrupted

Simple interrupted sutures use single, independent bites, ideal for skin closure and allowing removal of individual stitches.

Mattress sutures have four bites;

subcuticular sutures lie within dermis and are not externally visible.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In laparoscopic surgery, the angle between the right and the left working ports is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Manipulation angle

The manipulation angle represents the angle formed between the surgeon’s working instruments inside the abdomen. Optimal manipulation angle allows precise triangulation and effective ergonomic movement. The other angles relate to camera orientation.

Manipulation angle : Angle between working ports

Azimuth angle : Angle between telescope and working port

Elevation angle : Instrument angle from the horizontal

| Angle | Meaning

| ----- | -------

| Manipulation angle | Angle between working ports

| Azimuth angle | Horizontal orientation

| Elevation angle | Vertical instrument angle

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In patients undergoing elective colorectal surgery, when should parenteral antibiotic prophylaxis ideally be administered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Within 60 minutes before surgical incision

Parenteral antibiotic prophylaxis is most effective when adequate tissue concentrations are achieved at the time of skin incision. Therefore, prophylactic antibiotics should be administered within 60 minutes before surgical incision to minimize the risk of surgical site infection (SSI).

Why is B correct?

• Administration within 60 minutes before incision ensures optimal antibiotic levels in serum and tissues when bacterial contamination occurs during surgery.
• This is the recommended timing for most prophylactic antibiotics in elective colorectal surgery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Less than 10 minutes before incision: May not allow sufficient time to achieve effective tissue concentrations.
• C. 2 hours prior to surgery: Antibiotic levels may decline by the time of incision.
• D. 4 hours prior to surgery: Too early; inadequate tissue concentrations at the time of surgery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Open cardiac massage is what kind of wound?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Contaminated

Option B: Contaminated (open cardiac massage)

It is done in emergency situations (not planned, sterile surgery)

• Involves opening chest urgently (often in trauma/arrest) → break in sterile technique→ exposure to contaminants

Clean → planned, no entry into tracts

Clean-contaminated → controlled entry (GI, respiratory, etc.)

Contaminated → trauma, emergency, spillage, breaks in sterility

Dirty → already infected, pus present

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Perioperative benefit from transfusion is with a haemoglobin level of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6–8 g/dL

Current perioperative transfusion practice follows a restrictive transfusion strategy. Patients with hemoglobin <6 g/dL almost always require transfusion, while those with Hb 6–8 g/dL are the group most likely to benefit, depending on symptoms, ongoing blood loss, and comorbidities.

Why not the other options?

• A. <6 g/dL: Transfusion is generally mandatory, not merely a range where benefit is assessed.
• C. 8–10 g/dL: Routine transfusion is not recommended; consider only in selected high-risk patients.
• D. >10 g/dL: Transfusion is generally not indicated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The best measure of organ perfusion and the best monitor of adequacy of shock therapy is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urine output

Urine output is the most reliable bedside indicator of end-organ perfusion and the best clinical monitor of adequacy of shock resuscitation. Since the kidneys are highly sensitive to hypoperfusion, restoration of adequate urine output reflects successful improvement in renal blood flow, cardiac output, and tissue perfusion. Target urine output:

• Adults: ≥0.5 mL/kg/hour
• Children: ≥1 mL/kg/hour
• Burn patients: 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour (adults), 1 mL/kg/hour (children)

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Central venous pressure (CVP): CVP reflects right atrial pressure/preload, but is a poor predictor of tissue perfusion or fluid responsiveness.
• B. Pulmonary wedge pressure (PCWP): PCWP estimates left ventricular filling pressure and is mainly used in selected critically ill patients; it is not the best routine monitor of shock resuscitation.
• D. Restoring blood pressure/pulse vital parameters: Normal blood pressure and pulse do not necessarily indicate adequate tissue perfusion, as compensatory mechanisms may maintain vital signs despite ongoing organ hypoperfusion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The knot shown in the image is commonly used in various surgical procedures. Which type of knot does the image depict?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Surgeon's knot

• Surgeon's knot is identified by :  four loops from initial double throws,
• It provides more security when tying with needle holders→ especially for monofilament sutures.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The type of suture technique shown in the following diagram is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mattress

The diagram shows a mattress suture, in which the suture passes through the tissue in a way that distributes tension across a wider area rather than concentrating it at a single point.

A mattress suture is particularly useful for:

• Wound edge eversion
• Closing wounds under moderate tension
• Improving distribution of tension across the wound

The suture takes multiple bites on either side of the wound, producing broad tissue approximation and eversion.

Why not the other options?

• A. Simple interrupted: Each stitch is placed separately and crosses the wound once; it does not have the characteristic mattress configuration.
• C. Connell: A continuous inverting suture, mainly used for closure of hollow viscera.
• D. Donati: A vertical mattress suture with characteristic far-far and near-near bites; the configuration differs from the one shown.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Untidy wounds are characterised by which of the following? 1. Crushed or avulsed tissues 2. Contaminated wound 3. Devitalised tissue 4. No loss of tissue Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Untidy wounds are produced by high-energy trauma and are characterized by crushed, contaminated, and devitalized tissues, often with tissue loss. They require thorough debridement before definitive closure.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Crushed or avulsed tissues: Correct.
• 2. Contaminated wound: Correct.
• 3. Devitalised tissue: Correct.
• 4. No loss of tissue: Incorrect. Tissue loss is common in untidy wounds.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the angle between the laparoscopic working port and telescope called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Azimuth angle

Azimuth angle is the angle between telescope and working port, ideally 15–30° for ergonomics. Elevation angle is instrument–abdominal wall angle, manipulation angle is between two working ports.

Manipulation angle : Angle between working ports

Azimuth angle : Angle between telescope and working port

Elevation angle : Instrument angle from the horizontal

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following about Minimal Access Surgery are correct? I. Decreased intraoperative heat loss II. Improved visualization III. Increased chances of herniation IV. Improved mobility Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and IV

Minimal Access Surgery (MAS), also known as laparoscopic surgery, is performed through small incisions using a camera and specialized instruments. Compared with open surgery, MAS is associated with reduced surgical trauma, faster recovery, less postoperative pain, and shorter hospital stay.

The following statements are true:

• I. Decreased intraoperative heat loss: Smaller incisions and reduced exposure of abdominal viscera result in less evaporative heat loss, thereby reducing intraoperative hypothermia.
• II. Improved visualization: The laparoscope provides magnified, high-definition visualization, allowing better identification of anatomical structures and meticulous dissection.
• IV. Improved mobility: Patients experience less postoperative pain, allowing earlier ambulation, reduced pulmonary complications, and faster recovery.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. Increased chances of herniation: Laparoscopic surgery is associated with a lower incidence of incisional hernias because of the small port-site incisions. Although port-site hernias can occur, they are uncommon and mainly seen with ports ≥10 mm if fascial closure is inadequate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are components of SOFA scoring system? I. PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio II. Mean arterial pressure III. Glasgow Coma Scale IV. Prothrombin Time with INR Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is used to assess the severity of organ dysfunction in critically ill patients, particularly those with sepsis. It evaluates six organ systems, assigning a score from 0 to 4 for each system. A higher SOFA score is associated with an increased risk of mortality.

• I. PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio ✔

• Assesses respiratory function and is a component of the SOFA score.

• II. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) ✔

• Assesses cardiovascular function.
• SOFA uses MAP and the need for vasopressors to grade cardiovascular dysfunction.

• III. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ✔

• Assesses neurological function.
• Lower GCS scores indicate more severe neurological dysfunction.

• IV. Prothrombin Time with INR ✘

• Incorrect.
• SOFA assesses coagulation using platelet count, not PT/INR.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct in respect of Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS)? 1. It is caused by the release of lipopolysaccharide endotoxin from dying E. coli bacteria. 2. It is same as bacteraemia. 3. It results in Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS). 4. White cell counts of more than 12 × 10⁹/L are present. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) is a clinical syndrome of generalized inflammatory response that can be triggered by infectious or non-infectious insults such as trauma, burns, pancreatitis, or sepsis. If uncontrolled, SIRS may progress to Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS).

• 1. It is caused by the release of lipopolysaccharide endotoxin from dying E. coli bacteria. ✓

• Gram-negative endotoxins (lipopolysaccharides) are potent triggers of SIRS by stimulating massive cytokine release. Although SIRS can occur due to many infectious and non-infectious causes, this statement is correct.

• 2. It is same as bacteraemia. ✗

• Bacteremia refers to the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream, whereas SIRS is a systemic inflammatory response that may occur with or without infection.

• 3. It results in Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS). ✓

• Persistent or severe SIRS can progress to MODS, characterized by dysfunction of two or more organ systems.

• 4. White cell counts of more than 12 × 10⁹/L are present. ✓

• One of the diagnostic criteria for SIRS is WBC >12,000/mm³ (12 × 10⁹/L), <4,000/mm³, or >10% immature (band) forms.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for wound infection? 1. Malnutrition 2. Poor perfusion 3. Antibodies 4. Foreign body material Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Surgical site infection (SSI) develops when bacterial contamination overcomes host defense mechanisms. The risk depends on host factors (e.g., nutrition, tissue perfusion, immune status) and local wound factors (e.g., foreign bodies, dead tissue). Optimizing these factors before and after surgery reduces the incidence of wound infection.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Malnutrition ✅

• Protein-calorie malnutrition impairs collagen synthesis, immune function, and wound healing, increasing the risk of infection.

• 2. Poor perfusion ✅

• Reduced tissue oxygenation decreases delivery of immune cells and antibiotics to the wound, predisposing to infection.

• 3. Antibodies ❌

• Antibodies are protective against infection and are not a risk factor.

• 4. Foreign body material ✅

• Foreign materials (e.g., sutures, prostheses, retained debris) facilitate bacterial adherence and biofilm formation, markedly increasing infection risk.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in MEN 2B syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parathyroid adenoma

MEN 2B is caused by activating RET mutations and is characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Mucosal neuromas of lips, tongue, and gastrointestinal tract are hallmark features.

Patients often show marfanoid habitus and may have intestinal ganglioneuromatosis causing megacolon.

Parathyroid adenoma is seen in MEN 2A, not MEN 2B, making it the incorrect feature.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements about the suture material Polydioxanone (PDS) is accurate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is a monofilament suture

PDS (Polydioxanone) is a synthetic monofilament → delayed absorbable suture with - -

-       prolonged tensile strength.

-       ideal for Whipple’s surgery and port site closure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding sutures in surgery? I. Barbed sutures have the advantage of eliminating the need for knots. II. Vertical mattress sutures help in eversion of wound edges. III. Aberdeen knot is used for continuous suturing. IV. Silk is preferred for subcuticular suturing. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

An ideal surgical suture should provide adequate tensile strength, cause minimal tissue reaction, be easy to handle, and maintain wound approximation until healing occurs. Different suturing techniques and suture materials are selected according to the tissue involved and the desired wound healing characteristics. The following statements are true:

• I. Barbed sutures have the advantage of eliminating the need for knots: Barbed sutures contain unidirectional or bidirectional barbs that anchor the tissue, eliminating the need for knot tying, reducing operative time and distributing tension evenly.
• II. Vertical mattress sutures help in eversion of wound edges: The vertical mattress suture provides excellent wound edge eversion and distributes tension, making it useful for wounds under tension.
• III. Aberdeen knot is used for continuous suturing: The Aberdeen knot is a secure knot used to terminate continuous sutures, commonly in abdominal wall and skin closure.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Silk is preferred for subcuticular suturing: Subcuticular suturing is usually performed with absorbable monofilament sutures such as Monocryl (poliglecaprone), Vicryl Rapide, or PDS for better cosmetic results. Silk, a braided non-absorbable suture, causes greater tissue reaction and is not preferred.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding shock is true
options: Postpartum uterine inversion causes neurogenic shock
Gram positive bacteria cause endotoxic shock
Severe hypovolemic shock occurs when blood loss is >20%
There is hyper perfusion of organs due to increased cardiac output in shock
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Postpartum uterine inversion causes neurogenic shock

Shock is defined as inadequate tissue perfusion leading to cellular hypoxia. Postpartum uterine inversion can cause intense vagal stimulation, resulting in bradycardia and hypotension, producing neurogenic (vasovagal) shock, often disproportionate to blood loss.

Gram-negative bacteria, not Gram-positive, cause endotoxic shock due to lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Severe hypovolemic shock usually occurs when blood loss exceeds \~30–40%, not 20%. Shock generally involves reduced organ perfusion, not hyperperfusion.

Correct statement: Postpartum uterine inversion causes neurogenic shock.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) dressing are correct? 1. Reduces bacterial load 2. Maximum pressure is -125mm of Hg 3. Promotes granulation tissue 4. Reduces size of wound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3 and 4

All statements about Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) dressing are correct.

| Statement | Explanation

| --------- | -----------

| Reduces bacterial load | Continuous suction removes exudate, debris, and bacteria, lowering infection risk.

| Maximum pressure −125 mmHg | Standard optimal negative pressure used in VAC therapy is around −125 mmHg.

| Promotes granulation tissue | Negative pressure increases blood flow and angiogenesis, stimulating granulation tissue formation.

| Reduces size of wound | VAC causes macrodeformation, pulling wound edges together and decreasing wound size.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following suture material has the maximum tissue reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Catgut

Natural sutures produce more tissue reaction than synthetic sutures. Among the options, catgut is a natural absorbable suture that is degraded by enzymatic proteolysis, leading to greater inflammation and tissue reaction. In contrast, synthetic absorbable sutures such as Vicryl (polyglactin), PDS (polydioxanone), and Monocryl (poliglecaprone) are broken down by hydrolysis, causing minimal tissue reaction.

Hence, catgut causes the maximum tissue reaction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is not a wound prone to the development of tetanus?
options: Wound on forearm contaminated with soil
Donor site of a split-thickness skin graft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Donor site of a split-thickness skin graft

Clostridium tetani spores are found in soil and can enter wounds, particularly those with devitalized tissue, contamination, or poor oxygenation.

• (a) Compound fracture of tibia — Tetanus-prone: Open fractures involve tissue damage and contamination, providing favorable conditions for C. tetani.
• (b) Forearm wound contaminated with soil — Tetanus-prone: Soil contamination increases the risk of inoculation with C. tetani spores.
• (c) Donor site of split-thickness skin graft — Not typically tetanus-prone → Correct: It is a clean, surgically created superficial wound without the typical anaerobic environment or soil contamination associated with tetanus.
• (d) Dog bite over abdominal wall — Tetanus-prone: Animal bites are contaminated wounds and are considered potential tetanus-prone wounds.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which parameters are included in qSOFA score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. SBP, RR, GCS score

qSOFA (Quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment)

Screening tool for sepsis used outside the ICU to identify patients at risk of poor outcomes.

Includes:

1. Respiratory rate (RR) ≥ 22/min

2. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≤ 100 mmHg

3. Altered mentation → GCS < 15

Each parameter = 1 point

• Score ≥ 2 → High risk of sepsis / poor outcome

Why other options are incorrect

❌ A) BP, RR, CBC

CBC is not part of qSOFA.

❌ B) Creatinine, PR, BP

Creatinine is part of full SOFA, not qSOFA.

❌ C) RR, Body temperature, PR

These belong more to SIRS criteria, not qSOFA

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain. Serum amylase and lipase are elevated on two occasions, but exocrine pancreatic function is normal. An MRCP image is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Choledochal cyst

Features visible:

• Fusiform/cystic dilatation of the common bile duct
• Communication with biliary tree
• Typical MRCP appearance of a choledochal cyst

Most commonly:

• Todani Type I choledochal cyst

| Option | Reason

| ------ | ------

| Annular pancreas | Ring of pancreatic tissue around duodenum; not this biliary cystic dilatation

| Chronic pancreatitis | Shows irregular pancreatic duct dilatation/calcification

| Pancreatic divisum | Failure of duct fusion with dominant dorsal duct pattern

| Choledochal cyst | Correct — cystic CBD dilatation

Frequent confuser: Pancreatic divisum MRCP

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old female with fever, nausea, tenderness and migration of pain to the right iliac fossa (RIF), raised TLC of 15,000. What is the Alvarado score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 7

Alvarado Score (MANTRELS)

| Feature | Points

| ------- | ------

| Migration of pain to RIF | 1

| Anorexia | 1

| Nausea/Vomiting | 1

| Tenderness in RIF | 2

| Rebound tenderness | 1

| Elevated temperature (fever) | 1

| Leukocytosis (>10,000) | 2

| Shift to left (neutrophilia) | 1

Scoring in this patient

• Migration of pain → 1
• Nausea → 1
• RIF tenderness → 2
• Fever → 1
• Leukocytosis (TLC 15,000) → 2   → Total = 7

| Score | Meaning

| ----- | -------

| 1–4 | Appendicitis unlikely

| 5–6 | Possible appendicitis (observe / imaging)

| ≥7 | Strongly suggestive of appendicitis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 26-year-old female presents with dysphagia, weight loss, and halitosis. What is the most probable diagnosis based on the image provided?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Achalasia

The classic triad of dysphagia, weight loss, and regurgitation in a young patient, along with imaging showing smooth narrowing and gradual tapering, is highly suggestive of achalasia.

❌Option B: Ca  oesophagus

• Seen in lder age group
• Irregular narrowing, not smooth
• Dysphagia: solids first → then liquids

Option C : ❌Corrosive stricture

• History of acid/alkali ingestion
• Causes long, irregular strictures; Not typical smooth tapering on imaging

Option D : ❌Zenker’s diverticulum

• Seen in elderly
• Regurgitation of undigested food, Halitosis, gurgling
• Not typical smooth tapering on imaging

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male patient with enteric fever presents to the emergency with sudden onset of generalised abdominal pain, abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting and constipation for last 48 hours. On examination, patient is dehydrated with PR = 110/min and BP = 100/60 mmHg. There is generalised tenderness, rebound tenderness present and board like rigidity on per abdomen examination. The most likely complication of enteric fever in this patient is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Small bowel perforation

Enteric (typhoid) perforation is a life-threatening complication of typhoid fever, usually occurring in the third week due to necrosis of Peyer’s patches in the terminal ileum. It presents as acute generalized peritonitis. Features include sudden severe abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, constipation, dehydration, guarding, rebound tenderness, and board-like rigidity.

Why not the other options?

• A. Small bowel enteritis: Does not cause generalized peritonitis with board-like rigidity.
• C. Small bowel obstruction: Causes distension and vomiting but not generalized peritonitis unless perforation occurs.
• D. Cholecystitis: Causes right upper quadrant pain, not diffuse peritonitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with recurrent gastric ulcers and a nodule in the medial wall of the second part of the duodenum. What is the next step in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum gastrin levels

Recurrent gastric ulcers and a nodule in the medial wall of the 2nd part of the duodenum suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome occurs due to a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma).

• Most gastrinomas occur in the duodenum or pancreas, especially within the gastrinoma triangle (pancreas–duodenum region).
• So the first investigation —> check serum gastrin levels
• Initial test: Fasting serum gastrin (stop PPIs if possible).
• Diagnostic finding: Very high gastrin (>1000 pg/mL) with gastric pH <2.
• If gastrin is moderately elevated (100–1000 pg/mL), do the Secretin stimulation test → rise in gastrin ≥120 pg/mL confirms ZES.
• Localize tumor with Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT, CT/MRI, or EUS.
• Screen for Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 association.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 4-week-old child with a history of vomiting undergoes imaging as shown. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital Pyloric Stenosis

Age: 4-week-old infant with History of Vomiting. Ultrasound image: Thickened pyloric muscle

These features suggest Infantile Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (IHPS).

What happens in pyloric stenosis

The pyloric muscle becomes hypertrophied, causing gastric outlet obstruction—> leading to :-

• Projectile vomiting
• Non-bilious vomiting (because obstruction is before the bile duct entry in the duodenum).

On examination : Olive-shaped mass in epigastrium is seen

Metabolic change : Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis

Typical findings on USG:

• Pyloric muscle thickness > 3–4 mm
• Pyloric channel length > 14–17 mm

Signs described in imaging: Target sign, Donut sigand Cervix sign

Option B. Duodenal atresia

Causes bilious vomiting—> Shows double bubble sign on X-ray.

Option C. Annular pancreas

Causes duodenal obstruction with bilious vomiting.

Option D. Volvulus

Causes bilious vomiting and acute abdominal emergency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old lady underwent a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, which was uneventful other than some spillage of bile and gallstones during dissection. Postoperatively the patient was fine but she started complaining of right shoulder tip pain and developed high-grade fever on the 3rd postoperative day. Her pulse was found to be 110/min and RR 20/min. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right subdiaphragmatic abscess

The patient developed right shoulder-tip pain + high-grade fever on postoperative day 3 following laparoscopic cholecystectomy with spillage of bile and gallstones.

A right subdiaphragmatic (subphrenic) abscess is the most likely diagnosis.

• Shoulder-tip pain/right upper abdominal is due to referred pain via the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) from irritation of the diaphragm.
• Spilled infected bile/gallstones can act as a nidus for localized infection and abscess formation.
• Fever and tachycardia support a postoperative intra-abdominal infective complication.

Why not the other options?

• A. Ascending cholangitis: Usually presents with fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain; shoulder-tip pain is not characteristic.
• B. Liver abscess: Possible after biliary surgery but less specifically suggested by the combination of diaphragmatic irritation and shoulder-tip pain.
• D. DVT/PE: May cause tachycardia and respiratory symptoms, but high-grade fever with shoulder-tip pain after bile/gallstone spillage points toward an intra-abdominal abscess

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with dysphagia and regurgitation. A barium swallow study is performed. Which investigation is considered diagnostic for confirming this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oesophageal manometry

✅Option B: Oesophageal manometry is the diagnostic gold standard for achalasia, demonstrates→

• Incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES)
• Increased LES pressure
• Absent or disordered peristalsis

❌ Option A: CECT

• CECT is NOT diagnostic for achalasia because:
• Achalasia is a functional motility disorder and → CT cannot assess these dynamic abnormalities( LES relaxation, peristalsis etc).

❌ Option C: Upper GI endoscopy

• Helps to exclude malignancy ; Not diagnostic for primary motility disorder

❌Option D: NCCT : No role in diagnosing esophageal motility disorders

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman undergoes bariatric surgery for morbid obesity. Which of the following procedures is associated with the greatest risk of fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass

Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) is a combined restrictive and malabsorptive bariatric procedure. It bypasses the duodenum and proximal jejunum, the major sites for absorption of many nutrients, resulting in the highest risk of vitamin and mineral deficiencies, including fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K).

• RYGB decreases:

• Gastric volume (restrictive)
• Nutrient absorption (malabsorptive)

• Bypassing the proximal small intestine impairs absorption of:

• Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)
• Iron
• Calcium
• Vitamin B12
• Folate

Therefore, lifelong nutritional supplementation and monitoring are required.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sleeve gastrectomy: Primarily a restrictive procedure; nutritional deficiencies are less common than with RYGB.
• B. Adjustable gastric banding: Purely restrictive; lowest risk of vitamin deficiencies.
• D. Intragastric balloon: Temporary restrictive therapy with minimal effect on nutrient absorption.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient presents with a painless firm abdominal swelling of size 10 × 8 cm near the umbilicus. The swelling can be moved freely in a plane at right angle to the line of attachment of the mesentery. The most probable clinical diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mesenteric cyst

A mesenteric cyst classically presents as a painless, freely mobile intra-abdominal swelling. It exhibits Tillaux’s sign—the swelling is mobile at right angles to the line of attachment of the mesentery but has restricted mobility parallel to it.

Why not the other options?

• A. Dermoid cyst: Usually ovarian/sacrococcygeal; does not show Tillaux’s sign.
• B. Ovarian cyst: Arises from the pelvis and is not characteristically mobile perpendicular to the mesenteric attachment.
• D. Hydatid cyst: Commonly occurs in the liver and is relatively fixed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with chronic heartburn and retrosternal discomfort for several years. Upper GI endoscopy reveals salmon-colored velvety mucosa in the lower esophagus. Which of the following best describes the change in Barrett's esophagus?
options: Intestinal-type columnar epithelium to squamous epithelium
Squamous epithelium to simple columnar epithelium
Squamous epithelium to intestinal-type columnar epithelium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Squamous epithelium to intestinal-type columnar epithelium

Barrett’s esophagus is a metaplastic change due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux injury.

Normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

This represents an adaptive response to acidic injury.

On upper GI endoscopy: Salmon-pink mucosa

Barrett’s esophagus is a premalignant condition predisposing to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient presents to the emergency with sudden onset of upper abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and haematemesis. On examination, PR = 106/min, BP = 100/70 mmHg and pallor is present. CECT abdomen reveals a large exophytic tumor of size 13 × 8 cm at the fundus of the stomach. On upper GI endoscopy, the mucosa overlying the tumor is intact. The staining for CD117 in the upper GI endoscopic biopsy is positive. The most probable clinical diagnosis in this patient is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gastrointestinal stromal tumor

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) is the most common mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract. It arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal (pacemaker cells) and is characterized by KIT (CD117) positivity on immunohistochemistry.

The clinical scenario is classic for GIST:

• Large exophytic gastric mass
• Intact overlying mucosa on endoscopy
• CD117 (KIT) positive
• Upper GI bleeding due to mucosal ulceration/compression

Why not other options?

• A. Gastric lymphoma:

• Usually presents with diffuse gastric wall thickening or ulceration.
• Not characteristically CD117 positive.

• C. Carcinoid tumor:

• Usually a small neuroendocrine tumor.
• Positive for Chromogranin A and Synaptophysin, not CD117.

• D. Carcinoma stomach:

• Arises from the gastric mucosa and typically shows an ulceroproliferative or infiltrative mucosal lesion on endoscopy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old man presents with bleeding per rectum for 4 months. On examination, there is a 5 cm ulceroproliferative growth arising from the anal canal above the dentate line. Biopsy reveals squamous cell carcinoma. Contrast-enhanced CT shows no distant metastasis. What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the anal canal is treated primarily with definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT), which is the standard of care for localized disease without distant metastasis. This approach preserves the anal sphincter and achieves high rates of local control, avoiding the need for radical surgery in most patients.

Nigro Protocol

• 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) or Capecitabine
• Mitomycin C
• External beam radiotherapy

This is the gold standard treatment for anal canal SCC.

Why not the other options?

• A. Wide local excision: Reserved only for small, well-differentiated perianal (anal margin) tumors, not anal canal SCC.
• B. Surgery followed by radiotherapy: Surgery is not first-line because it requires abdominoperineal resection (APR) with permanent colostomy.
• C. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery: Routine surgery after CRT is not recommended. Surgery is reserved for persistent or recurrent disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive weight loss, altered bowel habits, and intermittent episodes of blood in the stool for the past four months. Colonoscopy reveals an ulceroproliferative lesion in the sigmoid colon, and histopathological examination confirms adenocarcinoma of the colon. Mutation in which of the following genes is most commonly associated with this malignancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. KRAS

Colorectal adenocarcinoma develops through the adenoma–carcinoma sequence, a multistep process involving accumulation of genetic mutations. One of the most common oncogene mutations is KRAS, which promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation by constitutively activating the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway. KRAS mutation is present in approximately 40–50% of colorectal cancers and is associated with progression from adenoma to carcinoma.

The patient has:

• Weight loss
• Altered bowel habits
• Hematochezia
• Sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma

KRAS mutation is one of the most frequent genetic alterations in sporadic colorectal carcinoma and plays a key role in tumor progression.

Why not the other options?

• A. RB1: Tumor suppressor gene mutated in retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma, not commonly associated with colorectal carcinoma.
• B. RET: Proto-oncogene associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) type 2 and medullary thyroid carcinoma, not colorectal adenocarcinoma.
• D. BRCA1: Tumor suppressor gene associated with breast and ovarian cancers, not a common mutation in colorectal cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old male underwent surgery for rectal prolapse, and a postoperative image was obtained. Can you identify the procedure that was most likely performed on the patient from the given image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thiersch stitch

The image shows a Thiersch stitch (anal encirclement procedure), a perineal operation used for rectal prolapse in which a nonabsorbable suture or synthetic material is placed subcutaneously around the anus to narrow the anal opening and prevent prolapse recurrence.

• Typically used in elderly, frail, or high-risk surgical patients who are poor candidates for major abdominal surgery.
• Performed through a perineal approach.
• Acts as a mechanical support to prevent protrusion of the rectum.
• May be combined with other perineal procedures.

Why Not the Other Options?

•

Stapled hemorrhoidopexy: Used for prolapsing hemorrhoids, not rectal prolapse.

•

Wells procedure (Ripstein/Wells rectopexy variants): An abdominal rectopexy using mesh fixation of the rectum to the sacrum.

•

Altemeier repair: Perineal rectosigmoidectomy for full-thickness rectal prolapse; involves resection of the prolapsed rectum rather than anal encirclement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with painless jaundice and pruritus without fever. On examination, the gallbladder is palpable and non-tender. Which among the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carcinoma head of pancreas

Painless progressive obstructive jaundice with a palpable, non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) is highly suggestive of malignant distal biliary obstruction, most commonly carcinoma of the head of the pancreas. The gradual obstruction allows progressive distension of the gallbladder, unlike gallstone disease, where chronic inflammation usually results in a fibrotic, contracted gallbladder.

• Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas classically presents with:

• Painless progressive jaundice
• Pruritus
• Palpable, non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign)
• Weight loss ± anorexia

Why not the other options?

• A. Cholangiocarcinoma: May cause obstructive jaundice, but a palpable gallbladder is less characteristic than in carcinoma of the pancreatic head.
• B. Gallbladder carcinoma: Usually presents with right upper quadrant pain, weight loss, and a gallbladder mass rather than Courvoisier sign.
• C. Choledocholithiasis: Typically causes painful obstructive jaundice, often with biliary colic, cholangitis, or a contracted gallbladder due to chronic cholelithiasis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with diabetes mellitus presents with intermittent anal discharge. Which of the following procedures is not considered a sphincter-preserving surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fistulectomy

The primary goal in the management of anal fistula is eradication of the fistulous tract while preserving anal sphincter function to maintain continence. Modern sphincter-preserving procedures are preferred for complex fistulas, whereas fistulectomy involves division of sphincter muscle and carries a higher risk of postoperative fecal incontinence.

• Fistulectomy involves complete excision of the fistulous tract, often requiring division of part of the anal sphincter.
• It is not a sphincter-preserving procedure and is associated with a greater risk of fecal incontinence, especially in high or complex fistulas.

Why not the other options?

• A. LIFT (Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract) ✓: Sphincter-preserving procedure performed in the intersphincteric plane.
• B. FiLaC (Fistula Laser Closure) ✓: Minimally invasive laser ablation of the fistula tract with preservation of the sphincter.
• C. VAAFT (Video-Assisted Anal Fistula Treatment) ✓: Endoscopic technique allowing identification and closure of the internal opening while preserving sphincter integrity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 72-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain. She describes excruciating pain, but abdominal examination reveals only mild tenderness, with pain out of proportion to physical findings. She has a history of atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Acute mesenteric ischemia is suspected. Which of the following statements are correct? 1. Serum lactate elevation is always present in the early stage. 2. Atrial fibrillation is a risk factor. 3. CT angiography is the investigation of choice. 4. Pain out of proportion to physical findings is a classic feature.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3 and 4

Acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) is a surgical emergency resulting from sudden interruption of intestinal blood flow. The classic presentation is severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings, particularly in patients with atrial fibrillation, which predisposes to superior mesenteric artery embolism. CT angiography (CTA) is the investigation of choice for early diagnosis.

• 2. Atrial fibrillation is a risk factor ✓: AF is the most common cause of arterial embolic acute mesenteric ischemia.
• 3. CT angiography is the investigation of choice ✓: It rapidly identifies arterial occlusion, bowel ischemia, and guides management.
• 4. Pain out of proportion to physical findings is a classic feature ✓: A hallmark of early acute mesenteric ischemia.

Why is statement 1 incorrect?

• 1. Serum lactate elevation is always present in the early stage ✗: False. Serum lactate may be normal early in the disease and typically rises only after significant bowel ischemia or infarction. Therefore, a normal lactate does not exclude AMI.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A child is having fecal discharge from the umbilicus. What is the abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Patent vitello-intestinal duct

Patent Vitellointestinal Duct (Omphalomesenteric Fistula)

• Connection: Ileum to Umbilicus
• Presentation:

• Fecal discharge from umbilicus
• May see mucosal prolapse

• Complete patency of duct

Omphalomesenteric (Vitellointestinal) Cyst

• Connection: Both ends closed, cyst in between
• Presentation:

• Umbilical swelling
• May get infected → painful mass

• No external discharge unless ruptured

Urachal Anomalies (Allantoic Remnant)

A. Patent Urachus

• Connection: Bladder to Umbilicus
• Presentation:

• Urine discharge from umbilicus

B. Urachal Cyst

• Connection: Both ends closed, cyst in midline
• Presentation:

• Infraumbilical swelling
• Infection → tender mass

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female presents with bleeding per rectum. On digital rectal examination, an ulcerated mass is palpated approximately 6 cm from the anal verge. Biopsy confirms intramucosal carcinoma. Based on this information, what is the correct stage of the rectal carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stage 0

| AJCC Stage | TNM Stage | Definition

| ---------- | --------- | ----------

| 0 | Tis N0 M0 | Intramucosal carcinoma; confined to mucosa, no nodal spread

| I | T1 N0 M0 | Tumour invades submucosa

| I | T2 N0 M0 | Tumour invades muscularis propria

| IIa | T3 N0 M0 | Tumour invades through muscularis propria into subserosa/pericolic tissues

| IIb | T4 N0 M0 | Tumour invades other organs or perforates visceral peritoneum

| IIIa | T1–T2 N1 M0 | Metastases to 1–3 regional lymph nodes

| IIIb | T3–T4 N1 M0 | Metastases to 1–3 regional lymph nodes

| IIIc | Any T N2 M0 | Metastases to ≥4 regional lymph nodes

| IV | Any T Any N M1 | Distant metastases

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A follow-up patient with long-standing GERD undergoes endoscopy, which reveals a nodule in the second part of the duodenum. Which hormone is most likely to be elevated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gastrin

What is Zollinger–Ellison Syndrome?

A gastrinoma is a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor, usually located in the:

Gastrinoma triangle
