(bounded by the cystic duct, pancreatic neck, and second part of the duodenum).

The tumor secretes excess gastri.Gastrin stimulates:

• Parietal cells
• Acid production

Excess gastrin → very high gastric acid levels → causing:

• Refractory GERD
• Recurrent ulcers

❌ B) Insulin

Associated with insulinoma, which causes:

• Hypoglycaemia
• Whipple’s triad

Not GERD.

❌ C) VIP

Associated with VIPoma, causing:

• Watery diarrhea
• Hypokalemia
• Achlorhydria

(WDHA syndrome)

❌ D) Glucagon

Associated with glucagonoma, causing:

• Necrolytic migratory erythema
• Diabetes
• Weight loss

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A neonate is born with protrusion of intestines from the abdominal wall without any covering. What should be the immediate next step in management?
options: Cover the content with a silo bag and shift to the NICU
Cover with saline-soaked gauze and wait for it to self-resolve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cover the content with a silo bag and shift to the NICU

Exposed bowel without membrane = gastroschisis.

First step is silo placement to protect bowel and allow gradual reduction preventing compartment syndrome.

Immediate closure may be unsafe; conservative waiting is dangerous.

| Feature | Gastroschisis | Omphalocele

| ------- | ------------- | -----------

| Covering sac | Absent | Present

| Location | Right of umbilicus | Midline

| Associated anomalies | Rare | Common

| Management | Silo reduction | Surgical repair

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient consumed 90% sodium hydroxide and has complete dysphagia. Which of the following would be the best next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Feeding jejunostomy

• This is a case of acute caustic ingestion.
• Alkali liquefactive necrosis→ leads to deep penetration → severe esophageal injury.
• The patient has complete dysphagia, meaning oral feeding is impossible.

Because the esophagus is severely injured, enteral nutrition must be administered via a route that bypasses it.

The safest option is Feeding jejunostomy (FJ), because → Allows the delay of definitive surgery until inflammation subsides

Why are the other options wrong

A) Esophago-jejunostomy

• A reconstructive surgery; Contraindicated in the acute phase
• Tissue is inflamed and friable → high risk of leak
• Done months later after stricture formation.

B) Stent placement

• Not done in acute caustic burns
• Risk of perforation and worsening injury

D) Gastrojejunostomy

• Requires a functional stomach
• Alkali ingestion often damages the stomach too (pyloric stenosis is a common feature)
• Does not solve the esophageal obstruction

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with acute appendicitis was brought to the hospital within 24 hours of symptom onset. Which of the following statements is/are true regarding this condition? 1. McBurney's point tenderness is a reliable clinical sign 2. Ultrasound (USG) is the preferred investigation in pregnant women and children 3. Ochsner-Sherren regimen is preferred for appendicular mass 4. Interval appendectomy is mandatory after conservative management
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

1) Acute Appendicitis

Typical progression:

Visceral pain phase

• Pain begins around the umbilicus
• Because visceral afferents from the appendix enter T10 spinal segment

Parietal peritoneal irritation

• Inflammation reaches parietal peritoneum
• Pain localizes to right lower quadrant

This is where McBurney’s point tenderness appears.

• Junction of lateral 1/3 and medial 2/3 of the line between: Umbilicus-Right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)

2) Ultrasound is preferred in pregnant women and children ✔️

• Ultrasound has no radiation
• Safe for pregnancy and pediatrics

It can detect:

• Inflamed appendix
• Appendix diameter > 6 mm
• Peri-appendiceal fluid

3) Ochsner-Sherren regimen is preferred for appendicular mass ✔️

An appendicular mass forms when the body tries to contain infection by surrounding the inflamed appendix with: Omentum and Bowel loops

Instead of immediate surgery, conservative treatment is given.

This is called Ochsner–Sherren regimen, which includes:

• Nil by mouth
• IV fluids
• Antibiotics
• Observation

Surgery is avoided initially because operating on a mass can injure surrounding bowel.

4) Interval appendectomy is mandatory-This is false.

Earlier practice:

• After conservative treatment, surgery was done 6–8 weeks later (interval appendectomy).

Current practice:

• Not mandatory anymore
• Done only if symptoms recur.

Many patients remain completely asymptomatic.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with esophageal perforation, and contrast leak is confirmed. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Early surgical exploration

Esophageal perforation is a life-threatening surgical emergency because leakage of saliva, gastric contents, and bacteria into the mediastinum rapidly leads to mediastinitis, sepsis, and multiorgan failure. Once contrast imaging confirms an esophageal leak, early surgical intervention (within 24 hours) is the treatment of choice in most patients.

The next best step is early surgical exploration and repair, along with:

• Nil per oral (NPO)
• Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
• IV fluids
• Drainage of contaminated mediastinum/pleural cavity as required

Why not the other options?

• A. Conservative management: Reserved only for small, contained cervical perforations or contained leaks in carefully selected stable patients without sepsis.
• C. Nasogastric tube feeds: Contraindicated initially as they may worsen contamination; enteral nutrition is considered only after stabilization.
• D. Observation: Inappropriate because untreated esophageal perforation has a very high mortality.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department with vomiting attempts after an alcohol binge, but unable to vomit, and experiencing chest pain. X-ray reveals a left pleural effusion. What is the next most appropriate diagnostic step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT chest

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophageal rupture) should be suspected in a patient with forceful vomiting after an alcohol binge, followed by sudden severe chest pain and left-sided pleural effusion. It is a life-threatening emergency due to mediastinal contamination.

Contrast-enhanced CT chest (preferably with water-soluble oral contrast) is the investigation of choice. It identifies:

• Esophageal perforation
• Pneumomediastinum
• Mediastinal fluid collection
• Left pleural effusion/hydropneumothorax
• Extraluminal contrast leak

Why not the other options?

• B. MRI: Not useful in the acute emergency setting.
• C. UGI endoscopy: Not the initial investigation; insufflation may worsen the perforation.
• D. Barium swallow: Barium leakage into the mediastinum can cause severe inflammation. If a contrast swallow is needed, water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) is preferred.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden hematemesis while taking aspirin and drinking alcohol occasionally. Which of these is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Peptic ulcer

• Sudden hematemesis (vomiting blood)
• Taking aspirin (NSAID)
• Occasional alcohol intake

Point toward NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with bleeding.

Why Aspirin Causes Peptic Ulcer

When prostaglandins decrease → gastric mucosal protection decreases → ulcer formation → bleeding.

Why Other Options Are Wrong

❌A) Mallory-Weiss tear

Occurs after forceful vomiting or retching

Caused by mucosal tear at gastro-esophageal junction

❌B) Esophagitis

Usually causes chronic symptoms like:

• Heartburn
• Dysphagia

Massive hematemesis is uncommon.

❌D) Esophageal varices

Occur due to portal hypertension

Usually seen in liver cirrhosis patients; No history suggesting chronic liver disease.

Common causes of upper GI bleeding

| Cause | Typical clue

| ----- | ------------

| Peptic ulcer | NSAIDs, epigastric pain

| Mallory-Weiss tear | Vomiting → hematemesis

| Esophageal varices | Cirrhosis, portal hypertension

| Gastritis | Alcohol, NSAIDs

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are considered premalignant conditions of the stomach, except: (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hiatus hernia

Several gastric conditions predispose to the development of gastric adenocarcinoma by promoting chronic inflammation, mucosal atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and dysplasia. However, hiatus hernia is not considered a premalignant condition of the stomach.

Premalignant Conditions of the Stomach:

• Chronic atrophic gastritis → Leads to intestinal metaplasia and increases gastric cancer risk.
• Pernicious anemia with achlorhydria → Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells causes chronic atrophic gastritis, a recognized precursor of gastric adenocarcinoma.
• Chronic gastric ulcer (especially longstanding ulcers) may harbor or mimic malignancy and warrant biopsy to exclude gastric cancer.

Why is Hiatus Hernia the Exception?

• Hiatus hernia is the herniation of part of the stomach through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm.
• It is primarily associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and may predispose to Barrett esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma, not gastric carcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following statements about stomas are true except?
options: Patients with a colostomy are at a higher risk of fluid and electrolyte imbalance.
Temporary stomas are fashioned as a loop
Colostomy stoma is everted and flushed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Patients with a colostomy are at a higher risk of fluid and electrolyte imbalance.

| Feature | Ileostomy | Colostomy

| ------- | --------- | ---------

| Location | Small intestine | Large intestine

| Output | Liquid | Semi-solid

| Volume | High | Low

| Electrolyte loss | High | Low

| Stoma type | Spouted | Flush

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An adult patient presents with right iliac fossa pain of 48 hours’ duration. Ultrasound examination is shown. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immediate surgery

Acute appendicitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis, with ultrasonography serving as a useful adjunct. An ultrasound showing a non-compressible, blind-ending tubular structure >6 mm in diameter with increased periappendiceal vascularity (“hyperemia”) is diagnostic of acute uncomplicated appendicitis, for which the treatment is urgent appendicectomy.

• The ultrasound demonstrates features of acute appendicitis:

• Dilated appendix (>6 mm)
• Non-compressible blind-ending tubular structure
• Increased vascularity on color Doppler (“ring of fire”)

• In a patient with 48 hours of right iliac fossa pain and confirmatory imaging, the appropriate management is immediate surgery (appendicectomy).

Why not the other options?

• A. USG-guided FNAC: Has no role in the diagnosis or management of acute appendicitis.
• B. CECT abdomen: Reserved for equivocal cases or when the diagnosis remains uncertain after ultrasound, especially in adults.
• C. USG-guided drainage: Indicated only for a localized appendicular abscess, not uncomplicated acute appendicitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An eight-month-old male child is brought to the emergency with recurrent episodes of screaming and drawing up of legs. The child appears to be listless in between the attacks. Local examination of abdomen reveals feeling of emptiness in the right iliac fossa and blood stained mucus is found on the finger on per rectal examination. The most probable clinical diagnosis in this child is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute intussusception

Acute intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants aged 6–18 months. It occurs when a segment of intestine telescopes into the adjacent distal bowel, most commonly ileocolic intussusception.

The classic triad consists of:

• Intermittent colicky abdominal pain (child screams and draws up the legs)
• Red currant jelly stools (blood and mucus)
• Palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass

Note: The classic triad is present in less than one-third of patients.

Why not other options?

• A. Caecal volvulus:

• Rare in infants.
• Presents with acute intestinal obstruction but not with intermittent colicky pain and red currant jelly stools.

• C. Rectal prolapse:

• Presents as a protruding rectal mass through the anus.
• Does not cause episodic colicky pain or Dance sign.

• D. Midgut volvulus:

• Presents with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and rapidly progressing intestinal ischemia.
• Blood-stained mucus is not the typical presentation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An image of a perianal disease is shown. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fistula in Ano

A fistula in ano : An abnormal tract connecting the anal canal to the perianal skin.

Usually develops after a perianal abscess.

On examination: small external opening near the anus with recurrent discharge (pus)

Why other options are wrong

B. Pilonidal sinus

• Located higher in the natal cleft
• Contains hair and sinus pits
• Not close to the anal verge.

C. Fissure in ano

• Linear tear in anal canal
• Causes severe pain during defecation
• No external sinus opening.

D. Hemorrhoids

• Dilated vascular cushions
• Appear as bluish or prolapsing masses, not a sinus opening.

Goodsall’s rule:

• Anterior openings → straight tract
• Posterior openings → curved tract to posterior midline

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Arrange the steps of inguinal hernioplasty in order: 1. Incision of the skin 2. Identify the hernia sac and reduce the contents 3. Wound closure 4. Mesh placement and fixation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 2 4 3

Standard steps of inguinal hernioplasty (Lichtenstein repair)

Skin incision

• Oblique inguinal incision parallel to the inguinal ligament.
• Opens the layers to reach the inguinal canal.

Open external oblique aponeurosis

• The external oblique aponeurosis is split along its fibers.
• This exposes the inguinal canal and spermatic cord.

Mobilize the spermatic cord

• The spermatic cord is isolated and lifted with a sling.
• This allows clear visualization of the hernia sac

Identify and manage the hernia sac

• Indirect hernia: sac separated from cord → ligated and excised.
• Direct hernia: sac reduced back into abdomen.

Prepare posterior wall

• The transversalis fascia/posterior wall is cleared to prepare for mesh placement.

Mesh placement (tension-free repair)

• A polypropylene mesh is placed over the posterior wall.
• Fixed to:

• Inguinal ligament (inferiorly)
• Conjoint tendon (superiorly)

• A slit is made in the mesh to accommodate the spermatic cord.

Wound closure

Layers closed sequentially:

• External oblique aponeurosis
• Subcutaneous tissue
• Skin

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on Park's classification, identify the type of anorectal fistula shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intersphincteric

Intersphincteric FISTULA:

Most common type in Park's classification of fistula-in-ano

• The tract runs between the internal and external sphincters
• It does NOT cross the external sphincter
• Usually opens near the anal verge

Option B : Suprasphincteric → goes above sphincter

Option C : Extrasphincteric → bypasses sphincters completely

Transsphincteric → crosses external sphincter

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the symptoms reported by the patient, what could be the possible diagnosis for a 30-year-old man who has been experiencing recurrent discharge and pain due to lesions around the anus for the past four years?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fistula in ano

What is Fistula-in-Ano?

A fistula-in-ano is a chronic abnormal tract connecting the anal canal to the skin around the anus.

It usually develops after a: Perianal abscess → persistent tract formation → chronic discharge

Common symptoms include:

• Recurrent pus discharge
• Pain around anus
• External opening near anal margin
• Intermittent swelling or irritation

The image shows a small external opening beside the anus, typical of a perianal fistula.

A) Pilonidal sinus

Occurs in the natal cleft above the anus.

Key features:

• Midline sinus
• Hair-containing tract

B) Carbuncle

A cluster of multiple boils caused by Staphylococcus infection.

Features:

• Acute
• Painful multiple pustules
• Not chronic for years

C) Boil (Furuncle)

A single acute infection of a hair follicle.

Features:

• Acute
• Painful swelling
• No chronic discharge

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding ‘Barrett’s Oesophagus’: 1. It is a pre-malignant condition. 2. The normal columnar mucosa of lower oesophagus is replaced by squamous cells. 3. It is an adaptive response to chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 3 only

• 1. It is a pre-malignant condition: Correct

• Barrett’s esophagus is a premalignant condition because intestinal metaplasia can progress through dysplasia → esophageal adenocarcinoma.

• 2. Normal columnar mucosa is replaced by squamous cells: Incorrect

• The opposite occurs.
• The normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by specialized intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells.

• 3. Adaptive response to chronic GERD: Correct

• Chronic exposure to gastric acid and bile causes injury and promotes metaplastic transformation of the distal esophageal epithelium.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Plummer-Vinson syndrome: I. Findings include cervical oesophageal web, iron deficiency anaemia and dysphagia. II. It is a rare disease, mainly affecting middle-aged women. III. There is predisposition to postcricoid, cervical oesophageal cancer. IV. Treatment is usually surgical. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and III

Plummer–Vinson syndrome (Paterson–Brown–Kelly syndrome) is a rare disorder characterized by the triad of:

• Iron deficiency anemia
• Upper (postcricoid/cervical) esophageal web
• Progressive dysphagia

It predominantly affects middle-aged women and is considered a premalignant condition, with an increased risk of postcricoid and upper esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

The following statements are true:

• I. Findings include cervical oesophageal web, iron deficiency anaemia and dysphagia: This is the classic triad of Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
• II. It is a rare disease, mainly affecting middle-aged women: Most commonly affects women between 40–70 years of age.
• III. There is predisposition to postcricoid, cervical oesophageal cancer: Patients have an increased risk of postcricoid and upper esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, necessitating long-term follow-up.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Treatment is usually surgical: Treatment is primarily conservative:

• Iron supplementation often improves dysphagia.
• Persistent esophageal webs are treated with endoscopic dilatation, not surgery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During an upper GI endoscopy, a constriction was observed at 40 cm from the upper incisors. What is the most likely cause of this constriction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diaphragmatic opening

The esophagus has four normal anatomical constrictions, which are important landmarks during upper GI endoscopy, bronchoscopy, and for the common sites of foreign body impaction and corrosive injury.

Normal esophageal constrictions from the upper incisors:

| Constriction | Distance from Upper Incisors

| ------------ | ----------------------------

| Pharyngoesophageal junction (C6, cricopharyngeus) | 15 cm

| Arch of the aorta | 25 cm

| Left main bronchus | 28 cm

| Diaphragmatic hiatus (esophageal hiatus) | 40 cm

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During splenectomy, bleeding is likely to occur from which source when separating spleen from stomach?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Short gastric artery

✅ Option A: Short gastric arteries

• Short gastric artery (branches of the splenic artery) supply the fundus of stomach.
• Run in the gastrosplenic ligament, between spleen and the stomach.
• During splenectomy, separating the spleen from the stomach → risk of tear of these vessels → bleeding.

❌ Option B and C: : Gastroepiploic arteries

• Gastroepiploic arteries lie along the greater curvature, are not in the plane of dissection during splenectomy.

❌ Option D: Splenic artery

• Splenic artery runs along the superior border of the pancreas and reaches the splenic hilum.
• During splenectomy, the splenic artery is usually identified and ligated or clipped at the hilum before the spleen is mobilized.
• When separating the spleen from the stomach, the splenic artery is already controlled and is not in the gastrosplenic ligament. (its the branches of splenic artery that bleed- short gastric)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Earliest symptom of carcinoma oesophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dysphagia more to solids

In Esophageal cancer, the earliest symptom is:

• Progressive dysphagia
• Initially for solids
• Later progresses to liquids

Esophageal carcinoma causes a mechanical obstruction of the lumen.

So:

• Solid food has difficulty passing first
• Liquids can still pass through relatively easily initially

As the tumor enlarges:

• Dysphagia progresses from:

Solids → semisolids → liquids

| Condition | Dysphagia Pattern

| --------- | -----------------

| Mechanical obstruction (e.g., carcinoma esophagus) | Solids first

| Motility disorder (e.g., achalasia) | Solids and liquids from beginning

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the bariatric surgery shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SADI-S

Sleeve Gastrectomy

• Removal of \~70–80% of stomach → Converts stomach into a tube (sleeve)
• No intestinal bypass, Mainly restrictive (↓ Ghrelin → reduces hunger)
• Only stomach reduction, NO intestinal bypass

Option B: SADI-S (Single Anastomosis Duodeno-Ileal bypass)

• Sleeve gastrectomy + one intestinal anastomosis
• Duodenum connected directly to distal ileum
• Restrictive + malabsorptive
• Simpler version of Duodenal Switch
• Lower complication risk compared to classic Duodenal switch
• Sleeve + single anastomosis (loop connection)
• Only ONE intestinal connection

Option C: Duodenal Switch (DS)

• Sleeve gastrectomy + two anastomoses  (Separate biliopancreatic and alimentary limbs)
• Highly effective weight loss, But ↑ risk of malnutrition & complications.
• Sleeve + TWO anastomoses
• More complex

Biliopancreatic Diversion (BPD)

• Older procedure, distal gastrectomy + bypass

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure based on the image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nissen Fundoplication

Why this is Nissen Fundoplication

The image shows the fundus of the stomach wrapped completely around the lower end of the esophagus→ This wrap is then sutured in place to strengthen the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and prevent reflux.

Nissen fundoplication = 360° wrap of gastric fundus around esophagus.

• Done when medical therapy fails.

| Procedure | Wrap | Key point

| --------- | ---- | ---------

| Nissen | 360° | Complete wrap

| Toupet | 270° | Posterior partial wrap

| Dor | 180–200° | Anterior partial wrap

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with carcinoma located at the anal verge, which of the following lymph node groups is most likely to be involved first?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Superficial inguinal nodes

Lymphatic drainage of the anal canal depends on its relation to the pectinate line.

Anal verge / below pectinate line Drains to:

• Superficial inguinal lymph nodes

Therefore, carcinoma at the anal verge first spreads to superficial inguinal nodes.

Important Anatomy

| Region | Lymphatic Drainage

| ------ | ------------------

| Above pectinate line | Internal iliac nodes

| Below pectinate line / anal verge | Superficial inguinal nodes

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In Barrett's esophagus, which of the following epithelial transformations occurs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Squamous to intestinal columnar epithelium

Chronic GERD induces intestinal metaplasia—replacement of normal squamous epithelium by goblet-cell–containing columnar epithelium, a premalignant change for adenocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Match the following conditions with their diagnostic modalities: 1. GERD 2. Biliary atresia 3. Parathyroid adenoma 4. Carcinoma oesophagus a. MRCP b. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) c. 24-hour pH monitoring d. Sestamibi scan
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b

| Condition | Best Diagnostic Modality | Reason

| --------- | ------------------------ | ------

| 1. GERD | c. 24-hour pH monitoring | Gold standard for detecting acid reflux episodes

| 2. Biliary atresia | a. MRCP | Visualizes biliary tract obstruction/absence

| 3. Parathyroid adenoma | d. Sestamibi scan | Localizes hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue

| 4. Carcinoma oesophagus | b. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) | Best for depth of invasion and nodal staging

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Patient presents with abdominal pain and anorexia. Endoscopy shows a flat lesion in lesser curvature of stomach. Genetic analysis shows down-regulation of E-cadherin. Which is the most likely malignancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse gastric carcinoma

• E-cadherin (gene CDH1, chromosome 16q22) is the transmembrane protein mediating calcium-dependent epithelial cell–cell adhesion. Its loss/down-regulation destroys intercellular cohesion, so tumour cells become discohesive and infiltrate singly rather than forming glands — the defining feature of the diffuse type (Lauren classification) of gastric adenocarcinoma. Histology shows signet-ring cells (mucin pushing the nucleus to the periphery); diffuse infiltration of the wall with desmoplasia produces the linitis plastica ("leather bottle") stomach, and the endoscopic appearance is typically a flat/plaque-like or thickened lesion rather than an ulcerated mass.
• Germline CDH1 mutation → Hereditary Diffuse Gastric Cancer (HDGC) — autosomal dominant, associated with lobular breast carcinoma (which also loses E-cadherin), managed with prophylactic total gastrectomy.

Other options:

• A. Intestinal adenocarcinoma → gland-forming, arises on intestinal metaplasia/atrophic gastritis (H. pylori), elderly males, antrum/lesser curve, APC/β-catenin, p53 — E-cadherin retained.
• C. GIST → mesenchymal tumour of interstitial cells of Cajal; c-KIT (CD117)/PDGFRA mutation; submucosal mass with central ulceration.
• D. Gastrinoma → neuroendocrine tumour of gastrinoma triangle → Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (refractory ulcers, diarrhea).

Pearl: E-cadherin loss = Diffuse gastric CA + Lobular breast CA + Signet ring cells + Linitis plastica.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) used in preoperative staging of gastro-oesophageal tumours is to detect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Distant metastatic disease

Positron Emission Tomography (PET-CT) is used in the preoperative staging of gastro-esophageal cancers primarily to detect occult distant metastases, thereby avoiding unnecessary surgery in patients with advanced disease.

Why not the other options?

• B. Extension into stomach: Best assessed by endoscopy and CT/endoscopic ultrasound (EUS).
• C. Local spread: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is the investigation of choice for T staging.
• D. Lymph node status: EUS ± FNA and CT are superior for regional nodal assessment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Resection of which part of intestine does not significantly affect fluid and electrolyte balance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proximal jejunum

The proximal jejunum is responsible for absorbing a large proportion of water, electrolytes, and nutrients. However, resection of the proximal jejunum is usually well tolerated because the remaining distal jejunum and ileum undergo structural and functional adaptation, compensating for the lost absorptive capacity.

In contrast, ileal resection has major consequences because the ileum has specialized absorptive functions that cannot be adequately compensated by other segments of the intestine.

Why not the other options?

• A. Ileum: Resection causes significant fluid and electrolyte loss, bile salt malabsorption, vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, steatorrhea, and short bowel syndrome. ⭐
• C. Distal jejunum: Better tolerated than ileal resection but less commonly emphasized than proximal jejunal resection.
• D. Colon: The colon absorbs approximately 1–1.5 L of water and sodium daily; colectomy increases stool water loss and predisposes to dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The first imaging modality for a 35-year-old lady, presenting to surgical emergency with complaints of colicky pain in right lower quadrant of abdomen and vomiting since last 2 days is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ultrasound abdomen

A 35-year-old woman presenting with right lower quadrant (RLQ) colicky abdominal pain and vomiting should initially undergo ultrasound (USG) of the abdomen. In women of reproductive age, ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality because it is non-invasive, radiation-free, readily available, and can evaluate both surgical and gynecological causes of acute abdominal pain. It can diagnose:

• Acute appendicitis
• Ovarian torsion
• Ruptured ovarian cyst
• Ectopic pregnancy (with transvaginal USG)
• Pelvic inflammatory disease
• Ureteric calculi with hydronephrosis

Why not the other options?

• A. Contrast CT abdomen:

• Highly accurate for appendicitis but not the initial investigation in young women due to radiation exposure.
• Used when ultrasound is inconclusive.

• B. Non-contrast CT abdomen: Preferred for suspected renal/ureteric calculi, not as the initial test for undifferentiated RLQ pain.
• D. Plain X-ray abdomen (erect):

• Limited value in RLQ pain.
• Mainly useful for detecting intestinal obstruction or perforation (free air under diaphragm).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The HPE section taken from the gastroesophageal junction is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Barrett esophagus

Barrett esophagus is an intestinal metaplasia in which the normal non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by non-ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). It is a premalignant condition that increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

• The biopsy from the gastroesophageal junction shows intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, which is diagnostic of Barrett esophagus.

Why not the other options?

• A. Adenocarcinoma: Would show invasive atypical malignant glands with stromal invasion, not simple intestinal metaplasia.
• B. Low-grade dysplasia: Shows cytologic atypia within Barrett mucosa; the image demonstrates metaplasia without clear dysplasia.
• C. Squamous cell carcinoma: Composed of malignant squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, not glandular epithelium.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The pathology seen in the image occurs due to weakness between which of the following muscles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thyropharyngeus & Cricopharyngeus

The image shows a Zenker diverticulum (pharyngoesophageal diverticulum), which develops due to herniation of the pharyngeal mucosa through Killian’s dehiscence, a weak area between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor.

Why not the other options?

• B. Cricopharyngeus & esophageal longitudinal muscle: This is not the site of the anatomical weakness causing Zenker diverticulum.
• C. Inferior constrictor & middle constrictor: No natural area of weakness exists between these muscles.
• D. Stylopharyngeus & palatopharyngeus: These longitudinal pharyngeal muscles are unrelated to Zenker diverticulum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The presence of which of the following is suggestive of metastatic spread of an underlying gastrointestinal malignancy? 1. Krukenberg Tumour 2. Virchow’s Node 3. Meigs’ Syndrome 4. Sister Mary Joseph’s Nodule Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

• 1. Krukenberg tumor: Correct

• Represents metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma, classically to the ovaries.
• Usually contains signet-ring cells.

• 2. Virchow’s node: Correct

• Left supraclavicular lymph-node enlargement due to metastatic spread, classically from gastric carcinoma.

• 3. Meigs’ syndrome: Incorrect

• Triad of ovarian fibroma + ascites + pleural effusion.
• It is a benign ovarian tumor syndrome, not a marker of gastrointestinal malignancy.

• 4. Sister Mary Joseph’s nodule: Correct

• A metastatic deposit at the umbilicus, commonly associated with gastrointestinal or gynecological malignancies.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the diagnosis based on the upper GI endoscopy image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Esophageal varices

Varices are -Dilated columns of veins in the esophagus.

• Endoscopy of esophageal varices → dilated tortuous submucosal veins, bulging longitudinal folds in the esophagus.

Clinical presentation : Hematemesis.

• Seen in portal hypertension→ most commonly due to liver cirrhosis.

Option A:  Barrett’s esophagus: red velvet mucosa is seen, not dilated veins.

Option C: Gastric erosions : small superficial erosions in mucosa.

Option D: Candidiasis shows white cheesy plaques, not dilated veins.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for an 8 cm chylo-lymphatic mesenteric cyst?
options: Resection of cyst along with adjacent bowel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enucleation

Chylolymphatic mesenteric cysts are separate from bowel and treated by enucleation, even when large.

Aspiration leads to recurrence, while bowel resection is only for enterogenous cysts attached to the intestine.

| Feature | Finding

| ------- | -------

| Location | Small bowel mesentery

| Content | Chyle or lymph

| Symptoms | Abdominal mass, pain

| Treatment | Complete surgical removal

| Type of cyst | Treatment

| ------------ | ---------

| Chylo-lymphatic mesenteric cyst | Enucleation

| Enterogenous cyst | Bowel resection

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common cause of perforation of the oesophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iatrogenic infection

Oesophageal perforation is a life-threatening surgical emergency associated with high morbidity and mortality due to rapid development of mediastinitis and sepsis. The most common cause is iatrogenic injury, usually occurring during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or oesophageal dilatation.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Barotrauma: Barotrauma can cause spontaneous oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome) after forceful vomiting, but it is less common than iatrogenic injury.
• B. Mediastinitis: Mediastinitis is a complication, not a cause, of oesophageal perforation.
• D. Malignancy: Oesophageal cancer may perforate, especially after radiotherapy or stenting, but it is not the most common cause.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common type of tumour of Vermiform Appendix?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carcinoid tumour

The most common tumor of the appendix overall is the Carcinoid tumor (Neuroendocrine Tumor/NET).

Key points for recall:

• Most common tumor of appendix (any type): Carcinoid/NET
• Most common site: Tip of appendix
• Most common malignant epithelial tumor: Mucinous adenocarcinoma
• Most common tumor to cause appendicitis-like presentation: Carcinoid (due to luminal obstruction)

Quick differentiator table:

| Tumor | Frequency | Location | Behavior

| ----- | --------- | -------- | --------

| Carcinoid (NET) | Most common overall | Tip | Usually indolent, malignant potential if >2cm

| Mucinous adenocarcinoma | Most common malignant epithelial | Base/body | Risk of PMP

| Goblet cell carcinoid (adenocarcinoid) | Rare | Variable | More aggressive than classic carcinoid

| Adenocarcinoma (colonic type) | Rare | Base | Behaves like colon cancer

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What value is called significant rectocele on MRI defecography?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 cm bulge

A rectocele is considered radiologically significant on MRI defecography (and conventional defecography) when there is an anterior rectal wall bulge of ≥ 2 cm beyond the expected margin of the anal canal/posterior vaginal wall.

What is a Rectocele?

A rectocele is a herniation of the anterior rectal wall into the posterior vaginal wall, occurring due to weakness or defect in the rectovaginal septum (fascia of Denonvilliers).

• Clinically: bulging in the posterior vaginal wall, incomplete evacuation, need to digitally splint the perineum/posterior vaginal wall to defecate ("digitation")
• Almost exclusively in females (posterior compartment prolapse)
• Classification is based on depth of protrusion measured on defecography

Classification by Depth (The Standard System)

The most widely used classification, derived from conventional proctography/defecography and validated for MRI defecography, is:

| Grade | Depth of Bulge | Clinical Significance

| ----- | -------------- | ---------------------

| Small | < 2 cm | Clinically insignificant, often incidental

| Moderate | 2 : 4 cm | May be symptomatic, assess with clinical correlation

| Large | > 4 cm | Significant, usually symptomatic, surgical consideration

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which among the following is considered the major risk factor for cecal volvulus in 30–70% of cases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Previous abdominal surgery

Cecal volvulus occurs due to twisting of a mobile cecum, ascending colon, and terminal ileum, leading to closed-loop intestinal obstruction with a risk of bowel ischemia and perforation. Previous abdominal surgery is the most common predisposing factor, being present in 30–70% of patients, as postoperative adhesions act as a fixed point for volvulus.

Why not the other options?

• A. Excessive use of laxatives: More commonly associated with sigmoid volvulus and chronic constipation, not cecal volvulus.
• B. High-fibre diet: Predisposes to sigmoid volvulus, especially in endemic regions.
• D. Female gender: Cecal volvulus has a slight female predominance in some studies but is not the major risk factor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which among the following is the oncological principle behind total mesorectal excision (TME) in rectal surgery?
options: Sharp resection of the entire mesorectum as a single intact unit
Blunt removal of the pelvic autonomic nerves
Excision of the peritumor fat around the mesorectum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sharp resection of the entire mesorectum as a single intact unit

Total Mesorectal Excision (TME) is the gold standard surgical technique for mid and low rectal cancers. The oncological principle is sharp dissection along the embryological (holy) plane to remove the rectum and the entire mesorectum intact, enclosed within its fascial envelope. This ensures complete excision of lymphovascular tissue and minimizes circumferential resection margin (CRM) positivity and local recurrence.

• Sharp resection of the entire mesorectum as a single intact unit is the fundamental principle of TME.
• It preserves the integrity of the mesorectal fascia, resulting in:

• Negative circumferential resection margins (CRM)
• Complete lymph node clearance
• Reduced local recurrence
• Improved long-term survival

Why not the other options?

• B. Blunt removal of the pelvic autonomic nerves: Incorrect. TME aims to preserve, not remove, the pelvic autonomic nerves to maintain urinary and sexual function.
• C. Excision of the peritumor fat around the mesorectum: Incorrect. The entire mesorectum, not just the peritumoral fat, must be removed en bloc.
• D. Ligation of internal iliac vessels: Incorrect. This is not a principle of TME and is not routinely performed in rectal cancer surgery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which kind of the following surgery will cause a profound decrease in vitamin B12?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. BPD-DS

Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD-DS) is the most malabsorptive bariatric procedure and is associated with the greatest risk of vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 absorption requires:

• Intrinsic factor (IF) produced by gastric parietal cells.
• An intact terminal ileum for absorption of the IF–B12 complex.

Following BPD-DS, reduced gastric acid and intrinsic factor production, along with bypass of a large segment of the small intestine, markedly impair vitamin B12 absorption. Lifelong vitamin B12 supplementation is therefore recommended.

• BPD-DS combines:

• Sleeve gastrectomy (reduced intrinsic factor production)
• Extensive intestinal bypass (marked malabsorption)

Why not the other options?

• B. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass: Can cause vitamin B12 deficiency due to reduced intrinsic factor and bypass of the duodenum, but the deficiency is less severe than with BPD-DS.
• C. Billroth I: Partial gastrectomy with gastroduodenostomy; causes relatively less vitamin B12 malabsorption because intestinal continuity is largely preserved.
• D. Billroth II: Partial gastrectomy with gastrojejunostomy; may lead to vitamin B12 deficiency over time due to loss of parietal cells, but less profound than BPD-DS.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are considered aetiological factors for Adenocarcinoma oesophagus? I. Barrett’s oesophagus II. Gastro-oesophageal reflux III. Obesity IV. Alcohol intake Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Esophageal adenocarcinoma most commonly arises in the distal esophagus and develops through the sequence: Chronic GERD → Barrett’s esophagus → Dysplasia → Adenocarcinoma.

The incidence has increased significantly with the rising prevalence of obesity and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

The following are established risk factors for esophageal adenocarcinoma:

• I. Barrett’s esophagus: The most important premalignant lesion for esophageal adenocarcinoma. It involves intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophageal squamous epithelium due to chronic acid reflux.
• II. Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD): Chronic acid reflux leads to Barrett’s esophagus and markedly increases the risk of adenocarcinoma.
• III. Obesity: Particularly central obesity, which increases intra-abdominal pressure, promotes GERD, and independently increases the risk of adenocarcinoma.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Alcohol intake: Alcohol is a major risk factor for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct for herniation via foramen of Morgagni? 1. It occurs posteriorly in chest. 2. Transverse colon is the commonest content. 3. Defect is between sternal and costal attachments. 4. It is a type of congenital hernia. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Foramen of Morgagni hernia is a rare congenital diaphragmatic hernia caused by a defect in the anterior diaphragm, located between the sternal and costal fibers of the diaphragm. It usually occurs on the right side and commonly contains the transverse colon or omentum.

Why is D correct?

• 1. It occurs posteriorly in chest. ✗

• Morgagni hernia is an anterior diaphragmatic hernia.
• The posterior diaphragmatic defect is the foramen of Bochdalek.

• 2. Transverse colon is the commonest content. ✓

• The transverse colon is the most common herniated viscus, followed by the omentum and occasionally the stomach or liver.

• 3. Defect is between sternal and costal attachments. ✓

• The foramen of Morgagni lies between the sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm (sternocostal triangle).

• 4. It is a type of congenital hernia. ✓

• Morgagni hernia is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, although it may remain asymptomatic until adulthood.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding late dumping? I. It usually occurs during the second hour after meal. II. It lasts for 30–40 minutes. III. Major symptoms are tremor, faintness, prostration. IV. It is relieved by lying down. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Late dumping syndrome is a complication seen after gastric surgery (e.g., gastrectomy, gastrojejunostomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass). It occurs due to rapid delivery of carbohydrates into the small intestine, causing a rapid rise in blood glucose followed by an exaggerated insulin response, resulting in reactive hypoglycemia. The following statements are true:

• I. It usually occurs during the second hour after meal: Late dumping typically develops 1–3 hours after eating, most commonly around 2 hours after a carbohydrate-rich meal.
• II. It lasts for 30–40 minutes: Symptoms usually persist for 30–60 minutes and resolve as blood glucose normalizes.
• III. Major symptoms are tremor, faintness, prostration: These are manifestations of reactive hypoglycemia and may include:

• Tremors
• Sweating
• Palpitations
• Hunger
• Dizziness/faintness
• Weakness (prostration)

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. It is relieved by lying down: Lying down helps relieve early dumping syndrome by slowing gastric emptying, but it is not a characteristic treatment for late dumping syndrome, which is caused by hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are indications of splenectomy? 1. Pseudomyxoma peritonei 2. Trauma 3. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) 4. Hypersplenism Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Splenectomy is indicated for splenic trauma, selected cases of refractory idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and hypersplenism causing significant cytopenias.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Pseudomyxoma peritonei ❌: Not a routine indication for splenectomy.
• 2. Trauma ✔️: Common indication, especially for uncontrolled splenic bleeding.
• 3. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) ✔️: Indicated in steroid-resistant/refractory cases.
• 4. Hypersplenism ✔️: Indicated when splenic sequestration causes symptomatic cytopenias.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are metabolic causes of splenic enlargement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amyloid and Gaucher’s disease

Splenomegaly has numerous causes and is commonly classified into infectious, hematological, congestive, neoplastic, inflammatory, and metabolic/storage disorders. Metabolic causes are mainly due to lysosomal storage diseases and abnormal protein deposition, leading to accumulation of substances within the spleen.

• Amyloidosis causes splenomegaly due to extracellular deposition of amyloid protein.
• Gaucher’s disease (β-glucocerebrosidase deficiency) is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and classically presents with massive splenomegaly.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Rickets and Still’s disease:

• Rickets is a metabolic bone disease and does not cause splenomegaly.
• Still’s disease is an inflammatory disorder and may cause splenomegaly, but it is not a metabolic disease.

• C. Porphyria and Felty’s syndrome:

• Porphyria is a metabolic disorder but splenomegaly is uncommon.
• Felty’s syndrome is an autoimmune disorder (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), not metabolic.

• D. Myelofibrosis and Weil’s disease:

• Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm.
• Weil’s disease is severe leptospirosis (infectious).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are the common complications after splenectomy? 1. Pancreatic fistula 2. Thrombocytopenia 3. Opportunistic infection 4. Left basal atelectasis Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Common complications following splenectomy include:

1. Pancreatic fistula — Correct

• The tail of the pancreas lies close to the spleen.
• Pancreatic injury during splenectomy can result in a pancreatic fistula.

2. Thrombocytopenia — Incorrect

• Splenectomy typically causes reactive thrombocytosis, not thrombocytopenia, because platelet sequestration in the spleen is removed.
• Thrombocytosis can increase the risk of portal/splenic vein thrombosis.

3. Opportunistic/severe infections — Correct

• Loss of splenic function increases susceptibility to overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI), particularly from encapsulated organisms such as S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis and H. influenzae.

4. Left basal atelectasis — Correct

• It is a common early postoperative pulmonary complication following upper abdominal surgery, including splenectomy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes small bowel obstruction and paralytic ileus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Colicky abdominal pain

Small bowel obstruction (SBO) is characterized by colicky (cramping) abdominal pain caused by vigorous peristaltic contractions attempting to overcome a mechanical obstruction. In contrast, paralytic ileus results from absent intestinal peristalsis and presents with diffuse, constant discomfort rather than colicky pain.

• Colicky abdominal pain is the hallmark of mechanical small bowel obstruction and helps distinguish it from paralytic ileus, in which bowel motility is absent.

Why not the other options?

• A. Abdominal distension: Seen in both SBO and paralytic ileus.
• C. Vomiting: Common in both conditions, especially in proximal SBO.
• D. Tachycardia: May occur in both due to dehydration, pain, or sepsis and is not a distinguishing feature.

| Feature | Small Bowel Obstruction | Paralytic Ileus

| ------- | ----------------------- | ---------------

| Pain | Colicky, intermittent | Constant, mild, diffuse

| Bowel sounds | High-pitched, hyperactive (“tinkling”) | Absent or markedly reduced

| Peristalsis | Increased initially | Absent

| Abdominal distension | Present | Present

| Vomiting | Common | Common

| X-ray | Multiple air-fluid levels with step-ladder pattern | Generalized gaseous distension of bowel

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding late dumping syndrome?
options: Aggravated by exercise and physical activity
Symptoms include tremors, dizziness, and palpitations
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Relieved by lying down

| Feature | Early Dumping | Late Dumping

| ------- | ------------- | ------------

| Time | 15–30 min | 1–3 hrs

| Cause | Osmotic fluid shift | Reactive hypoglycaemia

| Symptoms | GI + vasomotor symptoms | Hypoglycaemic symptoms

| Relief by lying down | ✔ Yes | ✘ No

Lying down helps in early dumping syndrome because early dumping happens due to fluid shifting in the intestine, causing vasomotor symptoms (tachycardia, flushing).

But late dumping is due to low sugar, not fluid shift.

Changing posture does nothing for hypoglycemia.

Early dumping = Fluid problem → posture helps

Late dumping = Sugar problem → posture doesn’t help

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrectly paired with its corresponding classification or criteria system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Achalasia – LA classification

• Achalasia is classified using the Chicago Classification.
• It is based on high-resolution esophageal manometry findings.
• LA (Los Angeles) classification is used to  grade reflux esophagitis (GERD) on endoscopy.

| Condition / Procedure | Classification / Score | Purpose

| --------------------- | ---------------------- | -------

| Peritonitis | Mannheim Peritonitis Index (MPI) | Predicts mortality and prognosis

| Colonoscopy | Boston Bowel Preparation Score | Assesses quality of bowel preparation

| Parathyroid resection | Miami Criteria | Confirms successful parathyroidectomy (↓ PTH ≥50%)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a classical symptom of acute appendicitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Constipation

Acute appendicitis classically presents with periumbilical visceral pain that later shifts to the right iliac fossa (McBurney’s point). The classical symptoms are:

• Anorexia (most consistent symptom)
• Periumbilical colicky pain migrating to the right iliac fossa
• Nausea and vomiting (usually after the onset of pain)

Constipation is not a classical symptom. Patients may have constipation or diarrhea, but neither is a characteristic feature.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. NRG-1

✔️Option A: KIT (CD117)

• Most common marker (\~95%)
• Gain of function mutations in KIT gene seen.

✔️Option B: PDGFRA (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor Receptor Alpha)

• Mutated in a subset of GISTs (usually KIT-negative tumors)

✔️Option C: SDH (Succinate Dehydrogenase complex)

• Seen in SDH-deficient GISTs ie loss of function mutation
• often seen in younger patients.
• Typically KIT/PDGFRA negative tumors.

❌ Option D: NRG- 1

• NRG-1 is seen in:Lung adenocarcinoma
• Some pancreatic, breast, and ovarian cancer

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following positions of the appendix is likely to present with suprapubic pain in a patient with acute appendicitis? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subcaecal

The subcaecal position is most likely to cause suprapubic pain among the given options. When the appendix is positioned below the cecum, it can extend inferiorly toward the pelvic brim. Inflammation in this position may spread downward, causing irritation to pelvic structures and resulting in suprapubic discomfort. This anatomical relationship explains why subcaecal appendicitis can present with symptoms similar to pelvic appendicitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding Barrett’s oesophagus? 1. It is a metaplastic change. 2. It is a risk factor for development of adenocarcinoma. 3. Ingestion of NSAIDs is the aetiological factor for its development. 4. Endoscopic mucosal resection is an effective treatment. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Barrett’s oesophagus is a premalignant condition in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). It is the most important precursor lesion for oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

Why is C correct?

• 1. It is a metaplastic change. ✅

• Barrett’s oesophagus is an example of intestinal metaplasia, where squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

• 2. It is a risk factor for development of adenocarcinoma. ✅

• Barrett’s oesophagus significantly increases the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, especially in the presence of dysplasia.

• 3. Ingestion of NSAIDs is the aetiological factor for its development. ❌

• The principal cause is chronic GERD, not NSAID use.

• 4. Endoscopic mucosal resection is an effective treatment. ✅

• Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR), often combined with radiofrequency ablation (RFA), is effective for high-grade dysplasia or early intramucosal adenocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the management of gastrointestinal bleeding in children? I. Somatostatin or octreotide infusion should be given for at least 7 days after stoppage of initial bleeding to prevent rebleeding II. Endoscopic Sclerotherapy (EST) involves endoscopic injection of N-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate or iso-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate III. EST has upto 90% efficacy in controlling acute bleeding IV. Following an episode of acute variceal bleeding, all patients should receive secondary prophylaxis to prevent rebleeding Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. III and IV

Acute variceal gastrointestinal bleeding in children is a life-threatening emergency, most commonly caused by portal hypertension. Management includes hemodynamic stabilization, vasoactive drugs, endoscopic therapy, and prevention of rebleeding (secondary prophylaxis).

Why is C correct?

• I. Somatostatin or octreotide infusion should be given for at least 7 days after stoppage of initial bleeding to prevent rebleeding. ✘

• Incorrect.
• Vasoactive therapy (octreotide or somatostatin) is generally continued for 2–5 days, not 7 days, after control of bleeding.

• II. Endoscopic Sclerotherapy (EST) involves endoscopic injection of N-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate or iso-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate. ✘

• Incorrect.
• Cyanoacrylate glue injection is used for gastric varices.
• Endoscopic sclerotherapy (EST) uses sclerosants such as ethanolamine oleate or sodium tetradecyl sulfate, not tissue glue.

• III. EST has up to 90% efficacy in controlling acute bleeding. ✔

• Correct.
• Endoscopic therapy (especially endoscopic variceal ligation and sclerotherapy) achieves hemostasis in approximately 80–90% of acute variceal bleeds.

• IV. Following an episode of acute variceal bleeding, all patients should receive secondary prophylaxis to prevent rebleeding. ✔

• Correct.
• Secondary prophylaxis with repeated endoscopic variceal ligation/sclerotherapy, with or without non-selective β-blockers (in selected children), is recommended to reduce the risk of recurrent bleeding.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Carcinoid tumour are correct? 1. Terminal ileum is the most common site for these tumours in the gastrointestinal tract. 2. These tumours arise from Kulchitsky cells situated at the base of intestinal crypts. 3. 5-Hydroxytryptamine is the most common vasoactive peptide produced by these tumours. 4. Serum chromogranin A is a useful marker for disease recurrence. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

Why is B correct?

• 2. These tumours arise from Kulchitsky cells situated at the base of intestinal crypts ✅: Correct. Carcinoid tumors arise from enterochromaffin (Kulchitsky) neuroendocrine cells.
• 3. 5-Hydroxytryptamine (Serotonin) is the most common vasoactive peptide produced by these tumours ✅: Correct. Serotonin is the principal secretory product responsible for carcinoid syndrome.
• 4. Serum Chromogranin A is a useful marker for disease recurrence ✅: Correct. Chromogranin A is the most widely used tumor marker for diagnosis and follow-up of neuroendocrine tumors.

Incorrect statement:

• 1. Terminal ileum is the most common site for these tumours in the gastrointestinal tract ❌ (As per exam key):

• In many standard surgical examinations, this statement is considered incorrect because the appendix is regarded as the most common individual GI site.
• However, clinically, the ileum is the most common site of malignant gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Ogilvie’s syndrome are correct? 1. It presents as acute large bowel mechanical obstruction. 2. Marked caecal dilatation is a common feature on X-ray abdomen. 3. Caecal perforation is a well recognized complication of this condition. 4. Intravenous Neostigmine is used for the treatment of this condition. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

Why is B. correct?

• 1. It presents as acute large bowel mechanical obstruction.

• Incorrect.
• Ogilvie’s syndrome is a pseudo-obstruction with no mechanical blockage.

• 2. Marked caecal dilatation is a common feature on X-ray abdomen.

• Correct.
• The caecum and right colon are usually markedly dilated.

• 3. Caecal perforation is a well-recognized complication of this condition.

• Correct.
• Risk increases when caecal diameter exceeds 10–12 cm or distension persists for >6 days.

• 4. Intravenous Neostigmine is used for the treatment of this condition.

• Correct.
• IV neostigmine is the drug of choice if conservative treatment fails and there are no contraindications.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements with regard to Enteric perforation are correct? 1. Salmonella typhi is the causative organism for Enteric fever. 2. Enteric perforation characteristically occurs during third week of illness. 3. Typhoid ulcers are placed transversely to the long axis of the gut. 4. Terminal ileum is the most common site for enteric perforation. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 4

Enteric perforation is the most serious complication of typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi. It usually occurs due to necrosis of Peyer’s patches in the terminal ileum, most commonly during the third week of illness.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Salmonella typhi is the causative organism for enteric fever ✔️: Correct.
• 2. Enteric perforation characteristically occurs during the third week of illness ✔️: Correct.
• 3. Typhoid ulcers are placed transversely to the long axis of the gut ❌: Incorrect. Typhoid ulcers are longitudinal (parallel) to the long axis of the bowel (contrast: tuberculous ulcers are transverse).
• 4. Terminal ileum is the most common site for enteric perforation ✔️: Correct.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of these are included in extra-oesophageal symptoms of GERD? a. Asthma b. Laryngitis c. Excessive phlegm d. Pulmonary fibrosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

Extra-oesophageal (atypical) manifestations of Gastroesophageal reflux disease include:

Option a. Asthma -correct

• Acid + pepsin from Gastroesophageal reflux disease reflux up the esophagus
• Small amounts spill over into the larynx and airways ( especially during sleep)--> leading to direct chemical irritation of bronchial mucosa

Option b. Laryngitis : Reflux laryngitis (part of laryngopharyngeal reflux) —> Direct irritation of laryngeal mucosa by acid/pepsin

• Patients usually present with morning hoarseness of voice.

Option c. Excessive phlegm / throat clearing

• Due to chronic irritation of upper airway mucosa.

Option d. Pulmonary fibrosis

• May occur rarely due to aspiration of acid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is a contraindication of doing a wireless capsule endoscopy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Small bowel stricture

Wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) is a noninvasive technique used to visualize the small intestine, particularly areas that are difficult to assess with conventional upper GI endoscopy or colonoscopy. The patient swallows a small camera-containing capsule that transmits images as it passes through the gastrointestinal tract.

The major contraindication to capsule endoscopy is a known or suspected small bowel stricture, obstruction, or fistula, because the capsule may become impacted, leading to capsule retention and possible intestinal obstruction.

Common Indications for Capsule Endoscopy

• Obscure gastrointestinal bleeding after negative upper and lower endoscopy
• Iron deficiency anemia of unknown source
• Suspected or known small bowel Crohn disease
• Small bowel tumors
• Celiac disease (selected cases with suspected complications or refractory disease)
• Positive fecal occult blood test with negative conventional evaluation

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

• A. Coeliac disease

• An indication in selected patients, especially when complications are suspected.

• C. Obscure gastrointestinal bleeding

• One of the most common and important indications for capsule endoscopy.

• D. FOBT positive but CT negative

• Capsule endoscopy may be useful to evaluate an occult small bowel source of bleeding.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of oesophageal motility disorders?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High resolution manometry

High-resolution esophageal manometry (HRM) is the gold standard investigation for diagnosing esophageal motility disorders. It measures esophageal peristalsis, lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure, LES relaxation, and esophageal body motility, allowing accurate classification of motility disorders according to the Chicago Classification. It diagnoses:

• Achalasia
• Diffuse esophageal spasm
• Hypercontractile (Jackhammer) esophagus
• Ineffective esophageal motility
• Esophagogastric junction outflow obstruction

Why not the other options?

• A. Upper GI endoscopy: Useful to exclude structural lesions (e.g., malignancy, strictures, esophagitis) but cannot diagnose motility disorders.
• B. Barium swallow: Demonstrates characteristic findings (e.g., bird-beak appearance in achalasia) but is not the gold standard.
• D. Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) oesophagus: Used for staging malignancy or evaluating extrinsic compression, not for assessing motility.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct regarding splenic artery aneurysm?
options: It is twice as common in men.
It is usually situated in the main arterial trunk.
It is caused due to blunt trauma to the abdomen.
It is generally multiple in number.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is usually situated in the main arterial trunk.

Splenic artery aneurysm (SAA) is the most common visceral artery aneurysm, accounting for approximately 60% of all visceral artery aneurysms. Most aneurysms occur along the main trunk of the splenic artery, particularly in its distal third, before it enters the splenic hilum.

Although many SAAs are asymptomatic, rupture is life-threatening, especially during pregnancy, with high maternal and fetal mortality.

Why not the other options?

• A. It is twice as common in men: Splenic artery aneurysms are actually more common in women, especially multiparous women.
• C. It is caused due to blunt trauma to the abdomen: Blunt trauma typically causes a splenic artery pseudoaneurysm, not a true aneurysm.
• D. It is generally multiple in number: Most splenic artery aneurysms are single (solitary).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct about mesenteric cysts?
options: It occurs most commonly in children less than 18 years of age.
It is more common in males as compared to females.
It presents most commonly as a painless abdominal swelling.
Percutaneous aspiration with injection of sclerosant is the preferred treatment option.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It presents most commonly as a painless abdominal swelling.

A mesenteric cyst is a rare benign intra-abdominal cyst arising from the mesentery of the small or large intestine, most commonly from the small bowel mesentery. It usually presents as a slow-growing, painless abdominal swelling and is treated by complete surgical excision to prevent recurrence and complications.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. It occurs most commonly in children less than 18 years of age: Mesenteric cysts can occur at any age. Although they are seen in children, most cases are diagnosed in adults (4th–5th decade).
• B. It is more common in males as compared to females: There is no significant male predominance; many studies report an equal or slight female predominance.
• D. Percutaneous aspiration with injection of sclerosant is the preferred treatment option: Aspiration has a high recurrence rate and risk of infection. Complete surgical excision (laparoscopic or open) is the treatment of choice.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding (UGIB)?
options: Esophageal varices are the most common cause.
Eradication of Helicobacter pylori in patients with bleeding ulcers decreases the rebleeding rates to less than 5%.
Patients with cardiovascular disease who are on aspirin for secondary prevention should not restart their aspirin.
Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS) should be considered as therapy only after one week of hospitalization for acute variceal bleeding.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Eradication of Helicobacter pylori in patients with bleeding ulcers decreases the rebleeding rates to less than 5%.

Upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) is bleeding originating proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Peptic ulcer disease is the most common cause of UGIB, and eradication of Helicobacter pylori in patients with bleeding peptic ulcers markedly reduces ulcer recurrence and lowers the risk of rebleeding to <5%.

Explanation of the options:

• A. Esophageal varices are the most common cause: Incorrect. Peptic ulcer disease, not esophageal varices, is the most common cause of UGIB.
• B. Eradication of Helicobacter pylori in patients with bleeding ulcers decreases the rebleeding rates to less than 5%: Correct. Successful H. pylori eradication after a bleeding peptic ulcer significantly reduces recurrent ulcer bleeding.
• C. Patients with cardiovascular disease who are on aspirin for secondary prevention should not restart their aspirin: Incorrect. In patients taking aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention, aspirin should generally be restarted early (usually within 3–5 days after achieving hemostasis) because prolonged discontinuation increases the risk of cardiovascular events.
• D. Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS) should be considered as therapy only after one week of hospitalization for acute variceal bleeding: Incorrect. Early or pre-emptive TIPS (within 72 hours) is recommended in selected high-risk patients with acute variceal bleeding, not after waiting one week.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is not correct regarding Gastric outlet obstruction associated with long standing peptic ulcer disease?
options: Hypochloraemic alkalosis is the usual metabolic abnormality in such cases.
Endoscopic biopsy is essential to exclude malignancy.
Medical therapy has no role in the treatment of this condition.
Operation is frequently required along with a drainage procedure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medical therapy has no role in the treatment of this condition.

Gastric outlet obstruction (GOO) is a complication of long-standing peptic ulcer disease (PUD) caused by chronic inflammation, edema, fibrosis, and cicatrization around the pylorus or duodenum, leading to obstruction of gastric emptying. The statement “Medical therapy has no role” is incorrect, because initial medical management is essential and may relieve obstruction due to edema.

Medical treatment plays an important role initially and includes:

• Nasogastric decompression
• Intravenous fluids and electrolyte correction
• Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)
• Helicobacter pylori eradication, if present

Patients with obstruction due to acute inflammatory edema may improve with medical therapy alone. Surgery is reserved for persistent or fibrotic obstruction.

Why are the other options correct?

• A. Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis is the usual metabolic abnormality: Repeated vomiting leads to loss of hydrogen and chloride ions, producing hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
• B. Endoscopic biopsy is essential to exclude malignancy: Since gastric carcinoma is now a common cause of GOO, upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is mandatory.
• D. Operation is frequently required along with a drainage procedure: Chronic fibrotic obstruction often requires surgery such as:

• Truncal vagotomy + pyloroplasty
• Truncal vagotomy + gastrojejunostomy
• Antrectomy with reconstruction

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain 4 days after undergoing cholecystectomy. Ultrasound reveals a collection of approximately 200 mL in the right upper quadrant. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. USG-guided pigtail insertion

After cholecystectomy, a bile leak can occur from:

• Cystic duct stump
• Accessory bile duct (duct of Luschka)
• Minor bile duct injury

Leading to accumulation of bile in the abdomen forming a biloma.

Typical features:

• Post-operative RUQ pain
• Fluid collection on ultrasound
• Occurs within a few days after surgery

The first-line management is: USG-guided drainage using a Pigtail catheter

Why?

• Relieves symptoms; Prevents infection
• Helps confirm bile leak if aspirated fluid contains bile.

A) Re-explore laparoscopically

This is not the first step unless:

• Patient deteriorates
• Major bile duct injury is suspected

B) Higher antibiotics

Antibiotics do not treat the collection that is already present The fluid must be drained.

C) MRCP

MRCP helps identify bile duct injury, but:

It is usually done after drainage, not before.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male with a history of chronic alcoholism presents with high-grade fever and right upper quadrant pain for 5 days. He gives a history of diarrhoea one week ago. On examination, he is febrile and has tender hepatomegaly. Ultrasound abdomen reveals a solitary liver abscess measuring 25 cc in the right lobe. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medical management

These findings suggest amoebic liver abscess.

Reason:

• Amoebiasis often follows intestinal infection → diarrhoea
• Infection spreads via portal vein to liver
• Right lobe involvement is most common.

The abscess is 25 cc, which is small.

| Abscess size | Treatment

| ------------ | ---------

| Small (<5 cm) | Medical therapy only

| Large (>5 cm) | Percutaneous drainage

| Risk of rupture / left lobe abscess | Drainage

So here → medical treatment first.

Drugs used

1. Metronidazole – kills tissue amoeba

2. Luminal agent (to clear intestinal cysts)

Diloxanide furoate

Paromomycin

❌ A) PAIR

PAIR = Puncture–Aspiration–Injection–Reaspiration

Used for hydatid cyst, not amoebic abscess.

❌ B) Surgery

Rarely required;  Only if rupture or complications.

❌D) Percutaneous drainage

Indicated when:

• Abscess >5 cm
• Left lobe abscess
• Risk of rupture
• No response to drugs

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old male is diagnosed with a tumor in the left lobe of the liver, and a left hemi-hepatectomy is planned. Which anatomical segments (lobes) of the liver will be resected in this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 3 and 4

Left hemi-hepatectomy removes segments 2, 3, and 4 (4a/4b) supplied by the left portal pedicle. Segment 1 is independent and usually preserved. Segments 5–8 belong to the right hemiliver.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis. While dissecting Calot's triangle, a lateral injury to the common bile duct occurred, leading to significant bile leakage into the operative field. The surgeon has limited experience in laparoscopy. What is the most appropriate intraoperative management step at this stage?
options: Continuing laparoscopic repair of the common bile duct
Placing a drainage tube in subhepatic space
Closing the abdomen and taking the patient for ERCP and biliary stenting
Converting the laparoscopic surgery to open surgery and placing a T-tube through the injured common bile duct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Converting the laparoscopic surgery to open surgery and placing a T-tube through the injured common bile duct

Bile duct injury is one of the most serious complications of laparoscopic cholecystectomy, most commonly occurring during dissection of Calot’s triangle due to misidentification of biliary anatomy. In this case:

• Lateral injury to the common bile duct (CBD)
• Significant bile leak
• Surgeon has limited laparoscopic experience

The safest management is to convert to open surgery and repair the injury over a T-tube, which decompresses the biliary tree and allows postoperative cholangiography.

Why not the other options?

• A. Continue laparoscopic repair of common bile duct: Not advisable in an inexperienced surgeon; increases the risk of further injury and stricture.
• B. Place only a drainage tube in subhepatic space: Inadequate for a recognized CBD injury.
• C. Close abdomen and perform ERCP and biliary stenting later: ERCP is useful for postoperative leaks but recognized major intraoperative bile duct injuries should be addressed immediately.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient with a history of cholecystectomy 4 years back for gallstones presents with symptoms of obstructive jaundice. Imaging studies reveal a stone in the common bile duct. What is the most probable type of stone causing this obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary

| Type | Definition

| ---- | ----------

| Primary | Formed de novo within the bile duct itself

| Secondary | Migrated from the gallbladder into the CBD

| Retained | Missed at the time of cholecystectomy (found within 2 years of surgery)

| Recurrent | Found after 2 years of a previous stone-clear CBD

Why "Primary" is Correct Here

The key detail is the 4-year gap after cholecystectomy:

• The gallbladder has been removed → stone cannot have migrated from GB → rules out Secondary
• Discovered 4 years post-op → beyond the 2-year window → rules out Retained
• Stone formed de novo in the CBD after cholecystectomy = Primary stone

Characteristics of Primary CBD Stones

• Typically brown pigment stones (vs. cholesterol in secondary)
• Associated with bile stasis, infection (E. coli, biliary stricture)
• Often soft, earthy, and friable
• Seen with biliary stricture, periampullary diverticulum, or biliary dyskinesia
• E. coli produces β-glucuronidase → deconjugates bilirubin → pigment stone formation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with fever and abdominal pain. Investigations showed the given findings. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?
options: Angioembolization is the treatment of choice
Echinococcus species is involved in Etiology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Echinococcus species is involved in Etiology
