This image shows a Hydatid cyst, most commonly caused by Echinococcus granulosus.

The Ultrasound/CT shows classic hydatid features:

• Cyst with internal floating membrane (“water-lily sign”).
• Daughter cysts inside the main cyst.
• Typically occurs in the liver.

Clinical clues in the question: Fever /Abdominal pain/ Cystic liver lesion with floating membrane.

Life cycle:

• Dog = definitive host
• Sheep = intermediate host
• Humans = accidental host

Humans ingest eggs → larvae reach liver via portal circulation → form hydatid cysts.

A) Surgery is mandatory ❌

Surgery is not always required. Management include:

• Albendazole
• PAIR technique

PAIR = Puncture ; Aspiration; Injection of scolicidal agent;  Reaspiration

Surgery is done only if:

• cyst is very large
• complicated
• ruptured
• PAIR not feasible

B) Fine needle aspiration cytology is diagnostic ❌

FNAC is contraindicated.

Why? If the cyst is punctured accidentally:

• Anaphylactic shock
• Dissemination of daughter cysts

C) Angioembolization is the treatment of choice ❌

Angioembolization is used for: bleeding tumors / vascular lesions / trauma

Hydatid cyst is a parasitic cyst, not vascular.

| Sign | Meaning

| ---- | -------

| Water lily sign | Floating detached membrane

| Daughter cysts | Multiple cysts inside mother cyst

| Hydatid sand | Parasite debris

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient reports pain in right upper abdomen. FNAC of liver cyst shows parasitic organism. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Echinococcus granulosus

• Hydatid cyst of liver is caused by Echinococcus granulosus.
• FNAC shows scolices and hooklets.
• Taenia solium causes neurocysticercosis, Taenia saginata and H. nana are intestinal parasites.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent a laparoscopic cholecystectomy and had a drain in place until postoperative day 7, as there was bilious output of 300 mL/day. A CECT scan was normal, and an MRCP showed a leakage from the cystic duct stump. What is the next best step in management?
options: Re-laparoscopy and suture ligation of the cystic duct
ERCP with sphincterotomy and peripapillary stent placement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ERCP with sphincterotomy and peripapillary stent placement

B. ERCP with sphincterotomy and biliary stent placement

Post-cholecystectomy bile leak most commonly arises from the cystic duct stump, often due to clip slippage.

First-line management is ERCP with sphincterotomy and biliary stent placement, which lowers biliary pressure and diverts bile into the duodenum, allowing the leak to heal spontaneously.

Surgery is reserved for major bile duct injuries or large persistent leaks.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent a laparoscopic cholecystectomy and presented on postoperative day 4 with abdominal pain and distension. Ultrasound shows approximately 200 mL of fluid in the right upper abdomen. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage

C. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage

After laparoscopic cholecystectomy, postoperative abdominal pain and distension with a localized fluid collection (e.g., biloma, seroma, or abscess) suggest a symptomatic postoperative collection. Symptomatic collections should be treated because they can become infected or lead to sepsis. The preferred management is ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage, which is a minimally invasive method that safely removes the fluid and relieves symptoms. Open surgery is reserved only for severe complications such as major bile duct injury or generalized peritonitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with peptic ulcer shows increased gastrin levels on pentagastrin stimulation. Probable diagnosis and anatomical boundaries?
options: Insulinoma; cystic duct, 2nd & 3rd part of duodenum
Gastrinoma; CBD, 3rd and 4th part of duodenum
Gastrinoma; cystic duct, 2nd & 3rd part of duodenum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastrinoma; cystic duct, 2nd & 3rd part of duodenum

✅Option C

• Peptic ulcer + increased gastrin on pentagastrin stimulation:  Gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome)
• Pentagastrin is a synthetic gastrin analog → stimulates G cells and gastrin-producing tumors.
• In gastrinoma → Basal gastrin may already be  high → After pentagastrin injection, gastrin rises paradoxically even more → because the tumor cells are autonomous and unregulated
• confirms gastrinoma as the cause of peptic ulcers, diarrhea, and acid hypersecretion.

Why not insulinoma?

• Insulinoma secretes insulin→ causes hypoglycemia, not peptic ulcers.
• no effect on gastrin levels.

Gastrinoma’s are usually located in passaro’s triangle.:-

| Boundary | Structure

| -------- | ---------

| Superior | Junction of cystic duct and common bile duct

| Inferior | Second and third parts of the duodenum

| Medial | Neck of the pancreas

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A trainee surgeon is performing his/her first cholecystectomy. The area marked with an asterisk in the diagram represents:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Calot’s triangle

The asterisk marks the Calot’s triangle (hepatocystic triangle), an important anatomical landmark during cholecystectomy.

It is bounded by:

• Cystic duct
• Common hepatic duct
• Inferior surface of the liver

The cystic artery is usually found within this triangle, making identification of the triangle crucial to avoid bile duct and vascular injuries during cholecystectomy.

Why not the other options?

• (a) Rouviere’s area: A landmark on the posterior aspect of the liver used to identify the plane of the common bile duct during laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
• (b) Bismuth’s triangle: Not the anatomical triangle shown here.
• (c) Calot’s triangle — Correct: Important surgical landmark containing the cystic artery.
• (d) Area of Lund: Another term associated with the region of the cystic artery/Calot’s triangle, but not the specific triangle indicated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An alcoholic patient with chronic pancreatitis has recurrent attacks and a 10 mm dilated duct with intraductal calculi. Which is the surgery of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy

Alcoholic chronic pancreatitis

Dilated pancreatic duct = 10 mm

Intraductal calculi (stones)

Indicate ductal obstruction with dilated main pancreatic duct.- The main goal of surgery here is ductal decompression.

Dilated pancreatic duct (>6 mm) + stones → Drainage procedure.

Best drainage surgery = Longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (Puestow procedure).

This surgery:

• Opens the pancreatic duct along its length
• Removes stones
• Anastomoses duct to jejunum
• Provides permanent drainage

❌A) Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple)

Done mainly for pancreatic head cancer;  Not for diffuse ductal dilation

❌C) ERCP with sphincterotomy.

Can remove stones temporarily; But does not provide long-term duct drainage

❌D) Coring of pancreas head (Frey procedure)

Used when disease is predominantly in the pancreatic head

Not first choice for diffuse duct dilation

| Pancreatic duct size | Surgery

| -------------------- | -------

| >6 mm dilated duct | Puestow (Longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy)

| Head dominant disease | Frey procedure

| Inflammatory mass in head | Beger procedure

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Arrange the steps of laparoscopic cholecystectomy in order: 1. Separation of the gallbladder from the liver bed 2. Create pneumoperitoneum 3. Dissect the Calot's triangle 4. Clip the cystic duct and cystic artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2341

• Step 1 — Pneumoperitoneum: CO₂ gas is insufflated to create working space; trocars are inserted
• Step 2 — Dissect Calot's triangle: Critical safety step to identify and achieve the Critical View of Safety (CVS) before clipping anything
• Step 3 — Clip cystic duct & artery: Once structures are clearly identified, they are double-clipped and divided
• Step 4 — Separate from liver bed: Gallbladder is dissected off the liver using electrocautery and retrieved through a port

Boundaries of hepatocystic triangle:

• Cystic duct
• Common hepatic duct
• Inferior surface of liver

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the given image, which type of injury is shown according to the Bismuth-Strasberg classification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type A

Strasberg Type A bile duct injury : characterized by cystic duct leak or leak from small ducts in the gallbladder bed, is the most common type of acute bile duct injury.

Management: ERCP and CBD stenting as it does not involve major bile ducts.

Revise Strassberg-Bismuth classification:

| Type | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Type A | Bile leak from cystic duct stump or small ducts in gallbladder bed (ducts of Luschka); main biliary tree intact

| Type B | Occlusion of an aberrant right hepatic duct (usually mistakenly clipped/ligated) without bile leak

| Type C | Transection of an aberrant right hepatic duct with bile leak (duct not connected to common bile duct)

| Type D | Lateral injury to a major bile duct (partial tear of common bile duct or hepatic duct)

| Type E | Complete transection or stricture of major bile duct (equivalent to Bismuth classification)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the incision marked in the image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gibson

Gibson incision :

• Oblique along inguinal ligament,
• used for pelvic kidney, ureter, or bladder surgery.

Robson (Gridiron incision)

• Located at McBurney’s point
• Used for appendicectomy

Kocher’s incision

• Right subcostal incision
• Used for gallbladder (cholecystectomy)

Battle incision

• Right paramedian incision
• Older approach for appendix

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In Pringle Manoeuvre, clamping includes which of the following? 1. Common bile duct 2. Hepatic artery 3. Portal vein 4. Inferior vena cava Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The Pringle manoeuvre is a temporary vascular control technique used during liver surgery or hepatic trauma to reduce bleeding by clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament, thereby occluding the portal triad.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Common bile duct ✔️: Part of the portal triad.
• 2. Hepatic artery ✔️: Part of the portal triad.
• 3. Portal vein ✔️: Part of the portal triad.
• 4. Inferior vena cava ❌: Not clamped in the Pringle manoeuvre.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In which scenario is liver transplant possible for secondary tumours?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ca testis

Why liver transplant is possible here:

• Testicular cancer (germ cell tumors) is Highly chemosensitive —> So , it can achieve complete remission
• Even with liver metastasis, if disease is controlled with no evidence of disease elsewhere→ Transplant can be considered.

❌ Melanoma

Highly aggressive tumor → High recurrence (even after transplant )

❌Breast cancer

No, because there is a risk of recurrence.

❌Active RCC

Active malignancy = absolute contraindication

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Incorrect statement about choledochal cyst is:
options: Cyst is opened and drainage done
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cyst is opened and drainage done

• It is a congenital condition characterized by dilatation of the biliary tree
• It carries a significant risk of malignancy, especially Cholangiocarcinoma.--> Because of this risk, the cyst should not be simply opened and drained.
• Classified by Todani system, and often linked to abnormal pancreatobiliary junction  (> 15mm, KOMI classification is used for this).
• Choledochal cysts are treated by complete excision with biliary reconstruction, not simple drainage.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Histopathology shows carcinoma invading muscularis propria. Next step in management would be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Radical cholecystectomy

Management by depth of invasion

• T1a (lamina propria) → Simple cholecystectomy is sufficient
• T1b (muscularis propria) → Completion radical cholecystectomy ( because T1b has higher risk of lymph node spread ; microscopic residual disease)--> Simple cholecystectomy is not sufficient

So what is done →

• Excision of gallbladder bed (segments IVb & V)-Regional lymphadenectomy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The manoeuvre marked with an asterisk shown in the following image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pringle

The image shows compression/clamping of the hepatoduodenal ligament at the porta hepatis, which is the Pringle manoeuvre.

The Pringle manoeuvre temporarily occludes the portal triad:

• Proper hepatic artery
• Portal vein
• Common bile duct

It is used during liver surgery or severe hepatic trauma to reduce hepatic inflow and control bleeding.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mattox: Left-sided abdominal visceral rotation to expose the retroperitoneum and major vessels.
• B. Kocher: Mobilization of the duodenum and pancreatic head by incising the lateral peritoneal attachment.
• C. Shoe-shine: Technique used during liver resection to mobilize/dissect liver tissue.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The Model for End Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score includes which of the following variables? 1. Serum bilirubin 2. Serum albumin 3. Serum creatinine 4. International Normalised Ratio (INR) Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score is used to assess the severity of chronic liver disease, estimate 3-month mortality, and prioritize patients for liver transplantation.

The MELD score is calculated using three laboratory variables:

• Serum bilirubin
• Serum creatinine
• International Normalized Ratio (INR)

Serum albumin is NOT included in the MELD score.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis based on the MRCP image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Choledochal cyst

The MRCP image you shared shows a large, smooth, cystic dilatation of the common bile duct with communication to the biliary tree.

Other options:

A) Choledochal cyst ✅

• Characterized by congenital cystic dilatation of the extrahepatic (± intrahepatic) bile ducts.
• MRCP: smooth, saccular or fusiform cystic dilatation of CBD → exactly as seen here.

B) Biliary ascariasis

• Would show a linear filling defect (worm) inside the bile duct, not a cystic dilatation.

C) Caroli disease

• Involves intrahepatic bile duct dilatation with “central dot sign.” This image shows extrahepatic dilatation, not typical of Caroli.

D) Choledocholithiasis

• Would show a filling defect (stone) inside CBD, not a large smooth cystic dilatation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which classification of bile duct injury considers bile duct and vascular injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hannover

Hannover classification  Includes:

• Bile duct injury (site)
• Type of damage (thermal/mechanical)
• Associated vascular injury

❌Bismuth

• Based on level of injury (relative to hepatic duct)
• No vascular component

❌ Strasberg

• Expanded version of Bismuth
• Includes minor leaks + major injuries
• Still no vascular injury

❌Stewart-Way

• Based on mechanism of injury (how injury occurred)
• Not vascular injury.

Strassberg bismuth classification:-

| Type | Description

| ---- | -----------

| A | Leak from cystic duct stump or small ducts (e.g., duct of Luschka)

| B | Occlusion of part of biliary tree (usually aberrant duct)

| C | Transection of aberrant duct with bile leak

| D | Lateral injury to major bile duct

| E1 | Transection >2 cm below hepatic duct confluence

| E2 | Transection <2 cm from confluence

| E3 | Injury at confluence (right & left ducts intact)

| E4 | Destruction of confluence (separate ducts)

| E5 | Injury to aberrant right duct + main duct

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is not a risk factor for Carcinoma of Gall bladder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Polyp <10 mm

•

Option A: Porcelain gallbladder

→ Chronic calcification due to long-standing inflammation→ this causes chronic irritation of mucosa → increased risk of dysplasia → hence, associated with malignancy risk

•

Option B: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)

→ Chronic biliary inflammation

→ Increases risk of hepatobiliary malignancies

•

Option D: Large gallstones (>3 cm)

→ Cause chronic irritation of the gallbladder mucosa

→ Leads to dysplasia → carcinoma

Why Polyp <10 mm is NOT a risk factor:

• Small gallbladder polyps (<10 mm) are usually: Cholesterol polyps (benign)

(Incidental and non-neoplastic)

• Polyps ≥10 mm → suspicious → consider cholecystectomy
• Polyps <10 mm → usually observed, not removed

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are congenital abnormalities of the gall bladder? I. The phrygian cap II. Floating gall bladder III. Absence of gall bladder IV. Spigelian gall bladder Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

The gallbladder may have several congenital anomalies involving its shape, position, number, and development. Most are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery, but some predispose to torsion, gallstone formation, or surgical complications.

The following are recognized congenital anomalies of the gallbladder:

• I. Phrygian cap: The most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder. It is a folding of the fundus over the body, resembling the cap worn by ancient Phrygians. It is usually clinically insignificant.
• II. Floating gall bladder: The gallbladder is suspended by a long mesentery, making it unusually mobile and predisposing it to gallbladder volvulus (torsion).
• III. Absence of gall bladder (Gallbladder agenesis): A rare congenital anomaly resulting from failure of gallbladder development.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Spigelian gall bladder: There is no recognized congenital anomaly known as a Spigelian gallbladder. The term Spigelian refers to a Spigelian hernia, which occurs through the Spigelian fascia of the abdominal wall.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are functions of the gall bladder? I. Reservoir for bile II. Production of bile III. Secretion of mucus IV. Concentration of bile Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

The gallbladder is a storage and concentrating organ for bile. It does not produce bile; bile is synthesized by hepatocytes in the liver. The gallbladder modifies bile by absorbing water and electrolytes and secreting mucus, which protects the mucosa and facilitates bile flow.

The normal functions of the gallbladder include:

• I. Reservoir for bile: Stores approximately 30–60 mL of bile between meals.
• III. Secretion of mucus: Mucus protects the gallbladder mucosa and lubricates bile flow.
• IV. Concentration of bile: The gallbladder absorbs water, sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate, concentrating bile 5–10 times.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Production of bile: Bile is produced by hepatocytes in the liver, not by the gallbladder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a boundary of hepatocystic triangle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystic artery

Hepatocystic triangle boundaries: cystic duct (lateral), common hepatic duct (medial), inferior liver border (superior). The cystic artery lies within the triangle as content, not as a boundary.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding hepatic adenomas are correct? 1. They are almost exclusively seen in females aged 25–50 years. 2. They are associated with use of oral contraceptive pills. 3. They do not have any malignant potential. 4. Majority are detected incidentally on imaging. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 4

Hepatic adenoma is a benign liver tumor seen predominantly in young women and is strongly associated with long-term oral contraceptive pill (OCP) use. Most lesions are incidentally detected on imaging, but they carry a risk of hemorrhage and malignant transformation.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Almost exclusively seen in females aged 25–50 years ✔️: Correct.
• 2. Associated with oral contraceptive pill use ✔️: Correct.
• 3. They do not have any malignant potential ❌: Incorrect. They can undergo malignant transformation (especially β-catenin-mutated adenomas).
• 4. Majority are detected incidentally on imaging ✔️: Correct.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is the investigation of choice for diagnosing the presence of stones in the gallbladder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transabdominal ultrasound

Transabdominal ultrasonography (USG) is the investigation of choice for diagnosing gallbladder stones (cholelithiasis). It is non-invasive, inexpensive, radiation-free, and has a sensitivity and specificity >95% for detecting gallstones larger than 2 mm.

Ultrasound can also identify:

• Gallbladder wall thickening
• Pericholecystic fluid
• Sonographic Murphy’s sign
• Biliary sludge
• Dilatation of the biliary tree

Why not the other options?

• B. Erect X-ray abdomen: Incorrect. Only 10–20% of gallstones are radiopaque (pigment stones). Most cholesterol stones are radiolucent and not visible on X-ray.
• C. Capsule endoscopy: Used to evaluate small bowel diseases, not gallbladder pathology.
• D. Computed Tomography (CT): Less sensitive than ultrasound for detecting gallstones, especially cholesterol stones. CT is mainly useful for detecting complications such as perforation, emphysematous cholecystitis, or malignancy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is the most common benign liver lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemangioma

Hepatic hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the liver.

• (a) Hepatic adenoma: Less common; associated with oral contraceptive use and anabolic steroids.
• (b) Hemangioma — Correct: Most common benign hepatic tumor, usually asymptomatic and incidentally detected.
• (c) Focal nodular hyperplasia: Second most common benign hepatic tumor; often seen in young women.
• (d) Simple liver cyst: A common benign cystic lesion, but the question asks for the most common benign liver lesion/tumor, for which hemangioma is the standard exam answer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding Budd-Chiari Syndrome (BCS)?
options: Venous drainage of the liver is occluded by IVC thrombus.
Abdominal discomfort and ascites are the main presenting features.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Abdominal discomfort and ascites are the main presenting features.

Budd–Chiari syndrome (BCS) is caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, anywhere from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava (IVC) with the right atrium. The obstruction leads to hepatic congestion, portal hypertension, and impaired liver function.

The classic clinical triad consists of:

• Abdominal pain/discomfort
• Ascites
• Hepatomegaly

Why not the other options?

• A. It principally affects young males: BCS is more common in young to middle-aged adults, with a female predominance in many populations due to associations with pregnancy, oral contraceptive use, and myeloproliferative disorders.
• B. Venous drainage of the liver is occluded by IVC thrombus: The obstruction most commonly involves the hepatic veins. IVC obstruction can occur but is not the defining or usual mechanism.
• C. Quadrate lobe (Segment 4 and 5) undergoes hypertrophy: The caudate lobe (Segment I) undergoes hypertrophy because it has independent venous drainage directly into the IVC, allowing it to remain relatively spared.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding Cantlie’s line is correct?
options: Runs between gall bladder fossa and right hepatic vein
Runs between gall bladder fossa and right branch of portal vein
Runs between gall bladder fossa and middle hepatic vein
Runs between gall bladder fossa and left branch of portal vein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Runs between gall bladder fossa and middle hepatic vein

Cantlie’s line is an imaginary line extending from the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the inferior vena cava posteriorly, following the course of the middle hepatic vein. It divides the liver into the functional right and left hemilivers based on vascular inflow and biliary drainage.

Why not the other options?

• A. Right hepatic vein: Right hepatic vein divides the right lobe into anterior and posterior sectors.
• B. Right branch of portal vein: Not the landmark for Cantlie’s line.
• D. Left branch of portal vein: Not the landmark for Cantlie’s line.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding choledochal cyst is not correct?
options: Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of intra- and/or extrahepatic biliary system.
Majority of patients are diagnosed after 10 years of age.
It is associated with an increased risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma.
Radical excision of the cyst is the treatment of choice.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Majority of patients are diagnosed after 10 years of age.

• (a) Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of intra- and/or extrahepatic biliary system: Correct. Choledochal cysts are congenital cystic dilatations of the biliary tree, involving the extrahepatic and/or intrahepatic ducts.
• (b) Majority of patients are diagnosed after 10 years of age: Incorrect. Most patients are diagnosed in childhood, although adult presentation is increasingly recognized. Therefore, saying that the majority are diagnosed after 10 years is not correct.
• (c) It is associated with an increased risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma: Correct. Choledochal cysts are associated with an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma, particularly with longstanding cysts.
• (d) Radical excision of the cyst is the treatment of choice: Correct.Complete excision of the cyst with biliary reconstruction, usually Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy, is the treatment of choice for most extrahepatic choledochal cysts.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-month-old male infant presents with scrotal swelling that has been present since birth. Now the swelling has become suddenly painful, red, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Strangulated inguinal hernia

In infants, inguinal hernias occur due to a persistent patent processus vaginalis.

Normally the processus vaginalis closes after birth.

• If it remains open, Abdominal contents (usually intestine) can herniate into the inguinal canal and scrotum.
• When the herniated bowel becomes trapped and its blood supply is compromised, it leads to→ Strangulated inguinal hernia

Typical features include:

• Pain
• Redness
• Irreducible swelling
• Infant irritability or vomiting

A) Acute epididymo-orchitis

• rare in infants
• Usually occurs in adolescents or adults
• Presents with fever and gradual pain, not swelling since birth.

B) Testicular torsion

Occurs mainly in:

• Neonates
• Adolescents

But it does not present as a swelling present since birth.

D) Hydrocele

Hydrocele features:

• Painless swelling
• Transilluminant
• Usually soft and reducible or fluctuant
• Not red or acutely painful

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient has undergone a surgical procedure for a swelling in his left groin. The image of the procedure is as shown. What procedure has been performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lichtenstein’s repair

The image represents Lichtenstein tension-free mesh hernioplasty, one of the standard open repairs for an inguinal hernia.

In this procedure:

• A polypropylene mesh is placed over the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.
• The mesh is fixed inferiorly to the inguinal ligament and superiorly to the conjoint tendon/internal oblique aponeurosis.
• A slit is made in the lateral part of the mesh to accommodate the spermatic cord.
• The two tails of the mesh overlap around the cord, creating a new internal ring.
• It is a tension-free repair, unlike traditional tissue-based repairs.

| Repair | Key feature

| ------ | -----------

| Lichtenstein | Tension-free polypropylene mesh repair

| Bassini | Conjoint tendon → inguinal ligament

| Shouldice | Multilayer reconstruction of transversalis fascia

| Desarda | Undetached strip of external oblique aponeurosis; no mesh

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient, a known case of left inguinal hernia presents to the emergency with an acute onset of pain abdomen associated with nausea, vomiting and abdominal distension. His pulse rate is 102/min, BP is 100/70 mmHg and respiratory rate is 24/min. On local examination, the skin overlying the swelling is tense and erythematous. There is localized tenderness over the swelling; the swelling is irreducible with absence of cough impulse. The most probable clinical diagnosis in this patient is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strangulated hernia

A strangulated hernia occurs when the blood supply to the herniated bowel is compromised, leading to ischemia. It presents with features of intestinal obstruction along with local signs of inflammation. Features include pain, irreducibility, absent cough impulse, localized tenderness, tense erythematous skin, and signs of intestinal obstruction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Obstructed hernia: Causes intestinal obstruction but blood supply is intact; skin is usually not erythematous or tense.
• C. Incarcerated hernia: Irreducible but without obstruction or vascular compromise.
• D. Irreducible hernia: Simply cannot be reduced; no features of obstruction or strangulation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male underwent a bilateral laparoscopic hernia repair for inguinal hernia. Postoperatively, he complained of pain in the right thigh. Which of the following nerve entrapment leads to this symptom?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is vulnerable during laparoscopic mesh fixation, causing meralgia paresthetica—burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral thigh.

During laparoscopic repair:

• Mesh is fixed with tacks/staples near the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).
• The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve passes near this area under the inguinal ligament.

So it can easily get compressed or trapped.

❌A) Ilioinguinal nerve

Supplies:

• Upper medial thigh
• Root of penis / scrotum

Injury causes groin or scrotal pain, not lateral thigh pain.

Also more commonly injured in open hernia repair, not laparoscopic.

❌B) Iliohypogastric nerve

Supplies:

• Lower abdominal wall
• Suprapubic skin

Damage causes suprapubic pain, not thigh pain.

❌C) Femoral nerve

Injury causes:

• Weak knee extension
• Loss of patellar reflex
• Quadriceps weakness

The question only mentions pain So, unlikely.

questions.subject: Surgery

options: Identified 5th intercostal space anterior to mid axillary line to place the tube
Inserted tube along the lower border of upper rib

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A mother brought her one-year-old child to a pediatric surgeon after noticing a groin swelling that appears during micturition or crying and moves medially. What is the most likely cause of this swelling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Indirect inguinal hernia

In children, the most common type of inguinal hernia is an indirect inguinal hernia, caused by failure of obliteration of the processus vaginalis (a congenital defect). The swelling:

• Appears during crying, coughing, or straining (increased intra-abdominal pressure)
• Is often intermittent and reducible
• Passes through the deep inguinal ring, traverses the inguinal canal, and may extend into the scrotum.
• On examination, it is felt medial to the examiner’s finger during invagination of the scrotum (a classical clinical finding for an indirect hernia).

Why not the other options?

• A. Direct inguinal hernia: Rare in children; acquired due to weakness of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal and occurs medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
• C. Femoral hernia: Rare in children and presents below the inguinal ligament.
• D. Undescended testis: Presents as an absent testis from the scrotum, not an intermittent groin swelling.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with groin swelling diagnosed as direct inguinal hernia. Weakness of which structure causes this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conjoint tendon

A direct inguinal hernia occurs due to weakness of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal→ The posterior wall is mainly formed by:

• Transversalis fascia
• Conjoint tendon (reinforces it medially)

If the conjoint tendon becomes weak, abdominal contents push directly through the wall.--> through Hesselbach’s triangle.

Hesselbach’s Triangle

| Boundary | Structure

| -------- | ---------

| Medial | Rectus abdominis muscle

| Lateral | Inferior epigastric vessels

| Inferior | Inguinal ligament

| Hernia Type | Relation to Inferior Epigastric Vessels

| ----------- | ---------------------------------------

| Direct inguinal hernia | Medial

| Indirect inguinal hernia | Lateral

❌  A) Pectineal ligament

• Part of Cooper’s ligament
• Important in hernia repair, not the cause.

❌  C) Reflected part of inguinal ligament

• Reinforces the superficial ring, not the posterior wall.

❌  D) Lacunar ligament

• Forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring, related to femoral hernia.

questions.text: A young female presents with pain in lower abdomen and vomiting. Swelling is lateral and below the pubic tubercle. X-ray is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Strangulated femoral hernia

Swelling lateral and below pubic tubercle

●     Femoral hernia → below & lateral to pubic tubercle

●     Inguinal hernia → above & medial to pubic tubercle

Option A: Adhesions

Cause intestinal obstruction but no external swelling and no relation to pubic tubercle

Option B: Strangulated Inguinal Hernia

Can cause obstruction but swelling here is above & medial to pubic tubercle

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are true about Late Dumping Syndrome, except? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diarrhea

Late dumping syndrome is a consequence of peptic ulcer surgery characterized by reactive hypoglycemia occurring typically 1-3 hours after meals. It develops when carbohydrate-rich food causes a rapid rise in blood glucose, triggering an excessive insulin response that leads to subsequent hypoglycemia. Diarrhea is typical of early dumping.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An asymptomatic patient presents with a reducible hernia below the inguinal ligament. Which of the following is the most appropriate management to consider? (NEET PG 2016)
options: Watchful waiting and follow-up if symptomatic
Surgical repair on the next elective list
Emergency surgical repair with exploration of the bowel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Surgical repair on the next elective list

A femoral hernia occurs below the inguinal ligament through the femoral ring. While this patient's hernia is currently asymptomatic and reducible, femoral hernias have rigid boundaries (femoral vein laterally, inguinal ligament superiorly, pubic arc inferiorly, and lacunar ligament medially), creating a high risk for strangulation. Femoral hernias warrant prompt elective surgical intervention regardless of symptoms, as they have a significantly higher risk of complications compared to other hernias.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An intra-operative image of a child undergoing inguinal hernia repair is shown, with a marked vein in the spermatic cord. What is the likely structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Testicular vein

The highlighted vein is within the spermatic cord.

The spermatic cord contains :

| Structure | Function

| --------- | --------

| Vas deferens | Transports sperm

| Testicular artery | Blood supply to testis

| Pampiniform plexus (testicular veins) | Venous drainage of testis

| Cremasteric vessels | Blood supply to cremaster muscle

| Genital branch of genitofemoral nerve | Motor supply to cremaster

The testicular vein is part of the pampiniform venous plexus, which surrounds the testicular artery.

Why the other options are incorrect

Femoral vein → Located in the femoral triangle, not inside the spermatic cord.

Obturator vein → Located in the pelvic region passing through the obturator canal.

Inferior epigastric vein→ Runs along the anterior abdominal wall, not within the cord.

During inguinal hernia repair, surgeons must protect:

• Vas deferens
• Testicular vessels

Damage to the testicular vein/artery may cause:

• Testicular ischemia
• Testicular atrophy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Ankle Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) suggesting imminent necrosis is indicated by which of the following values? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. <0.3

The Ankle Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is a quantitative assessment tool that measures the ratio of systolic blood pressure at the ankle to that in the ipsilateral arm. The normal resting ABPI ranges from 0.9-1.3. As ABPI decreases, it indicates progressively worsening arterial obstruction. An ABPI value of <0.3 specifically indicates imminent necrosis - the most severe stage of arterial insufficiency, where tissue death is about to occur.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During minimally invasive inguinal hernia surgery, in order to obtain the “critical view of MPO (Myopectineal orifice)”, the space of Retzius must be dissected. At what distance must the dissection be carried out from the pubic tubercle and Cooper’s ligament?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 cm

The “Critical View of the Myopectineal Orifice (MPO)” is an essential step during laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair (TEP/TAPP) to ensure complete mesh coverage of all potential hernia sites and minimize recurrence. Adequate dissection of the space of Retzius should extend at least 2 cm beyond the pubic tubercle and Cooper’s ligament.

• Dissection of the space of Retzius should be carried ≥2 cm medial to the pubic tubercle and Cooper’s ligament.
• This ensures:

• Complete exposure of the myopectineal orifice
• Adequate medial mesh overlap
• Reduced risk of mesh migration and hernia recurrence

Why not the other options?

• A. 0.5 cm: Inadequate medial dissection.
• B. 1 cm: Insufficient to achieve the critical view.
• D. 4 cm: More extensive than routinely required and not part of the standard definition of the critical view.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of hernia:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amyand

An Amyand hernia is an inguinal hernia that contains the appendix within the hernia sac. It’s typically right-sided and may present with features of appendicitis masquerading as hernia pain. Management depends on appendix status—normal vs inflamed—along with hernia repair. Littre hernia contains a Meckel’s diverticulum, Grynfeltt hernia is a superior lumbar hernia through the Grynfeltt triangle, and Gibbon hernia refers to a rare interparietal/lateral ventral hernia variant.

| Hernia | Contents

| ------ | --------

| Amyand hernia | Appendix within inguinal hernia sac

| Littre hernia | Meckel’s diverticulum in hernia sac

| Richter hernia | Only part of bowel wall (antimesenteric border) trapped

| Maydl hernia | Two bowel loops forming W configuration; strangulation occurs in intra-abdominal loop

| Garengeot hernia (often confused in notes) | Appendix within femoral hernia

| Gibbon hernia | Hernia containing ileocecal segment

questions.text: Mayo’s repair is done for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Umbilical hernia

Mayo’s repair (also called the vest-over-pants repair) is a tissue repair technique used for umbilical hernia, in which the fascial edges are overlapped to reinforce the defect.

Why not the other options?

• A. Inguinal hernia: Common repairs include Lichtenstein, Shouldice, Bassini.
• B. Femoral hernia: Common repairs include McVay (Cooper’s ligament), Lockwood, Lotheissen, McEvedy.
• D. Incisional hernia: Usually treated with mesh repair.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Open pre-peritoneal large mesh repair for complex inguinal hernia is associated with which of the following procedures? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stoppa operation

The Stoppa operation is the open pre-peritoneal large mesh repair technique for complex inguinal hernias. This procedure involves placing a large prosthetic mesh in the pre-peritoneal space that covers the entire myopectineal orifice bilaterally. It's specifically designed for complex, recurrent, or bilateral inguinal hernias. The Stoppa approach provides excellent coverage of all potential hernia sites while avoiding direct contact with nerves in the inguinal canal, reducing the risk of chronic pain.
