questions.text: What is the ideal pressure exerted by the method of dressing for a non-healing leg ulcer shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 110-130 mmHg

The pressure used in vacuum-assisted closure for wound healing is around –125 mmHg. That lies in the range of 110-130 mmHg

Applying negative pressure appears to hasten debridement and the formation of granulation tissue in chronic wounds and ulcers.

It acts by decreasing edema, by removing interstitial fluid, and as a result, helps in decreasing bacterial counts and cell proliferation increases.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the structure marked with the yellow arrow in the intraoperative image of spermatic cord of a patient with a congenital inguinal hernia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Testicular vein

The given clinical image is an open inguinal hernia repair of a child with a structure marked as the spermatic cord whose content includes the testicular vein.

Normally the funicular process of the peritoneum becomes obliterated after the testis has reached the scrotum. The scrotal part of the process remains patent and acquires the name 'tunica vaginalis'. In case of congenital hernia, the whole process remains patent. With the increase in abdominal pressure, abdominal contents come out through the patent peritoneal process. So it reaches the bottom of the scrotum very quickly. It may so happen that the funicular process remains patent up to the top of the testis. So the hernia stops at the top of the testis and is known as a congenital funicular hernia.

Indirect hernia comprises more than 80% of inguinal hernias which are common in women and children. It occurs earlier than a direct hernia and is often complete. The two forms often seen under indirect are congenital and acquired. Unlike congenital, acquired hernias do not become complete at once. They progress gradually. Clinically a congenital hernia may present at a later period.

The pearls attached below describe the inguinal canal and the differences between direct and indirect inguinal hernia.

Other options are not the contents of the spermatic cord. Contents are mentioned in the pearl below.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the treatment plan for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Split thickness skin grafting

The given clinical image is suggestive of partial thickness burns and the treatment plan for this condition is split thickness skin grafting.

Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis are called split-thickness skin grafts. Less dermis in the split-thickness skin graft translates into less primary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks in surface area after harvesting and before grafting) and more secondary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks during healing). Humby knife is used to harvest split-thickness skin grafts.

Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft:

• Large grafts can be harvested.
• In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such
as burns.
• Uptake is good.
• Meshing can be done, i.e., small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this, improving graft takeup. It also allows the graft to expand.

Other options

Option A: Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. More dermis in the full-thickness skin graft translates into more primary contraction and less secondary contraction.

Option C: VAC is a negative pressure dressing. An occlusive dressing is placed over the sore and it is connected to VAC that generates -125mmHg of pressure. It is used in chronic non-healing ulcers, venous ulcers, diabetic ulcers, burn wounds, and bed sores.

Venous ulcers are due to chronic venous insufficiency and are particularly seen in the lower ⅓ of the leg above the ankle on the medial aspect, known as the gaiter zone. Ambulatory venous hypertension is the most acceptable theory in the pathophysiology of venous ulcers. Venous ulcers have a sloping edge and the floor contains granulation tissue covered by slough and exudate. Marjolin’s ulcer is a type of squamous cell carcinoma seen in chronic long-standing venous ulcers.

Option D: Flaps are tissues with a blood supply, providing vascularity to a new area. Types include:

• Random Flaps: Rectangular, with no specific blood supply, length-to-breadth ratio ≤ 1.5:1.
• Axial Flaps: Long flaps based on known blood vessels, suitable for large distances.
• Pedicled/Isolated Flaps: Axial supply allows them to be moved on a stalk or fully isolated.
• Free Flaps: Blood supply disconnected and reconnected via microsurgery.
• Composite Flaps: Combine tissues like skin with bone or muscle.
• Perforator Flaps: Use small vessels from major blood vessels to supply the surface.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 26-year-old female presents with recurrent epigastric pain. On CECT, a cystic mass is found in the lesser sac, corresponding to the head and neck of the pancreas. Laboratory findings show high CEA and high mucin. Amylase levels were normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucinous cystic neoplasm

Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN)

MCN typically occurs in young or middle-aged women.

• Cystic mass in the lesser sac
• Located around head and neck of pancreas

Pancreatic cystic tumors commonly project into the lesser sac.

High CEA/ mucin

• Suggests mucin-producing tumor
• Amylase is normal-This helps rule out pseudocyst.

Lesion | Key Demographic | Location | Fluid Markers | Duct Communication | Clinchers

| ------ | --------------- | -------- | ------------- | ------------------ | ---------

| Serous Cystadenoma | Elderly females | Body/tail | Low CEA, low mucin | No | Honeycomb, central scar, benign

| Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN) | Middle-aged women | Body/tail (not head) | High CEA, high mucin, amylase low | No | Ovarian stroma, premalignant

| IPMN | Elderly males | Head predominant | High amylase, ± high CEA | Yes | Dilated duct, fish-mouth ampulla with mucin

| Pseudocyst | Post-pancreatitis | Anywhere | High amylase, low CEA | No | No epithelial lining, resolves/conservative first

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male has been diagnosed with achalasia cardia through esophageal manometry. The manometry results reveal simultaneous, high-pressure contractions in the distal esophagus, along with spasmodic contractions. What type of achalasia does this patient's presentation correspond among the provided options?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type III

The classification of achalasia into types I, II, and III is based on the Chicago Classification. This system uses high-resolution manometry to categorize esophageal motility disorders.

| Type of Achalasia | Description | Notes

| ----------------- | ----------- | -----

| Type I (Classic Achalasia) | Minimal to no esophageal body peristalsis and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing. | Also known as "minimal contractility" achalasia.

| Type II (Compression Achalasia) | Intermittent periods of pan-esophageal pressurization (> 20% of swallows) due to some preserved but uncoordinated esophageal body peristalsis and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax. | Good response to therapy.

| Type III (Spastic Achalasia) | Spastic contractions in the distal esophagus and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax. | Least common type. Often harder to treat and may require more aggressive therapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents to the hospital with an episode of acute cholecystitis. Symptoms are controlled with medical management. On ultrasound, there is a solitary gallstone of 1.5 cm. What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient? (NEET PG 2015)
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the next available elective list
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the next available elective list

• The patient presented with acute cholecystitis, and her symptoms have settled with medical management (IV fluids, antibiotics, analgesics, NPO).
• Once the acute attack has settled, the standard of care is laparoscopic cholecystectomy, since gallstone disease is a surgical condition and recurrence/complications (empyema, perforation, gangrene, recurrent cholecystitis) are common if left untreated.
• The key nuance is timing:

• Early cholecystectomy (within 72–96 hours of symptom onset) is preferred during the same admission if the patient presents early and is a good surgical candidate — this is now increasingly favored by most contemporary guidelines (e.g., Tokyo Guidelines) as it reduces overall hospital stay without increasing complication rates.

• Why not other options (commonly given as distractors in this question):

• Emergency cholecystectomy — not ideal once the acute attack has already settled; higher operative risk due to friable, edematous tissue.
• Conservative management only — inadequate, as gallstones with a prior attack of cholecystitis have a high risk of recurrent symptoms/complications.
• ERCP — not indicated here; there's no mention of choledocholithiasis, jaundice, or biliary obstruction — this is isolated gallbladder stone disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old malnourished patient presents with steatorrhea, progressive weight loss, and generalized weakness for the past year. On examination, the patient appears cachectic with fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. Investigations show normal serum amylase, lipase, and CA 19-9 levels. CECT abdomen reveals pancreatic atrophy and multiple intraductal calcifications in the head of the pancreas, suggestive of chronic pancreatitis, with no evidence of pancreatic head mass, biliary obstruction, or ductal dilatation requiring surgical decompression. What is the next step in this patient's management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy

This patient has chronic calcific pancreatitis with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI), evidenced by steatorrhea, weight loss, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and pancreatic calcifications, without features requiring surgery. The cornerstone of management is Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT).

• Normal CA 19-9 (against pancreatic carcinoma)
• No pancreatic head mass or ductal obstruction

Why not the other options?

• B. Total pancreatectomy: Reserved for refractory pain or selected hereditary pancreatitis; causes brittle diabetes.
• C. Steroids: Used only in autoimmune pancreatitis, not calcific chronic pancreatitis.
• D. Whipple’s operation: Indicated for pancreatic head malignancy or selected inflammatory head masses causing obstruction—not for isolated exocrine insufficiency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with anorexia, epigastric pain, jaundice, and pruritus for 2 months. The gallbladder is palpable but non-tender. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carcinoma head of pancreas

Jaundice + pruritus → obstructive jaundice

• Palpable, non-tender gallbladder → distended GB
• Chronic symptoms (2 months)

👉 This points to malignant obstruction, most commonly →  Carcinoma head of pancreas

This case illustrates Courvoisier's Law: “In obstructive jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely due to gallstones.”

Why this happens

Tumor in pancreatic head compresses common bile duct (CBD) → Bile backs up → gallbladder gradually distends → No inflammation → non-tender

❌A. Gall bladder carcinoma → GB usually irregular, hard; not smoothly enlarged

❌B. HCC → liver pathology, not classic obstructive pattern.

❌C. Cholelithiasis → GB is painful & fibrotic (not palpable)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In which of the following transplantations is organ/body size comparison believed to be least important? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pancreas

Organ size matching is specifically mentioned as important for heart, lung, liver and small bowel transplantation, but not for pancreas transplantation. Allocation of organs must take into account the relative size of the donor and recipient for most organ types. While kidney transplants can be performed between adults and children without significant size concerns, the heart, lung, liver, and small bowel require more careful size matching. The pancreas doesn't appear in discussions of organs requiring strict size compatibility.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The best method to obtain tissue for the diagnosis of pancreatic carcinoma is:
options: Transgastric FNAC guided by endoscopic ultrasound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transgastric FNAC guided by endoscopic ultrasound

Accurate diagnosis of pancreatic carcinoma requires histologic confirmation (especially before starting chemotherapy/radiation or when the tumor is unresectable/borderline resectable). The preferred method for obtaining tissue is one that provides high diagnostic yield with the lowest risk of complications, particularly tumor seeding.

Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided transgastric fine-needle aspiration/biopsy (FNAC/FNB) is the best method because it:

• Allows real-time high-resolution visualization of pancreatic masses
• Enables precise needle placement into the lesion
• Has high sensitivity and specificity
• Minimizes risk of peritoneal tumor seeding compared with percutaneous approaches
• Also permits sampling of regional lymph nodes

Percutaneous transperitoneal biopsy has a higher risk of needle tract/peritoneal seeding, and percutaneous transhepatic routes are technically limited and not preferred. Laparoscopic biopsy is invasive and reserved when less invasive options fail or staging laparoscopy is required.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common cause of shock in severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) is:
options: Hypovolemic shock resulting from third space loss
Septic shock resulting from infected pancreatic necrosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypovolemic shock resulting from third space loss

In severe acute pancreatitis (SAP), the most common cause of shock in the early phase is hypovolemic shock due to massive third-space fluid loss, vomiting, reduced oral intake, and increased capillary permeability. This leads to intravascular volume depletion and hypotension.

Why not the other options?

• B. Septic shock resulting from infected pancreatic necrosis: Occurs later (usually after 1–2 weeks) due to infected necrosis.
• C. Cardiogenic shock resulting from SIRS: SIRS causes vasodilation rather than primary cardiogenic shock.
• D. Abdominal compartment syndrome: A serious complication but not the commonest cause of shock.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common non-pancreatic site for tumour distribution in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Duodenum

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma). The most common site overall is the duodenum, followed by the pancreas. Thus, the most common non-pancreatic site is the duodenum.

Why not the other options?

• B. Ovaries: Extremely rare site for gastrinoma.
• C. Stomach: Gastrinomas do not commonly arise in the stomach.
• D. Liver: The liver is the most common site of metastasis, not the primary tumor.

questions.text: The most common site of acute limb ischemia from an embolic event is: (NEET PG 2015)
