None

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The Trapezoid of Disaster includes: (NEET PG 2015)
options: Triangle of death and circle of death
Triangle of doom and circle of death
Triangle of doom medially and triangle of pain laterally
Triangle of doom laterally and triangle of pain medially
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Triangle of doom medially and triangle of pain laterally

During laparoscopic hernia repair, the surgeon must navigate important anatomical landmarks in the inguinal region. The "Trapezoid of Disaster" contains two important triangles that require careful attention during mesh placement. The Triangle of Doom is bounded medially by the vas deferens and laterally by the testicular vessels, containing the external iliac vessels and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve. The Triangle of Pain is located lateral to this, bounded medially by testicular vessels and laterally by the iliopubic tract, containing the femoral nerve, anterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, and lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: TIGAR-O is an etiological classification used for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic pancreatitis

TIGAR-O classification system

• Used to classify the etiological causes (risk factors) of chronic pancreatitis.
• TIGAR-O helps clinicians identify the cause of chronic pancreatitis and choose cause-specific treatment, improving outcomes and preventing disease progression.

TIGAR-O stands for

T – Toxic-Metabolic

I – Idiopathic

G – Genetic: Mutations affecting pancreatic enzymes

Examples:

• PRSS1
• SPINK1
• CFTR

A – Autoimmune

R – Recurrent Acute Pancreatitis

O – Obstructive

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Tingling and numbness over the posteromedial part of the upper arm after Modified Radical Mastectomy is most likely caused by injury to which nerve? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intercostobrachial nerve

In Modified Radical Mastectomy (MRM), the intercostobrachial nerve (derived from T2-T3 nerve roots) is the most commonly injured nerve during the axillary dissection component of the procedure. This nerve crosses through the axilla and provides sensory innervation specifically to the posteromedial aspect of the upper arm. When injured, patients experience hypoesthesia (decreased sensation), numbness, and tingling in this characteristic distribution. This sensory disturbance is so predictable that patients should be warned about it preoperatively as part of the informed consent process.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the cut-off score for defining Severe Acute Pancreatitis from below? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. APACHE II Score > 8

Several prognostic scoring systems are used to predict severity in acute pancreatitis. The threshold for severe pancreatitis using the APACHE II scoring system is >8. This score helps clinicians identify patients at higher risk of complications who may require intensive monitoring and aggressive management. Severity stratification is particularly important to determine which patients might develop persistent organ failure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which artery is the most common source of Cirsoid Aneurysms of the scalp? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superficial temporal artery

Cirsoid aneurysm is an arteriovenous malformation that most commonly affects the superficial temporal vessels on the forehead and scalp. These lesions present as pulsatile masses and represent abnormal communications between arteries and veins without an intervening capillary network. The superficial temporal artery is the primary arterial feeder in these malformations, making it the most common source of cirsoid aneurysms of the scalp.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are complications of acute pancreatitis? 1. Hypoxia 2. Hypercalcemia 3. Hyperglycemia 4. Reduced serum albumin Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

Acute pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas that can cause both local and systemic complications due to the release of pancreatic enzymes and inflammatory mediators.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Hypoxia: Correct. Hypoxia is a common systemic complication due to acute lung injury/ARDS, pleural effusion, and systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
• Statement 2. Hypercalcemia: Incorrect. Acute pancreatitis is associated with hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia. Hypocalcemia occurs due to fat saponification, where calcium combines with free fatty acids in areas of fat necrosis.
• Statement 3. Hyperglycemia: Correct. Hyperglycemia occurs due to injury of pancreatic β-cells, resulting in decreased insulin secretion, along with stress-induced hyperglycemia.
• Statement 4. Reduced serum albumin: Correct. Reduced serum albumin occurs because of systemic inflammation, increased capillary permeability, and protein loss into the third space. Low serum albumin is also associated with more severe disease.

Other complications of acute pancreatitis:

• Local: Pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess, infected necrosis, hemorrhage.
• Systemic: Shock, acute kidney injury, DIC, ARDS, sepsis, multiorgan failure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are local complications of acute pancreatitis? 1. Pseudocyst 2. Pleural effusion 3. Ileus 4. Acute fluid collection Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Complications of acute pancreatitis are classified into local and systemic complications according to the Revised Atlanta Classification (2012). Local complications arise from inflammation or necrosis within and around the pancreas, whereas systemic complications involve distant organ dysfunction.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Pseudocyst ✅

• A pancreatic pseudocyst is a late local complication that usually develops ≥4 weeks after interstitial edematous pancreatitis and contains enzyme-rich fluid enclosed by a fibrous wall.

• 2. Pleural effusion ✅

• Pleural effusion, especially left-sided, is a recognized local extrapancreatic complication due to the spread of pancreatic inflammation or pancreaticopleural fistula.

• 3. Ileus ❌

• Ileus is considered a systemic manifestation of acute pancreatitis resulting from severe inflammation and electrolyte disturbances, rather than a local pancreatic complication.

• 4. Acute fluid collection ✅

• Acute peripancreatic fluid collection (APFC) develops within the first 4 weeks of interstitial edematous pancreatitis and is one of the earliest local complications.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are options for management of a pancreatic pseudocyst? 1. Pancreaticoduodenectomy 2. Cystogastrostomy 3. Percutaneous drainage 4. Endoscopic drainage Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

A pancreatic pseudocyst is managed based on its size, symptoms, and complications. Treatment options include internal drainage (cystogastrostomy), endoscopic drainage, or percutaneous drainage in selected cases.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Pancreaticoduodenectomy ❌: Not indicated for a pancreatic pseudocyst; reserved for malignancy or selected pancreatic head lesions.
• 2. Cystogastrostomy ✔️: Standard surgical internal drainage for pseudocysts adjacent to the stomach.
• 3. Percutaneous drainage ✔️: Option in selected patients, especially infected pseudocysts or poor surgical candidates.
• 4. Endoscopic drainage ✔️: Preferred minimally invasive approach (transmural or transpapillary) for suitable pseudocysts.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are probable sites for Ectopic pancreas? 1. Submucosa of the stomach and duodenum 2. Liver 3. Small bowel mesentery 4. Splenic hilum Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Ectopic (heterotopic) pancreas is pancreatic tissue located outside the normal pancreas without any anatomical or vascular continuity. It is most commonly found in the upper gastrointestinal tract but may occur at several other sites.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Submucosa of the stomach and duodenum ✔️: Correct. Most common site (also jejunum).
• 2. Liver ✔️: Correct. Rare but reported site.
• 3. Small bowel mesentery ✔️: Correct. Rare site.
• 4. Splenic hilum ❌: Incorrect. Not a recognized site of ectopic pancreas.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for the development of pancreatic cancer? 1. Cigarette smoking 2. Diabetes mellitus 3. Caucasian ethnicity 4. Male gender Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis because it is often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Several modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors increase the likelihood of developing pancreatic cancer, with cigarette smoking being the most important modifiable risk factor.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Cigarette smoking ✅

• Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor, increasing the risk of pancreatic cancer by 2–3 times.

• 2. Diabetes mellitus ✅

• Long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus is an established risk factor. Conversely, new-onset diabetes in older adults may be an early manifestation of pancreatic cancer.

• 3. Caucasian ethnicity ❌

• Pancreatic cancer is more common in African Americans than in Caucasians; therefore, Caucasian ethnicity is not considered a risk factor.

• 4. Male gender ✅

• The incidence is slightly higher in males, partly due to greater exposure to smoking and occupational carcinogens.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a boundary of the Gastrinoma triangle? (NEET PG 2016)
options: Second and third part of duodenum
Spleen vein and inferior mesenteric vein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spleen vein and inferior mesenteric vein

The Gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's Triangle) is an anatomical region where gastrinomas are most commonly found. This triangle is formed by specific anatomical boundaries that define the area where these tumors typically develop. The splenic vein and inferior mesenteric vein are not components of this triangle's boundaries, making this the incorrect option.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of these is a true statement about Crohn’s disease?
options: Antibiotics are the only effective treatment for a Crohn's mass
Symptomatic relapse following surgery is not related to the presence of disease during resection
Crohn's disease most commonly involves the proximal ileum
Continuous lesions observed during endoscopic examination are diagnostic of Crohn's disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Symptomatic relapse following surgery is not related to the presence of disease during resection

None

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of these is seen in acute pancreatitis?
options: Lipase is more specific than amylase
Lipase requires 30 days to return to baseline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lipase is more specific than amylase

✅ Lipase is more specific than amylase

• Lipase comes almost only from the pancreas, so elevations point to pancreatic injury.
• Amylase rises in many conditions (salivary gland disease, bowel perforation), so less specific.

❌ Lipase requires 30 days to return to baseline

• Lipase rises 4–8 h after onset, peaks at 24 h, and returns to baseline in 7–14 days.
• Lipase does not persist for a month;
• Prolonged elevation usually suggests ongoing pancreatic injury, chronic pancreatitis, or pseudocyst formation

❌ Lipase reflects severity of pancreatitis

• Level of lipase does not indicate how severe the pancreatitis is.
• Severity is assessed clinically (Ranson, BISAP, APACHE II).

❌ 75% cases have hypercalcemia on admission

• Actually, acute pancreatitis can cause hypocalcemia (from fat necrosis and saponification).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 13-year-old male presents with right testicular pain for 2 hours. On examination, there is severe testicular tenderness and an absent cremasteric reflex. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Surgical exploration

• Acute testicular pain for 2 hours
• Severe testicular tenderness
• Absent cremasteric reflex

Indicates testicular torsion→ Testicular torsion occurs when the spermatic cord twists, leading to:

• Cut-off blood supply to the testis; Rapid ischemia→ Possible testicular necrosis

The most important clinical sign is: Absent cremasteric reflex

(stroking the inner thigh normally elevates the testis — absence suggests torsion).

Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency. Immediate surgical exploration is required.

Do NOT delay surgery for Doppler ultrasound if clinical suspicion is high.

Why?

Testicular salvage rate falls rapidly after 6 hours.

Approximate salvage timeline:

• < 6 hours → \~90–100% salvage
• 6–12 hours → \~50% salvage
• > 24 hours → <10% salvage

A) Antibiotics

Used for epididymitis, which usually presents with:

• Gradual pain
• Fever
• Preserved cremasteric reflex

B) NSAIDs

Only provide symptomatic pain relief and do not treat torsion.

C) CT abdomen

Not indicated in this case

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-year-old boy presents to the paediatrician with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs). Upon further investigation, a micturating cystourethrogram is performed and which is shown below. The boy is currently asymptomatic and has no history of renal or bladder abnormalities. What could be the cause of the symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vesicoureteric reflux

• 2-year-old boy + Recurrent UTIs
• MCU (Micturating Cystourethrogram) image
• Image shows contrast going upward into dilated ureters
• When urine refluxes:
• Urine stagnates
• Bacteria travel upwards to kidney
• Leads to recurrent UTIs and pyelonephritis

VUR is graded I–V:

| Grade | Finding

| ----- | -------

| I | Reflux into ureter only

| II | Reflux into pelvis without dilation

| III | Mild dilation

| IV | Moderate dilation + tortuosity

| V | Severe dilation + loss of papillary impressions

The image here looks like higher-grade VUR because the ureters are dilated and tortuous.

B) Urinary bladder diverticulum

• Outpouching of bladder wall
• Would show contrast sac from bladder
• Does NOT cause dilated ureters bilaterally

C) Urinary bladder hernia

• Herniation of bladder into inguinal canal
• Seen on CT or cystography as bladder extending into hernia sac
• No ureteral dilation

D) Varicocele

• Dilated testicular veins
• Completely unrelated to UTIs or ureters

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old female patient with previous history of neck irradiation presents with thyroid swelling for last 6 months. The patient is clinically euthyroid. On examination, the right lobe of thyroid gland is enlarged with presence of ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. The most probable clinical diagnosis in this patient is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Papillary carcinoma thyroid

Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the most common thyroid malignancy and has a strong association with previous exposure to ionizing radiation, especially during childhood. It commonly presents as a painless thyroid nodule in a euthyroid patient and characteristically spreads via lymphatics, leading to cervical lymph node metastasis.

Why not other options?

• A. Medullary carcinoma thyroid

• Arises from parafollicular C. cells.
• Associated with MEN 2A/2B and elevated calcitonin, not prior neck irradiation.

• C. Lymphoma:

• Usually develops in patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis and presents as a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass.

• D. Follicular carcinoma thyroid

• More commonly associated with iodine deficiency.
• Spreads hematogenously to bone and lungs rather than to cervical lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient is brought to the emergency room after being involved in a motor vehicle accident. Upon examination, it is found that the patient is unable to pass urine and there is visible blood at the meatus. A retrograde urethrogram was performed as shown below. What is the most likely site of urethral injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Membranous urethra

Classic clues:

1. Motor vehicle accident
2. Inability to pass urine
3. Blood at the urethral meatus

Posterior urethral injury;  most common site is the membranous urethra.

Why membranous urethra specifically?

In pelvic fractures, the shearing force occurs at the bulbo-membranous junction, damaging the membranous urethra.

| Urethral part | Injury type | Common cause

| ------------- | ----------- | ------------

| Membranous urethra | Posterior urethral injury | Pelvic fracture / road traffic accident

| Bulbar urethra | Anterior urethral injury | Straddle injury (fall on bar/bicycle)

| Penile urethra | Rare | Direct penile trauma

In the RGU image:

• Contrast leaks at the bulbo-membranous region
• Contrast does not enter the bladder

This indicates posterior urethral disruption.

A) Bulbar urethra

• Usually due to straddle injury
• Example: falling on a bicycle bar.

B) Extraperitoneal bladder rupture

• Seen with pelvic fractures but no blood at the meatus typically.
• Contrast leak occurs around bladder, not urethra.

D) Penile urethra

• Requires direct penile trauma, which is not described.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient presents with a midline swelling in the neck. Upon examination, cervical node enlargement is also observed. Histopathological analysis of the lesion reveals the following findings is false. Identify the false statement of the following?
options: Excellent prognosis is associated with this condition.
Nuclear characteristics are used for identification
Fine needle aspiration cytology (FAC) is not diagnostic.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FAC) is not diagnostic.

Midline neck swelling ; Cervical lymph node enlargement

Histology shows papillary structures→ the histology image shows papillae with fibrovascular cores classic for Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC).

1. Excellent prognosis ✔

Papillary carcinoma has the best prognosis among thyroid cancers, especially in young patients.

2. Spread via lymphatics ✔

PTC characteristically spreads through lymphatics, which is why cervical lymph node metastasis is common.

3. Nuclear features are diagnostic ✔

Diagnosis is often based on classic nuclear changes:

• Orphan Annie eye nuclei
• Nuclear grooves
• Intranuclear inclusions
• Overlapping nuclei

4. FNAC is not diagnostic ❌

This statement is false because:

• FNAC is actually the primary diagnostic test for thyroid nodules.

Papillary carcinoma can be reliably diagnosed on FNAC due to its characteristic nuclear features.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. He was the driver of the car, and upon impact, he had hit his abdomen against the steering wheel. Upon examination, the patient was conscious but complained of severe abdominal pain and tenderness upon palpation. The physician noted bruising and swelling in the abdominal area. Further evaluation revealed the evisceration of omentum, which was protruding through a laceration in the abdominal wall. What would be the best management of the same?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Emergency laparotomy

Traumatic evisceration indicates a full-thickness abdominal wall breach and probable intra-abdominal injury → mandates immediate laparotomy because:

High risk of:

• Internal bleeding
• Bowel injury
• Peritonitis

You cannot assess or fix this externally ; hence, immediate laprotomy.

Observation or waiting risks peritonitis and hemorrhage; hydration alone does not address the underlying injury.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man sustains multiple injuries in a road traffic accident. He is initially conscious, but later becomes unresponsive and subsequently dies. Autopsy reveals numerous petechial haemorrhages in the corpus callosum. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse axonal injury

Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) follows severe head trauma, causing shearing at the grey-white matter junction.

Pathology shows petechial hemorrhages in the corpus callosum, often missed on CT but seen on MRI.

Clinically, patients may have brief consciousness followed by deep coma with very low GCS.

A. Epidural Hematoma (EDH)

• Classically: presents with → Lucid interval → rapid deterioration
• Lens-shaped bleed→ No petechial hemorrhages in corpus callosum

C. Subdural Hematoma

• Crescent-shaped bleed→ Due to rupture of bridging veins.
• Not diffuse axonal damage

D. Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH)

• Blood in the subarachnoid space
• Severe headache (“worst headache of life”); No corpus callosum petechiae.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old motorcycle rider is brought to the emergency with history of motor vehicle accident. On examination, the patient is tachycardic (pulse 110/min) with a BP of 90 systolic. He has an open wound in the thigh. What is the severity of haemorrhagic shock this patient is suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Class 3

According to the ATLS classification of hemorrhagic shock:

| Class | Blood loss | Clinical features

| ----- | ---------- | -----------------

| Class 1 | <15% (<750 mL) | HR <100, BP normal

| Class 2 | 15–30% (750–1500 mL) | HR 100–120, BP usually normal, anxiety

| Class 3 | 30–40% (1500–2000 mL) | HR >120, hypotension, confusion

| Class 4 | >40% (>2000 mL) | Severe hypotension, marked tachycardia, lethargy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old motorcycle rider is brought to the emergency with history of motor vehicle accident. On primary survey, he is found to open eyes in response to pain, speaking inappropriate words and localizes pain. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. E2 V3 M5

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) has three components:

E — Eye opening

• 4 = Spontaneous
• 3 = To voice
• 2 = To pain
• 1 = None

V — Verbal response

• 5 = Oriented
• 4 = Confused conversation
• 3 = Inappropriate words
• 2 = Incomprehensible sounds
• 1 = None

M — Motor response

• 6 = Obeys commands
• 5 = Localizes pain
• 4 = Withdraws from pain
• 3 = Abnormal flexion
• 2 = Extension
• 1 = None

In this patient:

• Opens eyes to pain → E2
• Speaking inappropriate words → V3
• Localizes pain → M5

Therefore, the actual GCS is E2 V3 M5 = 10/15.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old female presented to the urologist with complaints of abdominal pain and recurrent urinary tract infections. Upon examination, the physician noted tenderness in the lower abdomen and a palpable mass in the right flank area. Further evaluation revealed the following. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelviureteric junction obstruction

The most likely diagnosis is A) Pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction.

• Abdominal pain
• Recurrent urinary tract infections
• Palpable flank mass

These symptoms commonly occur with chronic hydronephrosis due to PUJ obstruction, where urine cannot drain properly from the renal pelvis into the ureter.

CT image findings

From the CT scan:

• Marked hydronephrosis (very dilated renal pelvis)
• Ballooned renal pelvis
• Calyceal dilatation
• Abrupt narrowing at the PUJ
• Ureter distal to the PUJ is not dilated

This pattern is classic for PUJ obstruction.

Why are the other options wrong

B) Putty kidney

• Seen in renal tuberculosis, the kidney becomes calcified and shrunken
• CT would show dense calcification, not hydronephrosis.

C) Staghorn calculus

• Large branching stone filling renal pelvis and calyces.
• CT would show hyperdense calculus, not a huge fluid-filled pelvis.

D) Cystic kidney (e.g., polycystic kidney disease)

• Shows multiple cysts in both kidneys, not a single massively dilated pelvis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old male with midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition and tongue protrusion. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroglossal cyst

Midline neck swelling that moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion almost pathognomonic for a thyroglossal duct cyst.

• Common in children and young adults.

Why it moves with tongue protrusion?

During embryological development:

• The thyroid gland descends from the foramen cecum of the tongue to the neck.
• It travels through the thyroglossal duct Sometimes the duct fails to disappear, forming a thyroglossal duct cyst.

The cyst remains attached to the tongue base via the duct, so when the tongue moves, the swelling also moves.

Why the other options are wrong

❌A) Branchial cyst

• Located laterally, along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid
• Does NOT move with tongue protrusion

❌C) Plunging ranula

• Comes from sublingual gland; Appears in submandibular region
• Not a midline swelling

❌D) Dermoid cyst

• Can be midline but does NOT move with tongue protrusion

Definitive treatment is Sistrunk operation:

This involves:

• Removal of the cyst, central part of the hyoid bone and Removal of the thyroglossal tract

→ purpose is to prevent recurrence.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. He has sudden breathlessness, absent breath sounds on the right side, and chest X-ray shows a large right-sided pneumothorax with complete lung collapse. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the next best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intercostal chest tube

A patient with a large traumatic pneumothorax and complete lung collapse who is hemodynamically stable should undergo tube thoracostomy (intercostal chest tube insertion) to evacuate air from the pleural cavity and allow lung re-expansion.

The patient has:

• Blunt chest trauma
• Large pneumothorax with complete lung collapse
• Hemodynamically stable

The treatment of choice is intercostal chest tube drainage (tube thoracostomy).

Why not the other options?

• B. Emergency thoracotomy: Indicated for massive hemothorax, cardiac injury, or persistent massive bleeding, not uncomplicated pneumothorax.
• C. Oxygen alone: Suitable only for small, stable pneumothoraces, not a complete lung collapse.
• D. Endotracheal intubation only: Does not treat the pneumothorax and may worsen it if positive-pressure ventilation is initiated without chest drainage.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old man meets with a road traffic accident. He is hemodynamically stable but complains of right flank pain. Examination shows mild abrasions over the right flank. Contrast-enhanced CT is given below that shows a perinephric hematoma. What is the next best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conservative (non-operative) management with close monitoring

The CT image shows a renal injury with a large perinephric hematoma, but the patient is hemodynamically stable. In hemodynamically stable patients, the standard of care for most blunt renal injuries (AAST Grades I–IV) is non-operative (conservative) management with close observation.

Therefore, conservative management is appropriate, including:

• Bed rest
• Serial monitoring of vital signs and hemoglobin
• Analgesia
• Repeat imaging if clinically indicated

Why not the other options?

• A. Immediate nephrectomy: Reserved for shattered kidney or uncontrollable bleeding in unstable patients.
• C. Exploratory laparotomy: Indicated only if there are associated intra-abdominal injuries requiring surgery or persistent hemodynamic instability.
• D. Renal artery embolization: Used for stable patients with active arterial contrast extravasation (ongoing bleeding/pseudoaneurysm) on CT, not for a stable perinephric hematoma without active bleeding.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old man sustains a stab injury to the neck. The wound is located between the cricoid cartilage and the angle of the mandible. Which neck zone is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zone II

The neck is divided into three anatomical zones in penetrating neck trauma to help assess the likelihood of injury to vital structures. The injury is located between the cricoid cartilage and the angle of the mandible, which corresponds to Zone II.

It is the most commonly injured neck zone and contains:

• Carotid arteries
• Internal jugular veins
• Larynx
• Hypopharynx
• Esophagus
• Trachea
• Vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves

Why not the other options?

• A. Zone I: Extends from the clavicles/sternal notch to the cricoid cartilage.
• C. Zone III: Extends from the angle of the mandible to the base of the skull.
• D. Zone IV: No anatomical Zone IV exists in the standard neck trauma classification.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old man was brought in with a stab injury to the anterior part of the neck. There was profuse bleeding and air bubbling observed at the injury site. The patient was tachycardiac (PR: 128/min) and hypotensive (BP: 80/50 mmHg). On examination, the wound extended from the cricoid to the angle of the mandible. What anatomical zone is involved, and what is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Zone 2: Immediate surgical exploration

Penetrating neck injuries are divided into three anatomical zones, which guide evaluation and management.

Neck Zones:

• Zone I: Clavicles/sternal notch → Cricoid cartilage
• Zone II: Cricoid cartilage → Angle of mandible ✔️
• Zone III: Angle of mandible → Base of skull

In this patient, the injury extends from the cricoid cartilage to the angle of the mandible, indicating a Zone II injury.

The presence of hard signs of vascular/aerodigestive injury:

• Profuse bleeding
• Air bubbling from the wound (suggesting tracheal/laryngeal injury)
• Hypotension (BP 80/50 mmHg)
• Tachycardia

mandates immediate surgical exploration without delay for imaging.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents to the ED with fever and altered mental status for 3 days. On examination, he opens his eyes in response to painful stimuli, produces incomprehensible sounds, and localizes pain to the painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 9

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a standardized tool used to assess the level of consciousness in patients with head injury or altered mental status. It evaluates eye opening (E), verbal response (V), and motor response (M), with a total score ranging from 3 to 15.

Why is D correct?

• Eye opening to pain = E2
• Incomprehensible sounds = V2
• Localizes pain = M5

Total GCS = E2 + V2 + M5 = 9

Why not the other options?

• A. 6: Would indicate a much poorer neurological status.
• B. 8: Incorrect combination of GCS components.
• C. 7: Incorrect calculation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with penetrating chest trauma and tracheal deviation. What is the most appropriate immediate step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. E-FAST

E-FAST (Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) is a rapid bedside ultrasound used in trauma to detect:

• Pneumothorax
• Hemothorax
• Pericardial tamponade
• Intra-abdominal bleeding

It is fast, non-invasive, and performed immediately in the ER.

In a trauma patient, the goal is to quickly identify life-threatening causes without delaying care.

E-FAST allows immediate detection of:

• Collapsed lung
• Pleural fluid
• Blood in thorax or abdomen

This guides urgent interventions like chest tube insertion.

❌ A) Needle decompression in 2nd intercostal space

This is done only if tension pneumothorax is clearly suspected and the patient is unstable.

Here, the diagnosis should first be confirmed quickly with E-FAST.

❌ B) CT scan

CT provides detailed imaging, but:

• Too slow
• Requires patient transfer

Not suitable as the immediate step in trauma resuscitation.

❌ D) Oxygen at 100%

Oxygen is supportive but does not diagnose the cause of tracheal deviation.

In chest trauma with suspected pneumothorax or hemothorax:

Immediate bedside evaluation → E-FAST

Then proceed to:

• Chest tube
• Needle decompression
• Further imaging if stable

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a stab injury to the left lower chest. His blood pressure is 90/59 mmHg. Chest X-ray is normal. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. eFAST

A patient with penetrating thoracoabdominal trauma who is hemodynamically unstable (BP 90/59 mmHg) should undergo an immediate eFAST examination as part of the primary survey (ATLS protocol). eFAST is a rapid bedside ultrasound used to detect hemoperitoneum, hemopericardium, pneumothorax, and hemothorax, allowing prompt life-saving intervention.

A normal chest X-ray does not exclude intra-abdominal or pericardial injury, especially in stab wounds involving the left lower chest, which can injure the diaphragm, spleen, stomach, or heart.

Why not the other options?

• B. CT chest: Requires a hemodynamically stable patient; not appropriate in unstable trauma.
• C. CT abdomen: Also reserved for stable patients after initial assessment.
• D. Diagnostic laparoscopy: Useful for stable patients with suspected diaphragmatic injury; it should not delay initial evaluation in an unstable patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old motorbike rider is brought to the emergency with history of a road traffic accident and altered consciousness. On secondary survey, the doctor notices presence of a bruise over the left mastoid process. The finding indicates:
options: Injury to the external auditory meatus
Soft tissue injury to the neck
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fracture of the skull base

Battle’s sign is ecchymosis over the mastoid process and is a classical clinical sign of a basilar skull fracture, particularly involving the middle cranial fossa (petrous temporal bone). It usually appears 6–24 hours after injury and should prompt evaluation for associated intracranial injuries.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Fracture of mastoid process: An isolated mastoid fracture is uncommon and does not classically produce Battle’s sign.
• B. Injury to the external auditory meatus: Injury to the external auditory canal may cause bleeding but does not produce mastoid ecchymosis.
• D. Soft tissue injury to the neck: Neck injuries do not cause bruising localized over the mastoid process.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient sustains circumferential full-thickness and deep partial-thickness burns on her limbs. The image shows the procedure performed on his right arm and forearm. What is the purpose of this procedure?
options: Protecting the vessels in the arm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Escharotomy for circumferential burns

The image shows escharotomy, an emergency procedure for circumferential fullthickness burns.

Concept : Rigid eschar acts like a tourniquet→ restrictions circulation → risking compartment syndrome and hence, loss of limb function.

• Longitudinal incisions are made (along anatomical lines)--> helps to release constriction and restore perfusion.
• You cut only the dead burnt skin (eschar) (It’s insensate = no sensation** (nerve endings are destroyed) → so patient does not feel pain and → gives immediate decompression, restoring the blood supply).

❌ Option B) : Surgical debridement

The goal is urgent decompression( in order to save the limb) ; not cleaning the wound.

❌ Option C) :  Protecting the vessels in the arm

Yes, escharotomy does help vessels indirectly ; BUT → That’s a secondary effect

The primary purpose is torelieve pressure → restore perfusion. (Done by escharotomy).

❌ Option D) : Early skin grafting

Yes, It is part of definitive management (later stage)--> when dead tissue is removed and the wound is clean; BUT

NOT an emergency procedure needed right now.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old road traffic accident victim is being taken up for emergency laparotomy for haemoperitoneum and suspected multiorgan trauma. Which one of the following will be an indication for performing damage control surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Coagulopathy

Damage Control Surgery (DCS) is a staged surgical approach used in severely injured trauma patients with profound physiological derangement. The goal is to rapidly control hemorrhage and contamination, correct the patient’s physiology in the ICU, and perform definitive surgery only after stabilization. The principal indication is the presence of the trauma lethal triad—coagulopathy, hypothermia, and acidosis.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Blood pressure <100 mm Hg: Mild hypotension alone is not a specific indication for DCS. Persistent hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation is more relevant.
• B. Acidosis with pH <7.32: Acidosis is an indication for DCS, but the classical threshold is severe acidosis (pH <7.2), not 7.32.
• C. Hypothermia <36°C: The accepted criterion is significant hypothermia (<35°C). A temperature of <36°C alone is insufficient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old female classical singer underwent total thyroidectomy for multinodular goiter. Post-surgery, she is unable to sing high-pitched notes, cannot modulate her voice, and experiences early vocal fatigue. Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. External branch of superior laryngeal nerve

The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN) supplies the cricothyroid muscle, the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The cricothyroid muscle tenses and elongates the vocal cords, enabling the production of high-pitched sounds.

Injury to the EBSLN during thyroidectomy results in:

• Inability to produce high-pitched notes
• Poor voice modulation
• Early vocal fatigue
• Difficulty singing (especially in professional voice users)

Why not the other options?

• A. Recurrent laryngeal nerve: Causes hoarseness, weak/breathy voice, and vocal cord paralysis, but loss of high pitch specifically suggests EBSLN injury.
• B. Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve: Provides sensory innervation above the vocal cords; injury causes loss of cough reflex and increased aspiration risk.
• C. Glossopharyngeal nerve: Supplies the pharynx and posterior one-third of the tongue; not involved in vocal cord tension.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents after a stab injury to the neck just above the clavicle. His pulse is 120/min and blood pressure is 90/70 mmHg. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediate surgical exploration

Penetrating neck injuries are managed based on the patient’s hemodynamic status and the presence of hard signs of vascular or aerodigestive injury.

This patient has:

• Penetrating neck trauma
• Hypotension (BP 90/70 mmHg)
• Tachycardia (120/min)

These findings indicate hemodynamic instability, which is an indication for immediate surgical exploration without delaying for imaging.

Why not the other options?

• B. Supportive treatment and observation: Appropriate only for stable patients without concerning signs.
• C. CT angiography of the neck: Investigation of choice only in hemodynamically stable patients.
• D. MRI neck: Not used in the acute trauma setting.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents with a painless, progressive swelling of the right scrotum for the past 4 months. On examination, the testis is enlarged, firm, and non-tender, with loss of testicular sensation. Scrotal USG reveals a homogeneous hypoechoic intratesticular mass with no areas of hemorrhage or necrosis. Serum tumor markers show normal AFP and slightly elevated beta-hCG levels. What is the most likely tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seminoma

Seminoma is the most common pure testicular germ cell tumor in men aged 30–40 years. It typically presents as a painless, progressively enlarging testicular mass with loss of testicular sensation.

• Homogeneous hypoechoic intratesticular mass on ultrasound
• Normal AFP
• Normal or mildly elevated β-hCG (due to syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells in some seminomas)
• No hemorrhage or necrosis on imaging

Why not the other options?

• B. Yolk sac tumor: Commonest testicular tumor in children; AFP is markedly elevated.
• C. Choriocarcinoma: Markedly elevated β-hCG, highly hemorrhagic, early hematogenous metastasis.
• D. Teratoma: Usually heterogeneous with cystic/calcific areas; in adults, often part of mixed germ cell tumors.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old man presents with a testicular bulky mass which was homogenous, grey-white and lobulated on the cut surface. It did not show hemorrhage or necrosis. Microscopic H&E image is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seminoma

Testicular mass

↓

Homogeneous, pale, lobulated

↓

No hemorrhage/necrosis

↓

Uniform tumor cells

↓

Seminoma

Seminoma typically presents as a bulky, homogeneous, gray-white, lobulated testicular mass without hemorrhage or necrosis. Microscopy shows sheets of uniform large cells with clear cytoplasm, central nuclei, and prominent nucleoli.

Large cells with clear cytoplasm (“fried egg” look 🍳)

Fibrous septa with lymphocytic infiltrate are characteristic histologic features.

Embryonal carcinoma shows hemorrhage and necrosis, yolk sac tumor has Schiller–Duval bodies, and lymphoma occurs in older men.

| Tumor | Key Feature

| ----- | -----------

| Seminoma | Homogeneous, no hemorrhage

| Embryonal carcinoma | Hemorrhage + necrosis

| Yolk sac tumor | AFP ↑, Schiller-Duval bodies

| Choriocarcinoma | β-hCG ↑, hemorrhagic

| Lymphoma | Older age

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male with motor traffic accident with BP 90/60mm Hg. On examination, he was stable with GCS 15/15. The pupil was reactive to light. Tenderness and bruising over the left lower chest wall with petechia were seen. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. eFAST

The next step in the evaluation of a trauma patient with the given findings is the Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (eFAST). This non-invasive imaging technique is crucial for rapidly identifying free fluid and organ injuries in the abdomen, as well as potential pneumothorax or hemothorax, which are critical in trauma cases. eFAST is used to quickly assess both stable and unstable patients following blunt abdominal trauma, providing immediate information that can dictate further management steps.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a stab wound to the epigastric region. He is tachycardic, hypotensive, and exhibits abdominal guarding and rigidity. What is the immediate intervention of choice in this scenario?
options: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Exploratory Laparotomy

The presence of peritonitis (abdominal guarding) and hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia) after a stab wound → absolute indications for exploratory laparotomy.

Indications for immediate laparotomy in penetrating trauma:

• Hemodynamic instability
• Evisceration
• Peritonitis
• Gunshot wound
• Impacted object
• Peritoneal breach
• Bleeding via orifice

❌Option A: FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma)

Used in stable or borderline stable patients

❌ because patient is already unstable and this would delay in definitive treatment

❌Option B:DPL (Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage)

Obsolete. Was done previously, but here surgical exploration is needed clearly.

❌Option D: CT Abdomen & Pelvis

Gold standard for stable patient; Contraindicated in unstable patients

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless, slowly enlarging testicular swelling for 3 months. There is no fever or history of trauma. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Seminoma

A painless, progressively enlarging testicular mass in a young or middle-aged man should be considered testicular cancer until proven otherwise. Seminoma is the most common pure germ cell tumor and classically presents as a painless testicular swelling with a slow, indolent course.

• Seminoma typically presents in men 30–40 years of age.
• Presents as a painless, firm, unilateral testicular mass.
• Ultrasound shows a homogeneous hypoechoic intratesticular lesion.
• Tumor markers:

• β-hCG: May be mildly elevated
• AFP: Never elevated in pure seminoma
• LDH: Often elevated

Why not the other options?

• A. Epididymitis: Painful swelling with fever, dysuria, and epididymal tenderness.
• C. Testicular torsion: Sudden onset of severe scrotal pain with a high-riding testis; surgical emergency.
• D. Hydrocele: Painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates and surrounds, rather than arises from, the testis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with nephrolithiasis and a palpable neck mass. His father died of pancreatic cancer at age 50. Which of the following gene mutations is most likely responsible for this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MEN1 gene

The presentation suggests multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1).

MEN1 mutation leads to parathyroid adenomas causing hypercalcemia and nephrolithiasis.

Associated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors explain the family history of pancreatic cancer.

MEN1 is a tumor suppressor gene encoding menin, unlike RET (MEN2) or VHL syndromes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient with hypercalcemia (12.8 mg%) and elevated PTH has a 1.5 cm mass below thyroid. Next step?
options: Scintigraphy followed by focused neck exploration for parathyroid removal
Perform DEXA scan, and if normal, rule out surgery
Assess Creatinine clearance, if >80 mandates surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scintigraphy followed by focused neck exploration for parathyroid removal

This is primary hyperparathyroidism due to parathyroid adenoma.

• Confirmed by elevated calcium  + elevated PTH + presence of a neck mass.

Next step:  Scintigraphy (Sestamibi scan), because:

• Helps localize the overactive gland.

Uses Tc-99m sestamibi tracer → is taken up by mitochondria-rich cells ( cells of parathyroid adenoma have high mitochondrial activity  → so, adenoma cells  retain the tracer longer than normal thyroid tissue  (because the radiotracer is lipid soluble )→Thyroid washes out and Adenoma “lights up” → exact localisation of adenoma.

•

Age <50 years

• Surgery recommended even if asymptomatic (long-term complications risk)

•

High calcium

• Risk of kidney stones, bone loss, neuro symptoms → hence surgery is indicated.

❌ Option B : DEXA scan, if normal avoid surgery

• DEXA checks bone density only → still need treatment

❌ Option C: Creatinine clearance >80 mandates surgery

• Renal function is just one criterion (supportive)→ Decision is not based only on this.

❌ Option D: No surgery, only surveillance

• Surveillance alone is inappropriate given significant biochemical abnormality and visible adenoma, especially in a young patient with clear disease.

Intraoperative success is confirmed by Miami criteria (>50% fall in PTH within 10 minutes).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of sweating, palpitations, and confusion that improve after glucose intake. She is diagnosed with an insulinoma. Which of the following tumors should be actively screened for in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pituitary adenoma

Insulinoma is a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin, causing recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia. It is classically associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutations in the MEN1 (menin) tumor suppressor gene. Therefore, patients diagnosed with insulinoma should be screened for other MEN1-associated tumors, especially pituitary adenomas and parathyroid adenomas/hyperplasia.

The patient has features of insulinoma:

• Sweating
• Palpitations
• Confusion
• Symptoms relieved by glucose (Whipple’s triad)

Insulinoma is a component of MEN 1, whose major tumors are:

• Parathyroid adenomas (most common)
• Pancreatic endocrine tumors (e.g., insulinoma, gastrinoma)
• Pituitary adenomas

Thus, the patient should be screened for a pituitary adenoma.

Why not the other options?

• B. Papillary thyroid carcinoma: Not associated with MEN syndromes.
• C. Medullary thyroid carcinoma: Associated with MEN 2A and MEN 2B (RET mutation), not MEN 1.
• D. Pheochromocytoma: Also associated with MEN 2, not MEN 1.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman undergoes surgery for a thyroid nodule. Postoperatively, she develops ptosis and miosis on the operated side. Which surgical approach is most likely associated with this complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Transaxillary endoscopic thyroidectomy

Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, ± anhidrosis) is caused by injury to the cervical sympathetic chain. It is a recognized but uncommon complication of transaxillary endoscopic thyroidectomy, where extensive lateral neck dissection and retraction may place the sympathetic chain at risk.

The patient develops Ptosis and Miosis. These are classic features of Horner syndrome, most likely due to cervical sympathetic chain injury during transaxillary endoscopic thyroidectomy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Conventional collar incision thyroidectomy: Common complications include recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve injury, and hypoparathyroidism. Horner syndrome is rare.
• C. Transoral vestibular thyroidectomy: More commonly associated with mental nerve injury causing numbness of the lower lip and chin.
• D. Lateral cervical lymph node biopsy: May injure the spinal accessory nerve or other cervical structures, but Horner syndrome is not the characteristic complication.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman, a chronic smoker and hypothyroid, on oral contraceptive pills (OCPs), presents with unilateral leg swelling and pain after a 14-hour flight. Which of the following is not a risk factor for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypothyroidism

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) occurs due to the mechanisms described in Virchow’s triad: venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. In this patient, prolonged immobility during a 14-hour flight causes venous stasis, leading to unilateral leg swelling and pain typical of DVT.

Smoking increases thrombosis risk by causing endothelial damage and platelet activation, while estrogen-containing oral contraceptive pills create a hypercoagulable state. Immobilization is a classic risk factor due to venous stasis.

Hypothyroidism is not a recognized major risk factor for DVT. Hence, the correct answer is Hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with difficulty urination and the finding shown in the image, and examination reveals that his prepuce cannot be retracted over the glans penis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Balanitis xerotica obliterans

The image demonstrates scarring of the prepuce and glans with inability to retract the foreskin,

This is phimosis → but the cause matters.

✅ Why Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans :

• It is a form of Lichen sclerosus.

Causes:

• White, fibrotic, scarred foreskin
• Tight ring → non-retractable prepuce (phimosis)
• May cause meatal narrowing → difficulty urination

❌ B. Meatal stenosis

• Narrow urethral opening → causing thin stream of urine
• Does NOT cause inability to retract foreskin

❌C. Hypospadias**

• Urethral opening on more ventrally, as compared to normal.
• Present since birth→ No relation to foreskin retraction problem.

❌D. Paraphimosis**

• This is exactly the opposite→ here,  Foreskin is retracted but cannot be pulled back → Leads to painful swelling of glans
• Here, foreskin cannot be retracted at all

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department with a complaint of acute-onset severe abdominal pain. The patient is conscious, alert, and hemodynamically stable. Upon examination, the patient reports that the pain began suddenly. A chest X-ray is performed, which reveals some abnormal findings. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Emergency laparotomy

On the chest X-ray :  free air under the diaphragm (subdiaphragmatic air) — especially beneath the right hemidiaphragm  indicates pneumoperitoneum.

Common causes include:

• Perforated peptic ulcer (most common)
• Perforated appendix
• Perforated diverticulum
• Bowel perforation

Why emergency laparotomy is required

When bowel perforates:

• Gas escapes into peritoneal cavity
• Peritonitis develops quickly
• Risk of sepsis and shock

So treatment is immediate surgical repair → Hence the next step is: Emergency laparotomy

Why other options are wrong

❌ A) Gastric lavage

• Used for poisoning/overdose
• No role in bowel perforation.

❌ C) Ultrasound

• Air blocks ultrasound waves
• Diagnosis already evident on X-ray.

❌ D) Chest tube insertion

• Used for pneumothorax
• Here the air is in abdomen, not pleural cavity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old patient presents with chest pain and hoarseness of voice for the past month. MRI of the patient is shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Dissecting aneurysm of arch of aorta
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Saccular aneurysm of aortic arch

A saccular aneurysm of the aortic arch appears as a localized sac-like outpouching from one side of the vessel wall. Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve causes hoarseness of voice (Ortner syndrome).

Chest pain with focal aneurysmal dilation favors saccular aneurysm over dissection or coarctation.

Thus, the findings are most consistent with a saccular aneurysm of the aortic arch.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presents with symptoms of heat intolerance, excessive sweating and weight loss since 10–12 months. After clinical examination, the surgeon orders an investigation which is shown in the image. The scan shown below is a/an:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radionuclide scan

• The image represents a thyroid radionuclide scan (thyroid scintigraphy).
• The patient has symptoms suggestive of hyperthyroidism—heat intolerance, excessive sweating and weight loss. A thyroid radionuclide scan helps determine the functional activity and distribution of thyroid tissue.
• The scan shown demonstrates increased, relatively diffuse uptake in the thyroid, which is characteristic of Graves disease.

Why not the other options?

• (a) MRI scan: Produces anatomical images using magnetic fields; not used to assess thyroid radioactive iodine uptake.
• (b) Non-contrast CT: Provides anatomical information but does not demonstrate thyroid functional activity.
• (c) Radionuclide scan — Correct: Uses a radiotracer such as I-123 or Tc-99m pertechnetate to assess thyroid uptake and function.
• (d) PET scan: Primarily used for metabolic imaging in malignancy and selected other conditions; not the routine functional scan for thyrotoxicosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient presents with erectile dysfunction and bilateral leg pain that worsens with rest. The patient reports a history of smoking and high blood pressure. Physical examination reveals reduced sensation in both legs and weak pulses in the feet. Identify the location of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aortoiliac bifurcation

Erectile dysfunction + bilateral claudication + absent pulses → Leriche syndrome, caused by occlusion at the aortoiliac bifurcation. Peripheral distal artery disease does not explain impotence.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient with prior neck radiation for lymphoma is diagnosed with 2 x 3 cm papillary thyroid cancer. No lymph node enlargement is present. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Total thyroidectomy

Total thyroidectomy (TT) is the preferred treatment in radiation-induced differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC), regardless of tumor size.

Differentiated thyroid cancers (DTC) include:

• Papillary carcinoma
• Follicular carcinoma
• Hürthle cell carcinoma

When is Hemithyroidectomy done?

• Tumor size 1–4 cm
• No extrathyroidal extension
• No nodal or distant metastasis

Indications for Total Thyroidectomy (TT):

• Tumor size ≥ 4 cm
• Gross extrathyroidal extension
• Metastatic disease present
• Radiation-induced DTC
• Familial non-medullary thyroid cancer
• Multifocal bilateral disease

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. On examination, he is noted to have subcutaneous emphysema and decreased breath sounds on the right side. His vital signs are unstable. What is the immediate management for this patient?
options: Insertion of wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space (ICS)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Insertion of wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space (ICS)

In trauma patients, subcutaneous emphysema + decreased unilateral breath sounds + hemodynamic instability strongly suggests a tension pneumothorax. This is a rapidly fatal condition due to:

• air trapping in pleural cavity under pressure

• collapse of the ipsilateral lung

• mediastinal shift → decreased venous return → obstructive shock

Immediate management is needle decompression (needle thoracostomy) and it must be done without waiting for imaging, as diagnosis is clinical.

Site (ATLS recommended):

• 5th intercostal space, anterior to mid-axillary line (or 2nd ICS midclavicular line)

• Use a wide-bore cannula to relieve pressure

After stabilization Insert intercostal chest drain (tube thoracostomy) definitively.

Why other options are not first:

• IV fluids do not treat obstructive shock from tension pneumothorax.

• Intubation with positive pressure ventilation can worsen tension pneumothorax if not decompressed first.

• eFAST should not delay life-saving decompression.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man undergoes liver transplantation. On postoperative day 2, he develops a sudden rise in liver enzymes. Doppler ultrasound shows absent hepatic arterial flow. The next best management is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Immediate surgical re-exploration

The patient has hepatic artery thrombosis (HAT), the most serious vascular complication after liver transplantation. It typically presents within the first week after transplantation with a sudden rise in liver enzymes. Absent hepatic arterial flow on Doppler ultrasonography confirms the diagnosis.

Because the hepatic artery is the sole arterial blood supply to the biliary tree, HAT can rapidly lead to graft ischemia, biliary necrosis, and graft failure. Therefore, immediate surgical re-exploration with thrombectomy/revascularization or urgent retransplantation is required.

Why not the other options?

• A. Broad-spectrum antibiotics: May be needed if infection develops but do not treat hepatic artery thrombosis.
• B. ERCP with biliary stenting: Used for biliary leaks or biliary strictures, not vascular occlusion.
• D. Observation: Delays treatment and may result in irreversible graft loss.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with midline neck swelling presented with odynophagia and dyspnoea. The swelling showed cells with variations in size and morphology. Amyloid deposit was also seen. The swelling was positive for IHC markers TTF-1, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medullary carcinoma

Medullary carcinoma of thyroid arises from parafollicular C cells - Shows neuroendocrine differentiation.( IHC is positive for neuroendocrine markers : chromogranin ,synaptophysin.)

• Tumor cells produce large amounts of abnormal/misfolded calcitonin (or its precursors) The excess calcitonin peptides get misfolded Body can’t properly clear them
• They accumulate in the tumor stroma- These proteins undergo amyloid transformation - stromal amyloid deposition

| Feature | Diagnosis

| ------- | ---------

| Amyloid in thyroid tumour | Medullary carcinoma

| Calcitonin elevated | Medullary carcinoma

| MEN-2 association | Medullary carcinoma

Papillary and follicular carcinomas are thyroglobulin-positive, while undifferentiated carcinoma lacks amyloid.

| Feature | Papillary carcinoma | Follicular carcinoma

| ------- | ------------------- | --------------------

| Frequency | Most common (\~80%) | Second most common

| Spread | Lymphatic | Hematogenous

| Common metastasis | Cervical lymph nodes | Bone, lung

| Age group | Younger patients | Middle-aged

| Prognosis | Excellent | Good

Anaplastic

• Undifferentiated
• ❌ No amyloid; Very aggressive

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man, 2 weeks post renal transplantation, presents for follow-up. His baseline serum creatinine was 1.2 mg/dL. On evaluation, a rise in creatinine is noted. Which of the following best suggests acute graft rejection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase in serum creatinine by 10%

• As per Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery:

• A ≥10% increase in serum creatinine is considered clinically meaningful and warrants evaluation for rejection.

• Smaller increases (e.g., 5% or “any rise”) may occur due to:

• Volume status changes
• Drug toxicity (e.g., tacrolimus, cyclosporine)
• Laboratory variability

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with progressive muscle weakness, particularly affecting the eyes and throat, leading to difficulty with swallowing and drooping eyelids. Imaging studies reveal a mediastinal mass. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thymoma

Thymoma is the most common anterior mediastinal mass associated with myasthenia gravis. Teratomas show fat/calcification, lymphoma presents with systemic symptoms, and PTH adenoma is cervical.

Key Radiology Features:

• Anterior mediastinal mass
• Well-defined, lobulated
• Homogeneous or mildly heterogeneous enhancement
• May show:

• Calcifications
• Local invasion (advanced cases)

| Feature | Thymoma | Teratoma | Lymphoma | Thyroid Mass

| ------- | ------- | -------- | -------- | ------------

| Location | Anterior mediastinum | Anterior | Anterior | Anterior

| Composition | Soft tissue | Fat + calcification | Soft tissue | Continuity with thyroid

| Association | Myasthenia gravis | None | B symptoms | Thyroid disease

| Age | Middle-aged | Young adults | Any | Adults

| Imaging clue | Homogeneous mass | Mixed density | Bulky nodes | Neck extension

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with a history of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1) syndrome presents with symptoms suggestive of a gastrinoma. Which of the following is the most common site of occurrence in MEN 1 syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Duodenum

None

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with recurrent renal stones, bone pain, and constipation. Laboratory evaluation shows hypercalcemia and elevated PTH. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parathyroid adenoma

Parathyroid adenoma is the most common cause (80–85%) of primary hyperparathyroidism. Excess secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) leads to hypercalcemia, producing the classic manifestations of:

• Bones: Bone pain, osteitis fibrosa cystica
• Stones: Renal calculi/nephrocalcinosis
• Abdominal groans: Constipation, abdominal pain, peptic ulcers, pancreatitis
• Psychiatric overtones: Fatigue, depression, confusion

Why not the other options?

• A. Parathyroid carcinoma: Rare (<1% of primary hyperparathyroidism); usually presents with very severe hypercalcemia (>14 mg/dL), markedly elevated PTH, and a palpable neck mass.
• C. Thyroid adenoma: Does not produce PTH or hypercalcemia.
• D. Medullary thyroid carcinoma: Produces calcitonin, not PTH, and is associated with MEN 2 syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman presents with a slowly enlarging anterior neck swelling for 1 year, along with recent onset hoarseness of voice. On examination, the swelling is hard, irregular in the right lobe, moves with deglutition, and is fixed to deeper structures. What investigation is performed to identify extra-thyroid spread of thyroid neoplasm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRI of neck

MRI of the neck is the best imaging modality for assessing extra-thyroidal extension of thyroid malignancy. It provides excellent soft-tissue resolution and helps determine invasion into adjacent structures such as the trachea, esophagus, larynx, strap muscles, recurrent laryngeal nerve, and major vessels, which is crucial for staging and surgical planning.

Why not the other options?

• B. USG of neck: First-line investigation for thyroid nodules and cervical lymph node evaluation, but less accurate for deep soft-tissue invasion.
• C. Radioiodine scan: Used to assess functional status of thyroid nodules (hot vs. cold), not local invasion.
• D. PET scan: Reserved for selected cases such as recurrent, metastatic, or radioiodine-negative differentiated thyroid cancer, not routine evaluation of local spread.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman presents with a slowly enlarging thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration is followed by thyroidectomy. Histopathology demonstrates nests of polygonal cells, with abundant eosinophilic amyloid deposition in the stroma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid

• Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, which originate from the neural crest and secrete calcitonin.
• The pathognomonic histological feature is amyloid deposition in the stroma, which is derived from altered calcitonin molecules produced by the tumor cells.
• Patients may present with:

• Solitary thyroid nodule
• Elevated serum calcitonin
• Cervical lymph node metastasis
• Occasionally diarrhea and flushing due to secretion of other peptides

MTC may occur sporadically or as part of MEN 2A or MEN 2B syndromes, which are associated with RET proto-oncogene mutations.

Why not the other options?

• A. Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid: Most common thyroid cancer; characterized by Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies. It arises from follicular cells, not C cells.
• B. Follicular carcinoma of the thyroid: Also arises from follicular cells and is diagnosed by capsular and/or vascular invasion. It commonly spreads hematogenously and lacks amyloid.
• D. Anaplastic carcinoma of the thyroid: A highly aggressive, undifferentiated tumor occurring in elderly patients. Histology shows marked pleomorphism and giant cells, not C-cell differentiation or amyloid.

High-yield pearl

| Thyroid carcinoma | Cell of origin | Characteristic feature

| ----------------- | -------------- | ----------------------

| Papillary | Follicular cell | Orphan Annie nuclei, nuclear grooves, psammoma bodies

| Follicular | Follicular cell | Capsular/vascular invasion; hematogenous spread

| Medullary | Parafollicular (C) cell | Calcitonin secretion + amyloid stroma

| Anaplastic | Undifferentiated follicular cell | Highly aggressive pleomorphic tumor

Exam tip:

• C cells + Calcitonin + Congo red–positive amyloid + RET mutation = Medullary thyroid carcinoma.

questions.text: A 48-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after suffering a stab injury to the lower chest. On presentation, he had bradycardia and hypotension which did not improve despite IV fluid administration. Chest radiography showed clear lung fields. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. E-FAST

None

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient presents to the hospital for a follow-up after undergoing a total thyroidectomy. He reports experiencing perioral numbness that started three days after the surgery. Upon further investigation, the patient has no history of nerve damage, facial trauma, or dental procedures. What diagnostic tests should be conducted to determine the cause of the perioral numbness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Calcium, Phosphate and Parathormone levels

Perioral numbness appearing after thyroidectomy (3 days later) : Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcemia

Why This Happens

During thyroidectomy, the parathyroid glands may:

• be accidentally removed, or
• become devascularized ( due to ligation of infrathyroid artery branches )

As a result, PTH drops → calcium levels fall.

Why Perioral Numbness Occurs :

Low calcium (hypocalcemia) causes neuromuscular irritability; symptoms include:

• Perioral numbness
• Tingling in fingers
• Muscle cramps

Later signs:

• Chvostek sign
• Trousseau sign
• Tetany

To confirm post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism, check:

Serum Calcium → ↓ low

Serum Phosphate → ↑ high

PTH levels → ↓ low→ This confirms hypoparathyroidism.

A) Serum Na, K, Cl

Electrolytes are not the cause of perioral numbness after thyroid surgery.

B) T3, T4, TSH

These evaluate thyroid function, not parathyroid injury.

C) Radioiodine scan

Used for:

• thyroid cancer follow-up
• hyperthyroidism

Not useful for postoperative numbness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient presents with pain in the right thigh during walking. Investigation reveals a finding as shown below. What will be the most appropriate surgical management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aortofemoral bypass

This image demonstrates aortoiliac occlusive disease (AIOD) involving the iliac artery/aortoiliac segment, causing exertional thigh claudication. The choice of revascularization depends on the anatomic level of arterial obstruction.

• Aortoiliac disease → Aortofemoral bypass is the gold-standard surgical treatment for extensive occlusive lesions.
• It provides durable long-term patency and restores blood flow from the abdominal aorta to the femoral arteries.

| Site of arterial disease | Preferred surgical treatment

| ------------------------ | -------------------------------

| Focal iliac stenosis | PTA ± stenting

| Unilateral iliac occlusion (high-risk patient) | Femoro-femoral (femorofemoral) bypass

| Extensive aortoiliac occlusive disease (Leriche syndrome) | Aortofemoral bypass

| Superficial femoral artery/popliteal disease | Femoro-popliteal bypass

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presented with tearing pain in the chest that intensely radiated to his back. He had non-specific ECG changes and his Trop I was negative. During the course of his evaluation, he passed away. Biopsy of the aorta obtained during autopsy is shown. What is the likely mechanism behind his disease?
options: Subintimal lipid infiltration with smooth muscle necrosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Connective tissue weakness

The key mechanism is: Weakness of connective tissue in the aortic media. This leads to cystic medial degeneration.

Features include:

• Fragmentation of elastic fibers
• Loss of smooth muscle cells
• Accumulation of mucoid material

The presentation of tearing chest pain radiating to the back with negative cardiac biomarkers is classic for aortic dissection.

Aortic dissection results from medial degeneration with connective tissue weakness, leading to an intimal tear. This allows blood to track between layers of the aortic wall.

| Risk factor | Mechanism

| ----------- | ---------

| Hypertension | Most common cause

| Marfan syndrome | Connective tissue defect

| Ehlers–Danlos syndrome | Collagen defect

| Bicuspid aortic valve | Aortic wall weakness

Fibrinoid necrosis and immune complex vasculitis are seen in vasculitides, not dissection.

A) Fibrinoid necrosis

Seen in malignant hypertension or vasculitis, not typical for dissection.

B) Subintimal lipid infiltration

Mechanism of atherosclerosis, not aortic dissection.

C) Immune complex vasculitis

Occurs in diseases like polyarteritis nodosa, not dissection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with LUTS underwent a fusion-guided prostate biopsy. Histopathological examination revealed acinar adenocarcinoma of the prostate with a Gleason score of 8 (4+4). According to the International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) grading system, what is the corresponding prognostic grade group?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Grade 4

The ISUP Grade Group system is a simplified prognostic classification based on the Gleason score and is routinely used for risk stratification, prognosis, and treatment planning in prostate adenocarcinoma.

• Gleason score = 8 (4+4) corresponds to ISUP Grade Group 4, indicating high-grade prostate cancer with an increased risk of extracapsular extension, metastasis, and disease progression.

ISUP Grade Group Classification:

| ISUP Grade Group | Gleason Score

| ---------------- | -------------

| Grade Group 1 | 3 + 3 = 6

| Grade Group 2 | 3 + 4 = 7

| Grade Group 3 | 4 + 3 = 7

| Grade Group 4 | 4 + 4 = 8, 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 3 = 8

| Grade Group 5 | 9–10 (4 + 5, 5 + 4, 5 + 5)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old with trauma 2 weeks ago presents with confusion and ataxia. CT image shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subdural hemorrhage

• History of trauma + symptoms after 2 weeks → delayed presentation
• Symptoms like confusion and ataxia are typical of chronic SDH
• Cause = rupture of bridging veins → slow bleed

On CT: Hypodense crescent-shaped collection along brain surface (can cross sutures)

A) Extradural (Epidural) hemorrhage

• Rapid onset, not delayed
• Classic lucid interval → sudden deterioration
• CT: lens-shaped (biconvex), does NOT cross sutures

C) Intra-parenchymal hemorrhage

• Bleeding within brain tissue
• Appears as localized hyperdense area, not crescent
• Usually acute neurological deficit, not gradual decline

D) Subarachnoid hemorrhage

• Sudden severe headache (“thunderclap”)
• Blood seen in sulci and cisterns, not as a collection
• Not typically delayed after minor trauma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman is evaluated for a solitary thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is reported as a follicular neoplasm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hemithyroidectomy

Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) cannot distinguish between follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma, as the diagnosis of carcinoma requires demonstration of capsular and/or vascular invasion, which can only be assessed on histopathological examination of the excised specimen. Therefore, the appropriate next step for a follicular neoplasm (Bethesda IV) is diagnostic hemithyroidectomy (thyroid lobectomy with isthmusectomy).

• Hemithyroidectomy provides the surgical specimen needed to evaluate capsular and vascular invasion, thereby differentiating follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma.
• It is both diagnostic and potentially therapeutic.

Why not the other options?

• B. Total thyroidectomy: Not routinely indicated as the initial procedure for an indeterminate follicular neoplasm unless there are high-risk features (large tumor, bilateral nodules, prior radiation, strong suspicion of malignancy).
• C. Radioactive iodine ablation: Used after confirmation of differentiated thyroid carcinoma, not before diagnosis.
• D. Repeat FNAC after 6 months: Repeating FNAC is unlikely to resolve the diagnosis because cytology cannot assess capsular or vascular invasion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old man with a history of untreated syphilis presents with difficulty initiating urination, chronic urinary retention, overflow incontinence, and an unsteady gait. Neurological examination reveals loss of vibration sense and sensory ataxia, suggestive of tabes dorsalis. Urodynamic evaluation demonstrates the following. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atonic bladder

The patient has tabes dorsalis, a manifestation of neurosyphilis involving degeneration of the posterior columns and dorsal roots of the spinal cord. Damage to the afferent sensory fibers from the bladder abolishes the normal micturition reflex.

This results in an atonic (flaccid) neurogenic bladder, characterized by:

• Large-capacity bladder
• Poor or absent detrusor contractions
• Chronic urinary retention
• Overflow incontinence
• Increased post-void residual urine

Urodynamic studies (cystometrogram) typically show a large-capacity bladder with markedly reduced detrusor activity, exactly as described.

Why not the other options?

• A. Automatic bladder: Occurs with spinal cord lesions above the sacral micturition center after the spinal shock phase. Reflex voiding returns, but bladder emptying is involuntary.
• C. Spastic bladder: Seen in suprasacral spinal cord lesions. The bladder has increased detrusor tone, small capacity, urgency, frequency, and reflex voiding—not a large flaccid bladder.
• D. Neurogenic uninhibited bladder: Results from frontal lobe or cerebral lesions, causing urgency, frequency, and urge incontinence with preserved detrusor contractions.

High-yield pearl

| Type of neurogenic bladder | Site of lesion | Bladder characteristics

| -------------------------- | -------------- | -----------------------

| Atonic (flaccid) bladder | Sacral cord, pelvic nerves, dorsal roots (e.g., tabes dorsalis, diabetic neuropathy) | Large-capacity bladder, urinary retention, overflow incontinence, ↓ detrusor contraction

| Automatic bladder | Spinal cord lesion above S2–S4 | Reflex emptying after spinal shock

| Spastic bladder | Suprasacral spinal cord lesion | Small-capacity, hyperreflexic bladder, urgency

| Neurogenic uninhibited bladder | Frontal cortex lesion | Urgency and urge incontinence

questions.subject: Surgery
