questions.text: A 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department with high-grade fever, chills, severe left flank pain, and vomiting. Imaging reveals a left proximal ureteric calculus causing hydronephrosis. Laboratory investigations show leukocytosis, and urinalysis is suggestive of infection. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Conservative management with analgesics and observation
Urgent urinary decompression with a Double-J (DJ) stent or percutaneous nephrostomy
Elective nephrectomy after the infection subsides
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent urinary decompression with a Double-J (DJ) stent or percutaneous nephrostomy

An obstructed infected urinary system (obstructive pyelonephritis/pyonephrosis) is a urological emergency. Obstruction prevents drainage of infected urine, predisposing the patient to urosepsis and septic shock.

The priority is:

• Immediate decompression of the collecting system using:

• Double-J (DJ) ureteric stent, or
• Percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN)

• Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
• Definitive stone removal is performed only after the infection has resolved.

Why not the other options?

• A. Conservative management with analgesics and observation: Contraindicated because infection with obstruction requires urgent drainage.
• B. Percutaneous nephrectomy: Nephrectomy is not the initial treatment unless the kidney is non-functioning and infection persists despite appropriate management.
• D. Elective nephrectomy after the infection subsides: Not indicated as first-line management in an acute obstructed infected kidney.

High-yield pearl:

• "Obstruction + Fever = Drain first, stone later."
• Never perform definitive stone removal before decompressing an infected obstructed collecting system.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old hypertensive patient arrives at the emergency department with sudden, severe chest pain radiating to the back. On physical examination, there is a noticeable difference in blood pressure between the arms, and unequal radial pulses are observed. A CT angiogram is done and shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
options: Aggressive blood pressure control and close monitoring
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aggressive blood pressure control and close monitoring

CT and clinical findings suggest Stanford A aortic dissection which are managed clinically initially to reduce BP followed by surgery.

| Classification | Description

| -------------- | -----------

| Stanford A | Ascending aorta involved

| Stanford B | Only descending aorta involved

Aggressive blood pressure and heart rate control reduces shear stress and prevents extension of dissection.

Initial treatment is medical management.

Goals:

• Reduce blood pressure
• Reduce heart rate
• Reduce shear stress on the aortic wall

Drugs commonly used:

• IV Beta blockers (Esmolol / Labetalol)
• Nitroprusside (if needed)

Target:

• HR < 60 bpm
• SBP 100–120 mmHg
•

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old male came with acute onset breathlessness and found to have pneumothorax. The resident doctor decided to insert intercostals drain. Which one of the following sites is suitable for such a procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Triangle of safety

The Triangle of Safety is the recommended site for insertion of an intercostal chest drain (tube thoracostomy) in patients with pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pleural effusion. Inserting the drain within this triangle minimizes the risk of injury to the lung, diaphragm, and major neurovascular structures.

Why is C correct?

• The Triangle of Safety is bounded by:

• Anteriorly: Lateral border of pectoralis major
• Posteriorly: Anterior border of latissimus dorsi
• Inferiorly: Line at the 5th intercostal space (approximately the level of the nipple/inframammary fold)
• Superiorly: Apex below the axilla

• The chest tube is usually inserted in the 4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line, and just above the upper border of the rib to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hesselbach’s triangle: Anatomical site of direct inguinal hernia.
• B. Petit’s triangle: Inferior lumbar triangle; site of lumbar hernia.
• D. Triangle of auscultation: Area where breath sounds are best heard; not used for chest tube insertion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old male recently diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, with imaging indicating a tumor size less than 4 cm, what would be the most suitable initial treatment approach for this patient's condition among the following options?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Partial nephrectomy

For localized renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with a tumor size <4 cm (clinical stage T1a), partial nephrectomy (nephron-sparing surgery) is the preferred initial treatment whenever technically feasible. This approach provides equivalent cancer-specific survival to radical nephrectomy while preserving renal function and reducing the risk of chronic kidney disease.

• Complete tumor excision with negative margins
• Preserves maximal functioning renal parenchyma
• Lower risk of long-term renal insufficiency
• Recommended for most T1a renal masses (<4 cm)

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect?

B. Partial nephrectomy + neoadjuvant chemotherapy

• RCC is generally resistant to conventional chemotherapy.
• Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is not standard treatment for localized RCC.

C. Radical nephrectomy

• Usually reserved for larger tumors, centrally located masses not amenable to nephron-sparing surgery, or when partial nephrectomy is technically impossible.

D. Radical nephrectomy + postoperative radiotherapy

• Adjuvant radiotherapy has no established role in localized RCC after complete surgical resection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents to the clinic with a history of unexplained weight loss, hematuria, and a palpable abdominal mass. Imaging studies reveal a large renal mass. A renal biopsy has the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chromophobe carcinoma

Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma arises from intercalated cells of the collecting duct and shows characteristic pale eosinophilic cells with prominent cell membranes and perinuclear halos on biopsy.

It often presents as a large renal mass with hematuria and abdominal lump.

Clear cell RCC shows lipid-rich clear cytoplasm, papillary RCC forms papillae with foamy macrophages, and Bellini duct carcinoma is rare and highly aggressive.

Large pale eosinophilic cells

• Perinuclear halo (very characteristic)
• Prominent cell membranes → “plant cell” look
• Wrinkled (raisinoid) nuclei

| Feature | Clear Cell RCC | Papillary RCC | Chromophobe RCC

| ------- | -------------- | ------------- | ---------------

| Cells | Clear, lipid-rich | Basophilic | Pale eosinophilic

| Pattern | Solid/alveolar | Papillary | Sheets

| Special feature | Rich vasculature | Foam cells | Perinuclear halo

| Nuclei | Round | Variable | Raisinoid

| Prognosis | Moderate | Good | Best

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 6-week-old infant is brought to the clinic with a history of projectile vomiting and poor weight gain. Physical examination reveals an abdominal mass in the epigastrium, and the diagnosis of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is suspected. An abdominal mass in a patient with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is best seen?
options: During palpation, over the left hypochondrium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. During feeding

None

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old lady presents with a recent onset increase in a long-standing swelling on the front of the neck. The swelling, which was small, had been present since last 30 years, but has now increased to more than twice the size in the last 2 months. On examination, the swelling is firm to hard in consistency and moves with deglutition. What is the most likely cause of this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malignant transformation

A long-standing thyroid swelling that shows rapid enlargement, especially in an older patient, should always raise suspicion for malignant transformation. A thyroid nodule that has been stable for many years but increases rapidly in size, becomes firm or hard, or develops compressive symptoms requires urgent evaluation for thyroid malignancy, particularly anaplastic carcinoma or carcinoma arising in a multinodular goiter.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Cystic degeneration: Usually produces a soft or fluctuant swelling and may cause gradual enlargement rather than a hard mass.
• B. Haemorrhage: Intranodular hemorrhage causes sudden painful enlargement, often with tenderness, not a progressively enlarging hard swelling.
• D. Myxomatous transformation: Not a recognized cause of rapid enlargement of a thyroid swelling.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a complaint of lower back pain. During the medical examination, it is discovered that the patient has prostate cancer. The medical team suspects that the cancer may have spread to the lumbar vertebrae. What is the likely route of spread for prostate cancer to the lumbar vertebrae?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prostatic venous plexus

• 60-year-old male
• Known prostate cancer
• Lower back pain
• Suspicion of spread to lumbar vertebrae

Suggests vertebral metastasis from prostate cancer.

Prostate cancer spreads to the spine through the Batson’s venous plexus (Prostatic venous plexus)

This plexus is:

• Valveless, connected to the internal vertebral venous plexus, allows retrograde venous flow

Because of the absence of valves, increased abdominal pressure can push tumor cells directly into the vertebral column, especially the lumbar vertebrae.

B) Trans-coelomic spread

This refers to spreading across the peritoneal surfaces.

Seen in:  Ovarian cancer,  Gastric cancer

Not typical for prostate cancer.

C) Inferior vesical vein

This vein drains the prostate, but it does not directly explain vertebral metastasis as the Batson plexus does.

D) Internal iliac vein

It drains pelvic organs but does not provide a direct valveless route to the vertebral column.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset shortness of breath and severe chest pain. The HRCT chest is shown below. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Needle thoracostomy

A 68-year-old man with sudden severe chest pain and dyspnea suggests an acute thoracic emergency. HRCT shows a large air collection in the pleural space with collapsed lung and absent lung markings, indicating pneumothorax. The severity of symptoms and significant lung compression suggest tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening condition where trapped air increases intrathoracic pressure and compresses mediastinal structures.

The immediate life-saving management is needle thoracostomy (needle decompression), typically at the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line or 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line, followed by chest tube insertion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset severe pain in the left lower limb for 5 hours. On examination, the limb is cold and pale. Distal pulses are absent. Sensory loss is present over the toes, and motor power is 4/5 at the ankle. There is no fixed mottling or muscle rigidity. What is the next best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent revascularization

The patient has acute limb ischemia (ALI) with a Rutherford Grade IIa (marginally threatened limb).

• Sudden onset severe limb pain
• Cold, pale limb
• Absent distal pulses
• Sensory loss limited to the toes
• No significant motor deficit (power 4/5)
• No fixed mottling or muscle rigidity

A viable but threatened limb requires urgent revascularization to salvage the extremity.

The patient has a salvageable limb with mild sensory loss and minimal motor weakness. The recommended management is:

• Immediate IV unfractionated heparin
• Urgent revascularization (catheter-directed thrombolysis, surgical embolectomy, or bypass depending on the cause and anatomy)

Rutherford classification of acute limb ischemia

| Grade | Limb Status | Clinical Features | Management

| ----- | ----------- | ----------------- | ----------

| I | Viable | No sensory or motor deficit | Anticoagulation ± imaging

| IIa | Marginally threatened | Toe sensory loss, minimal/no motor deficit | Urgent revascularization

| IIb | Immediately threatened | Sensory loss beyond toes, significant motor weakness | Immediate revascularization

| III | Irreversible | Profound anesthesia, paralysis, fixed mottling | Amputation

Why not the other options?

• A. Intravenous anticoagulation and observation: Anticoagulation is started immediately but observation alone is inappropriate because the limb is threatened.
• B. Catheter-directed thrombolysis: May be used as a revascularization technique in selected Rutherford I and IIa patients, but the broader and most appropriate answer is urgent revascularization.
• D. Amputation: Reserved for irreversible ischemia (Rutherford Grade III) with profound anesthesia, paralysis, fixed mottling, and muscle rigidity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with BPH underwent TURP under spinal anesthesia. During the procedure, 1.5% glycine was used as the irrigation fluid. After 45 minutes of resection, the patient developed restlessness, headache, nausea, altered sensorium, confusion, and mild hypotension. Intraoperative ABG and electrolyte analysis revealed acute dilutional electrolyte disturbance. What is the next appropriate step in intraoperative management?
options: Immediately stopping the procedure and administering hypertonic saline to correct acute symptomatic hyponatremia
Changing irrigation fluid to normal saline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediately stopping the procedure and administering hypertonic saline to correct acute symptomatic hyponatremia

This patient has TURP syndrome, a complication caused by systemic absorption of large volumes of hypotonic irrigation fluid (1.5% glycine) during monopolar transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). The diagnosis is suggested by:

• TURP under spinal anesthesia
• Use of 1.5% glycine irrigation
• Procedure lasting >45 minutes
• Restlessness, headache, nausea, confusion, altered sensorium
• Dilutional hyponatremia with mild hypotension

The first step is to stop the procedure immediately. Symptomatic acute hyponatremia requires careful administration of hypertonic (3%) saline.

Why not the other options?

• B. Fluid restriction: Appropriate only for mild, asymptomatic cases; inadequate in symptomatic patients.
• C. Change irrigation fluid to normal saline: Normal saline cannot be used with monopolar TURP and does not treat established TURP syndrome.
• D. Switch to bipolar diathermy: Bipolar TURP uses normal saline and reduces future risk but is not the immediate management once TURP syndrome has developed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 7-year-old male child was brought to the ER after a burn and was found to have 20% BSA burns. He was resuscitated as per Parkland's equation. After 6 hours, he was found to have cool extremities and hypotension, and urine output of 0.3ml/kg/hour. What is the next step in management?
options: Give bolus of 10 ml/kg Hartmann solution
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Give bolus of 10 ml/kg Hartmann solution

• 20% total body surface area (TBSA) burns
• Already resuscitated using Parkland formula
• After 6 hours:

• Cool extremities
• Hypotension
• Urine output = 0.3 mL/kg/hr

Indicate inadequate fluid resuscitation → burn shock / under-resuscitation.

The best indicator of adequate resuscitation in burns is:

Urine output

Targets:

• Adults → ≥0.5 mL/kg/hr
• Children → ≥1 mL/kg/hr

Here the child has:

0.3 mL/kg/hr → clearly inadequate perfusion.

Next Step in Management

Because the patient shows signs of hypovolemia, the immediate step is:

Give a 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus (Hartmann / Ringer lactate).

This helps restore→ Intravascular volume , Tissue perfusion, Urine output

❌ B) Give colloid bolus

Colloids are generally avoided during the first 24 hours after burns due to increased capillary permeability.

❌ C) Wait for 2 hours and reassess

Dangerous because the child already shows:

• Hypotension
• Poor perfusion
• Low urine output

Immediate fluid correction is required.

❌ D) Give bolus at 30 mL/kg

This is excessive and may lead to fluid overload or burn edema.

Standard correction bolus is 10 mL/kg.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 80-year-old male patient presents with a PSA level of 7 ng/mL and a small tumor focus in prostate with a Gleason score of 6, what would be the most appropriate course of action for management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Active surveillance

None

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A case of urinary bladder stone with a history of Proteus infection is likely to be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Triple Phosphate

How Proteus causes these stones→ Proteus produces urease enzyme, which breaks down urea:

Urea → Ammonia (NH₃) + CO₂

This causes: Alkaline urine (↑ pH); Precipitation of minerals

The minerals that combine are:

• Magnesium (Mg²⁺)
• Ammonium (NH₄⁺)
• Phosphate (PO₄³⁻)

These form Magnesium ammonium phosphate stones → Struvite stones (Triple phosphate stones).

Why other options are wrong

Oxalate stones

• Most common stones
• Associated with hypercalciuria, not infection.

Uric acid stones

• Occur in acidic urine
• Associated with gout.

Cystine stones

• Occur in cystinuria (genetic disorder).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A child is brought with a history of spilling hot milk on the hand 24 hours ago. What is the depth of burn in this case, as per the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superficial partial thickness

A scald burn presenting after 24 hours with red, moist, shiny skin and blistering/peeling indicates preserved dermal blood supply and intact nerve endings. These features are typical of a superficial partial-thickness (second-degree) burn, which is usually painful and well perfused.

In contrast, deep burns appear pale/dry with reduced pain, while full-thickness burns are white or charred and insensate.

Answer: Superficial partial-thickness burn.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A construction worker with white fingers for years while using heavy drills. What could be the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Raynauds phenomenon

A construction worker who has used heavy drills for years develops white fingers.

→ This is classic Raynaud’s phenomenon.

Concept:

Repeated vibration from tools like: Jackhammers/Power drills—> damage to small blood vessels and nerves in the fingers→  leads to vasospasm of digital arteries causing the fingers to temporarily lose blood supply.

Patients develop:

White fingers (blanching)--> Blue discoloration (cyanosis)--> Redness when blood flow returns.

White → Blue → Red

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female is cooking in the kitchen. Suddenly the cooker blasts, leading to dermo-epidermal burns of the face partly with singeing of eyebrows, bilateral upper limbs, and front of chest. What is the area of the burn?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 27-30%

• Using the Rule of Nines, both upper limbs contribute 18%, the anterior chest 9%, and the face (partial involvement) adds <9%%, totalling ≈27–30%.
• Facial burns with singed eyebrows also raise suspicion for inhalational injury, necessitating early airway assessment alongside fluid planning.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient presents to the clinic with a painful lump in her breast that has been increasing in size over the past few days. After examination, the doctor diagnoses her with a breast abscess and prescribes antibiotics to help clear the infection. The doctor attempts to aspirate the abscess using a needle and syringe, but no fluid is obtained. What is the next step in management?
options: Stop antibiotics as no aspirate was collected
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A second attempt at aspiration

For an uncomplicated breast abscess, needle aspiration (preferably ultrasound-guided) along with antibiotics is generally the initial approach.

If the first aspiration is unsuccessful, a repeat aspiration, preferably under ultrasound guidance, should be attempted rather than immediately proceeding to incision and drainage.

Incision and drainage is considered when:

• Repeated aspiration fails
• Abscess is large/multiloculated or has extensive skin involvement
• There is recurrence or failure to resolve

High-yield: Breast abscess → aspiration + antibiotics → repeat aspiration if required → I&D if aspiration fails.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident (RTA). The patient is in respiratory distress, hypotensive, and has distended, engorged neck veins. The chest x-ray is shown below. What is the next best immediate step in management?
options: Needle decompression at 2nd intercostal space in midclavicular line
Needle decompression at 7th intercostal space in midclavicular line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Needle decompression at 2nd intercostal space in midclavicular line

This patient has tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency characterized by:

• Respiratory distress
• Hypotension
• Distended neck veins (raised JVP)
• Chest X-ray showing a large pneumothorax with mediastinal shift

Immediate treatment is needle decompression, followed by definitive tube thoracostomy (intercostal chest drain).

Note: Current ATLS guidelines also recommend needle decompression at the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior to mid-axillary line, as it has a higher success rate due to a thinner chest wall. However, FMGE/NEET examinations often expect the traditional answer: 2nd ICS, midclavicular line.

Why not the other options?

• B. Needle decompression at 7th ICS in MCL: Incorrect anatomical site.
• C. Aggressive IV fluids: May support circulation but do not relieve the obstructive shock caused by tension pneumothorax.
• D. Endotracheal intubation: Positive-pressure ventilation can worsen an untreated tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man was brought to the emergency department after he fell from a motorbike and injured his perineum. He gets an urge to micturate but is unable to urinate. On examination, blood was seen at the tip of the urethra, and swelling of the penis and scrotum was seen. What is the site of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bulbar urethra injury

Bulbar (spongy) urethral injury is classically associated with straddle injuries (e.g., falling onto a bicycle or motorbike crossbar/perineal trauma). Patients typically present with:

• Blood at the urethral meatus
• Inability to urinate (urinary retention)
• Swelling/ecchymosis of the penis, scrotum, and perineum due to urine extravasation into the superficial perineal space

The bulbar urethra lies within the corpus spongiosum of the bulb of the penis and is vulnerable to direct perineal trauma. When it ruptures:

• Urine leaks into the superficial perineal pouch
• Swelling spreads to the scrotum, penis, and lower anterior abdominal wall (deep to Scarpa’s fascia)

Differentiation from Membranous Urethral Injury

• Membranous urethral rupture is usually caused by pelvic fractures
• Urine extravasates into the deep perineal space and pelvis
• Scrotal and penile swelling is less characteristic

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A midline neck swelling just below the hyoid bone and managed by Sistrunk’s operation leads to postoperative need for thyroxine replacement. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Thyroglossal cyst with only functioning thyroid tissue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thyroglossal cyst with only functioning thyroid tissue

A thyroglossal cyst (TGC) is the most common congenital midline neck swelling, arising from persistence of the thyroglossal duct. It typically presents as a midline swelling below the hyoid bone that moves with swallowing and protrusion of the tongue. The standard treatment is Sistrunk’s operation, which involves excision of the cyst, tract, and central part of the hyoid bone.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Lateral aberrant thyroid: Usually represents metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma to a cervical lymph node rather than ectopic thyroid tissue.
• B. Thyroglossal cyst: Most patients have a normally located thyroid gland, so thyroxine replacement is not required after surgery.
• C. Solitary thyroid nodule: Managed according to thyroid pathology and is unrelated to Sistrunk’s operation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient following head injury with altered consciousness, vomiting, and GCS of 7/15 undergoes CT scan as shown. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decompression

• Epidural Haematoma with low GCS is a neurosurgical emergency .
• Requires immediate decompression : to prevent further brain injury, because:-

(Blood accumulation between skull and dura → causes mass effects on brain parenchyma  → brain compression of neuroparenchyma → Can lead to herniation (fatal) if not treated quickly)

Option A: IV Mannitol ❌

• Temporarily reduces ICP and decreases brain swelling by pulling fluid out of the brain .
• But, Mannitol cannot remove the clot → Epidural hematoma is rapidly expanding
• Hence, needs immediate surgical removal.

Option B: Wait and watch❌

• EDH can deteriorate due to rapid expansion.  So, this option can be ruled out.

Option D: Anticoagulation ❌

• Cause thinning of blood→ hence worsen the bleed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient had enlarging nodules present on his scalp. He was taking prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus. His clinical lesion and the histopathological lesion are shown alongside. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malakoplakia

Image shows: multiple enlarging nodules / plaques. The patient is immunocompromised ( taking immunosuppressive drugs)

Malakoplakia classically occurs in immunosuppressed patients. (transplant recipients.)

The histology shows round basophilic inclusions inside macrophages (arrows). These are Michaelis–Gutmann bodies.

Malakoplakia occurs due to:

Defective macrophage killing of bacteria because of defective phagolysosomal activity (bacteria partially digested calcium + iron deposited  forms Michaelis–Gutmann bodies)

Most commonly associated organism: E coli.

Common sites of malakoplakia

| Organ | Frequency

| ----- | ---------

| Urinary bladder | Most common

| Kidney | Common

| Colon | Possible

| Skin | Rare

| Prostate | Occasional

A. Tuberculosis

• Shows caseating granulomas
• Langhans giant cells
• No Michaelis–Gutmann bodies

B. Pyoderma gangrenosum

• neutrophilic dermatosis; no macrophage inclusions

D. Drug-induced lesion

• no Michaelis–Gutmann bodies

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident has: • GCS: E4 V3 M4 • Respiratory rate: 28/min • Blood pressure: 90/60 mmHg What is the appropriate triage category?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Red

This patient should be triaged as Red (Immediate) because he has physiological instability and requires urgent life-saving intervention.

The patient has:

• GCS = E4 V3 M4 = 11 (altered mental status)
• Respiratory rate = 28/min (tachypnea)
• Blood pressure = 90/60 mmHg (hypotension suggesting shock)

These findings indicate a critically injured patient who requires immediate assessment and resuscitation.

Other Options:

• A. Green: Minor injuries; patient can walk (“walking wounded”).
• B. Yellow: Serious injuries but stable enough that treatment can be delayed.
• D. Black: Dead or injuries incompatible with survival despite available resources.

| Category | Color | Description

| -------- | ----- | -----------

| Immediate | Red | Airway compromise, shock, severe trauma, altered consciousness

| Delayed | Yellow | Serious but stable injuries; treatment can wait

| Minor | Green | Walking wounded; minor injuries

| Expectant/Dead | Black | Dead or unsurvivable injuries

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought to the casualty following a road traffic accident. On examination, the patient is conscious, BP is 90/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 40 breaths per minute, and pulse rate is 120 bpm. The X-ray is shown below. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Needle thoracostomy

The unstable patient with hyperlucent hemithorax and mediastinal shift indicates tension pneumothorax. Immediate needle thoracostomy in the 5th ICS midaxillary line relieves pressure. Chest tube insertion follows for definitive management.

Key Signs:

• Hyperlucent hemithorax (black side)
• Absent vascular markings
• Collapsed lung edge visible
• Mediastinal shift to opposite side (very important!)
• Depressed diaphragm
• Deep sulcus sign (in supine trauma patients)

| Option | Why Correct / Incorrect | Key Insight

| ------ | ----------------------- | -----------

| A. Pericardiocentesis | ❌ Used in cardiac tamponade | Beck’s triad: hypotension + JVD + muffled heart sounds

| B. Thoracotomy | ❌ Too invasive initially | Done in massive trauma or failed initial management

| C. Needle thoracostomy | ✅ FIRST step in tension pneumothorax | Emergency decompression

| D. Chest tube insertion | ❌ Definitive but NOT first | Done AFTER needle decompression

| Feature | Tension Pneumothorax | Cardiac Tamponade

| ------- | -------------------- | -----------------

| Breath sounds | Absent on one side | Normal

| Trachea | Deviated | Central

| Percussion | Hyperresonant | Normal

| JVP | ↑ | ↑

| X-ray | Hyperlucent lung + shift | Enlarged cardiac shadow

| Treatment | Needle thoracostomy | Pericardiocentesis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department after a building collapse. He initially loses consciousness but regains it shortly afterward. A non-contrast CT (NCCT) scan of the brain is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Extradural hematoma

An Extradural (Epidural) Hematoma (EDH) is a neurosurgical emergency caused by bleeding between the inner table of the skull and the dura mater, most commonly due to laceration of the middle meningeal artery following a temporal bone fracture. The diagnosis is suggested by:

• History of head trauma
• Brief loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval
• Progressive neurological deterioration
• CT showing a biconvex (lens-shaped), hyperdense hematoma that does not cross suture lines

Key differentiating features:

• Subdural hematoma (SDH):

• Tearing of bridging veins
• Crescent-shaped hematoma
• Crosses suture lines but not the falx
• Common in elderly and alcoholics

• Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH):

• Blood in basal cisterns and sulci
• Sudden “thunderclap” headache

• Diffuse axonal injury (DAI):

• Immediate prolonged unconsciousness
• CT may be normal or show multiple punctate hemorrhages

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department after sustaining a head injury. The CT scan is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epidural hematoma

An epidural hematoma (EDH) is an arterial hemorrhage that occurs between the inner table of the skull and the periosteal layer of the dura mater, most commonly due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery following a temporal bone (pterion) fracture. On CT scan, it appears as a hyperdense, biconvex (lentiform), extra-axial collection that is limited by cranial sutures because the dura is firmly attached at suture lines.

Why not the other options?

• B. Subdural hematoma: Caused by rupture of bridging veins. CT shows a crescent-shaped (concave) extra-axial collection that crosses sutures but is limited by the falx and tentorium.
• C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Blood is seen within the basal cisterns and cerebral sulci, producing a “star sign” on CT rather than a localized biconvex collection.
• D. Intracerebral hemorrhage: Appears as a hyperdense intraparenchymal lesion within the brain tissue, not as an extra-axial collection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is confused, opens his eyes on painful stimuli, flexes one limb on painful stimuli, and can localize the stimulus with the other limb. His Glasgow Coma Score is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 11

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a standardized tool used to assess the level of consciousness by evaluating eye opening, verbal response, and motor response. The total score ranges from 3 to 15, with lower scores indicating more severe neurologic impairment.

In this patient:

• Eye opening to pain = E2
• Confused verbal response = V4
• Localizes painful stimulus with one limb = M5

Although the other limb demonstrates abnormal flexion, the best motor response is used when calculating the GCS.

Total GCS = E2 + V4 + M5 = 11

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is found to have a solitary thyroid nodule. What is the first step in his management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thyroid profile/TSH

When a patient presents with a solitary thyroid nodule (STN  serum TSH is the first investigation.

(tells us whether the nodule is functioning (toxic) or non-functioning)

Stepwise approach to a thyroid nodule

| Step | Investigation | Purpose

| ---- | ------------- | -------

| 1 | TSH level | Determine thyroid function

| 2 | Ultrasound thyroid | Assess suspicious features

| 3 | FNAC | Confirm malignancy

| 4 | Radioiodine scan (if TSH low) | Identify hot vs cold nodule

TSH is low

●     Suggests hyperfunctioning nodule

●     Next step → Radioiodine scan (I-123)

●     These nodules are rarely malignant

TSH is normal/high

●     Do Ultrasound + FNAC

●     Higher suspicion of malignancy.

Radioiodine with I-123→ Used after TSH is low, not the first step.

Radioiodine with I-131→ Used for treatment, not diagnosis.

CECT→ Not part of initial evaluation of thyroid nodules.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient of blunt trauma to the abdomen is being explored in the emergency. Intraoperatively, a non-expanding haematoma is seen in the retroperitoneal colon. What is the appropriate management of this patient?
options: Haematoma to be explored, nothing to be done to the colon
Haematoma to be explored, the colon to be resected
Haematoma not to be explored, nothing to be done to the colon
Haematoma not to be explored, the colon to be resected
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Haematoma not to be explored, nothing to be done to the colon

Retroperitoneal hematomas are classified by anatomical zone, and management depends on both the zone and the mechanism of injury (blunt vs. penetrating):

| Zone | Location | Blunt trauma | Penetrating trauma

| ---- | -------- | ------------ | ------------------

| Zone 1 (Central/medial) | Aorta, IVC, pancreas, duodenum | Always explore | Always explore

| Zone 2 (Lateral/perinephric) | Kidney, ascending/descending (retroperitoneal) colon | Explore only if expanding, pulsatile, or ruptured | Explore

| Zone 3 (Pelvic) | Pelvic vessels | Explore only if expanding or uncontrolled (often better managed by angioembolization) | Explore

• The retroperitoneal colon (ascending and descending colon) lies in Zone 2. In blunt trauma, a non-expanding, non-pulsatile Zone 2 hematoma is generally left undisturbed — the retroperitoneum itself provides tamponade, and opening an intact hematoma risks converting a self-limited injury into uncontrolled hemorrhage or missing the chance for the body's own tamponade to work.
• Since the hematoma is not explored, the underlying retroperitoneal colon is also not visualized or manipulated — so no resection or repair is performed unless there's clear evidence of colonic perforation (free air, succus entericus, fecal contamination, or an expanding/pulsatile hematoma), in which case exploration becomes mandatory regardless of zone.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient of road traffic accident presents to the emergency with increasing restlessness and difficulty in breathing. The respiratory rate is 26 breaths/minute; there are distended neck veins; trachea is deviated to the right side with hyper-resonant note and absence of breath sounds on the left side. Which of the following statements are correct? 1. The most probable clinical diagnosis is left tension pneumothorax. 2. Immediate chest decompression using wide bore cannula in left second intercostal space should be done. 3. Immediate chest X-ray should be done to confirm the clinical diagnosis. 4. Definitive chest tube insertion in left fifth intercostal space should be done. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 4

The patient has left tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency characterized by respiratory distress, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, hyperresonance, and absent breath sounds.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Most probable clinical diagnosis is left tension pneumothorax: Correct.
• 2. Immediate chest needle decompression with a wide-bore cannula in the left 2nd intercostal space (midclavicular line) should be done: Correct. (Current ATLS also accepts the 4th/5th intercostal space, anterior/mid-axillary line.)
• 3. Immediate chest X-ray should be done to confirm the diagnosis: Incorrect. Do not delay treatment for imaging when tension pneumothorax is suspected clinically.
• 4. Definitive chest tube insertion in the left 5th intercostal space should be done: Correct.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A Patient presented with a growth on the penis, which invades corpus cavernosum without lymph node metastasis. What is the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Penectomy with bilateral ilio-inguinal dissection

For a patient with stage T3 carcinoma penis and no clinically palpable inguinal lymph nodes, the preferred treatment is:

• Penectomy (partial or total depending on residual stump length)
• Along with superficial inguinal lymph node dissection

Surgical management of the penis-

Partial penectomy:

Done when a functional penile stump >2 cm can be preserved after tumor excision.

Total penectomy:

Required when the remaining stump would be <2 cm after resection.

TNM staging of carcinoma penis

| Stage | Extent of invasion

| ----- | ------------------

| T1 | Limited to skin/subepithelial tissue

| T2 | Invades corpus spongiosum ± urethra

| T3 | Invades corpus cavernosum ± urethra

| T4 | Invades adjacent structures

Why inguinal node dissection in T3 disease?

T3 tumors invade deeper erectile tissue (corpus cavernosum), increasing the likelihood of micrometastatic lymph node spread, even if nodes are not clinically palpable.

• The first draining nodes are the superficial inguinal lymph nodes
• Hence management includes:

• Superficial inguinal lymph node dissection, or
• Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in selected cases

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with dilated veins in the lower limb as shown in the image. Venous Doppler is normal. What is the C stage of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. C1

The image shows telangiectasias (spider veins) without visible varicose veins, edema, skin changes, or ulceration. A normal venous Doppler indicates no significant deep venous reflux or obstruction.

According to the CEAP (Clinical–Etiological–Anatomical–Pathophysiological) classification, this corresponds to Clinical Class C1.

| Clinical Class | Features

| -------------- | --------

| C0 | No visible or palpable signs of venous disease

| C1 | Telangiectasias (spider veins) or reticular veins

| C2 | Varicose veins (≥3 mm diameter)

| C3 | Edema without skin changes

| C4a | Pigmentation or venous eczema

| C4b | Lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche

| C5 | Healed venous ulcer

| C6 | Active venous ulcer

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident, complaining of a severe headache. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

Characteristic CT Finding

• On non-contrast CT brain, SAH appears as: Hyperdense blood within the basal cisterns.
• This produces the classic radiological sign: “Star of death” ;

because blood outlines the suprasellar cistern and surrounding subarachnoid spaces.

❌ B) Subdural Hemorrhage

Typical CT appearance:

• Crescent-shaped collection
• Located between dura and arachnoid

Often due to bridging vein rupture.

❌ C) Epidural Hemorrhage

Classic CT sign:

• Biconvex (lens-shaped) hematoma
• Does not cross suture lines

Usually caused by middle meningeal artery injury.

❌ D) Intracerebral Hemorrhage

Appears as: Localized hyperdense bleed within brain parenchyma

Not within the cisterns.

| Hemorrhage | CT Appearance | Cause

| ---------- | ------------- | -----

| Subarachnoid | Star-shaped basal cistern blood | Aneurysm / trauma

| Subdural | Crescent-shaped | Bridging vein rupture

| Epidural | Biconvex (lens) | Middle meningeal artery

| Intracerebral | Focal parenchymal bleed | Hypertension / trauma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with the lesion shown in the image. He had a traumatic injury to the chest one year ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Keloid

The chest (especially sternum) is a very common site for keloids.

Why the answer is Keloid

• Grow beyond the original wound margins
• Firm, raised, shiny
• Progressively enlarge
• Do not regress spontaneously

They occur due to excess collagen deposition during wound healing.

Common sites include:

• Chest
• Shoulders
• Earlobes
• Upper back

❌ A) Hemangioma

• Red or bluish vascular lesion
• Often present in infancy
• Compressible and vascular

The image shows fibrous scar tissue, not a vascular tumor.

❌ B) Hypertrophic scar

Key difference from keloid:

| Feature | Hypertrophic scar | Keloid

| ------- | ----------------- | ------

| Extends beyond wound | ❌ No | ✅ Yes

| Growth pattern | Limited | Progressive

| Spontaneous regression | Often | Rare

❌ D) Neurofibroma

• Soft nodular lesions
• “Buttonhole sign”
• Associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1

This lesion clearly looks like scar tissue, not a nerve tumor.

Common treatments include:

• Intralesional steroids (triamcinolone)
• Silicone gel sheets
• Pressure therapy
• Laser therapy

Surgical excision alone is avoided because keloids recur frequently.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a lower limb wound as shown. The wound had healthy granulation tissue. What will be used as a cover?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Split thickness skin graft

Option A: Split  thickness grafts is ideal for large wounds with healthy granulation,  —> because it provides ideal coverage.

Concept: healthy granulation tissue means that the wound bed is clean and ready, just needs a skin cover

Option B. Full-thickness skin graft

●     Used for cosmetic areas (face, eyelids, fingers)

●     Needs better blood supply

●     Not ideal for large wounds like this.

Option C. VAC dressing

●     Used to promote granulation tissue formation

●     But here the wound already has healthy granulation.

Option D: Flap

●     Used when bone, tendon, vessels are exposed

●     Requires vascularized tissue transfer

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a tender pulsatile mass as shown in the image below. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CT angiogram

The image shows a tender pulsatile swelling on the scalp/forehead strongly suggests a vascular lesion, most commonly:

• Crisoid aneurysm
• Arteriovenous (AV) malformation

Both are high-flow vascular abnormalities of scalp vessels.

Why CT Angiography is the next step

• Before treating any vascular scalp lesion:need to Identify feeding arteries, draining veins
• This is done using CT angiography, which visualizes arterial and venous connections.

❌ A) FESS (Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery)

• Used for sinus disease.
• Completely unrelated to a vascular scalp mass.

❌ B) Needle aspiration

If the lesion is vascular (AV malformation / crisoid aneurysm), inserting a needle can cause:

• Massive hemorrhage
• Life-threatening bleeding

❌ D) Intravenous antibiotics

Antibiotics are used for infection (abscess, cellulitis).

But this lesion is vascular, not infective.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with neck swelling and undergoes a tissue biopsy which reveals the cells as shown in the image. Which of the following is the likely gene affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BRAF gene

The biopsy appearance is consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma, characterized by papillary architecture and nuclear features like clearing and grooves.

BRAF gene mutation (most commonly V600E) is the hallmark molecular abnormality in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

This mutation activates the MAP kinase pathway, driving tumorigenesis.

RET rearrangements and RAS mutations are seen in other thyroid tumours, while p53 is associated with anaplastic carcinoma.

| Thyroid tumor | Gene mutation

| ------------- | -------------

| Papillary carcinoma | BRAF / RET-PTC

| Follicular carcinoma | RAS

| Medullary carcinoma | RET

| Anaplastic carcinoma | P53

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden chest pain radiating to the neck and interscapular region. X-ray shows widened mediastinum. BP is 110/90 in right arm and 160/100 in left arm. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute aortic dissection

Sudden tearing chest pain + widened mediastinum + BP difference between arms

Almost always indicates acute aortic dissection.

❌A) Acute Coronary Syndrome

Pain usually pressure-like, not tearing; No mediastinal widening

No BP difference between arms

❌B) Acute Pulmonary Embolism

Presents with dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia

Chest X-ray often normal; No BP asymmetry

❌D) Esophageal Rupture (Boerhaave syndrome)

Usually occurs after severe vomiting

Shows mediastinal air, not widening; Associated with subcutaneous emphysema

Stanford Classification for aortic dissection

| Type | Involvement | Management

| ---- | ----------- | ----------

| Type A | Ascending aorta involved |   Emergency surgery (because can lead to aortic regurgitation)

| Type B | Only descending aorta | Medical management (beta blockers)

First step Control blood pressure and heart rate→ Drugs used Beta blockers (labetalol, esmolol)

Goal here: To reduce shear stress on aorta

Best test in stable patient: 👉 CT angiography; next best: trans esophageal echocardiography.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with varicose veins, as shown in the image below. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is true?
options: Sclerotherapy is first-line in the treatment of this condition
It can progress to eczema and ulceration
Pelvic mass is the most common cause
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It can progress to eczema and ulceration

The image shows varicose veins without any visible ulceration.

• This is CEAP C2 (varicose veins only)
• No ulcer, no eczema yet

The following complications occur when untreated.

Edema → pigmentation → dermatitis and eczema → lipodermatosclerosis → venous ulcer → deformities → inverted champagne bottle leg.

A. C6 stage

C6 = active ulcer present: Not seen in image

B. Sclerotherapy is not the first line for Varicose veins; Endovenous laser ablation is TOC.

D. Pelvic mass is most common cause

• Most common cause = valvular incompetence (great saphenous vein)
• Pelvic mass = rare secondary cause

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with weight gain, thinning of hair, and dry skin. Clinical features are suggestive of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which of the following antibodies is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody

• Weight gain
• Thinning of hair
• Dry skin

classic features of hypothyroidism suggests Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

Most Common Antibody in Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis

The hallmark antibody is: Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibody

• Present in \~90% of patients with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
• Targets the enzyme thyroid peroxidase, which is involved in thyroid hormone synthesis

❌ B) Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)

This antibody is associated with: Graves’ disease

It stimulates the TSH receptor, causing hyperthyroidism.

❌ C) TSH receptor antibody

Also seen in Graves’ disease, producing:

• Diffuse toxic goiter
• Hyperthyroidism
• Exophthalmos

❌D) Long-acting thyroid stimulator (LATS)

This is an older term for TSI, also linked to Graves’ disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient suffering from leprosy presents with an ulcer on his foot. There are no signs of inflammation. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Foot care, limb rehabilitation

Foot care, limb rehabilitation

Includes:

• Off-loading pressure (MCR footwear, rest)
• Daily foot inspection
• Protective footwear
• Physiotherapy & patient education

Cornerstone of trophic ulcer management

Debride and dressing:

• Indicated if slough, necrosis, or secondary infection is present
• Not the first step in a clean, non-inflamed trophic ulcer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient sustained burns and presented to the emergency department. His nasal hair was singed, and burns were noted on his face and neck. His carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) levels were raised to 18%, and his oxygen saturation was 80% on room air. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intubate and mechanical ventilation

This patient has evidence of inhalational injury following burns:

• Facial and neck burns
• Singed nasal hairs
• Elevated carboxyhemoglobin (COHb 18%)
• Hypoxemia (SpO₂ 80%)

The priority is early airway protection because progressive airway edema can rapidly lead to complete airway obstruction. Therefore, early endotracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation is indicated.

Why not the other options?

• A. 100% O₂ with NRBM: Although 100% oxygen is essential for carbon monoxide poisoning, this patient has signs of inhalational injury with impending airway compromise, so airway protection takes priority.
• C. Resuscitate using Parkland formula: Fluid resuscitation is important for major burns but is not the first priority in a patient with threatened airway.
• D. Hyperbaric O₂ therapy: Considered in selected cases of severe carbon monoxide poisoning (e.g., COHb >25%, neurological symptoms, pregnancy), but does not replace airway management.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoes total thyroidectomy. Which of the following complications is most likely to develop 2–3 days after the procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carpopedal spasm

Parathyroid glands get damaged / devascularized (To preserve parathyroids ligate inferior thyroid artery CLOSE to thyroid gland)

• They regulate calcium via PTH→ Injury to parathyroid leads to→ ↓ PTH → ↓ Calcium (hypocalcemia)

Concept :

• Calcium doesn’t drop immediately→ It takes 2–5 days for levels to fall

→ That’s when symptoms appear

Result: Hypocalcemia → Tetany → Carpopedal spasm (Trousseau’s sign)--> Hand goes into “obstetric position”

Other complaints include: peri oral numbness, tingling in fingers.

❌ B. Deviation of face

• Facial nerve issue, seen in parotid surgeries  (not related to thyroid surgery)

❌ C. Migratory thrombophlebitis

• Seen in malignancy especially pancreatic / any other adenocarcinomas (Trousseau syndrome); unrelated here.

❌ D. Gustatory sweating

• Frey’s syndrome (after parotid surgery), not thyroidectomy related.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent cystoscopy, which showed multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder. The histopathology image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malakoplakia

Malakoplakia is a chronic inflammatory condition seen in immunocompromised patients, commonly affecting the bladder trigone.

It results from defective macrophage phagolysosomal activity.

Histology shows von Hansemann histiocytes containing Michaelis–Gutmann bodies.

Yellow-white plaques on cystoscopy with these pathognomonic inclusions confirm malakoplakia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent split-thickness skin grafting for a burn injury on the arm. On the sixth postoperative day, he develops stiffness of the arm during physiotherapy. What should be the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graft
Remove the graft and regraft the area
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Continue physiotherapy without intervention

Post-Split thickness skin grafting

• Graft is in the phase of inosculation and revascularization
• Secondary contraction of STSG is expected
• Mild stiffness during early physiotherapy is physiological, not pathological

Aggressive stretching or surgery at this stage can disrupt neovascularization and cause graft shear or failure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. On presentation, he is in a stuporous state and has had 2 episodes of vomiting. CT of the head is done and is given below. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decompressive Craniotomy

A road traffic accident patient presenting with repeated vomiting suggests raised intracranial pressure.

•

CT brain shows a lens shaped hyperdense collection ---> characteristic of an acute epidural hematoma (EDH) along with mass effect and midline shift --> indicate significant brain compression and neurological deterioration.

•

In such cases, urgent surgical evacuation is required --> decompressive craniotomy/craniectomy with hematoma removal.

• Conservative treatment or burr hole drainage is inadequate for a large acute EDH.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a history of chest trauma with breathlessness on examination is found to have systolic BP of 90 mm of Hg, SpO₂ of 85%, GCS 8/15 and absent breath sounds. What is the next step?
options: Secure airway, needle thoracotomy and IV fluids
Blood transfusion and send for CT
Take history, administer IV Dextrose, and send for eFAST
CT scan of the head and secure the airway
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Secure airway, needle thoracotomy and IV fluids

According to the ATLS trauma management principle (ABCDE approach).

A – Airway

• GCS ≤ 8 → airway must be secured (intubation).

B – Breathing

• Absent breath sounds + chest trauma → suspect tension pneumothorax
• Immediate needle thoracotomy (needle decompression).

C – Circulation

• Hypotension (90 mmHg) indicates shock
• Start IV fluids for resuscitation.

Blood transfusion and CT❌

• CT is done only after patient stabilization.
• Patient is hemodynamically unstable, so immediate life-saving treatment is needed.

Take history, give IV dextrose, eFAST ❌

• Primary survey and life-saving interventions come first.
• History is secondary survey.

CT head and secure airway ❌

• Breathing problem (tension pneumothorax) must be treated immediately before CT→ because CT scan takes time and tension pneumothorax is life threatening.
• Tension pneumothorax → Air in pleural space → lung collapse→ This causes Mediastinal shift → ↓ venous return → hypotension
• Indicates respiratory compromise + obstructive shock, hence needs to be treated immediately with needle decompression.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a perforated peptic ulcer is hypotensive on arrival but becomes hemodynamically stable after fluid resuscitation. Which triage category should be assigned?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Yellow

In mass casualty triage, patients are categorized according to the urgency of treatment and likelihood of survival.

A patient with a perforated peptic ulcer who is initially hypotensive but responds to fluid resuscitation and becomes hemodynamically stable requires urgent surgical intervention, but treatment can be delayed briefly without immediate threat to life. Therefore, the patient is assigned to the Yellow (Delayed) category.

Why not the other options?

• A. Red (Immediate): Patients with life-threatening injuries requiring immediate intervention, e.g., persistent shock, airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax.
• C. Green (Minor): Walking wounded with minor injuries.
• D. Black (Expectant/Dead): Dead or injuries incompatible with survival despite available resources.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with chest trauma, BP 90 mmHg, SpO₂ 85%, GCS 8/15, absent breath sounds. Next step in his management will be?
options: Secure airway, ICD placement, and IV fluids
Start IV fluids, give atropine and send for chest x-ray
Administer IV Dextrose and send for CT
Evaluate for head injury and perform surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Secure airway, ICD placement, and IV fluids

• Hypotension, low SpO₂, GCS 8, and absent breath sounds strongly suggest a tension pneumothorax with airway compromise.
• Immediate priorities are securing the airway, rapid chest decompression/ICD placement, and IV fluid resuscitation.
• Imaging(CT)  is not done first in an unstable patient.

❌Start IV fluids + atropine + X-ray

• Atropine not indicated ; Taking X-ray delays immediate resuscitative measures.

❌ IV dextrose + CT

• Dextrose is not needed in this patient,
• CT is done only after initial stabilization

❌Evaluate head injury first

• Patient will die from airway/breathing issue first, hence , treated first.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with pressure sore shows partially broken skin with shallow ulcer. What is the grade?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

Pressure sore grading:

• Grade 1: Non-blanching erythema with intact skin
• Grade 2: Partial thickness skin loss involving epidermis/dermis, shallow ulcer
• Grade 3: Full thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat
• Grade 4: Full thickness tissue loss with exposed bone/muscle/tendon

In this case, partial skin loss with shallow ulcer indicates Grade 2.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with severe maxillofacial trauma following a road traffic accident presents with SpO₂ of 80% on room air. What is the most appropriate immediate step in management?
options: Do suction and again try intubation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cricothyrotomy

A “cannot intubate, cannot ventilate” scenario requires immediate front-of-neck access (cricothyrotomy).

Nasal/oral adjuncts are contraindicated in facial trauma, and repeated attempts worsen hypoxia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with suspected head injury is brought to the emergency following road traffic accident. At the time of examination, patient is conscious with GCS 14/15 and stable vitals. There is bleeding from right ear and CSF leak from nose. Bruising is present behind the right ear. The most probable clinical diagnosis in this patient is:
options: Fracture of the base of skull
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fracture of the base of skull

A basilar skull fracture is suggested by the presence of CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea, bleeding from the ear, and Battle’s sign (post-auricular ecchymosis). These are classic clinical features of a fracture involving the base of the skull.

Why not the other options?

• A. Extradural hematoma: Typically presents with lucid interval and signs of raised intracranial pressure, not CSF leak or Battle’s sign.
• C. Cerebral concussion: Causes transient loss of consciousness/amnesia without signs of basilar skull fracture.
• D. Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage: Presents with headache and altered sensorium but not characteristic external signs like CSF leak or Battle’s sign.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A typical ulcer as shown in the following diagram is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tuberculosis

The diagram shows an ulcer with undermined edges, which is characteristic of a tuberculous ulcer.

• A. Syphilis: Classically a punched-out ulcer with a clean base and indurated edge.
• B. Squamous cell carcinoma: Characteristically has everted, irregular edges with an indurated base.
• C. Tuberculosis: Correct. Classically shows undermined edges, with a pale granulating base.
• D. Basal cell carcinoma: Characteristically has rolled-out, pearly edges and may show central ulceration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A varicose vein patient presents with eczema over the same region. CEAP stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C4a

• CEAP C4a includes eczema and pigmentation.
• C4b includes lipodermatosclerosis/atrophie blanche→ Thus eczema corresponds to C4a classification.

| Class | Meaning

| ----- | -------

| C0 | No visible/palpable venous disease

| C1 | Telangiectasia / Reticular veins

| C2 | Varicose veins

| C3 | Edema

| C4a | Pigmentation / Eczema

| C4b | Lipodermatosclerosis / Atrophie blanche

| C5 | Healed venous ulcer

| C6 | Active venous ulcer

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A wound was left open initially, with debridement and cleaning for 5 days before closure by sutures. What type of wound healing is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tertiary intention

Primary intention

• Clean wound (edges are brought together )→ closed immediately (ie sutured)
• Heals with minimal inflammation, minimal scar fast healing and minimal granulation tissue formation → Example: surgical incision

Secondary intention :-

• The Wound left open completely
• Heals by:

• Granulation tissue
• Wound contraction
• Epithelialization

• Slower healing, heals with more scarring.
• Done for large diabetic ulcers, large traumatic wounds

Tertiary intention:-

• Wound is not closed immediately due to:

• Contamination / infection risk
• Devitalized tissue

• It is kept open for a few days (usually 3–5 days)
• During this time:

• Debridement is used to remove dead tissue (that hampers healing)
• Irrigation + dressings reduce bacterial load

• Once the wound looks clean and granulation tissue is formed, it is sutured.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young lady is brought to emergency department following stab injury to right chest. She is gasping for breath, with tachypnoea, distended neck veins and tracheal shift to left on examination. There is hyperresonance and absent breath sounds on right hemithorax. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right tension pneumothorax

The patient has classic features of a tension pneumothorax following penetrating chest trauma:

• Severe respiratory distress/gasping
• Tachypnea
• Distended neck veins → increased intrathoracic pressure and impaired venous return
• Tracheal deviation to the opposite side
• Hyperresonance on the affected side
• Absent breath sounds on the affected side

These findings indicate that air is accumulating under pressure in the pleural cavity, causing mediastinal shift and obstructive shock.

Why not other options?

• (a) Simple pneumothorax: May cause absent breath sounds and hyperresonance, but typically does not cause mediastinal shift, JVD, or severe hemodynamic compromise.
• (b) Tension pneumothorax — Correct: Respiratory distress + unilateral absent breath sounds + hyperresonance + JVD + tracheal deviation.
• (c) Cardiac tamponade: Causes JVD and hypotension, but typically has muffled heart sounds and does not cause unilateral hyperresonance or absent breath sounds.
• (d) Hydropneumothorax: Contains both air and fluid; percussion may be hyperresonant above and dull below, rather than uniformly hyperresonant.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young male presents to surgery OPD with a verrucous lesion over the penis as shown in the image. On examination, inguinal lymph nodes are not enlarged. What is the management of choice in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Partial penectomy

Verrucous carcinoma (Buschke–Löwenstein tumor) is a low-grade, locally aggressive variant of SCC that requires wide local excision/partial penectomy for complete clearance.

Topical therapies and ablative procedures are inadequate because the tumor invades deeply despite minimal metastasis risk.

Surgical excision provides best local control and prevents recurrence.

| Lesion | Management

| ------ | ----------

| Condyloma acuminata | Podophylline / laser

| Erythroplasia of Queyrat | 5-FU

| Verrucous carcinoma | Penectomy

Partial penectomy

Done when a functional penile stump >2 cm can be preserved after tumor excision.

Total penectomy

Required when the remaining stump would be <2 cm after resection.

A) CO₂ laser ablation

Used for condyloma accuminata.

But verrucous carcinoma invades deeply, so the laser is inadequate.

B) Podophyllin

Used for: genital warts (HPV); Not for carcinoma.

C) Topical 5-FU

Used for: Erythroplasia of Queyrat

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young man underwent a surgery on his chest after a trauma an year ago and has developed a lesion as shown. Which of the following is a probable diagnosis in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Keloid

The image shows : thick, raised scar over the sternum→ classic site for keloid formation.

KELOID:

A keloid is an excessive fibrous tissue response after skin injury.

It happens due to overproduction of collagen during wound healing.

Characteristics:

• Raised, shiny, firm scar
• Extends beyond the original wound margins
• Continues growing over time
• Common on chest, shoulders, earlobes

Histology : Keloids show: Thick, Hyalinized; Disorganized collagen bundles

❌ A) Hemangioma

• A vascular tumor
• Appears as red/blue lesion
• Usually present from childhood

❌ C) Normal scar

• Confined to wound edges
• Does not extend beyond the incision

❌ D) Hamartoma

• Congenital benign mass
• Not related to trauma or surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A) Assertion: For any scrotal swelling, the inguinal region has to be examined. B) Reason: Testis lymphatic drainage is to the superficial inguinal lymph node.
options: A is correct and B is incorrect
A is incorrect and B is correct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A is correct and B is incorrect

Evaluation of any scrotal swelling should always include examination of the inguinal region to assess for inguinal hernia, undescended testis, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. However, the lymphatic drainage of the testes is to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes, whereas the scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

Why is B correct?

• Assertion (A): ✓ Correct – Examination of the inguinal region is an essential part of assessing any scrotal swelling.
• Reason (B): ✗ Incorrect – Testicular lymphatics drain to the para-aortic (retroperitoneal/lumbar) lymph nodes, not the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: According to the Muir and Barclay resuscitation protocol, which of the following colloids is recommended for use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Albumin

Muir and Barclay protocol :-

• Used for burn resuscitation
• Combines:

• Colloids (Albumin) → maintains oncotic pressure-Preferably given after first 12 hours of burn
• Crystalloids → restores circulating volume

Unlike Parkland (crystalloids only), here colloids are used early to reduce edema.

The Formula:

The total required fluid for a given time period is calculated as:

Volume=Weight (kg)×TBSA burned (%)÷2

The calculated volume is delivered as one "ration." This ration is administered across 6 periods totaling 36 hours, distributed as follows:

• First 12 hours: 1 ration every 4 hours (3 infusions)
• Second 12 hours: 1 ration every 6 hours (2 infusions)
• Third 12 hours: 1 full ration administered over the 12 hours (1 infusion)
•

Pathophysiology in burns:

• Capillaries become leaky→ Fluid + proteins leak into tissues → interstitial fluid ↑ →  Fluid stays in tissues as edema
• Blood loses protein → oncotic pressure of blood ↓

Albumin is the main protein responsible for plasma oncotic pressure

• It increases oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure in blood
• Creates a pulling force that draws fluid from interstitium → back into vessels
• ↓ Interstitial fluid → less edema. ↑ Intravascular volume → better perfusion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: After a fall from a height, a 10-year-old child presented to the emergency department with complaints of abdominal pain. Upon examination, the child's vital signs were stable, but tenderness was noted in the left lumbar region. What would be the best investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Contrast enhanced CT scan

A hemodynamically stable child with blunt abdominal trauma (eg, fall from height) and localized flank/lumbar tenderness should be evaluated with a contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis, which is the investigation of choice for detecting and grading solid organ injuries, especially renal trauma.

• Gold standard in stable patients with suspected abdominal or renal injury.
• Accurately identifies:

• Renal contusions and lacerations
• Perinephric hematoma
• Urinary extravasation
• Injuries to spleen, liver, pancreas, and bowel

• Helps determine whether nonoperative management or intervention is needed.

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

B. Retrograde urethrogram

• Indicated for suspected urethral injury (blood at the urethral meatus, inability to void, pelvic fracture), not flank trauma.

C. Wait and watch

• Appropriate only after adequate imaging has excluded significant injury.

D. Emergency laparotomy

• Reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients or those with signs of peritonitis/ongoing hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are associated with recurrent urinary stone formation except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypercitraturia

• Citrate is protective against stone formation as it binds calcium, preventing precipitation with oxalate or phosphate.
• Hypercitraturia reduces stone risk, while hypocitraturia predisposes to recurrent stones.

So ↑ citrate (hypercitraturia) = ↓ stone risk

Hyperoxaluria : ↑ oxalate → combines with calcium → Forms calcium oxalate stones (most common)

Hyperuricosuria : ↑ uric acid → forms uric acid stones→ Also a nidus for calcium stones.

Hypercalciuria: ↑ calcium in urine → Leads to calcium oxalate / calcium phosphate stones.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following contribute to the circle of death, except: (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Femoral artery

The "circle of death" refers to the vascular anastomotic ring formed around the femoral ring, which is critical during femoral hernia and laparoscopic inguinal hernia surgery. This dangerous vascular circle is formed by the obturator artery, aberrant obturator artery (when present), and inferior epigastric artery. The femoral artery does not contribute to this vascular circle - it runs lateral to the femoral vein and outside the femoral ring.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Although different triage systems have been used as a part of disaster response, the most common classification uses the following internationally accepted four-colour code system: 1. Black 2. Green 3. Red 4. Yellow Which one among the following correctly represents the descending order (from the highest to the lowest) of priority for medical care and transportation to health centres?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 → 4 → 2 → 1

The internationally used four-colour disaster triage system prioritizes patients as follows:

| Colour | Priority | Meaning

| ------ | -------- | -------

| Red | 1st | Immediate care required; life-threatening but potentially salvageable

| Yellow | 2nd | Urgent/delayed care; serious but can tolerate some delay

| Green | 3rd | Minor injuries; “walking wounded”

| Black | 4th | Dead or injuries considered unsurvivable with available resources

Therefore, the descending order of priority is:

Red → Yellow → Green → Black

3 → 4 → 2 → 1 → C.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An adult weighing 50 kg has 20% TBSA second-degree burns. What is the fluid requirement in the first 24 hours according to Parkland formula?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4000 mL

Calculation (Parkland Formula)

Parkland formula:

Fluid requirement (first 24 hours) = 4 mL × Body weight (kg) × %TBSA burned

= 4 × 50 × 20

= 4000 mL

• First 8 hours (from the time of burn): 2000 mL
• Next 16 hours: 2000 mL

(Use Ringer’s lactate as the fluid of choice.)

The Parkland formula is used to calculate initial fluid resuscitation in adults with partial-thickness (second-degree) and full-thickness burns involving >20% TBSA. The formula recommends 4 mL/kg/%TBSA of Ringer’s lactate during the first 24 hours after the burn. Half of the calculated volume is given in the first 8 hours from the time of injury, and the remaining half over the next 16 hours. Fluid therapy should then be adjusted based on clinical response, especially maintaining a urine output of 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour in adults.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An intra-operative image of scrotal exploration is shown. Identify the pathology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Testicular torsion

Testicular torsion presents as acute testicular pain and requires urgent surgical intervention. The characteristic appearance on exploration includes a discoloured, possibly non-viable testis due to the loss of blood supply.

Emergency management-Immediate surgical exploration

| Feature | Finding

| ------- | -------

| Age | Adolescents

| Pain | Sudden severe scrotal pain

| Cremasteric reflex | Absent

| Testis position | High-riding, horizontal

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: As per the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) colon injury scale, >50% bowel perforation corresponds to which grade?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Grade 3

The American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) Colon Injury Scale grades colon injuries based on the extent of bowel wall damage and tissue loss. A laceration involving >50% of the bowel circumference without complete transection is classified as Grade III.

AAST Colon Injury Scale:

| Grade | Injury

| ----- | ------

| Grade I | Contusion/hematoma without devascularization or partial-thickness laceration

| Grade II | Laceration involving <50% of bowel circumference

| Grade III | Laceration involving >50% of bowel circumference without transection

| Grade IV | Full-thickness transection or segmental tissue loss with <25% circumferential loss

| Grade V | Transection with >25% tissue loss or devascularized colon

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Assertion (A): During blood transfusion, early initiation of blood products is preferred. Reason (R): Blood products increase oxygen delivery to the tissues.
options: A is correct and R is the correct reasoning of A
A is correct and R is not the correct reasoning of A
A is correct, R is wrong
A is wrong, R is correct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A is correct and R is the correct reasoning of A

Early initiation of blood products is a key principle of damage control resuscitation in patients with major hemorrhage. Prompt transfusion restores oxygen-carrying capacity, intravascular volume, and coagulation factors, thereby improving tissue oxygen delivery, limiting ongoing hemorrhage, and reducing mortality.

Why is A correct?

• Assertion (A): ✓ Early administration of blood products is recommended in patients with significant hemorrhage.
• Reason (R): ✓ Packed red blood cells increase oxygen delivery (DO₂) to tissues by restoring hemoglobin concentration.
• The reason correctly explains the assertion, as restoration of oxygen-carrying capacity is a major objective of early transfusion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the image shown below, which type of wound reconstruction technique is being used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Split thickness skin graft

The image shows a meshed Split-Thickness Skin Graft (STSG), characterized by its diamond/fish-net appearance, which allows the graft to expand and cover a larger wound area while permitting drainage of blood and serous fluid

Why not the other options?

• B. Full-thickness skin graft (FTSG): Not meshed routinely; used for small defects requiring superior cosmetic outcome.
• C. Free flap: Involves transfer of tissue with its vascular pedicle and microvascular anastomosis, not a meshed graft.
• D. Vacuum-assisted closure (VAC): Uses negative-pressure foam dressing and does not produce a mesh pattern.

| Feature | Split-Thickness Skin Graft (STSG) | Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG)

| ------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------

| Layers | Epidermis + part of dermis | Epidermis + entire dermis

| Meshing | Can be meshed | Usually not meshed

| Graft take | Better | Less reliable

| Secondary contraction | More | Less

| Cosmetic outcome | Fair | Better

| Donor site | Heals spontaneously | Requires primary closure

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Boyd's perforator vein is most frequently located: (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. In the proximal calf

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Calculate Burn Surface Area (BSA) for burns involving anterior chest + abdomen, right upper limb, and right thigh (circumferential) in an adult
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 36%

Wallace Rule of 9s for ADULT:

• Each arm = 9%

• Anterior trunk (chest + abdomen) = 18%

• Each leg ≈ 18%

• Head and neck = 9%

Calculation in this case:

Chest + abdomen: right arm, and right thigh (circumferential)

Burns involving:

1. Half of anterior chest + abdomen: 18%
2. Right arm = 9%
3. Right thigh

• Thigh corresponds to about half of one leg

• One leg = \~18%

• Thigh ≈ half of leg = 9%

Total approximate TBSA: 18 + 9 + 9 = 36%

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Calculate the percentage of burns in a 6-year-old child whose head and neck were burnt in an accident at school?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 18%
