According to the Wallace rule of 9, head + neck = 18% TBSA in a 1–14-year-old child. Hence the answer is 18%.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Consider the following findings in urine examination of suspected haematuria: Dipstick test is positive for: A. Myoglobinuria B. Hematuria C. Hemoglobinuria Urine microscopy: D. White blood cells E. No red cells F. Red cell casts Etiology: G. Glomerular bleeding H. Intravascular hemolysis I. Rhabdomyolysis Which one of the following triplets is correctly matched?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. B, F, G

A urine dipstick positive for blood detects the peroxidase activity of heme, and therefore cannot distinguish between hematuria (RBCs), hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria. Urine microscopy is essential to identify the underlying cause.

Correct correlation:

• Dipstick: Positive for hematuria
• Urine microscopy: Red cell casts
• Etiology: Glomerular bleeding (e.g., glomerulonephritis)

Explanation of the options:

• A. B, F, G: Correct. Red cell casts are virtually diagnostic of glomerular bleeding, indicating renal parenchymal disease.
• B. A, D, I: Incorrect. Rhabdomyolysis causes myoglobinuria with positive dipstick but no RBCs on microscopy; white blood cells are not a characteristic finding.
• C. B, E, H: Incorrect. Intravascular hemolysis causes hemoglobinuria, not hematuria. Microscopy shows no RBCs.
• D. C, F, H: Incorrect. Red cell casts indicate glomerular hematuria, not hemoglobinuria.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding flail chest: 1. Three or more ribs are fractured at two or more places. 2. The chest wall shows paradoxical motion. 3. An X-ray chest AP view is the gold standard for diagnosis. 4. Treatment involves oxygen support, analgesia and physiotherapy. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

1. Three or more ribs fractured at two or more places: Correct.

• This creates a free-floating segment of the chest wall, producing flail chest.

2. Paradoxical chest wall movement: Correct.

• The flail segment moves inward during inspiration and outward during expiration, opposite to normal chest-wall movement.

3. Chest X-ray AP view is the gold standard for diagnosis: Incorrect.

• Flail chest is primarily a clinical diagnosis, based on paradoxical movement and appropriate rib fractures.
• Chest X-ray helps identify rib fractures and associated complications such as pneumothorax and hemothorax, but is not the gold standard for diagnosing flail chest.

4. Treatment involves oxygen support, analgesia and physiotherapy: Correct.

• Management includes oxygenation, adequate analgesia, pulmonary toilet/physiotherapy, and ventilatory support when required.
• Associated injuries, especially pulmonary contusion, should also be treated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Consider the following: I. Diabetes II. Hypertension III. Renal failure IV. Jaundice Which of the above are the risk factors for post-operative wound dehiscence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Wound dehiscence (burst abdomen) is the partial or complete separation of a postoperative wound due to failure of fascial healing. It usually occurs between the 5th and 8th postoperative day, when wound tensile strength is at its lowest.

Several systemic factors impair collagen synthesis, wound healing, and immune function, thereby increasing the risk of wound dehiscence. The following are important risk factors:

• I. Diabetes: Causes impaired leukocyte function, poor collagen synthesis, microvascular disease, and delayed wound healing.
• III. Renal failure: Uremia, anemia, malnutrition, and impaired immune function delay wound healing and increase wound complications.
• IV. Jaundice: Associated with impaired collagen formation, malnutrition, immune dysfunction, and increased susceptibility to infection, all of which predispose to wound dehiscence.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Hypertension: Hypertension alone is not considered a major independent risk factor for wound dehiscence, although it may contribute indirectly in some patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Elderly male presents with history of trauma, with NCCT brain image as shown. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SDH (Subdural Hematoma)

Acute Subdural Hematoma (SDH) is often seen in elderly patients with a history of minor trauma, presenting weeks after the injury with symptoms such as headache, confusion, or neurological deficits.

The characteristic CT finding is a crescent-shaped collection along the convexity of the brain, distinguishing it from other types of intracranial haemorrhages.

A) Epidural Hematoma (EDH)

• Lens-shaped (biconvex) on CT
• Does NOT cross sutures
• Rapid onset + lucid interval ( Not delayed like 3 weeks)

C) Subarachnoid Haemorrhage (SAH)

• Blood in sulci and basal cisterns
• Presents with: Sudden severe headache (“worst headache of life”)
• Not a localized crescent collection

D) Contusion

• Patchy hemorrhages within brain tissue
• Appears as irregular hyperdense areas, not a smooth crescentic.crescent

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL) is most commonly used for the treatment of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urinary tract stones

Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL) is a non-invasive treatment for urinary tract calculi,  particularly stones ≤2 cm in size with favorable anatomy.  It uses high-energy shock waves generated outside the body to fragment stones into smaller pieces that can then pass spontaneously through the urinary tract.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Gallbladder stones: ESWL is not routinely used for gallstones because of high recurrence and limited efficacy. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the treatment of choice for symptomatic gallstones.
• C. Salivary gland stones: Although lithotripsy may be used in selected centers, it is not the most common indication for ESWL.
• D. Abdominal stony-hard tumour: ESWL has no role in the treatment of tumors.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Features of MEN2B are all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Parathyroid hyperplasia

MEN 2B is caused by activating RET mutations and is characterized by aggressive medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Mucosal ganglioneuromatosis involving lips, tongue, and GI tract is a hallmark feature.

Patients have marfanoid habitus due to connective tissue abnormalities.

Parathyroid hyperplasia is seen in MEN 2A, not MEN 2B, making it the incorrect feature.

| Feature | MEN1 | MEN2A | MEN2B

| ------- | ---- | ----- | -----

| Gene | MEN1 | RET | RET

| Parathyroid | Yes | Yes | No

| Pituitary | Yes | No | No

| Pancreatic tumors | Yes | No | No

| Medullary thyroid CA | No | Yes |  Yes (aggressive)

| Pheochromocytoma | No | Yes | Yes

| Mucosal neuromas | No | No | Yes

| Marfanoid habitus | No | No | Yes

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Features of MEN2B are all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PTH carcinoma

MEN Syndromes

| Syndrome | Chromosome & Gene | Tumors / Key Features

| -------- | ----------------- | ---------------------

| MEN 1 (Wermer syndrome) | Chromosome 11 (MEN1 gene) | 3 “P”s: Pituitary tumors, Parathyroid adenoma, Pancreatic tumors

| MEN 2A (Sipple syndrome) | Chromosome 10 (RET gene mutation) | Medullary carcinoma of thyroid, Pheochromocytoma, Parathyroid hyperplasia, Cutaneous amyloidosis

| MEN 2B | Chromosome 10 (RET gene mutation) | Medullary carcinoma of thyroid, Pheochromocytoma, Marfanoid habitus, Mucosal neuromas

| MEN 4 | Chromosome 12 (CDKN1B gene) | Parathyroid tumors, Anterior pituitary tumors, Thyroid tumors, Renal tumors, Adrenal tumors, Gonadal tumors

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Following a building collapse, a patient with airway obstruction and dirt particles in the mouth undergoes the procedure shown in the image below. Which of the following statements regarding this procedure is true?
options: Will be followed by a tracheostomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Will be followed by a tracheostomy

The image shows a needle cricothyrotomy being performed → is an emergency temporary airway procedure

This is needle cricothyrotomy

• Done through cricothyroid membrane
• Used in “can’t intubate, can’t ventilate”

→ provides ventilation for only 30 minutes due to risk of needle displacement and CO₂ retention; It must be followed by definitive secure airway (cuffed tracheostomy) , when oral intubation is not possible (in maxillofacial trauma or airway obstruction).

❌ A. Can provide ventilation for 4 hours

No — only short-term (\~30 min)

❌ C. Used for aspiration of secretions

No — it’s for oxygenation, not suction

❌ D. It is a secure airway

Not secure → temporary + unstable

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Following a mass casualty incident, a 20-year-old male is brought in with the injury shown on his foot. What level of triage does this injury correspond to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Yellow

Mass casualty triage is used to prioritize patients based on the urgency of treatment and the availability of resources. A patient with a severe limb injury that is not immediately life-threatening but requires urgent surgical intervention is categorized as Yellow (Delayed).

| Triage Category | Color | Priority | Examples

| --------------- | ----- | -------- | --------

| Immediate | Red | Life-threatening but salvageable with immediate intervention | Airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, uncontrolled hemorrhage, shock

| Delayed | Yellow | Serious injuries requiring surgery but can tolerate a delay | Open fractures, major soft-tissue injuries, stable abdominal injuries, limb-threatening injuries

| Minor | Green | Walking wounded | Minor lacerations, abrasions, sprains

| Expectant/Dead | Black | Dead or injuries incompatible with survival given available resources | Cardiac arrest, devastating head injury, unsurvivable burns

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Following a stab injury to the chest, the following imaging finding was noted. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemothorax

A White-out on the chest X-ray after a chest injury, especially with accompanying hypotension, indicates hemothorax (the accumulation of blood in the pleural space).

Pathophysiology :

• Blood accumulates in pleural space → Compresses lung → ↓ breath sounds
• Can cause shock if massive ( by compressing onto the major veins and hampering the preload→ decreased cardiac output.)

Option A ❌ :  Pneumothorax : Appears black (air), not white

Option C❌: Diaphragmatic rupture : Shows abdominal contents in chest, not uniform white-out appearance.

Option D❌: Lung contusion : Here patchy opacities are seen on Chest x ray, not complete white-out

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: How does this graft get nutrition on day 3?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inosculation

1. Plasmatic Imbibition (Day 1–2)

• The graft has no blood supply initially.
• It survives by absorbing nutrients and oxygen from the wound bed through diffusion.

2. Inosculation (Day 3–5)

• Around day 3, the existing vessels in the graft connect with vessels in the recipient bed.
• These tiny vascular channels start linking up; This stage is called inosculation.

3. Neovascularization (After Day 5)

• New blood vessels grow into the graft from the recipient site establishing a stable blood supply.

| Day | Process | Mechanism

| --- | ------- | ---------

| 1–2 | Imbibition | Diffusion of plasma

| 3–5 | Inosculation | Vessel-to-vessel connection

| >5 | Neovascularization | New vessel growth

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the condition shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trophic ulcer

Why this is a trophic ulcer:-

1. Location

The ulcer is on the plantar surface of the toe/foot, which is a pressure point.

Neuropathic ulcers commonly occur on weight-bearing areas like the heel, metatarsal heads, or toes.

2. Punched-out appearance

The ulcer has a deep, well-defined “punched-out” cavity.

3. Hyperkeratotic (callused) margins

The edges show thick callus formation, which is typical in diabetic neuropathic ulcers due to repeated pressure.

4. Minimal surrounding inflammation

These ulcers often appear relatively clean because pain sensation is reduced.

❌ Option A: Venous ulcer

• Usually around medial malleolus
• Irregular margins
• Associated with edema, pigmentation

❌Option B: Malignant ulcer

• Everted edges
• Irregular proliferative mass

❌Option C: Arterial ulcer

• Very painful
• Occurs on toes, heel, lateral malleolus
• Punched-out but pale with ischemic skin, no callus formation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the correct statement regarding Phase II of the given cystometrogram curve.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sympathetic-mediated detrusor relaxation

Phase II of the cystometrogram corresponds to the bladder filling (storage) phase, during which intravesical pressure remains nearly constant despite increasing bladder volume because of receptive relaxation (high bladder compliance). This phase is mediated by the sympathetic nervous system, where β₃-adrenergic receptor stimulation causes detrusor muscle relaxation, allowing the bladder to store urine without a significant rise in pressure.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sympathetic-mediated detrusor contraction: Incorrect; sympathetic stimulation relaxes the detrusor muscle.
• B. Parasympathetic-mediated detrusor contraction: Occurs during the voiding (micturition) phase, mediated by M₃ muscarinic receptors.
• D. Parasympathetic-mediated detrusor relaxation: Parasympathetic stimulation causes detrusor contraction, not relaxation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the correct statement regarding wound healing.
options: Inflammatory phase is followed by exudative phase
Type III collagen replaces Type I collagen in a 3– 1 ratio
Angiogenesis occurs in the proliferative phase
Tensile strength of collagen is due to random arrangement of Type I collagen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Angiogenesis occurs in the proliferative phase

Wound healing occurs in four overlapping phases:

1. Hemostasis
2. Inflammatory phase
3. Proliferative phase
4. Remodeling (maturation) phase

The proliferative phase is characterized by angiogenesis, fibroblast proliferation, collagen deposition (predominantly type III collagen), granulation tissue formation, epithelialization, and wound contraction.

• Angiogenesis is a hallmark of the proliferative phase, driven mainly by VEGF and FGF, and is essential for granulation tissue formation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Inflammatory phase is followed by exudative phase: Incorrect. The exudative phase is part of the inflammatory phase, not a separate phase that follows it.
• B. Type III collagen replaces Type I collagen in a 3– 1 ratio: Incorrect. Type III collagen is laid down first and is later replaced by stronger type I collagen during remodeling.
• D. Tensile strength of collagen is due to random arrangement of Type I collagen: Incorrect. Tensile strength results from cross-linking and organized alignment of type I collagen fibers, not random arrangement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the level of amputation:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Below Knee

• Image shows : tibia and fibula cut below knee joint, confirming below knee amputation.
• Below-knee amputation is preferred whenever possible because knee joint is preserved, resulting in better prosthetic function.
• Common indications of below-knee amputation are Peripheral Arterial Disease, Diabetic foot gangrene, Severe trauma, and infection.
• LisFranc is tarsometatarsal; Chopart is midfoot disarticulation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the mediastinal mass shown in the image. The measured Hounsfield unit in the mass revealed -70 HU.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Teratoma

Negative HU indicates fat, typical of teratomas, which often contain fat and calcification.

| Tissue | HU Value

| ------ | --------

| Air | –1000

| Fat | –50 to –100

| Water | 0

| Soft tissue | +20 to +60

| Bone | +1000

Key Radiology Features: Mixed density mass

• Contains:

• Fat (negative HU)
• Calcification (tooth/bone)
• Fluid levels

• Well-defined anterior mediastinal lesion

| Feature | Thymoma | Teratoma | Lymphoma | Thyroid

| ------- | ------- | -------- | -------- | -------

| HU | Soft tissue | Fat (- HU) | Soft tissue | Variable

| Composition | Homogeneous | Mixed | Homogeneous | Vascular

| Calcification | Rare | Common | Rare | Sometimes

| Association | Myasthenia gravis | Anti-NMDA encephalitis | B symptoms | Thyroid disease

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the most common neurological complication following ligation of the Inferior mesenteric artery during abdominoperineal resection for rectal carcinoma?
options: Parasympathetic - bladder dysfunction and retrograde ejaculation
Sympathetic - retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction
Sympathetic - Impotence and loss of cutaneous sensation in perineal region
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sympathetic - retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction

High ligation of the IMA risks injury to the superior hypogastric plexus (sympathetic) near the sacral promontory. -Sympathetic damage causes retrograde ejaculation + bladder dysfunction.

Loss of sympathetic tone → bladder neck fails to close → semen flows back into bladder.

Sympathetic fibers control:

| Function | Role

| -------- | ----

| Ejaculation | Emission phase

| Internal urethral sphincter | Prevents retrograde ejaculation

| Bladder neck tone | Maintains continence

Parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) supply is typically preserved. Parasympathetic injury causes urinary retention, not retrograde ejaculation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dog ear correction

• It occurs when unequal wound edges are closed.
• This causes redundant skin to bunch up at the ends of the incision, forming a cone-shaped bulge called a “dog ear.”

Correction of dog ear deformity

• Excision of redundant triangular skin at the wound end.---> Usually done at \~45° angle.
• This flattens the tissue and smoothens the scar, gives better cosmetic appearance.

Incision and drainage of abscess❌

• Used to drain pus from an infected cavity.
• Does not involve excision of triangular skin flaps.

Skin grafting ❌

• Involves transplanting skin from donor site to recipient site.
• Used for large wounds or burns, not scar edge correction.

Keloid excision ❌

• Removal of excess fibrous scar tissue.
• The procedure is scar removal, not scar edge correction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the stage of the pressure sore:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

Staging of bed sores:

Grade 1: Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin

Grade 2: Partial thickness skin loss

Grade 3: Full thickness skin loss

Grade 4: Damage to muscle, bone

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the surgical procedure:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Penectomy with inguinal dissection

The pictures show:

• Surgical removal of the penis (penectomy)
• Inguinal incision with drains, indicating inguinal lymph node dissection

Typically performed for penile carcinoma.

Why inguinal dissection is needed?

Penile cancer spreads primarily through lymphatics to the inguinal lymph nodes.

So treatment involves:

1. Penectomy → removal of the primary tumor
2. Inguinal lymph node dissection → remove regional metastasis

| First |  Superficial inguinal nodes

| ----- | ---------------------------

| Next |  Deep inguinal nodes

| Later |  External iliac nodes

Why other options are wrong

B. Orchiectomy : Removal of testis, not related to penile cancer surgery.

C. Debridement: Used for necrotic tissue (e.g., Fournier gangrene).

D. Penectomy with orchiectomy Testes are not removed in standard penile cancer surgery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of knot seen in the image given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reef knot

A reef knot (square knot) is formed by tying two opposite half-knots:

Right over left → Left over right

This produces a flat, symmetrical knot in which the two free ends lie on the same side as their corresponding standing parts.

High-yield:

• Reef knot = Square knot
• Commonly used surgical knot
• Same-direction half-knots → Granny knot, which is less secure
• Surgeon’s knot → first throw has an extra turn (double throw)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of ulcer based on the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Venous ulcer

Why this is a venous ulcer?

Site: Medial malleolus / gaiter area of leg

• Edges: Irregular
• Base: Granulation tissue
• Skin around ulcer: Pigmented, thickened (chronic venous changes (brownish skin due to hemosiderin deposition).
• Pain: Usually mild and relieved by leg elevation
• Associated with chronic venous insufficiency / varicose veins.

| Ulcer type | Typical site | Appearance

| ---------- | ------------ | ----------

| Venous ulcer | Medial malleolus | Irregular, shallow, pigmented skin

| Arterial (ischemic) | Toes / lateral malleolus | Punched-out, very painful

| Trophic (neuropathic) | Pressure points of foot | Painless, callus around

| Infectious | Variable | Inflamed, purulent

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of ulcer shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Venous ulcer

Typical Features of a Venous Ulcer

Location : Gaiter area of the leg (lower medial leg above the medial malleolus)

Appearance

• Irregular margins
• Shallow ulcer with sloping edges
• Granulation tissue at the base

Surrounding skin changes

• Hyperpigmentation
• Lipodermatosclerosis
• Edema
• Varicose veins

These occur due to chronic venous hypertension.

❌ A) Arterial ulcer

• Punched-out edges
• Located on toes, heel, or lateral malleolus
• Cold limb with poor pulses

❌ C) Diabetic ulcer

Occurs at pressure points of the foot, especially:

• Plantar surface
• Metatarsal heads

Often associated with diabetic neuropathy.

❌ D) Neuropathic ulcer

Seen in peripheral neuropathy.

• Painless ulcer
• Located on pressure areas of the sole
• Callus around the ulcer

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the vein involved in the image shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Great saphenous vein

The image shows varicose veins involving the medial aspect of the leg and thigh, which is the typical distribution of the Great Saphenous Vein (GSV). Varicosities in this distribution are most commonly due to saphenofemoral junction incompetence.

Why not the other options?

• A. Popliteal vein: Deep vein; does not present as visible superficial varicosities.
• B. Femoral vein: Deep vein; thrombosis causes leg swelling, not superficial tortuous veins.
• C. Short saphenous vein: Runs along the posterior calf and drains into the popliteal vein.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Image a of child with an orofacial cleft as shown. When can the repair be done the earliest?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3 months

The image shows a cleft lip (orofacial cleft).

The first surgical repair is cleft lip repair, which is typically done at around 3 months of age.

Millard’s “Rule of 10” before performing cleft lip repair:

• 10 weeks of age
• 10 pounds weight (≈4.5 kg)
• Hemoglobin ≥ 10 g/dL

On these conditions being met  surgery can be done safely  Usually corresponds to about 3 months of age.

| Procedure | Age

| --------- | ---

| Cleft lip repair | 3–6 months

| Cleft palate repair | 9–18 months

| Alveolar bone graft | 7–9 years

Why cleft lip is repaired FIRST (3–6 months)?

• Cleft lip interferes with proper sucking
• Early repair → better feeding → weight gain → safer .
• Too early (<3 months for lip):
• Not done before 3 months of age because: Baby not fit (low weight, poor Hb). ; Higher anesthesia risk
• Speech starts around 9–12 months
• Palate is needed for proper sound production (velopharyngeal function) Repair before speech develops → prevents speech defects.

Problems with early or late repair:

• Too late (e.g., 2 years for lip): because  Feeding issues persist.
• Too early palate repair can lead to : Maxillary growth problems.
• Too late palate repair (>18 months)  Speech defects become permanent.

Why other options are wrong

• 6 months – feeding issues persist, due to sucking abnormalities.
• 12 months – around this time is palate repair is done.
• 2 years – Too late for primary cleft lip repair.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a male child having recurrent urinary problems, an imaging as done as shown. What is the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endoscopic Ablation

This is a VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram) showing dilated posterior urethra, enlarged bladder, urinary obstruction which suggests Posterior Urethral Valves (PUV).

This condition occurs only in male children and causes recurrent urinary infections and obstructive uropathy.

Posterior urethral valves are congenital obstructing membranes in the posterior urethra, causing:

• Bladder outlet obstruction
• Recurrent UTIs
• Hydronephrosis
• Renal damage if untreated

The standard treatment is:

Endoscopic valve ablation (valve fulguration) using a cystoscope removes the obstructing valve and restores urine flow.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with renal stones, the following crystals suggest what etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Triple phosphate

Option A: Triple phosphate (struvite) crystals

• Indicate infection stones, typically due to urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella).
• These bacteria alkalinize urine → promoting struvite formation and staghorn calculi.

Option B. Uric acid crystals

• Seen in acidic urine, not alkaline.
• Associated with gout, high purine diet, and tumor lysis syndrome
• They are radiolucent stones (not seen on X ray)

Option C. Calcium oxalate monohydrate :

• Seen in ethylene glycol poisoning and severe dehydration
• Dumbbell-shaped crystals

Option D. Calcium oxalate dihydrate:

• The most common crystal in general idiopathic calcium stones
• Envelope-shaped, not specific to infection cases.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with severe polytrauma and physiological derangement, damage control surgery (DCS) is planned. Which of the following is the correct sequence of steps involved in damage control surgery? 1. Patient selection 2. Control of hemorrhage and contamination 3. ICU resuscitation and correction of physiology 4. Definitive abdominal closure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 → 2 → 3 → 4

Damage control sequence is:

1.     Patient selection

2.     Control of hemorrhage and contamination

3.     Temporary closure

4.     ICU resuscitation and correction of physiology

5.     Definitive abdominal closure

This minimizes mortality in physiologically unstable trauma patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In peripheral vascular disease (PVD), an Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) of which value indicates imminent risk of gangrene?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 0.3

• ABPI is the ratio of ankle systolic pressure to brachial systolic pressure.
• Values <0.4 indicate critical limb ischemia.
• At 0.3, perfusion is severely compromised, loss of tissue viability.
• Urgent revascularization is required to prevent irreversible tissue loss.

| ABPI Value | Severity of Disease

| ---------- | -------------------

| > 1.4 | Vessel calcification (non-compressible arteries)

| 0.81 – 1.30 | Normal / Mild or insignificant disease

| 0.5 – 0.80 | Moderate peripheral arterial disease

| < 0.5 | Severe disease

| < 0.3 | Critical limb ischemia (risk of gangrene)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Match the following images with their conditions: 1. Midline cleft lip 2. Bilateral cleft lip 3. Cleft palate 4. Oblique facial cleft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-B, 2-D, 3-A, 4-C

Cleft lip and cleft palate result from failure of fusion of embryonic facial prominences. Recognition of the different types is important because they differ in embryological origin, associated anomalies, and surgical management.

Correct Matching:

• 1. Midline cleft lip → B
• 2. Bilateral cleft lip → D
• 3. Cleft palate → A
• 4. Oblique facial cleft → C

Why is B correct?

• A (Cleft palate): Failure of fusion of the palatine shelves, resulting in a midline defect of the secondary palate.
• B (Midline cleft lip): Rare defect due to failure of fusion of the medial nasal prominences.
• C (Oblique facial cleft): Rare cleft extending from the upper lip toward the medial canthus due to failure of fusion of the maxillary and lateral nasal processes.
• D (Bilateral cleft lip): Failure of fusion of both maxillary prominences with the merged medial nasal prominences.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Meares-Stamey test is used in which one of the following clinical conditions?
options: Recurrent urinary tract infection in men
Urinary tract infection in pregnant women
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Recurrent urinary tract infection in men

The Meares–Stamey four-glass test is the gold standard for diagnosing chronic bacterial prostatitis and helps localize the source of infection in men with recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs). It compares cultures from:

• Initial voided urine (VB1)
• Midstream urine (VB2)
• Expressed prostatic secretions (EPS)
• Post-prostatic massage urine (VB3)

A significant increase in bacteria in EPS or VB3 indicates prostatic infection.

Why not the other options?

• B. Urinary tract infection in pregnant women: Diagnosed with routine urine culture; Meares–Stamey test has no role.
• C. Complicated cystitis in non-pregnant women: Evaluated with urine analysis and culture, not the Meares–Stamey test.
• D. Pelvic inflammatory disease: A gynecological infection diagnosed clinically with microbiological testing; unrelated to the Meares–Stamey test.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients is -
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malignancy

Malignancy

↓

1. PTHrP secretion (humoral)

2. Bone metastasis (osteolysis)

3. Vitamin D activation (lymphoma)

↓

↑ Bone resorption

↓

↑ Serum calcium

In hospitalized patients, hypercalcemia is most commonly due to malignancy.

Mechanisms include PTHrP secretion, osteolytic bone metastases, and increased vitamin D production by tumors.

Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia is typically acute, severe, and rapidly progressive.

Types of Malignancy Hypercalcemia

| Mechanism | Example

| --------- | -------

| PTHrP secretion | Squamous cell carcinoma

| Osteolytic metastasis | Breast cancer, myeloma

| Vitamin D mediated | Lymphoma

Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause in the outpatient setting, not in hospitalized patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Mutation in which of the following genes is most commonly associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. RET

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, which produce calcitonin.

The gene most strongly associated with MTC is the RET proto-oncogene.

Why RET?

• RET mutation is seen in:

• MEN 2A
• MEN 2B
• Familial medullary thyroid carcinoma
• 50% of sporadic MTC cases

RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase proto-oncogene. Activating mutations lead to uncontrolled cell proliferation.

Important associations of thyroid cancers

| Gene mutation | Commonly associated cancer

| ------------- | --------------------------

| RET | Medullary thyroid carcinoma

| BRAF | Papillary thyroid carcinoma

| RAS | Follicular thyroid tumors/carcinoma

| TP53 | Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma

High-yield exam points

MEN 2A

• Medullary thyroid carcinoma
• Pheochromocytoma
• Parathyroid hyperplasia

MEN 2B

• Medullary thyroid carcinoma
• Pheochromocytoma
• Mucosal neuromas
• Marfanoid habitus

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Patient presents with acute urinary retention, and suprapubic catheterization is done. Urethrogram show a long segment stricture. What is the best management?
options: Urethral repair with buccal mucosal graft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urethral repair with buccal mucosal graft

Long urethral strictures require reconstructive surgery with techniques such as urethral repair using a buccal mucosal graft : effective solution for restoring normal urethral function.

| Stricture type | Treatment

| -------------- | ---------

| Short (<1–2 cm) | Endoscopic urethrotomy

| Recurrent short stricture | Urethroplasty

| Long segment stricture | Buccal mucosal graft urethroplasty

(The Barbagli technique : dorsal onlay graft urethroplasty, developed for treating long or complex bulbar and penile urethral strictures).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Patient presents with urinary complaints with sterile pyuria on urine-analysis. A cystoscopy shows dilated ureteric orifice. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Golf hole ureteric orifice

Important findings:-

• Sterile pyuria (pus cells in urine but culture negative)
• Dilated ureteric orifice on cystoscopy

Suggestive of  “golf-hole ureteric orifice.”

Normally, the ureteric opening in the bladder is slit-like.

In some diseases (listed below)--> it may become wide, round ( Golf hole like) →  Leading to dilatation and incompetence of the ureteric orifice.

• Vesicoureteral reflux
• Chronic ureteric obstruction
• Renal tuberculosis
• Long-standing ureteric dilation

Why other options are wrong

B. Bladder diverticulum : Sac-like outpouching of bladder wall.

C. Bladder ulcer

• Local mucosal erosion; not a dilated ureteric opening.

D. Cystitis

• Diffuse bladder inflammation, not a dilated ureteric opening.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Phenomenon of renal colic, swelling in the loin which disappears after passing urine is called? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dietl’s crisis

Dietl's crisis refers to a clinical triad of renal colic (severe flank pain), intermittent loin swelling, and relief of symptoms with passage of a large volume of urine. This occurs in cases of intermittent hydronephrosis, particularly with pelvi-ureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction.

The swelling represents the distended renal pelvis that becomes temporarily obstructed, causing pain, and then relieves when the obstruction clears, allowing passage of the accumulated urine.

Other Options:

Option A. Murphy's triad - This refers to right lower quadrant pain\, vomiting\, and fever\, which are characteristic of acute appendicitis.

Option B. Saint's triad - This is the association of diverticular disease\, gallstones\, and hiatal hernia\, completely unrelated to urinary symptoms.

Option D. Charcot's triad - This includes right upper quadrant pain\, jaundice\, and fever\, associated with ascending cholangitis due to biliary obstruction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Pressure on the artery proximal to an A-V fistula causes all of the following, except: (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase in heart rate

In arteriovenous (A-V) fistulas, pressure on the artery proximal to the fistula reduces blood flow through the fistula. This causes a reduction in the size of the dilated veins, eliminates the thrill (palpable vibration), and stops the continuous bruit ("machinery murmur"). This occurs because proximal arterial compression blocks the arterial inflow to the fistula. However, heart rate is reduced, known as Branham’s bradycardia. This occurs as the hyperdynamic circulation due to the fistula reverts to normal.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Serum thyroglobulin level is an important tumor marker for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Papillary carcinoma thyroid

Note: Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a tumor marker for differentiated thyroid cancers (both papillary and follicular carcinoma). Since follicular carcinoma is not among the options, the best answer is papillary carcinoma thyroid.

Thyroglobulin (Tg) is a glycoprotein produced by normal thyroid follicular cells and differentiated thyroid cancers. It is not used for diagnosis but is an excellent tumor marker for postoperative surveillance after total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine ablation.

Why not other options?

• A. Medullary carcinoma thyroid:

• Arises from parafollicular C. cells.
• Tumor marker: Calcitonin (± CEA).

• C. Anaplastic carcinoma thyroid:

• Highly undifferentiated tumor.
• Does not produce thyroglobulin reliably, so Tg is not a useful marker.

• D. Thyroid lymphoma:

• Usually associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis.
• No role for thyroglobulin as a tumor marker.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The classical presentation of an acute embolic occlusion in a limb includes all of the following, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Purple discoloration

Acute arterial embolic occlusion classically presents with the 6 Ps:

1. Pain — sudden severe limb pain
2. Pallor — pale, cold limb
3. Pulselessness — absent distal pulses
4. Paresthesia — sensory loss
5. Paralysis — late sign indicating severe ischemia
6. Poikilothermia — cold limb

Purple discoloration is not one of the classical 6 Ps and therefore is the exception.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The commonest site of pressure sore is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ischium

A pressure sore (pressure ulcer/decubitus ulcer) is a localized injury to the skin and underlying soft tissue caused by prolonged pressure, shear, and friction, resulting in tissue ischemia and necrosis. Pressure ulcers occur most commonly over bony prominences.

In this question, the expected answer is ischium, which is the commonest site of pressure sores in patients who remain in the sitting position, such as wheelchair-bound or paraplegic patients.

Why not the other options?

• A. Heel: A common site in bedridden patients but not the commonest overall in sitting patients.
• B. Sacrum: The most common site in supine bedridden patients and often cited as the most common overall in general medical texts.
• D. Occiput: Common in infants and patients lying supine for prolonged periods, but less common in adults.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The complications of massive blood transfusion are listed below: 1. Hyperkalemia 2. Coagulopathy 3. Hypocalcemia 4. Hypothermia Which among the following are included in the lethal triad of trauma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 4

The lethal triad of trauma consists of coagulopathy, hypothermia, and metabolic acidosis. These abnormalities perpetuate hemorrhage, impair coagulation, and worsen tissue hypoperfusion, creating a vicious cycle associated with high mortality. During massive blood transfusion, coagulopathy and hypothermia are important contributors to this triad.

Why is A correct?

• 2. Coagulopathy ✓: Results from dilution of clotting factors, platelet consumption, and ongoing hemorrhage.
• 4. Hypothermia ✓: Caused by exposure, shock, and transfusion of cold blood products; it further impairs coagulation.

Why not the other options?

• 1. Hyperkalemia: A recognized complication of massive transfusion due to potassium leakage from stored RBCs, but not a component of the lethal triad.
• 3. Hypocalcemia: Occurs due to citrate toxicity from transfused blood, but is not part of the lethal triad.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The four-layer suture repair of an inguinal hernia with double breasting of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal is known as: (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Shouldice operation

None

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The image below shows a pressure sore. Which stage does this belong to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stage 4

Deep ulcer with exposed muscle/tissue = Stage 4 pressure injury.

Stage 1–3 do not involve full-thickness tissue loss exposing muscle/bone.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common cause for non-traumatic sub-arachnoid haemorrhage is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Saccular aneurysm rupture

The most common cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm, accounting for approximately 80–85% of spontaneous SAH cases. These aneurysms typically arise at branch points of the Circle of Willis due to congenital weakness of the arterial wall.

Patients classically present with a sudden-onset, severe “thunderclap headache”, often described as the “worst headache of my life.”

• Saccular (berry) aneurysm rupture is the leading cause of spontaneous (non-traumatic) SAH.
• Common sites include:

• Anterior communicating artery (most common) ⭐
• Posterior communicating artery
• Middle cerebral artery bifurcation
• Basilar artery tip

Why not the other options?

• A. Arteriovenous malformation (AVM): Can cause SAH but is less common than berry aneurysm rupture.
• C. Extension from primary intracerebral hemorrhage: May produce secondary SAH but is not the most common cause.
• D. Idiopathic: Most spontaneous SAH cases have an identifiable vascular cause.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common site of urethral opening in cases of hypospadias is:
options: At the junction of penile shaft and scrotum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Just proximal to the glans

Hypospadias is a congenital anomaly in which the external urethral meatus opens on the ventral (undersurface) of the penis due to incomplete fusion of the urethral folds during embryonic development. It is commonly associated with ventral curvature of the penis (chordee) and a dorsally hooded prepuce.

The most common site of the ectopic urethral opening is the distal penile (glanular/coronal or subcoronal) region, just proximal to the glans.

Why not the other options?

• B. On the penile shaft: Represents midshaft hypospadias, less common.
• C. At the junction of penile shaft and scrotum: Penoscrotal hypospadias, a proximal and more severe form.
• D. On the perineum: Perineal hypospadias, the rarest and most severe type.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The principle of adaptation shown in the following diagram is explained by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Monro-Kellie doctrine

The diagram illustrates the Monro–Kellie doctrine, which states that the adult skull is a rigid, fixed-volume compartment containing three major components:

• Brain tissue
• Arterial and venous blood
• Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)

When the volume of one component increases, the others must decrease to maintain a constant intracranial volume. Initially, CSF displacement and increased venous outflow compensate for an expanding mass. Once compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, intracranial pressure (ICP) rises rapidly.

Why not the other options?

• (a) Moynihan’s aphorism: Relates to surgical principles, not intracranial pressure.
• (b) Monro–Kellie doctrine — Correct: Explains the relationship between intracranial contents and ICP.
• (c) Cushing’s law: Describes the physiological response to raised ICP, particularly hypertension with bradycardia and respiratory changes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The sign seen in the image is due to:
options: Hypocalcemia causing increased excitability of neurons
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypocalcemia causing increased excitability of neurons

The video demonstrates Chvostek sign, which is elicited by tapping over the facial nerve anterior to the ear. A positive sign is characterized by ipsilateral contraction of the facial muscles and indicates neuromuscular hyperexcitability due to hypocalcemia. Low extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for opening of voltage-gated sodium channels, making peripheral nerves more excitable and resulting in spontaneous muscle contractions.

Why not the other options?

• Option A. Hyperkalemia causing muscle membrane depolarization – Causes muscle weakness, flaccid paralysis, and ECG changes (peaked T waves), not Chvostek sign.
• Option B. Hypercalcemia causing decreased neuromuscular excitability – Produces muscle weakness, constipation, polyuria, and shortened QT interval, rather than tetany.
• Option D. Hypomagnesemia causing decreased acetylcholine release – Although hypomagnesemia can produce tetany by impairing PTH secretion, the mechanism described (decreased acetylcholine release) is incorrect and does not explain Chvostek sign.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: There are four patients to be taken care of. You are the doctor on duty in the emergency room. Which of the following patients will you first attend to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 45-year-old unconscious male with noisy breathing

In triage, patients are prioritized using the ABCDE approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure), where the most immediate life-threatening problem is managed first. Airway compromise has the highest priority because obstruction can cause death within minutes. An unconscious patient with noisy breathing suggests airway obstruction, making this the most critical case.

Therefore, the 45-year-old unconscious male with noisy breathing should be attended to first.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Under categorization of triage, the immediately life-threatening injuries would be classified as under the color-coded category:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Red

| Category | Tagging Color | Priority | Examples

| -------- | ------------- | -------- | --------

| I | RED | EMERGENT | Airway obstruction, severe respiratory distress, massive hemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, shock, cardiac arrest

| II | YELLOW | URGENT | Long bone fractures, moderate controlled bleeding, abdominal injury without shock, open fractures, burns without airway compromise

| III | GREEN | NON-URGENT / DELAYED / MINIMAL | Minor cuts and abrasions, small lacerations, mild sprains/strains, minor burns

| IV | BLACK | EXPECTANT | No breathing after airway opening, massive head injury, severe burns (>90% TBSA), multi-organ failure with no chance of survival in disaster setting

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What could be the possible diagnosis of a 35-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension and multiple episodes of hematuria and loin pain, whose elder brother passed away due to stroke at the age of 40 and whose ultrasound abdomen is shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

The ultrasound shows multiple large cysts of varying sizes in the kidney.

This “cluster of cysts replacing normal renal tissue” appearance is classic for polycystic kidney disease.

Clinical clues:

Hypertension

ADPKD commonly causes early hypertension because cysts compress renal parenchyma → activates RAAS.

Hematuria + loin pain

These occur due to: Cyst rupture ; Cyst infection ; Stone formation

Very typical symptoms of ADPKD.

Family history of early stroke

ADPKD is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms, which can rupture and cause subarachnoid haemorrhage → early stroke or sudden death.

So the brother dying at 40 years strongly supports ADPKD.

A) Renal cell carcinoma

• Usually single solid mass, not multiple cysts.
• Does not show diffuse bilateral cystic kidneys.

C) Tuberculosis of kidney

• Causes calcified, shrunken kidney (“putty kidney”).
• Ultrasound would show destruction or calcification, not many cysts.

D) Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease

• Presents in infancy or childhood.
• Kidneys appear enlarged with tiny microcysts, not large cysts.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What instrument is used to insert this tube?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cysto-Urethroscope

DJ stents are inserted via cystourethroscopy,

Recognised by J shaped curl in kidney in urinary bladder.

(This prevents the DJ stent from migrating)

Purpose of DJ stent: to maintain urinary flow in cases of obstruction like obstrutive ureteric stones/ ureteric strictures.

Option A: Nephroscope is for kidney in PCNL procedures;

Option C: Ureteroscope : for intraureteral procedures like ureteric stone removal, no role in DJ stent placement.

Option D: USG guided

USG guidance is not used for DJ stent insertion through the bladder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bladder exstrophy

The image shows:

• Red, moist mucosal tissue - exposed on the lower abdominal wall
• The urinary bladder is open , visible outside the body
• Location: below the umbilicus

This is the classic appearance of bladder exstrophy, where the anterior abdominal wall and anterior bladder wall fail to develop, leaving the bladder mucosa exposed.

Associated with:

●     Wide pubic symphysis

●     Often associated with epispadias

| Condition | Key feature

| --------- | -----------

| Umbilical hernia | Skin-covered swelling at umbilicus

| Omphalocele | Abdominal organs in a sac at umbilicus

| Gastroschisis | Bowel outside abdomen without sac

| Bladder exstrophy | Exposed bladder mucosa in suprapubic region

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely procedure depicted?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IVP

Contrast-filled renal pelvis, ureters, and bladder indicate intravenous pyelogram. MCU evaluates bladder/urethra during voiding; RGU outlines urethra only; plain X-ray has no contrast.

| Investigation | Contrast route | Structure seen

| ------------- | -------------- | --------------

| IVP | IV injection | Kidney → ureter → bladder

| MCU | Catheter into bladder | Bladder & reflux

| RGU | Through urethra | Urethra

| Plain X-ray | No contrast | Stones

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the optimum pressure for VAC?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. -100 to 130 mm of Hg

The optimum pressure for Vacuum-Assisted Closure therapy is between -100 to 130 mm Hg, with -125 mm Hg being the most commonly used setting.

(promote effective wound healing)

At around −125 mmHg, VAC therapy improves local blood flow, promotes granulation tissue formation, removes exudate and bacteria and causes wound contraction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the Z-plasty surgical technique?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Technique for Scar Lengthening

Zplasty uses triangular transposition flaps at 45–60° angles to lengthen scars and release contractures→ lengthen + redirect/ reorient a scar.

• Involves making a Z-shaped incision → Creates two triangular flaps that are transposed
• It reorients scars along relaxed skin tension lines.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which among the following are complications of liver trauma? 1. Liver abscess 2. Biliary fistula 3. Portal thrombosis 4. Liver failure Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Liver trauma is the most common solid organ injury following blunt abdominal trauma. While most patients recover with appropriate management, delayed complications may occur due to bile leakage, infection, or extensive hepatic injury.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Liver abscess ✅

• May develop secondary to infected hematoma, biliary contamination, or devitalized liver tissue after trauma.

• 2. Biliary fistula ✅

• Results from injury to intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to persistent bile leakage or bilioma formation.

• 3. Portal thrombosis ❌

• Although possible, portal vein thrombosis is an uncommon complication and is not considered a typical complication of liver trauma in standard surgical teaching.

• 4. Liver failure ✅

• Can occur after massive hepatic injury, extensive hepatic resection, or prolonged hepatic ischemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which irrigation fluid is preferred during bipolar TURP?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Normal saline

Bipolar transurethral resection of the prostate (Bipolar TURP) uses normal saline (0.9% NaCl) as the irrigation fluid because the electrical current passes only between the two electrodes on the resectoscope, allowing the use of an electrolyte-containing solution. This significantly reduces the risk of TUR syndrome (hyponatremia due to absorption of hypotonic irrigation fluid).

• Normal saline is isotonic and electrically compatible with bipolar electrocautery.
• It minimizes the risk of dilutional hyponatremia and TUR syndrome.

Why not the other options?

• A. 1.5% Glycine: Used in monopolar TURP because it is a non-conductive irrigation fluid.
• B. 3% Sorbitol: Also used with monopolar TURP, not bipolar.
• D. Sterile water: Hypotonic; may cause hemolysis and severe hyponatremia. It is not used for TURP.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the below is the most preferred investigation for parathyroid adenoma localisation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sestamibi SPECT

For localization of Parathyroid adenoma, the preferred investigation is:

Tc-99m Sestamibi SPECT scan

It is more accurate than plain Sestamibi planar imaging because SPECT provides:

• Better 3D localization
• Improved sensitivity
• Detection of ectopic glands

Principle of Sestamibi Scan

Tc-99m sestamibi:

• Initially taken up by both thyroid and parathyroid tissue
• Washes out rapidly from thyroid
• Persists in parathyroid adenoma because adenoma cells are rich in mitochondria

Thus delayed images show persistent uptake in adenoma.

Why other options are incorrect

| Option | Reason

| ------ | ------

| CT | Used if sestamibi negative or reoperative cases

| USG | Operator dependent; less sensitive for ectopic glands

| Tc99m-Sestamibi scan | Correct principle, but SPECT is superior/preferred

Tc99m-Sestamibi (A) VS Sestamibi SPECT (B)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct about ectopic ureters? 1. They are more common in males. 2. They drain the upper pole of kidney. 3. They are associated with duplex ureter. 4. They may cause incontinence. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Ectopic ureters are more common in females and are usually associated with a duplex collecting system. According to the Weigert-Meyer rule, the upper pole ureter is the one that inserts ectopically and may open below the external urethral sphincter, causing continuous urinary incontinence.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. They are more common in males: Incorrect. They are more common in females.
• 2. They drain the upper pole of the kidney: Correct.
• 3. They are associated with duplex ureter: Correct.
• 4. They may cause incontinence: Correct, especially in females.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct for managing hypertrophic scars? 1. Silicone gel sheeting 2. Intralesional steroid injections 3. Vitamin A gel applications 4. Laser treatment Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Hypertrophic scars are raised, erythematous scars confined within the boundaries of the original wound. They result from excess collagen deposition during wound healing and may improve spontaneously over time.

• 1. Silicone gel sheeting ✓

• First-line non-invasive treatment for hypertrophic scars. It hydrates the scar, reduces collagen deposition, and improves scar thickness and erythema.

• 2. Intralesional steroid injections ✓

• Triamcinolone acetonide is the treatment of choice for symptomatic hypertrophic scars. It suppresses fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis.

• 3. Vitamin A gel applications ✗

• Vitamin A preparations are not standard evidence-based therapy for hypertrophic scars.

• 4. Laser treatment ✓

• Pulsed dye laser (PDL) and fractional CO₂ laser improve scar vascularity, thickness, pigmentation, and pliability.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are features of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease? 1. Cyst may also occur in liver, pancreas and arachnoid membrane. 2. Most commonly manifests between 20–30 years of age. 3. Clinical manifestations are renal and extrarenal. 4. Men tend to progress to renal failure more rapidly than women. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) is the most common inherited cystic kidney disease, caused by mutations in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes. It is characterized by progressive development of bilateral renal cysts along with multiple extrarenal manifestations.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Cyst may also occur in liver\, pancreas and arachnoid membrane. ✓

• ADPKD is associated with extrarenal cysts, most commonly in the liver, but also in the pancreas, spleen, seminal vesicles, and arachnoid membrane.

• 2. Most commonly manifests between 20–30 years of age. ✗

• Although cysts are present from birth, clinical manifestations usually appear between 30–50 years of age, most often in the 4th–5th decade.

• 3. Clinical manifestations are renal and extrarenal. ✓

• Renal manifestations include hypertension, hematuria, flank pain, recurrent UTIs, nephrolithiasis, and progressive CKD, while extrarenal manifestations include hepatic cysts, intracranial aneurysms, and cardiac valve abnormalities.

• 4. Men tend to progress to renal failure more rapidly than women. ✓

• Men generally have faster progression to end-stage renal disease, particularly in patients with PKD1 mutations.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are included in common causes of mediastinal masses in superior and anterior mediastinum? I. Goitre II. Thymic tumour III. Neurogenic tumour Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I and II only

Mediastinal masses are classified according to their anatomical compartment into anterior (superior), middle, and posterior mediastinum. The anterior (superior) mediastinum is classically remembered by the “4 Ts”:

• Thymoma
• Teratoma (and other germ cell tumors)
• Thyroid mass (retrosternal goitre)
• Terrible lymphoma ⭐

Thus, goitre and thymic tumors are common causes of anterior mediastinal masses, whereas neurogenic tumors are most commonly found in the posterior mediastinum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are stages of damage control surgery? 1. Patient’s selection 2. Control of haemorrhage 3. Resuscitation in ICU 4. Preventive surgery Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Damage Control Surgery (DCS) is a staged surgical strategy used in severely injured trauma patients with the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. The goal is to rapidly control hemorrhage and contamination, allow physiological recovery in the ICU, and then perform definitive surgical repair.

Why is A correct?

• 1. Patient selection ✅

• Appropriate selection of patients with severe physiological derangement (e.g., hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy, massive transfusion requirement) is the first step in the damage control approach.

• 2. Control of haemorrhage ✅

• The initial operation aims to rapidly control bleeding and contamination using packing, vessel ligation, stapling of bowel, and temporary abdominal closure.

• 3. Resuscitation in ICU ✅

• After abbreviated surgery, patients undergo aggressive correction of hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy, and electrolyte abnormalities in the ICU.

• 4. Preventive surgery ❌

• There is no stage called preventive surgery in the damage control surgery protocol.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are the causes of secondary lymphoedema? 1. Trauma 2. Deep venous thrombosis 3. Fungal infection 4. Viral infection Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Secondary lymphedema occurs when a previously normal lymphatic system is damaged or obstructed.

1. Trauma — Correct

• Trauma or surgery can damage lymphatic vessels and cause secondary lymphedema.

2. Deep venous thrombosis — Correct

• Chronic venous obstruction can impair lymphatic drainage and contribute to secondary lymphedema/phlebolymphedema.

3. Fungal infection — Correct

• Chronic fungal infections can damage lymphatic drainage and produce lymphedema.

4. Viral infection — Incorrect

• Viral infections are not a typical recognized cause of secondary lymphedema in standard exam classifications.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are the classical markers of a seminoma: 1. KIT 2. OCT 3 3. PLAP 4. HCG
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 3

Seminoma classically expresses KIT (CD117), OCT 3/4, and placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP) on immunohistochemistry.

These markers reflect germ cell origin and pluripotency.

Statement 1. KIT (CD117) — ✅ TRUE

• A tyrosine kinase receptor expressed on germ cells → strong membranous positivity in seminoma (\~90% of seminomas
• Helps differentiate from most non-seminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCTs)

Statement 2. OCT 3/4 — ✅ TRUE (Classical marker)

• Strong nuclear staining in seminoma
• Also positive in embryonal carcinoma, hence not completely specific.

Statement 3. PLAP (Placental Alkaline Phosphatase) — ✅ TRUE

• Shows membranous staining pattern
• Expressed in seminoma and intratubular germ cell neoplasia (ITGCN)

Statement 4. β-hCG — ❌ FALSE (Not a classical marker)

Hence, KIT, OCT 3/4, and PLAP are the correct classical markers of seminoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are the important parameters to be maintained in a patient with head trauma? 1. MAP 70–80 mm Hg 2. Intracranial pressure < 20 mm Hg 3. Cerebral perfusion pressure > 60 mm Hg 4. Na > 140 mEq/L Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

• In a patient with severe head trauma, the key goals are to maintain adequate cerebral perfusion and prevent secondary brain injury.
• The key targets shown for a head-injured patient in neurointensive care include: (Ref: Bailey-Love Surgery)

| Key parameters to maintain in head-injured patients in neurointensive care

| --------------------------------------------------------------------------

• PaCO₂ = 4.5–5.0 kPa
• PaO₂ > 11 kPa
• MAP = 80–90 mmHg
• ICP < 20 mmHg
• CPP > 60 mmHg
• [Na⁺] > 140 mmol/L
• [K⁺] > 4 mmol/L

High-yield:

• CPP = MAP − ICP.
• Maintaining adequate MAP while limiting ICP ensures sufficient cerebral perfusion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are the malignancies associated with lymphedema? I. Kaposi sarcoma II. Squamous cell carcinoma III. Malignant melanoma IV. Leukaemia Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Chronic lymphedema predisposes to the development of several cutaneous malignancies due to chronic lymphatic stasis, impaired immune surveillance, persistent inflammation, and tissue fibrosis. Although rare, these malignancies carry a poor prognosis and require early recognition.

The following malignancies are associated with chronic lymphedema:

• I. Kaposi sarcoma: Can occur in chronically lymphedematous limbs, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.
• II. Squamous cell carcinoma: Chronic inflammation and recurrent infections in lymphedematous tissue increase the risk of SCC.
• III. Malignant melanoma: Although uncommon, melanoma has been reported in patients with longstanding lymphedema.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Leukemia: Leukemia is not associated with chronic lymphedema as a complication.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are the symptoms commonly experienced by patients with lymphedema? I. Swelling II. Burning sensation III. Intolerance to cold IV. Cramps Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and IV

Lymphedema is a chronic condition caused by impaired lymphatic drainage, leading to accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid. It presents with progressive limb swelling, discomfort, recurrent infections, and skin changes. Symptoms worsen as fibrosis develops.

The following symptoms are commonly experienced by patients with lymphedema:

• I. Swelling: The cardinal feature of lymphedema. Initially pitting, it becomes non-pitting in later stages due to fibrosis.
• II. Burning sensation: Patients commonly complain of burning, aching, heaviness, tightness, and discomfort in the affected limb.
• IV. Cramps: Muscle cramps and a feeling of tightness or fatigue may occur due to chronic swelling and tissue fibrosis.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. Intolerance to cold: Cold intolerance is more characteristic of arterial insufficiency or Raynaud phenomenon, and is not a typical symptom of lymphedema.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are the techniques commonly used to close the raw area after excision of a pilonidal sinus in order to avoid a midline wound? I. Limberg procedure II. Y-V plasty III. Z-plasty IV. Karydakis procedure Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Pilonidal sinus is a chronic inflammatory condition of the natal cleft, usually caused by hair penetration into the skin, leading to chronic sinus formation. The goal of surgery is complete excision of the sinus with off-midline closure, as midline wounds have higher rates of infection, delayed healing, and recurrence.

The following techniques are commonly used to achieve off-midline closure after excision of a pilonidal sinus:

• I. Limberg procedure: A rhomboid transposition flap that flattens the natal cleft and shifts the suture line away from the midline. It has low recurrence rates.
• III. Z-plasty: A local flap technique that changes the direction of the scar and moves the wound away from the midline while reducing tension.
• IV. Karydakis procedure: An asymmetric advancement flap that lateralizes the incision and flattens the natal cleft. It is associated with excellent healing and low recurrence.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Y-V plasty: Although Y-V advancement flaps are useful in reconstructive surgery, they are not commonly used as standard procedures for pilonidal sinus closure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are types of wound healing? 1. Primary intention 2. Secondary intention 3. Tertiary intention 4. Quaternary intention Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Wound healing is classically divided into three types based on the method of wound closure:

1. Primary intention (Primary union) ✅

• Clean, incised wound with well-approximated edges.
• Minimal tissue loss.
• Rapid healing with minimal scar formation.
• Example: Surgical incision closed with sutures.

2. Secondary intention (Secondary union) ✅

• Wound edges are not approximated due to tissue loss.
• Heals by granulation tissue formation, wound contraction, and epithelialization.
• More inflammation, slower healing, and larger scar.
• Example: Pressure ulcers, infected wounds.

3. Tertiary intention (Delayed primary closure) ✅

• Wound is initially left open because of contamination or infection risk.
• After a few days, once the wound is clean, it is surgically closed.
• Combines features of primary and secondary healing.
• Example: Contaminated traumatic wounds.

4. Quaternary intention ❌

• Not a recognized type of wound healing.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following bariatric procedures has been shown to offer maximum weight reduction? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD/DS)

BPD/DS produces the greatest and most durable weight loss among the listed bariatric procedures because it combines:

• Restriction → sleeve-type gastrectomy
• Marked malabsorption → extensive intestinal bypass

A useful exam-oriented ranking for weight-loss efficacy is:

BPD/DS > Roux-en-Y gastric bypass > Sleeve gastrectomy > Adjustable gastric banding

High-yield:

Maximum weight loss → BPD/DS

Major drawback → highest risk of nutritional deficiencies/malabsorption
